Countless computerized activities are driven by timing measurements, often behind the user's back. When your screen dims after inactivity, a timer noticed the silence. When the scheduler preempts a CPU-bound process, a tick announced that the time slice expired. When a network protocol retransmits an unacknowledged packet, a timer detected the timeout. Linux 7.0.12 has completely overhauled its timekeeping architecture compared to the 2.6 era: the monolithic timer interrupt handler has given way to a layered framework of clocksources, clock event devices, high-resolution timers, and a tickless scheduler — all designed for nanosecond precision, power efficiency, and scalable multiprocessor operation.

Underneath all of it lies an awkward fact: a computer has no clock. It has oscillators, and counters that those oscillators increment. Nothing in the machine knows what time it is, and no register can be read to find out. What the kernel actually has is a number that grows at some rate, a stored belief about what that rate is, and a stored belief about what time it was when the counter last held a known value. Everything in this chapter — every framework, every structure, every correction — exists to turn those three things into an answer that a program can use.

The conversion itself is a single line, and it is worth seeing early because so much of the chapter is machinery arranged around it:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c — the heart of the matter */
return ((delta * tkr->mult) + tkr->xtime_nsec) >> tkr->shift;

A count of elapsed cycles is scaled into nanoseconds by a multiply and a right shift. There is no division, because this code runs on the hottest path in the kernel and a divide is far too expensive; mult and shift together encode the counter's frequency as a fixed-point scale factor, derived from the measured or declared frequency when the hardware is registered and thereafter continuously adjusted by NTP — the header describes this field as the “(NTP adjusted) multiplier for scaled math conversion”. Steering the clock means nudging that multiplier, not stepping the time. The rest of the expression is bookkeeping: delta is how far the counter has advanced since the last update, and xtime_nsec holds the readout offset in the same shifted units, so that fractional nanoseconds survive from one update to the next instead of being rounded away.

Almost everything that makes timekeeping difficult is a consequence of that line being an estimate. The frequency is not exactly what the kernel believes it is, so the result drifts and must be steered. The counter has a finite width, so it wraps. It may stop in deep idle states, or run at a different rate after a frequency change, or be reset by firmware across suspend, or — on virtual machines — be emulated by a hypervisor with its own ideas. And the answer must be produced concurrently on every CPU, and from user space without entering the kernel at all, while it is being adjusted underneath the readers.

The two architectures this book follows begin from opposite starting points, which explains why the chapter spends as long as it does on hardware. On x86_64 the Time Stamp Counter is fast and always present, but its frequency is not architecturally defined: the kernel must calibrate it against a slower reference at boot, storing the result in tsc_khz, and historically the TSC could not be trusted to run at a constant rate or stay synchronized across sockets — which is why a watchdog still checks it against an independent clock. On ARM64 the Generic Timer is part of the architecture: its frequency is published in CNTFRQ_EL0 and the driver treats it as authoritative, with a comment in drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c that leaves no room for doubt — “we have no mechanism to override the sysreg CNTFRQ value. This must be correct.” One architecture measures its clock and distrusts it; the other is told and believes. Both end up in the same framework.

One consequence is visible from the start. Because the requirements placed on “the time” conflict — a clock that an administrator can correct is useless for measuring an interval, and a clock that never jumps cannot be corrected — Linux does not maintain one clock. It maintains a single authoritative timekeeper and derives a family of time bases from it, each making a different bargain about whether it can jump, whether NTP steers it, and whether time spent suspended counts. Choosing correctly among them is the most common way that otherwise-careful code gets time wrong.

Two Kinds of Timing Measurement

We can distinguish two main kinds of timing measurement that must be performed by the Linux kernel:

  1. Keeping the current time and date — so they can be returned to user programs through clock_gettime(), gettimeofday(), and time(), and used by the kernel itself as timestamps for files, network packets, and audit records.
  2. Maintaining timers — mechanisms that notify the kernel or a user program that a certain interval of time has elapsed. The kernel uses timers for process scheduling (time slices), protocol retransmissions (TCP, USB), device management (screen blanking, disk spin-down), and deferred work. User programs use timers via timer_create(), timerfd_create(), setitimer(), alarm(), and clock_nanosleep().

The first duty is more plural than it looks. There is no single “current time” in Linux 7.0.12; there is a small family of clock bases, all derived from the same accumulated cycle count but differing in what they promise. CLOCK_REALTIME tracks wall-clock time and therefore jumps when settimeofday() or NTP steps it; CLOCK_MONOTONIC never jumps backwards but stops advancing across suspend; CLOCK_BOOTTIME is CLOCK_MONOTONIC plus the time spent suspended; and CLOCK_TAI is CLOCK_REALTIME shifted by the current leap-second offset, so it never repeats or skips a second. Choosing the wrong one is a classic source of bugs — a timeout measured against CLOCK_REALTIME can be made to fire immediately, or never, by an administrator setting the clock. Time Bases in Linux 7.0.12 works through the whole family and the offsets that relate them.

Two further points are worth flagging now, because both shape the design that follows. The bullet above asks that the counter be readable “ideally without a system call”: that wish is granted by the vDSO, a page of kernel-provided code mapped into every process so that clock_gettime() can be answered in user mode from a shared data page, with no privilege transition at all (see The vDSO). And the demand for stability is not taken on trust — the kernel verifies it at run time, continuously comparing the chosen clocksource against a known-good reference and demoting it if it misbehaves (see The Clocksource Watchdog).

These two duties place very different demands on the hardware:

  • Timekeeping requires a free-running counter with high resolution and stability — something the kernel can read at any moment to determine "what time is it now?" The counter must not stop during CPU idle states, must not drift with temperature or voltage changes, and should be readable cheaply (ideally without a system call).
  • Timer interrupts require a programmable event device that can generate an interrupt at a specified future time — either periodically (for the legacy tick) or as a one-shot event (for high-resolution timer expiry).

In Linux 2.6.11, these two roles were intertwined in a single timer_opts object per architecture. Linux 7.0.12 cleanly separates them into two generic frameworks:

Table 6-1. The Two Timing Duties and Their Kernel Abstractions
DutyHardware NeedKernel AbstractionKey Structure
Timekeeping (reading time)Free-running counterClocksource frameworkstruct clocksource
Timer events (generating interrupts)Programmable comparatorClock event frameworkstruct clock_event_device

Timing measurements are performed by several hardware circuits based on fixed-frequency oscillators and counters. On a modern x86_64 system you will typically find five or more independent clock circuits; on ARM64 the architecture provides a unified Generic Timer that serves both roles. The kernel abstracts all of them behind the two generic frameworks, selecting the best hardware automatically at boot.

Figure 6-1 shows the whole arrangement at once: the hardware circuits along the top, the two frameworks that abstract them, the core that sits above both, and the user-space interfaces they ultimately serve. It is worth returning to as the chapter proceeds, because nearly every later section is an expansion of one of its boxes.

The key insight of the modern architecture is the separation of concerns: reading time (clocksource) is completely independent of generating timer interrupts (clock events). This allows the kernel to use the TSC for sub-nanosecond time reads while using the LAPIC timer in TSC-deadline mode for precise interrupt delivery — two different hardware circuits serving two different purposes through two independent frameworks.

The old kernel interleaved timekeeping and timer-interrupt handling in a single timer_interrupt() ISR that performed time interpolation, jiffies update, process accounting, and software timer processing in one monolithic function. The modern kernel decomposes this into cleanly layered components, each independently configurable and replaceable.

Why the Separation Matters

Splitting one abstraction into two is not merely tidier. The two frameworks answer different questions, are registered through different calls — clocksource_register_hz() and clockevents_config_and_register() — and have different scopes, and several properties of the timing subsystem follow directly from that.

A clocksource is shared; a clock event device usually is not. There is one authoritative answer to “what time is it?”, so the kernel selects a single system-wide clocksource and every CPU reads it. Interrupts, by contrast, must be delivered to a particular CPU, so event devices are normally per-CPU. A machine with sixty-four CPUs has one clocksource and sixty-four clock event devices — plus, on hardware whose per-CPU timers stop in deep idle, one further shared device held back to wake them, which is the broadcast arrangement described below.

What expresses that per-CPU-ness is the device's cpumask, not a feature flag. A driver publishes clk->cpumask = cpumask_of(smp_processor_id()) as it registers — both drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c and the local APIC setup do exactly this — and tick_check_percpu() in kernel/time/tick-common.c decides a device is CPU-local by testing cpumask_equal(newdev->cpumask, cpumask_of(cpu)). There is a flag named CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU, and it is worth knowing that it does not mean what its name suggests: neither of the two canonical per-CPU devices sets it, and the entire kernel tests it in one file. In kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c it does two narrow jobs — it disqualifies a device from becoming the global broadcast device, since a broadcast device must be reachable from every CPU, and it is one of the conditions a device must satisfy to be installed as a per-CPU oneshot wakeup device. It is an assertion made for the benefit of the broadcast code, not the property that makes a timer per-CPU.

One piece of hardware may fill both roles, or neither. The frameworks describe capabilities, not chips. The ARM Generic Timer supplies a counter and a comparator from the same block, so drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c registers a struct clocksource and a per-CPU struct clock_event_device from the same driver. A typical x86_64 system splits the work between different circuits entirely: the TSC is read for time, while the local APIC timer generates the interrupts. And the ACPI power management timer, which can only be read, registers as a clocksource alone.

The interfaces are shaped by the question each answers. A clocksource is essentially one function — read() — plus the constants needed to interpret its result: a mask giving the counter's width, and the mult/shift pair that converts cycles to nanoseconds. A clock event device is a small state machine: set_next_event() or set_next_ktime() arms it, and explicit callbacks move it between the states DETACHED, SHUTDOWN, PERIODIC, ONESHOT and ONESHOT_STOPPED. It also advertises min_delta_ns and max_delta_ns, because a comparator can neither be armed arbitrarily far ahead nor be trusted to fire if armed for a moment that has almost arrived.

Independent does not mean unrelated. The one place the separation leaks is power management, and it leaks in a way worth knowing about early. Some event devices stop when the CPU enters a deep idle state — the local APIC timer is the classic offender, which is why include/linux/clockchips.h files CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP under the heading “x86(64) specific (mis)features”. On processors advertising ARAT — Always Running APIC Timer — the flag is cleared again at setup and the timer's rating is raised to 150 so that it is preferred over a per-CPU HPET channel, but on hardware without it, a device that stops cannot wake the CPU it was supposed to wake, so the kernel must arrange for some always-on device to take over the duty on its behalf. That mechanism is broadcast, and it is one of the reasons the tick layer is more intricate than it first appears.

A Third Kind: the Scheduler’s Clock

The two duties above are the ones the kernel exports. There is a third source of time inside the kernel that belongs to neither framework, and readers who assume that all kernel timestamps come from the timekeeper will be puzzled by the scheduler and the tracers.

Code that merely needs to know how much time has passed — how long a task has been running, how far apart two trace events were — cannot afford the timekeeper. It may be called from an NMI, from inside the timekeeper's own update, or from the scheduler on a hot path where even a seqlock read is unwelcome. For these callers the kernel provides sched_clock() and its wrappers cpu_clock() and local_clock(): a fast, per-CPU, nanosecond-resolution clock that is deliberately not disciplined.

What one gives up is stated bluntly in kernel/sched/clock.c. The value is “monotonic for constant i” — that is, per CPU — with only “bounded drift between CPUs”, and the file interrupts itself with a boxed warning that when comparing readings taken on two different CPUs, “time can go backwards!!”. There is also “no strict promise about the base”, so the value is meaningful only as a difference, never as a date. In exchange, cpu_clock() “can be used from any context, including NMI”.

On hardware whose counter is trustworthy the implementation is little more than a scaled counter read. Where it is not — the case CONFIG_HAVE_UNSTABLE_SCHED_CLOCK exists for — the kernel builds “a semi stable clock from a mixture of other clocks”, using the timekeeper's monotonic time as a base, improving its resolution with sched_clock() deltas, and filtering those deltas to preserve monotonicity. Because the raw counter can stop while a CPU is idle, that machinery also needs explicit sleep and wake notifications to account for time that is otherwise invisible — the reason the NOHZ code calls sched_clock_idle_sleep_event() and sched_clock_idle_wakeup_event(), discussed later in this chapter.

The distinction is a practical one. Use ktime_get() and its relatives when the value will be compared against something outside the current CPU, stored, or shown to a user. Use local_clock() when the value will only ever be subtracted from another reading taken on the same CPU, and the cost matters.

A Fourth Kind: Auxiliary Clocks

The clock bases named earlier are all steered together, because they are all views of one timekeeper reading one clocksource. That is exactly right for a machine that wants to agree with itself. It is wrong for a machine that must simultaneously agree with several other machines — a network element participating in more than one PTP domain, an audio or video device slaved to a media clock, a test system carrying an instrument's timebase. Each of those domains is disciplined by its own grandmaster, drifts on its own terms, and must not be allowed to perturb the system clock.

Linux 6.17 added auxiliary clocks for precisely this case, and they are the fourth kind of time in the kernel. An auxiliary clock is not an offset applied to CLOCK_REALTIME; it is a complete, independent timekeeper — its own timekeeper instance, its own NTP state, its own steering — that happens to read the same hardware counter as the core timekeeper. Eight of them are available. include/uapi/linux/time.h reserves clock IDs 16 through 23 for the purpose (CLOCK_AUX through CLOCK_AUX_LAST, with MAX_AUX_CLOCKS equal to 8), and its comment states the contract directly: these clocks “are dynamically configured by enabling a clock ID” and “can be steered independently of the core timekeeper”.

Because they cost memory and update work, they are inert unless asked for. The feature is compiled in under CONFIG_POSIX_AUX_CLOCKS, and each of the eight is enabled individually by writing to /sys/kernel/time/aux_clocks/N/aux_clock_enable. Until then a clock_gettime() on that ID simply fails. Once enabled, the clock behaves like any other POSIX clock: it can be read, it can be set, and hrtimers can be armed against it. Auxiliary Clocks returns to the mechanism — how a second timekeeper is fed from the same cycle count, and how user space disciplines one — once the timekeeping core has been described.

Hardware Clock Circuits

Everything in the previous section was a promise the kernel makes. This section is about the hardware that has to keep it. Whatever ktime_get() returns is ultimately a count of oscillations of a physical crystal, and whatever wakes a CPU at a chosen instant is ultimately a comparator on a physical counter. The kernel’s freedom to choose between devices is what makes the two frameworks worth having, but the choice itself is made on hardware terms, and those terms are what this section supplies.

Five properties decide whether a device is any good. They recur for every circuit below, so it is worth naming them once. Resolution is how finely it divides a second — a 3.58 MHz counter cannot distinguish events 100 ns apart. Access cost is what it takes to read: a register on the CPU core costs tens of cycles, a port or an MMIO read reaches off-chip and costs hundreds of nanoseconds, which for a clock read on a hot path is catastrophic. Width decides how long the kernel may go without looking, because a counter that wraps unobserved has lost time that cannot be recovered. Continuity is whether it keeps counting at a fixed rate while the CPU changes frequency, enters a deep idle state, or is suspended. And scope is whether there is one of them for the whole machine or one per CPU — a distinction that maps directly onto the clocksource/clock-event split, since a time base must be shared and a comparator is best owned.

The x86_64 collection is a historical record; the ARM64 one is a design. This is the most useful thing to know before reading the catalogue. A modern PC carries five timing devices not because five are needed, but because each was added to repair a defect in its predecessor and none could be removed without breaking something older. The RTC keeps the date across power-off but resolves only seconds. The PIT that once drove the tick was too coarse and too slow to read. The ACPI power management timer was introduced because it keeps a fixed rate when the CPU does not — but it is read over an I/O port. The HPET brought a decent rate and real comparators, at MMIO cost. The TSC is fast and fine-grained but was, for years, untrustworthy. The local APIC timer is per-CPU and cheap to arm but historically stopped in deep idle. ARM64 instead specifies one Generic Timer block in the architecture: a counter of architected width at a frequency the firmware declares, plus per-CPU comparators, available to every implementation. The practical consequence appears throughout this chapter — on ARM64 the kernel usually has exactly one candidate and takes it; on x86_64 it must choose, verify its choice at runtime, and be ready to revoke it.

The catalogue is not the whole population. Two later additions do not fit the pattern. On a virtual machine the most attractive time source is often not a device at all but a page of memory the hypervisor updates, which is why this section ends with the paravirtualised clocks before the summary comparison. And a device may be excellent as a time base yet useless as an interrupt source, or the reverse, so each entry below states which of the two duties it can serve.

Figure 6-2 shows the two collections side by side, with the frequency, width and role of each device.

Real Time Clock (RTC)

The RTC is a battery-backed device (CR2032 coin cell) that maintains wall-clock time when the system is off. On x86_64, it is the MC146818-compatible chip in the PCH, accessed through I/O ports 0x70–0x71. On ARM64, it is typically a PL031 MMIO device.

/* arch/x86/kernel/rtc.c — boot-time RTC read */
void mach_get_cmos_time(struct timespec64 *now)
{
    struct rtc_time tm;
    if (!pm_trace_rtc_valid()) {
        now->tv_sec = now->tv_nsec = 0;
        return;
    }
    if (mc146818_get_time(&tm, 1000)) {
        pr_err("Unable to read current time from RTC\n");
        now->tv_sec = now->tv_nsec = 0;
        return;
    }
    now->tv_sec = rtc_tm_to_time64(&tm);
    now->tv_nsec = 0;
}

When NTP-synchronized, the kernel writes back to the RTC every 11 minutes via sync_hw_clock() in kernel/time/ntp.c (SYNC_PERIOD_NS = 11×60×10⁹).

Interrupt Capabilities (x86_64 — IRQ 8)

The MC146818 RTC can generate three types of hardware interrupts on IRQ 8, controlled by bits in Status Register B:

  • Periodic Interrupt (PIE): Generates interrupts at programmable frequencies from 2 Hz to 8,192 Hz, in powers of two. The frequency is set via the rate field in Status Register A. The CMOS driver defaults to 1024 Hz:
/* drivers/rtc/rtc-cmos.c — cmos_do_probe() */
cmos_rtc.rtc->irq_freq = 1024;
CMOS_WRITE(RTC_REF_CLCK_32KHZ | 0x06, RTC_FREQ_SELECT);
  • Alarm Interrupt (AIE): Fires when the RTC reaches a programmed hour:minute:second value — effectively a 24-hour alarm clock. ACPI extensions (day_alrm, mon_alrm) allow alarms up to a month or year in the future.
  • Update-Ended Interrupt (UIE): Fires once per second when the RTC finishes updating its time registers — providing a clean 1 Hz signal.

In the old 2.6 kernel, the RTC driver was a monolithic character device tied to IRQ 8. In 7.0.12, these interrupt sources are abstracted through the generic RTC subsystem. On many modern systems, the HPET can "hijack" IRQ 8 and emulate the RTC's periodic and alarm interrupts, which the rtc-cmos driver detects:

/* drivers/rtc/rtc-cmos.c — interrupt handler selection */
if (use_hpet_alarm()) {
    rtc_cmos_int_handler = hpet_rtc_interrupt;
    hpet_register_irq_handler(cmos_interrupt);
} else
    rtc_cmos_int_handler = cmos_interrupt;

request_irq(rtc_irq, rtc_cmos_int_handler, 0,
            dev_name(&cmos_rtc.rtc->dev), cmos_rtc.rtc);

If no valid IRQ is available, the alarm feature is disabled entirely:

if (!is_valid_irq(rtc_irq))
    clear_bit(RTC_FEATURE_ALARM, cmos_rtc.rtc->features);

Userspace Access — /dev/rtc0

In kernel 2.6, processes accessed the RTC through the legacy /dev/rtc character device (major 10, minor 135). In 7.0.12, the RTC is exposed through the generic RTC class as /dev/rtc0 (and /dev/rtc1, etc., for systems with multiple RTCs). The driver (drivers/rtc/dev.c) provides a rich set of ioctl(2) commands:

Table 6-2. RTC ioctl Commands (/dev/rtc0)
ioctlDirectionDescriptionCapability Required
RTC_RD_TIMEReadRead current RTC date/timeNone
RTC_SET_TIMEWriteSet RTC date/timeCAP_SYS_TIME
RTC_ALM_READReadRead alarm timeNone
RTC_ALM_SETWriteSet alarm (up to 24h ahead)None
RTC_WKALM_SETWriteSet wake alarm (full date/time)None
RTC_WKALM_RDReadRead wake alarmNone
RTC_AIE_ON/OFFWriteEnable/disable alarm interruptNone
RTC_PIE_ON/OFFWriteEnable/disable periodic interruptCAP_SYS_RESOURCE (if >64 Hz)
RTC_UIE_ON/OFFWriteEnable/disable 1 Hz update interruptNone
RTC_IRQP_SETWriteSet periodic interrupt frequencyCAP_SYS_RESOURCE (if >64 Hz)
RTC_IRQP_READReadRead periodic interrupt frequencyNone
RTC_PARAM_GET/SETR/WGet/set RTC parameters (features, correction)Varies

A userspace process can read(2) or select(2) on /dev/rtc0 — either call blocks until the next interrupt occurs. The read returns an unsigned long where the low byte identifies the interrupt type (update-done, alarm, or periodic) and the upper bytes count interrupts since the last read. Setting periodic frequencies above 64 Hz requires CAP_SYS_RESOURCE (or root) to prevent unprivileged users from generating excessive interrupts.

The system administrator reads and sets the RTC using hwclock(8) (the modern replacement for the old clock utility), which opens /dev/rtc0 and issues RTC_RD_TIME / RTC_SET_TIME ioctls. On systemd-based systems, timedatectl provides a higher-level interface:

# Read current RTC time
$ hwclock --show
2026-06-20 07:56:42.123456+00:00

# Set RTC from system clock
$ hwclock --systohc

# systemd interface
$ timedatectl
               Local time: Fri 2026-06-20 00:56:42 PDT
           Universal time: Fri 2026-06-20 07:56:42 UTC
                 RTC time: Fri 2026-06-20 07:56:42
System clock synchronized: yes
              NTP service: active
          RTC in local TZ: no

The RTC subsystem also exposes attributes via sysfs at /sys/class/rtc/rtc0/, including date, time, since_epoch, wakealarm, max_user_freq, and offset (for fine-grained drift correction).

NVRAM Access

The MC146818 provides 64 bytes of CMOS NVRAM beyond the time registers (modern chips extend this to 128 or 256 bytes). Most of this memory is used by the BIOS/UEFI firmware for boot configuration. The rtc-cmos driver exports NVRAM via the nvmem framework:

/* drivers/rtc/rtc-cmos.c */
static int cmos_nvram_read(void *priv, unsigned int off, void *val, size_t count)
{
    unsigned char *buf = val;
    off += NVRAM_OFFSET;   /* Skip time registers */
    for (; count; count--, off++, buf++) {
        guard(spinlock_irq)(&rtc_lock);
        if (off < 128)
            *buf = CMOS_READ(off);
        else if (can_bank2)
            *buf = cmos_read_bank2(off);
        else
            return -EIO;
    }
    return 0;
}

ARM64 RTC (PL031)

On ARM64 systems, the PL031 RTC is a simple 32-bit seconds counter with memory-mapped registers. The driver (drivers/rtc/rtc-pl031.c) provides pl031_read_time() and pl031_set_time() via the generic RTC class. The kernel reads it at boot via read_persistent_clock64() and the same 11-minute write-back mechanism applies. The PL031 also supports a single alarm interrupt. Because ARM64 uses MMIO rather than port I/O, there is no equivalent to the x86 0x70/0x71 port convention — access is always through the /dev/rtc0 framework.

Table 6-3. RTC Register Access (x86_64 — MC146818)
RegisterPort AddrContent
Seconds0x00BCD 0x00–0x59
Alarm Seconds0x01BCD, or 0xC0 = don't care
Minutes0x02BCD 0x00–0x59
Alarm Minutes0x03BCD, or 0xC0 = don't care
Hours0x04BCD 0x00–0x23 (24h)
Alarm Hours0x05BCD, or 0xC0 = don't care
Day of Week0x061=Sunday
Day of Month0x07BCD 0x01–0x31
Month0x08BCD 0x01–0x12
Year0x09BCD 0x00–0x99
Status A0x0AUIP (bit 7), divider select, rate select
Status B0x0BSET, PIE, AIE, UIE, SQWE, DM, 24/12, DSE
Status C0x0CIRQF, PF, AF, UF (read-only, read clears)
Status D0x0DVRT — valid RAM and time (bit 7)

The I/O ports 0x70 and 0x71 serve as the CMOS address and data registers, defined in arch/x86/include/asm/mc146818rtc.h:

#ifndef RTC_PORT
#define RTC_PORT(x)     (0x70 + (x))
#endif

Writing the register address to port 0x70 and reading/writing data from port 0x71 is wrapped by CMOS_READ() and CMOS_WRITE() macros. Some chipsets provide a second bank at ports 0x72/0x73 for extended NVRAM.

The RTC's fundamental role is unchanged — it seeds wall time at boot, provides alarm wakeup, and receives periodic NTP write-back. Key differences: (1) the old monolithic /dev/rtc driver (major 10, minor 135) is replaced by the generic RTC class framework with /dev/rtc0, supporting multiple RTC devices; (2) the 11-minute write-back uses sync_hw_clock() work queue in ntp.c instead of direct port I/O in the timer interrupt; (3) HPET can emulate RTC interrupts when it hijacks IRQ 8; (4) the RTC_PARAM_GET/SET ioctls are new, exposing feature bits and hardware-assisted drift correction; (5) NVRAM access is handled through the nvmem framework instead of raw /dev/nvram; (6) sysfs attributes (/sys/class/rtc/rtc0/) provide a non-ioctl interface.

Time Stamp Counter (TSC) — x86_64

Starting with the Pentium, all x86 processors include a 64-bit Time Stamp Counter that is incremented with every clock cycle. On modern processors (Intel Core 2+, AMD Zen+), the TSC ticks at the CPU's base clock frequency (not the boosted/turbo frequency), making it independent of power management transitions. It is accessed via RDTSC/RDTSCP with ~20-cycle latency — the fastest time source on x86_64.

In kernel 2.6, the TSC was used primarily through calibrate_tsc() and its reliability was a constant concern. In 7.0.12, the TSC has become the primary clocksource on all modern x86_64 systems, driving the timekeeping core, scheduler clock (sched_clock()), perf timestamps, and the vDSO fast-path for clock_gettime().

How the TSC Works

The TSC is a Model-Specific Register (MSR_IA32_TSC, address 0x10). Each CPU core has its own TSC register counting cycles of the reference clock. On modern processors, the TSC is driven by an invariant crystal oscillator:

Table 6-4. TSC CPU Feature Flags
CPU Feature FlagMeaningDetection
X86_FEATURE_CONSTANT_TSCConstant rate regardless of P/C-stateCPUID.80000007H:EDX[8]
X86_FEATURE_NONSTOP_TSCContinues in deep C-states (C3/C6/C7)CPUID.80000007H:EDX[8]
X86_FEATURE_TSC_ADJUSTMSR_IA32_TSC_ADJUST available for offset correctionCPUID.07H:EBX[1]
X86_FEATURE_NONSTOP_TSC_S3Continues even in S3 suspendPlatform-specific
X86_FEATURE_TSC_RELIABLESkip watchdog verificationHypervisor/platform flag
X86_FEATURE_ARTAlways Running Timer — direct crystal-to-TSC ratioDetected by detect_art()

When CONSTANT_TSC, NONSTOP_TSC, and TSC_ADJUST are all present and the system has ≤ 4 packages, the kernel disables the clocksource watchdog entirely:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c — check_system_tsc_reliable() */
if (boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_CONSTANT_TSC) &&
    boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_NONSTOP_TSC) &&
    boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_ADJUST) &&
    topology_max_packages() <= 4)
        tsc_disable_clocksource_watchdog();

TSC Frequency Calibration

Determining the exact TSC frequency is critical — even a 1 ppm error accumulates to 86 ms/day. The kernel uses a multi-step calibration with fallback methods:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c — native_calibrate_tsc() */
unsigned long native_calibrate_tsc(void)
{
    unsigned int eax_denominator, ebx_numerator, ecx_hz, edx;

    /* Method 1: CPUID leaf 0x15 — TSC/crystal ratio + crystal Hz */
    cpuid(CPUID_LEAF_TSC, &eax_denominator, &ebx_numerator, &ecx_hz, &edx);
    if (ebx_numerator == 0 || eax_denominator == 0)
        return 0;

    crystal_khz = ecx_hz / 1000;

    /* Some SoCs don't report crystal freq — use CPUID leaf 0x16 */
    if (crystal_khz == 0 && boot_cpu_data.cpuid_level >= CPUID_LEAF_FREQ) {
        cpuid(CPUID_LEAF_FREQ, &eax_base_mhz, &ebx, &ecx, &edx);
        crystal_khz = eax_base_mhz * 1000 *
            eax_denominator / ebx_numerator;
    }
    return crystal_khz * ebx_numerator / eax_denominator;
}
Table 6-5. TSC Calibration Fallback Chain
PriorityMethodSourceAccuracyWhen Used
1CPUID leaf 0x15Crystal ratio × crystal HzExactIntel Skylake+, crystal freq reported
2CPUID 0x15 + 0x16Crystal ratio × (base MHz ÷ ratio)Very goodCrystal freq not reported
3MSR-basedPlatform-specific MSRGoodIntel Atom/SoC
4HPET referenceCount TSC ticks during HPET intervalGoodHPET enabled, CPUID fails
5ACPI PM timer refCount TSC ticks during PMTMR intervalGoodNo HPET, PMTMR available
6PIT calibrationTSC during PIT ~50 ms delayModerateLegacy fallback
7RefinementCompare TSC vs clocksource over ~1s< 1 ppmPost-boot work item

The refinement runs ~1 second after boot via tsc_refine_calibration_work(). If the refined value differs by more than 1% from the early calibration, the kernel discards it (assuming SMI interference):

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c — tsc_refine_calibration_work() */
static void tsc_refine_calibration_work(struct work_struct *work)
{
    /* Sample TSC and reference timer over ~1 second */
    tsc_stop = tsc_read_refs(&ref_stop, hpet);
    delta = tsc_stop - tsc_start;
    delta *= 1000000LL;
    if (hpet)
        freq = calc_hpet_ref(delta, ref_start, ref_stop);
    else
        freq = calc_pmtimer_ref(delta, ref_start, ref_stop);

    /* If refined calibration is off by 1%, use the early value */
    if (abs(tsc_khz - freq) > tsc_khz / 100)
        goto out;
    tsc_khz = freq;
}

Cycle-to-Nanosecond Conversion (cyc2ns)

The kernel pre-computes a fixed-point multiplier to avoid division in the hot path: ns = cycles × cyc2ns_mul >> cyc2ns_shift. The conversion is per-CPU and protected by a double-buffered seqcount latch for lock-free reads:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c */
static void __set_cyc2ns_scale(unsigned long khz, int cpu, unsigned long long tsc_now)
{
    unsigned long long ns_now = cycles_2_ns(tsc_now);
    struct cyc2ns_data data;

    clocks_calc_mult_shift(&data.cyc2ns_mul, &data.cyc2ns_shift,
                           khz, NSEC_PER_MSEC, 0);
    /* Offset absorbs recalibration to ensure time continuity */
    data.cyc2ns_offset = ns_now -
        mul_u64_u32_shr(tsc_now, data.cyc2ns_mul, data.cyc2ns_shift);

    /* Double-buffered latch — readers never see half-updated tuple */
    write_seqcount_latch_begin(&c2n->seq);
    c2n->data[0] = data;
    write_seqcount_latch(&c2n->seq);
    c2n->data[1] = data;
    write_seqcount_latch_end(&c2n->seq);
}

The Scheduler Clock (sched_clock)

The scheduler uses sched_clock() for task switch timestamps, CPU utilization, and CFS virtual runtime. On x86_64, native_sched_clock() provides the fastest nanosecond clock:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c */
noinstr u64 native_sched_clock(void)
{
    if (static_branch_likely(&__use_tsc)) {
        u64 tsc_now = rdtsc();
        return __cycles_2_ns(tsc_now);  /* inline cyc2ns */
    }
    /* Fallback to jiffies if no TSC */
    return (jiffies_64 - INITIAL_JIFFIES) * (1000000000 / HZ);
}

Importantly, sched_clock() continues using the TSC even after it is marked unstable for timekeeping — the scheduler cares about speed and monotonicity more than absolute accuracy.

Two-Phase Clocksource Registration

The kernel registers the TSC in two phases to solve the chicken-and-egg problem (verification needs a running clocksource):

/* Phase 1: Early — before refinement, lower rating */
static struct clocksource clocksource_tsc_early = {
    .name              = "tsc-early",
    .rating            = 299,
    .uncertainty_margin = 32 * NSEC_PER_MSEC,
    .flags             = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS |
                         CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY,
    .id                = CSID_X86_TSC_EARLY,
    .vdso_clock_mode   = VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TSC,
};

/* Phase 2: Final — after refinement, full rating */
static struct clocksource clocksource_tsc = {
    .name              = "tsc",
    .rating            = 300,
    .flags             = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS |
                         CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES |
                         CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY |
                         CLOCK_SOURCE_VERIFY_PERCPU,
    .id                = CSID_X86_TSC,
    .vdso_clock_mode   = VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TSC,
};

The early clocksource (rating 299) is registered during tsc_init(). After refinement confirms the frequency, the final clocksource (rating 300, with VALID_FOR_HRES) replaces it. VERIFY_PERCPU catches inter-socket TSC desynchronization.

TSC Synchronization Across CPUs

On multi-socket systems, each package has its own crystal oscillator. The kernel ensures synchronization with:

1. MSR_IA32_TSC_ADJUST — a per-core signed offset register. The kernel reads it at boot and verifies it hasn't been tampered with:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc_sync.c */
bool __init tsc_store_and_check_tsc_adjust(bool bootcpu)
{
    struct tsc_adjust *cur = this_cpu_ptr(&tsc_adjust);
    rdmsrq(MSR_IA32_TSC_ADJUST, bootval);
    cur->bootval = bootval;
    tsc_sanitize_first_cpu(cur, bootval, smp_processor_id(), bootcpu);
    return false;
}

2. Cross-CPU sync check — when a secondary CPU comes online, check_tsc_sync_target() compares its TSC against the boot CPU. If the difference exceeds the threshold, the TSC is marked unstable.

3. Periodic re-verification — a timer fires every SYNC_CHECK_INTERVAL to re-check during runtime, catching drift from BIOS SMI handlers modifying TSC_ADJUST.

Always Running Timer (ART)

Intel Skylake+ processors expose the ART — a direct hardware relationship between the crystal oscillator and the TSC. The kernel uses ART for hardware-correlated timestamps across audio/network devices:

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c — detect_art() */
static void __init detect_art(void)
{
    /* ART requires: not VM, non-stop TSC, TSC_ADJUST, no async resets */
    if (boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_HYPERVISOR) ||
        !boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_NONSTOP_TSC) ||
        !boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_ADJUST) || tsc_async_resets)
        return;

    cpuid(CPUID_LEAF_TSC, &art_base_clk.denominator,
          &art_base_clk.numerator, &art_base_clk.freq_khz, &unused);
    art_base_clk.freq_khz /= KHZ;
    rdmsrq(MSR_IA32_TSC_ADJUST, art_base_clk.offset);
    setup_force_cpu_cap(X86_FEATURE_ART);
}
Table 6-6. TSC Access Instructions (x86_64)
InstructionSerializing?ReturnsUse in Kernel
RDTSCNoEDX:EAX (64-bit)Fastest, used in native_sched_clock()
RDTSCPPartial (read fence)EDX:EAX + ECX (CPU ID)Preferred via rdtsc_ordered()
LFENCE; RDTSCYes (full serialize)EDX:EAXFallback when RDTSCP unavailable

TSC Initialization Flow

/* arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c */
void __init tsc_init(void)
{
    if (!cpu_feature_enabled(X86_FEATURE_TSC))
        return;

    if (!tsc_khz) {
        if (!determine_cpu_tsc_frequencies(false)) {
            mark_tsc_unstable("could not calculate TSC khz");
            return;
        }
        tsc_enable_sched_clock();
    }
    cyc2ns_init_secondary_cpus();
    if (!no_sched_irq_time)
        enable_sched_clock_irqtime();
    lpj_fine = get_loops_per_jiffy();
    check_system_tsc_reliable();

    if (unsynchronized_tsc()) {
        mark_tsc_unstable("TSCs unsynchronized");
        return;
    }
    if (tsc_clocksource_reliable || no_tsc_watchdog)
        tsc_disable_clocksource_watchdog();

    clocksource_register_khz(&clocksource_tsc_early, tsc_khz);
    detect_art();
}
Table 6-7. TSC Boot Initialization Steps
StepFunctionWhat It Does
1determine_cpu_tsc_frequencies()Try CPUID, MSR, then PIT calibration for tsc_khz
2tsc_enable_sched_clock()Enable TSC-backed sched_clock()
3cyc2ns_init_secondary_cpus()Initialize per-CPU cycle→ns tables
4enable_sched_clock_irqtime()Enable IRQ time accounting via TSC
5check_system_tsc_reliable()Check if watchdog can be disabled
6unsynchronized_tsc()Detect multi-socket desync
7clocksource_register_khz()Register tsc-early (rating 299)
8detect_art()Detect Always Running Timer
9tsc_refine_calibration_work()~1s later: refine, register final tsc (300)

The listing above is simplified in one respect that matters outside this subsection. Both of its failure returns are accompanied in the real function by setup_clear_cpu_cap(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER): if the TSC is absent, or its frequency cannot be determined, the kernel does not merely decline to use it for timekeeping — it also withdraws TSC-deadline mode from the local APIC timer. The two are the same counter, and a deadline programmed in units the kernel cannot convert to nanoseconds is worse than useless. This is the mechanism behind an otherwise puzzling observation: on a machine where the TSC has been rejected at boot, /proc/timer_list shows lapic rather than lapic-deadline as the event device, even though the CPU advertises the feature in CPUID.

Secure TSC on Confidential Guests

A guest running under AMD SEV-SNP has a problem the rest of this subsection does not consider: the hypervisor is not trusted, and the hypervisor is exactly who supplies the TSC offset, scaling, and the frequency the guest calibrates against. A malicious host can therefore make time appear to run fast or slow inside the guest — enough to defeat timeouts, skew cryptographic freshness checks, or mount timing attacks the guest believes it is protected from. None of the calibration methods described above helps, because every reference the guest could calibrate against is also emulated by the host.

Secure TSC answers this by moving the frequency out of the hypervisor’s reach. When the platform reports CC_ATTR_GUEST_SNP_SECURE_TSC, snp_secure_tsc_init() in arch/x86/coco/sev/core.c maps the SNP secrets page — memory the firmware populates and the hypervisor cannot alter — reads the guest TSC frequency from MSR_AMD64_GUEST_TSC_FREQ, and scales it by the tsc_factor the secrets page carries. It then sets X86_FEATURE_TSC_KNOWN_FREQ, which has a concrete effect on the two-phase registration described above: tsc_refine_calibration_work() skips the one-second refinement against a hardware timer — there is no trustworthy hardware timer to refine against — and registers the final tsc clocksource immediately. If any step fails the guest does not fall back — it calls sev_es_terminate() and stops, on the principle that a confidential guest that cannot trust its clock should not continue running.

The call sits in tsc_early_init() rather than tsc_init(), and it must: the frequency has to be established before anything calibrates against it or reads sched_clock(). Reads of the TSC MSRs from such a guest are themselves intercepted and handled in the #VC exception path.

When TSC Fails

The TSC can be unreliable on very old CPUs (pre-Core 2), some virtualized environments, multi-clock-domain NUMA systems, or platforms where firmware modifies TSC_ADJUST. When drift is detected (> ~0.03%), the kernel falls back:

clocksource: timekeeping watchdog on CPU0: Marking clocksource 'tsc' as unstable
clocksource: Switched to clocksource 'hpet'
Table 6-8. Kernel Boot Parameters for TSC
ParameterEffect
notscDisable TSC entirely as clocksource
tsc=reliableMark TSC as reliable — skip watchdog
tsc=unstableForce TSC unstable at boot
tsc=nowatchdogDisable clocksource watchdog for TSC
Linux 2.6 treated the TSC as a simple cycle counter calibrated against the PIT. In 7.0.12: (1) CPUID leaf 0x15 provides exact TSC/crystal ratios; (2) two-phase clocksource registration (tsc-early → tsc) solves boot ordering; (3) MSR_IA32_TSC_ADJUST enables per-core offset correction; (4) per-CPU cyc2ns with seqcount latches replaces the global fast_gettimeoffset_quotient; (5) ART provides hardware-correlated cross-device timestamps; (6) the watchdog detects drift as small as 0.03%; (7) sched_clock() uses static calls to avoid indirect-call overhead; (8) Secure TSC takes the frequency from the SNP secrets page so that a confidential guest need not trust the hypervisor for time.

Generic Timer — ARM64

ARM64 processors implement the ARM Generic Timer architecture (ARMv8-A), providing an elegant, unified timing solution — both a free-running counter and per-CPU comparators in a single block. Unlike x86_64 where clocksource and clock events come from different hardware, ARM64's Generic Timer serves both roles simultaneously.

The architecture provides a system counter (shared, always-on, fixed-frequency) and per-CPU timer comparators. The frequency is set by firmware in CNTFRQ_EL0 — typically 19.2 MHz (mobile), 25 MHz (server), or 100 MHz (embedded).

Physical vs. Virtual Timer

Table 6-9. ARM64 Timer Types and PPI Assignments
TimerCounterCompare RegisterControlPPIUse Case
Physical SecureCNTPCT_EL0CNTP_CVAL_EL0CNTP_CTL_EL029Secure firmware (EL3)
Physical Non-secureCNTPCT_EL0CNTP_CVAL_EL0CNTP_CTL_EL030Bare-metal / hypervisor
VirtualCNTVCT_EL0CNTV_CVAL_EL0CNTV_CTL_EL027Normal OS (EL1), VM guests
Hypervisor PhysicalCNTPCT_EL0CNTHP_CVAL_EL2CNTHP_CTL_EL226Hypervisor (EL2)
Hypervisor VirtualCNTVCT_EL0CNTHV_CVAL_EL2CNTHV_CTL_EL2—Hypervisor virtual

Linux at EL1 uses the virtual timer (ARCH_TIMER_VIRT_PPI). The virtual counter equals the physical counter minus a hypervisor-controlled offset: Virtual_Count = Physical_Count − CNTVOFF_EL2. Each VM sees time starting from zero at boot while the physical counter runs from power-on.

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
static enum arch_timer_ppi_nr arch_timer_uses_ppi __ro_after_init = ARCH_TIMER_VIRT_PPI;

static const char *arch_timer_ppi_names[ARCH_TIMER_MAX_TIMER_PPI] = {
    [ARCH_TIMER_PHYS_SECURE_PPI]    = "sec-phys",
    [ARCH_TIMER_PHYS_NONSECURE_PPI] = "phys",
    [ARCH_TIMER_VIRT_PPI]           = "virt",
    [ARCH_TIMER_HYP_PPI]            = "hyp-phys",
    [ARCH_TIMER_HYP_VIRT_PPI]       = "hyp-virt",
};

u64 (*arch_timer_read_counter)(void) __ro_after_init = arch_counter_get_cntvct;
EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL(arch_timer_read_counter);

Counter Width and Rollover

The kernel dynamically determines the counter width (minimum 56-bit, up to 64-bit) based on the minimum rollover requirement. At 19.2 MHz with 56 bits, the counter runs for ~119 years before rollover:

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
static int arch_counter_get_width(void)
{
    u64 min_cycles = MIN_ROLLOVER_SECS * arch_timer_rate;
    return clamp_val(ilog2(min_cycles - 1) + 1, 56, 64);
}

Clocksource Registration

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
static struct clocksource clocksource_counter = {
    .name   = "arch_sys_counter",
    .id     = CSID_ARM_ARCH_COUNTER,
    .rating = 400,          /* highest — architectural guarantee */
    .read   = arch_counter_read,
    .mask   = CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(56),
    .flags  = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS,
};

static void __init arch_counter_register(void)
{
    /* Select virtual or physical counter read */
    if (arch_timer_uses_ppi == ARCH_TIMER_VIRT_PPI) {
        if (arch_timer_counter_has_wa())
            rd = arch_counter_get_cntvct_stable;  /* erratum */
        else
            rd = arch_counter_get_cntvct;
    }
    arch_timer_read_counter = rd;
    width = arch_counter_get_width();
    clocksource_counter.mask = CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(width);

    if (!arch_counter_suspend_stop)
        clocksource_counter.flags |= CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP;

    clocksource_register_hz(&clocksource_counter, arch_timer_rate);
    sched_clock_register(scr, width, arch_timer_rate);
}

Rating 400 puts the counter in the framework’s top band, the one reserved for sources whose properties are guaranteed by an architecture specification rather than measured: the ARM counter is required to be monotonic, of constant frequency, and always-on. Because the guarantee is architectural there is nothing for the watchdog to check, and CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY is never set. 400 is the floor of that band rather than a ceiling, incidentally — the Hyper-V reference TSC page registers at 500.

The suspend behaviour is decided by a device-tree property, and it is easy to name the wrong one. Two distinct properties are in play. always-on describes the timer, and its absence sets arch_timer_c3stop, which adds CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP to the clock event device so the broadcast machinery knows the comparator stops in deep idle. arm,no-tick-in-suspend describes the counter, and it is the one that governs the clocksource: the driver sets arch_counter_suspend_stop from it and then adds CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP only when that flag is false. In other words the counter is assumed to keep running across suspend unless the firmware explicitly says it does not.

Register Access

/* arch/arm64/include/asm/arch_timer.h */
static inline u64 arch_timer_read_cntvct_el0(void)
{
    u64 cnt;
    asm volatile("mrs %0, cntvct_el0" : "=r" (cnt));
    return cnt;
}

static inline u32 arch_timer_get_cntfrq(void)
{
    u32 val;
    asm volatile("mrs %0, cntfrq_el0" : "=r" (val));
    return val;
}

CNTVCT_EL0 is readable from EL0, which is what allows clock_gettime() to be answered in the vDSO with no system call at all. The read itself, however, is not quite the single instruction it appears to be, and the reason is worth following because it is the one place where ARM64 timekeeping has a real cost.

Why the Counter Read Needs a Barrier — and FEAT_ECV

The ARM architecture permits MRS reads of the counter to be reordered with respect to surrounding loads and stores, and speculative execution may issue the read early. For a timestamp that is fatal: two CPUs sampling the counter around a shared lock could observe values in the wrong order, and a timestamp taken after an event could be satisfied by a value read before it. Baseline ARMv8.0 therefore requires an instruction-synchronization barrier before the read, and arch/arm64/include/asm/arch_timer.h emits exactly that:

/* arch/arm64/include/asm/arch_timer.h */
static inline notrace u64 arch_timer_read_cntvct_el0(void)
{
    u64 cnt;

    asm volatile(ALTERNATIVE("isb
 mrs %0, cntvct_el0",
                             "nop
" __mrs_s("%0", SYS_CNTVCTSS_EL0),
                             ARM64_HAS_ECV)
                 : "=r" (cnt));

    return cnt;
}

An ISB is not a cheap instruction. It flushes the pipeline and forces every preceding instruction to complete before the read is issued, which on a deep out-of-order core costs far more than the MRS it protects — tens of cycles rather than one. Since every ktime_get(), every vDSO clock_gettime() and every scheduler timestamp pays it, this single barrier has historically been the dominant cost of reading time on ARM64.

FEAT_ECV removes it. Enhanced Counter Virtualization, introduced in ARMv8.6-A and mandatory from ARMv9.1, adds self-synchronized views of the two counters: CNTPCTSS_EL0 and CNTVCTSS_EL0. These are architecturally defined to be ordered without an explicit barrier, so the barrier can be dropped. The ALTERNATIVE construct above is how the kernel takes advantage of that without a run-time branch: the assembler emits the conservative isb; mrs cntvct_el0 sequence into the instruction stream, and if the boot CPU reports the ARM64_HAS_ECV capability the alternatives patching pass rewrites those bytes in place with nop; mrs CNTVCTSS_EL0. Both sequences are two instructions wide, which is why the replacement is padded with a NOP — the patch must not change any code offsets. A kernel built once therefore runs the fast sequence on hardware that has ECV and the safe one on hardware that does not, with no cost for the check.

ECV shows up in one other place in the driver, and it is a consequence of the same architectural change. The event stream — the mechanism that turns transitions of a chosen counter bit into periodic wake-up events, used to bound how long a WFE loop can sleep, and described later under Busy-Wait Delays — selects its period with a four-bit divider in CNTKCTL_EL1, so it can name only bits 0 through 15. ECV parts tend to run the counter fast enough that the desired bit lies above that range. arch_timer_evtstrm_enable() therefore sets ARCH_TIMER_EVT_INTERVAL_SCALE when ECV is present and the required divider exceeds 15, which shifts the whole field up by eight bits and lets the driver subtract 8 from the divider it programs.

Enabling User-Space Access (vDSO)

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
static void arch_counter_set_user_access(void)
{
    u32 cntkctl = arch_timer_get_cntkctl();

    /* Disable all user access first */
    cntkctl &= ~(ARCH_TIMER_USR_PT_ACCESS_EN
                | ARCH_TIMER_USR_VT_ACCESS_EN
                | ARCH_TIMER_USR_VCT_ACCESS_EN
                | ARCH_TIMER_USR_PCT_ACCESS_EN);

    /* Enable virtual counter unless erratum requires trapping */
    if (arch_timer_this_cpu_has_cntvct_wa())
        pr_info("CPU%d: Trapping CNTVCT access\n", smp_processor_id());
    else
        cntkctl |= ARCH_TIMER_USR_VCT_ACCESS_EN;

    arch_timer_set_cntkctl(cntkctl);
}

If a CPU has a counter-read erratum, user-space access is trapped — the vDSO falls back to the syscall path on those CPUs.

Clock Event Device (Per-CPU Timer)

Each CPU registers its virtual timer as a oneshot clock event device at rating 450. That is far above anything x86_64 offers: the LAPIC timer registers at 100, rising to 150 when ARAT is present (Table 6-19), and the best x86 alternative, a per-CPU HPET MSI channel, sits at 110 — the shared legacy HPET channel is rated 50. The gap is not arbitrary — it reflects that the ARM comparator needs no calibration, has no errata table gating its use on most parts, and does not stop in idle unless the firmware says so.

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
static void __arch_timer_setup(struct clock_event_device *clk)
{
    clk->features = CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT;
    if (arch_timer_c3stop)
        clk->features |= CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP;
    clk->name = "arch_sys_timer";
    clk->rating = 450;
    clk->cpumask = cpumask_of(smp_processor_id());
    clk->irq = arch_timer_ppi[arch_timer_uses_ppi];

    switch (arch_timer_uses_ppi) {
    case ARCH_TIMER_VIRT_PPI:
        clk->set_state_shutdown = arch_timer_shutdown_virt;
        sne = erratum_handler(set_next_event_virt);
        break;
    case ARCH_TIMER_PHYS_NONSECURE_PPI:
        clk->set_state_shutdown = arch_timer_shutdown_phys;
        sne = erratum_handler(set_next_event_phys);
        break;
    }
    clk->set_next_event = sne;
    clockevents_config_and_register(clk, arch_timer_rate, 0xf, max_delta);
}

Per-CPU Initialization

static int arch_timer_starting_cpu(unsigned int cpu)
{
    struct clock_event_device *clk = this_cpu_ptr(arch_timer_evt);
    __arch_timer_setup(clk);
    enable_percpu_irq(arch_timer_ppi[arch_timer_uses_ppi], flags);
    arch_counter_set_user_access();  /* Enable vDSO */
    return 0;
}

When the Counter Is Not in the Core: the Memory-Mapped Timer

Everything above assumes the counter and comparator are reachable through system registers, which is the case for any CPU implementing the Generic Timer. The architecture also defines a memory-mapped variant, in which a timer block sits in the SoC address space and is described by its own device-tree node or by the ACPI GTDT. It exists for two situations: parts of the system that are not a CPU at all — a management controller, a secure element — and platforms where firmware has denied Linux access to the system-register view.

Linux 7.0 finished separating this case from the main driver. Commit 0f67b56d84b4 moved it into a standalone driver, drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer_mmio.c, which probes as an ordinary platform device rather than being tangled into the per-CPU probe path. The distinction that matters to the rest of the kernel is that a memory-mapped frame is not per-CPU: it is one block that any CPU can reach over the interconnect, so a read costs an MMIO access rather than an MRS, and its interrupt is an SPI rather than a PPI. The ratings reflect exactly that. The frame registers a clocksource at 300 — below the system-register counter's 400, since it is slower and carries no architectural read-ordering guarantee — and a clock event device at 400, below the per-CPU timer's 450. On a normal server or phone neither will ever be selected; on a platform with no usable system-register timer they are what keeps time.

ARM64 support did not exist in Linux 2.6; it was merged in Linux 3.7. The Generic Timer elegantly combines what requires 3–4 separate chips on x86. Key 7.0.12 features: (1) dynamic counter width (56–64 bit); (2) per-SoC erratum workaround framework with stable-read retry; (3) event stream for WFE spinlock guarantee; (4) CNTKCTL_EL1 user-access control for vDSO; (5) CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP driven by arm,no-tick-in-suspend; (6) KVM timecounter integration; (7) FEAT_ECV self-synchronized counter reads patched in via ALTERNATIVE, removing the ISB from the hot path; (8) the memory-mapped timer split into its own driver in 7.0.

High Precision Event Timer (HPET) — x86_64

The HPET is a chipset-integrated timer developed jointly by Intel and Microsoft. In the Linux 2.6.11 era it was still new and uncommon. Today, the HPET is universally present on x86_64 but rarely the primary clocksource — the invariant TSC beats it on resolution and access cost. Its modern value is as a TSC watchdog reference and early-boot timer.

Channel Modes

/* arch/x86/kernel/hpet.c */
enum {
    HPET_MODE_UNUSED,    /* Not claimed by kernel */
    HPET_MODE_LEGACY,    /* Legacy replacement (IRQ0=PIT, IRQ8=RTC) */
    HPET_MODE_CLOCKEVT,  /* Per-CPU clock event via MSI */
    HPET_MODE_DEVICE,    /* Reserved for /dev/hpet userspace */
};

Initialization

/* arch/x86/kernel/hpet.c — hpet_enable() */
int __init hpet_enable(void)
{
    if (!is_hpet_capable())
        return 0;
    if (hpet_is_pc10_damaged())  /* HPET stops in PC10 deep idle! */
        return 0;

    hpet_set_mapping();  /* ioremap ACPI-provided MMIO address */

    hpet_period = hpet_readl(HPET_PERIOD);
    if (hpet_period < HPET_MIN_PERIOD || hpet_period > HPET_MAX_PERIOD)
        goto out_nohpet;  /* 100,000 ≤ period ≤ 100,000,000 fs */

    freq = FSEC_PER_SEC;  /* 10^15 */
    do_div(freq, hpet_period);
    hpet_freq = freq;     /* e.g., 14,318,180 Hz */

    id = hpet_readl(HPET_ID);
    channels = ((id & HPET_ID_NUMBER) >> HPET_ID_NUMBER_SHIFT) + 1;

    /* Sanitize and read all channel configs */
    for (i = 0; i < channels; i++) {
        cfg = hpet_readl(HPET_Tn_CFG(i));
        hc->boot_cfg = cfg;
        cfg &= ~(HPET_TN_ENABLE | HPET_TN_LEVEL | HPET_TN_FSB);
        hpet_writel(cfg, HPET_Tn_CFG(i));
    }

    clocksource_register_hz(&clocksource_hpet, (u32)hpet_freq);

    if (id & HPET_ID_LEGSUP) {
        hpet_legacy_clockevent_register(&hpet_base.channels[0]);
        hpet_base.channels[0].mode = HPET_MODE_LEGACY;
    }
}

PC10 Deep Idle Problem

On modern Intel platforms supporting PC10 (Package C10), the HPET stops counting. The kernel detects this and auto-disables the HPET. The nonstop TSC is the only reliable counter through all idle states:

static bool __init hpet_is_pc10_damaged(void)
{
    if (!mwait_pc10_supported())
        return false;
    if (hpet_force_user) {
        pr_warn("HPET force enabled, but dysfunctional in PC10.\n");
        return false;
    }
    boot_hpet_disable = true;
    return true;
}

Clocksource

static struct clocksource clocksource_hpet = {
    .name   = "hpet",
    .rating = 250,       /* below TSC (300), above ACPI PMT (200) */
    .read   = read_hpet,
    .mask   = HPET_MASK, /* CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(32) — 32-bit reads only */
    .flags  = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS,
    .resume = hpet_resume_counter,
};

/* If TSC watchdog disabled, HPET itself needs verification */
if (tsc_clocksource_watchdog_disabled())
    clocksource_hpet.flags |= CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY;

Legacy Clock Event

/* Rating 50 — only used during early boot before LAPIC */
hpet_init_clockevent(hc, 50);

/* "Legacy horrors" — force periodic mode for QEMU/hardware compat */
hc->evt.features |= CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC;

hpet_enable_legacy_int();  /* Set HPET_CFG_LEGACY */
clockevents_config_and_register(&hc->evt, hpet_freq,
                                HPET_MIN_PROG_DELTA, 0x7FFFFFFF);
global_clock_event = &hc->evt;

The HPET was once expected to replace the PIT completely; instead, the invariant TSC eclipsed both. Key 7.0.12 changes: (1) PC10 deep-idle detection auto-disables HPET; (2) channel mode framework (HPET_MODE_*); (3) MSI per-CPU delivery; (4) deliberately low clock event rating (50); (5) conditional CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY; (6) 32-bit-only clocksource reads despite 64-bit hardware; (7) CONFIG_HPET_EMULATE_RTC for backward compatibility.

Local APIC Timer — x86_64

Each CPU's Local APIC includes a built-in timer — the kernel's primary per-CPU clock event device. Unlike the HPET (global/shared), the LAPIC timer is private to each CPU: no locking needed, interrupts delivered directly to the local core.

Linux 2.6 used the LAPIC timer only in periodic and one-shot modes, driven by the bus clock through power-of-two dividers. In 7.0.12, TSC-deadline mode (Intel Nehalem+, AMD Zen+) eliminates bus-clock dependency entirely.

LAPIC Timer Registers

Table 6-17. LAPIC Timer Registers
OffsetRegisterPurpose
0x320APIC_LVTTLVT Timer: vector, mode (bits 17–18), mask
0x380APIC_TMICTInitial Count: countdown start (periodic/oneshot)
0x390APIC_TMCCTCurrent Count: decrementing value (read-only)
0x3E0APIC_TDCRDivide Config: bus clock divider (÷1…÷128)
MSR 0x6E0MSR_IA32_TSC_DEADLINETarget TSC value (deadline mode only)

Three Operating Modes

Table 6-18. LAPIC Timer Modes
ModeLVT BitsHow It WorksProgrammingUse Case
Periodic01Count down, auto-reload on zeroWrite APIC_TMICTLegacy tick
One-shot00Count down, fire once, stopWrite APIC_TMICT each timehrtimer (fallback)
TSC-deadline10Fire when TSC ≥ MSR valueWrite MSR_IA32_TSC_DEADLINEhrtimer (preferred)

TSC-Deadline Programming

/* arch/x86/kernel/apic/apic.c */
#define TSC_DIVISOR  8

static int lapic_next_deadline(unsigned long delta,
                               struct clock_event_device *evt)
{
    u64 tsc;
    weak_wrmsr_fence();  /* xAPIC serialization */
    tsc = rdtsc();
    wrmsrq(MSR_IA32_TSC_DEADLINE, tsc + (((u64) delta) * TSC_DIVISOR));
    return 0;
}

/* Traditional one-shot: simple register write */
static int lapic_next_event(unsigned long delta,
                            struct clock_event_device *evt)
{
    apic_write(APIC_TMICT, delta);
    return 0;
}

LVT Register Programming

static void __setup_APIC_LVTT(unsigned int clocks, int oneshot, int irqen)
{
    unsigned int lvtt_value = LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR;

    if (!oneshot)
        lvtt_value |= APIC_LVT_TIMER_PERIODIC;
    else if (boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER))
        lvtt_value |= APIC_LVT_TIMER_TSCDEADLINE;

    apic_write(APIC_LVTT, lvtt_value);

    if (lvtt_value & APIC_LVT_TIMER_TSCDEADLINE) {
        asm volatile("mfence" : : : "memory"); /* serialize */
        return;  /* No divider or initial count needed */
    }
    /* Traditional: divider ÷16 */
    apic_write(APIC_TDCR, ... | APIC_TDR_DIV_16);
    if (!oneshot)
        apic_write(APIC_TMICT, clocks / APIC_DIVISOR);
}

Per-CPU Setup

static void setup_APIC_timer(void)
{
    struct clock_event_device *levt = this_cpu_ptr(&lapic_events);

    if (this_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_ARAT)) {
        lapic_clockevent.features &= ~CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP;
        lapic_clockevent.rating = 150;
    }
    memcpy(levt, &lapic_clockevent, sizeof(*levt));
    levt->cpumask = cpumask_of(smp_processor_id());

    if (this_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER)) {
        levt->name = "lapic-deadline";
        levt->features &= ~(CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC | CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY);
        levt->set_next_event = lapic_next_deadline;
        clockevents_config_and_register(levt,
                        tsc_khz * (1000 / TSC_DIVISOR),
                        0xF, ~0UL);  /* min 15, max unlimited */
    } else
        clockevents_register_device(levt);
}

Bus Clock Calibration

For periodic/one-shot modes, calibrate_APIC_clock() measures APIC decrements over ~100ms, cross-checking against the PM timer and TSC:

static void __init lapic_cal_handler(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    long tapic = apic_read(APIC_TMCCT);   /* current count */
    u32 pm = acpi_pm_read_early();         /* PM timer reference */
    u64 tsc = rdtsc();                     /* TSC reference */
    /* Sample at start and after LAPIC_CAL_LOOPS (HZ/10) ticks */
}

TSC-Deadline Errata

static __init bool apic_validate_deadline_timer(void)
{
    if (!boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER))
        return false;
    if (boot_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_HYPERVISOR))
        return true;  /* Hypervisor handles it */

    m = x86_match_cpu(deadline_match);
    if (!m) return true;

    if (boot_cpu_data.microcode >= (u32)m->driver_data)
        return true;

    setup_clear_cpu_cap(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER);
    pr_err("TSC_DEADLINE disabled due to Errata; "
           "please update microcode to: 0x%x\n", (u32)m->driver_data);
    return false;
}

Timer Shutdown

static int lapic_timer_shutdown(struct clock_event_device *evt)
{
    unsigned int v = apic_read(APIC_LVTT);
    v |= (APIC_LVT_MASKED | LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR);
    apic_write(APIC_LVTT, v);

    /* Belt and suspenders: mask AND zero counter/deadline */
    if (v & APIC_LVT_TIMER_TSCDEADLINE)
        wrmsrq(MSR_IA32_TSC_DEADLINE, 0);
    else
        apic_write(APIC_TMICT, 0);
    return 0;
}

C3STOP and Tick Broadcasting

The LAPIC timer stops in C3/C6/C7 unless X86_FEATURE_ARAT is present. Without ARAT, the kernel uses tick broadcasting — a global HPET timer sends IPIs to wake idle CPUs:

static void lapic_timer_broadcast(const struct cpumask *mask)
{
    apic->send_IPI_mask(mask, LOCAL_TIMER_VECTOR);
}

Rating Summary

Table 6-19. LAPIC Timer Configurations
ConfigurationRatingFeaturesset_next_event
Base (no ARAT)100PERIODIC + ONESHOT + C3STOPlapic_next_event()
With ARAT150PERIODIC + ONESHOTlapic_next_event()
TSC-deadline + ARAT150ONESHOT onlylapic_next_deadline()
Linux 2.6 used only periodic and one-shot modes with bus-clock dividers. In 7.0.12: (1) TSC-deadline mode is the default — sub-ns precision, no calibration; (2) ARAT eliminates C3STOP on Sandy Bridge+/Zen+; (3) deadline_match[] errata table auto-disables on old microcode; (4) weak_wrmsr_fence() + MFENCE handle xAPIC serialization; (5) belt-and-suspenders shutdown zeros both LVT and count/deadline; (6) lapic_update_tsc_freq() propagates recalibrated frequency to all CPUs; (7) per-CPU lapic_events array supports heterogeneous configs.

ACPI Power Management Timer (ACPI PMT)

The ACPI Power Management Timer (ACPI PMT) is a simple free-running counter specified by the ACPI standard, included in virtually every ACPI-based motherboard's southbridge/PCH. It runs at exactly 3.579545 MHz — derived from the legacy 14.318180 MHz crystal oscillator ÷ 4 (the same base clock used by the old 8254 PIT).

In Linux 2.6 the ACPI Power Management Timer was preferred over the TSC on machines where the operating system or the BIOS could lower the CPU frequency or voltage to save power: the TSC frequency changed with it, causing time warps, while the ACPI PMT frequency did not. In 7.0.12, the invariant TSC eliminates this concern on modern hardware, but the PM timer remains critical as a calibration reference and last-resort fallback.

How the ACPI PMT Works

The timer is a counter incremented at each 3.579545 MHz tick, accessed via a single I/O port read. The port address is discovered from the ACPI FADT during BIOS/firmware parsing:

/* drivers/clocksource/acpi_pm.c */
u32 pmtmr_ioport __read_mostly;  /* Set by ACPI FADT parsing */

static inline u32 read_pmtmr(void)
{
    return inl(pmtmr_ioport) & ACPI_PM_MASK;  /* Mask to 24 bits */
}
Table 6-20. ACPI PM Timer Counter Width
WidthMaskWrap PeriodFormula
24-bit (standard)0x00FFFFFF~4.69 s2²⁴ / 3,579,545
32-bit (extended)0xFFFFFFFF~1200 s2³² / 3,579,545

Clocksource Registration

/* drivers/clocksource/acpi_pm.c */
#define PMTMR_TICKS_PER_SEC    3579545

static struct clocksource clocksource_acpi_pm = {
    .name       = "acpi_pm",
    .rating     = 200,          /* below HPET (250), below TSC (300) */
    .read       = acpi_pm_read,
    .mask       = (u64)ACPI_PM_MASK,   /* CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(24) */
    .flags      = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS,
    .suspend    = acpi_pm_suspend,
    .resume     = acpi_pm_resume,
};

Chipset Errata: Triple-Read Workaround

Several early Intel chipsets (PIIX4, ICH4) have a hardware bug: when the counter increments, there is a 3 ns window every 69.8 ns where the read value is indeterminate (4.2% chance of incorrect data). The kernel works around this with a verified read:

u32 acpi_pm_read_verified(void)
{
    u32 v1 = 0, v2 = 0, v3 = 0;

    /* Broken chipsets (ICH4, PIIX4): PM clock not latched */
    do {
        v1 = read_pmtmr();
        v2 = read_pmtmr();
        v3 = read_pmtmr();
    } while (unlikely((v1 > v2 && v1 < v3) || (v2 > v3 && v2 < v1)
                      || (v3 > v1 && v3 < v2)));
    return v2;
}

When a buggy chipset is detected via PCI fixups, the rating drops from 200 to 120:

static inline void acpi_pm_need_workaround(void)
{
    clocksource_acpi_pm.read = acpi_pm_read_slow;  /* triple-read */
    clocksource_acpi_pm.rating = 120;
}

DECLARE_PCI_FIXUP_EARLY(PCI_VENDOR_ID_INTEL,
    PCI_DEVICE_ID_INTEL_82371AB_3, acpi_pm_check_blacklist);  /* PIIX4 */
DECLARE_PCI_FIXUP_EARLY(PCI_VENDOR_ID_INTEL,
    PCI_DEVICE_ID_INTEL_82801DB_0, acpi_pm_check_graylist);   /* ICH4 */

Initialization and Validation

The PM timer registers at fs_initcall priority (after PCI fixups, before device init), performing 10 monotonicity checks with increasing delays:

static int __init init_acpi_pm_clocksource(void)
{
    if (!pmtmr_ioport)
        return -ENODEV;

    /* 10 monotonicity checks with increasing delays */
    for (j = 0; j < ACPI_PM_MONOTONICITY_CHECKS; j++) {
        udelay(100 * j);
        value1 = clocksource_acpi_pm.read(&clocksource_acpi_pm);
        for (i = 0; i < ACPI_PM_READ_CHECKS; i++) {  /* 10000 reads */
            value2 = clocksource_acpi_pm.read(&clocksource_acpi_pm);
            if (value2 > value1) break;
            if ((value2 < value1) && (value2 < 0xFFF)) break; /* wrap */
        }
    }
    if (verify_pmtmr_rate() != 0)  /* cross-check vs PIT */
        return -ENODEV;

    if (tsc_clocksource_watchdog_disabled())
        clocksource_acpi_pm.flags |= CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY;

    return clocksource_register_hz(&clocksource_acpi_pm,
                                   PMTMR_TICKS_PER_SEC);
}
fs_initcall(init_acpi_pm_clocksource);

Role as Calibration Reference

Table 6-21. PM Timer as Calibration Reference
CallerFunctionPurpose
TSC calibrationcalc_pmtimer_ref() in tsc.cCross-check TSC frequency during boot
LAPIC calibrationcalibrate_by_pmtimer() in apic.cValidate bus clock measurement
Early bootacpi_pm_read_early()Available before clocksource framework init
 
/* include/linux/acpi_pmtmr.h — early boot access */
static inline u32 acpi_pm_read_early(void)
{
    if (!pmtmr_ioport)
        return 0;
    return acpi_pm_read_verified() & ACPI_PM_MASK;
}

Linux 2.6 preferred the ACPI PMT over the TSC when CPU frequency scaling was active. In 7.0.12: (1) invariant TSC makes the PM timer unnecessary as active clocksource on modern hardware; (2) the timer gains suspend/resume callbacks; (3) PCI fixup infrastructure detects errata automatically; (4) CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY flag integrates with clocksource watchdog; (5) primary role shifts to calibration reference for TSC and LAPIC measurements.

Paravirtualised Clocks — When the Host Keeps Time

Every device described so far exists, in some form, inside a virtual machine: the guest sees an emulated RTC, an emulated HPET, and a TSC that is the host’s TSC with an offset applied. That is precisely the problem. A guest is not told when it is descheduled, migrated to another host, or resumed from a snapshot, and each of those events can invalidate the calibration it performed at boot. Emulating the legacy devices faithfully is also expensive, because every access traps to the hypervisor.

The answer all three major hypervisors reached is the same, and it is not a device. The host publishes a small structure in a page of guest memory — struct pvclock_vcpu_time_info in arch/x86/include/asm/pvclock-abi.h, thirty-two bytes holding a version counter, a system_time reference timestamp, the tsc_timestamp it corresponds to, and the tsc_to_system_mul/tsc_shift pair. The guest reads the counter itself and applies the host’s conversion. Reading the clock therefore costs one counter read and some arithmetic, with no trap, and the host can correct the guest’s notion of time at any moment by rewriting the page. Because the guest still reads the counter directly, the vDSO fast path survives virtualisation: arch/x86/include/asm/vdso/clocksource.h defines the extra modes VDSO_CLOCKMODE_PVCLOCK and VDSO_CLOCKMODE_HVCLOCK for exactly this, and kvm_cs_enable() declares the first of them with vclocks_set_used().

The page is read under a seqlock, and there is a fallback that costs more than it looks. __pvclock_clocksource_read() in arch/x86/kernel/pvclock.c retries around pvclock_read_begin()/pvclock_read_retry() while it reads the parameters and calls __pvclock_read_cycles(src, rdtsc_ordered()) — the same pattern the timekeeper itself uses, for the same reason. If the host has set PVCLOCK_TSC_STABLE_BIT the result is returned immediately. If it has not, the guest cannot assume the underlying counter is monotonic across CPUs, so the function forces monotonicity by hand through a machine-wide last_value accumulator updated with raw_atomic64_try_cmpxchg(). That is a contended atomic on a global line for every clock read on every CPU, which is a good reason to care whether the host advertises a stable TSC.

The ratings tell the whole story of the relationship. Each paravirtual clocksource registers with a rating far above any real device, so that it wins by default — and each then demotes itself below the TSC when it can determine the host’s TSC is invariant and therefore that the indirection buys nothing. The comment in arch/x86/kernel/kvmclock.c puts it plainly: “Invariant TSC exposed by host means kvmclock is not necessary: can use TSC as clocksource.” Xen makes the same judgement about dom0, on the grounds that “Dom0 is never moved, no penalty on using TSC there.”

Table 6-24. Paravirtualised Clocksources and Their Self-Demotion
ClocksourceDriverRegistered ratingDemoted toCondition for demotion
hyperv_clocksource_tsc_pagedrivers/clocksource/hyperv_timer.c500250HV_ACCESS_TSC_INVARIANT, or running as the root partition
hyperv_clocksource_msrdrivers/clocksource/hyperv_timer.c495245same as above (MSR variant, used when the TSC page is unavailable)
kvm-clockarch/x86/kernel/kvmclock.c400299X86_FEATURE_CONSTANT_TSC and X86_FEATURE_NONSTOP_TSC and the TSC has not been marked unstable
xenarch/x86/xen/time.c400299, or 275 for dom0xen_tsc_safe_clocksource(); dom0 is demoted unconditionally

Two details in that table repay attention. The demotion targets are chosen relative to the TSC’s own ratings rather than being round numbers: 299 is exactly the rating of tsc-early, one below the 300 of the final tsc clocksource, so a demoted paravirtual clock is preferred over the early TSC and rejected in favour of the verified one. And the Hyper-V driver is shared with ARM64, where the reasoning inverts — the comment notes that TSC_INVARIANT “is not offered on ARM64, so the Hyper-V Reference TSC will be preferred over the virtualized ARM64 arch counter”.

ARM64 does not need any of this, and the reason is instructive. The Generic Timer is virtualised in the architecture rather than in software: the guest reads CNTVCT_EL0, which is the physical counter less the hypervisor-controlled offset CNTVOFF_EL2, so a guest gets a counter that starts at zero and runs at the declared frequency without any host cooperation on the read path. There is consequently no paravirtual clocksource for ARM64. What ARM does define, in DEN0057A, is a paravirtual time interface for the opposite problem — struct pvclock_vcpu_stolen_time in arch/arm64/include/asm/pvclock-abi.h reports how long a vCPU was descheduled, so the guest scheduler can discount time it never had. Reading the clock is a hardware problem that ARM64 solved in hardware; accounting for stolen time is not, and remains paravirtual on both architectures.

When a guest reports tsc rather than kvm-clock in /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource, that is normally the demotion above working as intended, not a misconfiguration. The case worth investigating is the reverse: a guest still using a paravirtual clock on a host whose TSC ought to be invariant, which usually means the host is not advertising the feature to the guest.

Comparison of Hardware Clocks

The table below summarizes all hardware timing circuits available on modern x86_64 and ARM64 platforms. Each device occupies a different niche: the TSC and ARM Arch Timer serve as primary high-resolution clocksources (read by ktime_get() and vDSO); the HPET and ACPI PMT provide fallback clocksources and calibration references; the LAPIC timer and ARM Generic Timer deliver per-CPU clock events (driving the scheduler tick, hrtimers, and timer wheel); and the RTC provides persistent wall-clock time across reboots.

The kernel's clocksource framework (described in the next section) uses the rating to automatically select the best available time source — higher ratings win. The clock event layer similarly picks the highest-rated per-CPU event device. This layered design means the kernel adapts to whatever hardware is present without architecture-specific selection logic.
