The Clocksource Framework

The previous section surveyed the counters themselves — half a dozen devices, no two alike, some counting up and some down, some 24 bits wide and some 64, some readable in a single instruction and some only through a bus transaction costing the better part of a microsecond. A kernel that wants to know what time it is cannot be written against any one of them. The clocksource framework is the layer that lets it be written against all of them at once.

A clocksource is the kernel's model of a counter, and the model is deliberately narrow. To qualify, a device need only satisfy four conditions: it counts monotonically upward, it advances at a rate the kernel can discover, it does not stop or restart of its own accord while the system is running, and it can be read. That is the whole contract. A clocksource cannot be programmed, cannot raise an interrupt, and is never asked to do anything at a particular moment — those are the responsibilities of the clock event device described in the next section. The two abstractions divide the same hardware along the line drawn at the start of this chapter: a clocksource answers how much time has passed, a clock event device arranges for something to happen at a chosen time. Several devices, the HPET and the ARM generic timer among them, register in both roles, but they do so through separate structures, because the two questions have almost nothing in common.

Linux 2.6 had no such layer. Each architecture chose its own timer through its own code — on x86 a timer_opts descriptor with four methods (mark_offset, get_offset, monotonic_clock and delay), a cur_timer pointer, and a select_timer() routine that encoded the preference order as a chain of conditionals. Adding a timer meant editing architecture code; changing the preference order meant editing it again; and the choice, once made during boot, was permanent. Linux 7.0.12 replaces all of it with roughly 1,500 lines of architecture-neutral code in kernel/time/clocksource.c that every counter on every architecture registers with, from the x86 TSC to the ARM generic timer to the paravirtualised clocks a guest inherits from its host.

Concentrating the logic in one place lets that code answer three questions the per-architecture versions never really addressed:

  1. Which counter should the system use? Every clocksource carries a rating, an integer from 1 to 500, and the framework keeps the registered sources in a list sorted by it. Because registration happens throughout boot — some counters are usable before the timer subsystem is initialised, others only once ACPI tables or the device tree have been parsed — the answer is recomputed each time a new source appears, and a system may switch clocksources several times before it finishes booting.
  2. Is that counter still telling the truth? This is the question the 2.6 code could not ask at all. Timer hardware fails in ways that are silent: a TSC that drifts apart between sockets, a counter that stops in a deep idle state, a virtual machine migrated to a host whose clock runs at a slightly different rate. A watchdog therefore cross-checks the chosen clocksource against a second, slower, more trustworthy one twice a second, and demotes it if the two disagree by more than their combined error margins.
  3. How are cycles turned into nanoseconds? Dividing by a frequency is far too expensive on a path taken millions of times a second, so the framework precomputes a multiplier and a shift when the source registers, and the conversion at runtime becomes a multiply and a shift. Choosing that pair correctly — precise enough to be accurate, small enough not to overflow — is the subject of the last part of this section.

Around those three answers sit the mechanics: a single registration call any driver can use, automatic fallback when the watchdog rejects a source, a sysfs interface through which an administrator can inspect the choice or override it, and a separate suspend clocksource that keeps count across S3 and S4 when the primary one has been powered off. Switching between sources is the one genuinely expensive operation in the framework — it runs under stop_machine(), with every other CPU held idle — which is why the decision is made as seldom as possible, and why the watchdog hands it to a work queue rather than performing it in timer context.

The subsections that follow work outward from the data structure. The clocksource structure comes first, then the three fields that drive every decision the framework makes: the flag bits describing what the hardware can do, the numeric identifier that replaced comparing names as strings, and the rating that orders the candidates. Registration and selection show how a static structure in a driver becomes the system clock; the watchdog and the suspend clocksource show what keeps it honest and what covers for it while it sleeps; the sysfs interface shows what an administrator can see and change. The section closes with the arithmetic that all of it exists to serve.

The clocksource Structure

The struct clocksource is the central abstraction in the timekeeping subsystem. Every hardware counter that can serve as a time reference — whether an on-chip TSC, an external HPET, a platform-specific SoC timer, or a paravirtualized clock in a VM — must instantiate this structure and register it. The structure serves three purposes simultaneously:

  1. Hardware abstraction — the read() callback hides architecture-specific access (RDTSC, MMIO, I/O port) behind a uniform function pointer
  2. Conversion parameters — the mult/shift pair enables zero-division nanosecond conversion at every ktime_get() call
  3. Lifecycle management — enable/disable/suspend/resume callbacks let the framework power-manage the hardware

A driver author implementing a new clocksource declares a static instance, fills in the hardware-specific fields, and calls clocksource_register_hz(). The framework handles everything else — computing mult/shift, inserting into the sorted list, triggering selection, and starting watchdog verification.

/* include/linux/clocksource.h */
struct clocksource {
    u64         (*read)(struct clocksource *cs);
    u64         mask;           /* bitmask for valid bits */
    u32         mult;           /* cycle → nanosecond multiplier */
    u32         shift;          /* fixed-point shift for mult */
    u64         max_idle_ns;    /* max ns before wrap danger */
    u64         max_cycles;     /* max raw cycles before overflow */
    u32         maxadj;         /* max NTP adjustment to mult */
    u32         uncertainty_margin; /* ns margin for watchdog check */

    const char  *name;
    int         rating;         /* selection priority; kerneldoc bands run 1–499 */
    enum clocksource_ids id;    /* CSID_X86_TSC, CSID_ARM_ARCH_COUNTER... */
    unsigned long flags;

    /* Power management */
    int         (*enable)(struct clocksource *cs);
    void        (*disable)(struct clocksource *cs);
    void        (*suspend)(struct clocksource *cs);
    void        (*resume)(struct clocksource *cs);

    /* Watchdog state */
    struct list_head wd_list;
    u64         cs_last, wd_last;

    /* vDSO acceleration */
    enum vdso_clock_mode vdso_clock_mode;
};
Table 6-26. Key Fields — Who Sets What
FieldPurposeSet By
readReturns current cycle count. Must be fast — called on every ktime_get(). Must never sleep or take locks.Driver
maskBitmask of valid counter bits. Use CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(n) for n-bit counters. Framework uses this for correct wrap handling.Driver
mult / shiftConvert cycles → ns: ns = (Δcycles × mult) >> shift. Computed automatically from frequency — drivers should NOT set manually.Framework
ratingAutomatic selection priority (higher wins). See Rating System below.Driver
max_idle_nsMax nanoseconds system can idle before Δcycles × mult overflows. NOHZ uses this to cap idle duration.Framework
max_cyclesMax raw cycle delta for safe multiplication. Beyond this, slower mul_u64_u32_shr() is used.Framework
uncertainty_marginTolerance (ns) for watchdog skew. If unset, computed from clock period (min 500 ppm).Driver (opt) / Framework
idTyped ID for fast vDSO dispatch without string comparison. Default: CSID_GENERIC.Driver
vdso_clock_modeWhich userspace fast-path for clock_gettime(). VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE → syscall fallback.Driver
flagsCapability/state bits — see Flags section below.Driver + Framework
enable/disableCalled when clocksource becomes/stops being active. For power-gated timers.Driver (optional)
suspend/resumeCalled during system sleep. Must NOT be set for SUSPEND_NONSTOP clocksources.Driver (optional)

Minimal driver example:

/* Registering a simple MMIO-based SoC timer */
static u64 my_timer_read(struct clocksource *cs)
{
    return readl(timer_base + COUNTER_REG) & cs->mask;
}

static struct clocksource my_timer_cs = {
    .name   = "my_soc_timer",
    .rating = 200,
    .read   = my_timer_read,
    .mask   = CLOCKSOURCE_MASK(32),
    .flags  = CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS,
};

static int __init my_timer_init(void)
{
    /* Framework computes mult, shift, max_idle_ns automatically */
    return clocksource_register_hz(&my_timer_cs, 24000000); /* 24 MHz */
}

Clocksource Flags

The flags field is a bitmask that describes both the capabilities of the hardware (set by the driver) and the runtime state (set by the framework). Understanding these flags is essential for driver developers who need to know which to set, and for kernel developers debugging clocksource issues.

Table 6-27. Clocksource Flags
FlagValueSet ByMeaning
CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS0x01DriverCounter is free-running, not tick-based. Required for high-res timer support — jiffies can never be promoted to HRES.
CLOCK_SOURCE_MUST_VERIFY0x02DriverNot trusted until watchdog verifies it. Used when TSC watchdog is disabled.
CLOCK_SOURCE_WATCHDOG0x10FrameworkInternal: first watchdog measurement taken. Set after initial cs_watchdog_read().
CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES0x20FrameworkValidated for high-res timers. Set when continuous clocksource passes watchdog. Required for oneshot/hres mode.
CLOCK_SOURCE_UNSTABLE0x40FrameworkWatchdog detected excessive skew. Triggers clocksource_select_fallback().
CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP0x80DriverCounter keeps running in S3/S4. Selected for suspend time accounting. Must NOT have suspend/resume callbacks.
CLOCK_SOURCE_RESELECT0x100FrameworkStatus changed (e.g., HRES promotion) — needs re-evaluation.
CLOCK_SOURCE_VERIFY_PERCPU0x200DriverVerify monotonicity across CPUs via IPI sampling. Critical for multi-socket TSC.

Typical flag combinations:

Table 6-28. Clocksource Flags: Driver-Set vs Framework-Added
ClocksourceDriver SetsFramework Adds
TSCIS_CONTINUOUS | VERIFY_PERCPUVALID_FOR_HRES
HPETIS_CONTINUOUSVALID_FOR_HRES
ACPI PMTIS_CONTINUOUSVALID_FOR_HRES (after watchdog)

Driver guidance: At minimum set CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS for any free-running counter. Add SUSPEND_NONSTOP if hardware keeps counting during all sleep states. Add VERIFY_PERCPU if the counter exists independently on each CPU and cross-CPU sync might fail.

Clocksource IDs

Before kernel 5.x, clocksource identification relied on string comparison (strcmp(cs->name, "tsc")), which was slow and fragile. The enum clocksource_ids provides typed, compile-time-checked identifiers that enable fast switch-based dispatch in performance-critical paths:

/* include/linux/clocksource_ids.h */
enum clocksource_ids {
    CSID_GENERIC = 0,          /* Default for untyped clocksources */
    CSID_ARM_ARCH_COUNTER,     /* ARM architectural counter */
    CSID_S390_TOD,             /* s390 Time-of-Day clock */
    CSID_X86_TSC_EARLY,        /* Early boot TSC (before validation) */
    CSID_X86_TSC,              /* Validated x86 TSC */
    CSID_X86_KVM_CLK,          /* KVM paravirtual clock */
    CSID_X86_ART,              /* Always Running Timer (Intel ART) */
    CSID_MAX,
};

Where IDs are used:

  1. vDSO fast-path selection — The vDSO data page includes the current clocksource ID. Userspace clock_gettime() uses it to select the correct read method (RDTSC, MRS, etc.) without kernel involvement.
  2. Timekeeping optimization — The tk_read_base structure caches the ID for branch-free read function selection in ktime_get() hot paths.
  3. ART correlation — CSID_X86_ART identifies Intel's Always Running Timer for hardware-correlated cross-timestamps (PTP/IEEE 1588, sub-µs sync).
  4. TSC lifecycle — CSID_X86_TSC_EARLY vs CSID_X86_TSC reflects two-phase registration: early (pre-watchdog, lower rating) replaced by validated TSC.

Driver guidance: Most clocksources should use CSID_GENERIC (the default). Only set a specific ID if your clocksource has a corresponding vDSO fast-path or needs special timekeeping handling. Adding a new ID requires changes to both clocksource_ids.h and vDSO code.

Rating System

The rating system is the framework's primary mechanism for automatic quality-based selection. When multiple clocksources are available (always the case — at minimum jiffies is registered), the framework picks the highest-rated valid one. The rating is a simple integer reflecting the driver author's assessment of the hardware's quality — the framework trusts it directly for sorting.

Table 6-29. Clocksource Rating Ranges
RatingQualityExamplesRationale
400+Perfect — architectural / paravirtARM arch timer (400), kvm-clock (400), Hyper-V TSC page (500)Spec guarantees monotonicity + invariance + cross-CPU sync
300Very good — hardware stablex86 TSC (invariant)Constant freq guaranteed, but cross-socket needs verification
250Good — reliable, slower accessHPETAlways correct but MMIO ~200 ns access cost
200Acceptable — fallbackACPI PM timerImmune to DVFS but I/O port ~500 ns and 24-bit wrap
100–150Functional but poorPIT / i8253 (110)Limited precision/width/access
1–99Last resortjiffies (1), refined jiffies (2)Tick-based or intentionally low-quality fallback

Boot-time selection sequence (typical x86_64):

/* Typical dmesg output showing rating-based switching */
clocksource: jiffies: mask: 0xffffffff ...          /* rating 1 */
clocksource: tsc-early: mask: 0xffffffffffffffff ... /* rating 299 */
clocksource: Switched to clocksource tsc-early
clocksource: hpet: mask: 0xffffffff ...              /* rating 250 — no switch */
clocksource: acpi_pm: mask: 0x00ffffff ...           /* rating 200 — no switch */
clocksource: tsc: mask: 0xffffffffffffffff ...       /* rating 300 */
clocksource: Switched to clocksource tsc

Driver guidance for choosing a rating:

  • Architecturally guaranteed monotonic + synchronized across CPUs: 350–400
  • Reliable, invariant, but needs watchdog verification: 300
  • Correct but significant access latency: 200–250
  • Works but has limitations (narrow width, slow): 100–200
  • Never use rating 0 — it means "do not select"

Registration and Selection

The registration process transforms a driver's static struct clocksource into a live, watchdog-monitored, selectable time source. Understanding this flow is essential for driver developers adding new clocksources.

Registration Flow

Clocksources register via two convenience macros that expand to the same core function:

clocksource_register_hz(cs, freq);   /* freq in Hz */
clocksource_register_khz(cs, freq);  /* freq in kHz */

The core function performs five steps atomically under clocksource_mutex:

int __clocksource_register_scale(struct clocksource *cs, u32 scale, u32 freq)
{
    /* Step 1: Architecture-specific init (e.g., x86 vDSO setup) */
    clocksource_arch_init(cs);

    /* Step 2: Validate vdso_clock_mode and clocksource ID */
    if (cs->vdso_clock_mode < 0 || cs->vdso_clock_mode >= VDSO_CLOCKMODE_MAX)
        cs->vdso_clock_mode = VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE;

    /* Step 3: Compute mult/shift, max_idle_ns, maxadj, uncertainty_margin */
    __clocksource_update_freq_scale(cs, scale, freq);

    mutex_lock(&clocksource_mutex);

    /* Step 4: Insert into sorted list + watchdog list */
    clocksource_enqueue(cs);             /* sorted by rating */
    clocksource_enqueue_watchdog(cs);    /* add to watchdog monitoring */

    /* Step 5: Trigger selection of best clocksource */
    clocksource_select();                /* pick the winner */
    clocksource_select_watchdog(false);  /* pick watchdog reference */
    __clocksource_suspend_select(cs);    /* check if suspend-capable */

    mutex_unlock(&clocksource_mutex);
    return 0;
}

Step 3 (__clocksource_update_freq_scale()) computes all derived fields:

void __clocksource_update_freq_scale(struct clocksource *cs, u32 scale, u32 freq)
{
    /* Compute max safe seconds before counter wrap */
    sec = cs->mask;
    do_div(sec, freq * scale);
    if (sec > 600 && cs->mask > UINT_MAX)
        sec = 600;   /* Cap at 10 minutes for precision */

    /* Compute mult/shift for cycle→ns conversion */
    clocks_calc_mult_shift(&cs->mult, &cs->shift, freq,
                           NSEC_PER_SEC / scale, sec * scale);

    /* Compute uncertainty margin (min 500 ppm) */
    if (!cs->uncertainty_margin)
        cs->uncertainty_margin = max(NSEC_PER_SEC / (scale * freq),
                                     2 * WATCHDOG_MAX_SKEW);

    cs->maxadj = clocksource_max_adjustment(cs);  /* 11% of mult */
    clocksource_update_max_deferment(cs);          /* max_idle_ns, max_cycles */

    pr_info("%s: mask: 0x%llx max_cycles: 0x%llx, max_idle_ns: %lld ns\n",
            cs->name, cs->mask, cs->max_cycles, cs->max_idle_ns);
}

Selection Algorithm

clocksource_enqueue() inserts into a sorted linked list (highest rating first), then __clocksource_select() picks the winner:

static void __clocksource_select(bool skipcur)
{
    bool oneshot = tick_oneshot_mode_active();
    struct clocksource *best = clocksource_find_best(oneshot, skipcur);
    if (!best) return;

    /* Check for user override via sysfs or boot parameter */
    if (strlen(override_name)) {
        list_for_each_entry(cs, &clocksource_list, list) {
            if (strcmp(cs->name, override_name) != 0) continue;
            /* Must be HRT-compatible in oneshot mode */
            if (!(cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES) && oneshot) {
                if (cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_UNSTABLE)
                    override_name[0] = 0;  /* Give up */
            } else
                best = cs;
            break;
        }
    }

    if (curr_clocksource != best && !timekeeping_notify(best)) {
        pr_info("Switched to clocksource %s\n", best->name);
        curr_clocksource = best;
    }
}

Key design decisions:

  • Oneshot mode filter — only VALID_FOR_HRES clocksources are eligible, preventing jiffies from being used with hrtimers
  • User override — clocksource= boot param or sysfs write takes precedence, but only if HRT-compatible
  • timekeeping_notify() — switches the timekeeping core's tk_read_base over to the new source
  • Boot deferral — before finished_booting (set at fs_initcall), selection is deferred to avoid churn

That third point deserves more than a line, because it is the reason clocksource switching is treated as a rare event rather than a routine one. A running system reads the current clocksource from every CPU, from interrupt context, from the vDSO in user space, and from inside the seqlock-protected timekeeping read loop. There is no way to swap the counter underneath all of those readers with a lock, so the kernel does not try:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
int timekeeping_notify(struct clocksource *clock)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;

    if (tk->tkr_mono.clock == clock)
        return 0;
    stop_machine(change_clocksource, clock, NULL);
    tick_clock_notify();
    return tk->tkr_mono.clock == clock ? 0 : -1;
}

stop_machine() halts every other CPU in the system and runs change_clocksource() with nothing else executing anywhere. Only under that guarantee is it safe to recompute the timekeeper's cycle base, install the new mult and shift, and republish the vDSO data. The cost is measured in tens of microseconds across the whole machine, which is negligible if it happens three times during boot and unacceptable if it happens on a schedule. Two consequences follow, and both appear later in this section: the watchdog never switches sources itself but marks the offender unstable and schedules a work item, so the stop_machine() call happens in process context rather than in a timer callback; and selection is skipped entirely until finished_booting is set, so the several clocksources that register in quick succession during early boot cause one switch at the end rather than one apiece.

The final call, tick_clock_notify(), sets a bit in every CPU's tick_sched structure asking the tick layer to reconsider its mode. tick_check_oneshot_change() picks the bit up on each CPU in turn and, if timekeeping_valid_for_hres() now holds, moves that CPU to one-shot ticks. The check runs in one direction only: a new clocksource can grant high-resolution mode, but nothing takes it away again. Once a CPU has switched, hres_active is cleared only when the CPU is brought back up after a hotplug operation — there is no runtime demotion, even if the system later falls back to a clocksource as poor as jiffies.

The Clocksource Watchdog

The watchdog continuously monitors registered clocksources for instability — detecting drift, jitter, or failure — and automatically falls back to a working alternative. Without it, a malfunctioning TSC on a multi-socket system could cause silent time corruption.

Why a watchdog? Hardware timers can become unreliable due to multi-socket TSC desync, CPU frequency changes on old hardware, firmware bugs, or virtualization artifacts (VM migration between hosts).

The Three-Point Read

The cs_watchdog_read() function uses a careful three-point measurement to bound the read window:

static enum wd_read_status cs_watchdog_read(struct clocksource *cs,
                                             u64 *csnow, u64 *wdnow)
{
    for (nretries = 0; nretries <= max_retries; nretries++) {
        local_irq_disable();
        *wdnow = watchdog->read(watchdog);  /* reference start */
        *csnow = cs->read(cs);               /* clocksource sample */
        wd_end = watchdog->read(watchdog);   /* reference end */
        wd_end2 = watchdog->read(watchdog);  /* consecutive check */
        local_irq_enable();

        wd_delay = cycles_to_nsec_safe(watchdog, *wdnow, wd_end);
        if (wd_delay <= md + cs->uncertainty_margin)
            return WD_READ_SUCCESS;

        /* Consecutive reads too far apart → system overloaded */
        wd_seq_delay = cycles_to_nsec_safe(watchdog, wd_end, wd_end2);
        if (wd_seq_delay > md)
            return WD_READ_SKIP;  /* Suspend watchdog 5 minutes */
    }
    return WD_READ_UNSTABLE;  /* Too many retries */
}

Two questions that listing raises are worth answering, because md carries most of the weight and the listing never says what it is.

What md is. It is the watchdog’s own uncertainty_margin — how far apart two readings of the reference may legitimately be before the reading is considered disturbed rather than merely slow. The read is bracketed by two watchdog samples precisely so this can be measured: if the reference advanced by more than md + cs->uncertainty_margin between them, something interrupted the sequence — an SMI, an NMI, or, on a virtual machine, the vCPU being descheduled by the host — and the clocksource sample taken in the middle cannot be trusted. The function retries rather than concluding anything. Only when every retry is disturbed does it return WD_READ_UNSTABLE.

Where does uncertainty_margin come from? A driver may state one, and if it does not, __clocksource_update_freq_scale() derives it from the clock period — one tick, NSEC_PER_SEC / freq — and then raises it to a floor of 2 × WATCHDOG_MAX_SKEW. That floor is what matters in practice, because for any modern counter the period is far below it: a 3 GHz TSC has a period of a third of a nanosecond and ends up with the floor instead. The floor is chosen so that the sum of the two margins in a comparison comes to 500 ppm of the half-second watchdog interval, and the comment in kernel/time/clocksource.c justifies the figure briskly: it comes from NTP’s own limits, and “if a clocksource is good enough for NTP, it is good enough for us”. The point is that what is being bounded is not the counter’s resolution but the software’s ability to read it promptly, so a more precise counter earns no tighter a margin.

A driver overrides the default when it knows the reading conditions are unusual, and arch/x86/kernel/tsc.c gives the clearest example: clocksource_tsc_early declares .uncertainty_margin = 32 * NSEC_PER_MSEC — thirty-two milliseconds, some two hundred times the floor. Early boot is single-threaded, firmware is still taking SMIs, and the calibration behind tsc-early is deliberately rough; holding it to the normal margin would reject a counter that is merely imprecise rather than broken. The final tsc clocksource states no margin at all and takes the floor.

Why the two margins must match. This bracket margin and the interval margin used in the main loop below were not always the same expression, and the difference was a real bug fixed only in December 2025 (commit c06343be0b4e). The readout limit was 2 × watchdog->uncertainty_margin + cs->uncertainty_margin while the interval check allowed only watchdog->uncertainty_margin + cs->uncertainty_margin — in the worked example accompanying the fix, 750 µs against 500 µs. A readout could therefore be accepted as valid and still leave enough displacement to fail the interval comparison on the following cycle, because the intervals are computed against the previous cycle’s samples. The consequence was not a missed fault but the opposite: perfectly good TSCs were marked unstable on busy machines. Both checks now use the same margin, which is the property that had been assumed all along.

The Main Watchdog Loop

static void clocksource_watchdog(struct timer_list *unused)
{
    spin_lock(&watchdog_lock);
    list_for_each_entry(cs, &watchdog_list, wd_list) {
        if (cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_UNSTABLE) {
            schedule_work(&watchdog_work);
            continue;
        }

        read_ret = cs_watchdog_read(cs, &csnow, &wdnow);
        if (read_ret == WD_READ_UNSTABLE) { __clocksource_unstable(cs); continue; }
        if (read_ret == WD_READ_SKIP) { extra_wait = HZ * 300; break; }

        /* Convert elapsed cycles to nanoseconds */
        wd_nsec = cycles_to_nsec_safe(watchdog, cs->wd_last, wdnow);
        cs_nsec = cycles_to_nsec_safe(cs, cs->cs_last, csnow);

        /* THE KEY CHECK: compare elapsed times */
        md = cs->uncertainty_margin + watchdog->uncertainty_margin;
        if (abs(cs_nsec - wd_nsec) > md) {
            __clocksource_unstable(cs);
            continue;
        }

        /* Promote to high-res valid */
        if (!(cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES) &&
            (cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS))
            cs->flags |= CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES;
    }

    /* Rotate to next CPU and re-arm */
    next_cpu = cpumask_next_wrap(raw_smp_processor_id(), cpu_online_mask);
    add_timer_on(&watchdog_timer, next_cpu);
    spin_unlock(&watchdog_lock);
}

Per-CPU Verification

For clocksources with VERIFY_PERCPU (notably TSC), the framework verifies cross-CPU monotonicity via IPI sampling:

void clocksource_verify_percpu(struct clocksource *cs)
{
    clocksource_verify_choose_cpus();  /* Pick up to verify_n_cpus random CPUs */
    for_each_cpu(cpu, &cpus_chosen) {
        csnow_begin = cs->read(cs);
        smp_call_function_single(cpu, clocksource_verify_one_cpu, cs, 1);
        csnow_end = cs->read(cs);
        /* If target's reading is outside [begin, end] → desync */
    }
    /* Log: "CPUs X,Y behind CPU Z for clocksource tsc" */
}

The sampling is a compromise forced by cost. Each probe is a synchronous smp_call_function_single(), so checking every CPU on a large machine would be an expensive storm of IPIs for a test that almost always passes; sampling a handful at random still catches a genuinely desynchronised socket within a few rounds. The count is the module parameter verify_n_cpus, writable at runtime and defaulting to 8; setting it to −1 checks every online CPU, and setting it to 0 disables the check altogether. Note that the test is one-sided by design — it reads the counter on the local CPU, then on the target, then locally again, and only complains if the target’s value falls outside that bracket — so it cannot mistake ordinary read latency for skew.

Watchdog State Machine

Current StateEventNext StateAction

Suspend Clocksource

When the system enters S3/S4 sleep, most hardware clocks stop. But the kernel needs to know how long the system was asleep to correctly update CLOCK_MONOTONIC on resume. The suspend clocksource mechanism selects a clock that keeps running through sleep states.

Selection

static void __clocksource_suspend_select(struct clocksource *cs)
{
    if (!(cs->flags & CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP))
        return;
    /* Nonstop clocks must NOT provide suspend/resume callbacks */
    if (cs->suspend || cs->resume)
        pr_warn("Nonstop clocksource %s should not supply "
                "suspend/resume interfaces\n", cs->name);
    if (!suspend_clocksource || cs->rating > suspend_clocksource->rating)
        suspend_clocksource = cs;
}

Suspend/Resume Flow

/* Called late in suspend (after CPUs stopped, IRQs disabled) */
void clocksource_start_suspend_timing(struct clocksource *cs, u64 start_cycles)
{
    if (!suspend_clocksource) return;
    if (clocksource_is_suspend(cs)) {
        suspend_start = start_cycles;  /* Reuse current reading */
        return;
    }
    if (suspend_clocksource->enable)
        suspend_clocksource->enable(suspend_clocksource);
    suspend_start = suspend_clocksource->read(suspend_clocksource);
}

/* Called early in resume (single CPU, no IRQs) */
u64 clocksource_stop_suspend_timing(struct clocksource *cs, u64 cycle_now)
{
    u64 now = clocksource_is_suspend(cs) ? cycle_now
            : suspend_clocksource->read(suspend_clocksource);
    u64 nsec = 0;
    if (now > suspend_start)
        nsec = cycles_to_nsec_safe(suspend_clocksource, suspend_start, now);
    /* Disable to save power if not also the active clocksource */
    if (!clocksource_is_suspend(cs) && suspend_clocksource->disable)
        suspend_clocksource->disable(suspend_clocksource);
    return nsec;  /* Added to CLOCK_MONOTONIC by timekeeping_resume() */
}

Key design: The calling sequence runs late in suspend / early in resume — processes are frozen, non-boot CPUs stopped, IRQs disabled. No locking needed, readings are reliable.

Driver guidance: If your hardware keeps counting in all sleep states, set CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP and do NOT provide suspend/resume callbacks.

Cycle-to-Nanosecond Conversion

This conversion runs on every ktime_get(), clock_gettime(), and vDSO call — millions of times per second on busy systems. It uses fixed-point arithmetic to avoid the 20–90 cycle cost of hardware division.

The Core Formula

nanoseconds = (delta_cycles × mult) >> shift

/* Replaces the expensive: ns = delta_cycles × (1,000,000,000 / freq) */
/* Fixed-point: 1 MUL + 1 SHR (3-5 cycles) vs division (20-90 cycles) */

Computing mult and shift

void clocks_calc_mult_shift(u32 *mult, u32 *shift, u32 from, u32 to, u32 maxsec)
{
    u64 tmp;
    u32 sft, sftacc = 32;

    /* to = NSEC_PER_SEC, from = frequency (Hz), maxsec = safe range */
    tmp = ((u64)maxsec * from) >> 32;
    while (tmp) { tmp >>= 1; sftacc--; }

    for (sft = 32; sft > 0; sft--) {
        tmp = (u64)to << sft;
        tmp += from / 2;    /* round to nearest */
        do_div(tmp, from);
        if ((tmp >> sftacc) == 0) {
            *mult = (u32)tmp;
            *shift = sft;
            return;
        }
    }
}

Worked Examples

Table 6-33. mult/shift Values for Common Clocks
ClockFrequencymultshift1 cycle → nsGranularity of one mult step
TSC @ 3 GHz3,000,000,0005,592,405240.3333 ns0.179 ppm
TSC @ 4 GHz4,000,000,0002,097,152230.2500 ns0.477 ppm
HPET @ 14.3 MHz14,318,1802,343,484,4372569.8413 ns0.0004 ppm
ACPI PMT3,579,5452,343,484,43723279.3651 ns0.0004 ppm
ARM @ 19.2 MHz19,200,000873,813,3332452.0833 ns0.0011 ppm
ARM @ 100 MHz100,000,000167,772,1602410.0000 ns0.0060 ppm

Three things in that table are worth explaining, because each of them looks like an error until the algorithm is followed through.

The shift is not maximised. A larger shift means a finer mult, so one might expect clocks_calc_mult_shift() to return the largest shift that keeps mult inside 32 bits. It does not. The loop counts down from 32 and stops at the first shift for which mult fits within sftacc bits, where sftacc was derived from maxsec × freq. The constraint being satisfied is not “mult is representable” but “cycles × mult does not overflow 64 bits for any interval up to maxsec seconds”. A wide, fast counter is therefore given a smaller shift than a narrow, slow one, which is the reverse of the intuition.

That is why the 600-second cap appears in the registration path. For a 64-bit counter, mask / freq is astronomical, and honouring it would drive the shift down to almost nothing and destroy precision. Capping sec at 600 for masks wider than 32 bits bounds the requirement to a ten-minute conversion range. The kernel comment states the resulting number outright — “a shift value of 24 for a clocksource with mask ≥ 40-bit and f ≥ 4GHz” — and the table above reproduces it: every wide counter in it lands on shift 24, whether it ticks at 19.2 MHz or 3 GHz, and only the 4 GHz TSC is pushed down to 23. A narrow counter is capped by its own mask long before the 600-second rule applies: the 24-bit ACPI PMT wraps in under five seconds, so sec is 4, sftacc stays at its full 32 bits, and the shift is then limited by nothing but the requirement that mult fit in 32 bits.

The HPET and the ACPI PMT share a mult. This is not a coincidence and not a typo. The HPET’s 14.318180 MHz is exactly four times the PMT’s 3.579545 MHz — both are derived from the same NTSC colour-burst crystal — so the two conversions differ by a factor of four, which is absorbed entirely by the shift (25 against 23) and leaves the multiplier identical.

The last column is the granularity of NTP steering rather than of a single reading: adjusting mult by one is the smallest rate change the kernel can make, and it corresponds to a fractional change of 1/mult. For the TSC that is about 0.18 ppm, comfortably finer than the drift NTP needs to correct.

Overflow Protection

static inline void clocksource_update_max_deferment(struct clocksource *cs)
{
    /* max_cycles: largest delta where (delta × (mult+maxadj)) fits in u64 */
    cs->max_idle_ns = clocks_calc_max_nsecs(cs->mult, cs->shift,
                                             cs->maxadj, cs->mask,
                                             &cs->max_cycles);
    /* Includes 50% safety margin — returns half the safe maximum */

    /* max_raw_delta: 87.5% of mask — detects negative counter motion */
    cs->max_raw_delta = (cs->mask >> 1) + (cs->mask >> 2) + (cs->mask >> 3);
}

/* Runtime safe conversion */
static noinline u64 cycles_to_nsec_safe(struct clocksource *cs, u64 start, u64 end)
{
    u64 delta = clocksource_delta(end, start, cs->mask, cs->max_raw_delta);
    if (likely(delta < cs->max_cycles))
        return clocksource_cyc2ns(delta, cs->mult, cs->shift);  /* fast */
    return mul_u64_u32_shr(delta, cs->mult, cs->shift);  /* slow but safe */
}

The 87.5% figure deserves a word, because the obvious choice would be half the mask — the point at which a forward wrap and a backward step become indistinguishable — and that is indeed what the kernel used until late 2024. It was widened by commit 76031d9536a0 after a report of boot stalls on an emulated 32-bit ARM machine with a 24-bit clocksource. There, max_idle_ns works out to about 597 ms while the half-mask tripping point sits at roughly 671 ms: a legal tickless idle that overran its wakeup slightly could cross the threshold, at which point clocksource_delta() returned zero, the clock froze, and the next timeout was computed from a stale base — which made the following interval longer still. Moving the cut-off to seven-eighths lifts the tripping point to about 1.17 s and restores the gap. For wide counters the change is invisible, because the overflow arithmetic already holds max_idle_ns nowhere near half the mask; it only matters when the counter is narrow enough that the two limits are neighbours.

The suppression itself is deliberately blunt. clocksource_delta(), in kernel/time/timekeeping_internal.h, simply returns 0 when the masked difference exceeds max_delta: time stands still for that update rather than leaping backwards by most of a counter period. Standing still is recoverable; leaping backwards corrupts every timestamp derived from it.

NTP Adjustments

NTP corrects clock drift by adjusting mult — speeding up or slowing down time without discontinuity:

mult_adjusted = mult + ntp_correction
nanoseconds = (delta_cycles × mult_adjusted) >> shift

/* maxadj = 11% of mult — allows ±110,000 ppm correction */
static u32 clocksource_max_adjustment(struct clocksource *cs)
{
    return (u64)cs->mult * 11 / 100;
}

Impact on NOHZ Idle

The max_idle_ns value directly limits tickless idle duration:

Table 6-34. Clocksource Width and Maximum Tickless Idle
Clocksourcemax_idle_ns (approx)Max Tickless Idle
64-bit TSC @ 3 GHz~hundreds of secondsEffectively unlimited
32-bit HPET @ 14 MHz~150 seconds~2.5 minutes
24-bit ACPI PMT~2.3 seconds~2 seconds
The Linux 2.6 timer_opts with four methods is gone. The 7.0.12 clocksource framework: (1) supports unlimited registrations on a single sorted list; (2) adds a watchdog with configurable uncertainty margins, three-point reads, and per-CPU verification; (3) introduces typed IDs (enum clocksource_ids) for fast vDSO dispatch; (4) handles suspend time accounting via suspend_clocksource; (5) provides sysfs + boot-param runtime control; (6) integrates with timekeeping via timekeeping_notify(); (7) computes max_idle_ns with 50% safety margin for NOHZ.

Clock Event Devices

A clock event device is a piece of timer hardware that satisfies the mirror image of the clocksource contract of the previous section. A clocksource must be readable and must never stop; it cannot be programmed and cannot interrupt. A clock event device is the opposite on every point:

  • It can be programmed to raise an interrupt at a chosen future time. This is the whole reason it exists, and it is the one capability a clocksource does not have.
  • It has a known frequency and a known programmable range. The driver declares an input clock in Hz and the smallest and largest delta it will accept, in hardware ticks. Without these the framework cannot turn a deadline expressed in nanoseconds into a register write.
  • It need not be readable. The framework never asks a clock event device what time it is; that question always goes to the clocksource. A device that is write-only is perfectly acceptable.
  • It need not keep running. A timer that stops when its CPU enters a deep C-state is still usable, provided it says so with the C3STOP feature flag; the broadcast machinery described later in this chapter then covers for it.

Because a clock event device cannot tell the time and a clocksource cannot cause an interrupt, the two are always used together, and neither is useful alone. Every scheduler tick, every hrtimer expiry, and every timer wheel callback in the system arrives because some clock event device was programmed to interrupt and did. On a typical x86_64 machine the Local APIC timer plays this role; on ARM64 it is the per-CPU generic timer comparator.

Linux 2.6 had no such abstraction. Interrupts were driven by named hardware from architecture-specific code: the PIT provided the global tick, the Local APIC timer the per-CPU tick, and each architecture wired its own. Linux 7.0.12 places all of it behind one structure, struct clock_event_device, and one framework, kernel/time/clockevents.c (794 lines). That framework exists to answer three questions:

  1. Which device drives which CPU? Devices announce themselves with clockevents_config_and_register(), carrying a rating and a cpumask; the tick layer picks a winner per CPU and is free to change its mind later when better hardware appears. Covered under Registration and Programming and Per-CPU Assignment.
  2. What is the device doing right now? A five-state machine — detached, shutdown, periodic, oneshot, oneshot-stopped — governs every transition, so a driver always receives its callbacks in a predictable order and the framework always knows whether an interrupt can still arrive. Covered under Clock Event States and Features and Capabilities.
  3. How does a deadline become a register write? clockevents_program_event() converts an absolute ktime_t into a hardware delta using precomputed mult/shift factors, clamps it to what the hardware will accept, and — since Linux 7.0 — refuses to reprogram in a way that would starve the interrupt it is trying to schedule. Covered under Registration and Programming.

Two further concerns cut across all three. Power management is handled by the C3STOP flag and the broadcast device that stands in for stopped per-CPU timers, and by the suspend and resume callbacks. CPU hotplug requires that a dying CPU hand off any global duty and release its device before it goes, and that an incoming CPU re-register cleanly. Both are covered under Suspend, Resume, and CPU Hotplug, and the last subsection describes the sysfs interface that lets you see the result from user space.

The clock_event_device Structure

The struct clock_event_device is the central abstraction for all interrupt-generating timers in the kernel. It serves three distinct roles:

  1. Hardware abstraction — wraps architecture-specific timer programming (writing LAPIC registers, ARM timer comparators, HPET channels) behind a uniform interface
  2. Framework integration — provides the metadata (rating, cpumask, features) that the tick layer needs to select the best device for each CPU
  3. Power management — includes suspend/resume callbacks and C3STOP awareness so the kernel can maintain timekeeping across idle states

Every timer driver allocates one clock_event_device per hardware instance (typically one per CPU for LAPIC/ARM, one per channel for HPET) and fills in the fields before calling clockevents_config_and_register(). The framework then takes ownership of the device lifecycle.

/* include/linux/clockchips.h */
struct clock_event_device {
    /* Event delivery */
    void    (*event_handler)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int     (*set_next_event)(unsigned long evt,
                              struct clock_event_device *);
    int     (*set_next_ktime)(ktime_t expires,
                              struct clock_event_device *);
    ktime_t next_event;

    /* Timing range (computed by framework from ticks + frequency) */
    u64             max_delta_ns;
    u64             min_delta_ns;
    u32             mult;           /* ns → cycles multiplier (reverse of clocksource) */
    u32             shift;          /* ns → cycles divisor */

    /* Device state and capabilities */
    enum clock_event_state  state_use_accessors;
    unsigned int            features;
    unsigned int            next_event_forced;  /* Last arming was a forced min-delta */
    unsigned long           retries;

    /* State transition callbacks (driver-provided) */
    int (*set_state_periodic)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int (*set_state_oneshot)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int (*set_state_oneshot_stopped)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int (*set_state_shutdown)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int (*tick_resume)(struct clock_event_device *);

    /* Broadcast function (for C3STOP devices) */
    void (*broadcast)(const struct cpumask *mask);

    /* Power management */
    void (*suspend)(struct clock_event_device *);
    void (*resume)(struct clock_event_device *);

    /* Registration range (driver-provided) */
    unsigned long   min_delta_ticks;
    unsigned long   max_delta_ticks;

    /* Identity and affinity */
    const char              *name;
    int                     rating;
    int                     irq;
    int                     bound_on;
    const struct cpumask    *cpumask;
    struct list_head        list;
    struct module           *owner;
} ____cacheline_aligned;
Table 6-35. Key clock_event_device Fields
FieldPurposeWho Sets It
event_handlerCalled when the timer interrupt fires. Set to tick_handle_periodic() (periodic) or hrtimer/NOHZ handler (oneshot). Drivers must never set this directly.Framework
set_next_eventPrograms the next interrupt in hardware ticks (delta from now). This is the driver's core function — writes to hardware registers. Must return 0 on success.Driver
set_next_ktimeAlternative: programs next interrupt using absolute ktime. Used by devices with CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_KTIME.Driver (optional)
next_eventCached ktime of the next programmed event. Useful for debugging and broadcast layer.Framework
mult / shiftConvert ns → cycles: ticks = (ns × mult) >> shift. Reverse of clocksource (cycles → ns). Auto-computed from frequency.Framework
min_delta_ticks / max_delta_ticksHardware limits on programmable range. Min prevents events expiring before write completes; max bounds counter range. ARM64: min=0xf typical; LAPIC: min=0x6.Driver
min_delta_ns / max_delta_nsNanosecond equivalents of tick limits. max_delta_ns caps the requested delta in clockevents_program_event(); a delta below min_delta_ns takes the forced path instead of being clamped.Framework
featuresCapability flags (see Features table below). Determines what modes the tick layer can use.Driver
ratingSelection priority — higher-rated devices replace lower-rated ones. LAPIC: 400–500; ARM timer: 450; HPET: 110.Driver
cpumaskWhich CPUs this device can serve. Per-CPU: cpumask_of(smp_processor_id()). Global: multiple CPUs but less preferred.Driver
broadcastFunction to send IPIs when used as broadcast timer. Wakes target CPUs from deep idle.Driver
set_state_*Driver callbacks for state transitions. set_state_shutdown is mandatory.Driver
tick_resumeCalled when tick device resumes from deep idle (distinct from full system resume).Driver
next_event_forcedSet when the last arming was a forced minimum-delta event. Suppresses further reprogramming until that event fires, preventing interrupt starvation (new in Linux 7.0).Framework
retriesCounter incremented on each programming retry. Useful for diagnosing min_delta issues; reported in /proc/timer_list.Framework

Contrast with clocksource: A clocksource's mult/shift convert cycles→ns (for reading time), while a clock event device's mult/shift convert ns→cycles (for programming the next event). They are inverse operations using the same fixed-point technique.

Minimal driver example (ARM64 Generic Timer):

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c — simplified */
static void __arch_timer_setup(struct clock_event_device *clk)
{
    clk->features = CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT;
    if (arch_timer_c3stop)
        clk->features |= CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP;

    clk->name = "arch_sys_timer";
    clk->rating = 450;
    clk->cpumask = cpumask_of(smp_processor_id());
    clk->irq = arch_timer_ppi[arch_timer_uses_ppi];

    clk->set_state_shutdown = arch_timer_shutdown_virt;
    clk->set_state_oneshot_stopped = arch_timer_shutdown_virt;
    clk->set_next_event = arch_timer_set_next_event_virt;

    clockevents_config_and_register(clk, arch_timer_rate,
                                    0xf,              /* min: 15 ticks */
                                    max_delta);       /* max: 56-bit */
}
Driver guidance: Always set name, rating, cpumask, features, set_state_shutdown, and set_next_event before registration. Set min_delta_ticks conservatively — too small causes retries; too large wastes resolution. Use CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP if there is any doubt about timer behavior in deep idle.

Clock Event States

The clock event framework uses a well-defined state machine to manage each device's lifecycle. State transitions are driven by the tick layer and enforce valid sequencing — for example, a device cannot enter ONESHOT_STOPPED unless it is currently in ONESHOT.

The state machine exists to ensure that:

  1. Drivers receive a predictable callback sequence — they know shutdown always precedes any mode switch
  2. The framework can safely assume device state — a device in SHUTDOWN is guaranteed not to fire interrupts
  3. Power management is explicit — the ONESHOT_STOPPED state lets hardware actually stop the timer counter (saving power) while preserving the ability to quickly restart it
enum clock_event_state {
    CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED,          /* Not registered or released */
    CLOCK_EVT_STATE_SHUTDOWN,          /* Registered, not generating IRQs */
    CLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC,          /* Generating periodic interrupts */
    CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT,           /* Programmed for single interrupt */
    CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT_STOPPED,   /* Oneshot but currently idle */
};
static int __clockevents_switch_state(struct clock_event_device *dev,
                                       enum clock_event_state state)
{
    /* A dummy device has no hardware behind it: accept every transition */
    if (dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY)
        return 0;

    /* On state transitions clear the forced flag unconditionally */
    dev->next_event_forced = 0;

    switch (state) {
    case CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED:
    case CLOCK_EVT_STATE_SHUTDOWN:
        return dev->set_state_shutdown ? dev->set_state_shutdown(dev) : 0;

    case CLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC:
        if (!(dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC))
            return -ENOSYS;  /* Hardware doesn't support periodic */
        return dev->set_state_periodic ? dev->set_state_periodic(dev) : 0;

    case CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT:
        if (!(dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
            return -ENOSYS;  /* Hardware doesn't support oneshot */
        return dev->set_state_oneshot ? dev->set_state_oneshot(dev) : 0;

    case CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT_STOPPED:
        if (WARN_ONCE(!clockevent_state_oneshot(dev), "Current state: %d\n",
                      clockevent_get_state(dev)))
            return -EINVAL;  /* Must be in oneshot first */
        return dev->set_state_oneshot_stopped ?
               dev->set_state_oneshot_stopped(dev) : -ENOSYS;

    default:
        return -ENOSYS;
    }
}

That is the inner function. Callers do not reach it directly; they go through a wrapper whose four lines carry more weight than their length suggests:

void clockevents_switch_state(struct clock_event_device *dev,
                              enum clock_event_state state)
{
    if (clockevent_get_state(dev) != state) {
        if (__clockevents_switch_state(dev, state))
            return;                 /* failed: keep the recorded state */

        clockevent_set_state(dev, state);

        /* A nsec2cyc multiplicator of 0 is invalid and we would crash on it */
        if (clockevent_state_oneshot(dev)) {
            if (WARN_ON(!dev->mult))
                dev->mult = 1;
        }
    }
}

The outer test makes the transition idempotent: if the device is already recorded as being in the requested state, the driver callback is not invoked at all. That is normally exactly what one wants — a redundant shutdown should not cost a register write — but it makes the recorded state authoritative in a way that is easy to forget. Anything that sets state_use_accessors behind the framework’s back will cause the very next transition to that state to be silently skipped. This is not hypothetical: it produced a real bug in the CPU-offline path, described later in this section.

The early return on failure is the second point. When the inner function reports an error the wrapper leaves the recorded state unchanged, so the framework’s view continues to match hardware that refused the request rather than optimistically recording a transition that did not happen. A driver whose set_state_oneshot() fails leaves a device that the framework still believes is in SHUTDOWN, which is the safe belief.

The third is the mult fix-up, which looks like paranoia and is not. Entering ONESHOT means the device is about to be handed to clockevents_program_event(), which computes (delta × mult) >> shift; a mult of zero would convert every future deadline to zero ticks. Rather than divide the machine by zero, the framework warns and substitutes 1 — a wildly wrong conversion factor, but one that keeps the system alive and leaves a backtrace naming the guilty driver. It fires for a device that has reached ONESHOT without its conversion factors ever having been computed — typically a driver that called clockevents_register_device() directly, leaving mult at zero, where clockevents_config_and_register() would have derived it from the declared frequency.

Three things in the inner function are worth pausing on. A DUMMY device returns success before anything else happens, which is what makes the placeholder devices used during early boot harmless — every transition is accepted and nothing is programmed. The PERIODIC and ONESHOT cases return -ENOSYS if the corresponding feature bit is absent; reaching that line means the tick layer asked for a mode the device never advertised, which is a kernel bug rather than a runtime condition. And a missing callback is not an error for the shutdown, periodic, and oneshot states — a driver that has nothing to do for a transition may simply leave the pointer NULL — but it is an error for ONESHOT_STOPPED, which returns -ENOSYS so the tick layer knows the power optimisation is unavailable and can fall back to leaving the timer armed.

Table 6-36. Clock Event Device States
StateMeaningWhen EnteredDriver Callback
DETACHEDNot registered, or released after replacementInitial state, or after clockevents_exchange_device()set_state_shutdown()
SHUTDOWNRegistered but generating no interruptsAfter registration, before tick layer configures itset_state_shutdown()
PERIODICGenerating interrupts at a fixed interval (HZ rate)Legacy periodic tick modeset_state_periodic()
ONESHOTProgrammed for a single future interruptSwitched by tick layer when hrtimers/NOHZ enabledset_state_oneshot()
ONESHOT_STOPPEDOneshot mode but timer idle (power saving)When no pending events; re-enters ONESHOT on next programset_state_oneshot_stopped()
Table 6-37. Typical State Transition Sequences
ScenarioState Sequence
Boot (periodic mode)DETACHED → SHUTDOWN → PERIODIC
Boot then switch to hrtimersDETACHED → SHUTDOWN → PERIODIC → SHUTDOWN → ONESHOT
Idle CPU (NOHZ)ONESHOT → ONESHOT_STOPPED → (wake-up) → ONESHOT
Device replacementONESHOT → DETACHED (a single transition — the DETACHED case falls through to set_state_shutdown)

Driver guidance: set_state_shutdown must disable all timer interrupts — the framework assumes silence after this call. set_state_oneshot_stopped is optional — if not provided, the timer stays in ONESHOT (slightly less power efficient but functional). Never access state_use_accessors directly — use clockevent_state_detached(), clockevent_state_oneshot(), etc.

Features and Capabilities

Clock event devices advertise their capabilities through feature flags. The tick layer uses these to determine which modes are available and whether broadcast is needed. Features are set once during driver initialization and remain constant for the device's lifetime (except C3STOP which may be cleared if the platform has the Always-Running APIC Timer — ARAT).

The feature flags serve as a contract between the driver and the framework:

  • PERIODIC/ONESHOT tell the tick layer which modes it can request
  • C3STOP triggers the broadcast mechanism (critical for correct timekeeping during deep idle)
  • PERCPU is an assertion read only by the broadcast code — it bars the device from becoming the global broadcast device, and is required of a per-CPU oneshot wakeup device. What actually binds a device to one CPU is its cpumask.
  • KTIME/HRTIMER enable software-emulated devices that bypass the normal ns→ticks conversion
Table 6-38. Clock Event Feature Flags
Feature FlagValueMeaningImpact on FrameworkExample
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC0x01Can generate periodic interruptsFramework can set PERIODIC state; tick layer uses auto-reloadLAPIC periodic, HPET ch0
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT0x02Can be programmed for single interruptEnables hrtimers and NOHZ; required for modern kernelsLAPIC one-shot, ARM timer
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_KTIME0x04Accepts absolute ktime directlyclockevents_program_event() calls set_next_ktime(), skipping conversionhrtimer broadcast
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP0x08Timer stops in deep idle (C3+)Tick layer registers CPU with broadcast; on idle, broadcast takes overLAPIC without ARAT
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY0x10Placeholder (no real hardware)State transitions are no-ops; programming is silently ignoredBoot-time LAPIC pre-calibration
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DYNIRQ0x20IRQ affinity can be set dynamicallyBroadcast layer can reassign device's IRQ to any CPUarch_mem_timer, ARM SoC timers — not the HPET
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU0x40Asserts the device can only ever serve one CPURead only in tick-broadcast.c: bars the device from becoming the global broadcast device, and is required of a per-CPU oneshot wakeup device. It is not what makes a device per-CPU — the cpumask is.arm_global_timer, exynos_mct; notably not the LAPIC or the ARM architected timer
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER0x80Software-emulated via hrtimerUsed as broadcast when no global timer availableARM broadcast emulation

LAPIC (no ARAT)PERIODIC | ONESHOT | C3STOP | DUMMYFull-featured but stops in deep idle; DUMMY is cleared once calibration completes

LAPIC TSC-deadlineONESHOT (+ C3STOP without ARAT)setup_APIC_timer() clears PERIODIC and DUMMY; programs the TSC deadline MSR
