Driver guidance: Always set CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT unless your hardware physically cannot do one-shot — without it, the kernel cannot enable hrtimers or NOHZ (a severe performance/power regression). Set CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP if there is any doubt about timer behavior in deep idle. The DUMMY flag is for early boot only — clear it once calibration is complete.

Registration and Programming

Registration

Clock event devices register with clockevents_config_and_register(), which is the single entry point that computes timing parameters and integrates the device into the framework. The function performs three steps internally:

  1. Store hardware limits — saves min_delta_ticks and max_delta_ticks from the driver
  2. Compute conversion parameters — clockevents_config() calculates mult, shift, min_delta_ns, and max_delta_ns from the device frequency and tick range
  3. Register and notify — clockevents_register_device() adds the device to the global list and notifies the tick layer
/* kernel/time/clockevents.c */
void clockevents_config_and_register(struct clock_event_device *dev,
                                     u32 freq,
                                     unsigned long min_delta,
                                     unsigned long max_delta)
{
    dev->min_delta_ticks = min_delta;
    dev->max_delta_ticks = max_delta;
    clockevents_config(dev, freq);     /* Compute mult/shift, min/max_delta_ns */
    clockevents_register_device(dev);  /* Add to list, notify tick layer */
}

The clockevents_config() function internally:

static void clockevents_config(struct clock_event_device *dev, u32 freq)
{
    u64 sec;

    if (!(dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
        return;   /* No conversion needed for periodic-only devices */

    /* Calculate max sleep time (capped at 600s for >32-bit counters) */
    sec = dev->max_delta_ticks;
    do_div(sec, freq);
    if (!sec)
        sec = 1;
    else if (sec > 600 && dev->max_delta_ticks > UINT_MAX)
        sec = 600;

    clockevents_calc_mult_shift(dev, freq, sec);
    dev->min_delta_ns = cev_delta2ns(dev->min_delta_ticks, dev, false);
    dev->max_delta_ns = cev_delta2ns(dev->max_delta_ticks, dev, true);
}
void clockevents_register_device(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    clockevent_set_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED);

    if (!dev->cpumask)
        dev->cpumask = cpumask_of(smp_processor_id());

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&clockevents_lock, flags);
    list_add(&dev->list, &clockevent_devices);
    tick_check_new_device(dev);          /* Let tick layer evaluate */
    clockevents_notify_released();       /* Check for displaced devices */
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&clockevents_lock, flags);
}
Table 6-40. Device Selection Rules (tick_check_replacement)
PriorityRuleLogic
1CPU affinityDevice must be able to serve this CPU (cpumask test)
2Local preferencePer-CPU devices preferred over global ones
3IRQ affinityGlobal devices must support IRQ steering
4Oneshot preferenceOneshot-capable preferred when oneshot mode is active
5Rating comparisonHigher rating wins among comparable devices
6Fallback to broadcastIf rejected as tick device, try as broadcast
Driver guidance: Call clockevents_config_and_register() from a per-CPU context (e.g., CPU hotplug callback) for per-CPU devices. The freq parameter is the timer's input clock in Hz. Pass min_delta = 0 and max_delta = 0 for periodic-only devices. Registration is IRQ-safe.

Programming the Next Event

Once registered and assigned to a CPU, the framework programs events through clockevents_program_event(). This function is called by the tick layer, hrtimer subsystem, and broadcast mechanism — never directly by drivers.

int clockevents_program_event(struct clock_event_device *dev,
                              ktime_t expires, bool force)
{
    unsigned long long clc;
    int64_t delta;

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(expires < 0))
        return -ETIME;

    dev->next_event = expires;

    if (clockevent_state_shutdown(dev))
        return 0;

    /* We must be in ONESHOT state here */
    WARN_ONCE(!clockevent_state_oneshot(dev), "Current state: %d\n",
              clockevent_get_state(dev));

    /* Shortcut: devices with FEAT_KTIME handle conversion internally */
    if (dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_KTIME)
        return dev->set_next_ktime(expires, dev);

    delta = ktime_to_ns(ktime_sub(expires, ktime_get()));

    /* Required for tick_periodic() during early boot */
    if (delta <= 0 && !force)
        return -ETIME;   /* Already in the past */

    /* Comfortably far out: convert to ticks and program it */
    if (delta > (int64_t)dev->min_delta_ns) {
        delta = min(delta, (int64_t)dev->max_delta_ns);
        clc = ((unsigned long long)delta * dev->mult) >> dev->shift;
        if (!dev->set_next_event((unsigned long)clc, dev)) {
            dev->next_event_forced = 0;
            return 0;
        }
    }

    /* Too close, or the write failed. A forced minimum-delta event is
     * already pending, so leave it alone rather than pushing it out. */
    if (dev->next_event_forced)
        return 0;

    if (dev->set_next_event(dev->min_delta_ticks, dev)) {
        if (!force || clockevents_program_min_delta(dev))
            return -ETIME;
    }
    dev->next_event_forced = 1;
    return 0;
}

The structure is a fast path followed by a fallback. If the deadline is comfortably further out than the hardware minimum, the delta is capped at max_delta_ns, converted to ticks, and written; that is the case almost every time. Everything after it deals with deadlines that are already past, are nearer than the hardware can express, or that the driver simply refused. Note that the value is not clamped into [min_delta_ns, max_delta_ns] — only the upper bound is applied on the fast path. A delta below the minimum falls through to the fallback, which programs min_delta_ticks directly rather than a converted value, avoiding a rounding error at exactly the point where it would matter most.

Table 6-41. Event Programming Flow
StepActionFailure Mode
1Reject negative expiry: WARN_ON_ONCE(expires < 0)Returns -ETIME; indicates a caller bug
2Cache event: dev->next_event = expires—
3State check: skip if SHUTDOWN; warn if not ONESHOTReturns 0 (silent success)
4KTIME shortcut: call set_next_ktime() for software devicesDriver returns error
5Compute delta: expires - ktime_get()Negative = already past
6Past check: if delta ≤ 0 and not forced, return -ETIMECaller retries with force
7If delta > min_delta_ns: cap at max_delta_ns, convert ticks = (delta_ns × mult) >> shift, programOverflow protected by the cap; on success clears next_event_forced
8Otherwise, if a forced event is already pending, return 0 and leave itNone — this is the starvation guard
9Program min_delta_ticks directly and set next_event_forcedOn failure: -ETIME, or retry via clockevents_program_min_delta() when forced

The force parameter handles the case where the event is slightly in the past — the framework retries with min_delta_ticks to guarantee at least one interrupt fires. This is essential for the hrtimer subsystem which needs forward progress guarantees.

Guarding Against Interrupt Starvation

Steps 8 and 9 above, and the next_event_forced field they read and write, are new in Linux 7.0 and deserve their own explanation, because they fix a denial of service that had been latent in the framework since clock events were introduced in 2007.

The reproducer is short. A user-space program creates a timerfd and rearms it in a loop with an absolute expiry of 1 ns — always in the past. Each rearm reaches clockevents_program_event() with a negative delta, the framework dutifully programs the hardware minimum, and control returns to user space, which rearms again before the minimum delta has elapsed. On a sufficiently fast machine the loop closes: the deadline is pushed out by one minimum delta on every iteration, so the interrupt the kernel is trying to schedule never actually fires. The CPU spins in user space, the hrtimer that drives the lockup detector never runs, and the NMI watchdog eventually reports a hard lockup — confusingly, one attributed to user space.

The fix is the next_event_forced flag. When the framework is forced to program the bare minimum delta it records that fact; on the next reprogramming request, if a forced event is still pending and the new deadline is no further out than the minimum, it returns success without touching the hardware. The already-armed interrupt is allowed to arrive. Once it does — or once any normal, comfortably-distant event is programmed successfully — the flag is cleared and ordinary behaviour resumes.

Getting the flag cleared everywhere it needed clearing took a follow-up fix, because a stale flag is worse than the original bug: if the pending event is far in the future, suppressing reprogramming stops timer interrupts entirely. The clearing rule is simple once you see it — the flag is cleared the moment the forced event can no longer be pending. That happens in three situations:

  • The interrupt arrived. Every event handler clears the flag on entry: tick_handle_periodic(), tick_nohz_lowres_handler(), hrtimer_interrupt(), and the three handlers in kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c — tick_handle_periodic_broadcast(), tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast() and tick_oneshot_wakeup_handler().
  • A normal event was armed instead. The success path of the fast branch in clockevents_program_event() clears it, since the hardware now holds a genuine deadline rather than a forced minimum.
  • The device changed state. __clockevents_switch_state() clears it unconditionally on every transition and clockevents_shutdown() clears it again, so it cannot survive a shutdown/startup cycle. The broadcast code clears it directly at three more points where a device changes hands or is restarted: tick_broadcast_start_periodic(), tick_broadcast_setup_oneshot() and hotplug_cpu__broadcast_tick_pull().
For driver writers: this mechanism only works if min_delta_ticks is honest. A driver that advertises a minimum its hardware cannot actually meet will see set_next_event() fail repeatedly, and the framework's recovery path — described next — is a poor substitute for an accurate value. Measure it.

When the Hardware Refuses: Minimum-Delta Recovery

Step 9 of the table can still fail. A driver's set_next_event() returns -ETIME when it discovers that the deadline it was asked to program has already passed by the time it wrote the register — a real possibility when the requested delta is the hardware minimum and an SMI, a hypervisor exit, or a long instruction stream intervened. If the caller passed force, the framework must not give up, because some caller is depending on an interrupt to make forward progress. clockevents_program_min_delta() is the recovery path, and it has two implementations selected at build time.

Most architectures, ARM64 among them, get the simple version: try again with a progressively larger delta, up to ten times, and then admit defeat.

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c — !CONFIG_GENERIC_CLOCKEVENTS_MIN_ADJUST */
static int clockevents_program_min_delta(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    unsigned long long clc;
    int64_t delta = 0;
    int i;

    for (i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        delta += dev->min_delta_ns;            /* 1x, 2x, 3x ... 10x */
        dev->next_event = ktime_add_ns(ktime_get(), delta);

        if (clockevent_state_shutdown(dev))
            return 0;

        dev->retries++;
        clc = ((unsigned long long)delta * dev->mult) >> dev->shift;
        if (dev->set_next_event((unsigned long)clc, dev) == 0)
            return 0;
    }
    return -ETIME;
}

Note that dev->min_delta_ns itself is never modified here — the device's advertised minimum is taken as correct and only the requested delta grows. The retries counter is reported per device in /proc/timer_list, and a device accumulating retries is telling you its minimum is optimistic.

Adaptive Minimum Delta (x86 only)

Selecting CONFIG_GENERIC_CLOCKEVENTS_MIN_ADJUST replaces that loop with one that, on repeated failure, permanently raises the device's min_delta_ns. In Linux 7.0.12 exactly one architecture selects it — x86 (arch/x86/Kconfig) — which is worth knowing when reading dmesg on ARM64 and wondering why the message below never appears.

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c — CONFIG_GENERIC_CLOCKEVENTS_MIN_ADJUST */
#define MIN_DELTA_LIMIT     (NSEC_PER_SEC / HZ)   /* one jiffy */

static int clockevents_increase_min_delta(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    /* Nothing to do if we already reached the limit */
    if (dev->min_delta_ns >= MIN_DELTA_LIMIT) {
        printk_deferred(KERN_WARNING
                        "CE: Reprogramming failure. Giving up\n");
        dev->next_event = KTIME_MAX;
        return -ETIME;
    }

    if (dev->min_delta_ns < 5000)
        dev->min_delta_ns = 5000;            /* floor: jump straight to 5us */
    else
        dev->min_delta_ns += dev->min_delta_ns >> 1;   /* otherwise +50% */

    if (dev->min_delta_ns > MIN_DELTA_LIMIT)
        dev->min_delta_ns = MIN_DELTA_LIMIT;

    printk_deferred(KERN_WARNING
                    "CE: %s increased min_delta_ns to %llu nsec\n",
                    dev->name ? dev->name : "?",
                    (unsigned long long)dev->min_delta_ns);
    return 0;
}

Three details are easy to miss. The first failure of a device advertising a sub-microsecond minimum does not increase it by 50 % — it jumps straight to 5 µs, because growing by half of a very small number would take many rounds to reach anything useful. The ceiling is one jiffy, and reaching it produces "Reprogramming failure. Giving up" and sets next_event to KTIME_MAX, effectively disarming the device. And both messages use printk_deferred() rather than pr_warn(), because this code runs with the timer machinery in a delicate state and a synchronous console write could deadlock.

The calling loop retries three times at the current minimum before invoking the increase, then resets its counter and tries again at the new value:

for (i = 0;;) {
    delta = dev->min_delta_ns;
    dev->next_event = ktime_add_ns(ktime_get(), delta);
    ...
    if (++i > 2) {
        if (clockevents_increase_min_delta(dev))
            return -ETIME;
        i = 0;
    }
}

Either message in dmesg is a useful diagnostic — frequent min_delta increases indicate the driver's initial min_delta_ticks was too optimistic, or that the system has unusually high interrupt latency (e.g., from virtualization overhead).

Frequency Update at Runtime

Clock event devices may need their frequency recalculated after initial registration. The most common scenario is the TSC-deadline timer on x86_64: the TSC frequency is initially estimated during boot, then refined later through calibration against other timers (PIT, HPET, or ACPI PM timer). Once the refined frequency is known, the LAPIC clock event device must update its mult/shift parameters so that nanosecond-to-tick conversions remain accurate.

Other scenarios requiring frequency updates include:

  • CPU frequency scaling (DVFS) — on platforms where the timer clock is derived from the CPU clock (rare in modern designs, but seen in some ARM SoCs)
  • Clock reparenting — embedded timer blocks whose input clock can be switched between sources at runtime
  • Hot-recalibration — the kernel periodically checks TSC stability and may refine its calibration

The kernel provides two APIs:

/* Internal: called with appropriate locking already held */
int __clockevents_update_freq(struct clock_event_device *dev, u32 freq)
{
    clockevents_config(dev, freq);    /* Recompute mult/shift/min/max_delta_ns */

    if (clockevent_state_oneshot(dev))
        return clockevents_program_event(dev, dev->next_event, false);

    if (clockevent_state_periodic(dev))
        return __clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC);

    return 0;
}

/* Public: handles broadcast devices and serialization */
int clockevents_update_freq(struct clock_event_device *dev, u32 freq)
{
    unsigned long flags;
    int ret;

    local_irq_save(flags);
    ret = tick_broadcast_update_freq(dev, freq);
    if (ret == -ENODEV)
        ret = __clockevents_update_freq(dev, freq);
    local_irq_restore(flags);
    return ret;
}

Why reprogramming is needed after a frequency change: The mult/shift values encode the ratio between nanoseconds and hardware ticks. If the timer frequency changes but mult/shift are stale, the framework would program incorrect tick counts — events would fire too early or too late. After updating the conversion parameters, the framework must:

  • In oneshot mode: reprogram the pending event (dev->next_event) using the new parameters
  • In periodic mode: re-issue the set_state_periodic() callback so the driver reloads the hardware auto-reload register with the correct tick count

Real-world example — LAPIC TSC-deadline recalibration (x86_64):

/* arch/x86/kernel/apic/apic.c */
static void __lapic_update_tsc_freq(void *info)
{
    struct clock_event_device *levt = this_cpu_ptr(&lapic_events);

    if (!this_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER))
        return;

    clockevents_update_freq(levt, tsc_khz * (1000 / TSC_DIVISOR));
}

void lapic_update_tsc_freq(void)
{
    /* Schedule frequency update on each CPU via IPI —
     * mult/shift must be updated on the CPU that owns the device */
    smp_call_function(__lapic_update_tsc_freq, NULL, 0);
    __lapic_update_tsc_freq(NULL);
}
Important constraints: clockevents_update_freq() must be called on the CPU that owns the device for per-CPU timers (runs with local IRQs disabled). For broadcast devices, tick_broadcast_update_freq() handles serialization. May return -ETIME if the scheduled event is already past after recalculation.
Driver guidance: If your timer's input clock can change at runtime, register a clock notifier (clk_notifier_register()) and call clockevents_update_freq() from the callback. For per-CPU devices needing update on all CPUs (like LAPIC), use smp_call_function() to ensure each CPU updates its own device. Never call from interrupt context on a different CPU than the device owner.

Per-CPU Assignment

In Linux 2.6, per-CPU timer assignment was hardwired: on UP systems the PIT was the sole tick source, while on SMP each CPU's Local APIC timer was set up during boot with architecture-specific initialization code. There was no generic mechanism for evaluating, comparing, or replacing timer devices at runtime.

Linux 7.0.12 replaces this with a fully dynamic per-CPU assignment system. Each CPU gets assigned exactly one clock event device — the "tick device" — that drives all periodic and one-shot interrupts for that CPU. The assignment can change at runtime as better devices register (e.g., LAPIC replacing PIT at boot, then TSC-deadline replacing LAPIC).

The per-CPU assignment is stored in:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct tick_device, tick_cpu_device);

struct tick_device {
    struct clock_event_device   *evtdev;     /* The assigned clock event device */
    enum tick_device_mode        mode;       /* TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC or TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT */
};

On x86_64, the typical per-CPU device is the Local APIC timer (rating 100, or 150 with ARAT); on ARM64, it's the per-CPU virtual timer from the Generic Timer (rating 450). Global devices like HPET (rating 110 for the legacy channel, 50 for an MSI channel) serve as fallbacks or broadcast devices.

The tick_do_timer_cpu Duty

Among all CPUs, exactly one is designated as the "timekeeping CPU" — responsible for calling do_timer() (which increments jiffies and updates wall time). This avoids a thundering-herd problem where all CPUs would contend for the timekeeping lock every tick:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
int tick_do_timer_cpu __read_mostly = TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT;
Table 6-42. Timekeeping Duty Assignment Rules
ScenarioBehavior
BootFirst CPU to register a tick device takes the duty (TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT → CPU 0)
Normal operationOne CPU holds tick_do_timer_cpu; all others only call update_process_times()
NOHZ idle entryDuty CPU going idle sets tick_do_timer_cpu = TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE; next CPU to tick picks it up
CPU hotplug (offline)tick_cpu_dying() transfers duty to first online CPU
NO_HZ_FULLBoot CPU may transfer duty to first non-full-NOHZ secondary CPU

The tick_periodic() function shows how only the duty CPU updates global time:

static void tick_periodic(int cpu)
{
    if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == cpu) {
        raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
        write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
        tick_next_period = ktime_add_ns(tick_next_period, TICK_NSEC);
        do_timer(1);                 /* jiffies_64++ */
        write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        update_wall_time();          /* Update timekeeper */
    }

    update_process_times(user_mode(get_irq_regs()));  /* Every CPU does this */
    profile_tick(CPU_PROFILING);
}

The Selection Algorithm

The clock event selection algorithm is the heart of the per-CPU tick assignment system. It runs every time a new clock event device registers — whether during boot, CPU hotplug, or module load — and determines whether the new device should replace the current per-CPU tick source, serve as a broadcast device, or be rejected entirely.

The algorithm must handle a surprisingly complex set of constraints: it must respect CPU affinity (a device that can only interrupt CPU 0 cannot serve CPU 3), IRQ routing capabilities (a global device with a fixed IRQ cannot be steered to arbitrary CPUs), capability requirements (once the system switches to oneshot mode, periodic-only devices are useless as tick sources), and rating preferences (a high-precision device should replace a lower-precision one).

When a new clock event device registers, tick_check_new_device() runs on the CPU that receives the registration:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
void tick_check_new_device(struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    struct clock_event_device *curdev;
    struct tick_device *td;
    int cpu;

    cpu = smp_processor_id();
    td = &per_cpu(tick_cpu_device, cpu);
    curdev = td->evtdev;

    /* Step 1: Can this device replace the current one? */
    if (!tick_check_replacement(curdev, newdev))
        goto out_bc;    /* No → try as broadcast instead */

    /* Step 2: Take module reference to prevent unload during use */
    if (!try_module_get(newdev->owner))
        return;

    /* Step 3: Handle broadcast device specially */
    if (tick_is_broadcast_device(curdev)) {
        clockevents_shutdown(curdev);
        curdev = NULL;   /* Don't return broadcast device to released list */
    }

    /* Step 4: Exchange devices and set up the new one */
    clockevents_exchange_device(curdev, newdev);
    tick_setup_device(td, newdev, cpu, cpumask_of(cpu));

    /* Step 5: Notify oneshot layer if capable */
    if (newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT)
        tick_oneshot_notify();
    return;

out_bc:
    /* Device can't replace current — try as broadcast */
    tick_install_broadcast_device(newdev, cpu);
}

Note that Step 3 handles a subtle corner case: if the current device happens to be the system-wide broadcast device, it must not be returned to the released list (where it would be re-evaluated and potentially reassigned), because the broadcast device is managed separately.

The replacement check is decomposed into two independent filters, applied in sequence by tick_check_replacement():

bool tick_check_replacement(struct clock_event_device *curdev,
                            struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    if (!tick_check_percpu(curdev, newdev, smp_processor_id()))
        return false;
    return tick_check_preferred(curdev, newdev);
}

Filter 1 — CPU Affinity (tick_check_percpu): This filter determines whether the new device can serve this CPU at all, and whether it should based on locality:

static bool tick_check_percpu(struct clock_event_device *curdev,
                              struct clock_event_device *newdev, int cpu)
{
    if (!cpumask_test_cpu(cpu, newdev->cpumask))
        return false;                    /* Can't serve this CPU at all */
    if (cpumask_equal(newdev->cpumask, cpumask_of(cpu)))
        return true;                     /* Local device — always OK */
    if (newdev->irq >= 0 && !irq_can_set_affinity(newdev->irq))
        return false;                    /* Global but IRQ can't be steered */
    if (curdev && cpumask_equal(curdev->cpumask, cpumask_of(cpu)))
        return false;                    /* Don't replace local with global */
    return true;
}

The logic encodes a strong preference for per-CPU devices: a local LAPIC timer (whose cpumask contains only one CPU) will never be replaced by a global HPET (whose cpumask covers all CPUs), regardless of rating. This is critical because per-CPU timers generate interrupts directly on the target CPU with no IPI overhead, while global devices require IRQ affinity steering which adds latency and may not be reliable across C-state transitions.

Filter 2 — Capability and Rating (tick_check_preferred): If the affinity check passes, this filter compares the capabilities and quality of the two devices:

static bool tick_check_preferred(struct clock_event_device *curdev,
                                 struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    /* Prefer oneshot-capable when oneshot mode is active */
    if (!(newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT)) {
        if (curdev && (curdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
            return false;
        if (tick_oneshot_mode_active())
            return false;
    }

    /* Higher rating wins; local devices preferred over global */
    return !curdev ||
           newdev->rating > curdev->rating ||
           !cpumask_equal(curdev->cpumask, newdev->cpumask);
}

The oneshot check is asymmetric by design: once the system switches to oneshot mode (which happens when hrtimers are activated), a periodic-only device will never replace an oneshot-capable device, even if it has a higher rating. This prevents a late-registering PIT (rating 110, periodic-only) from displacing a LAPIC (rating 400, oneshot) after the system has transitioned to high-resolution timing.

Table 6-43. Device Selection Priority Rules
PriorityRuleRationaleExample
1Per-CPU device always preferred over globalPer-CPU interrupts have zero IPI overhead and work in all C-statesLAPIC (local, rating 100) beats HPET (global, rating 110) — note the per-CPU device wins despite the lower rating
2Oneshot-capable preferred when oneshot activehrtimers and NOHZ require oneshot; periodic devices cannot serveLAPIC-oneshot beats PIT periodic-only
3Higher rating wins among equal-class devicesRating reflects precision, resolution, and reliabilityLAPIC-deadline (500) beats LAPIC-periodic (400)
4New per-CPU beats existing globalA newly registered local device replaces a steered global oneARM arch_timer replaces temporary broadcast timer
5If rejected as tick device, try as broadcastNo device is wasted — globals can serve C3STOP CPUsHPET → becomes broadcast for C3STOP CPUs

For driver developers: The selection algorithm is fully automatic — drivers never explicitly choose their role. A driver simply calls clockevents_config_and_register() and the framework decides whether the device becomes a tick source or broadcast device. However, drivers can influence the outcome through: cpumask (set to cpumask_of(cpu) for per-CPU devices, or cpu_possible_mask for global), rating (higher ratings win; use 100–199 for basic, 300–399 for reliable, 400+ for high-precision), and features (include CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT whenever the hardware supports it — without it, the device will be rejected once hrtimers activate).

Device Setup

After the selection algorithm decides a new device should replace (or be the first device on) a CPU, tick_setup_device() performs a multi-step initialization sequence. This function is responsible for five distinct tasks: timekeeping duty assignment, state preservation during replacement, IRQ affinity configuration, broadcast integration, and operating mode configuration.

Understanding tick_setup_device() is important because it is the function that ties together the clock event framework, the per-CPU tick infrastructure, and the timekeeping subsystem. Every tick interrupt that will ever fire on a CPU passes through the handler installed by this function.

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
static void tick_setup_device(struct tick_device *td,
                              struct clock_event_device *newdev,
                              int cpu, const struct cpumask *cpumask)
{
    void (*handler)(struct clock_event_device *) = NULL;
    ktime_t next_event = 0;

    if (!td->evtdev) {
        /*
         * First device on this CPU — assign timekeeping duty if unclaimed.
         * TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT means no CPU has claimed the duty yet.
         */
        if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT) {
            WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
            tick_next_period = ktime_get();

            /* NO_HZ_FULL: if boot CPU is nohz_full, record it
             * so a housekeeping secondary can take over later */
            if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu))
                tick_do_timer_boot_cpu = cpu;

        } else if (tick_do_timer_boot_cpu != -1 &&
                   !tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu)) {
            /* First non-nohz_full secondary — steal duty from boot CPU */
            tick_do_timer_boot_cpu = -1;
            WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
        }

        td->mode = TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC;    /* Always start periodic */
    } else {
        /* Replacing existing device — preserve handler and next event
         * so the transition is seamless (no missed ticks) */
        handler = td->evtdev->event_handler;
        next_event = td->evtdev->next_event;
        td->evtdev->event_handler = clockevents_handle_noop;
    }

    td->evtdev = newdev;

    /* Pin IRQ affinity for global devices serving a specific CPU.
     * Per-CPU devices already interrupt the correct CPU. */
    if (!cpumask_equal(newdev->cpumask, cpumask))
        irq_set_affinity(newdev->irq, cpumask);

    /* Check if this device should operate in broadcast mode instead.
     * This handles the x86 "C3STOP" case where LAPIC timers stop in
     * deep idle. */
    if (tick_device_uses_broadcast(newdev, cpu))
        return;

    /* Configure the operating mode and install the event handler */
    if (td->mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
        tick_setup_periodic(newdev, 0);       /* → tick_handle_periodic */
    else
        tick_setup_oneshot(newdev, handler, next_event);  /* → hrtimer handler */
}
Table 6-44. tick_setup_device() Initialization Steps
StepConditionActionWhy
1aFirst device (!td->evtdev)Claim tick_do_timer_cpu if TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOTExactly one CPU must run do_timer() — first wins
1bFirst device + NO_HZ_FULL boot CPURecord tick_do_timer_boot_cpuBoot CPU is nohz_full, needs handoff to housekeeping CPU
1cFirst device + first non-nohz_full secondarySteal duty from boot CPUHousekeeping CPU takes over timekeeping from nohz_full boot CPU
2Replacing (td->evtdev exists)Save event_handler + next_event, install noop on oldEnsures no interrupts fire on old device during transition
3Global device (cpumask ≠ target)irq_set_affinity()Steer global device's IRQ to this CPU
4Device has C3STOP + deep idletick_device_uses_broadcast() returns trueDevice stops in idle — must use broadcast wake-up instead
5aPeriodic modetick_setup_periodic() → tick_handle_periodicEarly boot or nohz=off kernel parameter
5bOneshot modetick_setup_oneshot() → preserved handlerNormal operation after hrtimers activate

The periodic setup path (tick_setup_periodic()) itself handles two cases depending on hardware capabilities:

void tick_setup_periodic(struct clock_event_device *dev, int broadcast)
{
    tick_set_periodic_handler(dev, broadcast);
    if (!tick_device_is_functional(dev))
        return;

    if ((dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC) &&
        !tick_broadcast_oneshot_active()) {
        /* Hardware supports periodic mode — use it directly */
        clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC);
    } else {
        /* Hardware is oneshot-only — emulate periodic ticks by
         * reprogramming after each event */
        ktime_t next = tick_next_period;
        clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT);
        for (;;) {
            if (!clockevents_program_event(dev, next, false))
                return;
            next = ktime_add_ns(next, TICK_NSEC);
        }
    }
}

This means that even if a system uses periodic ticking (e.g., with nohz=off), the framework can run on hardware that only supports oneshot mode — it simply reprograms the device every TICK_NSEC nanoseconds. This is how the TSC-deadline timer (which has no periodic mode at all) can serve as a tick source during early boot before hrtimers are activated.

Event Handler Chain: The event_handler installed by tick_setup_device() determines how every timer interrupt is processed. The framework supports four distinct handlers, each optimized for a different operating mode:

Table 6-45. Event Handler Chain
Modeevent_handlerWhat It DoesTransition TriggerWhen Used
Periodictick_handle_periodic()Updates jiffies (on duty CPU), calls update_process_times() + profile_tick(), emulates periodic on oneshot HWtick_setup_periodic() during first device setupEarly boot, nohz=off, or no CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS
Oneshot (hrtimers)hrtimer_interrupt()Processes expired hrtimers from the per-CPU red-black tree, reprograms for next earliest expirytick_switch_to_oneshot() from hrtimer_run_queues()Normal operation after CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS activates
NOHZ idletick_nohz_handler()Handles tick after idle wake-up, catches up accumulated jiffies, re-evaluates idletick_nohz_idle_enter() when CPU enters idleCPU returning from extended idle period
Broadcasttick_handle_periodic_broadcast() or tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast()Scans broadcast mask, sends IPIs to CPUs whose timers have stopped in deep idletick_install_broadcast_device()Global device (HPET) waking C3-idle CPUs

The transition between handlers happens at well-defined points during boot. The initial handler is always tick_handle_periodic(). When the hrtimer subsystem starts and detects a capable oneshot device, it calls tick_switch_to_oneshot() which atomically swaps the handler to hrtimer_interrupt(). This transition is one-way — once a CPU switches to oneshot mode, it never goes back to periodic (except during shutdown).

Typical boot sequence on x86_64:

On a modern x86_64 system with HPET, LAPIC timer, and TSC-deadline support, the boot sequence involves up to five device replacements as progressively better clock event devices register. Each replacement triggers the full tick_check_new_device() → tick_setup_device() pipeline:

Table 6-46. x86_64 Boot Sequence — Per-CPU Device Assignment
StepBoot PhaseEventPer-CPU DeviceBroadcastModeKernel Function
1Early bootPIT initialized (global, rating 110)PIT (all CPUs share)—Periodicsetup_default_timer_irq()
2APIC initLAPIC calibrated (per-CPU, rating 150–400)LAPIC replaces PITPIT → released listPeriodicsetup_APIC_timer()
3HPET initHPET registers (global, rating 110)LAPIC (unchanged — local preferred)HPET becomes broadcastPeriodichpet_enable()
4Late boothrtimers activateLAPICHPETOneshothrtimer_run_queues() → tick_switch_to_oneshot()
5SMP initTSC-deadline re-registration (per-CPU, rating unchanged at 100/150)LAPIC-deadline replaces LAPICHPETOneshotsetup_APIC_timer() with X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER

Note that in Step 2, the LAPIC timer's rating varies: CPUs with the ARAT (Always Running APIC Timer) feature get rating 150 with C3STOP cleared (meaning the LAPIC runs even in deep idle). CPUs without ARAT get a higher base rating but have C3STOP set, requiring broadcast wake-ups. The actual x86 registration code shows this:

/* arch/x86/kernel/apic/apic.c — setup_APIC_timer() */
if (this_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_ARAT)) {
    lapic_clockevent.features &= ~CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP;
    lapic_clockevent.rating = 150;  /* Lower but always running */
}

if (this_cpu_has(X86_FEATURE_TSC_DEADLINE_TIMER)) {
    levt->name = "lapic-deadline";
    levt->features &= ~(CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC | CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY);
    levt->set_next_event = lapic_next_deadline;
    clockevents_config_and_register(levt, tsc_khz * 1000/TSC_DIVISOR, 0xF, ~0UL);
} else
    clockevents_register_device(levt);

Typical boot sequence on ARM64:

ARM64 systems have a simpler boot sequence because the ARM Generic Timer is a per-CPU device from the start — there is no need for the PIT-to-LAPIC replacement dance that x86 requires:

Table 6-47. ARM64 Boot Sequence — Per-CPU Device Assignment
StepBoot PhaseEventPer-CPU DeviceBroadcastModeKernel Function
1Timer probeARM arch timer probed (per-CPU, rating 450)arch_sys_timer—Periodicarch_timer_setup() via clockevents_config_and_register()
2Late boothrtimers activatearch_sys_timer—Oneshothrtimer_run_queues() → tick_switch_to_oneshot()
3Idle initC3STOP detected on SoC (timer stops in deep idle)arch_sys_timerhrtimer broadcast (software)Oneshottick_broadcast_init() — uses CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER

The ARM arch timer registration is simpler — a single call covers all the setup:

/* drivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.c */
clockevents_config_and_register(clk, arch_timer_rate, 0xf, max_delta);

On ARM64 SoCs that implement C3STOP (where the per-CPU timer stops in certain PSCI idle states), the kernel creates a software-based broadcast device using CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER. Unlike x86 which uses the HPET as a hardware broadcast device, ARM64 uses a software hrtimer on a non-idle CPU to send IPIs — no additional hardware timer is needed.

CPU Hotplug and Duty Transfer

CPU hotplug is a common operation in modern systems — from server capacity management to power-saving on mobile SoCs. The tick layer must handle both directions: taking a CPU offline (cleanly releasing its tick device and transferring any duties) and bringing it back online (re-registering and reassigning devices).

The offline path is especially critical because it involves the timekeeping duty. If the CPU being taken offline is the one currently running do_timer() (i.e., tick_do_timer_cpu == dying_cpu), the duty must be transferred before the CPU stops — otherwise jiffies would stop incrementing and the entire system's sense of time would freeze.

The CPU hotplug framework calls tick_cpu_dying() during the "dying" phase — when the CPU is still executing but about to stop — from a dedicated state in the hotplug state machine:

/* kernel/cpu.c — the CPU hotplug state table */
[CPUHP_AP_TICK_DYING] = {
    .name            = "tick:dying",
    .startup.single  = NULL,          /* nothing to do on the way up */
    .teardown.single = tick_cpu_dying,
},

Giving the tick its own state, CPUHP_AP_TICK_DYING, is what fixes its position in the teardown order. Hotplug tears states down from the highest number to the lowest, and CPUHP_AP_HRTIMERS_DYING sits immediately below CPUHP_AP_TICK_DYING in include/linux/cpuhotplug.h, so the ordering is: stop this CPU's tick and hand over the timekeeping duty first, then migrate its hrtimers to a surviving CPU. That is the right way round — migrating the hrtimers first would leave a CPU still taking ticks with nothing left to expire.

Both callbacks run on the dying CPU itself, with interrupts disabled, while every other CPU is held in stop_machine(). That is the only window in which the outgoing CPU can hand over the duty and reach its own timer hardware to switch it off — and until recently the kernel did not take advantage of it.

Before commit 3b1596a21fbf (October 2024), the teardown ran on a surviving CPU after the target was already dead. A surviving CPU cannot touch another CPU’s local timer registers, so tick_shutdown() did the only thing it could: it marked the device detached and unlinked it, leaving the hardware itself alone. That was acceptable only because the CPU was about to lose power anyway. Moving the work into CPUHP_AP_TICK_DYING, executed by the outgoing CPU itself, removed the restriction — but not, at first, the workaround.

The leftover cost eleven months to notice, and it is a direct consequence of the idempotence guard described earlier under Clock Event States. tick_shutdown() still opened by setting the device’s state to DETACHED by hand, and then called clockevents_exchange_device(), which calls clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED). The wrapper compared the requested state against the recorded one, found them equal, and returned without invoking set_state_shutdown(). The result was that the timer hardware of an offlined CPU was never actually switched off — on most systems harmless, since the core was losing power, but not on platforms where the timer block survives the core, and not on virtual machines where “offline” is a software fiction. Commit fe2a449a45b1 (September 2025) fixed it by deleting one line: the manual state assignment, leaving the transition to the framework that knows how to perform it.

It is worth naming the general shape, because it recurs. A hand-written state assignment that was compensating for an inability to reach the hardware became, once that inability was removed, the very thing preventing the hardware from being reached. Neither commit was wrong on its own; the defect lived in the gap between them.

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
int tick_cpu_dying(unsigned int dying_cpu)
{
    /*
     * If the current CPU is the timekeeper, it's the only one that can
     * safely hand over its duty. Also all online CPUs are in stop
     * machine, guaranteed not to be idle, therefore there is no
     * concurrency and it's safe to pick any online successor.
     */
    if (tick_do_timer_cpu == dying_cpu)
        tick_do_timer_cpu = cpumask_first(cpu_online_mask);

    /* Make sure the CPU won't try to retake the timekeeping duty */
    tick_sched_timer_dying(dying_cpu);

    /* Remove CPU from timer broadcasting */
    tick_offline_cpu(dying_cpu);
    return 0;
}

Note the comment about stop-machine: when tick_cpu_dying() executes, all other CPUs are held in stop_machine(), which means they are not idle and not contending for tick_do_timer_cpu. This eliminates race conditions that would otherwise require complex locking.

After the duty transfer, tick_shutdown() runs on the dying CPU itself (with clockevents_lock held and interrupts disabled) to release the hardware:

void tick_shutdown(void)
{
    struct tick_device *td = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
    struct clock_event_device *dev = td->evtdev;

    td->mode = TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC;   /* Reset to initial state */
    if (dev) {
        clockevents_exchange_device(dev, NULL);  /* Release to framework */
        dev->event_handler = clockevents_handle_noop;
        td->evtdev = NULL;
    }
}

Finally, the framework cleans up any orphaned per-CPU devices:

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c — called during CPU offline */
list_for_each_entry_safe(dev, tmp, &clockevent_devices, list) {
    if (cpumask_test_cpu(cpu, dev->cpumask) &&
        cpumask_weight(dev->cpumask) == 1 &&
        !tick_is_broadcast_device(dev)) {
        BUG_ON(!clockevent_state_detached(dev));
        list_del(&dev->list);   /* Remove from global list entirely */
    }
}
Table 6-48. CPU Hotplug Tick Lifecycle
PhaseFunctionWhat HappensContext
Offline — dyingtick_cpu_dying()Transfer tick_do_timer_cpu if needed, cancel tick_sched hrtimer, remove from broadcastDying CPU, in stop_machine
Offline — detachtick_offline_cpu()Called by tick_cpu_dying(): runs tick_broadcast_offline(), then tick_shutdown(), then unregisters the devices those releasedDying CPU, clockevents_lock held
Offline — shutdowntick_shutdown()Called by tick_offline_cpu(): release clock_event_device, install noop handler, clear td->evtdevDying CPU, IRQs disabled
Online — startupArchitecture-specific (e.g., setup_APIC_timer())Re-register per-CPU clock event deviceOnlining CPU
Online — checktick_check_new_device()Re-evaluate device, assign as tick source, possibly reclaim dutyOnlining CPU

When a CPU comes back online, its per-CPU clock event device re-registers through the architecture-specific CPU hotplug callback (e.g., setup_APIC_timer() on x86, arch_timer_starting_cpu() on ARM64). This triggers the full tick_check_new_device() → tick_setup_device() pipeline, which treats the device as a fresh registration. If no other CPU has claimed tick_do_timer_cpu, the newly online CPU may take over the timekeeping duty.

For driver developers: Clock event device drivers generally do not need to handle CPU hotplug explicitly — the framework manages device release and re-registration automatically. However, drivers for per-CPU hardware timers should ensure their set_state_shutdown callback fully quiesces the hardware, because tick_shutdown() will call it during CPU offline. The device should be ready to re-register cleanly when the CPU comes back online.

Device Replacement

Device replacement is the mechanism that allows the tick system to improve over time — as better clock event devices register (either during boot or via module load), they automatically replace inferior ones. The replacement is seamless: no ticks are lost during the transition because the framework preserves the old device's handler and next-event time and transfers them to the new device.

The core of device replacement is clockevents_exchange_device(), which manages the lifecycle transition for both the outgoing and incoming devices:

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c */
void clockevents_exchange_device(struct clock_event_device *old,
                                 struct clock_event_device *new)
{
    if (old) {
        module_put(old->owner);          /* Release module reference */
        clockevents_switch_state(old, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED);
        list_move(&old->list, &clockevents_released);  /* Keep for reuse */
    }
    if (new) {
        BUG_ON(!clockevent_state_detached(new));
        clockevents_shutdown(new);       /* Start in SHUTDOWN state */
    }
}

The old device is not destroyed — it is moved to the clockevents_released list. After each new device registration, the framework calls clockevents_notify_released() which iterates the released list and re-evaluates each device:

static void clockevents_notify_released(void)
{
    struct clock_event_device *dev;

    while (!list_empty(&clockevents_released)) {
        dev = list_entry(clockevents_released.next,
                         struct clock_event_device, list);
        list_move(&dev->list, &clockevent_devices);
        tick_check_new_device(dev);  /* Re-evaluate: might become broadcast */
    }
}

This recycling mechanism is elegant: when a LAPIC timer is replaced by a TSC-deadline timer, the original LAPIC device is not lost — it re-enters the evaluation pipeline and may be selected as a broadcast device or assigned to a different role.

There is also a direct replacement path for modules that need to swap devices on the current CPU without going through the full registration pipeline:

void tick_install_replacement(struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    struct tick_device *td = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    clockevents_exchange_device(td->evtdev, newdev);
    tick_setup_device(td, newdev, cpu, cpumask_of(cpu));
    if (newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT)
        tick_oneshot_notify();
}
Table 6-49. Device Replacement Scenarios
ScenarioOld DeviceNew DeviceOutcome for OldExample
Boot upgradePIT (global, rating 110)LAPIC (per-CPU, rating 100/150)Released → re-evaluated → may become broadcastx86 early boot
Deadline upgradeLAPIC (per-CPU, rating 100/150)LAPIC-deadline (same rating; only the name and set_next_event change)Released → re-evaluated → likely unusedx86 with TSC-deadline
Module loadCurrent tick deviceNew device from moduleReleased → re-evaluatedExternal timer driver loaded
CPU offlinePer-CPU deviceNULLReleased → cleaned upCPU hotplug offline
Broadcast promotionReleased global device—Re-evaluated by notify_released() → becomes broadcastHPET after PIT→LAPIC transition

For driver developers: Device replacement is transparent to drivers — the framework handles the full lifecycle. However, there are two important contracts:

1. State callbacks must be idempotent: set_state_shutdown may be called on a device that is already shut down (e.g., during exchange). Drivers should handle this gracefully without failing.

2. Module reference counting: The framework calls try_module_get() when selecting a device and module_put() when releasing it. This means a module providing a clock event device cannot be unloaded while its device is active — the module reference prevents rmmod from succeeding. Drivers that need to support unloading should implement a shutdown sequence that transitions the device to DETACHED state first.

Suspend, Resume, and CPU Hotplug

In Linux 2.6, power management for timing was rudimentary — the timer interrupt was simply disabled during suspend and re-enabled during resume, with xtime updated from the RTC or persistent clock to account for the time spent suspended. There was no generic framework for suspending individual clock devices, no broadcast device management, and no "freeze" path for suspend-to-idle.

Linux 7.0.12 implements a layered suspend/resume architecture that carefully orchestrates clock event devices, clocksources, broadcast timers, and the timekeeping core. The ordering is critical — components must be suspended in reverse dependency order and resumed in forward order to avoid using a stopped clock or programming a suspended device.

System Suspend (S3/S4)

During full system suspend (initiated by writing to /sys/power/state; Chapter 21, §3.1 follows the whole sequence), the kernel follows the syscore_ops path. The timekeeping_suspend() function serves as the master orchestrator, calling each subsystem in the correct order:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
int timekeeping_suspend(void)
{
    /* 1. Read persistent clock for later sleep-time calculation */
    read_persistent_clock64(&timekeeping_suspend_time);

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    /* 2. Forward the timekeeper to "now" — accumulate pending cycles */
    timekeeping_forward_now(tks);
    timekeeping_suspended = 1;

    /* 3. Save current cycle count for nonstop clocksource timing */
    cycle_now = tks->tkr_mono.cycle_last;
    clocksource_start_suspend_timing(curr_clock, cycle_now);

    /* 4. Compensate for persistent-clock drift across suspend/resume */
    if (persistent_clock_exists) {
        delta = timespec64_sub(tk_xtime(tks), timekeeping_suspend_time);
        /* adjust to avoid accumulated ~1s drift per cycle */
    }

    timekeeping_update_from_shadow(&tk_core, 0);
    halt_fast_timekeeper(tks);     /* Stop vDSO fast path */
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    /* 5. Suspend in reverse dependency order */
    tick_suspend();                /* Tick devices + broadcast */
    clocksource_suspend();         /* Clocksources */
    clockevents_suspend();         /* Clock event hardware */

    return 0;
}

The resume path runs in the opposite order, with sleep-time injection:

void timekeeping_resume(void)
{
    /* 1. Read persistent clock to measure elapsed suspend time */
    read_persistent_clock64(&ts_new);

    /* 2. Resume hardware in forward dependency order */
    clockevents_resume();          /* Clock event hardware first */
    clocksource_resume();          /* Then clocksources */

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    /* 3. Calculate time spent in suspend from best available source:
     *    Priority: nonstop clocksource → persistent clock → RTC */
    cycle_now = tk_clock_read(&tks->tkr_mono);
    nsec = clocksource_stop_suspend_timing(clock, cycle_now);
    if (nsec > 0) {
        ts_delta = ns_to_timespec64(nsec);   /* Nonstop clocksource */
    } else if (ts_new > timekeeping_suspend_time) {
        ts_delta = ts_new - timekeeping_suspend_time;  /* Persistent clock */
    }

    /* 4. Inject sleep time into all time bases */
    if (inject_sleeptime)
        __timekeeping_inject_sleeptime(tks, &ts_delta);

    /* 5. Re-base cycle counters */
    tks->tkr_mono.cycle_last = cycle_now;
    tks->tkr_raw.cycle_last  = cycle_now;
    timekeeping_suspended = 0;
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    /* 6. Resume tick devices and notify hrtimers */
    tick_resume();
    timerfd_resume();              /* Notify timerfd as clock_was_set */
}
Table 6-50. System Suspend/Resume Ordering
OrderSuspend (timekeeping_suspend)Resume (timekeeping_resume)Why This Order
1Read persistent clockRead persistent clockCapture timestamps before/after suspend
2Forward timekeeper, set timekeeping_suspended = 1Resume clock event hardware (clockevents_resume)Hardware must be re-enabled before framework uses it
3Start suspend timing (nonstop clocksource)Resume clocksources (clocksource_resume)Clocksource needed to read cycles
4Halt vDSO fast pathCalculate and inject sleep timeAccumulated suspend time added to MONOTONIC/BOOTTIME
5tick_suspend() — shutdown tick + broadcastRe-base cycle_last for all read basesPrevents stale cycle values causing time jumps
6clocksource_suspend() — suspend clocksourcestick_resume() — restart tick + broadcastTick devices program against clocksource — must come after
7clockevents_suspend() — suspend HW lasttimerfd_resume() — notify userspaceUserspace timers see updated time

Clock Event Device Callbacks

The clock event framework provides three separate callbacks that drivers can implement for power management. Each serves a different purpose in the suspend lifecycle:

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c */
void clockevents_suspend(void)
{
    struct clock_event_device *dev;
    /* Iterate in REVERSE order — last registered suspended first */
    list_for_each_entry_reverse(dev, &clockevent_devices, list)
        if (dev->suspend && !clockevent_state_detached(dev))
            dev->suspend(dev);
}

void clockevents_resume(void)
{
    struct clock_event_device *dev;
    /* Iterate in FORWARD order — first registered resumed first */
    list_for_each_entry(dev, &clockevent_devices, list)
        if (dev->resume && !clockevent_state_detached(dev))
            dev->resume(dev);
}

Note the asymmetric iteration order: suspend walks the list in reverse (LIFO) while resume walks it forward (FIFO). This mirrors the general Linux driver model convention where devices registered later (which may depend on earlier ones) are suspended first and resumed last.

Table 6-51. Clock Event Power Management Callbacks
CallbackWhen CalledPurposeExample
suspend(dev)System suspend, after tick shutdownSave hardware state, disable clocks, release power domainsHPET: save configuration registers
resume(dev)System resume, before tick restartRestore hardware state, re-enable clocksHPET: restore configuration, re-enable counter
tick_resume(dev)Per-CPU resume (local tick restart)Quick re-initialization without full resumeLAPIC: re-enable timer vector, restore divider
set_state_shutdown(dev)tick_suspend_local(), CPU offlineQuiesce the timer hardware (stop counting/interrupting)LAPIC: mask timer LVT entry

The tick_resume callback (called via clockevents_tick_resume()) is distinct from resume — it provides a per-CPU fast path for bringing the local tick device back to operational state without a full hardware re-initialization. This is particularly important for the freeze path (suspend-to-idle) where only the local CPU's timer needs restarting.

Tick Layer Suspend/Resume

The tick layer (tick-common.c) manages the per-CPU and broadcast aspects of suspend:

/* Suspend: shutdown local tick device, then broadcast device */
void tick_suspend(void)
{
    tick_suspend_local();        /* Shutdown this CPU's evtdev */
    tick_suspend_broadcast();    /* Shutdown broadcast device */
}

/* Resume: restart broadcast first, then local (reverse order) */
void tick_resume(void)
{
    tick_resume_broadcast();     /* Restart broadcast device */
    tick_resume_local();         /* Restart this CPU's evtdev */
}

The local suspend simply shuts down the per-CPU device:

void tick_suspend_local(void)
{
    struct tick_device *td = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
    clockevents_shutdown(td->evtdev);  /* → set_state_shutdown callback */
}

The local resume is more involved — it must restore the correct operating mode and check whether this CPU should use the broadcast device:

void tick_resume_local(void)
{
    struct tick_device *td = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
    bool broadcast = tick_resume_check_broadcast();

    clockevents_tick_resume(td->evtdev);   /* → tick_resume callback */

    if (!broadcast) {
        if (td->mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
            tick_setup_periodic(td->evtdev, 0);
        else
            tick_resume_oneshot();
    }

    /* Ensure hrtimers are up to date and device is reprogrammed */
    hrtimers_resume_local();
}

The broadcast resume path handles both periodic and oneshot broadcast modes:

void tick_resume_broadcast(void)
{
    struct clock_event_device *bc = tick_broadcast_device.evtdev;

    if (bc) {
        clockevents_tick_resume(bc);

        switch (tick_broadcast_device.mode) {
        case TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC:
            if (!cpumask_empty(tick_broadcast_mask))
                tick_broadcast_start_periodic(bc);
            break;
        case TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT:
            if (!cpumask_empty(tick_broadcast_mask))
                tick_resume_broadcast_oneshot(bc);
            break;
        }
    }
}

Suspend-to-Idle (Freeze)

Modern systems increasingly use suspend-to-idle (also called "s2idle" or "freeze") instead of full S3 suspend. In this mode, CPUs enter their deepest idle state rather than being powered off, and peripherals may remain powered. The tick layer has a dedicated freeze/unfreeze path:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
void tick_freeze(void)
{
    raw_spin_lock(&tick_freeze_lock);

    tick_freeze_depth++;
    if (tick_freeze_depth == num_online_cpus()) {
        /* Last CPU to freeze — suspend timekeeping globally */
        system_state = SYSTEM_SUSPEND;
        sched_clock_suspend();
        timekeeping_suspend();
    } else {
        /* Not the last — only suspend local tick */
        tick_suspend_local();
    }

    raw_spin_unlock(&tick_freeze_lock);
}

void tick_unfreeze(void)
{
    raw_spin_lock(&tick_freeze_lock);

    if (tick_freeze_depth == num_online_cpus()) {
        /* First CPU to unfreeze — resume timekeeping globally */
        timekeeping_resume();
        sched_clock_resume();
        system_state = SYSTEM_RUNNING;
    } else {
        /* Not the first — only resume local tick */
        touch_softlockup_watchdog();
        tick_resume_local();
    }

    tick_freeze_depth--;

    raw_spin_unlock(&tick_freeze_lock);
}

The freeze path uses a depth counter (tick_freeze_depth) protected by tick_freeze_lock to determine when all CPUs have entered the freeze state. Only the last CPU to freeze calls timekeeping_suspend() (which handles the full suspend sequence), while all other CPUs only shut down their local tick device. On unfreeze, the first CPU to wake calls timekeeping_resume(), and subsequent CPUs only restart their local ticks.

Table 6-52. Suspend vs. Freeze Path Comparison
AspectFull Suspend (S3/S4)Suspend-to-Idle (Freeze)
Entry pathsyscore_suspend() → timekeeping_suspend()tick_freeze() per CPU
CPUs involvedAll non-boot CPUs offlined first; boot CPU runs suspendAll CPUs enter idle; last one suspends timekeeping
Timekeeping suspendCalled by boot CPU with IRQs disabledCalled by last-to-freeze CPU under tick_freeze_lock
Clock event hardwareclockevents_suspend() powers down HWtick_suspend_local() shuts down per-CPU device
Broadcast devicetick_suspend_broadcast() shuts downMay remain active (depends on freeze depth)
Resume triggerHardware interrupt (e.g., power button, RTC alarm)Any interrupt (IRQ, timer, wake source)
Sleep time sourcePersistent clock or nonstop clocksourceNonstop clocksource (preferred) or persistent clock
Resume pathtimekeeping_resume() → tick_resume()tick_unfreeze() — first CPU resumes timekeeping

Sleep Time Accounting

A key challenge during resume is determining how long the system was suspended, so that CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME remain accurate. The kernel uses three sources, in priority order:

1. Nonstop clocksource (e.g., TSC with CLOCK_SOURCE_SUSPEND_NONSTOP): If the clocksource continued counting during suspend, the kernel computes the elapsed time from the cycle delta. This is the most accurate method (nanosecond precision).

2. Persistent clock (e.g., CMOS RTC via read_persistent_clock64()): The kernel reads the persistent clock at suspend and resume, computing the delta. Accuracy is typically ±1 second.

3. RTC device (handled separately by rtc_resume()): As a last resort, the RTC subsystem injects the sleep time. This has the same ±1 second accuracy but works even when no persistent clock driver is available.

/* Sleep time injection during resume */
cycle_now = tk_clock_read(&tks->tkr_mono);
nsec = clocksource_stop_suspend_timing(clock, cycle_now);
if (nsec > 0) {
    /* Source 1: Nonstop clocksource — nanosecond precision */
    ts_delta = ns_to_timespec64(nsec);
    inject_sleeptime = true;
} else if (timespec64_compare(&ts_new, &timekeeping_suspend_time) > 0) {
    /* Source 2: Persistent clock — second precision */
    ts_delta = timespec64_sub(ts_new, timekeeping_suspend_time);
    inject_sleeptime = true;
}

if (inject_sleeptime)
    __timekeeping_inject_sleeptime(tks, &ts_delta);

The injected sleep time is added to CLOCK_BOOTTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC (the latter only if the sleep was a full suspend, not just idle). CLOCK_REALTIME is also adjusted by the same amount. CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW is not adjusted — it reflects only actual hardware ticks.

To prevent drift from accumulating across many suspend/resume cycles (each of which can add ~1 second of error from the persistent clock), timekeeping_suspend() implements a drift compensation algorithm that tracks the delta between system time and persistent clock time and adjusts subsequent readings to keep the offset stable.

CPU Hotplug Integration

CPU hotplug (covered in detail in the Per-CPU Assignment section above) interacts with the suspend/resume path at several points. During full S3 suspend, all non-boot CPUs are taken offline before timekeeping_suspend() runs — this means tick_cpu_dying() and tick_offline_cpu() have already cleaned up all per-CPU tick devices except the boot CPU's. The boot CPU's device is then shut down by tick_suspend().

On resume, the sequence reverses: timekeeping_resume() restarts the boot CPU's tick device, and then the CPU hotplug framework brings secondary CPUs back online one by one, each re-registering its per-CPU clock event device through tick_check_new_device().

For driver developers: Implementing power management callbacks is essential for any clock event device driver. At minimum, drivers should implement set_state_shutdown (called during tick_suspend_local()) to quiesce the hardware. For devices that need re-initialization after resume (e.g., HPET which loses its configuration), implement resume. For per-CPU devices that need only minimal restart (e.g., LAPIC timer which only needs its LVT entry unmasked), implement tick_resume for the fast path. All callbacks are called with interrupts disabled and must not sleep.

Sysfs Interface

The clock event framework exposes a per-CPU sysfs interface under /sys/devices/system/clockevents/ that allows administrators, debugging tools, and automated test suites to inspect the current tick device assignment and unbind devices for testing or troubleshooting. Unlike the clocksource sysfs (which allows switching the active clocksource by writing a name), the clock event sysfs is more limited — you can see what's assigned and unbind devices, but you cannot directly force a specific device onto a CPU.

Sysfs Paths

The directory structure mirrors the per-CPU tick assignment:

/sys/devices/system/clockevents/
├── clockevent0/           # CPU 0
│   ├── current_device     # Read-only: name of assigned clock event device
│   └── unbind_device      # Write-only: unbind a named device from this CPU
├── clockevent1/           # CPU 1
│   ├── current_device
│   └── unbind_device
├── ...
└── broadcast/             # Broadcast device (if CONFIG_GENERIC_CLOCKEVENTS_BROADCAST)
    └── current_device     # Read-only: name of broadcast clock event device
Table 6-53. Clock Event Sysfs Files
FilePermissionsPurposeExample Value
current_devicer--r--r--Shows the name of the clock event device currently assigned to this CPUlapic-deadline, arch_sys_timer
unbind_device-w-------Write a device name to unbind it from this CPU; framework selects a replacementWrite lapic-deadline to force fallback
broadcast/current_devicer--r--r--Shows the current broadcast device (global timer for C3STOP wake-ups)hpet, or empty if no broadcast needed

Querying Current Assignments

# Show which clock event device is assigned to each CPU
$ for i in /sys/devices/system/clockevents/clockevent*/current_device; do
    echo "$(dirname $i | xargs basename): $(cat $i)"
done
clockevent0: lapic-deadline
clockevent1: lapic-deadline
clockevent2: lapic-deadline
clockevent3: lapic-deadline

# On ARM64:
clockevent0: arch_sys_timer
clockevent1: arch_sys_timer

# Show the broadcast device (x86 with HPET)
$ cat /sys/devices/system/clockevents/broadcast/current_device
hpet

The implementation reads the per-CPU tick_cpu_device structure under clockevents_lock:

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c */
static ssize_t current_device_show(struct device *dev,
                                   struct device_attribute *attr, char *buf)
{
    struct tick_device *td;
    ssize_t count = 0;

    raw_spin_lock_irq(&clockevents_lock);
    td = tick_get_tick_dev(dev);
    if (td && td->evtdev)
        count = sysfs_emit(buf, "%s\n", td->evtdev->name);
    raw_spin_unlock_irq(&clockevents_lock);
    return count;
}

Unbinding a Device

The unbind_device file allows removing a clock event device from a CPU, forcing the framework to select a replacement (if one exists) or fall back to broadcast:

# Unbind the lapic-deadline timer from CPU 0
$ echo lapic-deadline > /sys/devices/system/clockevents/clockevent0/unbind_device

# The framework will try to find a replacement device
# If no replacement exists, the CPU relies on broadcast wake-ups

The unbind mechanism works through an SMP function call to the target CPU, because the clock event device can only be safely manipulated on its owning CPU:

static int __clockevents_try_unbind(struct clock_event_device *ced, int cpu)
{
    /* Fast track: device is already unused (DETACHED state) */
    if (clockevent_state_detached(ced)) {
        list_del_init(&ced->list);
        return 0;
    }

    /* Device is the active tick device — need replacement */
    return ced == per_cpu(tick_cpu_device, cpu).evtdev ? -EAGAIN : -EBUSY;
}

static int clockevents_unbind(struct clock_event_device *ced, int cpu)
{
    struct ce_unbind cu = { .ce = ced, .res = -ENODEV };
    /* Must execute on the owning CPU to safely exchange devices */
    smp_call_function_single(cpu, __clockevents_unbind, &cu, 1);
    return cu.res;
}

The IPI is not always needed, and the store handler is careful about it. Writing to unbind_device first walks clockevent_devices under clockevents_lock looking for a device of that name, and calls __clockevents_try_unbind() straight away on the writing CPU. If the device is already DETACHED the whole operation is a list removal — there is no hardware to quiesce and no reason to disturb another CPU — so it returns 0 immediately. Only the -EAGAIN case, meaning the device is the CPU’s live tick device, escalates to clockevents_unbind() and its smp_call_function_single(), where the same test is repeated on the owning CPU and this time followed by a replacement attempt. -EBUSY — the device is registered but belongs to some other CPU — fails outright.

clockevents_replace() is more restrictive than it may appear. It considers only devices that are currently DETACHED, that is, devices previously released and still on the global list; a device actively serving another CPU is never stolen. Each candidate is put through tick_check_replacement(), the same rating-and-capability test used during registration, and a module reference is taken with try_module_get() before it is accepted, so a timer driver cannot be unloaded out from under a tick that is about to be installed on it. When a better candidate displaces an earlier one the earlier module reference is dropped again. If the walk finds nothing the function returns -EBUSY and the original device stays where it is — unbinding never leaves a CPU without a tick source.

The user-visible consequence is that an unbind can legitimately fail, and that the failure is reported to the shell as a write error rather than silently. A single-timer machine — most ARM64 SoCs, where the architected timer is the only per-CPU clock event device there is — will therefore refuse the unbind with EBUSY, which is the correct answer rather than a limitation.

The exported entry point behind all of this is clockevents_unbind_device(), which is simply clockevents_unbind() wrapped in clockevents_mutex. It is EXPORT_SYMBOL_GPL’d for drivers that need to withdraw a device they own — a timer on a hot-removable board, for instance — rather than for general use. The mutex is what lets the store handler drop clockevents_lock before issuing the IPI and still be sure the device it found by name has not been freed in the meantime.

Table 6-54. Use Cases for Unbinding
ScenarioPurposeEffect
Testing fallback pathsUnbind high-quality device to exercise lower-rated fallbackLAPIC unbound → system falls back to HPET or broadcast
Debugging timing issuesIsolate which device is causing jitter or missed ticksUnbind suspect device, observe if problem disappears
Driver developmentTest device hot-removal code pathsExercises the full replacement pipeline
Power analysisForce broadcast mode to measure C-state behaviorUnbind per-CPU device → CPU uses broadcast wake-ups

Comparison with Clocksource Sysfs

Related Kernel Parameters

Several kernel command-line parameters affect clock event device behavior and can be observed through sysfs:

Table 6-56. Kernel Parameters Affecting Clock Events
ParameterEffectObservable via Sysfs
nohz=offDisable tickless idle; keep periodic tickingAll CPUs show tick device, all in periodic mode
highres=offDisable high-resolution timersDevices remain in periodic mode after boot
clocksource=hpetForce HPET as clocksource (may affect tick selection)Clocksource shows hpet; tick devices unchanged
