Version history. Linux 2.6.11 had no generic clock event framework at all — the PIT and the Local APIC timer were wired directly into architecture-specific interrupt handlers, and there was no common notion of a programmable timer device. struct clock_event_device and the per-CPU sysfs interface arrived together in 2.6.21 (2007) with the clockevents overhaul, alongside the Generic Time Subsystem. The rest accumulated slowly: CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_KTIME in 2011, for devices that take an absolute time and need no conversion; hrtimer-based broadcast and CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER in 2014, for platforms with no global timer to wake a sleeping CPU; ONESHOT_STOPPED in 2015. The only part of this section that is genuinely new in 7.0 is the interrupt-starvation guard and its next_event_forced flag, together with the CPU-offline shutdown fix — both described above.

The Timekeeping Core

The previous two sections described hardware that can be read but not programmed, and hardware that can be programmed but not read. Neither knows what time it is. A clocksource returns an opaque, free-running cycle count that begins wherever the counter happened to be at boot; a clock event device returns nothing at all. Something has to stand between that cycle count and a caller asking for the date, and that something is the timekeeping core in kernel/time/timekeeping.c.

Its job is to answer "what time is it?" — but that innocuous question hides four separate obligations that pull in different directions:

  • It must be correct. Cycles must be accumulated into nanoseconds without drift and without losing the fractional remainder, across counters that wrap, across suspend, and across a clocksource being swapped out underneath it.
  • It must be steerable. An NTP or PTP daemon in user space is continuously telling the kernel that it is running slightly fast or slightly slow. The core has to absorb those corrections smoothly, without ever letting a monotonic clock jump backwards.
  • It must be fast. ktime_get() is one of the most frequently executed functions in the kernel, and clock_gettime() one of the most frequently executed system calls. A design that took a lock would serialise the entire machine on the clock.
  • It must be safe to read from anywhere. Tracing, perf, and machine-check handlers need timestamps from NMI context, where even a seqcount retry loop can deadlock against a writer that was interrupted mid-update.

These four obligations explain almost every design decision in this section. Correctness produces the shifted-nanosecond accumulator and the logarithmic catch-up loop; steerability produces the split between tkr_mono and tkr_raw; speed produces the deliberate cacheline layout, the seqcount instead of a lock, and the vDSO; and NMI safety produces the latched fast timekeeper that stands beside the main one.

Linux 2.6 had no such core. Wall-clock time lived in a global struct timespec called xtime, guarded by a seqlock called xtime_lock; monotonic time was not stored at all but recomputed by every caller; sub-tick precision came from per-architecture interpolation code; and NTP state sat in a scatter of loose global variables. Linux 7.0.12 replaces all of it with one structure, struct timekeeper, one publication mechanism, and one accumulation loop. This section works through that machinery in the order the data flows:

  1. What does the conversion machinery look like? struct tk_read_base holds the clocksource pointer and the mult/shift pair that turns cycles into nanoseconds, and it is sized and placed so that the common read touches exactly one cacheline. struct timekeeper wraps two of them — one NTP-steered, one raw — and adds the offsets that derive every other clock. Covered under The tk_read_base Structure and The timekeeper Structure.
  2. How is an update made visible without a lock? Writers never modify the live timekeeper. They modify a shadow copy at leisure and then publish it inside a very short seqcount write section, so readers see either the whole old state or the whole new one. Covered under The tk_data Wrapper and Shadow Pattern.
  3. How many clocks are there, and how do they differ? Seven time bases are derived from the same accumulated cycle count, differing only in whether NTP steers them, whether suspend advances them, and whether the administrator can set them. Linux 6.17 added a family of auxiliary clocks on top, steerable independently of all seven. Covered under Time Bases in Linux 7.0.12.
  4. How is time read, and how is it updated? Five distinct read paths trade precision against latency and context-safety, from the vDSO fast path down to the NMI-safe latch. One accumulation path, driven by the tick, feeds them all. Covered under Reading Time and Updating Time.

The section closes with jiffies — the oldest and crudest time base in the kernel, which survives not because it is accurate but because reading a variable is cheaper than anything described above, and because a great deal of kernel code needs nothing better.

Evolution from Linux 2.6 to 7.0.12

In Linux 2.6, timekeeping was distributed across several loosely connected components: xtime held wall-clock time, jiffies counted ticks, wall_to_monotonic tracked the monotonic offset, and per-architecture do_gettimeofday() implementations interpolated between ticks using the TSC or other counters. NTP corrections were applied through a complex set of global variables (time_offset, time_freq, time_adj) that were difficult to reason about.

This approach had several fundamental problems:

  • No clean separation between time bases. Monotonic time was computed on-the-fly by adding wall_to_monotonic to xtime, which meant every caller paid the cost of an addition and there was no pre-computed monotonic value for the vDSO to export.
  • Per-architecture interpolation. Each architecture implemented its own do_gettimeofday() with TSC interpolation, leading to duplicated code and subtle bugs (especially around TSC instability and frequency changes).
  • Fragile NTP integration. NTP corrections were applied by modifying time_freq and time_adj — global variables that were coupled to the update loop but not to the xtime structure itself, creating race windows.
  • No CLOCK_BOOTTIME or CLOCK_TAI. The kernel had no concept of a clock that includes suspend time, or an atomic time without leap seconds.
  • 32-bit seconds. xtime.tv_sec was a time_t (32-bit on 32-bit architectures), creating the Year 2038 problem.

Linux 7.0.12 consolidates all timekeeping into a single subsystem (kernel/time/timekeeping.c) with a clean layered architecture:

  1. Hardware layer — Clocksources provide raw cycle counts (TSC, arch timer, etc.)
  2. Accumulation layer — timekeeping_advance() converts cycles to nanoseconds and applies NTP corrections
  3. Publication layer — tk_core publishes consistent time via seqcount; vDSO mirrors data to userspace
  4. Consumer layer — ktime_get*() functions read time locklessly; hrtimers and timers consume time values

Each layer has a well-defined interface:

  • The hardware layer only provides clocksource->read() — a function that returns raw cycle counts.
  • The accumulation layer calls clocksource->read(), computes the delta since the last update, converts cycles to nanoseconds using (delta × mult) >> shift, applies NTP frequency corrections, and writes the result into a shadow copy of struct timekeeper.
  • The publication layer atomically copies the shadow into the live tk_core.timekeeper under a seqcount write section, then pushes updates to the vDSO data page and fast timekeepers.
  • The consumer layer reads the published timekeeper via a seqcount retry loop (or the vDSO for userspace).
Table 6-57. Timekeeping Core — Old vs. New Architecture
AspectLinux 2.6Linux 7.0.12
Wall clock storagextime (struct timespec, 32-bit seconds)struct timekeeper.xtime_sec (64-bit seconds)
Protectionxtime_lock (seqlock)tk_core.seq (seqcount) + tk_core.lock (raw_spinlock)
Monotonic timeDerived: xtime + wall_to_monotonicNative: tkr_mono.base (accumulated nanoseconds)
Raw monotonicDid not existtkr_raw (separate read base, no NTP)
Boot timeDid not existCLOCK_BOOTTIME = monotonic + offs_boot
TAI timeDid not existCLOCK_TAI = realtime + offs_tai
Coarse timeDid not existcoarse_nsec updated per tick
NTP integrationSeparate variables (time_freq, time_adj)Integrated: ntp_error, ntp_err_mult in timekeeper
Userspace fast pathvsyscall page (x86 only, limited)vDSO (all architectures, full clock support)
Update functiondo_timer() + per-arch update_wall_time()Generic timekeeping_advance() (all architectures)
Multi-tick catchupNot supported cleanlyLogarithmic accumulation (ilog2 shift)
Shadow patternNone — direct modificationShadow timekeeper → atomic publish
Cacheline layoutNot optimizedDeliberately laid out across 5 cachelines
Year 2038 safetytime_t (32-bit on 32-bit arch)u64 xtime_sec (always 64-bit)

The table above deserves elaboration on several key transitions:

Shadow timekeeper pattern. In Linux 2.6, update_wall_time() modified xtime directly while holding xtime_lock. If a reader was in the middle of reading xtime when the update happened, it would see the seqcount change and retry. This was acceptable because xtime was small (just two fields), so updates were fast. But struct timekeeper is much larger (spanning 5 cachelines), and updating it field-by-field under the seqcount would create a long write-side critical section. The shadow pattern solves this: the tick handler modifies shadow_timekeeper (which nobody else reads), then copies the entire struct into tk_core.timekeeper in a single memcpy under the seqcount write section. This minimizes the time readers can observe an inconsistent state.

Cacheline-optimized layout. The kernel comments in timekeeper_internal.h explicitly document the cacheline layout:

  • Cacheline 0: seqcount + tkr_mono (the data for ktime_get() — the most common reader)
  • Cacheline 1: xtime_sec, ktime_sec, wall_to_monotonic, offset fields, coarse_nsec, id
  • Cacheline 2: tkr_raw, raw_sec (for CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW readers)
  • Cachelines 3-4: Internal accumulation variables (cycle_interval, xtime_interval, NTP state)

This means ktime_get() — the most frequently called function — only touches cachelines 0 and 1, which are hot in the CPU cache. CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW readers touch cacheline 2. The tick handler touches all 5 cachelines, but that only happens once per tick (typically every 1-4ms).

The tk_read_base Structure

Before examining the full struct timekeeper, it is important to understand struct tk_read_base — the embedded sub-structure that provides the cycle-to-nanosecond conversion for each clock type. The kernel maintains two instances: tkr_mono (for NTP-adjusted MONOTONIC/REALTIME/BOOTTIME/TAI) and tkr_raw (for RAW monotonic with no NTP adjustment):

/* include/linux/timekeeper_internal.h */
struct tk_read_base {
    struct clocksource  *clock;       /* current clocksource */
    u64                 mask;         /* bitmask for non-64-bit counters */
    u64                 cycle_last;   /* last clocksource reading */
    u32                 mult;         /* NTP-adjusted multiplier */
    u32                 shift;        /* shift for scaled math */
    u64                 xtime_nsec;   /* shifted fractional ns offset */
    ktime_t             base;         /* accumulated ktime_t base */
    u64                 base_real;    /* CLOCK_REALTIME base for vDSO */
};
Table 6-58. tk_read_base Fields
FieldTypeSizePurpose
clockstruct clocksource *8BPointer to the active clocksource (TSC, arch_timer, etc.)
masku648BBitmask for two's-complement subtraction on counters < 64 bits
cycle_lastu648BClocksource cycle value at last timekeeping_advance() call
multu324BMultiplier for (cycles × mult) >> shift conversion; NTP-adjusted for tkr_mono
shiftu324BShift factor for scaled-math conversion
xtime_nsecu648BAccumulated fractional nanoseconds (shifted); carried forward between ticks
basektime_t8BPre-computed base time in nanoseconds; readers add sub-tick interpolation to this
base_realu648Bbase + offs_real, pre-computed so that a realtime reader gets base and delta from one consistent snapshot. Used by the vDSO CLOCK_REALTIME fast path and by ktime_get_real_fast_ns().

The struct is exactly 56 bytes on 64-bit systems. Together with the 8-byte seqcount that precedes it in tk_data, tkr_mono occupies a single 64-byte cacheline — ensuring that the most common time-reading path (ktime_get()) touches exactly one cacheline.

The mult field deserves special attention. Unlike the clocksource's own mult, which is fixed at registration time, tkr_mono.mult is continuously adjusted by the NTP subsystem via timekeeping_adjust(). This is how NTP steers the clock: by slightly increasing or decreasing mult, each tick accumulates slightly more or fewer nanoseconds, gradually converging on the correct time. tkr_raw.mult, by contrast, always matches the clocksource's original mult — this is what makes CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW immune to NTP adjustments.

The timekeeper Structure

In Linux 2.6, the kernel stored wall-clock time in a single global variable xtime — a struct timespec containing seconds and nanoseconds since the Unix epoch. It was protected by xtime_lock (a seqlock) and updated by the timer interrupt handler. This was simple but limited: there was only one time base, NTP corrections were applied directly to xtime, and there was no separation between monotonic and wall-clock time at the data-structure level.

Linux 7.0.12 replaces xtime with the much richer struct timekeeper, which maintains multiple time bases simultaneously, integrates NTP corrections, caches coarse-time values for fast access, and supports the vDSO for userspace reads without syscalls. The complete structure with its cacheline layout:

/* include/linux/timekeeper_internal.h */
struct timekeeper {
    /* === Cacheline 0 (with prepended seqcount) === */
    struct tk_read_base tkr_mono;       /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC readout base */

    /* === Cacheline 1 === */
    u64                 xtime_sec;      /* seconds since epoch (REALTIME) */
    unsigned long       ktime_sec;      /* MONOTONIC seconds */
    struct timespec64   wall_to_monotonic; /* offset: mono = real + this */
    ktime_t             offs_real;      /* mono → real offset */
    ktime_t             offs_boot;      /* mono → boot offset */
    union {
        ktime_t         offs_tai;       /* mono → TAI offset */
        ktime_t         offs_aux;       /* mono → AUX clock offset */
    };
    u32                 coarse_nsec;    /* nanosecond part for coarse getters */
    enum timekeeper_ids id;            /* TIMEKEEPER_CORE or AUX */

    /* === Cacheline 2 === */
    struct tk_read_base tkr_raw;        /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW readout base */
    u64                 raw_sec;        /* RAW monotonic seconds */

    /* === Cachelines 3-4 (internal, updated only per tick) === */
    unsigned int        clock_was_set_seq;   /* clock-set event sequence */
    u8                  cs_was_changed_seq;  /* clocksource-change sequence */
    u8                  clock_valid;          /* clocksource valid flag */
    union {
        struct timespec64 monotonic_to_boot;  /* for vDSO BOOTTIME update */
        struct timespec64 monotonic_to_aux;   /* for vDSO AUX clock update */
    };
    u64                 cycle_interval;  /* cycles per NTP tick interval */
    u64                 xtime_interval;  /* shifted ns per NTP tick interval */
    s64                 xtime_remainder; /* rounding remainder */
    u64                 raw_interval;    /* shifted raw ns per tick */
    ktime_t             next_leap_ktime; /* when next leap second occurs */
    u64                 ntp_tick;        /* cached ntp_tick_length() */
    s64                 ntp_error;       /* accumulated NTP error */
    u32                 ntp_error_shift; /* NTP error shift conversion */
    u32                 ntp_err_mult;    /* NTP error multiplication factor */
    u32                 skip_second_overflow; /* avoid double NTP update */
    s32                 tai_offset;      /* current UTC-TAI offset in seconds */
};
Table 6-59. struct timekeeper Field Groups
GroupCachelineFieldsReaderUpdate Frequency
Monotonic readoutCL 0tkr_mono.*ktime_get(), ktime_get_real(), ktime_get_boottime(), ktime_get_clocktai()Every tick
Time offsetsCL 1xtime_sec, ktime_sec, wall_to_monotonic, offs_real/boot/tai, coarse_nsecktime_get_real(), ktime_get_coarse_*(), clock_gettime()Every tick
Raw readoutCL 2tkr_raw.*, raw_secktime_get_raw()Every tick
NTP stateCL 3-4ntp_error, ntp_err_mult, ntp_tick, cycle_interval, xtime_intervalTick handler onlyEvery tick (internal)
Event trackingCL 3-4clock_was_set_seq, cs_was_changed_seq, clock_validhrtimers (for reprogramming check)On clock set/change events
Leap secondCL 3-4next_leap_ktime, tai_offset, skip_second_overflowktime_get_clocktai(), NTPOn leap-second insertion

How time is derived from the structure:

Every ktime_get*() variant reads the timekeeper and computes time using this formula:

time = tkr_mono.base + ((clocksource->read() - tkr_mono.cycle_last) × tkr_mono.mult) >> tkr_mono.shift

The different clock types are then derived by adding the appropriate offset:

Table 6-60. Clock Derivation from struct timekeeper
ClockFormula
CLOCK_MONOTONICtkr_mono.base + delta_ns
CLOCK_REALTIMEMONOTONIC + offs_real (or equivalently xtime_sec × 10⁹ + nanoseconds)
CLOCK_BOOTTIMEMONOTONIC + offs_boot
CLOCK_TAIREALTIME + offs_tai
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAWtkr_raw.base + delta_ns_raw (no NTP)
CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSEPre-computed per-tick snapshot (no sub-tick interpolation)
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSEPre-computed per-tick snapshot (no sub-tick interpolation)

The tk_data Wrapper and Shadow Pattern

The struct timekeeper does not live alone — it is embedded in a tk_data wrapper that implements the shadow-copy pattern:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
struct tk_data {
    seqcount_raw_spinlock_t  seq;              /* reader sequence counter */
    struct timekeeper        timekeeper;       /* live — readers access this */
    struct timekeeper        shadow_timekeeper; /* shadow — writers modify this */
    raw_spinlock_t           lock;             /* writer exclusion */
} ____cacheline_aligned;

static struct tk_data timekeeper_data[TIMEKEEPERS_MAX];
#define tk_core  (timekeeper_data[TIMEKEEPER_CORE])

The array is recent (Linux 6.17) and deserves a word. Through Linux 6.16 there was exactly one tk_data, the global tk_core. It became an array when auxiliary POSIX clocks were added, so that each independently steerable clock domain gets its own timekeeper, its own shadow, its own seqcount and its own lock — and therefore its own accumulation state, entirely decoupled from system time. tk_core survives as a macro naming slot zero, so all the existing code that refers to it is unchanged. Auxiliary clocks occupy the remaining slots and are described later in this section; everything that follows here applies to any slot, because the shadow mechanism is per-tk_data, not global.

The shadow pattern works as follows:

  1. During update: the writer modifies shadow_timekeeper freely, under tkd->lock — no reader ever looks at the shadow, so this can take as long as it needs and can proceed in many small steps.
  2. To publish: timekeeping_update_from_shadow() opens a seqcount write section, recomputes the derived state (leap-second state, ktime_sec, tkr_mono.base_real), pushes the new values out to the vDSO with update_vsyscall(), to the paravirt notifier chain with update_pvclock_gtod(), and to the two NMI-safe latches with update_fast_timekeeper(); then it memcpy()s the shadow over the live timekeeper and closes the write section.
  3. To abandon an update: timekeeping_restore_shadow() copies the live timekeeper back over shadow_timekeeper, discarding the half-finished edit.

The third step is worth dwelling on, because the direction of the copy makes it easy to misread. timekeeping_restore_shadow() is not a preparation step run before each update; it is the rollback path. Because publication ends by copying the shadow over the live copy, the two are already identical whenever a writer begins, so no preparation is needed. A restore is required only when a writer has already dirtied the shadow and then discovers that the result would be invalid — for example do_settimeofday64() finding that the requested wall time would drive monotonic time negative:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c — the abort path, not the setup path */
if (timespec64_compare(&tks->wall_to_monotonic, &ts_delta) > 0) {
        timekeeping_restore_shadow(&tk_core);
        return -EINVAL;
}

This gives the writer side transaction-like semantics: dirty the shadow, and either commit it with timekeeping_update_from_shadow() or roll it back with timekeeping_restore_shadow(). The live timekeeper is never observed in an intermediate state, and a rejected settimeofday() leaves no trace.

Note also that the seqcount protects rather more than the final memcpy(). The vDSO update happens inside the write section deliberately: if it did not, a thread could read the already-updated vDSO page, then make a kernel call that read the not-yet-updated timekeeper, and observe time going backwards across the two.

Table 6-61. Timekeeper Fields — Old xtime vs. Modern timekeeper
FieldPurposeOld xtime Equivalent
xtime_secSeconds since Unix epoch (wall-clock seconds)xtime.tv_sec
tkr_mono.baseAccumulated ns for CLOCK_MONOTONIC(no equivalent — derived on-the-fly)
tkr_mono.cycle_lastLast raw clocksource value read(per-architecture interpolation)
tkr_mono.mult / shiftNTP-adjusted conversion factorstime_adj in NTP daemon
wall_to_monotonicOffset: REALTIME ↔ MONOTONIC(concept didn't exist cleanly)
offs_bootAccumulated suspend time (CLOCK_BOOTTIME)(did not exist)
offs_taiTAI offset / leap seconds(did not exist)
coarse_nsecNanoseconds part for coarse-time getters (per-tick)(did not exist)

The entire timekeeper lives inside the global tk_core structure (the #define macro above). This replaces the old xtime_lock seqlock with a more efficient seqcount + raw_spinlock combination. Writers (the tick handler calling timekeeping_advance()) take tk_core.lock and bump the sequence; readers (any ktime_get*() caller) only need the lockless seqcount retry loop. Because the seqcount is a separate type (seqcount_raw_spinlock_t), lockdep can verify that writers hold the correct lock.

The old kernel stored time in xtime (a simple struct timespec) protected by xtime_lock (seqlock). The modern kernel uses the much richer struct timekeeper with separate read bases for each clock type, NTP integration, and coarse-time caches — all protected by a seqcount inside tk_core. The shadow-copy pattern and deliberate cacheline layout are entirely new in the modern kernel.

Time Bases in Linux 7.0.12

In Linux 2.6, the kernel effectively had only two time references: xtime (wall-clock / REALTIME) and jiffies (a tick counter). Monotonic time was derived on-the-fly by adding wall_to_monotonic to xtime, and there was no concept of boot time, raw time, TAI, or coarse-grained time.

Linux 7.0.12 maintains seven distinct time bases simultaneously, each optimized for different use cases. All seven are derived from the same struct timekeeper and therefore from the same accumulated cycle count; they differ only in whether they are affected by NTP frequency steering, whether they include time spent in suspend, and whether they can be set (jumped) by the administrator. A further family of auxiliary clocks, described at the end of this subsection, sits outside that shared fate entirely.

Table 6-62. Kernel Time Bases
Clock IDValueMonotonic?NTP Adjusted?Includes Suspend?Settable?Use Case
CLOCK_REALTIME0NoYesYesYesWall clock, timestamps, file times
CLOCK_MONOTONIC1YesYesNoNoIntervals, timeouts, scheduling
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW4YesNoNoNoHardware benchmarks, profiling
CLOCK_BOOTTIME7YesYesYesNoTotal system uptime, Android timers
CLOCK_TAI11NoYesYesNoAtomic time (no leap seconds)
CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE5NoYesYes—Fast path (±tick accuracy)
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE6YesYesNo—Fast path (±tick accuracy)

Detailed clock descriptions:

CLOCK_REALTIME — The "human" clock that corresponds to calendar time (seconds since the Unix epoch, 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC). It is settable by settimeofday() or clock_settime(), which means it can jump forward or backward. NTP adjusts it continuously to keep it synchronized with UTC. Use this for timestamps that need to correspond to real-world time (file modification times, log entries, certificates). Caution: Because it can jump, never use REALTIME for measuring durations or as a timer expiry base — a settimeofday() call could cause your timer to fire immediately or never.

CLOCK_MONOTONIC — The workhorse clock for the kernel and most applications. It starts at zero at boot and advances at a constant rate (NTP-adjusted to match wall-clock rate, but never jumps). It does not include time spent in suspend — if the system sleeps for 8 hours, MONOTONIC does not advance during that time. This is the default clock for hrtimers, timerfd, nanosleep(), and most timeout logic. The kernel function ktime_get() returns this clock.

CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW — Like MONOTONIC but completely unaffected by NTP frequency adjustments. It reflects the raw clocksource cycles converted to nanoseconds using the original (fixed) mult/shift values. Use this for hardware benchmarking where you want to measure the actual oscillator rate without NTP interference. Over long periods, RAW and MONOTONIC can diverge by hundreds of ppm if NTP is steering the clock. The kernel function ktime_get_raw() returns this.

CLOCK_BOOTTIME — Identical to MONOTONIC plus the time spent in suspend states (S3/S4/s2idle). When the system resumes from a 2-hour sleep, BOOTTIME jumps forward by 2 hours but MONOTONIC does not. This clock represents "time since the machine was powered on" and is important for:

  • Android's AlarmManager (which needs timers that fire even across suspend)
  • System uptime reporting (/proc/uptime uses BOOTTIME)
  • Network protocols that need to track absolute elapsed time

The kernel function ktime_get_boottime() returns this, and offs_boot in the timekeeper accumulates all suspend durations.

CLOCK_TAI — International Atomic Time (TAI), which is REALTIME without leap-second adjustments. TAI = UTC + tai_offset, where tai_offset is currently 37 seconds (as of 2024) and increases by 1 each time a leap second is inserted. TAI never jumps backward (unlike UTC at a leap-second insertion) and is used in financial systems, telecommunications, and any application where a monotonically-increasing wall clock is required. The kernel tracks tai_offset in the timekeeper and NTP daemons update it via adjtimex().

CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE / CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE — Provide time at tick granularity (typically ±1ms with HZ=1000) but without reading the clocksource hardware. These return the cached value from the last tick update, making them extremely fast — just a few nanoseconds on modern hardware, even faster than the vDSO fast path for the full clocks. Use these when millisecond precision is acceptable and call frequency is very high (e.g., logging timestamps in high-throughput systems).

Mathematical relationships between clocks:

CLOCK_REALTIME      = CLOCK_MONOTONIC + offs_real
                    = CLOCK_MONOTONIC - wall_to_monotonic  (equivalent)
CLOCK_BOOTTIME      = CLOCK_MONOTONIC + offs_boot
CLOCK_TAI           = CLOCK_REALTIME  + tai_offset  (37 seconds in 2024)
CLOCK_*_COARSE      = Cached per-tick snapshot (no clocksource read)
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW = tkr_raw.base + raw_delta  (independent of NTP)
Table 6-63. Kernel API Functions for Each Time Base
ClockIn-kernel FunctionUserspacevDSO?Typical Latency
CLOCK_MONOTONICktime_get() / ktime_get_ns()clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, ...)Yes~20ns (vDSO)
CLOCK_REALTIMEktime_get_real() / ktime_get_real_ns()clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME, ...)Yes~20ns (vDSO)
CLOCK_BOOTTIMEktime_get_boottime()clock_gettime(CLOCK_BOOTTIME, ...)Yes~20ns (vDSO)
CLOCK_TAIktime_get_clocktai()clock_gettime(CLOCK_TAI, ...)Yes~20ns (vDSO)
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAWktime_get_raw()clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, ...)Yes~20ns (vDSO)
CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSEktime_get_coarse_real()clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE, ...)Yes~5ns (no HW read)
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSEktime_get_coarse()clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE, ...)Yes~5ns (no HW read)
(NMI-safe)ktime_get_mono_fast_ns()——~10ns (latch)
(jiffies)jiffies / jiffies_64——Direct variable read
Table 6-64. Choosing the Right Clock — Developer Decision Guide
ScenarioRecommended ClockWhy
Measuring function execution timeCLOCK_MONOTONICNever jumps, NTP-smooth
Kernel timeout / sleepCLOCK_MONOTONICStandard timer base
File timestamps (stat.st_mtime)CLOCK_REALTIMEMust match wall clock
"Wake me up at 3:00 AM even if device sleeps"CLOCK_BOOTTIME (alarm)Advances through suspend
System uptime displayCLOCK_BOOTTIMEIncludes all time since boot
Hardware cycle-accurate profilingCLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAWNo NTP interference

High-frequency logging (>100K msg/s)CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSEMinimal overhead
Network packet timestamps (PTP)CLOCK_REALTIME or CLOCK_TAINeeds absolute time
Timer that should NOT fire during suspendCLOCK_MONOTONICDoesn't advance in S3

Auxiliary Clocks: CLOCK_AUX

Every clock described so far is a view of the same accumulated cycle count. Set the wall clock and CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_TAI both move; let NTP steer the frequency and CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_BOOTTIME and CLOCK_TAI all change rate together. That shared fate is exactly what you want for system time, and exactly what you do not want when the machine has to track a clock that is not system time at all.

The motivating case is PTP. A machine on a precision-time network may participate in several clock domains at once — a grandmaster on one network segment, a different one on another, an audio or automotive bus with its own notion of time. These domains are not related to UTC, not related to each other, and each needs its own frequency correction. Before Linux 6.17 the only way to expose such a domain to applications was a character device (/dev/ptpN) read through ioctl() — correct, but a system call per timestamp, with no vDSO path.

Auxiliary clocks, added in Linux 6.17 by commit 9094c72c3d81 ("time: Introduce auxiliary POSIX clocks") under CONFIG_POSIX_AUX_CLOCKS, solve this by giving each such domain a complete timekeeper of its own. This is why tk_data became an array: an auxiliary clock is not a new offset applied to system time, it is a parallel instance of the entire machine described in this section — its own tkr_mono, its own shadow copy, its own seqcount, its own NTP state.

/* include/uapi/linux/time.h */
#define MAX_CLOCKS              16
#define CLOCK_AUX               MAX_CLOCKS              /* 16 */
#define MAX_AUX_CLOCKS          8
#define CLOCK_AUX_LAST          (CLOCK_AUX + MAX_AUX_CLOCKS - 1)  /* 23 */

/* include/linux/timekeeper_internal.h */
enum timekeeper_ids {
        TIMEKEEPER_CORE,
        TIMEKEEPER_AUX_FIRST,
        TIMEKEEPER_AUX_LAST = TIMEKEEPER_AUX_FIRST + MAX_AUX_CLOCKS - 1,
        TIMEKEEPERS_MAX,
};

Clock IDs 16 through 23 are therefore auxiliary clocks, and the id field added to struct timekeeper is what lets shared code such as timekeeping_update_from_shadow() tell which slot it is operating on. It is also what the two unions in the structure key off: an auxiliary timekeeper has no TAI offset and no boot offset to track, so offs_tai is reused as offs_aux (the offset from that domain's monotonic base to the time the domain publishes) and monotonic_to_boot is reused as monotonic_to_aux. The core timekeeper never uses the aux arms and an auxiliary timekeeper never uses the others, so the overlap is safe.

Auxiliary clocks are disabled by default and enabled individually from user space through sysfs — there is no in-kernel registration API and no autodetection, because only the application managing the clock domain knows whether it wants one:

# Enable auxiliary clock 0 (becomes CLOCK_AUX, clock ID 16)
$ echo 1 > /sys/kernel/time/aux_clocks/0/aux_clock_enable

# ... and disable it again
$ echo 0 > /sys/kernel/time/aux_clocks/0/aux_clock_enable

Enabling a clock runs aux_clock_enable(), which zeroes the slot's shadow timekeeper, restores its id, and calls tk_setup_internals() with the core timekeeper's raw clocksource. The new clock therefore starts out counting the same hardware at the same nominal frequency as system time — the kernel makes no attempt to guess the domain's real rate. From that starting point it is entirely the responsibility of user space to discipline it, via clock_settime() to set the offset and clock_adjtime() to steer the frequency. Disabling is simply a matter of clearing clock_valid and republishing; every reader then fails cleanly.

That failure mode is the one respect in which auxiliary clocks differ from every other clock in this chapter at the API level. A disabled auxiliary clock is a valid clock ID that has no time, so the read accessors return a bool rather than assuming success:

/* Returns false if the clock is not enabled — callers MUST check */
bool ktime_get_aux(clockid_t id, ktime_t *kt);
bool ktime_get_aux_ts64(clockid_t id, struct timespec64 *ts);

From user space the same condition surfaces as -ENODEV from clock_gettime(), clock_getres() and clock_adjtime(). Because an auxiliary clock is steered independently, several adjtimex() operations that make sense for system time are rejected on one: leap-second insertion and deletion (STA_INS, STA_DEL), TAI offset changes (ADJ_TAI) and the PPS modes (STA_PPSFREQ, STA_PPSTIME) all return -EINVAL. Like TAI, an auxiliary clock has no leap seconds.

Table 6-65. Auxiliary Clocks Compared with the Core Time Bases
PropertyCore time bases (REALTIME, MONOTONIC, BOOTTIME, TAI)Auxiliary clocks (CLOCK_AUX … CLOCK_AUX_LAST)
Timekeeper instanceOne, shared — timekeeper_data[TIMEKEEPER_CORE]One each — up to 8 further slots
Frequency steeringShared; NTP steers all of them togetherIndependent per clock, via clock_adjtime()
AvailabilityAlways presentOff by default; enabled individually through sysfs
Read failure possible?NoYes — -ENODEV / false when disabled
Leap secondsREALTIME observes them; TAI does notNever; STA_INS/STA_DEL are rejected
Advances across suspendBOOTTIME and REALTIME yes; MONOTONIC noNo — suspend is not injected into auxiliary clocks
vDSO acceleratedYesYes — aux_clock_data[MAX_AUX_CLOCKS] in the vDSO data page
hrtimer baseYesNo — timers cannot be armed on an auxiliary clock
Kernel accessorktime_get(), ktime_get_real(), …ktime_get_aux(), ktime_get_aux_ts64()

The last two rows are the practical limits. There is no hrtimer clock base for an auxiliary clock and no RTC behind it, so nothing can be scheduled against one — aux_clock_adj() discards the adjtimex result that would normally be used to notify hrtimers, with a comment saying exactly that. An auxiliary clock is a timestamp source, not a timer base: its purpose is to let an application read a foreign clock domain at vDSO speed instead of paying a system call, and that is all it does.

Table 6-66. Auxiliary Clock Interfaces
InterfaceDirectionPurpose
/sys/kernel/time/aux_clocks/N/aux_clock_enablewrite 0/1Enable or disable auxiliary clock N (0–7)
clock_gettime(CLOCK_AUX + N, …)readRead the clock; vDSO-accelerated, -ENODEV if disabled
clock_settime(CLOCK_AUX + N, …)writeSet the clock's offset (aux_clock_set())
clock_adjtime(CLOCK_AUX + N, …)read/writeSteer the clock's frequency (aux_clock_adj())
clock_getres(CLOCK_AUX + N, …)readResolution, from aux_clock_resolution_ns()
ktime_get_aux_ts64()in-kernelRead the clock from kernel code; returns false if disabled
Auxiliary clocks are the reason several fields in this section look odd in isolation: the id member of struct timekeeper, the two unions that overlay offs_aux on offs_tai and monotonic_to_aux on monotonic_to_boot, and above all the promotion of tk_data from a single global to an array. None of these exist in older 6.x-era or 2.6-era sources.

Reading Time

Reading time is one of the most frequently performed operations in any operating system. Every scheduling decision, timeout check, timestamp, and performance measurement requires reading the current time. In Linux 2.6, reading time was relatively simple: call do_gettimeofday() which read xtime under xtime_lock, then performed per-architecture TSC interpolation. The main optimization was the x86-only vsyscall page that avoided the syscall overhead.

Linux 7.0.12 provides five distinct reading paths, each optimized for different contexts and precision requirements. The choice of path depends on whether the caller is in userspace or kernel, whether NMI safety is needed, and whether tick-level precision is acceptable:

Table 6-67. Time Reading Paths — From Fastest to Most Precise
PathContextLatencyPrecisionMonotonic?When to Use
Coarse (cached)Kernel / vDSO~5ns±1 tick (1-4ms)Yes (steps)High-frequency logging, coarse timestamps
vDSO fast-pathUserspace~15-25nsSub-tick (ns)YesAll userspace clock_gettime() calls
In-kernel seqcountKernel (process/IRQ)~20-40nsSub-tick (ns)Yesktime_get*() family
NMI-safe (latch)Kernel (NMI/tracing)~10-20nsSub-tick (ns)No (rare inversion)perf, ftrace, NMI handlers
Syscall fallbackUserspace~200-800nsSub-tick (ns)YesvDSO unavailable, dynamic clocks
Note: The kernel's printk() timestamping does not use the coarse APIs. In vprintk_store(), the timestamp is taken via local_clock(), which maps to sched_clock() — a per-CPU, NMI-safe monotonic clock that typically reads the TSC directly (on x86) or uses the architecture timer (on ARM64). This is equivalent to the NMI-safe latch path in the diagram, providing nanosecond precision without blocking.

The vDSO Fast Path (Userspace)

The virtual Dynamic Shared Object (vDSO) is a small shared library that the kernel maps into every process's address space. It contains a read-only data page (vdso_time_data) that the kernel updates every tick, plus code that can read the hardware clocksource directly from userspace (e.g., rdtsc on x86, mrs cntvct_el0 on ARM64).

When a userspace application calls clock_gettime(), the C library redirects to the vDSO implementation rather than making a syscall. The vDSO code:

  1. Reads the sequence counter from the shared data page
  2. Reads the hardware counter directly (arch-specific)
  3. Computes nanoseconds: ns = (cycles - cycle_last) × mult >> shift + base_nsec
  4. Checks if the sequence counter changed (concurrent kernel update); if so, retries
  5. Falls back to a real syscall if the clocksource is not vDSO-compatible
/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c — simplified */
static bool do_hres(const struct vdso_time_data *vd, const struct vdso_clock *vc,
                    clockid_t clk, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    u64 sec, ns;
    u32 seq;

    do {
        seq = vdso_read_begin(vc);           /* read seqcount */
        cycles = __arch_get_hw_counter(vc->clock_mode, vd);  /* rdtsc / cntvct */
        ns = vdso_calc_ns(vc, cycles, vdso_ts->nsec);
        sec = vdso_ts->sec;
    } while (vdso_read_retry(vc, seq));

    ts->tv_sec = sec + ns / NSEC_PER_SEC;
    ts->tv_nsec = ns % NSEC_PER_SEC;
    return true;
}

/* The main vDSO entry point dispatches by clock type */
static bool __cvdso_clock_gettime_common(const struct vdso_time_data *vd,
                                         clockid_t clock, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    u32 msk = 1U << clock;
    if (msk & VDSO_HRES)       return do_hres(vd, vc, clock, ts);
    if (msk & VDSO_COARSE)     return do_coarse(vd, vc, clock, ts);
    if (msk & VDSO_RAW)        return do_hres(vd, &vc[CS_RAW], clock, ts);
    return false;  /* → syscall fallback */
}

The vDSO supports CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_BOOTTIME, CLOCK_TAI, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, and both COARSE variants — all without a syscall. The kernel pushes updates to the vDSO data page via update_vsyscall() during timekeeping_update_from_shadow().

In-Kernel Reading: The Seqcount Path

All in-kernel time readers (ktime_get(), ktime_get_real(), ktime_get_boottime(), etc.) follow the same pattern — read the struct timekeeper under a seqcount retry loop:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
ktime_t ktime_get(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;
    unsigned int seq;
    ktime_t base;
    u64 nsecs;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&tk_core.seq);
        base = tk->tkr_mono.base;
        nsecs = timekeeping_get_ns(&tk->tkr_mono);
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&tk_core.seq, seq));

    return ktime_add_ns(base, nsecs);
}

The timekeeping_get_ns() function computes the sub-tick interpolation — the nanoseconds elapsed since the last tick:

static inline u64 timekeeping_get_ns(const struct tk_read_base *tkr)
{
    u64 delta = clocksource_delta(tk_clock_read(tkr),
                                  tkr->cycle_last, tkr->clock->mask);
    return ((delta * tkr->mult) + tkr->xtime_nsec) >> tkr->shift;
}

This reads the clocksource hardware (e.g., rdtsc), subtracts the last-known cycle value (cycle_last) to get a delta, multiplies by mult, adds the fractional nanosecond accumulator (xtime_nsec), and shifts down. The result is nanoseconds elapsed since the last timekeeping_advance() update.

Why the seqcount retry loop? The tick handler updates tk_core.timekeeper periodically. If a reader is in the middle of reading fields when the writer updates them, the fields could be inconsistent (e.g., base updated but cycle_last not yet). The seqcount detects this: if seq changed between the begin and retry check, the reader discards its results and tries again. In practice, retries are rare (only when a read coincides with the exact moment of a tick update).

Table 6-68. In-Kernel Time Reader Functions
FunctionReturnsClock BaseUsed By
ktime_get()ktime_tMONOTONIChrtimers, scheduling, most subsystems
ktime_get_ns()u64 (ns)MONOTONICPerformance measurements
ktime_get_real()ktime_tREALTIMETimestamps, inode times
ktime_get_boottime()ktime_tBOOTTIMEUptime, Android timers
ktime_get_clocktai()ktime_tTAIPTP, financial
ktime_get_raw()ktime_tRAWHardware benchmarks
ktime_get_ts64()struct timespec64 *MONOTONICLegacy interfaces
ktime_get_real_ts64()struct timespec64 *REALTIMEgetnstimeofday64() replacement
ktime_get_clock_ts64()struct timespec64 *selected at runtimePTP and other callers holding a clock ID

The last entry was added in Linux 6.17 and is the odd one out: every other function in the table names its clock base at compile time, whereas ktime_get_clock_ts64() takes a POSIX clock ID and dispatches to the appropriate reader. It exists for callers such as PTP drivers that are told at runtime which clock to timestamp against, and that would otherwise have to carry their own switch statement. Because it accepts clock IDs that may not be available — an auxiliary clock that nobody enabled, for instance — it reports failure in-band by setting ts->tv_sec to -1 rather than by returning a value:

struct timespec64 ts;

ktime_get_clock_ts64(id, &ts);
if (ts.tv_sec == -1)
        return -ENODEV;        /* clock @id is not available */

Coarse-Grained Reading (No Hardware Access)

The coarse time functions return the cached time snapshot from the last tick update — they do not read the clocksource hardware. This makes them extremely fast (~5ns) but limits precision to ±1 tick interval:

void ktime_get_coarse_real_ts64(struct timespec64 *ts)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;
    unsigned int seq;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&tk_core.seq);
        *ts = tk_xtime_coarse(tk);   /* just reads xtime_sec + coarse_nsec */
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&tk_core.seq, seq));
}

void ktime_get_coarse_ts64(struct timespec64 *ts)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;
    struct timespec64 now, mono;
    unsigned int seq;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&tk_core.seq);
        now = tk_xtime_coarse(tk);
        mono = tk->wall_to_monotonic;
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&tk_core.seq, seq));

    set_normalized_timespec64(ts, now.tv_sec + mono.tv_sec,
                              now.tv_nsec + mono.tv_nsec);
}

Notice: no call to timekeeping_get_ns() (no clocksource read). The coarse functions only read pre-computed values from the timekeeper — xtime_sec and coarse_nsec — which are updated once per tick by tk_update_coarse_nsecs(). This is ideal for code that calls clock_gettime() millions of times per second.

The dedicated coarse_nsec field is worth a note, because it is recent (Linux 6.15) and it exists to fix a bug that had been latent for years. Until commit b71f9804f66c ("timekeeping: Prevent coarse clocks going backwards") the coarse getters had no field of their own; they simply shifted the live accumulator down themselves:

/* Linux 6.15+ — computed once per update, read verbatim by the coarse getters */
static inline void tk_update_coarse_nsecs(struct timekeeper *tk)
{
        tk->coarse_nsec = tk->tkr_mono.xtime_nsec >> tk->tkr_mono.shift;
}

The problem was that tkr_mono.xtime_nsec is not monotonic in isolation. When timekeeping_adjust() steers the multiplier forward it compensates by subtracting from xtime_nsec, so that callers who scale the outstanding cycle delta by the new multiplier still see a continuous line. The full-precision readers do exactly that and never notice. The coarse readers do not read the clocksource at all, so for them the subtraction was simply time moving backwards.

Normally the accumulation that precedes the adjustment is much larger than the correction, so the net movement stays positive and the window never opens. But adjtimex() calls into timekeeping_advance() to apply a frequency change immediately, and on that path there may have been no accumulation at all — leaving xtime_nsec smaller than it was before, and CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE visibly going backwards until the next tick.

The history here is instructive. The first fix (757b000f7b93) forwarded the timekeeper so the offset was zero at the point of adjustment. That worked, but it moved the update out of its period and cleared the accumulated NTP error, which changed adjtimex() behaviour that user space depends on — so it was reverted. The fix that stuck inverts the approach: rather than making the shared accumulator safe to read, give the coarse clocks their own snapshot that is only ever written at points where the value is known to be consistent. Two classes of reader with different consistency requirements were sharing one field; the fix was to stop sharing it.

Multigrain Timestamps: When Coarse Is Not Good Enough

Coarse time is fast because it is stale, and for most callers that trade is fine. Filesystems are the exception, and Linux 6.13 added a small set of accessors for them. The difficulty is that a file’s ctime and mtime serve two masters. Local workloads write files far faster than the tick, so a coarse timestamp is cheap and nobody notices that a thousand consecutive writes share one value. But NFSv3 clients and change-attribute consumers use those same timestamps to decide whether a file was modified, and two modifications that land in the same tick become indistinguishable — a genuine cache-coherence bug.

Taking a fine-grained timestamp on every write would fix it and cost a clocksource read each time. The multigrain scheme instead takes the fine-grained timestamp only when one is actually needed — when a file is being queried after modification — while guaranteeing that the cheap coarse timestamps handed out elsewhere never appear to precede it. That guarantee is what the machinery is for:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
static __cacheline_aligned_in_smp atomic64_t mg_floor;

mg_floor is a single system-wide monotonic ktime_t: the latest fine-grained timestamp ever handed out as a file timestamp. The two accessors work against it from opposite directions. ktime_get_coarse_real_ts64_mg() reads the ordinary coarse time, converts the floor to realtime, and returns whichever is later — so a coarse timestamp can never fall behind a fine-grained one already issued. ktime_get_real_ts64_mg() reads a fresh fine-grained time and attempts to install it as the new floor with atomic64_try_cmpxchg(). If a concurrent caller wins the race the failure needs no retry: whatever that caller installed is by definition later than the floor this one saw, so either outcome satisfies the invariant.

Two caveats are worth stating because they are easy to mistake for bugs. A backward step of CLOCK_REALTIME can still make one file timestamp precede another, since the floor is monotonic while the value returned is realtime — the kerneldoc calls this out explicitly. And these interfaces are documented as filesystem-specific: the global atomic64_t is a system-wide contended cacheline, which is acceptable at the rate inodes are stamped and would not be at the rate ktime_get() is called.

NMI-Safe Reading: The Latch Technique

Some kernel contexts cannot use the regular seqcount path because they might interrupt the writer itself. If an NMI fires while the tick handler holds tk_core.lock and is updating the timekeeper, a normal seqcount read would spin forever waiting for the write to complete.

The solution is the latch technique: a separate pair of tk_read_base copies (tk_fast_mono and tk_fast_raw) that use seqcount_latch — a lock-free algorithm where the writer alternates between two copies, and readers always have at least one consistent copy available:

/* The NMI-safe fast timekeeper */
static struct tk_fast {
    seqcount_latch_t     seq;
    struct tk_read_base  base[2];  /* two alternating copies */
} tk_fast_mono, tk_fast_raw;

static u64 __ktime_get_fast_ns(struct tk_fast *tkf)
{
    struct tk_read_base *tkr;
    unsigned int seq;
    u64 now;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_latch(&tkf->seq);
        tkr = tkf->base + (seq & 0x01);   /* pick the "stable" copy */
        now = ktime_to_ns(tkr->base);
        now += timekeeping_get_ns(tkr);
    } while (read_seqcount_latch_retry(&tkf->seq, seq));

    return now;
}

u64 ktime_get_mono_fast_ns(void)  { return __ktime_get_fast_ns(&tk_fast_mono); }
u64 ktime_get_raw_fast_ns(void)   { return __ktime_get_fast_ns(&tk_fast_raw); }

The derived clocks are where this gets interesting, because they are not built the same way and the difference is observable. Boot and TAI really are the monotonic value plus an offset read separately:

u64 notrace ktime_get_boot_fast_ns(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;

    return ktime_get_mono_fast_ns() + ktime_to_ns(data_race(tk->offs_boot));
}

u64 notrace ktime_get_tai_fast_ns(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;

    return ktime_get_mono_fast_ns() + ktime_to_ns(data_race(tk->offs_tai));
}

The data_race() annotation is an admission, not a decoration: the offset is read outside any seqcount, so the two halves of the sum are not consistent with each other. The kerneldoc spells out both consequences. A timestamp taken between the injection of sleep time and the timekeeper update adds the new boot offset to the old monotonic base, making the boot clock appear to jump forward early; and on 32-bit systems the 64-bit offset can be read half-updated. Both are tolerated because updating a boot or TAI offset is a rare event and the users of these functions are tracers, which post-process anyway.

CLOCK_REALTIME is deliberately not built this way:

u64 ktime_get_real_fast_ns(void)
{
    struct tk_fast *tkf = &tk_fast_mono;
    struct tk_read_base *tkr;
    u64 baser, delta;
    unsigned int seq;

    do {
        seq = raw_read_seqcount_latch(&tkf->seq);
        tkr = tkf->base + (seq & 0x01);
        baser = ktime_to_ns(tkr->base_real);   /* not base + offs_real */
        delta = timekeeping_get_ns(tkr);
    } while (raw_read_seqcount_latch_retry(&tkf->seq, seq));

    return baser + delta;
}

It runs its own latch loop and reads base_real — the realtime base that the writer precomputed and stored inside the same tk_read_base copy. Because the base and the cycle delta come from one latch-consistent snapshot, there is no window in which a realtime timestamp can mix a new offset with an old base. That is what base_real is for: the publication path computes tkr_mono.base_real = tkr_mono.base + offs_real once, inside the seqcount write section, so that no reader ever has to combine the two itself. The field had to exist anyway for the vDSO realtime fast path, which makes the atomic in-kernel reader almost free; boot and TAI have no equivalent precomputed base and would need one added before they could be given the same guarantee.

Trade-off: the latch technique is wait-free — it never spins, which is the entire point in NMI context — but ktime_get_mono_fast_ns() does not guarantee monotonicity across an update. The value is base_mono + clock_delta × slope, and the two copies are updated one at a time, so while base[1] still holds the old mult a reader steered onto it computes the delta with the old, steeper slope. A reader arriving just afterwards uses the new copy and the shallower slope, and can produce a smaller value than its predecessor. The kerneldoc draws the little ASCII graph that makes this obvious and notes that reader 6 observes time going backwards relative to reader 5.

Two qualifications keep this from being worse than it sounds. First, the anomaly is normally only observable between CPUs; for a single CPU to see its own timestamps go backwards, an NMI must land in the middle of the update and take a timestamp from the copy the interrupted code was not going to use. Callers that correlate timestamps across CPUs — which is most tracers — have to cope with it; callers that only compare their own do not, except across an NMI. Second, the hazard is specific to the monotonic fast clock. ktime_get_raw_fast_ns() is documented as always correct, because tkr_raw.mult is never touched by NTP or PTP: with a conversion factor that does not change, the two copies never disagree about the slope and the entire failure mode disappears. When a fast timestamp must not go backwards and an unsteered timebase is acceptable, that is the function to reach for.

None of these are suitable for timer expiry logic, which needs the ordinary seqcount path and its stronger guarantees.

The writer (update_fast_timekeeper()) uses the latch protocol:

static void update_fast_timekeeper(const struct tk_read_base *tkr, struct tk_fast *tkf)
{
    write_seqcount_latch_begin(&tkf->seq);  /* force readers to base[1] */
    memcpy(&tkf->base[0], tkr, sizeof(*tkr));
    write_seqcount_latch(&tkf->seq);        /* force readers back to base[0] */
    memcpy(&tkf->base[1], &tkf->base[0], sizeof(tkf->base[0]));
    write_seqcount_latch_end(&tkf->seq);
}

Syscall Fallback Path

When the vDSO cannot service a request (unsupported clocksource, dynamic clock ID, or architecture without vDSO support), userspace falls back to a real syscall:

/* In vDSO code */
int __cvdso_clock_gettime_data(const struct vdso_time_data *vd,
                               clockid_t clock, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    bool ok = __cvdso_clock_gettime_common(vd, clock, ts);
    if (unlikely(!ok))
        return clock_gettime_fallback(clock, ts);  /* real syscall */
    return 0;
}

The syscall path (sys_clock_gettime()) enters the kernel's POSIX clock layer, which dispatches to the appropriate timekeeping accessor based on clock ID:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c */
SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_gettime, const clockid_t, which_clock,
                struct __kernel_timespec __user *, tp)
{
    const struct k_clock *kc = clockid_to_kclock(which_clock);
    struct timespec64 kernel_tp;
    int error;

    if (!kc)
        return -EINVAL;
    error = kc->clock_get_timespec(which_clock, &kernel_tp);
    if (!error && put_timespec64(&kernel_tp, tp))
        error = -EFAULT;
    return error;
}

/* Dispatch table routes to the same ktime_get*() accessors */
/* CLOCK_REALTIME    → ktime_get_real_ts64()    → seqcount path */
/* CLOCK_MONOTONIC   → ktime_get_ts64()         → seqcount path */
/* CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW → ktime_get_raw_ts64()   → seqcount path */
/* CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE → ktime_get_coarse_real_ts64() → cached */
/* CLOCK_BOOTTIME    → ktime_get_boottime_ts64() → seqcount path */

Thus, the syscall fallback is not a separate timekeeping mechanism — it re-enters the same seqcount read path (or coarse cache for CLOCK_*_COARSE) that in-kernel callers use. The only difference is the ~200-800ns overhead from the user→kernel transition (mode switch, KPTI page-table flip on x86, and Spectre mitigations).

Table 6-69. When the Syscall Fallback Triggers
ConditionWhy vDSO FailsExample
Clocksource not vDSO-capableCannot read HW from userspaceHPET (MMIO, no userspace mapping)
Dynamic/process clock IDCLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID etc.Per-process CPU time
Time namespace with offsetNeeds kernel namespace lookupContainers with shifted clocks
Architecture lacks vDSONo vDSO implementationSome embedded/uncommon archs
TSC unstable (x86)Kernel disables vDSO clocksourceOld hardware, VM migration

Updating Time

While the reading paths described above are passive (they never modify the timekeeper), updating time is an active operation that modifies the authoritative tk_core data. In the old 2.6 kernel, update_wall_time() was the only significant update path. In Linux 7.0.12, there are five distinct update paths, each triggered by different events and modifying different aspects of the timekeeper:

Overview: The Five Update Paths

Unlike reading time (which is a lockless operation), updating time always requires the tk_core.lock raw spinlock and operates through the shadow timekeeper pattern. Every update path follows the same three-step protocol:

  1. Acquire lock: raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tk_core.lock, flags)
  2. Modify shadow: All changes target tkd->shadow_timekeeper
  3. Publish: timekeeping_update_from_shadow() atomically copies shadow → live under seqcount write protection
Table 6-70. Time Update Paths in Linux 7.0.12
PathTriggerEntry FunctionWhat ChangesFrequencyAffects Which Clocks
Periodic tickTimer interrupt on duty CPUupdate_wall_time()Accumulate cycles→ns, NTP mult steering, coarse cachesEvery 1/HZ sec (1ms at HZ=1000)All clocks
NTP frequencyadjtimex(ADJ_FREQUENCY)__do_adjtimex() → __timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_FREQ)Update mult, re-run advance if offset availableNTP daemon polls (typically 16-1024s)MONOTONIC, REALTIME
Set wall clocksettimeofday() / clock_settime()do_settimeofday64()Jump xtime, adjust wall_to_monotonicRare (boot, NTP step)REALTIME only (MONO preserved)
Suspend/ResumeSystem power state transitiontimekeeping_suspend() / timekeeping_resume()Inject sleep time into BOOTTIME + wall, re-base cycle_lastEach suspend/resume cycleREALTIME, BOOTTIME
TAI offsetLeap second via NTP__timekeeping_set_tai_offset()Change tai_offset field~1 per 18 monthsCLOCK_TAI only

Path 1: Periodic Tick — timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_TICK)

This is the primary update path, called every tick from the timekeeping-duty CPU. It is the only path that accumulates new time from the clocksource:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
void update_wall_time(void)
{
    if (timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_TICK))
        clock_was_set_delayed();   /* Notify hrtimers of time change */
    tk_aux_advance();              /* Update auxiliary timekeepers */
}

The timekeeping_advance() function is the heart of the timekeeping core. It reads the clocksource, accumulates elapsed cycles into nanoseconds (handling multi-tick catch-up for NOHZ), applies NTP corrections, updates coarse-time caches, and publishes the new time:

static bool __timekeeping_advance(struct tk_data *tkd,
                                  enum timekeeping_adv_mode mode)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tkd->shadow_timekeeper;
    unsigned int clock_set = 0;
    int shift = 0, maxshift;
    u64 offset, orig_offset;

    if (unlikely(timekeeping_suspended))
        return false;

    /* Step 1: Read clocksource and compute elapsed cycles */
    offset = clocksource_delta(tk_clock_read(&tk->tkr_mono),
                               tk->tkr_mono.cycle_last,
                               tk->tkr_mono.mask,
                               tk->tkr_mono.clock->max_raw_delta);
    orig_offset = offset;

    /* Step 2: Check if there's enough to accumulate */
    if (offset < real_tk->cycle_interval && mode == TK_ADV_TICK)
        return false;   /* Less than one tick — nothing to do */

    /* Step 3: Logarithmic accumulation for multi-tick catch-up (NOHZ)
     * Find the largest power-of-2 multiple of cycle_interval that fits,
     * then work down. This converts O(n) tick catch-up to O(log n). */
    shift = ilog2(offset) - ilog2(tk->cycle_interval);
    shift = max(0, shift);
    /* Bound shift to one less than what overflows tick_length */
    maxshift = (64 - (ilog2(ntp_tick_length(tk->id)) + 1)) - 1;
    shift = min(shift, maxshift);
    while (offset >= tk->cycle_interval) {
        offset = logarithmic_accumulation(tk, offset, shift, &clock_set);
        if (offset < tk->cycle_interval << shift)
            shift--;
    }

    /* Step 4: Apply NTP frequency adjustment to mult */
    timekeeping_adjust(tk, offset);

    /* Step 5: Handle nanosecond overflow → seconds */
    clock_set |= accumulate_nsecs_to_secs(tk);

    /* Step 6: Update the coarse caches only if time was actually accumulated */
    if (orig_offset != offset)
        tk_update_coarse_nsecs(tk);

    /* Step 7: Publish — write seqcount, update vDSO, fast timekeepers */
    timekeeping_update_from_shadow(tkd, clock_set);

    return !!clock_set;
}

Three details in that listing repay attention, because each is a guard rather than a step.

The fourth argument to clocksource_delta() is max_raw_delta, the 87.5%-of-mask negative-motion cut-off described earlier under The Clocksource Framework. This is where that guard actually bites. If the clocksource reports a delta beyond the cut-off — a counter that appears to have run backwards, or a wrap that cannot be distinguished from one — offset comes back as zero, the accumulation loop below does nothing, and time stands still for this tick instead of leaping backwards by most of a counter period. The next tick, reading against the same unchanged cycle_last, will usually produce a sane delta and recover.

maxshift bounds the ambition of the logarithmic loop. The first two lines pick the largest doubling of cycle_interval that fits inside the outstanding offset, which is what makes catch-up logarithmic; but the accumulation multiplies that interval by ntp_tick_length(), and a shift chosen purely from the offset can push that product past 64 bits. The bound is one less than the shift at which tick_length would overflow, so a very long idle period accumulates in a few more, smaller chunks rather than in one that computes garbage. It is the reason the declared variable exists at all.

The conditional coarse update is the other half of the fix discussed under Coarse-Grained Reading. orig_offset records the offset before the loop, so the comparison asks a precise question: did this call actually accumulate anything? On the TK_ADV_FREQ path it often did not — adjtimex() can arrive with less than a tick outstanding, run timekeeping_adjust(), and leave xtime_nsec slightly smaller than it found it. Refreshing coarse_nsec from that value is exactly what made CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE visibly run backwards. Skipping the refresh when nothing accumulated means the coarse snapshot is only ever taken at a point where it is known to have moved forward. Giving the coarse clocks their own field was one half of commit b71f9804f66c; this test is the other.

Logarithmic accumulation is a key optimization for NOHZ systems. When a CPU has been idle for a long time (e.g., 100ms at HZ=1000 = 100 ticks to catch up), naively looping 100 times would be wasteful. Instead, the algorithm uses binary decomposition — if 100 ticks are pending, it first accumulates 64 (2^6), then 32, then 4, covering 100 ticks in just 3 iterations:

static u64 logarithmic_accumulation(struct timekeeper *tk, u64 offset,
                                    u32 shift, unsigned int *clock_set)
{
    u64 interval = tk->cycle_interval << shift;

    if (offset < interval)
        return offset;

    offset -= interval;
    tk->tkr_mono.cycle_last += interval;
    tk->tkr_raw.cycle_last  += interval;

    /* Accumulate into both MONOTONIC and RAW bases */
    tk->tkr_mono.xtime_nsec += tk->xtime_interval << shift;
    *clock_set |= accumulate_nsecs_to_secs(tk);

    tk->tkr_raw.xtime_nsec += tk->raw_interval << shift;

    /* Track NTP error accumulation */
    tk->ntp_error += tk->ntp_tick << shift;
    tk->ntp_error -= (tk->xtime_interval + tk->xtime_remainder) <<
                     (tk->ntp_error_shift + shift);

    return offset;
}

The shadow timekeeper pattern: timekeeping_advance() operates on a shadow copy of the timekeeper (tkd->shadow_timekeeper). All modifications happen on the shadow. Only at the end does timekeeping_update_from_shadow() atomically publish the result by copying the shadow to the live timekeeper under the seqcount write section. This minimizes the time spent inside the critical section, reducing reader-side retries.

The do_timer() function handles the jiffies side:

void do_timer(unsigned long ticks)
{
    jiffies_64 += ticks;
    calc_global_load();    /* Update loadavg samples */
}
Table 6-71. Timekeeping Update Call Chain
CallerFunctionWhat It UpdatesFrequency
tick_periodic() (duty CPU)do_timer(1)jiffies_64, global load averageEvery tick (1/HZ seconds)
tick_periodic() (duty CPU)update_wall_time()All time bases, NTP error, coarse caches, vDSOEvery tick
tick_nohz_idle_exit()tick_do_update_jiffies64()jiffies_64 (catch up N ticks)On idle exit
NTP daemon (adjtimex())timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_FREQ)mult adjustment only (no accumulation)When NTP adjusts frequency
The old kernel's update_wall_time() was a simple loop that accumulated one cycle_interval at a time — O(n) for n missed ticks. The modern kernel uses logarithmic accumulation (O(log n)), the shadow timekeeper pattern for minimal reader contention, and a unified function that handles both periodic ticks and NOHZ catch-up. The split between do_timer() (jiffies) and update_wall_time() (nanosecond time) remains, but both are now called from the generic tick layer rather than architecture-specific code.

Path 2: NTP Frequency Adjustment — timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_FREQ)

When the NTP daemon calls adjtimex() with ADJ_FREQUENCY or ADJ_TICK, the kernel updates the clock frequency multiplier. This path re-uses the same __timekeeping_advance() function but with TK_ADV_FREQ mode. The key difference: the offset < cycle_interval early-exit check is bypassed for TK_ADV_FREQ, so the mult adjustment and publication happen even if less than one tick has elapsed:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c — inside __do_adjtimex() */
/* Update the multiplier immediately if frequency was set directly */
if (txc->modes & (ADJ_FREQUENCY | ADJ_TICK))
    result->clock_set |= __timekeeping_advance(tkd, TK_ADV_FREQ);

/* In __timekeeping_advance(): */
/* TK_ADV_TICK returns false if offset < cycle_interval (nothing to do) */
/* TK_ADV_FREQ proceeds regardless — mult is re-applied via timekeeping_adjust() */
if (offset < real_tk->cycle_interval && mode == TK_ADV_TICK)
    return false;  /* Only skips for TK_ADV_TICK */

This ensures that NTP frequency corrections take effect immediately rather than waiting for the next tick — important for precision time synchronization (PTP, chrony).

Path 3: Setting the Wall Clock — do_settimeofday64()

When userspace calls settimeofday() or clock_settime(CLOCK_REALTIME, ...), the kernel jumps the wall clock to the specified value. This is the only path that can make CLOCK_REALTIME go backward:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
int do_settimeofday64(const struct timespec64 *ts)
{
    struct timespec64 ts_delta, xt;

    if (!timespec64_valid_settod(ts))
        return -EINVAL;

    scoped_guard(raw_spinlock_irqsave, &tk_core.lock) {
        struct timekeeper *tks = &tk_core.shadow_timekeeper;

        /* Forward shadow to current time first */
        timekeeping_forward_now(tks);

        xt = tk_xtime(tks);
        ts_delta = timespec64_sub(*ts, xt);  /* How much to jump */

        /* Prevent CLOCK_MONOTONIC from going backward */
        if (timespec64_compare(&tks->wall_to_monotonic, &ts_delta) > 0) {
            timekeeping_restore_shadow(&tk_core);
            return -EINVAL;
        }

        /* Adjust wall_to_mono so MONOTONIC is unaffected by the jump */
        tk_set_wall_to_mono(tks, timespec64_sub(tks->wall_to_monotonic, ts_delta));
        tk_set_xtime(tks, ts);
        timekeeping_update_from_shadow(&tk_core, TK_UPDATE_ALL);
    }

    clock_was_set(CLOCK_SET_WALL);  /* Notify hrtimers, timerfd */
    audit_tk_injoffset(ts_delta);
    return 0;
}

Key design principle: wall_to_monotonic is adjusted in the opposite direction of the wall clock jump, so CLOCK_MONOTONIC = CLOCK_REALTIME + wall_to_monotonic remains unchanged. This is how Linux guarantees that CLOCK_MONOTONIC never jumps, even when wall time is set backward.

Path 4: Suspend and Resume

When the system enters a sleep state (suspend-to-RAM, hibernate), the clocksource stops counting. On resume, the kernel must account for the time spent sleeping. This is a two-phase process:

Suspend phase (timekeeping_suspend()):

int timekeeping_suspend(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tks = &tk_core.shadow_timekeeper;

    /* Record persistent clock (RTC) time at suspend entry */
    read_persistent_clock64(&timekeeping_suspend_time);

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tk_core.lock, flags);
    timekeeping_forward_now(tks);   /* Flush pending cycles */
    timekeeping_suspended = 1;      /* Block advance() calls */

    /* Start suspend timing if clocksource supports it */
    cycle_now = tks->tkr_mono.cycle_last;
    clocksource_start_suspend_timing(curr_clock, cycle_now);

    timekeeping_update_from_shadow(&tk_core, 0);
    halt_fast_timekeeper(tks);      /* Freeze NMI-safe paths */
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    tick_suspend();
    clocksource_suspend();
    clockevents_suspend();
}

Resume phase (timekeeping_resume()):

void timekeeping_resume(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tks = &tk_core.shadow_timekeeper;

    read_persistent_clock64(&ts_new);
    clockevents_resume();
    clocksource_resume();

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    /* Three sources for sleep time, in priority order:
     * 1) Non-stop clocksource (e.g., TSC with CONSTANT_TSC)
     * 2) Persistent clock (RTC readable with IRQs off)
     * 3) RTC (handled separately by rtc core)
     */
    cycle_now = tk_clock_read(&tks->tkr_mono);
    nsec = clocksource_stop_suspend_timing(clock, cycle_now);
    if (nsec > 0) {
        ts_delta = ns_to_timespec64(nsec);
        inject_sleeptime = true;
    } else if (ts_new > timekeeping_suspend_time) {
        ts_delta = timespec64_sub(ts_new, timekeeping_suspend_time);
        inject_sleeptime = true;
    }

    if (inject_sleeptime)
        __timekeeping_inject_sleeptime(tks, &ts_delta);

    /* Re-base cycle_last to current clocksource value */
    tks->tkr_mono.cycle_last = cycle_now;
    tks->tkr_raw.cycle_last  = cycle_now;

    timekeeping_suspended = 0;
    timekeeping_update_from_shadow(&tk_core, TK_CLOCK_WAS_SET);
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tk_core.lock, flags);

    tick_resume();
    timerfd_resume();
}

The sleep time injection advances CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_BOOTTIME, and the sleep-time accumulator, while CLOCK_MONOTONIC is adjusted via wall_to_monotonic so it also advances by the sleep duration. CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW does not advance during sleep — it only counts time when the clocksource is actively running.

Table 6-72. Sleep Time Sources (priority order)
PrioritySourceAccuracyAvailabilityExample
1 (best)Non-stop clocksourceNanosecondTSC with CONSTANT_TSC + NONSTOP_TSCModern Intel/AMD x86_64
2Persistent clock (RTC)~1 secondread_persistent_clock64() works with IRQs offMost x86 platforms
3RTC subsystem~1 secondI2C/SPI RTC (needs IRQs enabled)ARM embedded boards

Path 5: TAI Offset and Leap Seconds

International Atomic Time (TAI) differs from UTC by an integer number of leap seconds (currently 37). When a leap second is inserted, the NTP daemon calls adjtimex() which updates the TAI offset:

static void __timekeeping_set_tai_offset(struct timekeeper *tk, s32 tai_offset)
{
    tk->tai_offset = tai_offset;
    tk->offs_tai = ktime_add(tk->offs_real, ktime_set(tai_offset, 0));
}

This is followed by timekeeping_update_from_shadow() with TK_CLOCK_WAS_SET, which triggers clock_was_set() to notify subsystems (hrtimers, timerfd) that a clock discontinuity occurred.

The Publication Mechanism: timekeeping_update_from_shadow()

All five update paths converge on this single function, which atomically publishes the modified shadow timekeeper to all readers:

static void timekeeping_update_from_shadow(struct tk_data *tkd, unsigned int action)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tkd->shadow_timekeeper;

    lockdep_assert_held(&tkd->lock);

    /* Block readers during update */
    write_seqcount_begin(&tkd->seq);

    if (action & TK_CLEAR_NTP) {
        tk->ntp_error = 0;
        ntp_clear(tk->id);
    }

    tk_update_leap_state(tk);
    tk_update_ktime_data(tk);
    tk->tkr_mono.base_real = tk->tkr_mono.base + tk->offs_real;

    /* Update all publication targets */
    if (tk->id == TIMEKEEPER_CORE) {
        update_vsyscall(tk);                          /* vDSO data page */
        update_pvclock_gtod(tk, action & TK_CLOCK_WAS_SET); /* KVM PV clock */
        update_fast_timekeeper(&tk->tkr_mono, &tk_fast_mono); /* NMI-safe */
        update_fast_timekeeper(&tk->tkr_raw,  &tk_fast_raw);
    }

    if (action & TK_CLOCK_WAS_SET)
        tk->clock_was_set_seq++;

    /* Copy shadow → live (why not pointer swap? cacheline optimization) */
    memcpy(&tkd->timekeeper, tk, sizeof(*tk));
    write_seqcount_end(&tkd->seq);
}

The memcpy rather than pointer-swap design is deliberate: it keeps the reader-visible tkd->timekeeper at a fixed address with optimized cacheline layout. Pointer swapping would add an indirection on every read and break the cacheline packing.

The jiffies Variable

In Linux 2.6, jiffies was treated as a fundamental 32-bit counter that overflows after approximately 497 days (at HZ=1000) and required careful comparison macros. In Linux 7.0.12, jiffies remains conceptually the same — it counts elapsed ticks since boot — but the implementation has been refined.

The 64-bit / 32-bit duality:

/* include/linux/jiffies.h */
extern u64 __cacheline_aligned_in_smp jiffies_64;
extern unsigned long volatile __jiffy_arch_data jiffies;

jiffies_64 is the authoritative 64-bit counter; the 32-bit jiffies is aliased to its lower half via linker magic. On x86_64 and ARM64 (64-bit architectures), unsigned long is 64 bits, so both are effectively identical and never overflow in practice.

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — tick_periodic() */
static void tick_periodic(int cpu)
{
    if (tick_do_timer_cpu == cpu) {
        raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
        write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
        do_timer(1);         /* jiffies_64++ */
        write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
    }
    update_process_times(user_mode(get_irq_regs()));
}

Only one CPU (designated by tick_do_timer_cpu) updates jiffies per tick — this avoids lock contention. In NOHZ mode, this duty can migrate between CPUs.

Wrapping and Safe Comparisons

On 32-bit systems, jiffies wraps around after 2³² ticks. To handle wrapping correctly, the kernel provides comparison macros that use signed subtraction:

#define time_after(a, b)     ((long)((b) - (a)) < 0)
#define time_before(a, b)    time_after(b, a)
#define time_after_eq(a, b)  ((long)((a) - (b)) >= 0)
#define time_before_eq(a, b) time_after_eq(b, a)
#define time_in_range(a, b, c) (time_after_eq(a,b) && time_before_eq(a,c))

Never write: if (jiffies > timeout) — this breaks on wrap.
Always write: if (time_after(jiffies, timeout)) — this is wrap-safe.

Conversion Functions

Table 6-73. Jiffies Conversion API
FunctionDirectionNotes
msecs_to_jiffies(ms)Milliseconds → jiffiesHandles MAX_JIFFY_OFFSET overflow
usecs_to_jiffies(us)Microseconds → jiffiesRounds up to nearest tick
nsecs_to_jiffies(ns)Nanoseconds → jiffiesRounds up
jiffies_to_msecs(j)Jiffies → millisecondsTruncates (no rounding)
jiffies_to_usecs(j)Jiffies → microseconds
jiffies_to_nsecs(j)Jiffies → nanosecondsVia jiffies_to_usecs() × 1000

Typical usage in drivers:

/* Set a 5-second timeout */
unsigned long timeout = jiffies + msecs_to_jiffies(5000);

/* Wait for condition or timeout */
while (!condition_met()) {
    if (time_after(jiffies, timeout))
        return -ETIMEDOUT;
    schedule();
}

10010 ms100~497 daysServers (minimal overhead)
2504 ms250~199 daysDefault — balanced
