Linux 2.6.11 used HZ = 1000 as the x86 default. Modern kernels default to HZ = 250, and with NO_HZ (tickless) the periodic tick can be stopped entirely during idle. The INITIAL_JIFFIES value is set to -(5 minutes in ticks) to trigger early wrap-around bugs during testing.

The Tick Layer

The three preceding sections built a kernel that knows what time it is. Nothing in them makes anything happen. A clocksource is read on demand; a clock event device will fire an interrupt if somebody programs it; the timekeeping core converts and publishes. None of them decides that an interrupt should be programmed at all. The tick layer (kernel/time/tick-*.c, roughly 3,830 lines across six files) is what makes that decision, on every CPU, continuously. It is the subsystem that turns a programmable timer into the kernel's heartbeat.

The obvious design — program every CPU's timer to fire at HZ and be done — is what Linux 2.6 did, and essentially all of the complexity in this section exists because that design fails in four different directions at once:

  • Exactly one CPU may count jiffies, and it must never be nobody. jiffies_64 and update_wall_time() are global, so having every CPU update them would be both wrong and a contention disaster on a large machine. Having a single fixed CPU do it is simple, but that CPU can then never go idle, and it can be hotplugged out. The tick layer therefore has to hand the duty around at runtime, using an assignment protocol that stays correct even though CPUs pick it up and drop it without coordinating.
  • Every CPU nevertheless needs its own tick. Scheduler preemption, CPU time accounting, RCU quiescent states and per-CPU timer expiry are all local work that no other CPU can do on this CPU's behalf. So the duty is global but the tick is per-CPU, and the two are separate concerns that happen to travel on the same interrupt.
  • The per-CPU timer stops in deep idle. The hardware that is cheapest to use for a per-CPU tick — the x86 local APIC timer — is powered down in C3 and deeper. A CPU that entered idle relying on it would never wake up. Recovering from this without giving up deep idle is what the entire broadcast machinery exists for.
  • Most ticks do nothing. On an idle CPU, or on a CPU running a single CPU-bound task, the tick fires, finds no work, and returns. At HZ=1000 that is a thousand pointless wakeups per second per CPU — measurable power on a laptop, measurable jitter on a real-time or HPC workload. The modern tick layer spends much of its code trying not to tick.

These four pressures explain the shape of everything that follows. The first produces tick_do_timer_cpu and its handover protocol; the second produces the per-CPU tick_device and tick_sched pair; the third produces the broadcast device and the cpumasks that track who depends on it; the fourth produces the three operating modes and, ultimately, NOHZ. They also conflict: the CPU that wants to go idle may be the one holding the timekeeping duty, and the CPU that needs a broadcast wakeup may be the one that was about to take the duty over. Much of the subtlety in this section is the tick layer arbitrating between them.

Version history. In Linux 2.6 there was effectively no tick layer. Each architecture wired its timer interrupt straight to do_timer() plus update_process_times(), the rate was fixed at HZ, and CPU 0 held the timekeeping duty for the lifetime of the system. Everything in this section — the three operating modes, dynamic duty assignment, broadcasting, and tick suppression — postdates Linux 2.6.11. The one piece that survives unchanged in spirit is tick_handle_periodic(), which is still what runs on hardware too limited to do anything better.

The section answers five questions, in order.

Where does the tick layer sit, and what state does a CPU keep? It occupies the gap between the clock event device framework below it and the scheduler, timer wheel and RCU above it. Each CPU carries two structures: a tick_device, which is the binding to its hardware, and a tick_sched, which is the far larger record of what mode that CPU is in and what it is doing about the tick.

What modes can a CPU be in? Three, entered in a fixed order as capabilities become available: periodic at boot, high-resolution once a one-shot-capable device and a good clocksource exist, and NOHZ once the CPU has nothing to tick for. The first transition happens once and is permanent; the last is entered and left thousands of times a second.

Who counts jiffies? One CPU at a time, named by tick_do_timer_cpu, which is dropped when that CPU goes idle and claimed by whichever CPU next takes a tick. This is deliberately racy, and understanding why it is nevertheless safe — and what happens when the holder stalls inside a VM exit or stop_machine() — is the most interesting protocol in the section.

How does a CPU get a tick device in the first place? Through tick_check_new_device(), which every clock event device registration passes through, and which decides whether the newcomer replaces the CPU's current device, becomes the global broadcast device, or is rejected outright.

What happens when the local timer dies in idle? A second device, shared by all CPUs, takes over the wakeups on their behalf and delivers them by IPI. Five cpumasks track the arrangement: two record which CPUs need the service at all, and three more record, for the one-shot case, which are currently asleep under it, which already have a wakeup pending, and which must be woken unconditionally.

A final subsection follows the tick all the way through: from the three entry points that converge on update_process_times(), out into the scheduler, timer wheel, RCU and posix-cpu-timers, with measured costs for each stage.

Tick Layer Architecture

The tick layer sits between clock event devices (hardware) and kernel subsystems (consumers). It performs three critical functions: (1) selects and configures the best clock event device for each CPU, (2) dispatches timer interrupts to the appropriate handler based on the current mode, and (3) manages the timekeeping duty assignment to avoid lock contention. The following figure shows how these components relate:

The tick layer consists of six source files, each handling a distinct aspect:

Table 6-75. Tick Layer Source Files
FileLinesPurposeKey Functions

The layered design allows the kernel to start with a simple periodic tick at boot and progressively enable features as hardware capabilities are discovered — first one-shot mode, then high-resolution timers, then NOHZ tick suppression. Each transition is triggered by the clock event or clocksource framework calling into the tick layer.

Key Data Structures

The tick layer relies on three categories of data: per-CPU device bindings, per-CPU scheduler tick state, and global coordination variables. Understanding the relationship between these structures is essential for understanding how ticks flow through the system.

struct tick_device — Per-CPU HW Binding

Each CPU has exactly one tick_device that binds it to its assigned clock event device. This is a simple wrapper:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.h */
enum tick_device_mode {
    TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC,   /* Device generates fixed-rate interrupts */
    TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT,    /* Device programmed for next specific event */
};

struct tick_device {
    struct clock_event_device *evtdev;  /* Pointer to assigned HW device */
    enum tick_device_mode     mode;    /* Current operating mode */
};

/* One per CPU — defined in tick-common.c */
DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct tick_device, tick_cpu_device);

The evtdev pointer is set by tick_check_new_device() when a clock event device is registered. The mode starts as TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC and transitions to TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT when the tick layer switches to high-resolution mode. A CPU's tick_device can change during the system's lifetime (e.g., when a higher-rated device is registered, or on CPU hotplug).

struct clock_event_device — Hardware Timer Abstraction

The clock_event_device is the hardware abstraction that tick_device wraps. Each physical timer (LAPIC, HPET, ARM Arch Timer, etc.) registers one of these structures. It is the "event source" half of the timing subsystem — while clocksources provide time reading, clock event devices provide time interrupts:

/* include/linux/clockchips.h */
struct clock_event_device {
    /* === Dispatch === */
    void  (*event_handler)(struct clock_event_device *);  /* Current tick handler */
    int   (*set_next_event)(unsigned long evt, struct clock_event_device *);
    int   (*set_next_ktime)(ktime_t expires, struct clock_event_device *);
    ktime_t         next_event;         /* Next event in oneshot mode */

    /* === Timing parameters === */
    u64             max_delta_ns;       /* Max programmable interval */
    u64             min_delta_ns;       /* Min programmable interval */
    u32             mult;               /* ns→cycles multiplier */
    u32             shift;              /* ns→cycles divisor (power of 2) */

    /* === State machine === */
    enum clock_event_state  state_use_accessors;
    unsigned int    features;           /* CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_* bitmask */
    unsigned int    next_event_forced;  /* Last arming was a forced min-delta */
    unsigned long   retries;            /* Programming retry count */

    /* === State transition callbacks (driver-provided) === */
    int  (*set_state_periodic)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int  (*set_state_oneshot)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int  (*set_state_oneshot_stopped)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int  (*set_state_shutdown)(struct clock_event_device *);
    int  (*tick_resume)(struct clock_event_device *);

    /* === Broadcast support === */
    void (*broadcast)(const struct cpumask *mask);
    void (*suspend)(struct clock_event_device *);
    void (*resume)(struct clock_event_device *);
    unsigned long   min_delta_ticks;
    unsigned long   max_delta_ticks;

    /* === Identity and binding === */
    const char     *name;               /* "lapic", "arch_sys_timer", "hpet" */
    int             rating;             /* Quality: higher = preferred */
    int             irq;                /* IRQ number (non-percpu devices) */
    int             bound_on;           /* CPU this device is bound to */
    const struct cpumask *cpumask;      /* CPUs this device can serve */
    struct list_head list;              /* Global clockevent list */
    struct module   *owner;
} ____cacheline_aligned;

Only the fields the tick layer touches are annotated here; the framework side of this structure — how mult and shift are computed, what each set_state_* callback must guarantee, and the meaning of the next_event_forced flag added in Linux 7.0 to break a reprogramming loop that could starve a CPU of timer interrupts — is covered under Registration and Programming.

Table 6-76. clock_event_device Feature Flags
FlagValueMeaningExample Hardware
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC0x01Can generate periodic interruptsLAPIC (divisor mode), HPET
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT0x02Can be programmed for single future eventLAPIC (TSC-deadline), ARM Arch Timer
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_KTIME0x04Accepts ktime_t directly (no ns→cycles conversion)Hyper-V synthetic timer
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP0x08Timer stops in deep idle (C3+) — needs broadcastLAPIC on most x86
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY0x10Placeholder with no real hardware behind it; state changes are no-ops and programming is ignored. The broadcast selection code tests this flag first (see Broadcast Device Selection)LAPIC before calibration
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DYNIRQ0x20The core may retarget the device\'s interrupt affinity at runtime, so a broadcast wakeup is delivered straight to the CPU that asked for it. Read in exactly one place, tick_broadcast_set_affinity()arch_mem_timer and many ARM SoC timers; no x86_64 device sets it
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU0x40Asserts the device can only ever serve one CPU (read only by the broadcast code; the cpumask is what binds a device to a CPU)arm_global_timer, exynos_mct — not the LAPIC or the ARM architected timer
CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER0x80Broadcast device is hrtimer-based (software)hrtimer broadcast emulation

Clock Event Device States

A clock event device moves through a well-defined state machine managed by the clockevents core:

Device Selection: Rating and Replacement

When a new clock event device registers, the tick layer decides whether to adopt it via tick_check_new_device(). The selection is based on the rating field — higher rating wins. Unlike clocksource ratings, which are spread thinly across a wide range, clock event ratings on the two architectures this book covers occupy a narrow band, and the values are chosen relative to one another rather than on any absolute scale:

Table 6-77. Clock Event Device Ratings on x86_64 and ARM64
DeviceRatingScopeRegistered byNotes
jiffies clockevent1Globalkernel/time/jiffies.cLowest valid rating; the floor that guarantees a tick exists at all
HPET legacy channel50Globalhpet_legacy_clockevent_register()Deliberately low — must lose to any per-CPU device
LAPIC timer100Per-CPUarch/x86/kernel/apic/apic.cCarries CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP; needs broadcast in deep idle
i8253 PIT110Globaldrivers/clocksource/i8253.cLast-resort legacy device
HPET per-CPU MSI channel110Per-CPUinit_one_hpet_msi_clockevent()Beats a plain LAPIC, loses to an ARAT-capable one
LAPIC timer with ARAT150Per-CPUsame, raised in setup_APIC_timer()C3STOP cleared; raised specifically to outrank the per-CPU HPET
ARM arch timer, MMIO frame400Globaldrivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer_mmio.carch_mem_timer; one block reachable by any CPU
ARM arch timer, per-CPU450Per-CPUdrivers/clocksource/arm_arch_timer.carch_sys_timer; the highest rating either architecture registers

Two things in that table are easy to misread. The first is that a clock event rating and a clocksource rating for the same piece of hardware are unrelated numbers: the HPET registers a clocksource at 250 but its legacy channel is a clock event device rated 50, and the ARM architected counter is a clocksource rated 400 while the timer built on it is a clock event device rated 450. They are separate frameworks with separate orderings, and the only thing a rating means is better than another device in the same framework.

The second is that the numbers encode deliberate policy, not a quality score. The two HPET channels differ by sixty points in the direction that looks wrong at first glance — the shared legacy channel is 50, the per-CPU MSI channel 110 — because the tick layer wants a per-CPU device wherever one exists, and a global device is useful mainly as a broadcast fallback. The LAPIC entries make the same point more sharply. A plain LAPIC timer is rated 100, below the per-CPU HPET at 110, because it stops in deep idle and will drag the broadcast machinery in with it. When the CPU advertises ARAT the timer no longer stops, CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP is cleared, and the rating is raised to 150 for the express purpose of overtaking that HPET channel — the comment in arch/x86/kernel/apic/apic.c says so directly: “Make LAPIC timer preferable over percpu HPET”. Note that this is the only runtime clock event rating change on x86_64 — the paravirtual clocksource demotions described earlier are a separate framework — and TSC-deadline mode is not what triggers it. A deadline-capable LAPIC changes its name to lapic-deadline and its programming path, but not its rating.

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — device selection logic */
void tick_check_new_device(struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    struct clock_event_device *curdev;
    struct tick_device *td;
    int cpu;

    cpu = smp_processor_id();
    td = &per_cpu(tick_cpu_device, cpu);
    curdev = td->evtdev;

    /* tick_check_replacement() compares rating + features */
    if (!tick_check_replacement(curdev, newdev))
        goto out_bc;  /* Rejected as per-CPU — try as broadcast device */

    /* Pin the driver module for as long as we hold the device */
    if (!try_module_get(newdev->owner))
        return;             /* note: return, not goto out_bc */

    /* If the device being displaced is the broadcast device, do not
     * hand it back to the clockevents layer — other CPUs still need it. */
    if (tick_is_broadcast_device(curdev)) {
        clockevents_shutdown(curdev);
        curdev = NULL;
    }

    /* Winner: swap in the new device */
    clockevents_exchange_device(curdev, newdev);
    tick_setup_device(td, newdev, cpu, cpumask_of(cpu));

    /* If new device supports oneshot, notify tick layer for mode upgrade */
    if (newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT)
        tick_oneshot_notify();
    return;

out_bc:
    /* Loser for per-CPU — can it serve as the broadcast device? */
    tick_install_broadcast_device(newdev, cpu);
}

The two steps between the gate and the swap are easy to skip past and both are load-bearing. try_module_get() pins the driver module for as long as the tick layer holds a reference to its device; a module already on its way out fails the call, and the function then returns rather than jumping to out_bc. That asymmetry is deliberate. A device that merely lost the per-CPU contest is still a perfectly good broadcast candidate, but a device whose module is disappearing is no use to anyone, so it is dropped outright instead of being offered a second role.

The broadcast check guards a subtler case. clockevents_exchange_device() normally releases the outgoing device back to the clockevents layer, where it becomes available for reuse. If the device currently installed as this CPU\'s tick device is also the system\'s broadcast device, releasing it would pull it out from under every other CPU that is relying on it to wake them from deep idle. So the code shuts it down and sets curdev to NULL, which makes the exchange a pure install with nothing given back — the kernel\'s own comment ends with an exclamation mark, which is rare enough in this file to be worth noticing.

In Linux 2.6, clock event device selection was simpler — the first device with the right features won. The rating system lets a better device displace a working one at runtime, which is what allows a per-CPU timer to take over from the global device set up early in boot, and lets a device rejected for per-CPU duty fall through to broadcast service instead of being discarded. The ONESHOT_STOPPED state (added in 2015 by commit 8fff52fd5093, not new in 7.0.12) covers a narrower case: a device that was programmed in one-shot mode and is temporarily stopped, so the kernel can leave it unarmed across a long NOHZ idle without tearing down its configuration and without it delivering an event nobody asked for.

Tick State Lifecycle: CPU Boot → Idle → Wake

The following figure shows how the tick_sched flags and tick_device mode evolve through a CPU's typical lifecycle — from boot through high-res activation, idle entry, tick stop, and wake:

Table 6-78. Tick Lifecycle Phase Summary
PhaseTriggerKey ActionsDuration
①BootFirst clock_event_device registeredtick_setup_device() sets periodic mode; HW generates HZ-rate IRQs~100ms (calibration)
②High-restick_check_oneshot_change() detects capable clocksourcetick_setup_sched_timer(): creates hrtimer, sets HIGHRES|NOHZ flags, switches device to ONESHOTIndefinite (running)
③Idle enterdo_idle() → tick_nohz_idle_enter()Sets INIDLE flag; evaluates whether tick can be stoppedBrief (decision point)
④Tick stoppedNo timers pending within next ticktick_nohz_stop_tick(): cancels sched_timer, programs next event to earliest timer, sets STOPPED; device enters ONESHOT_STOPPED~1ms to seconds
⑤WakeIRQ / timer expiry / IPItick_nohz_idle_exit(): clears INIDLE|STOPPED, catches up jiffies via tick_do_update_jiffies64(), restarts sched_timerBrief (resume)

struct tick_sched — Per-CPU Tick State Machine

The tick_sched structure is the central control block for the tick layer on each CPU. It manages tick emulation, idle accounting, and NOHZ state:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.h */
struct tick_sched {
    /* Common flags — bitfield controlling mode and state */
    unsigned long           flags;

    /* Tick handling: jiffies stall detection */
    unsigned int            stalled_jiffies;
    unsigned long           last_tick_jiffies;

    /* Tick handling: hrtimer-based emulated tick */
    struct hrtimer          sched_timer;    /* THE emulated periodic tick */
    ktime_t                 last_tick;      /* When sched_timer last fired */
    ktime_t                 next_tick;      /* Next programmed tick (NOHZ) */
    unsigned long           idle_jiffies;   /* jiffies at idle entry */
    ktime_t                 idle_waketime;  /* When CPU woke from idle */
    unsigned int            got_idle_tick;  /* Tick fired while idle */

    /* Idle entry tracking */
    seqcount_t              idle_sleeptime_seq;
    ktime_t                 idle_entrytime; /* When CPU entered idle */

    /* NOHZ: tick stop state */
    unsigned long           last_jiffies;   /* jiffies when tick was stopped */
    u64                     timer_expires_base;
    u64                     timer_expires;  /* Next timer deadline (absolute) */
    u64                     next_timer;     /* Debug: next timer expiry */
    ktime_t                 idle_expires;   /* Debug: next tick in idle */
    unsigned long           idle_calls;     /* Total idle entries */
    unsigned long           idle_sleeps;    /* Idle entries with tick stopped */

    /* Idle exit accounting */
    ktime_t                 idle_exittime;
    ktime_t                 idle_sleeptime;  /* Sum of tick-stopped idle time */
    ktime_t                 iowait_sleeptime; /* IO-wait portion of idle time */

    /* NO_HZ_FULL: tick dependency tracking */
    atomic_t                tick_dep_mask;  /* Subsystems needing the tick */

    /* Clocksource change notification */
    unsigned long           check_clocks;
};
Table 6-79. struct tick_sched — Field Groups and Purposes
GroupFieldsPurposeUsed By

Tick emulationsched_timer, last_tick, next_tickhrtimer that fires at HZ rate; tracks last/next fire timeHigh-res mode, NOHZ handler

Idle accountingidle_entrytime, idle_sleeptime, iowait_sleeptime, idle_callsTrack idle time for /proc/stat reportingcpufreq, scheduler, procfs

The flags field is a bitmask that tracks the current state of the tick on this CPU:

Tick Dependency Bits (NO_HZ_FULL)

When CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL is enabled, the kernel tracks which subsystems need the tick running via tick_dep_mask. If any bit is set, the tick cannot be stopped even if the CPU has only one runnable task:

Table 6-81. Tick Dependency Bits
BitConstantSubsystemWhen Set
0TICK_DEP_BIT_POSIX_TIMERPOSIX CPU timersProcess has active ITIMER_VIRTUAL / ITIMER_PROF
1TICK_DEP_BIT_PERF_EVENTSPerf event subsystemTick-based sampling events active on this CPU
2TICK_DEP_BIT_SCHEDSchedulerMore than 1 runnable task, or bandwidth throttling

/* include/linux/tick.h — tick dependency API */
void tick_dep_set(enum tick_dep_bits bit);          /* Global: all CPUs */
void tick_dep_clear(enum tick_dep_bits bit);

void tick_dep_set_cpu(int cpu, enum tick_dep_bits bit);   /* Per-CPU */
void tick_dep_clear_cpu(int cpu, enum tick_dep_bits bit);

void tick_dep_set_task(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit);
void tick_dep_clear_task(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit);

void tick_dep_set_signal(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit);
void tick_dep_clear_signal(struct signal_struct *signal, enum tick_dep_bits bit);

This dependency tracking is a key innovation of NO_HZ_FULL — it allows the kernel to precisely know when the tick is truly unnecessary, avoiding the subtle bugs that would result from blindly stopping the tick while subsystems still depend on it.

Global Coordination Variables

Three global variables coordinate the tick across all CPUs:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
int tick_do_timer_cpu __read_mostly = TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT;
    /* Which CPU updates jiffies + wall time.
     * TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT (-2): pre-boot, first tick device takes over
     * TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE (-1): duty dropped (NOHZ), next waker claims it
     * 0..NR_CPUS-1: specific CPU has the duty */

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
ktime_t tick_next_period;
    /* Absolute time of next jiffies update — used for fast lockless
     * check on 64-bit: if now < tick_next_period, skip jiffies update */

/* kernel/time/jiffies.c */
__cacheline_aligned_in_smp DEFINE_RAW_SPINLOCK(jiffies_lock);
__cacheline_aligned_in_smp seqcount_raw_spinlock_t jiffies_seq =
    SEQCNT_RAW_SPINLOCK_ZERO(jiffies_seq, &jiffies_lock);
    /* Serializes jiffies_64 updates.  The seqcount allows lockless
     * readers (read_seqcount_begin/retry) for timestamps */

The tick_do_update_jiffies64() function demonstrates the optimized locking pattern — on 64-bit architectures, it uses smp_load_acquire() for a lockless fast path that avoids the spinlock entirely when jiffies is already up to date:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_do_update_jiffies64(ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long ticks = 1;
    ktime_t delta, nextp;

    /* 64-bit fast path: lockless check with acquire semantics */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_64BIT)) {
        if (ktime_before(now, smp_load_acquire(&tick_next_period)))
            return;  /* No update needed — skip the lock entirely */
    }

    raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
    /* Re-check under lock (another CPU may have updated) */
    if (ktime_before(now, tick_next_period)) {
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        return;
    }

    write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);

    /* Compute missed ticks for NOHZ catch-up */
    delta = ktime_sub(now, tick_next_period);
    if (unlikely(delta >= TICK_NSEC)) {
        s64 incr = TICK_NSEC;
        ticks += ktime_divns(delta, incr);
        last_jiffies_update = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update,
                                           incr * ticks);
    } else {
        last_jiffies_update = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update, TICK_NSEC);
    }

    /* Advance jiffies */
    jiffies_64 += ticks;

    /* Keep tick_next_period up to date */
    nextp = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update, TICK_NSEC);
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_64BIT))
        smp_store_release(&tick_next_period, nextp); /* Pairs with acquire */
    else
        tick_next_period = nextp;

    write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);

    calc_global_load();
    raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
    update_wall_time();
}
Developer note: The smp_load_acquire() / smp_store_release() pair is a memory ordering optimization. On x86_64 (which has strong memory ordering), these compile to plain loads/stores. On ARM64 (which has weak ordering), they emit LDAR/STLR instructions to ensure the jiffies update is visible before tick_next_period advances.

The Three Operating Modes

The tick layer operates in one of three progressively more capable modes. At boot, the system starts in periodic mode — the simplest configuration where the hardware generates a fixed-rate interrupt at HZ frequency. Once the kernel discovers a high-resolution clocksource (such as the TSC or ARM Arch Timer counter) and confirms the clock event device supports one-shot programming, it transitions to high-resolution mode, replacing the hardware periodic interrupt with an hrtimer-based software tick. Finally, when the CPU enters idle with no imminent timers, the tick layer enters NOHZ (dynamic tick) mode, stopping the periodic tick entirely and programming the next event for the earliest pending timer.

These transitions are one-directional during normal operation — once a CPU reaches high-resolution mode, it stays there. The NOHZ state is entered and exited repeatedly as the CPU cycles between idle and running. The key insight is that each mode builds on the previous one:

Table 6-82. Three Tick Modes at a Glance
ModeHandlerHW ModeTick IntervalPowerTimer Precision
Periodictick_handle_periodic()PERIODIC (or SW-emulated ONESHOT)Fixed at 1/HZ (1–10ms)Low (constant IRQs)HZ granularity only
High-restick_nohz_handler()ONESHOT1/HZ via hrtimerMedium (still ticking)Nanosecond (hrtimer)
NOHZ (dyntick)tick_nohz_handler()ONESHOT / ONESHOT_STOPPEDVariable (next event)High (tick suppressed)Nanosecond

The transition from periodic to high-resolution is triggered by tick_check_oneshot_change() which runs inside the tick interrupt itself — the periodic handler checks whether the conditions for upgrade are met (one-shot capable device + CLOCK_SOURCE_VALID_FOR_HRES clocksource). Once triggered, tick_setup_sched_timer() creates the hrtimer-based emulated tick and sets the TS_FLAG_HIGHRES and TS_FLAG_NOHZ flags, enabling both high-resolution timers and tick suppression. The following figure illustrates these three modes, their transition triggers, and what each tick produces:

Mode 1: Periodic (Legacy)

In the simplest configuration (or at boot before high-resolution clocksources are registered), each CPU's clock event device generates a periodic interrupt at HZ frequency. The handler is tick_handle_periodic():

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
static void tick_periodic(int cpu)
{
    if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == cpu) {
        raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
        write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);

        tick_next_period = ktime_add_ns(tick_next_period, TICK_NSEC);
        do_timer(1);

        write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        update_wall_time();
    }

    update_process_times(user_mode(get_irq_regs()));
    profile_tick(CPU_PROFILING);
}

void tick_handle_periodic(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();
    tick_periodic(cpu);

    /* If the device doesn't support periodic mode natively,
     * reprogram it for the next tick (SW-emulated periodic) */
    if (!dev->event_handler)
        return;
    if (dev->state != CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT)
        return;
    /* ... reprogram for next TICK_NSEC ... */
}

Key points:

  • Only the duty CPU (tick_do_timer_cpu) updates jiffies and wall time — other CPUs skip this.
  • ALL CPUs run update_process_times() for their own scheduler and timer accounting.
  • If the hardware only supports one-shot mode, the periodic tick is SW-emulated by reprogramming the next event after each interrupt.

Mode 2: High-Resolution

Once a high-resolution clocksource is registered and the clock event device supports one-shot mode, the tick layer switches to high-resolution mode via tick_setup_sched_timer(). In this mode, the periodic tick becomes an hrtimer (ts->sched_timer) rather than a direct hardware periodic interrupt:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
void tick_setup_sched_timer(bool hrtimer)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    /* Register the tick as a CLOCK_MONOTONIC hard-IRQ hrtimer */
    hrtimer_setup(&ts->sched_timer, tick_nohz_handler,
                  CLOCK_MONOTONIC, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_HARD);

    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS) && hrtimer)
        tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_HIGHRES);

    hrtimer_set_expires(&ts->sched_timer, tick_init_jiffy_update());

    /* Offset the tick to avoid jiffies_lock contention across CPUs */
    if (sched_skew_tick) {
        u64 offset = TICK_NSEC >> 1;
        do_div(offset, num_possible_cpus());
        offset *= smp_processor_id();
        hrtimer_add_expires_ns(&ts->sched_timer, offset);
    }

    hrtimer_forward_now(&ts->sched_timer, TICK_NSEC);
    hrtimer_start_expires(&ts->sched_timer, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_PINNED_HARD);
    tick_nohz_activate(ts);
}

The handler tick_nohz_handler() fires at each tick period, calls tick_sched_do_timer() (which handles the duty CPU's jiffies/timekeeping update) and tick_sched_handle() (which calls update_process_times()), then re-arms itself for the next TICK_NSEC period.

Why this matters: In high-resolution mode, the hardware clock event device is in one-shot mode and can serve both hrtimer expiries (nanosecond precision) and the emulated periodic tick. The hrtimer_interrupt() handler processes all expired hrtimers including the tick, then programs the device for the earliest next expiry — which might be a sleep timer, a networking retransmit, or the next tick, whichever comes first.

Table 6-83. Periodic vs High-Resolution Mode Comparison
AspectPeriodic ModeHigh-Resolution Mode
HW modePeriodic (or SW-emulated oneshot)One-shot
Timer precision1/HZ (1-4ms)Nanosecond (clocksource limited)
Tick sourceDirect HW interrupthrtimer (sched_timer)
Next-event decisionFixed: always tick_next_periodEarliest of: next hrtimer, next tick, NOHZ deadline
NOHZ capableNoYes (tick can be suppressed)
Boot phaseInitial defaultAfter clocksource + oneshot HW ready

Mode 3: NOHZ (Tickless)

NOHZ mode extends high-resolution mode by suppressing the tick when it's not needed. This is covered in detail in the next section (NOHZ: The Tickless Kernel), but the key tick-layer interaction is:

  • Idle entry: tick_nohz_idle_enter() → tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() — cancels/defers the sched_timer to the next real event
  • Idle exit: tick_nohz_idle_exit() — restarts tick, catches up jiffies
  • IRQ during idle: tick_nohz_irq_exit() — re-evaluates whether tick should remain stopped

The Timekeeping Duty CPU

A critical design decision in the tick layer is that exactly one CPU is responsible for updating jiffies and calling update_wall_time(). This avoids thundering-herd contention on jiffies_lock — if every CPU tried to update jiffies simultaneously, the spinlock would become a scalability bottleneck on large systems. The designated CPU is identified by the global variable tick_do_timer_cpu.

In the Linux 2.6 era (before NOHZ), the duty CPU was static — typically CPU 0 held it for the entire system lifetime. In 7.0.12, the duty is dynamic: it migrates between CPUs as they enter and exit idle, and a stall-detection mechanism ensures jiffies still advances even if the duty CPU gets stuck in a VM exit or stop_machine().

The Duty Variable

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
int tick_do_timer_cpu __read_mostly = TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT;

/* Special values: */
#define TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT  (-2)  /* Pre-boot: first tick device takes over */
#define TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE  (-1)  /* Duty dropped (NOHZ): next waker claims it */
/* 0..NR_CPUS-1: specific CPU has the duty */

Duty Transfer Protocol

When the duty CPU stops its tick on entering NOHZ idle, it drops the duty by writing TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE; the next CPU to run a tick handler sees that value and claims it. The kernel comment above the variable gives it two jobs, and it is worth reading them in order, because the second is the one this subsection is about while the first explains why the variable exists at all:

  1. to prevent a thundering herd — without a designated CPU, every CPU taking a tick would try to grab the timekeeping lock at once, and the comment’s phrasing is “a gazillion of CPUs”;
  2. to hand the duty off in the NOHZ idle case, by parking it on a CPU number that does not exist so that whichever CPU next looks will take over. The same mechanism covers CPU hotplug.

So the handover is deliberately unsynchronised, but that is not the same as the update itself being racy. Two CPUs can certainly both decide they are the new duty CPU and both call tick_do_update_jiffies64(); what makes that harmless is the structure of that function rather than anything about the claim. It opens with a lockless check of tick_next_period and returns immediately if the next period has not yet arrived, so the overwhelming majority of calls never touch a lock at all. Only when that check says an update is due does it take jiffies_lock and then re-test the same condition with the lock held — the kernel comments the re-test with “Another CPU might have done the update already” — so the loser of the race unlocks and returns without advancing anything. This is an ordinary double-checked update, not a tolerated race.

The lockless half of that check is one of the few places in the tick layer where 32-bit and 64-bit builds genuinely diverge. On 64-bit the read is a single smp_load_acquire() of tick_next_period, paired with the release store made later in the same function. On 32-bit a ktime_t store is two 32-bit stores, and the first of them can become visible long before the second, so the quick check has to be wrapped in a jiffies_seq seqcount loop instead — the sequence count is doing here exactly what it does in the timekeeping core, guarding a multi-word value that cannot be read atomically.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c — tick_sched_do_timer() */
static void tick_sched_do_timer(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    int tick_cpu, cpu = smp_processor_id();

    tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);

    /* If duty was dropped (NOHZ idle), claim it.  Race is harmless:
     * jiffies_lock serializes the actual jiffies update. */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON) &&
        unlikely(tick_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE)) {
        WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
        tick_cpu = cpu;
    }

    /* Only the duty CPU updates jiffies + wall time */
    if (tick_cpu == cpu)
        tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);

    /* Stall detection: if jiffies hasn't changed for MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES
     * ticks, force an update even if we're not the duty CPU.
     * This handles VM-exit delays and stop_machine() blocking. */
    if (ts->last_tick_jiffies != jiffies) {
        ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
        ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
    } else {
        if (++ts->stalled_jiffies >= MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES) {
            /* Only clear the counter if we actually did the update.
             * If another CPU held the guard we retry on the next tick. */
            if (tick_limited_update_jiffies64(ts, now)) {
                ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
                ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
            }
        }
    }
}

/* Duty drop on NOHZ idle entry: */
/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c — inside tick_nohz_stop_tick() */
tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
if (tick_cpu == cpu) {
    WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE);
    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST);
}
Table 6-84. Timekeeping Duty Transfer — All Scenarios
EventConditionActionNew Value
Boottick_do_timer_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOTtick_setup_device() claims duty for first CPU registering a tick deviceCPU 0 (typically)
Duty CPU enters NOHZ idletick_cpu == cpu in tick_nohz_stop_tick()WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, NONE); sets TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LASTTICK_DO_TIMER_NONE
Any CPU fires ticktick_do_timer_cpu == NONEtick_sched_do_timer() claims: WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu)Waking CPU number
Duty CPU hotplug-offtick_do_timer_cpu == dying_cputick_cpu_dying(): assigns to first online CPU (in stop_machine, no races)cpumask_first(cpu_online_mask)
NO_HZ_FULL bootBoot CPU is nohz_fullFirst non-nohz_full secondary takes over via tick_do_timer_boot_cpu handoffHousekeeping CPU
Stall detectedstalled_jiffies >= 5tick_limited_update_jiffies64(): non-duty CPU forces jiffies update (atomic guard prevents pileup)Unchanged (temporary assist)

Stall Detection and Recovery

A new feature in Linux 7.0.12 is jiffies stall detection. If the duty CPU gets stuck — for example during a VM exit on a KVM guest where the host doesn't schedule the vCPU for several milliseconds, or during stop_machine() which halts all other CPUs — jiffies can fall behind. Each tick handler tracks whether jiffies has advanced since its last invocation. After MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES (5) consecutive ticks without jiffies advancing, a non-duty CPU forces an update via tick_limited_update_jiffies64():

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static bool tick_limited_update_jiffies64(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    static atomic_t in_progress;
    int inp;

    /* Prevent pile-up: only one CPU does the forced update at a time */
    inp = atomic_read(&in_progress);
    if (inp || !atomic_try_cmpxchg(&in_progress, &inp, 1))
        return false;

    if (ts->last_tick_jiffies == jiffies)
        tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);   /* Force catch-up */

    atomic_set(&in_progress, 0);
    return true;
}

This mechanism ensures that even if the duty CPU is temporarily unresponsive, time still advances. The atomic_t in_progress guard prevents multiple CPUs from all trying to force the update simultaneously — exactly one wins, catches up jiffies, and the others see the advance on their next tick.

NO_HZ_FULL: Pinned Duty

When CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL is active, the duty CPU never relinquishes. The kernel restricts the duty to a housekeeping CPU (one not in the nohz_full mask), ensuring that tick-free CPUs (running latency-sensitive workloads) are never burdened with jiffies updates. The comment in tick_sched_do_timer() explicitly warns:

/* If nohz_full is enabled, this should not happen because the
 * 'tick_do_timer_cpu' CPU never relinquishes. */
if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON) &&
    unlikely(tick_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE)) {
#ifdef CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL
    WARN_ON_ONCE(tick_nohz_full_running);  /* Bug if we get here! */
#endif
    WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
}

During boot, if the boot CPU itself is in the nohz_full mask, it temporarily holds the duty. When the first non-nohz_full secondary CPU comes online and registers its tick device, it takes over via the tick_do_timer_boot_cpu handoff mechanism in tick_setup_device().

Device Registration: tick_check_new_device()

When a clock event device is registered (e.g., LAPIC timer during CPU bringup, or HPET during PCI enumeration), the tick layer runs a multi-step evaluation to decide its fate. The device can end up in one of three roles: per-CPU tick source (replacing the current device), broadcast device (serving CPUs in deep idle), or rejected (if neither role applies).

The Decision Flowchart

The Replacement Checks

The decision involves two sub-checks, called together by tick_check_replacement():

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
bool tick_check_replacement(struct clock_event_device *curdev,
                            struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    if (!tick_check_percpu(curdev, newdev, smp_processor_id()))
        return false;
    return tick_check_preferred(curdev, newdev);
}
Table 6-85. Device Replacement Decision Logic
CheckFunctionCriteria (must all pass)Rationale
1. Per-CPU eligibility tick_check_percpu() • newdev->cpumask includes this CPU
• If not strictly per-CPU: IRQ affinity must be settable
• If current device is already CPU-local: prefer it over a shared device 		Ensures the device can actually deliver interrupts to this CPU. Prefers truly local devices (zero cross-CPU latency).
2. Quality preference tick_check_preferred() • Prefer one-shot capable over periodic-only
• Higher rating wins
• CPU-local device preferred even with lower rating than shared device 		One-shot is required for hrtimers and NOHZ. Rating reflects precision and latency. Local avoids IPI overhead.

Device Setup: First vs Replacement

Once a device wins the replacement check, tick_setup_device() handles two fundamentally different scenarios. For the first device on a CPU, it must bootstrap the entire tick subsystem — claiming timekeeping duty, setting the tick period origin, and installing the periodic handler. For a replacement, it must perform a seamless hot-swap: transfer the active handler and pending event to the new hardware without losing a single tick.

The full function also handles an important NO_HZ_FULL corner case: when the boot CPU is configured as a nohz_full CPU, it temporarily holds the timekeeping duty but immediately marks itself for handoff to the first non-nohz_full secondary CPU that comes online.

Full Annotated Code
/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — tick_setup_device() */
static void tick_setup_device(struct tick_device *td,
                              struct clock_event_device *newdev,
                              int cpu, const struct cpumask *cpumask)
{
    void (*handler)(struct clock_event_device *) = NULL;
    ktime_t next_event = 0;

    if (!td->evtdev) {
        /*
         * First device on this CPU.  Claim timekeeping duty if
         * no CPU has taken it yet (TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT = -2).
         */
        if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT) {
            WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
            tick_next_period = ktime_get();
#ifdef CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL
            /* Boot CPU is nohz_full → mark for handoff */
            if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu))
                tick_do_timer_boot_cpu = cpu;
        } else if (tick_do_timer_boot_cpu != -1 &&
                   !tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu)) {
            /* First non-nohz_full secondary — steal duty */
            tick_do_timer_boot_cpu = -1;
            WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
#endif
        }
        td->mode = TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC;
    } else {
        /* Replacement: save current state before swap */
        handler = td->evtdev->event_handler;
        next_event = td->evtdev->next_event;
        /* Prevent old device from calling stale handler */
        td->evtdev->event_handler = clockevents_handle_noop;
    }

    td->evtdev = newdev;

    /* Pin IRQ to this CPU if device serves multiple CPUs */
    if (!cpumask_equal(newdev->cpumask, cpumask))
        irq_set_affinity(newdev->irq, cpumask);

    /*
     * If this CPU uses broadcast (C3STOP device entering idle),
     * don't program the device — broadcast will wake us.
     */
    if (tick_device_uses_broadcast(newdev, cpu))
        return;

    /* Program hardware for current operating mode */
    if (td->mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
        tick_setup_periodic(newdev, 0);
    else
        tick_setup_oneshot(newdev, handler, next_event);
}
The NO_HZ_FULL Boot CPU Handoff

When CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULL is enabled and the boot CPU is in the nohz_full mask, it cannot permanently hold the timekeeping duty (its goal is to run tick-free for real-time workloads). The kernel handles this with a temporary marker:

Table 6-86. NO_HZ_FULL Boot CPU Duty Handoff
Stagetick_do_timer_cputick_do_timer_boot_cpuAction
1. Boot CPU claims dutyCPU 0CPU 0 (marked nohz_full)Normal claim, but marks itself for handoff
2. Secondary nohz_full CPUs come onlineCPU 0 (unchanged)CPU 0 (unchanged)Other nohz_full CPUs skip — they can't take duty either
3. First housekeeping CPU online← CPU N← -1 (done)Non-nohz_full CPU steals duty; handoff complete

This ensures the tick duty always ends up on a housekeeping CPU that will maintain periodic ticks, while the nohz_full CPUs remain free to go tick-less once the system is fully booted.

clockevents_exchange_device(): The Old Device Lifecycle

Before tick_setup_device() is called, clockevents_exchange_device(old, new) handles the ownership transfer at the clockevents layer:

/* kernel/time/clockevents.c */
void clockevents_exchange_device(struct clock_event_device *old,
                                 struct clock_event_device *new)
{
    if (old) {
        module_put(old->owner);     /* Release module reference */
        clockevents_switch_state(old, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_DETACHED);
        list_move(&old->list, &clockevents_released);
    }
    if (new) {
        BUG_ON(!clockevent_state_detached(new));
        clockevents_shutdown(new);  /* DETACHED → SHUTDOWN */
    }
}

The old device transitions through: active state → DETACHED → released list. Later, clockevents_notify_released() processes the released list and may re-evaluate devices (e.g., for broadcast use). The new device starts in DETACHED state and is moved to SHUTDOWN before tick_setup_device() programs it into PERIODIC or ONESHOT.

What Happens After Setup: tick_handle_periodic()

Once the device is programmed in periodic mode, interrupts arrive at tick_handle_periodic(). This handler is the heartbeat of the kernel during boot:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
void tick_handle_periodic(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();
    ktime_t next = dev->next_event;

    tick_periodic(cpu);  /* Core per-tick work */

    /* May have transitioned to HIGHRES via update_process_times()
     * → run_local_timers() → hrtimer_run_queues() */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_TICK_ONESHOT) &&
        dev->event_handler != tick_handle_periodic)
        return;  /* Handler was replaced — exit gracefully */

    if (!clockevent_state_oneshot(dev))
        return;  /* True periodic HW — no reprogramming needed */

    /* Oneshot HW emulating periodic: reprogram for next tick */
    for (;;) {
        next = ktime_add_ns(next, TICK_NSEC);
        if (!clockevents_program_event(dev, next, false))
            return;
        if (timekeeping_valid_for_hres())
            tick_periodic(cpu);
    }
}

static void tick_periodic(int cpu)
{
    if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == cpu) {
        raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
        write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
        tick_next_period = ktime_add_ns(tick_next_period, TICK_NSEC);
        do_timer(1);              /* Advance jiffies */
        write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        update_wall_time();       /* Update timekeeper */
    }
    update_process_times(user_mode(get_irq_regs()));
    profile_tick(CPU_PROFILING);
}
Table 6-87. tick_periodic() Per-Tick Work Breakdown
ActionDuty CPU Only?Function CalledPurpose
Advance jiffiesYesdo_timer(1)Increment jiffies_64 by 1 tick
Update wall timeYesupdate_wall_time()Read clocksource, adjust NTP, update timekeeper
Process timersNo — all CPUsupdate_process_times()Run timer wheel, scheduler tick, RCU, accounting
CPU profilingNo — all CPUsprofile_tick()Statistical profiling sample
Oneshot Emulation of Periodic

Many modern timer hardware (LAPIC TSC-deadline, ARM arch timer) only supports oneshot mode. When such hardware is first configured as a tick device, tick_setup_periodic() programs it in oneshot emulation: the hardware is set to CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT, but the handler reprograms the next event at tick_next_period + TICK_NSEC intervals — appearing periodic to the rest of the kernel. This is why tick_handle_periodic() contains the reprogram loop.

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — tick_setup_periodic() excerpt */
void tick_setup_periodic(struct clock_event_device *dev, int broadcast)
{
    tick_set_periodic_handler(dev, broadcast);

    if (!tick_device_is_functional(dev))
        return;

    if ((dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERIODIC) &&
        !tick_broadcast_oneshot_active()) {
        /* True periodic HW — set-and-forget */
        clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC);
    } else {
        /* Oneshot emulation — read tick_next_period under seqcount */
        unsigned int seq;
        ktime_t next;

        do {
            seq = read_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
            next = tick_next_period;
        } while (read_seqcount_retry(&jiffies_seq, seq));

        clockevents_switch_state(dev, CLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT);
        clockevents_program_event(dev, next, false);
    }
}
Table 6-88. tick_setup_device() — First Device vs Replacement (complete)
AspectFirst Device (boot)Replacement (upgrade)
Duty claimClaims tick_do_timer_cpu if still BOOT; NO_HZ_FULL may mark for later handoffNo change to duty assignment
ModeForced to TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODICPreserves current mode (periodic or oneshot)
Handlertick_handle_periodic() installed via tick_setup_periodic()Existing handler transferred to new device verbatim
next_eventComputed from tick_next_periodPreserved from old device (pending event not lost)
Old device stateNone — first deviceHandler → clockevents_handle_noop; state → DETACHED; moved to released list
IRQ affinityPinned to this CPU if not already per-CPUSame
Broadcast checkMay become broadcast client immediately (C3STOP device)Same
HW programmingCLOCK_EVT_STATE_PERIODIC or oneshot emulationCLOCK_EVT_STATE_ONESHOT with preserved next_event
Module refcountTaken for new deviceOld device released via module_put()
The basic first-vs-replacement logic existed in Linux 2.6.18 when the generic clockevents framework was introduced. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) the NO_HZ_FULL boot CPU handoff logic ensuring nohz_full CPUs never permanently hold timekeeping duty, (2) the tick_device_uses_broadcast() early-return that prevents programming a device already managed by broadcast, and (3) the clockevents_handle_noop safety net that ensures a late interrupt on the old device doesn't call a handler that now references new device state.

When Does Registration Happen?

Table 6-89. Clock Event Device Registration Points
WhenDeviceTriggered ByTypical Outcome
Early boot (BSP)HPET channel 0hpet_legacy_clockevent_register()First tick device on CPU 0, periodic mode
Each CPU bringupLAPIC timersetup_APIC_timer() → clockevents_register_device()Replaces HPET (higher rating + per-CPU)
ARM boot (each CPU)Arch Timerarch_timer_starting_cpu()Per-CPU tick device, oneshot capable
RuntimeTSC-deadline LAPICAfter TSC calibration validates deadline modeReplaces divisor-mode LAPIC (higher rating)
VirtualizationHyper-V / KVM synthetic timerParavirt initReplaces LAPIC (avoids VM-exit overhead)
In Linux 2.6, timer registration was ad-hoc — each architecture had its own setup path and there was no generic replacement logic. In 7.0.12, the tick_check_new_device() framework provides a uniform algorithm that works across x86, ARM64, RISC-V, and virtualized environments. The rating-based hot-swap allows seamless upgrades: at boot, a CPU might start with HPET (rating 110), then upgrade to LAPIC (rating 250) when each CPU comes online, then upgrade again to TSC-deadline LAPIC (rating 300+) once calibration completes — all without missing a tick.

Tick Broadcasting

Some hardware timers stop in deep CPU idle states (C3+ on x86, deeper cluster idle on ARM). These devices advertise CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP. When a CPU with such a timer enters deep idle, it cannot rely on its local timer for wakeup — instead, the broadcast mechanism provides a substitute. This is one of the most important power-management features of the tick layer: without it, a CPU wanting to save power by entering C3 would have to stay awake just for its timer interrupt.

The Problem: C3-Stopped Local Timers

On x86, the LAPIC timer (which is the primary per-CPU clock event device) stops counting in C3 and deeper idle states. The hardware simply freezes the timer counter when the CPU enters deep idle, meaning no interrupt will fire — even if a timer was programmed to expire. On ARM64, similar behavior occurs with some implementations of the arch timer when entering deep cluster idle states. The kernel discovers this via the CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP feature flag at device registration time.

Broadcast Architecture

Key Data Structures

The broadcast framework is built around a single global tick_device (the broadcast device), five CPU bitmask variables that track different CPU states, a per-CPU wakeup device pointer, and a raw spinlock. Understanding the relationship between these masks is essential for understanding broadcast behavior — each mask represents a different phase of the CPU's lifecycle relative to deep idle.

The broadcast framework maintains several cpumask bitmaps, each tracking a different aspect of CPU state:

Table 6-90. Broadcast Framework CPU Masks
VariableTypePurposeSet WhenCleared When
tick_broadcast_mask cpumask_var_t CPUs registered for periodic broadcast (C3STOP devices) Device has CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP or non-functional device registered Device replaced by non-C3STOP device, or CPU goes offline
tick_broadcast_on cpumask_var_t CPUs explicitly enabled for broadcast via tick_broadcast_control(ON) TICK_BROADCAST_ON or TICK_BROADCAST_FORCE TICK_BROADCAST_OFF (unless forced)
tick_broadcast_oneshot_mask cpumask_var_t CPUs currently in deep idle relying on broadcast for wakeup tick_broadcast_enter() — CPU entering deep idle tick_broadcast_exit() — CPU waking up
tick_broadcast_pending_mask cpumask_var_t CPUs whose deadline expired and IPI has been sent but not yet processed tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast() finds expired event CPU processes IPI in tick_broadcast_exit()
tick_broadcast_force_mask cpumask_var_t CPUs that must be force-woken (raced with broadcast handler) CPU exits idle and finds its next_event already expired tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast() processes the force mask
The Global Broadcast Device

The broadcast device is a single system-wide tick_device — the same structure used for per-CPU tick devices, but serving all CPUs collectively:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.h */
struct tick_device {
    struct clock_event_device *evtdev;  /* The hardware device */
    enum tick_device_mode mode;         /* TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC or _ONESHOT */
};

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c — global broadcast state */
static struct tick_device tick_broadcast_device;

/* Masks: allocated at boot via alloc_cpumask_var() */
static cpumask_var_t tick_broadcast_mask __cpumask_var_read_mostly;
static cpumask_var_t tick_broadcast_on __cpumask_var_read_mostly;
static cpumask_var_t tmpmask __cpumask_var_read_mostly;  /* scratch for handler */
static int tick_broadcast_forced;   /* Set once → never cleared */

static __cacheline_aligned_in_smp DEFINE_RAW_SPINLOCK(tick_broadcast_lock);

#ifdef CONFIG_TICK_ONESHOT
/* Oneshot-specific masks (only exist if CONFIG_TICK_ONESHOT) */
static cpumask_var_t tick_broadcast_oneshot_mask __cpumask_var_read_mostly;
static cpumask_var_t tick_broadcast_pending_mask __cpumask_var_read_mostly;
static cpumask_var_t tick_broadcast_force_mask __cpumask_var_read_mostly;

/* Per-CPU dedicated wakeup device (ARM always-on timers) */
static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct clock_event_device *, tick_oneshot_wakeup_device);
#endif
Locking and Synchronization

All broadcast operations are serialized under tick_broadcast_lock, a raw spinlock acquired with interrupts disabled. This is critical because the broadcast handler runs in interrupt context on one CPU while other CPUs may be concurrently entering or exiting deep idle:

Table 6-91. Broadcast Lock Usage Contexts
ContextFunctionWhy Lock Is Needed
CPU entering idle___tick_broadcast_oneshot_control(ENTER)Must atomically set oneshot_mask + reprogram broadcast device
CPU exiting idle___tick_broadcast_oneshot_control(EXIT)Must atomically clear oneshot_mask + check pending/force state
Broadcast IRQ handlertick_handle_oneshot_broadcast()Must atomically scan masks + send IPIs + reprogram next event
Device registrationtick_install_broadcast_device()Must atomically swap device + start/stop broadcast
Mode controltick_broadcast_control()Must atomically update on/mask + start/stop local/broadcast
CPU hotplugtick_broadcast_offline()Must clear all masks for departing CPU

One exception: tick_check_broadcast_expired() reads force_mask without the lock. It is marked noinstr (no instrumentation allowed) for use in the idle entry path after disabling interrupts — it uses arch_test_bit() for a single atomic read.

The tmpmask Scratch Variable

The handler uses a pre-allocated tmpmask to collect the set of CPUs to wake, avoiding dynamic allocation in interrupt context. The handler builds this mask by scanning oneshot_mask, then ORs in force_mask, then passes it to tick_do_broadcast() which calls the device's broadcast() callback (typically lapic_timer_broadcast() on x86 or IPI-based on ARM).

Mode Transitions

The broadcast device starts in TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC and transitions to TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT when the first CPU switches to high-res/NOHZ mode. This transition is one-way — once in oneshot mode, it never reverts:

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
void tick_broadcast_switch_to_oneshot(void)
{
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tick_broadcast_lock, flags);

    oldmode = tick_broadcast_device.mode;
    tick_broadcast_device.mode = TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT;
    bc = tick_broadcast_device.evtdev;
    if (bc)
        tick_broadcast_setup_oneshot(bc, oldmode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC);

    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tick_broadcast_lock, flags);
}

When transitioning from periodic, tick_broadcast_setup_oneshot() copies all CPUs from tick_broadcast_mask into tick_broadcast_oneshot_mask to ensure they continue receiving wakeups in the new mode. It programs the broadcast device for tick_next_period so that CPUs waiting for the next periodic tick still get woken.

Broadcast Device Selection

When a clock event device is rejected as a per-CPU tick device (by tick_check_new_device()), it falls through to tick_install_broadcast_device(). This function implements a three-stage evaluation: (1) try as a per-CPU wakeup device, (2) check suitability as a shared broadcast device, (3) install and configure. The entire function runs under clockevents_lock with interrupts disabled.

The Full Installation Code
/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
void tick_install_broadcast_device(struct clock_event_device *dev, int cpu)
{
    struct clock_event_device *cur = tick_broadcast_device.evtdev;

    /* Stage 1: Try as per-CPU oneshot wakeup device (ARM optimization) */
    if (tick_set_oneshot_wakeup_device(dev, cpu))
        return;  /* Accepted as wakeup device — done */

    /* Stage 2: Check broadcast eligibility */
    if (!tick_check_broadcast_device(cur, dev))
        return;  /* Not suitable — device goes unused */

    /* Stage 3: Module reference (prevent unload while in use) */
    if (!try_module_get(dev->owner))
        return;

    /* Swap: old device → DETACHED, new device → SHUTDOWN */
    clockevents_exchange_device(cur, dev);
    if (cur)
        cur->event_handler = clockevents_handle_noop;
    tick_broadcast_device.evtdev = dev;

    /* If CPUs already need broadcast, start immediately */
    if (!cpumask_empty(tick_broadcast_mask))
        tick_broadcast_start_periodic(dev);

    /* Oneshot support check */
    if (!(dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
        return;

    /* System already in oneshot? Switch broadcast device too */
    if (tick_broadcast_oneshot_active()) {
        tick_broadcast_switch_to_oneshot();
        return;
    }

    /*
     * Notify all CPUs — they might be stuck in periodic mode
     * because their C3STOP devices couldn't switch to oneshot
     * without a oneshot-capable broadcast device backing them.
     */
    tick_clock_notify();
}
The Eligibility Check in Detail
/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
static bool tick_check_broadcast_device(struct clock_event_device *curdev,
                                        struct clock_event_device *newdev)
{
    /* Reject: dummy devices, per-CPU devices, C3STOP devices */
    if ((newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY) ||
        (newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU) ||
        (newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP))
        return false;

    /* In oneshot mode, broadcast device must support oneshot */
    if (tick_broadcast_device.mode == TICKDEV_MODE_ONESHOT &&
        !(newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
        return false;

    /* Accept if no current device, or higher rating */
    return !curdev || newdev->rating > curdev->rating;
}
Table 6-92. Broadcast Device Eligibility Requirements
CheckRequirementRationalePasses ✓ / Fails ✗
1. Not DUMMY!(features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_DUMMY)Must be real hardware, not a placeholderHPET ✓, dummy ✗
2. Not PERCPU!(features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU)Broadcast must serve all CPUs via IPI; a device that declares itself per-CPU can only reach one. Note that the LAPIC and the ARM architected timer do not set this flag — they are excluded by check 3 and by their single-CPU cpumask.HPET ✓, arm_global_timer ✗
3. Not C3STOP!(features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP)Must keep running when CPUs are in deep idle — it is the wakeup sourceHPET ✓, LAPIC ✗
4. Oneshot capableRequired only if system already in oneshot modeCannot reprogram periodic-only device for per-CPU deadlinesHPET ✓ (has ONESHOT), PIT ✗ (periodic only)
5. Higher ratingnewdev->rating > curdev->ratingBetter precision/latency wins; first device always accepted (curdev == NULL)—
The Unblocking Effect: tick_clock_notify()

A crucial subtlety: on many x86 systems, per-CPU LAPIC timers have CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP. When such CPUs try to switch to oneshot/high-res mode, the tick layer blocks the switch because there's no broadcast device to provide wakeup backup. Installing a oneshot-capable broadcast device (typically HPET) unblocks all CPUs — tick_clock_notify() triggers each CPU to re-evaluate the oneshot transition:

Table 6-93. Boot Sequence: How Broadcast Unblocks High-Res Mode
StepEventState
1LAPIC timers registered (per-CPU, C3STOP)Periodic mode, no broadcast device
2CPUs try tick_check_oneshot_change()Blocked: C3STOP device without broadcast backup
3HPET registered → tick_install_broadcast_device()HPET becomes broadcast device
4tick_clock_notify() → IPIs to all CPUsEach CPU re-checks oneshot readiness
5CPUs switch to oneshot modeHigh-res timers + NOHZ enabled system-wide
Typical Broadcast Devices by Platform
Table 6-94. Common Broadcast Devices
PlatformBroadcast DeviceRatingFeaturesNotes
x86 (HPET present)HPET channel 0110ONESHOTMost common broadcast device on x86
x86 (no HPET)hrtimer-based pseudo—HRTIMERFallback; one CPU cannot enter deep idle
ARM (always-on timer)SP804 / Synopsys DW150+ONESHOTPlatform-specific always-on timer
ARM (no always-on)hrtimer-based pseudo—HRTIMERSame fallback as x86
Virtualized (KVM)Usually not needed——Synthetic timers typically don't have C3STOP
Linux 2.6 had a simpler broadcast selection — first suitable device won, no hot-swap. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) the per-CPU wakeup device path (checked first, avoids IPI overhead entirely on ARM), (2) rating-based replacement allowing a better broadcast device to take over at runtime, (3) the tick_clock_notify() unblocking mechanism that enables high-res mode system-wide when a suitable broadcast device appears, and (4) the try_module_get() safety check preventing module unload while the broadcast device is active.

Per-CPU Oneshot Wakeup Devices (ARM Optimization)

On some ARM SoCs, each CPU has access to a dedicated always-on timer that doesn't stop in deep idle (separate from the main arch timer). These can serve as per-CPU wakeup devices, avoiding the overhead of the shared broadcast + IPI path entirely:

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
static bool tick_set_oneshot_wakeup_device(struct clock_event_device *newdev,
                                           int cpu)
{
    /* Must be per-CPU, oneshot capable, not C3STOP, not dummy */
    if (!(newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_PERCPU) ||
        !(newdev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_ONESHOT))
        return false;

    if (!cpumask_equal(newdev->cpumask, cpumask_of(cpu)))
        return false;

    /* Higher rating wins over current wakeup device */
    if (curdev && newdev->rating <= curdev->rating)
        return false;

    newdev->event_handler = tick_oneshot_wakeup_handler;
    per_cpu(tick_oneshot_wakeup_device, cpu) = newdev;
    return true;
}

When a per-CPU wakeup device is available, __tick_broadcast_oneshot_control() programs it directly instead of going through the shared broadcast device — eliminating the IPI entirely.

Broadcast Modes: Periodic vs Oneshot

Table 6-95. Broadcast Operating Modes
AspectPeriodic BroadcastOneshot Broadcast
When usedSystem in periodic tick mode; some CPUs in deep idleSystem in high-res / NOHZ mode; CPUs entering deep idle
Handlertick_handle_periodic_broadcast()tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast()
Firing patternEvery TICK_NSEC, unconditionallyOnly at earliest deadline among idle CPUs
Wakeup targetAll CPUs in tick_broadcast_maskOnly CPUs with expired next_event
After fireReprograms for next tick (or auto-repeats for true periodic HW)Reprograms for next earliest deadline
Power costHigher — wakes all idle CPUs every tickLower — wakes only needed CPUs, at precise times
TransitionSwitches to oneshot when first CPU enters high-res modeNever reverts to periodic

The Oneshot Broadcast Handler

The oneshot handler is the heart of the broadcast framework. When the broadcast device fires, this handler scans all idle CPUs to find which ones have expired deadlines, sends IPIs to wake them, and reprograms the broadcast device for the next earliest deadline:

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
static void tick_handle_oneshot_broadcast(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    struct tick_device *td;
    ktime_t now, next_event;
    int cpu, next_cpu = 0;
    bool bc_local;

    raw_spin_lock(&tick_broadcast_lock);
    dev->next_event = KTIME_MAX;
    next_event = KTIME_MAX;
    cpumask_clear(tmpmask);
    now = ktime_get();

    /* Scan all CPUs in oneshot broadcast mask */
    for_each_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_oneshot_mask) {
        td = &per_cpu(tick_cpu_device, cpu);
        if (td->evtdev->next_event <= now) {
            /* Expired — add to wakeup mask */
            cpumask_set_cpu(cpu, tmpmask);
            cpumask_set_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_pending_mask);
        } else if (td->evtdev->next_event < next_event) {
            /* Not yet — track earliest for reprogram */
            next_event = td->evtdev->next_event;
            next_cpu = cpu;
        }
    }

    cpumask_clear_cpu(smp_processor_id(), tick_broadcast_pending_mask);

    /* Include force-wakeup CPUs */
    cpumask_or(tmpmask, tmpmask, tick_broadcast_force_mask);
    cpumask_clear(tick_broadcast_force_mask);

    /* Send IPIs to expired CPUs */
    bc_local = tick_do_broadcast(tmpmask);

    /* Reprogram for next earliest deadline */
    if (next_event != KTIME_MAX)
        tick_broadcast_set_event(dev, next_cpu, next_event);

    raw_spin_unlock(&tick_broadcast_lock);

    /* Handle local CPU's expired event (avoids IPI to self) */
    if (bc_local) {
        td = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
        td->evtdev->event_handler(td->evtdev);
    }
}

The Enter/Exit Protocol

CPUs interact with the broadcast framework through a well-defined enter/exit protocol when transitioning to and from deep idle states. The cpuidle governor calls tick_broadcast_enter() before entering deep idle and tick_broadcast_exit() upon waking:

The Ping-Pong Problem

A subtle race exists when a CPU exits idle at the same time the broadcast handler fires for that CPU. The broadcast handler has already found the CPU's next_event expired and is about to send an IPI. Meanwhile, the CPU wakes from a different interrupt and starts to reprogram its local timer. If the CPU reprograms its timer with an already-expired time, the timer fires immediately, the handler runs, and the CPU goes back to idle — where it re-enters broadcast, causing a ping-pong between broadcast registration and immediate expiry.

The kernel solves this with the pending_mask and force_mask:

Table 6-96. Broadcast Race Resolution
ScenarioDetectionResolution
Broadcast handler already sent IPI CPU finds itself in tick_broadcast_pending_mask Skip local reprogram — the IPI will arrive and the broadcast handler will invoke our event handler
CPU woke before IPI, event already expired dev->next_event <= now in exit path Set force_mask bit — the broadcast handler will include this CPU in the next wakeup batch, avoiding the reprogram-then-idle ping-pong
CPU woke from different interrupt, event not expired dev->next_event > now and not in pending mask Normal reprogram: tick_program_event(dev->next_event, 1)

The hrtimer-Based Broadcast

On systems where no always-on hardware timer exists for broadcast (common in some virtualized environments), the kernel creates a pseudo-broadcast device backed by an hrtimer. This is marked with CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER and introduces a special constraint: the hrtimer broadcast device runs on some CPU's local timer, so that CPU cannot enter deep idle (it would stop the broadcast device). The broadcast_needs_cpu() check prevents this:

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
static int broadcast_needs_cpu(struct clock_event_device *bc, int cpu)
{
    if (!(bc->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER))
        return 0;      /* Real HW device — any CPU can sleep */
    if (bc->next_event == KTIME_MAX)
        return 0;      /* No pending event — safe to sleep */
    return bc->bound_on == cpu ? -EBUSY : 0;  /* This CPU hosts broadcast */
}
Table 6-97. Hardware vs hrtimer Broadcast
AspectHardware Broadcast (HPET)hrtimer-Based Broadcast
Device typeDedicated always-on timerPseudo-device backed by local hrtimer
Feature flagNone (default)CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER
Hosting CPUN/A — hardware fires independentlybc->bound_on = CPU running the hrtimer
Deep idle restrictionNone — all CPUs can enter C3+Hosting CPU cannot enter deep idle
Local handler callSafe to call recursivelyMust avoid hrtimer recursion (special check in tick_do_broadcast())
Common platformsx86 with HPET, ARM always-on timerVMs without paravirt timers, some embedded

tick_broadcast_control(): Runtime Mode Switching

The idle subsystem uses tick_broadcast_control() to dynamically enable or disable broadcast mode for the current CPU based on the selected C-state:

/* kernel/time/tick-broadcast.c */
void tick_broadcast_control(enum tick_broadcast_mode mode)
{
    struct clock_event_device *bc, *dev;
    struct tick_device *td;
    int cpu, bc_stopped;
    unsigned long flags;

    /* Protects also the local clockevent device. */
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&tick_broadcast_lock, flags);
    td  = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_device);
    dev = td->evtdev;

    /* Only acts on devices that actually stop in deep idle */
    if (!dev || !(dev->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP))
        goto out;
    if (!tick_device_is_functional(dev))
        goto out;

    cpu = smp_processor_id();
    bc  = tick_broadcast_device.evtdev;
    bc_stopped = cpumask_empty(tick_broadcast_mask);  /* state on entry */

    switch (mode) {
    case TICK_BROADCAST_FORCE:
        tick_broadcast_forced = 1;
        fallthrough;
    case TICK_BROADCAST_ON:
        cpumask_set_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_on);
        /* test_and_set: only act on the 0 → 1 edge */
        if (!cpumask_test_and_set_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_mask)) {
            if (bc && !(bc->features & CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_HRTIMER) &&
                tick_broadcast_device.mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
                clockevents_shutdown(dev);
        }
        break;

    case TICK_BROADCAST_OFF:
        if (tick_broadcast_forced)
            break;  /* FORCE is permanent */
        cpumask_clear_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_on);
        /* test_and_clear: only act on the 1 → 0 edge */
        if (cpumask_test_and_clear_cpu(cpu, tick_broadcast_mask)) {
            if (tick_broadcast_device.mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
                tick_setup_periodic(dev, 0);
        }
        break;
    }

    if (bc) {
        if (cpumask_empty(tick_broadcast_mask)) {
            if (!bc_stopped)
                clockevents_shutdown(bc);      /* last client left */
        } else if (bc_stopped) {               /* first client arrived */
            if (tick_broadcast_device.mode == TICKDEV_MODE_PERIODIC)
                tick_broadcast_start_periodic(bc);
            else
                tick_broadcast_setup_oneshot(bc, false);
        }
    }
out:
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&tick_broadcast_lock, flags);
}

Almost every line of this function is an edge detector, and that is the point. cpuidle calls it on every idle entry and exit, so it must be safe to call repeatedly with the same argument. The two cpumask_test_and_set_cpu() / cpumask_test_and_clear_cpu() forms are what make it so: the local device is shut down only on the transition into the broadcast mask and restarted only on the transition out of it, never on a repeat call that finds the bit already in the state it wants. The same idea appears at the other end of the function, where bc_stopped is sampled before the switch runs. Comparing that snapshot against the mask afterwards is how the code distinguishes “the mask is empty and was already empty” — nothing to do — from “the last client just left”, which is what actually warrants powering the broadcast device down.

The two guards at the top are equally important. A device without CLOCK_EVT_FEAT_C3STOP keeps running in every idle state the platform offers, so it has no need of a stand-in and the whole function is a no-op for it — on an ARM64 system whose firmware leaves the architected timer running, this is the path every cpuidle call takes. The tick_device_is_functional() test excludes a device that is merely a placeholder. Note also that everything after the lock is taken runs under tick_broadcast_lock, and the kernel comment is explicit that this lock covers the local clock event device as well as the broadcast one, which is why the goto out style is used rather than bare returns.

Table 6-98. tick_broadcast_control() Modes
ModeEffectCallerReversible?
TICK_BROADCAST_ONEnable broadcast for this CPUcpuidle before entering C3+Yes
TICK_BROADCAST_OFFDisable broadcast, restart local timercpuidle after exiting to C1/C2Yes
TICK_BROADCAST_FORCEPermanently enable broadcastBIOS/ACPI quirk detectionNo — cannot be undone
The broadcast framework in Linux 2.6 was relatively simple — periodic-only, x86-centric, and tightly coupled to HPET. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) per-CPU oneshot wakeup devices for ARM SoCs, avoiding IPI overhead entirely, (2) the hrtimer-based pseudo-broadcast for systems without always-on hardware, (3) the pending_mask/force_mask ping-pong prevention logic, (4) TICK_BROADCAST_FORCE for BIOS quirks that permanently disable local timers, and (5) the oneshot broadcast handler that precisely targets only expired CPUs rather than waking all idle CPUs every tick.

The Tick Handler Path (Detailed)

Every tick — whether delivered by a periodic clock event, an hrtimer callback, or a NOHZ re-entry — ultimately executes the same per-CPU housekeeping pipeline. The path splits into two phases: a global duty (timekeeping, executed by one CPU) and per-CPU work (executed by every CPU on every tick).

Entry Points: Three Modes, One Pipeline

The kernel has three distinct tick entry points depending on the operating mode, but they all converge at the same two functions:

Phase 1: Global Timekeeping Duty

Only one CPU — the tick_do_timer_cpu — performs global timekeeping on each tick. This is the kernel's heartbeat:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c — NOHZ/highres path */
static void tick_sched_do_timer(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    int tick_cpu, cpu = smp_processor_id();

    /* Reclaim duty if previous owner went to sleep */
    tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON) &&
        unlikely(tick_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE)) {
        WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
        tick_cpu = cpu;
    }

    /* Only the duty CPU updates jiffies */
    if (tick_cpu == cpu)
        tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);

    /* Stall detection: force update after MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES */
    if (ts->last_tick_jiffies != jiffies) {
        ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
        ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
    } else if (++ts->stalled_jiffies >= MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES) {
        if (tick_limited_update_jiffies64(ts, now)) {
            ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
            ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
        }
    }
}

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c — the actual jiffies update */
static void tick_do_update_jiffies64(ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long ticks = 1;

    /* Fast path: 64-bit lockless check */
    if (ktime_before(now, smp_load_acquire(&tick_next_period)))
        return;

    raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
    /* Double-check under lock (another CPU may have updated) */
    if (ktime_before(now, tick_next_period)) {
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        return;
    }

    write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);

    /* Handle catch-up: may advance multiple ticks at once */
    ktime_t delta = ktime_sub(now, tick_next_period);
    if (unlikely(delta >= TICK_NSEC))
        ticks += ktime_divns(delta, TICK_NSEC);

    tick_next_period = ktime_add_ns(tick_next_period, ticks * TICK_NSEC);
