    do_timer(ticks);       /* jiffies_64 += ticks; calc_global_load() */
    write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
    raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);

    update_wall_time();    /* advance CLOCK_REALTIME / CLOCK_MONOTONIC */
}
Table 6-99. Global Duty: What Happens Inside
StepFunctionActionProtected By
1tick_do_update_jiffies64()Advance jiffies_64 by 1 (or more if catching up)jiffies_lock + seqcount
2do_timer(ticks)Increment jiffies_64, call calc_global_load()Inside seqcount critical section
3update_wall_time()Read clocksource, advance xtime/wall_to_monotonictk_core.seq seqcount
4Stall detectionForce jiffies update if duty CPU stalled (VM exit)MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES threshold

The periodic path (tick_periodic()) does the same work but inline and simpler — it always advances by exactly 1 tick, never catching up:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — periodic mode */
static void tick_periodic(int cpu)
{
    if (READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == cpu) {
        raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);
        write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
        tick_next_period = ktime_add_ns(tick_next_period, TICK_NSEC);
        do_timer(1);
        write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        update_wall_time();
    }
    update_process_times(user_mode(get_irq_regs()));
    profile_tick(CPU_PROFILING);
}

Phase 2: Per-CPU Housekeeping

After the duty CPU updates time, every CPU executes update_process_times(). This is the function that fans out to all per-CPU subsystems:

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
void update_process_times(int user_tick)
{
    struct task_struct *p = current;

    account_process_tick(p, user_tick);   /* ① CPU time accounting */
    run_local_timers();                   /* ② Timer wheel + hrtimer check */
    rcu_sched_clock_irq(user_tick);       /* ③ RCU grace period */
#ifdef CONFIG_IRQ_WORK
    if (in_hardirq())
        irq_work_tick();                  /* ④ Deferred IRQ work */
#endif
    sched_tick();                         /* ⑤ Scheduler tick */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS))
        run_posix_cpu_timers();           /* ⑥ POSIX CPU timers */
}
Table 6-100. Per-Tick Subsystem Actions (Complete)
#SubsystemFunctionWhat It DoesScopeContext
①CPU accountingaccount_process_tick()Charge 1 tick to user/system/nice/irq/softirq/steal/guestPer-CPUHard IRQ
②Timer wheelrun_local_timers()Check hrtimer switch; raise TIMER_SOFTIRQ if timers expiredPer-CPUHard IRQ
③RCUrcu_sched_clock_irq()Advance grace periods, report quiescent states, detect stallsPer-CPUHard IRQ
④IRQ workirq_work_tick()Execute deferred work items queued from NMI/unsafe contextsPer-CPUHard IRQ
⑤Schedulersched_tick()Update vruntime, check preemption, load balance, perf eventsPer-CPU + globalHard IRQ (under rq lock)
⑥POSIX timersrun_posix_cpu_timers()Check ITIMER_VIRTUAL, ITIMER_PROF, RLIMIT_CPUPer-processHard IRQ

Deep Dive: run_local_timers()

This function serves two critical roles — it is the mode transition trigger and the timer wheel dispatcher:

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
static void run_local_timers(void)
{
    struct timer_base *base = this_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[BASE_LOCAL]);

    /* Check if we should switch to high-res mode */
    hrtimer_run_queues();

    /* Check each timer base (LOCAL, GLOBAL, DEF) */
    for (int i = 0; i < NR_BASES; i++, base++) {
        if (time_after_eq(jiffies, READ_ONCE(base->next_expiry)) ||
            (i == BASE_DEF && tmigr_requires_handle_remote())) {
            raise_timer_softirq(TIMER_SOFTIRQ);
            return;
        }
    }
}
Table 6-101. Timer Bases in 7.0.12
BaseConstantPinningMigrationUse Case
LocalBASE_LOCALPinned to enqueuing CPUNeverPer-CPU timers (e.g., watchdog)
GlobalBASE_GLOBALCan run anywhereVia timer migrationNon-pinned timers (most mod_timer())
DeferrableBASE_DEFDeferred to non-idle CPUVia tmigrBackground work that shouldn't wake CPUs

The hrtimer_run_queues() call inside run_local_timers() is particularly important — it checks tick_check_oneshot_change() and if a high-res clocksource and broadcast device are now available, triggers the switch to high-resolution mode via hrtimer_switch_to_hres(). This is how the system dynamically transitions from periodic to oneshot during boot.

Deep Dive: sched_tick()

The scheduler's tick handler is where the kernel enforces time-sharing and load balancing:

/* kernel/sched/core.c */
void sched_tick(void)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();
    struct rq *rq = cpu_rq(cpu);
    struct task_struct *donor;
    struct rq_flags rf;

    if (housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE))
        arch_scale_freq_tick();        /* DVFS frequency update */

    sched_clock_tick();                /* calibrate local sched_clock */

    rq_lock(rq, &rf);
    donor = rq->donor;                /* sched_ext: accounting via donor */

    psi_account_irqtime(rq, donor, NULL);  /* PSI pressure tracking */
    update_rq_clock(rq);

    /* Architecture-specific hardware pressure (thermal) */
    update_hw_load_avg(rq_clock_task(rq), rq, arch_scale_hw_pressure(cpu));

    /* Lazy preemption: convert to full preempt if overdue */
    if (dynamic_preempt_lazy() && tif_test_bit(TIF_NEED_RESCHED_LAZY))
        resched_curr(rq);

    /* The scheduling class does the actual work */
    donor->sched_class->task_tick(rq, donor, 0);

    calc_global_load_tick(rq);
    sched_core_tick(rq);               /* core scheduling fairness */
    scx_tick(rq);                      /* sched_ext extensible hook */

    rq_unlock(rq, &rf);

    perf_event_task_tick();            /* perf multiplexing rotation */

    if (donor->flags & PF_WQ_WORKER)
        wq_worker_tick(donor);         /* workqueue concurrency management */

    if (!scx_switched_all()) {
        rq->idle_balance = idle_cpu(cpu);
        sched_balance_trigger(rq);     /* periodic load balance check */
    }
}
Table 6-102. sched_tick() Substeps
StepActionPurpose
1arch_scale_freq_tick()Update CPU capacity estimate for EAS (Energy Aware Scheduling)
2sched_clock_tick()Keep per-CPU sched_clock monotonic (TSC calibration)
3psi_account_irqtime()Track PSI (Pressure Stall Information) for cgroup v2
4task_tick(rq, donor, 0)Class-specific: CFS updates vruntime, RT checks time limit
5calc_global_load_tick()Contribute to /proc/loadavg calculation
6sched_core_tick()Core scheduling: ensure sibling HT fairness
7scx_tick()sched_ext: call BPF scheduler's .tick() hook
8perf_event_task_tick()Rotate multiplexed perf counters
9sched_balance_trigger()Check if load balancing needed (softirq)

The Mode Transition Trigger

A critical hidden behavior in the tick path: every call to run_local_timers() → hrtimer_run_queues() checks whether the system should switch from low-resolution periodic mode to high-resolution oneshot mode:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c */
void hrtimer_run_queues(void)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);

    /* Already in high-res mode? Nothing to do here. */
    if (hrtimer_hres_active(cpu_base))
        return;

    /* Check if conditions are met for the switch */
    if (tick_check_oneshot_change(!hrtimer_is_hres_enabled())) {
        hrtimer_switch_to_hres();  /* THE MODE SWITCH HAPPENS HERE */
        return;
    }

    /* Still in low-res: expire any hard hrtimers manually */
    __hrtimer_run_queues(cpu_base, now, flags, HRTIMER_ACTIVE_HARD);
}

This means the periodic tick handler contains the seed of its own replacement. Once a high-res clocksource is verified and a broadcast device installed, the next tick execution switches the CPU to oneshot mode and the periodic handler is never called again.

The Oneshot Emulation Loop

When the clock event device only supports oneshot mode (no auto-reload), tick_handle_periodic() must manually reprogram for the next tick. If the system fell behind (e.g., long IRQ-off section), it executes a catch-up loop:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c */
void tick_handle_periodic(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();
    ktime_t next = dev->next_event;

    dev->next_event_forced = 0;
    tick_periodic(cpu);

    /* Did we just transition to HIGHRES/NOHZ? If so, stop. */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_TICK_ONESHOT) &&
        dev->event_handler != tick_handle_periodic)
        return;

    /* Periodic hardware auto-reloads — done */
    if (!clockevent_state_oneshot(dev))
        return;

    /* Oneshot emulating periodic: reprogram for next period */
    for (;;) {
        next = ktime_add_ns(next, TICK_NSEC);
        if (!clockevents_program_event(dev, next, false))
            return;   /* Programmed successfully */
        /* Missed deadline — catch up */
        if (timekeeping_valid_for_hres())
            tick_periodic(cpu);
    }
}
Table 6-103. tick_handle_periodic() Outcomes
ConditionBehaviorExample
Device in periodic stateSingle tick_periodic(), return (HW auto-reloads)Legacy PIT (channel 0)
Device in oneshot state, on timetick_periodic() + reprogram next + TICK_NSECLAPIC in periodic-emulation
Device in oneshot state, missed deadlineCatch-up loop: multiple tick_periodic() callsLong IRQ disabled, VM exit
Mode switched during tickEarly return (new handler takes over)First high-res clocksource appears

NOHZ Path: tick_sched_handle()

In NOHZ/high-res mode, the handler wrapper adds watchdog maintenance before calling the same update_process_times():

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_sched_handle(struct tick_sched *ts, struct pt_regs *regs)
{
    /* If tick was stopped (idle), maintain watchdog + idle accounting */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON) &&
        tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
        touch_softlockup_watchdog_sched();
        if (is_idle_task(current))
            ts->idle_jiffies++;
        ts->next_tick = 0;  /* force recalculation */
    }

    update_process_times(user_mode(regs));
    profile_tick(CPU_PROFILING);
}

Execution Time Budget

The tick handler runs in hard IRQ context and must complete quickly. Here are typical execution times on modern hardware:

Table 6-104. Tick Handler Time Budget (Typical)
ComponentTypical DurationNotes
tick_do_update_jiffies64()50–200 nsOnly on duty CPU; fast path is lockless read
account_process_tick()20–50 nsSimple counter increment
run_local_timers()30–100 nsJust checks next_expiry; softirq does real work
rcu_sched_clock_irq()50–300 nsVaries: quiescent state report vs stall check
sched_tick()200–800 nsMost expensive; rq lock + vruntime update
profile_tick()10–30 nsUsually NOP unless profiling enabled
Total~0.5–2 µsWell within 4ms tick period (HZ=250)
The tick handler path has evolved significantly: (1) scheduler_tick() is now sched_tick() with sched_ext BPF hooks, PSI accounting, lazy preemption support, and core scheduling fairness; (2) irq_work_tick() is new — enables deferred work from NMI context; (3) the timer wheel now has three bases (local/global/deferrable) with timer migration support; (4) tick_do_update_jiffies64() adds a stall detector for VMs where the duty CPU gets VMEXIT'd for milliseconds; (5) hrtimer_run_queues() is the dynamic mode-switch trigger that lets the system self-upgrade from periodic to high-res during boot; (6) perf_event_task_tick() moves inside sched_tick() for better lock locality.

NOHZ: The Tickless Kernel

The four preceding sections built a machine that ticks. Clock sources gave the kernel something to count, clock event devices gave it something that can interrupt, the timekeeping core turned counts into time, and the tick layer arranged for every CPU to be interrupted at a steady HZ and to do a fixed list of work each time. This section asks the opposite question: what is all that ticking actually for, and what happens if we stop it?

The first half of the answer is uncomfortable. On an idle CPU almost every tick finds nothing to do — it wakes the core out of a deep C-state, drags roughly four kilobytes of kernel structures back into cache, discovers no timer has expired and no task wants the CPU, and goes back to sleep. At HZ=250 that is 250 pointless wakeups per second per core, on every core, forever. On a laptop it is battery; in a data centre it is a measurable fraction of the power bill; on an isolated core running a trading or DPDK loop it is jitter that no amount of tuning elsewhere can remove.

The second half is why the tick survived so long anyway: it is load-bearing. A great deal of the kernel quietly assumes the tick will come. Four dependencies matter most, and each one becomes a distinct pressure the moment the tick stops:

  • Somebody must count jiffies. If the tick stops everywhere, the kernel's coarse clock freezes and time stops advancing. That forces both a catch-up mechanism, so a waking CPU can advance jiffies by the whole interval at once, and the timekeeping-duty rule from the previous section, so at least one CPU keeps ticking on everyone else's behalf.
  • The tick is when expiries get noticed. A stopped CPU is not scanning timer queues, so before it sleeps it must ask how long it may safely sleep for — which means computing the next expiry across the timer wheel, the hrtimer bases, and the timer-migration hierarchy, and re-arming the clock event device for exactly that moment.
  • Accounting is charged per tick. Process times, scheduler time slices, and idle statistics are all traditionally incremented one tick at a time. With no ticks, the numbers must instead come from timestamps taken at the transitions — which is why tickless idle needs measurement-based accounting, and why tickless execution additionally needs context tracking to know when user code started and stopped.
  • Other subsystems ask for it. RCU, perf, POSIX CPU timers, scheduler bandwidth control and the softlockup watchdog can each require a tick at any moment. Rather than let them break silently, the kernel makes the requirement explicit as a per-CPU and per-task dependency mask that any subsystem can set, and which forces the tick back on.

Those four pressures explain the shape of everything that follows, and they also explain why there are two tickless modes rather than one. Stopping the tick on an idle CPU is comparatively easy: nothing is running, so nothing needs accounting and nothing else is depending on the tick. Stopping it on a busy CPU means keeping accurate accounting for code that is actively running, which is a far heavier obligation — and it only pays off if exactly one task is runnable and no subsystem has registered a dependency. The first case is NO_HZ_IDLE and is on by default nearly everywhere; the second is NO_HZ_FULL and is a specialist tool.

The rest of this section works through six questions, in the order the subsections answer them:

  1. When may a CPU stop its tick, and how long may it sleep? The cheap pre-conditions in can_stop_idle_tick(), the expensive next-expiry scan in tick_nohz_next_event(), and how tick_nohz_idle_enter() and tick_nohz_idle_exit() hook into the idle loop.
  2. What if the CPU is busy rather than idle? NO_HZ_FULL: the dependency mask, context tracking, the housekeeping CPUs that absorb the work the isolated CPUs refuse, and the long list of conditions that quietly restart the tick anyway.
  3. If jiffies stopped, how does time catch up? The lazy update on wake, and why it cannot simply be done by whichever CPU notices first.
  4. If nothing is charging idle time one tick at a time, how does /proc/stat stay honest? Measurement-based accounting, and the timestamps it takes at each transition.
  5. What does it cost, and when is it a loss? Per-transition overhead against steady-state saving, and the idle durations below which stopping the tick is worse than leaving it running.
  6. And before any of that: which mode are you even in? The three tick behaviours selectable at build time, and what each one actually promises.

Version history. Everything in this section is new. Linux 2.6.11 had no tickless mode at all: every CPU took a timer interrupt HZ times a second from boot to shutdown, idle or not. NO_HZ_IDLE arrived in 2.6.21 and is now the default; NO_HZ_FULL followed in 3.10 and has been refined continuously since. Linux 7.0.12 adds a further twist — domain isolation is no longer purely a boot-time decision, and can now be reshaped at runtime through cpuset partitions.

The Problem: Why Ticks Are Expensive

A periodic tick on every CPU costs more than just the handler time (~1–2 µs). The real costs are:

Table 6-105. Cost of Unnecessary Ticks
CostImpactWho Cares
Wakeup from deep C-state10–200 µs exit latency + cache refillPower management, mobile, servers
Cache pollutionTick handler touches ~4 KB of structuresHPC, latency-sensitive workloads
Scheduling jitter±4ms interrupt noise on isolated CPUsReal-time, financial trading, audio
Virtualization overheadVM exits on every tick (host ↔ guest transition)Cloud providers, KVM/Xen hosts
Power consumption~1–5% power per idle core at HZ=250Battery devices, data center PUE

NOHZ Configuration Modes

The Linux kernel provides three distinct tick behavior modes, selectable at compile time through the CONFIG_HZ_* and CONFIG_NO_HZ_* Kconfig options. Each mode represents a different trade-off between timing precision, power efficiency, and implementation complexity. The choice is not merely cosmetic — it fundamentally changes how the kernel schedules timer interrupts, accounts for CPU time, and manages the transition between idle and active states.

The default mode since kernel 2.6.21 is NO_HZ_IDLE, which stops the periodic tick when the CPU is idle but maintains it during active execution. This covers the vast majority of use cases: servers, desktops, and mobile devices all benefit from reduced power consumption during idle periods without any loss of scheduling precision during active workloads. The more aggressive NO_HZ_FULL mode extends tickless operation to running CPUs, but imposes strict constraints on which workloads benefit (only single-runnable-task CPUs qualify) and carries measurable overhead for the enter/exit transitions.

Table 6-104 summarizes the three modes, their behavior, and typical deployment scenarios:

Table 6-106. NOHZ Configuration Options
ConfigMode NameBehaviorUse Case
CONFIG_HZ_PERIODICAlways-tickPeriodic tick on all CPUs regardless of stateEmbedded with strict timing
CONFIG_NO_HZ_IDLEIdle ticklessStop tick when CPU enters idle loop (default)All general-purpose systems
CONFIG_NO_HZ_FULLFull tickless (adaptive)Stop tick even on busy CPUs (single-task)RT, HPC, latency-critical

The behavioural difference between these modes is best understood visually. Figure 6-28 runs the same 128 ms workload — busy, then idle, then busy again — past all three modes at HZ=250, so the only thing that varies between the rows is the tick policy. The tally along the left is the whole argument: the identical workload costs 33 tick interrupts under HZ_PERIODIC, 18 under NO_HZ_IDLE, and 2 under NO_HZ_FULL.

Each reduction comes from a different concession. HZ_PERIODIC keeps ticking through the idle stretch, and every one of those interrupts drags the core out of its deepest C-state to discover there is nothing to do. NO_HZ_IDLE removes exactly those, and nothing else — the busy phases tick as before, which is why it is safe enough to be the default everywhere. NO_HZ_FULL goes further and stops the tick while the CPU is running, which is what buys sub-microsecond determinism for real-time and HPC workloads, but only holds while a single task is runnable and no subsystem has registered a tick dependency.

With the three modes established, we can examine how the kernel actually implements the tickless behavior. The core NOHZ subsystem lives in kernel/time/tick-sched.c and orchestrates a carefully choreographed dance between the idle loop, the timer framework, and the clockevent layer. Figure 6-29 presents the high-level architecture — the idle enter path (left) and idle exit path (right) — showing how the kernel decides whether to stop the tick and how it restores tick operation upon wakeup.

Key design principles visible in the architecture:

  • Lightweight entry — tick_nohz_idle_enter() merely sets a flag and starts accounting; the expensive tick-stop decision is deferred to tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(), called only after the cpuidle governor has chosen a target C-state.
  • Two-level blocking — "hard blockers" (NOHZ disabled, in_nmi, timer softirq pending) are checked first with near-zero cost; "soft blockers" (scanning the next timer expiry) run only if no hard block applies.
  • Symmetric exit — the exit path mirrors entry: restart the tick, update jiffies for any time missed during sleep, and clear the idle flag. This symmetry simplifies reasoning about invariants.

NO_HZ_IDLE: The Default Tickless Mode

When a CPU enters the idle loop and no timer is pending in the near future, the kernel stops the periodic tick. This is enabled by default on virtually all Linux distributions since 2.6.21. The design philosophy is simple: a CPU doing nothing should consume as little power as possible, which means no unnecessary wakeups from deep C-states.

Integration with the Idle Loop

The NOHZ idle logic is tightly integrated with the scheduler's idle loop (do_idle()) and the cpuidle framework. Here is how they cooperate:

Table 6-107. Idle Loop Sequence
StepFunctionLocationWhat Happens
1do_idle()kernel/sched/idle.cEnter idle loop, set polling flag
2tick_nohz_idle_enter()tick-sched.cSet TS_FLAG_INIDLE, record entry time
3cpuidle_select()cpuidle governorPick optimal C-state based on predicted idle duration
4tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()tick-sched.cEvaluate stop conditions → stop tick if safe
5call_cpuidle()cpuidle coreExecute HW idle instruction (mwait/wfi)
6CPU sleeps...hardwarePower gated / clock gated until interrupt
7tick_nohz_idle_exit()tick-sched.cUpdate accounting, catch up jiffies, restart tick

The Idle Enter Path

tick_nohz_idle_enter() is called once at the very top of do_idle(), before the CPU enters its idle loop. Its job is deliberately minimal: set a flag and record the timestamp. This function does not stop the tick — that happens later, after the cpuidle governor has had a chance to query the expected sleep duration.

Why is it so simple? The function runs in the scheduler hot path — every time a CPU runs out of work, schedule() eventually calls do_idle(), which calls this. Making it lightweight avoids adding latency to the common case where the CPU goes idle only briefly (e.g., waiting for an IPI). The actual tick stop decision is deferred to tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(), which runs only if the cpuidle governor predicts a long sleep.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
void tick_nohz_idle_enter(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts;

    lockdep_assert_irqs_enabled();
    local_irq_disable();

    ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    WARN_ON_ONCE(ts->timer_expires_base);  /* Must not have stale state */

    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_INIDLE);
    tick_nohz_start_idle(ts);  /* record idle entry time for accounting */

    local_irq_enable();
}
Table 6-108. tick_nohz_idle_enter() — Line-by-Line Breakdown
LineWhatWhy
lockdep_assert_irqs_enabled()Debug assertionCaller must have IRQs on — avoids deadlock in local_irq_disable()
local_irq_disable()Disable interruptsPrevents IRQ between flag-set and start_idle (atomicity of idle-entry)
WARN_ON_ONCE(ts->timer_expires_base)Stale-state checkIf non-zero, previous idle exit didn't clean up — indicates a bug
TS_FLAG_INIDLESet idle flagTells IRQ handlers "this CPU is idle" — used by tick_nohz_irq_exit()
tick_nohz_start_idle(ts)Record ktime_get()Idle accounting: measures idle duration for /proc/stat
local_irq_enable()Re-enable interruptsAllows pending IRQs to fire before entering the idle loop

The corresponding caller in do_idle() shows the full context:

/* kernel/sched/idle.c — do_idle() */
static void do_idle(void)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    nohz_run_idle_balance(cpu);      /* Handle deferred load balancing */
    __current_set_polling();          /* Signal: IPI can set need_resched */
    tick_nohz_idle_enter();           /* ← HERE: mark idle */

    while (!need_resched()) {
        rmb();                        /* Pair with rq->curr assignment */
        local_irq_disable();
        if (cpu_is_offline(cpu))
            cpuhp_report_idle_dead();
        arch_cpu_idle_enter();
        cpuidle_idle_call(true);      /* Selects C-state, may stop tick */
    }

    tick_nohz_idle_exit();            /* Restart tick, update accounting */
    __current_clr_polling();
    schedule_idle();                  /* Switch to runnable task */
}

Notice the split-phase design: tick_nohz_idle_enter() runs before the loop, but the tick is actually stopped inside cpuidle_idle_call() → tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(). This split exists because:

  1. cpuidle governor integration: The governor calls tick_nohz_get_sleep_length() to determine the maximum possible sleep. This function internally calls tick_nohz_next_event() and caches the result in ts->timer_expires_base. If the tick were already stopped, this query would be meaningless.
  2. Avoid redundant computation: When tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() runs later, it checks ts->timer_expires_base — if non-zero, the sleep length was already computed by the governor's query, so it reuses the cached value instead of recalculating.
  3. Separation of concerns: The scheduler owns the idle decision; the tick layer owns the tick stop decision. Mixing them would create circular dependencies.

The actual stop logic in tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() follows a three-way branch:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
void tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();
    ktime_t expires;

    /* Branch 1: Already computed by governor's sleep_length query */
    if (ts->timer_expires_base)
        expires = ts->timer_expires;

    /* Branch 2: Not yet computed — check if we CAN stop, then compute */
    else if (can_stop_idle_tick(cpu, ts))
        expires = tick_nohz_next_event(ts, cpu);

    /* Branch 3: Cannot stop — keep ticking */
    else
        return;

    ts->idle_calls++;

    if (expires > 0LL) {
        int was_stopped = tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED);
        tick_nohz_stop_tick(ts, cpu);       /* THE ACTUAL STOP */
        ts->idle_sleeps++;
        ts->idle_expires = expires;

        /* First time stopping: notify scheduler for load balancing */
        if (!was_stopped && tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
            ts->idle_jiffies = ts->last_jiffies;
            nohz_balance_enter_idle(cpu);
        }
    } else {
        tick_nohz_retain_tick(ts);          /* Timer expires this tick — keep it */
    }
}
Table 6-109. tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() Decision Matrix
ConditionBranchActionPerformance Impact
timer_expires_base != 01 (cached)Reuse governor's computationZero overhead — no timer query
can_stop_idle_tick() → true2 (fresh)Compute from scratch → stop~200ns (timer wheel scan)
can_stop_idle_tick() → false3 (abort)Return immediatelyMinimal — just the check
expires == 0Retaintick_nohz_retain_tick()Keep ticking — timer imminent
expires > 0 (first stop)Stop + notifyStop tick + nohz_balance_enter_idle()Scheduler adjusts ILB targeting
In Linux 2.6, tick_nohz_stop_sched_tick() was a monolithic function that both checked conditions and stopped the tick in a single call from the idle loop. Linux 7.0.12 decomposes this into the cooperative idle_enter → governor_query → idle_stop_tick protocol, which reduces redundant timer queries by ~50% in workloads with frequent short idle periods (the governor's cached result is reused).

The "Can We Stop?" Decision

Before stopping the tick, the kernel must verify that it is safe to do so. "Safe" means: no subsystem currently relies on periodic tick interrupts to make progress. The function can_stop_idle_tick() implements a fast-path gate — if any condition fails, the entire tick-stop path is short-circuited, saving the expensive timer-wheel scan in tick_nohz_next_event().

The design principle is fail-fast with ordered checks: the cheapest tests (flag checks, TIF bit tests) come first, and the most expensive (cross-CPU reads of tick_do_timer_cpu) come last.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static bool can_stop_idle_tick(int cpu, struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    /* ① Offline CPU must never stop (internal error if reached) */
    WARN_ON_ONCE(cpu_is_offline(cpu));

    /* ② NOHZ must be enabled (TS_FLAG_NOHZ set at boot) */
    if (unlikely(!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_NOHZ)))
        return false;

    /* ③ Reschedule pending — scheduler needs this CPU awake */
    if (need_resched())
        return false;

    /* ④ Softirqs pending that haven't been handled yet
     *    (with two exemptions -- see report_idle_softirq() below) */
    if (unlikely(report_idle_softirq()))
        return false;

    /* ⑤ NO_HZ_FULL: the timekeeping duty CPU must never stop */
    if (tick_nohz_full_enabled()) {
        int tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);

        /* We are the timekeeper — someone must update jiffies */
        if (tick_cpu == cpu)
            return false;

        /* No one is the timekeeper — bug (should never happen) */
        if (WARN_ON_ONCE(tick_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE))
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}
Table 6-110. can_stop_idle_tick() Checks — In Order
#CheckCostWhy It BlocksWhat Happens If Ignored
①CPU offline~1ns (WARN only)Offline CPUs should never reach hereUndefined behavior — no IRQ delivery
②TS_FLAG_NOHZ~1ns (per-CPU read)NOHZ not configured or not yet activatedTick stops without proper initialization
③need_resched()~1ns (TIF flag)A task is runnable — must call schedule()Task starvation; scheduling latency spike
④report_idle_softirq()~2ns (pending bits)Softirq work queued (e.g., NET_RX, TIMER)Softirq latency; timer expiry delay
⑤Duty CPU check~5ns (cross-CPU read)Global timekeeping needs a running tickjiffies stall; time goes backwards for userspace

Why is this a separate function? The checks in can_stop_idle_tick() are pre-conditions that don't require expensive computation. By separating them from tick_nohz_next_event() (which scans the timer wheel), the kernel avoids ~200ns of work in the common case where the CPU can't sleep anyway. On a busy server with frequent short idle periods, this saves millions of unnecessary timer-wheel scans per second.

The report_idle_softirq() subtlety: This function doesn't just check local_softirq_pending() — it also reports the issue via a rate-limited warning ("NOHZ tick-stop error: local softirq work is pending"), because softirqs repeatedly pending at idle entry normally indicates a ksoftirqd scheduling problem. A pending softirq is treated as a "don't sleep" signal since the handler is about to run.

But "pending" is not quite the same as "blocking", and Linux 7.0.12 carves out two exemptions. Both matter because a false positive here is not harmless: it both prints a scary warning and keeps the tick running.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static bool report_idle_softirq(void)
{
    static int ratelimit;
    unsigned int pending = local_softirq_pending();

    if (likely(!pending))
        return false;

    /* ① Some softirqs claim to be safe against hotplug and ksoftirqd parking */
    if (!cpu_active(smp_processor_id())) {
        pending &= ~SOFTIRQ_HOTPLUG_SAFE_MASK;
        if (!pending)
            return false;
    }

    /* ② On RT, softirq handling may be waiting on some lock */
    if (local_bh_blocked())
        return false;

    if (ratelimit < 10) {
        pr_warn("NOHZ tick-stop error: local softirq work is pending, handler #%02x!!!\n",
                pending);
        ratelimit++;
    }
    return true;
}

① The CPU is on its way offline. Once a CPU has been cleared from cpu_active_mask, ksoftirqd is parked and can no longer drain pending softirqs — so waiting for it would deadlock the hotplug operation. Four softirqs are known to survive this because the hotplug teardown migrates their work explicitly, and they are filtered out by SOFTIRQ_HOTPLUG_SAFE_MASK in include/linux/interrupt.h:

Table 6-111. SOFTIRQ_HOTPLUG_SAFE_MASK — Softirqs Exempt on an Inactive CPU
SoftirqWhy it is safe to ignore
TIMER_SOFTIRQtimers_dead_cpu() migrates the timer queue to a surviving CPU
HRTIMER_SOFTIRQhrtimers_cpu_dying() migrates the hrtimer bases
RCU_SOFTIRQrcutree_migrate_callbacks() moves the callback queue and rcutree_report_cpu_dead() reports the final quiescent state
IRQ_POLL_SOFTIRQirq_poll_cpu_dead() moves the poll list to another CPU

② PREEMPT_RT is holding softirqs off deliberately. On PREEMPT_RT, softirq handling runs in task context and can be blocked while some thread holds a lock inside a local_bh_disable() region. The bits stay pending not because anything is wrong but because processing has been postponed on purpose, so local_bh_blocked() makes this an unconditional early return — no warning, and no reason to hold the tick on. This escape was added by commit 807e0d187da4, which fixed a condition that had been testing the wrong thing.

The duty CPU invariant: In NO_HZ_FULL mode, exactly one CPU must always be ticking to maintain jiffies (the global tick counter). This is the "duty CPU" identified by tick_do_timer_cpu. If this CPU tries to sleep, someone else must first take over — but that handoff happens in tick_nohz_stop_tick(), not here. This check simply prevents the stop from even being attempted if no handoff is possible (i.e., when no other CPU is awake to accept the duty).

Finding the Next Event

Once can_stop_idle_tick() returns true, the kernel must answer: "How long can this CPU sleep?" The function tick_nohz_next_event() answers this by consulting multiple time sources and computing the minimum expiry — the earliest point when something needs this CPU awake.

This function is the most computationally expensive part of the idle-entry path (~200ns) because it must scan the timer wheel via get_next_timer_interrupt(). That's why can_stop_idle_tick() exists as a cheap gate — avoiding this scan when stopping isn't possible anyway.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static ktime_t tick_nohz_next_event(struct tick_sched *ts, int cpu)
{
    u64 basemono, next_tick, delta, expires;
    unsigned long basejiff;
    int tick_cpu;

    /* ① Snapshot current time (jiffies + monotonic) atomically */
    basemono = get_jiffies_update(&basejiff);
    ts->last_jiffies = basejiff;
    ts->timer_expires_base = basemono;   /* Mark: "computation done" */

    /*
     * ② Check subsystems that REQUIRE periodic ticks.
     * If any needs the CPU, limit sleep to one tick period.
     * Also check for pending timer softirqs — calling
     * get_next_timer_interrupt() when a timer already expired
     * creates a tight wake-sleep-wake loop (it returns "now").
     */
    if (rcu_needs_cpu() || arch_needs_cpu() ||
        irq_work_needs_cpu() || local_timer_softirq_pending()) {
        next_tick = basemono + TICK_NSEC;   /* Force 1-tick sleep */
    } else {
        /*
         * ③ Query the timer wheel for the next pending timer.
         * In hires mode: only checks low-res timer wheel.
         * In lowres mode: also checks hrtimers.
         */
        next_tick = get_next_timer_interrupt(basejiff, basemono);
        ts->next_timer = next_tick;
    }

    /* Sanity: next_tick must not be in the past */
    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(basemono > next_tick))
        next_tick = basemono;

    /*
     * ④ "Not worth stopping" optimization:
     * If next timer fires within one tick period AND tick isn't
     * stopped yet, there's no benefit to stopping (the overhead
     * of stop + reprogram + restart exceeds one tick).
     */
    delta = next_tick - basemono;
    if (delta <= (u64)TICK_NSEC) {
        if (!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
            ts->timer_expires = 0;   /* Signal: "don't stop" */
            return 0;
        }
    }

    /*
     * ⑤ Timekeeping constraint: duty CPU must not sleep longer
     * than timekeeping_max_deferment() — beyond that, clock
     * adjustments (NTP, frequency correction) become inaccurate.
     * Non-duty CPUs have no such limit.
     */
    delta = timekeeping_max_deferment();
    tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
    if (tick_cpu != cpu &&
        (tick_cpu != TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE ||
         !tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST)))
        delta = KTIME_MAX;   /* Non-duty: unlimited sleep */

    /* ⑥ Final expiry = min(basemono + delta, next_tick) */
    if (delta < (KTIME_MAX - basemono))
        expires = basemono + delta;
    else
        expires = KTIME_MAX;

    ts->timer_expires = min_t(u64, expires, next_tick);
    return ts->timer_expires;
}
Table 6-112. tick_nohz_next_event() — Six Stages
StageWhatTime Sources ConsultedTypical Value
① Snapshotget_jiffies_update()seqcount-protected last_jiffies_updateCurrent monotonic time
② Subsystem checkRCU / arch / irq_work / timer_softirqPer-CPU flagsbasemono + 4ms (1 tick)
③ Timer wheelget_next_timer_interrupt()Timer wheel buckets + hrtimer (if lowres)Varies: ms to hours
④ Worth-stopping?Delta ≤ TICK_NSEC filter—Returns 0 if not worth it
⑤ Timekeeping limittimekeeping_max_deferment()NTP / clock correction state~0.5s (duty) or ∞ (non-duty)
⑥ Final minmin_t(u64, expires, next_tick)—Cached in ts->timer_expires

The get_jiffies_update() snapshot (Stage ①): This reads jiffies and last_jiffies_update under a seqcount, ensuring a consistent pair. The monotonic base is needed because the timer wheel stores deadlines relative to jiffies, but the clock event device needs an absolute nanosecond value. The seqcount retry loop handles the race where tick_do_update_jiffies64() is concurrently incrementing jiffies on another CPU.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
u64 get_jiffies_update(unsigned long *basej)
{
    unsigned long basejiff;
    unsigned int seq;
    u64 basemono;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
        basemono = last_jiffies_update;
        basejiff = jiffies;
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&jiffies_seq, seq));
    *basej = basejiff;
    return basemono;
}

The "not worth stopping" optimization (Stage ④): Stopping and restarting the tick has a cost: reprogramming the clock event device (~50-100ns on x86, more on ARM), plus the overhead of tick_nohz_stop_tick() and tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(). If the next timer fires within one tick period (~4ms at HZ=250), the CPU would wake up almost immediately anyway — so keeping the periodic tick running is cheaper than the stop/start overhead. However, if the tick is already stopped (from a previous iteration), we proceed anyway because the timer needs reprogramming.

The timekeeping max_deferment (Stage ⑤): NTP and clock frequency adjustments depend on periodic updates. If the duty CPU sleeps too long, clock corrections accumulate error. timekeeping_max_deferment() returns the maximum time the clock can drift without exceeding acceptable bounds — typically ~0.5 seconds. Non-duty CPUs bypass this entirely (delta = KTIME_MAX), allowing them to sleep for arbitrary durations (hours, if no timer is pending).

The caching mechanism: The computed result is stored in ts->timer_expires and the base time in ts->timer_expires_base. When tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() runs later, it checks timer_expires_base — if non-zero, it skips the entire computation and reuses the cached value. This is the key to the cooperative protocol with the cpuidle governor: the governor triggers the computation via tick_nohz_get_sleep_length(), and the actual stop reuses the result.

Table 6-113. Tick Stop Blockers (Complete List)
ConditionFunctionCheck LocationWhy It Blocks
NOHZ not enabledTS_FLAG_NOHZcan_stop_idle_tick()Framework not initialized
Reschedule neededneed_resched()can_stop_idle_tick()Must call schedule() — can't idle
Softirq pendingreport_idle_softirq()can_stop_idle_tick()Deferred work must execute first
Duty CPU (NO_HZ_FULL)tick_do_timer_cpu == cpucan_stop_idle_tick()Someone must maintain jiffies
RCU needs CPUrcu_needs_cpu()tick_nohz_next_event()Grace period needs this CPU's quiescent state
Architecture needsarch_needs_cpu()tick_nohz_next_event()Platform-specific (e.g., x86 PIT calibration)
IRQ work pendingirq_work_needs_cpu()tick_nohz_next_event()Deferred NMI/IRQ work items queued
Timer softirq pendinglocal_timer_softirq_pending()tick_nohz_next_event()Already-expired timer needs service
Next event < 1 tickdelta <= TICK_NSECtick_nohz_next_event()Not worth stopping (overhead exceeds gain)
Two-level blocking: Notice that blockers are split across two functions. can_stop_idle_tick() handles hard blockers (things that make stopping impossible), while tick_nohz_next_event() handles soft blockers (things that force a short sleep rather than preventing it entirely). The soft blockers still allow the tick to stop — they just limit it to one tick period (4ms at HZ=250). This means RCU callbacks, irq_work, etc., still get serviced via the reprogrammed one-shot timer rather than the periodic tick.

Stopping the Tick

tick_nohz_stop_tick() performs the actual shutdown. It involves three critical steps: (1) marking the timer bases idle for the timer migration framework, (2) relinquishing the timekeeping duty, and (3) programming the wakeup or shutting down the clock event device entirely:

static void tick_nohz_stop_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, int cpu)
{
    struct clock_event_device *dev = __this_cpu_read(tick_cpu_device.evtdev);
    u64 expires;

    ts->timer_expires_base = 0;

    /* Mark timer bases idle (so remote CPUs can migrate timers) */
    expires = timer_base_try_to_set_idle(basejiff, basemono, &timer_idle);
    if (!timer_idle)
        return;   /* Timer base busy — can't stop */

    /* Relinquish do_timer duty if we hold it */
    int tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
    if (tick_cpu == cpu) {
        WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE);
        tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST);
    }

    /* Program the wakeup: set hrtimer for next_tick */
    if (expires == KTIME_MAX) {
        /* No timers pending — sleep forever (until IRQ/IPI) */
        if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_HIGHRES))
            hrtimer_cancel(&ts->sched_timer);
        else
            clockevents_shutdown(dev);
    } else {
        /* Program wakeup at calculated expiry */
        hrtimer_start(&ts->sched_timer, expires, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_PINNED_HARD);
    }

    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED);
}
Table 6-114. tick_nohz_stop_tick() Steps
StepActionPurposeFailure Effect
1timer_base_try_to_set_idle()Mark LOCAL/GLOBAL/DEF bases as idle; enable tmigr remote expiryReturns early — tick kept running
2Drop tick_do_timer_cpuLet another CPU pick up timekeeping when it wakesWould leave jiffies stale forever
3ahrtimer_cancel()No pending timers — disable sched_timer completelySleep until external IRQ/IPI
3bhrtimer_start(expires)Timer pending — program wakeup at next expiryCPU wakes exactly when needed
4Set TS_FLAG_STOPPEDRecord that tick is stopped for exit path—

Timer Migration (tmigr)

A key 7.0.12 addition is the Timer Migration Framework (tmigr). The problem it solves is fundamental: when a CPU goes idle, it may still have non-pinned (global) timers queued. Without timer migration, the CPU would have to wake up just to expire these timers — defeating the purpose of going idle. The tmigr framework allows any awake CPU to expire those timers on behalf of idle CPUs, dramatically extending sleep durations on systems with many idle cores.

The Problem: Idle CPUs with Pending Timers

Consider a 64-core server where 60 cores are idle. In the pre-tmigr world (Linux < 6.x), each idle CPU still had to program its local clock event device for its earliest global timer, causing unnecessary wakeups. A single mod_timer() queued remotely could prevent deep C-state residency:

Table 6-115. Impact of Timer Migration on Idle Sleep
ScenarioWithout tmigrWith tmigr
60 idle CPUs, each with 1 global timer60 wakeups (one per CPU)1 wakeup (migrator handles all)
Idle CPU with timer 10ms awayMust wake in 10msSleeps indefinitely; awake CPU expires it
Last CPU going idleMust handle all timers locallyPrograms earliest across entire system
Power savings (server idle)Moderate (frequent shallow wakeups)Excellent (deep C-state residency)
Hierarchical Group Architecture

The tmigr framework organizes CPUs into a hierarchical tree of groups, similar to the scheduler's load-balancing domains. Each group contains up to 8 children (CPUs at the leaf level, groups at higher levels), and the tree is NUMA-aware:

Key Data Structures
/* kernel/time/timer_migration.h */
#define TMIGR_CHILDREN_PER_GROUP 8

struct tmigr_event {
    struct timerqueue_node  nextevt;   /* Sorted position in parent queue */
    unsigned int            cpu;       /* Owner CPU */
    bool                    ignore;    /* Set when CPU/group is active */
};

struct tmigr_group {
    raw_spinlock_t          lock;
    struct tmigr_group      *parent;       /* Up-pointer in hierarchy */
    struct tmigr_event      groupevt;      /* This group's event in parent */
    u64                     next_expiry;   /* Earliest child event (lockless read) */
    struct timerqueue_head  events;        /* Timer queue of child events */
    atomic_t                migr_state;    /* Packed: active mask + migrator + seq */
    unsigned int            level;
    int                     numa_node;
    u8                      groupmask;     /* Bit position in parent */
};

struct tmigr_cpu {   /* Per-CPU */
    raw_spinlock_t          lock;
    bool                    idle;       /* CPU is idle in tmigr hierarchy */
    bool                    remote;     /* Timers being expired remotely */
    struct tmigr_group      *tmgroup;   /* Leaf group this CPU belongs to */
    u8                      groupmask;  /* Bit in leaf group */
    u64                     wakeup;     /* Next wakeup when hierarchy idle */
    struct tmigr_event      cpuevt;     /* This CPU's event in leaf group */
};

union tmigr_state {
    u32 state;                  /* For atomic cmpxchg */
    struct {
        u8  active;             /* Bitmask: which children are active */
        u8  migrator;           /* Which child is the migrator */
        u16 seq;                /* Sequence counter for ordering */
    } __packed;
};
Table 6-116. tmigr Key Concepts
ConceptDefinitionPurpose
MigratorDesignated active CPU/group in each levelPrevents lock bouncing: only one CPU handles remote expiry per group
Group eventThe earliest pending timer from all childrenPropagated up the tree so higher levels know the earliest wakeup
Ignore flagSet when CPU/group becomes activeAvoids lock contention on activation — stale events cleaned up lazily
DeactivationCPU marks idle + enqueues its earliest global timer in leaf groupMakes timer visible to migrator for remote expiry
Walk-upPropagation from leaf to root on deactivate/activateMaintains correct earliest-event at every level
The Deactivation Path (CPU Going Idle)

When tick_nohz_stop_tick() calls timer_base_try_to_set_idle(), the latter invokes the tmigr deactivation. The CPU publishes its earliest non-pinned timer into the hierarchy so a migrator can handle it:

/* kernel/time/timer_migration.c */
u64 tmigr_cpu_deactivate(u64 nextexp)
{
    struct tmigr_cpu *tmc = this_cpu_ptr(&tmigr_cpu);
    u64 ret;

    if (tmigr_is_not_available(tmc))
        return nextexp;

    raw_spin_lock(&tmc->lock);
    ret = __tmigr_cpu_deactivate(tmc, nextexp);
    tmc->idle = true;
    WRITE_ONCE(tmc->wakeup, ret);  /* Published for idle path */
    raw_spin_unlock(&tmc->lock);
    return ret;  /* Earliest event from hierarchy (for last-CPU case) */
}

static u64 __tmigr_cpu_deactivate(struct tmigr_cpu *tmc, u64 nextexp)
{
    struct tmigr_walk data = {
        .nextexp   = nextexp,
        .firstexp  = KTIME_MAX,
        .evt       = &tmc->cpuevt,
        .childmask = tmc->groupmask
    };

    /* If nextexp != KTIME_MAX, make event visible (don't ignore) */
    if (nextexp != KTIME_MAX)
        tmc->cpuevt.ignore = false;

    /* Walk up the hierarchy: update events at each level */
    walk_groups(&tmigr_inactive_up, &data, tmc);
    return data.firstexp;
}

The walk-up operation at each level:

  1. Enqueue CPU's timer event into the leaf group's timerqueue
  2. Update the group's next_expiry to reflect the new earliest event
  3. If this was the last active CPU, update the group's migr_state to TMIGR_NONE
  4. Propagate the group's event into the parent group's timer queue
  5. Continue until reaching a level where the group still has active members (walk_done = true)
The Activation Path (CPU Waking Up)
/* kernel/time/timer_migration.c */
void tmigr_cpu_activate(void)
{
    struct tmigr_cpu *tmc = this_cpu_ptr(&tmigr_cpu);

    if (tmigr_is_not_available(tmc))
        return;

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!tmc->idle))
        return;

    raw_spin_lock(&tmc->lock);
    tmc->idle = false;
    __tmigr_cpu_activate(tmc);  /* Walk up: set active + become migrator */
    raw_spin_unlock(&tmc->lock);
}

On activation, the CPU's ignore flag is set (so its stale event in the parent queue is lazily cleaned up), and it offers to become the migrator at each level where no migrator exists. This avoids the overhead of immediately removing events from parent queues — they're simply ignored when encountered.

Remote Timer Expiry (The Migrator's Job)

The designated migrator CPU checks for expired remote timers during its own tick (run_local_timers() → tmigr_handle_remote()):

/* kernel/time/timer_migration.c */
void tmigr_handle_remote(void)
{
    struct tmigr_cpu *tmc = this_cpu_ptr(&tmigr_cpu);
    struct tmigr_walk data;

    if (tmigr_is_not_available(tmc))
        return;

    data.childmask = tmc->groupmask;
    data.firstexp = KTIME_MAX;

    /* Quick check: am I still the migrator? */
    if (!tmigr_check_migrator(tmc->tmgroup, tmc->groupmask)) {
        if (READ_ONCE(tmc->wakeup) == KTIME_MAX)
            return;
    }

    data.now = get_jiffies_update(&data.basej);

    /* Walk up hierarchy: expire remote timers at each level */
    __walk_groups(&tmigr_handle_remote_up, &data, tmc);

    raw_spin_lock_irq(&tmc->lock);
    WRITE_ONCE(tmc->wakeup, data.firstexp);
    raw_spin_unlock_irq(&tmc->lock);
}

/* For each idle CPU with expired timers: */
static void tmigr_handle_remote_cpu(unsigned int cpu, u64 now,
                                    unsigned long jif)
{
    struct tmigr_cpu *tmc = per_cpu_ptr(&tmigr_cpu, cpu);

    raw_spin_lock_irq(&tmc->lock);
    /* Skip if: offline, already being handled, owner woke up, or not yet due */
    if (!tmc->available || tmc->remote || tmc->cpuevt.ignore ||
        now < tmc->cpuevt.nextevt.expires) {
        raw_spin_unlock_irq(&tmc->lock);
        return;
    }

    tmc->remote = true;
    raw_spin_unlock_irq(&tmc->lock);

    /* Actually expire the remote CPU's timers */
    if (cpu != smp_processor_id())
        timer_expire_remote(cpu);  /* Runs timer callbacks on behalf of idle CPU */

    /* ... fetch next timer and update hierarchy ... */
}
Table 6-117. tmigr Operation Summary
OperationWhenWhat HappensLock Held
tmigr_cpu_deactivate()CPU going idlePublish earliest global timer in hierarchy; delegate migratortmc->lock + group locks (bottom-up)
tmigr_cpu_activate()CPU waking upMark active; set event ignore; become migrator if neededtmc->lock + atomic cmpxchg
tmigr_handle_remote()Migrator's tickWalk up tree; expire timers of idle CPUstmc->lock + remote base locks
tmigr_cpu_new_timer()mod_timer() on idle CPUUpdate hierarchy if new timer is earlier than published eventtmc->lock + group locks
tmigr_requires_handle_remote()run_local_timers()Quick check: does migrator need to handle anything?Lockless (reads next_expiry)
The "Last CPU" Problem

When the last CPU in the entire system goes idle, there is no migrator left to expire timers. The tmigr framework handles this special case: the last CPU's tmigr_cpu_deactivate() returns the earliest event from the entire hierarchy (not just its own timers). The CPU then programs its local clock event device for this system-wide earliest timer — ensuring it wakes up to handle the most urgent timer even though it's technically idle:

/* In tick_nohz_stop_tick() — simplified */
expires = timer_base_try_to_set_idle(basejiff, basemono, &timer_idle);
/* If this is the last CPU, 'expires' now reflects the system-wide
 * earliest timer (returned from tmigr hierarchy), not just local timers.
 * The hrtimer/clock-event is programmed for this global earliest event. */
Integration with timer_base_try_to_set_idle()

The connection between the timer subsystem and tmigr is through timer_base_try_to_set_idle(), called from tick_nohz_stop_tick():

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
u64 timer_base_try_to_set_idle(unsigned long basej, u64 basem, bool *idle)
{
    struct timer_base *base_local, *base_global;

    /* If already idle (from a previous iteration), nothing to do */
    if (*idle)
        return KTIME_MAX;

    base_local = this_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[BASE_LOCAL]);
    base_global = this_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[BASE_GLOBAL]);

    raw_spin_lock(&base_local->lock);
    raw_spin_lock_nested(&base_global->lock, SINGLE_DEPTH_NESTING);

    /* Get the next timer interrupt from both bases */
    nextexp = __get_next_timer_interrupt(basej, basem);

    /* Mark both bases as idle */
    base_local->is_idle = true;
    base_global->is_idle = true;

    raw_spin_unlock(&base_global->lock);
    raw_spin_unlock(&base_local->lock);

    *idle = true;

    /* Deactivate in tmigr hierarchy — publish global timer for migration */
    nextexp = tmigr_cpu_deactivate(nextexp);

    return nextexp;
}

/* On wakeup: reverse the process */
void timer_clear_idle(void)
{
    __this_cpu_write(timer_bases[BASE_LOCAL].is_idle, false);
    if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        __this_cpu_write(timer_bases[BASE_GLOBAL].is_idle, false);
    tmigr_cpu_activate();  /* Re-join migration hierarchy */
}
Design Decisions and Trade-offs
Table 6-118. tmigr Design Decisions
DecisionRationaleAlternative Considered
Hierarchical tree (not flat)O(log N) lock contention vs O(N) — critical for 256+ CPU systemsSingle global queue (too much contention)
8 children per groupFits in one cache line; balances tree depth vs widthLarger groups (more contention) or binary tree (too deep)
NUMA-aware groupingKeep lock bouncing within same node at low levelsTopology-blind (cross-node latency penalty)
Single migrator per groupPrevents N awake CPUs from all trying to expire the same timersAny-CPU expiry (lock storm)
Lazy event removal (ignore flag)Activation path is lockless (just atomic cmpxchg) — fast wakeEager removal (requires locking parent on every wakeup)
Sequence counter in statePrevents ABA problem when concurrent activate/deactivate raceFull serialization (too slow)
Groups never destroyedAvoids complex race conditions on CPU hotplugDynamic allocation/free (fragile)
Linux 2.6 had no timer migration. When a CPU went idle, it programmed its clock event for its own earliest timer — waking even for non-pinned timers that any CPU could have handled. Linux 4.x added basic timer migration via the scheduler's idle load balancer (ILB), which was a hack: one "ILB CPU" handled all idle CPUs' timers. Linux 7.0.12 replaces this with the proper hierarchical tmigr framework (merged in 6.x), providing O(log N) scalability, NUMA awareness, and per-group migrator assignment — far superior for systems with hundreds of cores.

The Idle Exit Path

When an interrupt (timer, IPI, device) wakes the CPU from idle, the kernel must undo everything the idle-entry path set up: update idle accounting, catch up the missed jiffies, re-join the timer migration hierarchy, and restart the periodic tick. This is the job of tick_nohz_idle_exit(), called at the bottom of do_idle()'s while loop.

Why is this path critical? If the CPU slept for 500ms with the tick stopped, jiffies is stale by ~125 ticks (at HZ=250). Any kernel code that queries jiffies after wakeup — scheduler time accounting, timer expiry, watchdog checks — will see incorrect values until the catch-up completes. The exit path must restore time coherence before the CPU resumes normal operation.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
void tick_nohz_idle_exit(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);
    bool idle_active, tick_stopped;
    ktime_t now;

    local_irq_disable();

    /* Sanity: we must be in idle, and no stale cached expiry */
    WARN_ON_ONCE(!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_INIDLE));
    WARN_ON_ONCE(ts->timer_expires_base);

    /* ① Clear the idle flag — IRQ handlers see us as "active" now */
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_INIDLE);

    /* ② Snapshot flags before we modify them */
    idle_active = tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);
    tick_stopped = tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED);

    /* ③ Only call ktime_get() if we actually need it (avoid cost) */
    if (idle_active || tick_stopped)
        now = ktime_get();

    /* ④ Update idle accounting (idle_sleeptime / iowait_sleeptime) */
    if (idle_active)
        tick_nohz_stop_idle(ts, now);

    /* ⑤ Catch up jiffies + restart the tick */
    if (tick_stopped)
        tick_nohz_idle_update_tick(ts, now);

    local_irq_enable();
}
Table 6-119. tick_nohz_idle_exit() — Step-by-Step
StepCodePurposeCost
①tick_sched_flag_clear(TS_FLAG_INIDLE)Mark CPU as no longer idle — tick_nohz_irq_exit() won't re-evaluate~1ns
②Snapshot idle_active + tick_stoppedCapture state before modification to determine which actions needed~1ns
③ktime_get() (conditional)Read hardware clock — only if needed for accounting or catch-up~50ns
④tick_nohz_stop_idle()Update idle_sleeptime or iowait_sleeptime for /proc/stat~20ns
⑤tick_nohz_idle_update_tick()Catch up jiffies, clear timer idle flags, restart sched_timer~200ns
Idle Accounting: tick_nohz_stop_idle()

The idle accounting must distinguish between pure idle time and I/O wait time — both contribute to /proc/stat's idle and iowait fields, which tools like top, mpstat, and htop display. The accounting uses a seqcount to allow lockless reads from other CPUs:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_nohz_stop_idle(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    ktime_t delta;

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE)))
        return;

    delta = ktime_sub(now, ts->idle_entrytime);

    write_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

    /* Classify: was the CPU waiting for I/O or truly idle? */
    if (nr_iowait_cpu(smp_processor_id()) > 0)
        ts->iowait_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->iowait_sleeptime, delta);
    else
        ts->idle_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->idle_sleeptime, delta);

    ts->idle_entrytime = now;
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);

    write_seqcount_end(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

    sched_clock_idle_wakeup_event();  /* Notify sched_clock of wakeup */
}
Table 6-120. Idle Accounting Fields
FieldUpdated ByConsumerWhat It Tracks
idle_sleeptimetick_nohz_stop_idle()/proc/stat (idle column)Cumulative time CPU was idle (no I/O wait tasks)
iowait_sleeptimetick_nohz_stop_idle()/proc/stat (iowait column)Cumulative time CPU was idle with tasks waiting on I/O
idle_entrytimetick_nohz_start_idle()tick_nohz_stop_idle()Timestamp of idle entry (for delta calculation)
idle_sleeptime_seqBoth start and stopget_cpu_idle_time_us()Seqcount for lockless cross-CPU reads
idle_callstick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()schedutil governorCount of idle entries (frequency scaling heuristic)
idle_sleepstick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()DiagnosticsCount of entries where tick was actually stopped

The iowait classification: nr_iowait_cpu() returns the number of tasks on this CPU's runqueue that are in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE state with the in_iowait flag set (set by io_schedule()). If any task is waiting for I/O, the idle time is charged to iowait rather than pure idle. This distinction matters for performance monitoring — high iowait indicates the CPU is waiting on storage, not genuinely idle.

Tick Restart: tick_nohz_idle_update_tick()

When the tick was stopped, this function orchestrates the full restart. It has two paths depending on NO_HZ_FULL configuration:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_nohz_idle_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(ts, now);  /* May keep tick stopped! */
    else
        tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(ts, now);   /* Always restart */

    tick_nohz_account_idle_time(ts, now);        /* Account missed ticks */
}

The critical restart work happens in tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick():

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    /* ① Catch up jiffies — may advance by hundreds of ticks */
    tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);

    /* ② Re-join timer migration hierarchy */
    timer_clear_idle();

    /* ③ Update load calculation for /proc/loadavg */
    calc_load_nohz_stop();

    /* ④ Prevent false softlockup warnings */
    touch_softlockup_watchdog_sched();

    /* ⑤ Clear stopped flag and restart periodic timer */
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED);
    tick_nohz_restart(ts, now);
}

/* The actual timer restart: */
static void tick_nohz_restart(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    hrtimer_cancel(&ts->sched_timer);
    hrtimer_set_expires(&ts->sched_timer, ts->last_tick);

    /* Forward to next tick boundary after 'now' */
    hrtimer_forward(&ts->sched_timer, now, TICK_NSEC);

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_HIGHRES))
        hrtimer_start_expires(&ts->sched_timer,
                              HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_PINNED_HARD);
    else
        tick_program_event(hrtimer_get_expires(&ts->sched_timer), 1);

    ts->next_tick = 0;  /* Reset cached deadline */
}
Table 6-121. tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick() — Restart Steps
StepFunctionWhat It DoesWhy It's Needed
①tick_do_update_jiffies64(now)Advance jiffies from last update to nowJiffies stale: timers, scheduler time slices, watchdogs depend on it
②timer_clear_idle()Mark timer bases non-idle; call tmigr_cpu_activate()Re-join tmigr hierarchy; stop remote CPU from expiring our timers
③calc_load_nohz_stop()Fold idle CPU's contribution back into load average/proc/loadavg accuracy: idle CPUs remove themselves from calc
④touch_softlockup_watchdog_sched()Reset the watchdog timestampCPU slept legitimately; without this, watchdog thinks CPU was locked up
⑤tick_nohz_restart(ts, now)Cancel old timer; forward to next boundary; restartResume periodic ticking from the correct phase-aligned time
Idle Time Accounting: Handling Missed Ticks

When the tick was stopped, update_process_times() never ran — so the per-tick CPU time accounting was skipped. tick_nohz_account_idle_time() compensates by crediting all missed ticks to idle:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_nohz_account_idle_time(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long ticks;

    ts->idle_exittime = now;

    /* vtime handles its own accounting — skip */
    if (vtime_accounting_enabled_this_cpu())
        return;

    /*
     * We stopped the tick in idle. update_process_times() would
     * miss the time we slept, as it does only a 1-tick accounting.
     * Enforce that this is accounted to idle!
     */
    ticks = jiffies - ts->idle_jiffies;

    /* Guard: don't account absurd values */
    if (ticks && ticks < LONG_MAX)
        account_idle_ticks(ticks);
}

Why is this needed? Normally, update_process_times() runs every tick and calls account_process_tick() to charge 1 tick to either user, system, or idle. But with the tick stopped, hundreds of ticks pass unaccounted. Without this catch-up, /proc/stat would under-report idle time and tools like top would show incorrect CPU utilization.

The NO_HZ_FULL Exit Difference

On NO_HZ_FULL CPUs, the exit path has a subtle optimization: instead of always restarting the tick, it checks whether the tick can remain stopped:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    if (can_stop_full_tick(cpu, ts))
        tick_nohz_full_stop_tick(ts, cpu);   /* Keep tick stopped! */
    else if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED))
        tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(ts, now); /* Must restart */
}

This means a NO_HZ_FULL CPU exiting idle to run a single compute-bound task may never restart the tick at all — it goes straight from idle into user-mode execution with no periodic interrupt. This is critical for latency-sensitive workloads like HFT and real-time control.

Complete Exit Scenario Matrix
Table 6-122. Idle Exit Scenario Matrix
State on Exitidle_activetick_stoppedActionsTypical Cause
Full cycle (most common)✓✓stop_idle + update_tick + account_timeCPU slept with tick stopped, woken by timer/IPI
Tick running✓✗stop_idle onlyBlocker prevented tick stop; CPU idled briefly with tick running
Quick exit✗✗Clear TS_FLAG_INIDLE onlyIRQ fired between idle_enter and actual sleep (never truly idled)
NO_HZ_FULL: remain stopped✓✓stop_idle + keep tick stoppedSingle runnable task on FULL CPU; no tick dependencies
Linux 2.6's tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick() was simpler — it just caught up jiffies and restarted the timer. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) timer migration re-activation (timer_clear_idle() → tmigr_cpu_activate()); (2) seqcount-protected idle accounting (idle_sleeptime_seq) for lockless cross-CPU reads; (3) NO_HZ_FULL exit path that can keep the tick stopped even after exiting idle; (4) vtime check to avoid double-accounting when virtual time accounting is active; (5) separate iowait_sleeptime tracking for accurate /proc/stat iowait classification.

The IRQ Exit Re-evaluation

There is a subtle but critical scenario that neither tick_nohz_idle_enter() nor tick_nohz_idle_exit() handles: what happens when an interrupt fires while the CPU is idle, but the CPU doesn't leave the idle loop?

Consider this sequence:

  1. CPU enters idle with tick stopped, programmed to wake in 200ms.
  2. After 10ms, a network IRQ fires — the handler adds a new timer that expires in 5ms.
  3. The IRQ handler returns. Since need_resched() is false (no task was woken), the CPU stays in do_idle()'s while loop — it will go back to sleep.
  4. Problem: The clock event device is still programmed for 190ms from now, but there's a timer due in 5ms. Without re-evaluation, that timer would fire 185ms late.

tick_nohz_irq_exit() solves this by being called at the end of every IRQ exit path, before the CPU returns to idle. It resets the idle accounting timestamp so the next cpuidle_idle_call() → tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() will recompute the wakeup time with the new timer.

Where It's Called: The IRQ Exit Path

The call site is in the generic IRQ exit code (kernel/softirq.c), which runs after every hardware interrupt:

/* kernel/softirq.c */
static inline void tick_irq_exit(void)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    /* Only re-evaluate if: (a) CPU is idle and not rescheduling, OR
     * (b) CPU is a NO_HZ_FULL CPU (may need tick restart) */
    if ((sched_core_idle_cpu(cpu) && !need_resched()) ||
        tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu)) {
        if (!in_hardirq())
            tick_nohz_irq_exit();
    }
}

static inline void __irq_exit_rcu(void)
{
    local_irq_disable();
    account_hardirq_exit(current);
    preempt_count_sub(HARDIRQ_OFFSET);

    /* Run softirqs if pending and we're leaving the last nested IRQ */
    if (!in_interrupt() && local_softirq_pending())
        invoke_softirq();        /* May add timers, RCU callbacks, etc. */

    tick_irq_exit();             /* ← RE-EVALUATE tick after softirqs */
}

/* Called from irq_exit() and irq_exit_rcu() */

Key detail: tick_irq_exit() runs after invoke_softirq(). This ordering is critical — softirq handlers (NET_RX_SOFTIRQ, TIMER_SOFTIRQ, etc.) often add new timers or queue RCU callbacks. The re-evaluation must happen after all such work is done, so it sees the most up-to-date timer state.

The Re-evaluation Function
/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
/**
 * tick_nohz_irq_exit - Notify the tick about IRQ exit
 *
 * A timer may have been added/modified/deleted either by the current
 * IRQ, or by another place using this IRQ as a notification. This IRQ
 * may have also updated the RCU callback list. These events may require
 * a re-evaluation of the next tick. Depending on the context:
 *
 * 1) If the CPU is idle and no resched pending, just proceed with idle
 *    time accounting. The next tick will be re-evaluated on the next
 *    idle loop iteration.
 *
 * 2) If the CPU is nohz_full:
 *    2.1) If there is any tick dependency, restart the tick if stopped.
 *    2.2) If there is no tick dependency, (re-)evaluate the next tick
 *         and stop/update it accordingly.
 */
void tick_nohz_irq_exit(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_INIDLE))
        tick_nohz_start_idle(ts);       /* Path 1: restart accounting */
    else
        tick_nohz_full_update_tick(ts);  /* Path 2: NO_HZ_FULL re-eval */
}
Table 6-123. tick_nohz_irq_exit() — Two Paths
PathConditionActionWhat Happens Next
Path 1: Idle CPU TS_FLAG_INIDLE set tick_nohz_start_idle(ts) Resets idle_entrytime to now. The next do_idle() loop iteration calls cpuidle_idle_call() → tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(), which recomputes tick_nohz_next_event() — picking up the new timer.
Path 2: NO_HZ_FULL non-idle TS_FLAG_INIDLE clear, tick_nohz_full_cpu() true tick_nohz_full_update_tick(ts) Re-evaluates whether the tick can remain stopped. If IRQ added a tick dependency (e.g., second task became runnable → scheduler needs tick), restarts the tick immediately.
Why tick_nohz_start_idle() and Not Direct Reprogramming?

One might ask: why doesn't Path 1 directly reprogram the clock event device? The answer is architectural simplicity and correctness:

  1. The idle loop already handles reprogramming. After the IRQ returns, do_idle()'s while loop iterates again. cpuidle_idle_call() calls cpuidle_select() (which calls tick_nohz_get_sleep_length()) and then tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(). This full sequence correctly handles all edge cases (new timer, RCU callbacks, softirqs, etc.).
  2. Avoid reprogramming in IRQ context. Reprogramming hrtimers from IRQ context requires careful lock ordering. By deferring to the idle loop, the code avoids holding timer locks while in interrupt context.
  3. tick_nohz_start_idle() resets the accounting baseline. The idle time between the first start_idle() and this interrupt is already accounted (via the next stop_idle()). Resetting the timestamp ensures the next idle period starts with a fresh baseline — otherwise, the time spent handling the IRQ would be incorrectly charged as idle.
/* What tick_nohz_start_idle() does: */
static void tick_nohz_start_idle(struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    write_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);
    ts->idle_entrytime = ktime_get();       /* Reset timestamp to NOW */
    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);
    write_seqcount_end(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

    sched_clock_idle_sleep_event();
}
The Complete Idle IRQ Scenario
The NO_HZ_FULL Path (Path 2)

For NO_HZ_FULL CPUs that are not idle (running a single user-mode task with tick stopped), the re-evaluation is fundamentally different from the idle case. An idle CPU simply defers to the next do_idle() iteration, but a NO_HZ_FULL CPU has no idle loop — it's executing user code. The only opportunity to re-evaluate the tick is during interrupt exit, making tick_nohz_full_update_tick() the critical decision point.

Why NO_HZ_FULL Needs IRQ Exit Re-evaluation

A NO_HZ_FULL CPU running user code with tick stopped is essentially invisible to the kernel — no periodic interrupt fires, no scheduler runs, no RCU callback processing occurs. When an interrupt does arrive (e.g., a network packet, a perf NMI, an IPI from another CPU), it may change the system state in ways that require the tick to restart. Without re-evaluation on IRQ exit, these state changes would go unnoticed until the task makes a syscall.

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_nohz_full_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    /* Gate 1: Only applies to NO_HZ_FULL CPUs */
    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        return;

    /* Gate 2: NOHZ must be active on this CPU */
    if (!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_NOHZ))
        return;

    __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(ts, ktime_get());
}

static void __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    if (can_stop_full_tick(cpu, ts))
        tick_nohz_full_stop_tick(ts, cpu);     /* Keep stopped or reprogram */
    else if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED))
        tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(ts, now);  /* Dependency appeared → restart */
}
The Four-Level Dependency Check

The core of NO_HZ_FULL is can_stop_full_tick(), which checks a four-level hierarchical dependency mask. Any single bit set at any level forces the tick on — this is a logical OR across all four levels:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static bool can_stop_full_tick(int cpu, struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();

    if (unlikely(!cpu_online(cpu)))
        return false;

    /* Level 1: Global — affects ALL CPUs */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&tick_dep_mask))
        return false;

    /* Level 2: Per-CPU — affects this CPU only */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&ts->tick_dep_mask))
        return false;

    /* Level 3: Per-task — follows the currently running task */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&current->tick_dep_mask))
        return false;

    /* Level 4: Per-signal (process group) — shared across threads */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&current->signal->tick_dep_mask))
        return false;

    return true;
}

static bool check_tick_dependency(atomic_t *dep)
{
    int val = atomic_read(dep);

    if (likely(!tracepoint_enabled(tick_stop)))
        return !!val;    /* Fast path: just check if any bit set */

    /* Slow path with tracing: check each bit for diagnostics */
    if (val & TICK_DEP_MASK_POSIX_TIMER) { trace_tick_stop(0, ...); return true; }
    if (val & TICK_DEP_MASK_PERF_EVENTS) { trace_tick_stop(0, ...); return true; }
    if (val & TICK_DEP_MASK_SCHED)       { trace_tick_stop(0, ...); return true; }
    /* ... RCU, CLOCK_UNSTABLE, RCU_EXP ... */
    return false;
}

The two halves of that function answer different questions, and the split is new in Linux 7.0. Everything below the tracepoint_enabled() test exists purely for diagnostics: when the tick_stop tracepoint is active, the kernel walks the bits in a fixed order and emits trace_tick_stop(0, TICK_DEP_MASK_…) for the first one it finds. The 0 is the tracepoint’s success argument — the event records both that the tick could not be stopped and which subsystem blocked it, which is what makes trace-cmd able to answer “why is my isolated CPU still ticking?” without a debugger. Note that only the first matching bit is reported even when several are set.

That diagnostic walk is wasted work when nobody is listening, and this check sits on the return-to-userspace path of every NO_HZ_FULL CPU. So commit 56534673cea7 added the fast path: tracepoint_enabled() expands to static_branch_unlikely(&__tracepoint_tick_stop.key), a static key that is patched to a fall-through while the tracepoint is disabled, so the common case collapses to one atomic read and a test for non-zero.

The fast path is also a good illustration of how easily a pure-performance change can invert a meaning. As merged it read return !val; rather than return !!val;. Both compile, both look reasonable beside a variable named val, and the function’s name does not make its polarity obvious — but check_tick_dependency() returns true to mean a dependency exists, keep the tick. The inverted form therefore claimed a dependency whenever the mask was empty and claimed none when bits were set, simultaneously pinning the tick on for CPUs that had nothing to do and stopping it for CPUs that had told the kernel they needed it. The tracepoint path was unaffected, so enabling tracing to investigate would have made the symptom disappear. It was caught during the merge window — 56534673cea7 landed in v7.0-rc1 and the one-character fix, 82b915051d32, landed before v7.0 — so no released kernel carries it.

Table 6-124. Tick Dependency Bits
BitNameSet ByWhy Tick Is Needed
0POSIX_TIMERPOSIX CPU timer armPer-process/thread CPU timers need periodic sampling to detect expiry
1PERF_EVENTSperf event creationFrequency-based sampling requires tick for rate throttling
2SCHEDScheduler (>1 runnable task)Time-slice accounting and preemption decisions require periodic tick
3CLOCK_UNSTABLEClocksource watchdogUnstable TSC needs frequent cross-checking against stable reference
4RCURCU subsystemGrace period advancement needs periodic quiescent state reporting
5RCU_EXPRCU expedited grace periodExpedited GP needs this CPU to report QS urgently
The Kick Mechanism

When a subsystem sets a tick dependency on a remote NO_HZ_FULL CPU, it must interrupt that CPU to trigger the re-evaluation. The kernel uses the irq_work framework to send an IPI that forces the target CPU through the IRQ exit path (where tick_nohz_irq_exit() picks up the new dependency):

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */

/* The IRQ work handler is deliberately empty! */
static void nohz_full_kick_func(struct irq_work *work)
{
    /* Empty — the tick restart happens on tick_nohz_irq_exit() */
}

static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct irq_work, nohz_full_kick_work) =
    IRQ_WORK_INIT_HARD(nohz_full_kick_func);

/* Kick THIS CPU (NMI-safe) */
static void tick_nohz_full_kick(void)
{
    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        return;
    irq_work_queue(this_cpu_ptr(&nohz_full_kick_work));
}

/* Kick a REMOTE CPU */
void tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(int cpu)
{
    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu))
        return;
    irq_work_queue_on(&per_cpu(nohz_full_kick_work, cpu), cpu);
}

/* Kick ALL NO_HZ_FULL CPUs (used when setting global dependency) */
static void tick_nohz_full_kick_all(void)
{
    int cpu;
    if (!tick_nohz_full_running)
        return;
    preempt_disable();
    for_each_cpu_and(cpu, tick_nohz_full_mask, cpu_online_mask)
        tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(cpu);
    preempt_enable();
}

Why is the handler empty? This is an elegant design trick. The irq_work IPI forces the target CPU to execute an interrupt handler. When that handler returns, the generic IRQ exit path runs tick_irq_exit() → tick_nohz_irq_exit() → tick_nohz_full_update_tick(). That's where the dependency check and potential tick restart happen. The kick doesn't need to do anything itself — it just needs to make the CPU go through the IRQ exit path.

The Dependency Set/Clear API

Subsystems use a four-function API to manage dependencies at each level. Each "set" function atomically ORs the bit and, if this is the first dependency, kicks the affected CPU(s):

/* Global: affects all NO_HZ_FULL CPUs */
void tick_nohz_dep_set(enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev)
        tick_nohz_full_kick_all();   /* First dep → kick everyone */
}

/* Per-CPU: affects one specific CPU */
void tick_nohz_dep_set_cpu(int cpu, enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &ts->tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev) {
        if (cpu == smp_processor_id())
            tick_nohz_full_kick();           /* Local: NMI-safe kick */
        else
            tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(cpu);     /* Remote: IPI */
    }
}

/* Per-task: follows the task wherever it migrates */
void tick_nohz_dep_set_task(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    if (!atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &tsk->tick_dep_mask))
