        tick_nohz_kick_task(tsk);   /* Kick CPU where task runs */
}

/* Per-signal: shared by all threads in process */
void tick_nohz_dep_set_signal(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &sig->tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev) {
        __for_each_thread(sig, t)
            tick_nohz_kick_task(t); /* Kick ALL threads' CPUs */
    }
}

/* Clear is simpler — just atomic AND-NOT, no kick needed */
void tick_nohz_dep_clear(enum tick_dep_bits bit) {
    atomic_andnot(BIT(bit), &tick_dep_mask);
}
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_cpu(int cpu, enum tick_dep_bits bit) { ... }
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_task(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit) { ... }
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_signal(struct signal_struct *sig, enum tick_dep_bits bit) { ... }
Table 6-125. Dependency API — Set vs Clear Asymmetry
OperationAtomic OpSide EffectWhy
dep_set*()atomic_fetch_or()IPI kick if first bitMust interrupt tickless CPU immediately to restart tick
dep_clear*()atomic_andnot()NoneCPU will notice on next tick_nohz_irq_exit() or when tick fires — no urgency
Task Switch Re-evaluation

When the scheduler switches to a new task on a NO_HZ_FULL CPU, the per-task and per-signal dependency masks may change. The kernel checks this on every context switch:

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c — called from __schedule() */
void __tick_nohz_task_switch(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts;

    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        return;

    ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
        /* New task has dependencies? → restart tick */
        if (atomic_read(&current->tick_dep_mask) ||
            atomic_read(&current->signal->tick_dep_mask))
            tick_nohz_full_kick();
    }
}
Complete Re-evaluation Scenario Matrix
Table 6-126. NO_HZ_FULL IRQ Exit Scenarios — Expanded
ScenarioIRQ Did WhatDependency Changecan_stop_full_tick()Action
Timer IRQ, no new workExpired timer, no new tasksNonetrueKeep tick stopped; reprogram for next timer
Network IRQ, added timerNew timer in 5msNonetrueReprogram wakeup to 5ms, tick stays stopped
IPI: task wakeupSecond task enqueuedSCHED bit set by schedulerfalseRestart tick (scheduler needs time-slicing)
IPI: perf event startperf opens frequency eventPERF_EVENTS bit setfalseRestart tick (perf rate throttling)
RCU: callback queuedRCU wants grace periodRCU bit setfalseRestart tick (QS reporting needed)
RCU: expedited GPUrgent grace periodRCU_EXP bit setfalseRestart tick immediately
POSIX timer armedsetitimer() from threadPOSIX_TIMER on signalfalseRestart tick (CPU time sampling)
Clocksource unstableWatchdog detected driftCLOCK_UNSTABLE globalfalseAll FULL CPUs restart (TSC cross-check)
Linux 2.6 had no NO_HZ_FULL — the tick was only stopped during idle. NO_HZ_FULL was introduced in Linux 3.10 with a basic dependency check. Linux 7.0.12 refines it with: (1) four-level hierarchy (global/CPU/task/signal) instead of simple boolean; (2) atomic_fetch_or() for lock-free dependency management; (3) NMI-safe self-kick via irq_work; (4) per-process POSIX timer dependency via the signal struct; (5) task switch integration via __tick_nohz_task_switch(); (6) tracepoint support for debugging tick stop decisions (trace_tick_stop).
Guard Conditions in tick_irq_exit()

Not every IRQ exit calls tick_nohz_irq_exit(). The wrapper tick_irq_exit() in kernel/softirq.c applies two guards:

Table 6-127. tick_irq_exit() Guard Conditions
GuardCheckRationale
CPU is idle + no resched OR NO_HZ_FULL (sched_core_idle_cpu(cpu) && !need_resched()) || tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu) Only re-evaluate if CPU will stay idle or is a FULL CPU. If need_resched(), the CPU exits do_idle() entirely — tick_nohz_idle_exit() handles tick restart.
Not in nested hardirq !in_hardirq() If this IRQ interrupted another IRQ (nested), defer to the outermost IRQ exit to avoid redundant re-evaluations.
Linux 2.6 had a simpler tick_nohz_update_jiffies() called on IRQ entry (not exit), which caught up jiffies but didn't re-evaluate the next wakeup. Linux 7.0.12's tick_nohz_irq_exit() is called on IRQ exit (after softirqs), handles both idle and NO_HZ_FULL paths, and correctly resets idle accounting timestamps. The placement after invoke_softirq() is crucial — softirq handlers frequently add timers that must be visible to the re-evaluation.

cpuidle Governor Integration

The NOHZ tick subsystem and the cpuidle framework are tightly coupled through a cooperative protocol that optimizes both tick stopping and C-state selection. The fundamental challenge: the cpuidle governor needs to know the expected sleep duration to pick the right C-state, but the sleep duration depends on whether the tick will be stopped — and the tick stop depends on the governor's decision. Linux 7.0.12 solves this circular dependency with a clever compute-once, reuse pattern.

The Cooperation Protocol

The sequence within cpuidle_idle_call() is carefully ordered:

tick_nohz_get_sleep_length() — The Bridge Function

This function is the interface between the cpuidle governor and the NOHZ tick subsystem. It answers the question: "If we stop the tick, how long until the next event that requires this CPU?"

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
ktime_t tick_nohz_get_sleep_length(ktime_t *delta_next)
{
    struct clock_event_device *dev = __this_cpu_read(tick_cpu_device.evtdev);
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    /*
     * Use idle_entrytime as "now" — avoid expensive ktime_get().
     * It was recorded in tick_nohz_idle_enter() and is close enough
     * (typically <1µs old).
     */
    ktime_t now = ts->idle_entrytime;
    ktime_t next_event;

    WARN_ON_ONCE(!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_INIDLE));

    /*
     * Return 1: "next tick" duration — the baseline if we CAN'T stop.
     * The governor uses this as a fallback.
     */
    *delta_next = ktime_sub(dev->next_event, now);

    /*
     * Return 2: If we can't stop the tick, the governor can only pick
     * C-states with residency ≤ one tick period.
     */
    if (!can_stop_idle_tick(cpu, ts))
        return *delta_next;

    /*
     * Return 3: Compute the full sleep length.
     * This is the expensive path — scans the timer wheel.
     * The result is CACHED in ts->timer_expires_base for later reuse.
     */
    next_event = tick_nohz_next_event(ts, cpu);
    if (!next_event)
        return *delta_next;   /* Timer imminent — stick with tick */

    /*
     * Also consider hrtimers that might fire before the timer-wheel
     * event. Exclude our own sched_timer (it will be reprogrammed
     * or cancelled by tick_nohz_stop_tick).
     */
    next_event = min_t(u64, next_event,
                       hrtimer_next_event_without(&ts->sched_timer));

    return ktime_sub(next_event, now);
}
Table 6-128. tick_nohz_get_sleep_length() — Return Values
Return PathConditionValue ReturnedGovernor Uses It For
Baseline (*delta_next)Always setTime until currently-programmed clock eventFallback when tick can't stop
Can't stopcan_stop_idle_tick() → falseSame as baselineLimits C-state to ≤ 1 tick residency
Timer imminenttick_nohz_next_event() → 0Same as baselineNo benefit to stopping tick
Full sleepAll checks passmin(next_timer, next_hrtimer) - nowCan pick deep C-states (ms to hours)
How Governors Use the Sleep Length

Linux 7.0.12 ships with two cpuidle governors: menu (default for servers) and TEO (Timer Events Oriented, default for mobile/embedded). Both use the sleep length differently:

Table 6-129. Governor Comparison — Sleep Length Usage
Aspectmenu governorTEO governor
AlgorithmStatistical: predicts next wakeup from historical intervalsPattern-based: tracks timer vs non-timer wakeup ratios
Sleep length useUpper bound for prediction; combined with correction_factorDirectly compared to state target_residency
Tick stop decisionStops if predicted sleep > RESIDENCY_THRESHOLD_NSStops if selected state residency ≥ TICK_NSEC
Short idle optimizationUses get_typical_interval() histogramSkips sleep length query if short_idles ≥ 50%
Best forGeneral purpose, variable workloadsPredictable workloads, latency-sensitive

The TEO governor has a notable optimization: it skips calling tick_nohz_get_sleep_length() entirely when historical data shows the CPU is waking frequently from non-timer sources (e.g., IPIs, network interrupts). This avoids the ~200ns timer-wheel scan in workloads where the CPU never sleeps long enough to benefit from it.

The stop_tick Output Parameter

The governor returns a stop_tick boolean to the caller. This tells cpuidle_idle_call() whether to call tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() or tick_nohz_idle_retain_tick():

/* kernel/sched/idle.c — inside cpuidle_idle_call() */
stop_tick = true;   /* Default: governors may stop the tick */

/* Governor selects C-state and may clear stop_tick */
next_state = cpuidle_select(drv, dev, &stop_tick);

/* Stop or retain based on governor's decision */
idle_call_stop_or_retain_tick(stop_tick);

/* Execute the selected idle state */
entered_state = call_cpuidle(drv, dev, next_state);

/* Let governor learn from what actually happened */
cpuidle_reflect(dev, entered_state);
Table 6-130. stop_tick Decision Outcomes
stop_tickMeaningActionWhen
trueGovernor expects long sleeptick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()Deep C-state selected, sleep ≥ tick period
falseGovernor expects short sleeptick_nohz_idle_retain_tick()Polling state or sleep < tick period
The Reflect Phase

After the CPU wakes from idle, cpuidle_reflect() gives the governor feedback on what actually happened. The TEO governor uses this to update its timer/non-timer wakeup statistics, which feed into the next cpuidle_select() decision — including whether to even query the sleep length:

/* TEO governor uses tick_nohz_idle_got_tick() to check if the tick
 * fired (meaning the CPU didn't sleep as long as expected) */
bool tick_nohz_idle_got_tick(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);
    if (ts->got_idle_tick) {
        ts->got_idle_tick = 0;
        return true;    /* Tick fired during idle — wakeup was from tick */
    }
    return false;       /* Non-tick wakeup (IPI, device interrupt, etc.) */
}
The Complete Cooperative Lifecycle
Table 6-131. cpuidle ↔ NOHZ — Complete Lifecycle
StepWhoFunctionNOHZ State After
1Idle looptick_nohz_idle_enter()TS_FLAG_INIDLE set; timer_expires_base = 0
2Governortick_nohz_get_sleep_length()timer_expires_base = basemono (computed)
3Governorcpuidle_select() returns stop_tickC-state chosen, stop_tick decided
4Idle looptick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()Reuses cached timer_expires; sets TS_FLAG_STOPPED
5Hardwarecall_cpuidle() → mwait/wfiCPU sleeping; clock event programmed
6InterruptWakeupIRQ fires
7Governorcpuidle_reflect()Statistics updated for next iteration
8Idle looptick_nohz_idle_exit()TS_FLAG_STOPPED cleared; tick restarted; timer_expires_base = 0
Linux 2.6 had no cpuidle governor integration with the tick subsystem — the governor (menu, only) used next_timer_interrupt() directly, and tick stop was a separate, uncoordinated decision in the idle loop. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) the cooperative compute-once protocol via timer_expires_base caching; (2) the TEO governor (4.17+) with pattern-based wakeup prediction that can skip the timer scan entirely; (3) the stop_tick output parameter allowing governors to prevent tick stop for short idles; (4) hrtimer_next_event_without() to correctly exclude the sched_timer from sleep length; (5) tick_nohz_idle_got_tick() for governor feedback; (6) idle_entrytime reuse instead of calling ktime_get() again (~50ns saved per idle entry).

The tick_sched Structure

Each CPU has a per-CPU tick_sched structure (declared in kernel/time/tick-sched.h) that serves as the central state machine for the NOHZ subsystem. It tracks everything: whether the tick is running or stopped, how long the CPU has been idle, what the next wakeup event is, and whether any subsystem depends on the tick. Understanding this structure is key to understanding how the idle/tickless paths interact.

Declaration and Per-CPU Allocation
/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct tick_sched, tick_cpu_sched);

struct tick_sched *tick_get_tick_sched(int cpu)
{
    return &per_cpu(tick_cpu_sched, cpu);
}

Being per-CPU means most fields require no locking — only the owning CPU modifies them. The exception is idle_sleeptime_seq (a seqcount) which protects idle-time accounting fields that are read by other CPUs (e.g., /proc/stat readers).

Full Structure (Linux 7.0.12)
/* kernel/time/tick-sched.h */
struct tick_sched {
    /* ═══ Common Flags ═══ */
    unsigned long   flags;              /* TS_FLAG_* bitmask (6 bits) */

    /* ═══ Tick Handling: Jiffies Stall Detection ═══ */
    unsigned int    stalled_jiffies;    /* consecutive ticks w/o jiffies advance */
    unsigned long   last_tick_jiffies;  /* jiffies snapshot at last tick */

    /* ═══ Tick Handling: The Sched Timer ═══ */
    struct hrtimer  sched_timer;        /* THE periodic/oneshot tick hrtimer */
    ktime_t         last_tick;          /* when tick last fired (for nohz resume) */
    ktime_t         next_tick;          /* next programmed expiry */
    unsigned long   idle_jiffies;       /* jiffies at idle entry */
    ktime_t         idle_waketime;      /* timestamp of last wakeup from idle */
    unsigned int    got_idle_tick;      /* tick fired while in idle (for governor) */

    /* ═══ Idle Entry ═══ */
    seqcount_t      idle_sleeptime_seq; /* protects sleeptime fields (readers on other CPUs) */
    ktime_t         idle_entrytime;     /* ktime when idle was entered (reused as "now") */

    /* ═══ Tick Stop: Timer Cache ═══ */
    unsigned long   last_jiffies;       /* jiffies base for timer_expires computation */
    u64             timer_expires_base; /* base clock mono for cache (0 = invalid) */
    u64             timer_expires;      /* cached: earliest timer wakeup time */
    u64             next_timer;         /* next timer expiry (debug only) */
    ktime_t         idle_expires;       /* next tick when in idle (debug only) */
    unsigned long   idle_calls;         /* total idle entries (statistics) */
    unsigned long   idle_sleeps;        /* idle entries where tick was stopped */

    /* ═══ Idle Exit ═══ */
    ktime_t         idle_exittime;      /* when CPU left idle */
    ktime_t         idle_sleeptime;     /* accumulated idle time (non-IO) */
    ktime_t         iowait_sleeptime;   /* accumulated idle time (IO wait) */

    /* ═══ Full Dynticks (NO_HZ_FULL) ═══ */
    atomic_t        tick_dep_mask;      /* per-CPU dependency bits (OR of dep bits) */

    /* ═══ Clocksource Change Notification ═══ */
    unsigned long   check_clocks;       /* bit 0: clocksource/event change pending */
};
Flags: The 6-Bit State Machine

The flags field encodes the current state of this CPU's tick subsystem. All flag operations (tick_sched_flag_set/clear/test) require IRQs disabled — this eliminates races without requiring spinlocks:

static inline void tick_sched_flag_set(struct tick_sched *ts, unsigned long flag)
{
    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();
    ts->flags |= flag;
}

static inline void tick_sched_flag_clear(struct tick_sched *ts, unsigned long flag)
{
    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();
    ts->flags &= ~flag;
}
Table 6-132. tick_sched Flags
FlagBitSet WhenCleared WhenPrimary Users
TS_FLAG_INIDLE0tick_nohz_idle_enter()tick_nohz_idle_exit()IRQ exit path checks this to decide re-evaluation
TS_FLAG_STOPPED1tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() (tick actually stopped)tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick()Idle exit decides whether to restart; governor checks this
TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE2tick_nohz_start_idle()tick_nohz_stop_idle()Idle accounting: /proc/stat readers use with seqcount
TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST3Before sleeping if duty CPUOn wake if reclaimedcan_stop_idle_tick() uses for hand-off logic
TS_FLAG_NOHZ4tick_nohz_switch_to_nohz() at bootNever (permanent)Guards all NOHZ paths — early exit if not set
TS_FLAG_HIGHRES5tick_setup_sched_timer(hrtimer=true)Never (permanent)Tick restart chooses hrtimer vs. tick_program_event
Field Groups Explained

Jiffies Stall Detection — The stalled_jiffies/last_tick_jiffies pair detects pathological situations where the duty CPU (responsible for tick_do_update_jiffies64()) is stuck in stop_machine() or a VM exit for several milliseconds. If MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES (5) consecutive ticks fire without jiffies advancing, any CPU forces an update via tick_limited_update_jiffies64():

#define MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES 5

/* In tick_sched_do_timer(): */
if (ts->last_tick_jiffies != jiffies) {
    ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
    ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
} else {
    if (++ts->stalled_jiffies >= MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES) {
        if (tick_limited_update_jiffies64(ts, now)) {
            ts->stalled_jiffies = 0;
            ts->last_tick_jiffies = READ_ONCE(jiffies);
        }
    }
}

The sched_timer — This is the single most important field. It is a high-resolution timer that fires periodically at HZ frequency (or one-shot when NOHZ stops the tick). When NOHZ stops the tick, it cancels this hrtimer; when restarting, it reprograms it. The last_tick field records when this timer last fired — essential for correctly resuming in the timeline after a long NOHZ sleep.

Timer Cache (Compute-Once Protocol) — Three fields implement the cooperative caching between cpuidle and NOHZ:

Table 6-133. Timer Cache Fields
FieldTypeMeaningInvalidation
timer_expires_baseu64Clock monotonic base when cache was computed; 0 means invalidSet to 0 on tick_nohz_idle_exit()
timer_expiresu64The cached earliest wakeup time (ns)Only valid when timer_expires_base ≠ 0
last_jiffiesunsigned longJiffies snapshot when cache was computed (detects stale results)Compared against current jiffies

Idle Accounting (seqcount-protected) — The idle_sleeptime and iowait_sleeptime accumulators feed /proc/stat's idle% and iowait% columns. They are updated on idle exit (not entry) by tick_nohz_stop_idle(). The seqcount protects against torn reads when /proc/stat readers on other CPUs access these fields concurrently:

static void tick_nohz_stop_idle(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    ktime_t delta = ktime_sub(now, ts->idle_entrytime);

    write_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);
    if (nr_iowait_cpu(smp_processor_id()) > 0)
        ts->iowait_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->iowait_sleeptime, delta);
    else
        ts->idle_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->idle_sleeptime, delta);
    ts->idle_entrytime = now;
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);
    write_seqcount_end(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);
}

The got_idle_tick Flag — Set to 1 in tick_sched_do_timer() when the tick fires while the CPU is in idle (i.e., TS_FLAG_INIDLE is set). The cpuidle governor's tick_nohz_idle_got_tick() reads and clears it — this tells the governor "you were woken by the tick, not by an external event" which helps TEO distinguish timer wakeups from device wakeups for C-state prediction.

Clocksource Change Notification — check_clocks uses bit 0 as a per-CPU notification flag. When a better clocksource or clock event device becomes available, tick_oneshot_notify() sets the bit. On the next timer softirq, tick_check_oneshot_change() tests-and-clears it, potentially switching the CPU from low-res periodic mode to high-res oneshot mode:

void tick_oneshot_notify(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);
    set_bit(0, &ts->check_clocks);
}

int tick_check_oneshot_change(int allow_nohz)
{
    if (!test_and_clear_bit(0, &ts->check_clocks))
        return 0;  /* No change pending */
    if (!timekeeping_valid_for_hres() || !tick_is_oneshot_available())
        return 0;  /* Hardware not ready */
    /* ... switch to oneshot/nohz mode ... */
}
Key Design Decisions
Table 6-134. tick_sched Design Decisions
DecisionRationale
Per-CPU, no spinlockHot path (every idle entry/exit) — lock contention would destroy scalability on 256+ CPU systems
IRQs-disabled for flag opstick_sched_flag_set/clear assert lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled() — prevents IRQ handler from seeing half-updated state
Seqcount for idle timesOnly 2 fields need cross-CPU visibility; seqcount is ~3ns read cost vs. spinlock ~12ns
timer_expires_base = 0 as sentinelZero is impossible for a valid clock-monotonic timestamp (time can't be zero after boot) — no extra "valid" flag needed
Separate idle_sleeptime / iowait_sleeptimeMatches /proc/stat columns; avoids post-hoc classification
got_idle_tick as u32 (not bool)Avoids read-modify-write on byte fields; u32 is naturally atomic on all architectures
stalled_jiffies counterGracefully handles VM guests where the host may schedule the vCPU out for many milliseconds
Linux 2.6.11's tick_sched equivalent was split across several ad-hoc variables. Linux 7.0.12 consolidates all NOHZ state into a single per-CPU structure with: (1) bitfield flags replacing boolean fields (saves ~40 bytes), (2) seqcount replacing raw spinlock for idle accounting, (3) timer cache fields (timer_expires_base/timer_expires) for the compute-once protocol (2.6 had no cpuidle integration), (4) tick_dep_mask for NO_HZ_FULL (didn't exist in 2.6), (5) stall detection for virtualized environments, (6) got_idle_tick for governor feedback loop.

NO_HZ_FULL: Adaptive Ticks (Full Dynticks)

For latency-sensitive workloads (HPC, real-time, financial trading, DPDK networking), NO_HZ_FULL eliminates the periodic tick even on busy CPUs — provided only one runnable task exists and no kernel subsystem depends on the tick. This removes the last source of periodic kernel interference (jitter), achieving sub-microsecond worst-case latency on isolated cores.

Motivation and Use Cases

Even with NO_HZ_IDLE, a running task still receives ~1000 interrupts/second from the scheduler tick. Each tick causes:

  • Cache pollution (kernel code/data replaces application hot lines)
  • Pipeline flush (interrupt entry/exit costs ~1–5µs)
  • TLB shootdowns (if kernel/user share TLB entries)
  • Non-deterministic latency spikes (jitter) of up to 10µs

For workloads that need uninterrupted CPU time, this is unacceptable:

Table 6-135. NO_HZ_FULL Target Workloads
WorkloadWhy Tick-Free MattersTypical Isolation
High-Frequency TradingEvery µs of jitter = lost moneyisolcpus=2-15 nohz_full=2-15
DPDK / Packet ProcessingPoll-mode driver must not be interruptednohz_full=1-7 rcu_nocbs=1-7
Real-Time Control (PREEMPT_RT)Deterministic loop timingnohz_full=2-3 isolcpus=domain,2-3
HPC / Scientific ComputingMaximize FLOPS per corenohz_full=1-63 (leave CPU 0)
Telecommunications (5G)L1/L2 processing with strict timingPer-core isolation with cgroups

Configuration and Boot Parameters

# Kernel command line:
nohz_full=2-7       # CPUs 2-7 run tickless when single-task
isolcpus=2-7        # Also isolate from scheduler load balancing
rcu_nocbs=2-7       # Offload RCU callbacks to housekeeping CPUs

# At least 1 CPU must remain as housekeeping:
# - Handles timekeeping (tick_do_timer_cpu)
# - Processes unbound timers/workqueues
# - Services RCU grace periods
# CPU 0 is housekeeping by default

Housekeeping CPUs and the hk_type Masks

"Housekeeping" is the inverse of isolation, and it is the concept the rest of the kernel actually queries. Isolating a CPU is never enough on its own — the work that CPU refuses does not disappear, it has to land somewhere. Unbound workqueues, unpinned timers, RCU callbacks, unbound kthreads and the timekeeping duty must all be steered onto the CPUs that were not isolated. Rather than have each subsystem re-derive that set from nohz_full=, isolcpus= and their variants, kernel/sched/isolation.c maintains one set of cpumasks and exposes them through housekeeping_cpumask(), housekeeping_cpu() and housekeeping_any_cpu().

Linux 7.0.12 keeps only four distinct masks, indexed by enum hk_type in include/linux/sched/isolation.h:

Table 6-136. hk_type — The Housekeeping Masks
hk_typePopulated fromGovernsMutable at runtime?
HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOTInverse of boot-time isolcpus=The boot-time domain isolation, kept as the immutable baselineNo
HK_TYPE_DOMAINHK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT minus cpuset isolated partitionsScheduler domains, unbound workqueues, unbound kthreads, timer migrationYes
HK_TYPE_MANAGED_IRQInverse of isolcpus=managed_irq,…Managed interrupt affinityNo
HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISEInverse of nohz_full= or isolcpus=nohz,…Tick, timers, RCU, workqueues, kthreads, misc — everything NOHZ cares aboutNo

Older kernels had a separate hk_type per subsystem. Because nohz_full= was the only thing that ever set any of them, they were always identical, and Linux 7.0.12 collapses them into aliases of a single mask:

/* include/linux/sched/isolation.h -- all six are the same mask */
HK_TYPE_TICK    = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE,
HK_TYPE_TIMER   = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE,
HK_TYPE_RCU     = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE,
HK_TYPE_MISC    = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE,
HK_TYPE_WQ      = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE,
HK_TYPE_KTHREAD = HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE

The names survive so that call sites still document why they are asking, but there is now exactly one answer. HK_TYPE_SCHED was removed outright, and isolcpus=nohz,… became an exact synonym for nohz_full= — note that, unlike a bare isolcpus=, it sets only HK_FLAG_KERNEL_NOISE and does not imply domain isolation as well.

The kernel does not refuse to boot on a bad isolation mask. If nohz_full= or isolcpus= would leave no present housekeeping CPU, housekeeping_setup() forces the boot CPU back into the housekeeping set and warns "Housekeeping: must include one present CPU, using boot CPU:N". A mismatched combination — a second nohz_full=/isolcpus= that disagrees with the first — is rejected with "nohz_full= must match isolcpus=" and simply ignored. In every case the system boots; it just may not be isolated the way you asked.

Runtime Isolation: housekeeping_update() and cpuset Partitions

Through Linux 6.x, isolation was frozen at boot: the masks were parsed from the command line and never changed again. That made isolation an all-or-nothing property of the machine — to re-partition a host between a latency-sensitive workload and a general one, you rebooted it. Linux 7.0.12 breaks that assumption for domain isolation. A cpuset isolated partition can now be created, resized or dissolved at runtime, and the change is pushed down into the housekeeping masks by housekeeping_update().

/* kernel/sched/isolation.c (abridged) */
int housekeeping_update(struct cpumask *isol_mask)
{
    struct cpumask *trial, *old = NULL;

    trial = kmalloc(cpumask_size(), GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!trial)
        return -ENOMEM;

    /* New domain set = the boot baseline minus the newly isolated CPUs */
    cpumask_andnot(trial, housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_DOMAIN_BOOT), isol_mask);

    /* Refuse to isolate every online CPU */
    if (!cpumask_intersects(trial, cpu_online_mask)) {
        kfree(trial);
        return -EINVAL;
    }
    ...
    rcu_assign_pointer(housekeeping.cpumasks[HK_TYPE_DOMAIN], trial);
    synchronize_rcu();                  /* readers finish with the old mask */

    /* Drain anything already queued against the old set ... */
    pci_probe_flush_workqueue();
    mem_cgroup_flush_workqueue();
    vmstat_flush_workqueue();

    /* ... then re-steer each subsystem at the new set */
    workqueue_unbound_housekeeping_update(housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_DOMAIN));
    tmigr_isolated_exclude_cpumask(isol_mask);
    kthreads_update_housekeeping();

    kfree(old);
    return 0;
}

Three details are worth drawing out, because they are what make a runtime change safe rather than merely possible.

First, the new mask is published by RCU pointer assignment followed by synchronize_rcu(). The housekeeping masks are read on hot paths — every unbound timer enqueue and every workqueue dispatch consults them — so they cannot be protected by a lock. Converting them to RCU pointers is what allows them to change at all, and the synchronize_rcu() guarantees no reader is still looking at the old mask before it is freed.

Second, the update is bracketed by flushes. Changing the mask only affects future placement decisions; work already queued against a CPU that is about to become isolated would still run there. The PCI probe, memcg and vmstat workqueues are therefore drained first, so the newly isolated CPUs start clean.

Third, and most important for this chapter: housekeeping_update() writes only HK_TYPE_DOMAIN. It never touches HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE. Domain isolation — scheduler placement, unbound work, timer migration — is now dynamic, but the nohz_full set itself is still fixed at boot. A CPU cannot be made tickless by writing to a cgroup file; what a cpuset partition can do is stop the scheduler and the unbound-work machinery from aiming at it. Tickless execution still requires nohz_full= on the command line, because the per-CPU state it depends on — context tracking, the tick dependency masks, the timekeeping-duty handoff — is established during tick_nohz_init() before the system is running.

Initialization (tick_nohz_init)
void __init tick_nohz_init(void)
{
    if (!tick_nohz_full_running)
        return;

    /* NO_HZ_FULL requires arch support for IRQ work self-IPIs */
    if (!arch_irq_work_has_interrupt()) {
        pr_warn("NO_HZ: Can't run full dynticks because arch "
                "doesn't support IRQ work self-IPIs\n");
        cpumask_clear(tick_nohz_full_mask);
        tick_nohz_full_running = false;
        return;
    }

    /* Boot CPU cannot be nohz_full (needs to be timekeeper) */
    if (cpumask_test_cpu(smp_processor_id(), tick_nohz_full_mask)) {
        pr_warn("NO_HZ: Clearing %d from nohz_full for timekeeping\n",
                smp_processor_id());
        cpumask_clear_cpu(smp_processor_id(), tick_nohz_full_mask);
    }

    /* Enable user/kernel transition tracking for these CPUs */
    for_each_cpu(cpu, tick_nohz_full_mask)
        ct_cpu_track_user(cpu);

    /* Register CPU hotplug callback to prevent removing duty CPU */
    cpuhp_setup_state_nocalls(CPUHP_AP_ONLINE_DYN,
        "kernel/nohz:predown", NULL, tick_nohz_cpu_down);

    pr_info("NO_HZ: Full dynticks CPUs: %*pbl.\n",
            cpumask_pr_args(tick_nohz_full_mask));
}

Tick Dependency Tracking

Unlike NO_HZ_IDLE (which only needs to check timers), NO_HZ_FULL must track multiple kernel subsystems that require the tick to function correctly. The kernel uses a four-level hierarchical dependency mask — any bit set at any level forces the tick back on:

/* include/linux/tick.h */
enum tick_dep_bits {
    TICK_DEP_BIT_POSIX_TIMER   = 0,  /* Active POSIX CPU timer */
    TICK_DEP_BIT_PERF_EVENTS   = 1,  /* Perf needs tick sampling */
    TICK_DEP_BIT_SCHED         = 2,  /* >1 runnable task (need preemption) */
    TICK_DEP_BIT_CLOCK_UNSTABLE = 3, /* TSC unstable, need tick for correction */
    TICK_DEP_BIT_RCU           = 4,  /* RCU callback pending */
    TICK_DEP_BIT_RCU_EXP       = 5,  /* RCU expedited grace period waiting */
};

/* Checked at 4 levels (OR logic across all): */
static atomic_t tick_dep_mask;                /* Level 1: Global system-wide */
per_cpu: ts->tick_dep_mask;                   /* Level 2: Per-CPU */
current->tick_dep_mask;                       /* Level 3: Per-task */
current->signal->tick_dep_mask;               /* Level 4: Per-signal group */
The Four-Level Check
static bool can_stop_full_tick(int cpu, struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();

    if (unlikely(!cpu_online(cpu)))
        return false;

    /* Check all 4 levels — any bit at any level → cannot stop */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&tick_dep_mask))            return false;  /* Global */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&ts->tick_dep_mask))        return false;  /* Per-CPU */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&current->tick_dep_mask))   return false;  /* Per-task */
    if (check_tick_dependency(&current->signal->tick_dep_mask))
                                                          return false;  /* Per-signal */
    return true;
}

/* check_tick_dependency: reads atomic, traces which bit blocked */
static bool check_tick_dependency(atomic_t *dep)
{
    int val = atomic_read(dep);
    if (likely(!tracepoint_enabled(tick_stop)))
        return !!val;               /* Fast path: just check non-zero */
    /* Slow path: trace which specific bit is set */
    if (val & TICK_DEP_MASK_POSIX_TIMER) { trace_tick_stop(0, ...); return true; }
    if (val & TICK_DEP_MASK_PERF_EVENTS) { trace_tick_stop(0, ...); return true; }
    /* ... same for SCHED, CLOCK_UNSTABLE, RCU, RCU_EXP ... */
    return false;
}
Table 6-137. Tick Dependencies — What Forces the Tick Back On
DependencyLevel(s)Set ByCleared WhenExample Trigger
POSIX_TIMERTask, Signalposix_cpu_timer_create()Timer expires/deletedsetitimer(ITIMER_PROF)
PERF_EVENTSCPU, Globalperf_event_open()Event closed/disabledperf record -C 3
SCHEDCPUsched_update_tick_dependency()Drops back to 1 runnable taskAny wake_up() on isolated CPU
CLOCK_UNSTABLEGlobalTSC marked unstableNever (until reboot)TSC drift detected across sockets
RCUCPURCU callback queued on this CPUCallbacks drained/offloadedcall_rcu() from this CPU
RCU_EXPCPUExpedited grace period needs this CPUGP completessynchronize_rcu_expedited()
Why Four Levels?

Different subsystems operate at different scopes. The four-level design allows precise, minimal-cost dependency management:

Table 6-138. Why Four Dependency Levels
LevelScopeWhy SeparateExample
GlobalAll CPUsRare system-wide events; single atomic check covers all CPUsTSC marked unstable affects every CPU
Per-CPUOne CPUCPU-local events (RCU callbacks queued here); no need to kick otherscall_rcu() adds callback → sets bit on this CPU only
Per-TaskFollows taskWhen task migrates, its deps move with it; checked on task switchPOSIX timer attached to thread
Per-SignalProcess-wideProcess-level timers affect all threads; setting once covers them allITIMER_VIRTUAL on a multi-threaded process

The Dependency Set/Clear API

The API exhibits a deliberate set/clear asymmetry: setting a dependency is urgent (must interrupt tickless CPU), while clearing is lazy (noticed on next IRQ exit):

/* ═══ SET: atomic OR + immediate IPI kick ═══ */
void tick_nohz_dep_set(enum tick_dep_bits bit)         /* Global */
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev)
        tick_nohz_full_kick_all();   /* Kick ALL full-dynticks CPUs */
}

void tick_nohz_dep_set_cpu(int cpu, enum tick_dep_bits bit)  /* Per-CPU */
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &ts->tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev) {
        if (cpu == smp_processor_id())
            tick_nohz_full_kick();         /* NMI-safe self-kick */
        else
            tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(cpu);  /* Remote IPI */
    }
}

void tick_nohz_dep_set_task(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    if (!atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &tsk->tick_dep_mask))
        tick_nohz_kick_task(tsk);    /* Kick CPU where task is running */
}

void tick_nohz_dep_set_signal(struct task_struct *tsk, enum tick_dep_bits bit)
{
    int prev = atomic_fetch_or(BIT(bit), &tsk->signal->tick_dep_mask);
    if (!prev) {
        /* Must kick ALL threads in the process */
        __for_each_thread(sig, t)
            tick_nohz_kick_task(t);
    }
}

/* ═══ CLEAR: atomic AND-NOT, NO kick (lazy) ═══ */
void tick_nohz_dep_clear(enum tick_dep_bits bit)       { atomic_andnot(BIT(bit), &tick_dep_mask); }
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_cpu(int cpu, ...)             { atomic_andnot(BIT(bit), &ts->tick_dep_mask); }
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_task(struct task_struct *, ..) { atomic_andnot(BIT(bit), &tsk->tick_dep_mask); }
void tick_nohz_dep_clear_signal(struct signal_struct *, ...) { atomic_andnot(BIT(bit), &sig->tick_dep_mask); }
Table 6-139. Set vs Clear Asymmetry
OperationAtomic OpSide EffectRationale
dep_set*()atomic_fetch_orIPI kick (if first bit)Must interrupt tickless CPU immediately — it won't check otherwise
dep_clear*()atomic_andnotNoneCPU notices on next IRQ exit via tick_nohz_irq_exit() — no urgency

The Kick Mechanism

When a dependency changes, the kernel kicks the tickless CPU to force it to re-evaluate. The mechanism is ingeniously simple: an empty IRQ work handler:

/* The handler does NOTHING — the magic is in the IRQ exit path */
static void nohz_full_kick_func(struct irq_work *work) { }

static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct irq_work, nohz_full_kick_work) =
    IRQ_WORK_INIT_HARD(nohz_full_kick_func);

/* Self-kick: NMI-safe (uses local irq_work queue) */
static void tick_nohz_full_kick(void)
{
    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        return;
    irq_work_queue(this_cpu_ptr(&nohz_full_kick_work));
}

/* Remote kick: sends IPI to target CPU */
void tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(int cpu)
{
    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu))
        return;
    irq_work_queue_on(&per_cpu(nohz_full_kick_work, cpu), cpu);
}

/* Kick all full-dynticks CPUs */
static void tick_nohz_full_kick_all(void)
{
    for_each_cpu_and(cpu, tick_nohz_full_mask, cpu_online_mask)
        tick_nohz_full_kick_cpu(cpu);
}

Why an empty handler works: The IPI causes an interrupt. On interrupt exit, tick_nohz_irq_exit() runs, which calls tick_nohz_full_update_tick(), which calls can_stop_full_tick(). If the dependency bit is now set, the tick is restarted. The kick doesn't do anything itself — it merely ensures the CPU goes through the IRQ exit path where the real decision happens.

The Scheduler Integration (SCHED Dependency)

The most common dependency is TICK_DEP_BIT_SCHED — the tick is needed for preemption when more than one task is runnable. The scheduler maintains this via sched_update_tick_dependency():

/* kernel/sched/sched.h — called on every enqueue/dequeue */
static inline void sched_update_tick_dependency(struct rq *rq)
{
    int cpu = cpu_of(rq);

    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(cpu))
        return;

    if (sched_can_stop_tick(rq))
        tick_nohz_dep_clear_cpu(cpu, TICK_DEP_BIT_SCHED);
    else
        tick_nohz_dep_set_cpu(cpu, TICK_DEP_BIT_SCHED);
}

/* kernel/sched/core.c */
bool sched_can_stop_tick(struct rq *rq)
{
    /* Deadline tasks always need the tick */
    if (rq->dl.dl_nr_running)
        return false;

    /* Multiple RR tasks need tick for round-robin */
    if (rq->rt.rr_nr_running > 1)
        return false;

    /* Single FIFO task: no preemption needed */
    if (rq->rt.rt_nr_running - rq->rt.rr_nr_running > 0)
        return true;

    /* SCX: ask the BPF scheduler */
    if (scx_enabled() && !scx_can_stop_tick(rq))
        return false;

    /* Multiple CFS tasks: need tick for involuntary preemption */
    if (rq->cfs.h_nr_queued > 1)
        return false;

    /* Single CFS task with bandwidth constraint: keep tick */
    if (cfs_task_bw_constrained(rq->curr))
        return false;

    return true;  /* Can stop! */
}
Table 6-140. sched_can_stop_tick() Decision Matrix
Scheduling ClassConditionCan Stop?Reason
SCHED_DEADLINEAny DL task running❌ NoDL needs tick for bandwidth enforcement
SCHED_RR>1 RR task❌ NoRound-robin timeslice needs tick
SCHED_RRExactly 1 RR task✅ YesNo one to preempt
SCHED_FIFOAny count✅ YesFIFO never preempts same-priority
SCHED_OTHER (CFS)>1 task❌ NoCFS needs tick for fair timeslicing
SCHED_OTHER (CFS)1 task, bandwidth-constrained❌ Nocgroup CPU limit enforcement
SCHED_OTHER (CFS)1 task, no BW limit✅ YesNo preemption needed
SCX (BPF)BPF says no❌ NoBPF scheduler decision

Task Switch Re-evaluation

When a task switch occurs on a NO_HZ_FULL CPU, the new task might carry different per-task dependencies. __tick_nohz_task_switch() handles this:

void __tick_nohz_task_switch(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts;

    if (!tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        return;

    ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
        /* Tick is currently stopped — check if new task needs it */
        if (atomic_read(&current->tick_dep_mask) ||
            atomic_read(&current->signal->tick_dep_mask))
            tick_nohz_full_kick();  /* Force re-evaluation */
    }
}
/* Called from context_switch() → finish_task_switch() path */

This is critical for correctness: if task A runs tickless (no deps) and task B is scheduled in (has a POSIX timer), the tick must restart immediately. Without this check, task B's timer would never fire.

The Full Tick Stop/Restart Cycle

The actual tick stop for NO_HZ_FULL happens through __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(), which is called from two places: (1) tick_nohz_irq_exit() on IRQ exit, and (2) schedule() when returning to a single-task state:

static void __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    int cpu = smp_processor_id();

    if (can_stop_full_tick(cpu, ts))
        tick_nohz_full_stop_tick(ts, cpu);       /* Stop or reprogram */
    else if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED))
        tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(ts, now);   /* Must restart! */
}

static void tick_nohz_full_stop_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, int cpu)
{
    if (tick_nohz_next_event(ts, cpu))   /* Find next timer */
        tick_nohz_stop_tick(ts, cpu);    /* Program wakeup */
    else
        tick_nohz_retain_tick(ts);       /* Timer too soon, keep tick */
}

Context Tracking Integration

NO_HZ_FULL requires context tracking (ct_cpu_track_user()) to know when the CPU transitions between kernel and user mode. This is how the kernel knows the CPU is actually running user code (and can safely stop the tick):

/* During init: enable context tracking on nohz_full CPUs */
for_each_cpu(cpu, tick_nohz_full_mask)
    ct_cpu_track_user(cpu);

/* On kernel→user transition (return from syscall/IRQ): */
/* context_tracking detects user entry → tick can be stopped */
/* On user→kernel transition (syscall/IRQ entry): */
/* context_tracking detects kernel entry → tick may be restarted */

Without context tracking, the kernel cannot distinguish "CPU running user code" from "CPU running kernel code." In kernel mode, the tick may be needed for softirq processing, RCU quiescent state reporting, etc.

NO_HZ_FULL Requirements and Limitations

Table 6-141. NO_HZ_FULL Requirements
RequirementReasonConsequence if Violated
At least 1 housekeeping CPUMust maintain jiffies + handle unbound work + RCUBoot CPU is forced back into the housekeeping set, with a warning
Exactly 1 runnable taskNo fair scheduling possible without tickTick restarts (SCHED dep set)
rcu_nocbs= recommendedOffload RCU callbacks to housekeeping CPUsRCU dep forces tick frequently
arch_irq_work_has_interrupt()Kick mechanism needs self-IPI capabilityNO_HZ_FULL disabled at boot
No perf counters on isolated CPUsTick-based sampling impossible without tickTick restarts (PERF dep)
No POSIX CPU timers on isolated tasksITIMER_VIRTUAL needs tick-based accountingTick restarts (POSIX dep)
Stable TSC (x86)Unstable TSC forces tick for clock correctionTick restarts permanently (global)
Not bandwidth-constrained (CFS BW)CPU limits need tick for enforcementTick cannot stop

CPU Hotplug Interaction

The tick_do_timer_cpu (timekeeping duty CPU) cannot be offlined when NO_HZ_FULL is active — this would leave the system without a timekeeper:

bool tick_nohz_cpu_hotpluggable(unsigned int cpu)
{
    /* The duty CPU handles housekeeping on behalf of full dynticks CPUs */
    if (tick_nohz_full_running && READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu) == cpu)
        return false;  /* Cannot offline this CPU */
    return true;
}

static int tick_nohz_cpu_down(unsigned int cpu)
{
    return tick_nohz_cpu_hotpluggable(cpu) ? 0 : -EBUSY;
}

Performance Impact and Tradeoffs

Table 6-142. NO_HZ_FULL Performance Tradeoffs
AspectBenefitCost
Tick elimination0 jitter from tick (vs ~1–10µs per tick)Context tracking overhead on every syscall/IRQ (~200ns)
IsolationPredictable, deterministic executionLess work capacity on housekeeping CPUs
CacheNo kernel cache pollution from tick handlerFirst syscall after long tickless run is cold
RCU offloadNo RCU callback processing on isolated CPUsHousekeeping CPU handles all callbacks
DiagnosticsTracepoints for dependency trackingHarder to debug (no periodic sampling)
NO_HZ_FULL did not exist in Linux 2.6. It was introduced in Linux 3.10 (2013) with basic full dynticks support. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) Four-level dependency tracking (3.10 only had per-CPU), (2) atomic_fetch_or() lock-free management (replacing spinlocks), (3) NMI-safe self-kick via irq_work, (4) Per-process signal-level deps for POSIX timers, (5) Task switch integration (__tick_nohz_task_switch()), (6) SCX (BPF scheduler) integration in sched_can_stop_tick(), (7) Context tracking via ct_cpu_track_user() (replaces vtime), (8) Tracepoint diagnostics (trace_tick_stop), (9) CPU hotplug safety for duty CPU.

NOHZ and Timekeeping: The Jiffies Catch-Up

When the tick is stopped, jiffies — the kernel's coarse-grained time counter — is not updated in real time. This creates a fundamental problem: any code that reads jiffies during an interrupt on a tickless CPU would see a stale value, potentially causing timers to fire late, load accounting to be wrong, and the softlockup watchdog to trigger falsely. Linux 7.0.12 solves this with a lazy catch-up mechanism: jiffies are advanced all at once when the CPU wakes up or receives an interrupt.

The Core Update Function

/* kernel/time/tick-sched.c */
static void tick_do_update_jiffies64(ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long ticks = 1;
    ktime_t delta, nextp;

    /* ① Quick check: is it even time for a tick? */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_64BIT)) {
        /* 64-bit: lockless check with acquire semantics */
        if (ktime_before(now, smp_load_acquire(&tick_next_period)))
            return;
    } else {
        unsigned int seq;
        /* 32-bit: need seqcount to read tick_next_period atomically */
        do {
            seq = read_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);
            nextp = tick_next_period;
        } while (read_seqcount_retry(&jiffies_seq, seq));
        if (ktime_before(now, nextp)) return;
    }

    /* ② Acquire the jiffies lock (only one CPU advances) */
    raw_spin_lock(&jiffies_lock);

    /* Re-check under lock (another CPU may have updated) */
    if (ktime_before(now, tick_next_period)) {
        raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);
        return;
    }

    write_seqcount_begin(&jiffies_seq);

    /* ③ Calculate missed ticks */
    delta = ktime_sub(now, tick_next_period);
    if (unlikely(delta >= TICK_NSEC)) {
        /* Long sleep: advance multiple ticks at once */
        ticks += ktime_divns(delta, TICK_NSEC);
        last_jiffies_update = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update,
                                           TICK_NSEC * ticks);
    } else {
        last_jiffies_update = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update, TICK_NSEC);
    }

    /* ④ Advance jiffies atomically */
    jiffies_64 += ticks;

    /* ⑤ Set next tick boundary */
    nextp = ktime_add_ns(last_jiffies_update, TICK_NSEC);
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_64BIT))
        smp_store_release(&tick_next_period, nextp); /* pairs with ① */
    else
        tick_next_period = nextp;   /* seqcount already covers it */

    write_seqcount_end(&jiffies_seq);

    /* ⑥ Global load average update (not under seqcount) */
    calc_global_load();

    raw_spin_unlock(&jiffies_lock);

    /* ⑦ Update wall clock (NTP, timekeeping) */
    update_wall_time();
}
Table 6-143. tick_do_update_jiffies64() Steps
StepWhatCostWhy
①Lockless quick check~1ns (64-bit)Avoid lock contention — most calls return here
②Acquire jiffies_lock~5ns uncontendedSerialize concurrent update attempts
③Calculate missed ticks~2ns (division)Handle long sleeps (may be thousands of ticks)
④Advance jiffies_64~1nsThe actual time advance all consumers see
⑤Update tick_next_period~1ns (store_release)Set boundary for next quick check
⑥calc_global_load()~50nsLoad average uses jiffies; must be up to date
⑦update_wall_time()~100nsAdvance NTP-corrected wall clock for gettimeofday()

When is the Catch-Up Triggered?

The catch-up happens in two contexts:

/* ═══ Context 1: IRQ entry on idle/tickless CPU ═══ */
/* kernel/softirq.c */
void irq_enter_rcu(void)
{
    __irq_enter_raw();
    if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()) ||
        (is_idle_task(current) && (irq_count() == HARDIRQ_OFFSET)))
        tick_irq_enter();   /* ← triggers catch-up */
    account_hardirq_enter(current);
}

void tick_irq_enter(void)
{
    tick_check_oneshot_broadcast_this_cpu();
    tick_nohz_irq_enter();
}

static inline void tick_nohz_irq_enter(void)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = this_cpu_ptr(&tick_cpu_sched);

    if (!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED | TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE))
        return;

    ktime_t now = ktime_get();

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE))
        tick_nohz_stop_idle(ts, now);  /* Update idle accounting */

    if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED))
        tick_nohz_update_jiffies(now); /* THE jiffies catch-up */
}

/* ═══ Context 2: Idle exit (tick_nohz_idle_exit) ═══ */
/* Also calls tick_do_update_jiffies64() via tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick() */

The tick_nohz_update_jiffies() Function

/**
 * tick_nohz_update_jiffies - update jiffies when idle was interrupted
 * @now: current ktime_t
 *
 * Called from interrupt entry when the CPU was idle.
 * We do this unconditionally on any CPU, as we don't know whether the
 * CPU which has the update task assigned is in a long sleep.
 */
static void tick_nohz_update_jiffies(ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long flags;

    __this_cpu_write(tick_cpu_sched.idle_waketime, now);

    local_irq_save(flags);
    tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);   /* Advances jiffies + wall time */
    local_irq_restore(flags);

    touch_softlockup_watchdog_sched();  /* Prevent false watchdog trigger */
}

The touch_softlockup_watchdog_sched() call is critical: after a long tickless sleep, the softlockup watchdog would see a huge gap since the last tick and incorrectly conclude the CPU is stuck. Touching the watchdog resets its counter.

The Duty CPU Hand-Off Protocol

Only one CPU at a time is responsible for calling tick_do_update_jiffies64() from the normal tick path. This prevents a "thundering herd" of all CPUs trying to grab jiffies_lock simultaneously. The duty is tracked in tick_do_timer_cpu:

/* kernel/time/tick-common.c — declared globally */
int tick_do_timer_cpu __read_mostly = TICK_DO_TIMER_BOOT;

/*
 * Purpose:
 * 1) Prevent thundering herd on jiffies_lock (only duty CPU updates)
 * 2) Hand off in NOHZ idle by setting TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE;
 *    next waking CPU reclaims
 */

The hand-off code in tick_nohz_stop_tick():

/* When stopping the tick: */
tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
if (tick_cpu == cpu) {
    /* I was the duty CPU — relinquish */
    WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE);
    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST);
} else if (tick_cpu != TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE) {
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST);
}

/* When the tick fires (tick_sched_do_timer): */
tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);
if (unlikely(tick_cpu == TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE)) {
    /* Nobody owns it — I'll take it */
    WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, cpu);
    tick_cpu = cpu;
}
if (tick_cpu == cpu)
    tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);   /* Only duty CPU updates */

The Timekeeping Max Deferment Limit

A CPU cannot sleep indefinitely without updating timekeeping. Every clocksource has a max_idle_ns value — the maximum time the clocksource can drift before its cycle counter wraps or accumulates unacceptable error:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
u64 timekeeping_max_deferment(void)
{
    struct timekeeper *tk = &tk_core.timekeeper;
    unsigned int seq;
    u64 ret;

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&tk_core.seq);
        ret = tk->tkr_mono.clock->max_idle_ns;
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&tk_core.seq, seq));

    return ret;  /* e.g., ~1.5 seconds for TSC */
}

This limits how long the duty CPU can sleep. If the duty CPU goes idle, it uses timekeeping_max_deferment() as its maximum sleep time (not KTIME_MAX). Non-duty CPUs can sleep indefinitely:

/* In tick_nohz_next_event(): */
delta = timekeeping_max_deferment();
tick_cpu = READ_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu);

if (tick_cpu != cpu &&
    (tick_cpu != TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE ||
     !tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST)))
    delta = KTIME_MAX;  /* Not duty CPU: sleep as long as needed */

/* Duty CPU: capped at max_deferment (typically ~1.5s for TSC) */
expires = basemono + delta;
Table 6-144. Max Deferment by Clocksource
ClocksourceTypical max_idle_nsLimiting Factor
TSC (x86)~1.5 secondsNTP correction accumulation
ARM arch timer~5 seconds56-bit counter, lower frequency
HPET~100ms32-bit counter at 14.3 MHz
ACPI PM timer~2.7 seconds24-bit counter at 3.58 MHz

The 64-bit vs 32-bit Split

The quick check in tick_do_update_jiffies64() uses different strategies based on word size:

Table 6-145. Architecture-Specific Jiffies Update Strategy
ArchitectureQuick CheckWhy
64-bit (x86_64, ARM64)smp_load_acquire(&tick_next_period)ktime_t (64-bit) is atomically readable; no torn read risk
32-bit (ARMv7, etc.)seqcount read of tick_next_period64-bit ktime_t stored as two 32-bit words; CPU can reorder stores

On 64-bit, the fast path is completely lockless: a single smp_load_acquire() paired with smp_store_release() in the update path. This means the common case (tick not yet due) costs only ~1ns.

The asymmetry runs through the write side as well, and it is worth following because it shows how narrowly a memory barrier can be scoped. Step ⑤ publishes tick_next_period with smp_store_release() on 64-bit but with a plain store on 32-bit. That is not an oversight. The release store exists solely to pair with the lockless acquire load in step ①, and to stop the compiler or the CPU reordering the update of jiffies_64 after the store that advertises the new period — a reader that saw the new tick_next_period but the old jiffies_64 would conclude the tick had already been accounted for when it had not. On 32-bit there is no lockless reader to pair with: the quick check is inside a jiffies_seq retry loop, and the store is inside the matching write_seqcount section, so the seqcount already provides the ordering and the barrier would be redundant. As the kernel puts it, “A plain store is good enough on 32-bit, as the quick check above is protected by the sequence count.”

Why This is Transparent to Most Code

Table 6-146. Why Jiffies Catch-Up is Transparent
SubsystemWhy It Doesn't Notice
High-resolution timingUses ktime_get() (clocksource-based), not jiffies
Timer wheelTimers are relative to jiffies; they don't fire until CPU wakes and runs softirqs anyway
SchedulerUses sched_clock() for per-CPU time, independent of jiffies
RCUQuiescent state is reported on idle entry, not based on jiffies ticking
User-space gettimeofday()update_wall_time() called in catch-up, so wall clock is correct
Load averagecalc_global_load() called in catch-up; values are correct
Softlockup watchdogtouch_softlockup_watchdog_sched() prevents false alarms

The "All CPUs Idle" Corner Case

When every CPU in the system goes idle (common on laptops and embedded), no CPU is updating jiffies. The resolution is simple but effective:

  1. The last CPU to sleep was the duty CPU → it wrote TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE
  2. All CPUs sleep; jiffies is frozen
  3. First IRQ wakes any CPU → tick_nohz_irq_enter() calls tick_nohz_update_jiffies(now)
  4. Inside, tick_do_update_jiffies64() advances jiffies by all missed ticks at once
  5. In tick_sched_do_timer(), this CPU sees TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE → reclaims duty

This means jiffies can jump by thousands in a single call after a long system-wide sleep. Kernel subsystems must handle this:

/* Example: after 10 seconds of sleep at HZ=1000 */
/* tick_do_update_jiffies64() advances jiffies by 10,000 in ONE call */
ticks = ktime_divns(delta, TICK_NSEC);  /* = 10000 */
jiffies_64 += ticks;                     /* atomic 64-bit add */

Stall Detection During Long Sleeps

If the duty CPU is stuck (e.g., in stop_machine() or a VM exit) and can't update jiffies, other CPUs detect the stall after MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES (5) ticks via tick_limited_update_jiffies64():

static bool tick_limited_update_jiffies64(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    /* Only one CPU at a time can do this (atomic cmpxchg) */
    int inp = atomic_read(&in_progress);
    if (inp || !atomic_try_cmpxchg(&in_progress, &inp, 1))
        return false;

    /* Force jiffies update even though we're not duty CPU */
    if (ts->last_tick_jiffies == jiffies)
        tick_do_update_jiffies64(now);

    atomic_set(&in_progress, 0);
    return true;
}
Table 6-147. Jiffies Update Scenarios Summary
ScenarioWho UpdatesTriggerTicks Advanced
Normal operationDuty CPUTick handler (tick_sched_do_timer)1 per tick
Duty CPU idle, others busyFirst waking CPUtick_sched_do_timer() sees NONE1 (duty was only briefly idle)
All CPUs idleFirst to waketick_nohz_update_jiffies() in IRQ entryN (all missed)
Long single-CPU sleepThat CPU on waketick_nohz_restart_sched_tick()N (all missed)
Duty CPU stuck (VM exit)Any non-duty CPUtick_limited_update_jiffies64() after 5 stallsN (catch-up)
NO_HZ_FULL busy CPUHousekeeping CPUNormal tick on housekeeping1 per tick (always running)
Linux 2.6.11 called tick_nohz_update_jiffies() on every IRQ entry unconditionally. Linux 7.0.12 optimizes this with: (1) TS_FLAG_STOPPED check — only calls when tick was actually stopped, (2) 64-bit lockless quick path via smp_load_acquire/smp_store_release, (3) tick_limited_update_jiffies64() for VM stall recovery, (4) TS_FLAG_DO_TIMER_LAST tracking so duty can be reclaimed without races, (5) timekeeping_max_deferment() cap that's clocksource-aware (not a hardcoded constant).

NOHZ Idle Accounting

When ticks are stopped during idle, the traditional tick-based accounting (which charges one tick to idle every time the tick fires while idle) breaks down. The NOHZ subsystem must replace it with precise, measurement-based accounting — recording exact entry/exit timestamps and computing durations. This feeds /proc/stat, CPU frequency governors, and power management decisions.

The Problem: Tick-Based vs Measurement-Based Accounting

Table 6-148. Accounting Approaches Compared
ApproachMethodAccuracyUsed When
Tick-based (legacy)update_process_times() charges 1 tick per interrupt±1 tick (1-10ms)Tick is running (HZ_PERIODIC)
NOHZ measurementktime_get() at entry/exit, compute delta±clocksource resolution (~1ns)Tick is stopped (NOHZ)
vtime (virtual time)Timestamp at every user/kernel boundary: syscall and IRQ entry and exit, guest enter and exit, idle enter and exit, and context switchClocksource resolution, paid for with a clock read on every transitionVIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_GEN, required by NO_HZ_FULL

The Accounting Lifecycle

Idle accounting is managed through three key functions called at precise points in the idle cycle:

Entry: tick_nohz_start_idle()

static void tick_nohz_start_idle(struct tick_sched *ts)
{
    write_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);
    ts->idle_entrytime = ktime_get();      /* Record precise entry time */
    tick_sched_flag_set(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);  /* Mark as actively idle */
    write_seqcount_end(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

    sched_clock_idle_sleep_event();  /* Notify sched_clock of idle entry */
}

This is called from two places, and it is worth knowing both. The primary caller is tick_nohz_idle_enter(), on the way into the idle loop. The second is tick_nohz_irq_exit(): when an interrupt arrives on a CPU that is already idle, the handler runs, tick_nohz_stop_idle() closes the accounting segment on the way in, and on the way out tick_nohz_irq_exit() opens a fresh one. That is why tick_nohz_stop_idle() resets ts->idle_entrytime to now rather than clearing it — a single visit to the idle loop is recorded as a sequence of segments, one per interruption, and the interrupt handling time between them is correctly excluded from the idle totals. The seqcount protects the pair of counters against readers on other CPUs, which reach them through /proc/stat.

Exit: tick_nohz_stop_idle()

static void tick_nohz_stop_idle(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    ktime_t delta;

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE)))
        return;

    delta = ktime_sub(now, ts->idle_entrytime);

    write_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);
    if (nr_iowait_cpu(smp_processor_id()) > 0)
        ts->iowait_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->iowait_sleeptime, delta);
    else
        ts->idle_sleeptime = ktime_add(ts->idle_sleeptime, delta);

    ts->idle_entrytime = now;      /* Reset for next idle segment */
    tick_sched_flag_clear(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE);
    write_seqcount_end(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

    sched_clock_idle_wakeup_event();  /* Notify sched_clock of wakeup */
}

The nr_iowait_cpu() classification determines whether this idle time is "pure idle" or "waiting for I/O." This distinction matters for /proc/stat and CPU frequency governors — iowait signals the CPU could be doing useful work if I/O were faster.

That is the intent, but the reader should be told that the kernel does not really believe in it. “iowait” is a per-CPU counter of tasks that blocked on I/O while last running on this CPU, and nothing pins those tasks to it: when the I/O completes the task is woken by the scheduler and may well run somewhere else entirely. So a CPU can show high iowait while having no relationship to the work that is about to happen. The comment above nr_iowait_cpu() in kernel/sched/core.c is unusually blunt about this: “Consumers of these two interfaces, like for example the cpuidle menu governor, are using nonsensical data. Preferring shallow idle state selection for a CPU that has IO-wait which might not even end up running the task when it does become runnable.”

The counter survives because /proc/stat is ABI and the %iowait column of top, vmstat and mpstat is derived from it. Treat it as a system-wide hint that I/O is a bottleneck somewhere, never as a statement about the CPU it is reported against. The race described later in this section is a second, narrower problem layered on top of this semantic one.

Tick Accounting: account_idle_ticks()

When the tick was stopped, update_process_times() (which normally charges 1 tick per interrupt) never ran. On exit, the missed ticks must be charged to idle:

static void tick_nohz_account_idle_time(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    unsigned long ticks;

    ts->idle_exittime = now;

    /* vtime handles accounting for NO_HZ_FULL CPUs */
    if (vtime_accounting_enabled_this_cpu())
        return;

    /*
     * We stopped the tick in idle. update_process_times() would miss
     * the time we slept, as it does only a 1-tick accounting.
     * Enforce that this is accounted to idle!
     */
    ticks = jiffies - ts->idle_jiffies;

    /* Sanity: don't account a huge number (protects against wrap) */
    if (ticks && ticks < LONG_MAX)
        account_idle_ticks(ticks);  /* → account_idle_time(ticks * TICK_NSEC) */
}
Table 6-149. Idle Accounting Fields and Their Consumers
FieldUpdated ByConsumerPurpose
idle_sleeptimetick_nohz_stop_idle()get_cpu_idle_time_us() → /proc/stat, cpufreqTotal non-IO idle time (µs since boot)
iowait_sleeptimetick_nohz_stop_idle()get_cpu_iowait_time_us() → /proc/statTotal IO-wait idle time (µs since boot)
idle_callstick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()tick_nohz_get_idle_calls_cpu() → schedutilTotal idle entries (frequency governor uses for utilization)
idle_sleepstick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()/proc/timer_listEntries where tick was actually stopped
idle_jiffiestick_nohz_idle_stop_tick()tick_nohz_account_idle_time()Jiffies base for tick accounting on exit
idle_entrytimetick_nohz_start_idle()tick_nohz_stop_idle(), governorTimestamp for delta computation
idle_exittimetick_nohz_account_idle_time()Debugging, /proc/timer_listWhen CPU last left idle
idle_waketimetick_nohz_update_jiffies()IRQ entry pathTimestamp of interrupt that woke us

The Reader API: get_cpu_idle_time_us()

External consumers (cpufreq, /proc/stat) call get_cpu_idle_time_us() which handles the tricky case of reading while the CPU is currently idle:

u64 get_cpu_idle_time_us(int cpu, u64 *last_update_time)
{
    struct tick_sched *ts = &per_cpu(tick_cpu_sched, cpu);
    return get_cpu_sleep_time_us(ts, &ts->idle_sleeptime,
                                 !nr_iowait_cpu(cpu), last_update_time);
}

static u64 get_cpu_sleep_time_us(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t *sleeptime,
                                  bool compute_delta, u64 *last_update_time)
{
    ktime_t now, idle;
    unsigned int seq;

    if (!tick_nohz_active)
        return -1;  /* NOHZ disabled — use legacy accounting */

    now = ktime_get();
    if (last_update_time)
        *last_update_time = ktime_to_us(now);

    do {
        seq = read_seqcount_begin(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq);

        if (tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE) && compute_delta) {
            /* CPU is CURRENTLY idle — add in-progress time */
            ktime_t delta = ktime_sub(now, ts->idle_entrytime);
            idle = ktime_add(*sleeptime, delta);
        } else {
            idle = *sleeptime;
        }
    } while (read_seqcount_retry(&ts->idle_sleeptime_seq, seq));

    return ktime_to_us(idle);
}

Key insight: When the target CPU is currently idle (TS_FLAG_IDLE_ACTIVE), the reader adds the in-progress delta (now - idle_entrytime) to the accumulated total. This gives a live, accurate reading without requiring the idle CPU to wake up. The seqcount ensures consistency if the idle CPU exits concurrently.

The IO-Wait Classification Problem

The nr_iowait_cpu() classification has a known race condition acknowledged in the kernel comments:

/*
 * Note that this is partially broken due to the counter of iowait tasks
 * that can be remotely updated without any synchronization. Therefore
 * it is possible to observe backward values within two consecutive reads.
 */

The race occurs because:

  1. CPU A calls get_cpu_iowait_time_us(cpu=B)
  2. Concurrently, a task on CPU B completes its I/O → nr_iowait_cpu(B) drops from 1 to 0
  3. The next idle segment on CPU B gets classified differently (idle vs iowait)
  4. Result: iowait_sleeptime appears to decrease between readings

This is tolerated because the total (idle + iowait) is always correct — only the split between them can momentarily glitch.

Integration with /proc/stat

/* fs/proc/stat.c */
u64 get_idle_time(struct kernel_cpustat *kcs, int cpu)
{
    u64 idle_usecs = -1ULL;

    if (cpu_online(cpu))
        idle_usecs = get_cpu_idle_time_us(cpu, NULL);

    if (idle_usecs == -1ULL)
        /* !NO_HZ or cpu offline — use tick-based cpustat */
        idle = kcs->cpustat[CPUTIME_IDLE];
    else
        idle = idle_usecs * NSEC_PER_USEC;  /* Convert µs → ns */

    return idle;
}

When NOHZ is active, /proc/stat uses the measurement-based values (accurate). When disabled, it falls back to tick-based cpustat counters (±1 tick accuracy).

Integration with CPU Frequency Governors

The schedutil and ondemand governors use get_cpu_idle_time_us() and tick_nohz_get_idle_calls_cpu() to compute CPU utilization:

/* drivers/cpufreq/cpufreq.c */
static inline u64 get_cpu_idle_time(unsigned int cpu, u64 *wall, int io_busy)
{
    u64 idle_time = get_cpu_idle_time_us(cpu, io_busy ? wall : NULL);

    if (!io_busy)
        idle_time += get_cpu_iowait_time_us(cpu, wall);

    return idle_time;
}
/* Utilization = 1 - (idle_time / wall_time) */
Table 6-150. How Governors Use NOHZ Accounting
GovernorMetric UsedDecision
schedutilidle_calls counter changesDetects if CPU was idle since last sample → affects frequency ramp
ondemandidle_time / wall_time ratioHigh idle% → lower frequency; low idle% → higher frequency
conservativeidle_time / wall_time ratioSame as ondemand but ramps gradually

The sched_clock Integration

The scheduler clock (sched_clock()) must know when a CPU enters/exits idle to avoid accumulating time that would confuse scheduler fairness calculations:

/* Called from tick_nohz_start_idle(): */
sched_clock_idle_sleep_event();    /* Mark sched_clock as "frozen" */

/* Called from tick_nohz_stop_idle(): */
sched_clock_idle_wakeup_event();   /* Resume sched_clock; catch up */

Without these notifications, sched_clock() would see a huge gap and potentially cause scheduling anomalies (e.g., a task appearing to have consumed no CPU time during the idle period).

Statistics Counters

/* In tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(): */
ts->idle_calls++;      /* Every time we attempt to stop the tick */

if (expires > 0LL) {
    tick_nohz_stop_tick(ts, cpu);
    ts->idle_sleeps++;  /* Only when tick was actually stopped */
    ts->idle_expires = expires;

    if (!was_stopped && tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_STOPPED)) {
        ts->idle_jiffies = ts->last_jiffies;  /* Base for exit accounting */
        nohz_balance_enter_idle(cpu);           /* Inform scheduler */
    }
}

The ratio idle_sleeps / idle_calls indicates how effective NOHZ is: a low ratio means the tick couldn't be stopped often (e.g., timers too frequent).

Table 6-151. NOHZ Accounting Statistics
FieldMeaningTypical ValueDiagnostic Use
idle_callsTotal idle entriesMillions/hourHigher = more idle transitions = less efficient
idle_sleepsEntries where tick stopped~90-99% of callsLow ratio = timers preventing tick stop
idle_sleeptimeTotal non-IO idle (ns)Grows monotonicallyFeeds /proc/stat idle%

Preservation Across CPU Hotplug

When a CPU is hotplugged, the kernel preserves accounting statistics across the transition:

/* During CPU hotplug reset: */
idle_sleeptime = ts->idle_sleeptime;
iowait_sleeptime = ts->iowait_sleeptime;
idle_calls = ts->idle_calls;
idle_sleeps = ts->idle_sleeps;

memset(ts, 0, sizeof(*ts));  /* Clear everything */

/* Restore the counters */
ts->idle_sleeptime = idle_sleeptime;
ts->iowait_sleeptime = iowait_sleeptime;
ts->idle_calls = idle_calls;
ts->idle_sleeps = idle_sleeps;

This ensures /proc/stat doesn't show sudden drops in idle time when CPUs go offline and come back online.

Linux 2.6.11 used only tick-based idle accounting (accurate to ±1 tick = 1-10ms). Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) ktime_get()-based measurement accounting (±1ns accuracy), (2) seqcount protection for cross-CPU readers, (3) iowait/idle split with nr_iowait_cpu() classification, (4) sched_clock_idle_sleep/wakeup_event() for scheduler clock coherence, (5) live-reading for currently-idle CPUs (no wakeup needed), (6) idle_calls counter for schedutil frequency governor, (7) hotplug-safe counter preservation.

Performance Impact

The NOHZ subsystem introduces a fundamental trade-off: per-transition overhead versus steady-state savings. Every time a CPU transitions between ticked and tickless states, it must perform work — scanning timer queues, reprogramming clockevent devices, updating accounting structures, and coordinating with the timer migration hierarchy. These costs are amortized over the duration of the idle (or busy-tickless) period. The longer a CPU stays in one state, the better the amortization; frequent transitions (short idle periods of <1ms) can actually increase total overhead compared to simply leaving the tick running.

Transition Overhead Breakdown

When a CPU decides to stop its tick via tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick(), the kernel performs a series of operations whose cumulative cost varies by hardware platform and timer queue depth:

/* Simplified cost model of tick_nohz_idle_stop_tick() */

/* Step 1: Check hard blockers (can_stop_idle_tick) — ~5ns */
if (!tick_sched_flag_test(ts, TS_FLAG_NOHZ))   // flag read
    return;
if (need_resched())                              // TIF flag read
    return;
if (report_idle_softirq())                       // softirq pending check
    return;

/* Step 2: Scan timer queues (tick_nohz_next_event) — ~200-800ns */
/* Checks hrtimer next expiry across 8 clock bases,
 * timer wheel next expiry, and timer migration tree */
expires = tick_nohz_next_event(ts, cpu);

/* Step 3: Mark timer bases idle (timer_base_try_to_set_idle) — ~100-300ns */
/* Acquires timer_base lock, marks idle, handles pending timers */
expires = timer_base_try_to_set_idle(basejiff, basemono, &timer_idle);

/* Step 4: Duty CPU hand-off — ~50ns (if this CPU is duty CPU) */
if (tick_cpu == cpu)
    WRITE_ONCE(tick_do_timer_cpu, TICK_DO_TIMER_NONE);

/* Step 5: Reprogram clock event device — ~100-500ns (hardware) */
hrtimer_start(&ts->sched_timer, expires,
              HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_PINNED_HARD);

/* Step 6: Notify scheduler (nohz_balance_enter_idle) — ~50-100ns */
nohz_balance_enter_idle(cpu);

/* Step 7: Stop load calculation (calc_load_nohz_start) — ~20ns */
calc_load_nohz_start();

/* Total: ~500-1800ns typical, up to ~5µs on heavily loaded timer queues */

The restart path (tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick()) carries similar costs: reprogramming the clockevent device, reclaiming the duty CPU role, and catching up on missed jiffies. If the CPU was sleeping for many ticks, tick_do_update_jiffies64() performs the jiffies catch-up in O(1) through a single division rather than iterating — a critical optimization for CPUs waking from multi-second sleeps.

Table 6-152. NOHZ Transition Cost Breakdown
OperationCost (typical)Scales WithAmortized Over
Hard blocker check (can_stop_idle_tick)~5nsConstant (flag reads)—
Timer queue scan (tick_nohz_next_event)200–800nsNumber of active hrtimer basesIdle duration
Timer base idle marking100–300nsPending timer countIdle duration
Clockevent reprogramming100–500nsHardware (MSR vs MMIO)Idle duration
Scheduler NOHZ balance entry50–100nsBlocked CPUs in groupIdle duration
Jiffies catch-up on wake50–200nsO(1) division; constant—
Timer migration tree update100–400nsHierarchy depth (log₂ CPUs)Idle duration
Total enter + exit~1–3µs—Must be < saved tick cost

The critical insight is that a single tick interrupt costs approximately 2–5µs of CPU time (entering the interrupt handler, running tick_sched_handle(), updating timekeeping, running the scheduler tick, and returning). Stopping and restarting the tick costs roughly the same again, which is why the break-even sits at one full tick period: a CPU that skips fewer than one tick has paid the transition cost for nothing.

It is worth doing the arithmetic on what is actually saved, because the answer is smaller than the emphasis usually placed on it. Taking 3µs as a round figure for one tick, a CPU that stays idle for a full second at HZ=250 avoids 250 ticks and therefore 750µs of work — 0.075% of that CPU. At HZ=1000 it avoids 1000 ticks, or 3ms, which is 0.3%. Recovering three tenths of a percent of a core is not why anyone enables NO_HZ_IDLE.

The saving that matters is indirect, and it is the reason the table below is expressed in wakeups rather than in microseconds: every tick that does not fire is a C-state exit that does not happen. The CPU time spent in the handler is almost incidental next to the cost of dragging a core out of a deep sleep state and back into it, and next to the fact that a core which is woken 250 times a second never reaches the deepest states at all.
