NO_HZ_FULL-Specific Overheads

The full-dynticks mode imposes unique costs that don't exist in NO_HZ_IDLE. These must be carefully weighed against the jitter reduction benefits for real-time and HPC workloads:

Context tracking — Every kernel entry and exit point (syscall, interrupt, exception) must update the per-CPU context_tracking state via ct_kernel_enter() / ct_kernel_exit(). This adds ~300–500ns per system call and is marked noinstr to avoid instrumentation recursion. The overhead exists because the kernel needs to know whether a CPU in userspace is in an "extended quiescent state" for RCU purposes — without ticks, there's no other way to detect this.

/* kernel/context_tracking.c — entry on every syscall/interrupt in NO_HZ_FULL */
static void noinstr ct_kernel_enter(bool user, int offset)
{
    struct context_tracking *ct = this_cpu_ptr(&context_tracking);
    /* ... */
    if (!ct->nesting++)     /* First entry from user: report to RCU */
        ct_kernel_enter_state(offset);
}

/* The cost: ~300ns per syscall just for this state transition.
 * On a syscall-heavy workload (100K syscalls/sec), this adds
 * ~30ms/sec of pure overhead — 3% of one CPU. */

Tick dependency checking — The four-level dependency system (tick_dep_mask at global, per-CPU, per-task, and per-signal levels) must be re-evaluated on every kernel exit to determine whether the tick should restart. This is fast (bitwise OR of 4 atomics, ~20ns) but occurs on every return-to-userspace path:

/* Called on return to userspace from tick_nohz_full CPUs */
static void __tick_nohz_full_update_tick(struct tick_sched *ts, ktime_t now)
{
    /* Check all dependency levels */
    if (can_stop_full_tick(cpu, ts))
        tick_nohz_stop_tick(ts, cpu);   // Stay tickless
    else
        tick_nohz_restart_sched_tick(ts, now);  // Restart tick
}

RCU callbacks offloading — NO_HZ_FULL CPUs should use rcu_nocbs (callback offloading) to avoid the tick being restarted solely for RCU callback processing. Without rcu_nocbs, any pending RCU callback sets TICK_DEP_BIT_RCU, forcing the tick back on. The offloading itself is free in steady state but adds IPI cost when callbacks are queued from a nohz_full CPU.

Scheduler limitations — A CPU can only be tickless if it has exactly 0 or 1 runnable tasks. The moment a second task becomes runnable, sched_can_stop_tick() returns false and the tick restarts for time-slicing. This means NO_HZ_FULL benefits are limited to carefully isolated CPUs running single-threaded workloads.

Impact on Scheduler Load Balancing

When CPUs go idle with NOHZ, the scheduler's periodic load balancing stops running on those CPUs. In a periodic kernel it is driven from the tick: sched_tick() ends by calling sched_balance_trigger(), which raises SCHED_SOFTIRQ when the current CPU's balancing interval has expired. (This function was called trigger_load_balance() until Linux 6.9, when commit 983be0628c06 renamed the balancing entry points to a common sched_balance_* prefix; the older name is still what most existing documentation and blog posts use.) Since Linux 6.12 the call is also conditional on !scx_switched_all() — if a sched_ext scheduler has taken over every task, the fair-class balancer is not driven from the tick at all. With the tick stopped, neither path runs, so to compensate the kernel uses an IPI-based "NOHZ balance kick" mechanism:

/* kernel/sched/fair.c — nohz_balancer_kick(), abridged */
/* Called from sched_balance_trigger(), i.e. from every tick */
static void nohz_balancer_kick(struct rq *rq)
{
    unsigned long now = jiffies;
    unsigned int flags = 0;

    if (unlikely(rq->idle_balance))   /* this CPU is itself going idle */
        return;

    nohz_balance_exit_idle(rq);       /* first busy tick after idle */

    /* Blocked-load decay is due: refresh statistics, migrate nothing. */
    if (READ_ONCE(nohz.has_blocked_load) &&
        time_after(now, READ_ONCE(nohz.next_blocked)))
        flags = NOHZ_STATS_KICK;

    if (time_before(now, nohz.next_balance))
        goto out;
    if (unlikely(cpumask_empty(nohz.idle_cpus_mask)))
        return;               /* nobody is NOHZ-idle: nothing to kick */

    /* Each of the following says "there is work an idle CPU could take". */
    if (rq->nr_running >= 2) {                       /* plainly overloaded */
        flags = NOHZ_STATS_KICK | NOHZ_BALANCE_KICK;
        goto out;
    }
    if (rq->cfs.h_nr_runnable >= 1 &&
        check_cpu_capacity(rq, sd))                  /* capacity stolen by IRQ/RT */
        flags = NOHZ_STATS_KICK | NOHZ_BALANCE_KICK;
    else if (sched_asym(sd, i, cpu))                 /* ASYM_PACKING */
        flags = NOHZ_STATS_KICK | NOHZ_BALANCE_KICK;
    else if (check_misfit_status(rq))                /* ASYM_CPUCAPACITY */
        flags = NOHZ_STATS_KICK | NOHZ_BALANCE_KICK;
out:
    if (flags)
        kick_ilb(flags);      /* IPI the idle load balancer */
}

Two things about that function are easy to misread. First, it is not a special path taken by "the CPU that notices an imbalance" — it is called from sched_balance_trigger(), so every busy CPU runs it on every tick, and the early rq->idle_balance return is what keeps a CPU that is itself heading for idle from kicking anyone. Second, the two flags are not cumulative steps. NOHZ_STATS_KICK on its own means "the blocked-load averages of the idle CPUs have gone stale, please decay them"; no task will move. NOHZ_BALANCE_KICK is only ever set together with it, at one of four independent trigger conditions: two or more runnable tasks, a runnable CFS task on a CPU whose capacity is being eaten by interrupts or RT work, an ASYM_PACKING topology where a more preferred CPU is idle, and a misfit task that wants a bigger CPU. That last one is the ASYM_CPUCAPACITY case, so on a big.LITTLE ARM64 system the tick is what notices that a task has outgrown its little core — which is precisely the observation that makes stopping the tick on such systems a trade-off rather than a free win. If no condition fires, flags stays zero and no IPI is sent at all.

The idle load balancer (ILB) is a designated idle CPU that is woken by that IPI to perform load balancing on behalf of all NOHZ-idle CPUs. This design avoids waking every idle CPU just to check balance, but introduces latency — an imbalanced state may persist for up to one tick period on the busy CPU before the ILB is kicked. On systems with many idle CPUs, this is a significant power advantage: instead of N idle CPUs waking N times per second, only 1 wakes on demand.

Power Savings Quantification

The actual power savings from NOHZ depend on the workload's idle pattern and the hardware's C-state characteristics:

Table 6-154. Power Impact by Idle Pattern
Idle PatternHZ_PERIODIC CostNO_HZ_IDLE SavingsExplanation
Deep idle (seconds)HZ wakeups × C-state exit cost95–99% reduction in wakeupsCPU stays in deepest C-state uninterrupted; DRAM can enter self-refresh
Medium idle (10–100ms)2–25 unnecessary tick wakeups80–95% reductionAllows C3–C6 entry without premature exit; significant on mobile/laptop
Short idle (1–4ms)0–1 tick wakeupsMarginal (~0-50%)Transition overhead approaches savings; NOHZ may retain tick
Very short idle (<1ms)No tick wakes anywayNegative (overhead only)NOHZ transition cost wasted; tick_nohz_idle_retain_tick() avoids this

The kernel's cpuidle governor integration (described in the cpuidle Governor Integration section) ensures that for very short predicted idle durations, tick_nohz_idle_retain_tick() is called instead of stopping the tick — avoiding the overhead when it wouldn't pay off. This adaptive behavior means the NOHZ subsystem rarely makes things worse in practice.

Measurement and Tuning

The kernel exposes several interfaces for measuring NOHZ effectiveness and tuning behavior:

/* Per-CPU statistics (from tick_sched structure) */
ts->idle_calls    // Total idle entries (with tick stop attempted)
ts->idle_sleeps   // Entries where tick was actually stopped

/* Effectiveness ratio: idle_sleeps / idle_calls
 * Close to 1.0 = NOHZ is effective (most idles are long enough)
 * Close to 0.0 = Frequent short idles (NOHZ overhead may dominate)
 */

/* /proc/timer_list — shows per-CPU NOHZ state */
/* Tick Device mode: highres | oneshot | periodic */
/* idle_sleeptime:   total time with tick stopped (ns) */
/* iowait_sleeptime: time classified as iowait (ns) */

/* nohz_full CPUs: /sys/devices/system/cpu/nohz_full */
/* Shows which CPUs are in full-dynticks mode */

/* ftrace: tick_stop event */
/* trace_tick_stop(1, TICK_DEP_MASK_NONE); — logged when tick stops */
/* trace_tick_stop(0, dep_mask);           — logged when tick retained */

For production tuning, the key metric is the idle_sleeps / idle_calls ratio visible in /proc/timer_list. A ratio below 0.5 indicates that the workload generates many short idle periods where NOHZ overhead isn't amortized — in such cases, consider whether the workload's timer pattern can be adjusted (batching timers, using timer_slack_ns) rather than disabling NOHZ.

Architecture-Specific Considerations

The actual cost numbers vary significantly between x86_64 and ARM64 due to differences in clockevent hardware and cache architectures:
