Operationx86_64 (TSC + LAPIC)ARM64 (arch timer)Notes
Read current time (ktime_get())~20ns~40nsWhole read, not the counter instruction alone — RDTSC and MRS CNTVCT_EL0 cost roughly half that on their own (Table 6-173); the rest is the seqcount retry loop and the mult/shift arithmetic
Reprogram next event~100ns (LAPIC TSC-deadline)~80ns (CNTV_CVAL_EL0)x86 LAPIC TSC-deadline mode; ARM direct register write
C-state exit latency~1–200µs (C1–C10)~1–500µs (WFI–powerdown)Dominates total wake time; NOHZ avoids triggering this
IPI delivery (NOHZ kick)~1–5µs~2–10µs (GIC)ARM GIC-v3 slightly slower for cross-cluster IPIs
Context tracking (NO_HZ_FULL)~300ns~400nsARM slightly higher due to additional barrier requirements

On x86_64, the TSC-deadline mode of the Local APIC allows sub-microsecond reprogramming, making NOHZ transitions very cheap. On ARM64, the architected timer provides similar efficiency through direct system register access (CNTV_CVAL_EL0), though some older SoCs with memory-mapped timer access pay higher latency. Both architectures benefit enormously from NOHZ during deep idle: avoiding a C6/cluster-powerdown exit that costs 100–500µs is worth many thousands of 1µs NOHZ transition costs.

Linux 2.6 had only CONFIG_NO_HZ (equivalent to NO_HZ_IDLE), introduced in 2.6.21. Linux 7.0.12 adds: (1) NO_HZ_FULL (3.10+) with hierarchical tick dependency tracking at 4 levels (global/CPU/task/signal); (2) Timer migration (tmigr) so idle CPUs don't need to wake for global timers; (3) timer_base_try_to_set_idle() marking timer bases as idle for safe remote expiry; (4) tick_nohz_full_kick() IRQ work mechanism for instant tick restart; (5) rcu_nocbs integration for fully offloading RCU callbacks; (6) Stall detection (MAX_STALLED_JIFFIES) for virtual machines; (7) idle_sleeptime_seq seqcount for consistent idle time reporting without locks.

High-Resolution Timers (hrtimers)

The hrtimer subsystem provides nanosecond-resolution timers independent of the HZ tick frequency. Unlike the timer wheel (described in the next section), which groups timeouts into coarse buckets and tolerates significant expiry jitter, hrtimers are designed for precision: a timer set to expire in exactly 5.000000ms will fire at that time to within the hardware's interrupt delivery latency — typically under 1µs on modern x86_64 and ARM64 systems.

In Linux 7.0.12, hrtimers have become the universal timing primitive. They are the foundation for:

  • nanosleep() and clock_nanosleep() — precise user-space sleep
  • POSIX interval timers (timer_create() / timer_settime())
  • timerfd_create() — file-descriptor-based timers for epoll()-driven event loops
  • Scheduler tick emulation (tick_setup_sched_timer()) — the tick itself runs as an hrtimer in oneshot mode
  • Futex timeouts (futex_wait() with timeout)
  • io_uring timeout operations
  • Network protocol timers (TCP retransmit, keepalive)
  • DRM vblank simulation, IIO trigger generation, perf event mux

The design is built on three key ideas: (1) per-CPU, per-clock sorted trees for O(log n) insertion and O(1) next-timer lookup; (2) one-shot clockevent programming so the hardware only fires when a timer actually expires; and (3) a hard/soft IRQ split that keeps latency-critical timers in hardirq context while deferring less urgent ones to softirq.

Those three ideas are answers. The rest of this section is easier to follow if the questions come first, because almost every structure and function below exists to relieve one of five pressures:

  • Finding the next expiry must be cheap, and it is asked constantly. The previous section showed that a CPU cannot go tickless without first computing when it must next wake up, and that question is asked on every idle entry. With thousands of timers pending, the answer has to be available without walking anything — which is why timers live in sorted trees with a cached leftmost node, and why each CPU keeps a bitmask of which of its queues are non-empty so empty ones are never even visited.
  • “The clock” is not one clock. CLOCK_MONOTONIC never jumps, CLOCK_REALTIME can be moved by settimeofday() or slewed by NTP, CLOCK_BOOTTIME counts suspend and CLOCK_TAI ignores leap seconds. A timer armed against one of them must not be disturbed by adjustments to another. This is why timers are partitioned into separate per-clock queues, each carrying an offset from the monotonic base, and why an administrator stepping the wall clock has to force a re-evaluation of every affected queue.
  • Not every timer deserves hardirq context. Running all callbacks in the timer interrupt keeps latency low for the timers that need it and inflates it for everyone else — and on PREEMPT_RT, where callbacks must be preemptible, it is not acceptable at all. Hence the hard/soft split that doubles the number of queues per CPU, and the mode flags that let each caller state which half it belongs in.
  • Every expiry costs an interrupt. A timer that fires alone wakes the CPU for one callback; five timers that fire within a microsecond of each other can share a single wakeup if the kernel is allowed to slide them together. That permission is what the timer range mechanism grants, and it is the reason an hrtimer carries two expiry times rather than one.
  • The CPU that armed a timer may not be the one that should run it. If that CPU has gone tickless-idle, waking it to service a timer defeats the purpose of stopping its tick; if it has gone offline, nothing will service the timer at all. Both cases force timers to move between CPUs while remaining safely cancellable by code running elsewhere.

The rest of this section works through eleven questions, in the order the subsections answer them:

  1. How is a timer represented, and where does it live? The three-level hierarchy of timer, per-clock queue, and per-CPU container — and why the “callback running” state is deliberately not stored in the timer.
  2. Why eight queues per CPU and not four? The four clock bases, doubled by the hard/soft split.
  3. What is a caller actually choosing when it picks a mode? Absolute versus relative, pinned versus migratable, hard versus soft — and which of those choices PREEMPT_RT overrides.
  4. What happens between setup and the callback returning? The full lifecycle: initialization, arming, enqueue, cancellation from another CPU, and self-rearming periodic timers.
  5. How does one clockevent interrupt become a batch of callbacks? The hardirq handler, the queue walk, the execution of a single timer — and the hang-detection logic that stops a slow callback from live-locking the CPU.
  6. Which timers are deferred, and what runs them? The soft-IRQ path and its extra locking on PREEMPT_RT.
  7. What if the hardware cannot do one-shot at all? The low-resolution fallback, where hrtimers still work but are checked once per tick.
  8. How does deliberately imprecise timing save power? Slack, coalescing, and where the default slack value comes from.
  9. When is the hardware reprogrammed, and what happens to timers whose CPU goes idle or disappears? Reprogramming, remote enqueue, migration between CPUs, and the hotplug teardown path.
  10. How is an ordinary user-space sleep built from these pieces? nanosleep(), the sleeper wrapper, and how a sleep survives a signal and resumes for the correct remaining time.
  11. Who else depends on all this? The subsystems that would break if hrtimers did.

Version history. All of it. Linux 2.6.11 predates hrtimers entirely — in that kernel every kernel timeout, without exception, went through the timer wheel described in the next section, and the finest granularity any caller could ask for was one jiffy. The hrtimer subsystem was merged in 2.6.16 and has been reworked repeatedly since: the hard/soft split and the move to eight clock bases arrived in 4.16, PREEMPT_RT support brought sleeping expiry locks and automatic promotion of unmarked timers into softirq context, and Linux 7.0.12 completes a multi-release API change that retires hrtimer_init() in favour of hrtimer_setup() and makes the callback pointer private so it can no longer be assigned behind the subsystem's back.

Core Data Structures

The hrtimer subsystem is organized into a three-level hierarchy: individual timers (struct hrtimer), per-clock queues (struct hrtimer_clock_base), and per-CPU containers (struct hrtimer_cpu_base). Understanding these structures is essential for understanding the enqueue, expiry, and migration paths.

The hrtimer Structure

Each high-resolution timer is represented by a struct hrtimer, defined in include/linux/hrtimer_types.h:

struct hrtimer {
    struct timerqueue_node      node;           /* RB-tree node; node.expires = hard expiry */
    ktime_t                     _softexpires;   /* Earliest allowed expiry (for range/slack) */
    enum hrtimer_restart        (*__private function)(struct hrtimer *);  /* Callback */
    struct hrtimer_clock_base   *base;          /* Current per-CPU, per-clock base */
    u8                          state;          /* INACTIVE or ENQUEUED */
    u8                          is_rel;         /* Armed with relative time? */
    u8                          is_soft;        /* Expire in softirq context? */
    u8                          is_hard;        /* Expire in hardirq even on PREEMPT_RT? */
};

The __private annotation on function arrived in Linux 6.15 (commit 04257da0c99c), and it makes the field off-limits to the idiom that had been used throughout the kernel for two decades: timer->function = my_callback;. The enforcement is static-analysis rather than compiler enforcement. __private expands to __attribute__((noderef)) only when the source is being analysed by sparse, and to nothing at all in an ordinary gcc or clang build, so a direct assignment still compiles — but make C=1 reports it, and the kernel's CI runs sparse. The sanctioned way through the annotation is the ACCESS_PRIVATE() macro, which casts the noderef away with __force. In practice this means callbacks are supplied to hrtimer_setup() at initialization time, or, for the rare cases that genuinely need to change a callback afterwards, through hrtimer_update_function():

/* include/linux/hrtimer.h */
static inline void hrtimer_update_function(struct hrtimer *timer,
                                           enum hrtimer_restart (*function)(struct hrtimer *))
{
#ifdef CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING
    guard(raw_spinlock_irqsave)(&timer->base->cpu_base->lock);

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(hrtimer_is_queued(timer)))
        return;
    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!function))
        return;
#endif
    ACCESS_PRIVATE(timer, function) = function;
}

The accessor exists to make two rules checkable. First, the callback may only be changed while the timer is not queued — swapping it under a timer that is already in the tree races with an expiry that may be about to call the old pointer. Second, it may never be set to NULL. Both checks are compiled out unless CONFIG_PROVE_LOCKING is enabled, so the production cost is a plain assignment; the debug build is what catches the misuse. This is a good example of a recurring pattern in modern kernel code: rather than documenting an invariant in a comment and hoping, the field is made unwritable and the only legal way in performs the check.

The dual-expiry design (_softexpires and node.expires) enables the timer range mechanism: the timer may fire at any time between _softexpires (the earliest acceptable time) and node.expires (the latest, = _softexpires + range_ns). This allows the kernel to coalesce nearby timers into a single wakeup, reducing interrupt frequency. For timers with no slack (e.g., hrtimer_start() with range_ns=0), both fields are identical.

The state field uses only two values:

Table 6-156. hrtimer State Values
StateValueMeaning
HRTIMER_STATE_INACTIVE0x00Timer is not enqueued in any tree
HRTIMER_STATE_ENQUEUED0x01Timer is in the RB-tree, waiting to expire

Notably, there is no "callback running" state bit. Instead, the kernel tracks running callbacks via base->running == timer. This design avoids a subtle race: if the callback state were stored in the timer itself, clearing it after the callback returns would require touching the timer after the callback — but the callback might have freed the timer. By storing the running state in the base, the timer can be safely freed from within its own callback.

The hrtimer_clock_base Structure

Each clock type (MONOTONIC, REALTIME, BOOTTIME, TAI) has a separate queue, and each queue exists in both hard-IRQ and soft-IRQ variants, giving 8 bases per CPU:

struct hrtimer_clock_base {
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base     *cpu_base;  /* Back-pointer to per-CPU container */
    unsigned int                index;      /* HRTIMER_BASE_MONOTONIC..TAI_SOFT */
    clockid_t                   clockid;    /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_REALTIME, etc. */
    seqcount_raw_spinlock_t     seq;        /* Protects running/state consistency */
    struct hrtimer              *running;   /* Currently executing timer (or NULL) */
    struct timerqueue_head      active;     /* RB-tree of enqueued timers */
    ktime_t                     offset;     /* Offset from MONOTONIC to this clock */
};

The active field is a timerqueue_head — a red-black tree sorted by expiry time, with a cached pointer to the leftmost (earliest) node. This gives O(log n) insertion and removal, and O(1) access to the next timer to expire. The offset field converts between the internal monotonic representation and the clock's actual time (e.g., for CLOCK_REALTIME, offset = wall_to_monotonic).

The hrtimer_cpu_base Structure

The per-CPU container is where the subsystem keeps everything that is true of a CPU as a whole rather than of any individual timer. Three responsibilities account for most of its fields. It must be able to answer “when is this CPU's next expiry?” without inspecting any queue, because the tickless code asks that question on every idle entry — hence the cached expires_next and the active_bases bitmask that lets empty queues be skipped entirely. It must track where it is in the expiry cycle, so that a timer armed from inside a callback does not trigger a redundant hardware reprogram that will be undone moments later. And it must survive misbehaving callbacks, which is what the hang-detection counters are for. It holds all 8 clock bases plus that global state:

struct hrtimer_cpu_base {
    raw_spinlock_t          lock;                   /* Protects all bases on this CPU */
    unsigned int            cpu;                    /* CPU number */
    unsigned int            active_bases;           /* Bitmask: which bases have timers */
    unsigned int            clock_was_set_seq;      /* Detects REALTIME clock changes */

    /* Status flags (bitfields) */
    unsigned int            hres_active       : 1,  /* High-res mode enabled? */
                            in_hrtirq         : 1,  /* Inside hrtimer_interrupt()? */
                            hang_detected     : 1,  /* Interrupt overrun detected */
                            softirq_activated : 1,  /* HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ already raised */
                            online            : 1;  /* CPU is online */

    /* Hang detection statistics (CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS) */
    unsigned int            nr_events;              /* Total interrupt events */
    unsigned short          nr_retries;             /* Retries within single interrupt */
    unsigned short          nr_hangs;               /* Detected hang count */
    unsigned int            max_hang_time;           /* Maximum hang duration (ns) */

    /* PREEMPT_RT only: let hrtimer_cancel() sleep instead of spin */
    spinlock_t              softirq_expiry_lock;    /* Held across soft callbacks */
    atomic_t                timer_waiters;          /* Cancellers waiting */

    /* Next-event tracking */
    ktime_t                 expires_next;           /* Next hard timer expiry (absolute) */
    struct hrtimer          *next_timer;            /* Pointer to earliest hard timer */
    ktime_t                 softirq_expires_next;   /* Next soft timer expiry */
    struct hrtimer          *softirq_next_timer;    /* Earliest soft timer */

    /* The 8 clock bases */
    struct hrtimer_clock_base clock_base[HRTIMER_MAX_CLOCK_BASES];  /* [0..7] */

    call_single_data_t      csd;  /* For remote CPU reprogramming via IPI */
} ____cacheline_aligned;

The active_bases bitmask is a critical optimization: instead of iterating all 8 clock bases to find expired timers, __hrtimer_run_queues() only visits bases that have at least one timer enqueued, using for_each_active_base().

The expires_next / next_timer pair tracks the globally earliest timer across all hard-IRQ clock bases. This is what gets programmed into the clockevent device — the hardware will fire an interrupt at exactly this time. The separate softirq_expires_next / softirq_next_timer pair does the same for soft-IRQ timers, which are raised via HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ rather than run directly in the interrupt handler.

Figure 6-42 shows the overall architecture. Each CPU has its own hrtimer_cpu_base containing 8 clock bases (4 hard + 4 soft). Timers are sorted in red-black trees within each base. The hrtimer_interrupt() handler runs all expired hard timers, raises HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ if any soft timers have expired, and reprograms the clockevent device for the next event.

Clock Bases and the Hard/Soft Split

The obvious design would give each CPU one sorted queue holding every pending timer. Linux gives it eight, and the reason is that two entirely separate distinctions have to be made before a timer can be compared with its neighbours.

The first is which clock the timer was armed against. Expiry times are stored as absolute values, so two timers can only be ordered against each other if they are measured on the same time base — and a CLOCK_REALTIME timer and a CLOCK_MONOTONIC timer are not. Worse, the relationship between them is not fixed: settimeofday() can step the realtime clock forwards or backwards at any moment, which would silently corrupt the ordering of a shared tree. Keeping each clock in its own queue, with a single per-queue offset field recording its current distance from monotonic time, means a clock adjustment updates one number rather than re-sorting a tree.

The second distinction is which context the callback will run in. A timer expiring in hardirq context runs with interrupts disabled and must therefore be short and non-blocking; a timer expiring in softirq context may take longer and, on PREEMPT_RT, may sleep. These cannot share a queue because the two halves are dispatched at different times by different code — the hard half directly from the timer interrupt, the soft half from a raised softirq. Multiplying four clocks by two contexts gives the eight queues:

Table 6-157. hrtimer Clock Bases
IndexClockContextDescriptionTypical Users
0MONOTONICHard IRQMonotonically increasing, unaffected by clock changesScheduler tick, futex timeouts, kernel internal timers
1REALTIMEHard IRQWall-clock time, adjusted by settimeofday()/NTPPOSIX timers with CLOCK_REALTIME
2BOOTTIMEHard IRQLike MONOTONIC but includes time spent in suspendAndroid alarm timers, network timers
3TAIHard IRQInternational Atomic Time (no leap seconds)PTP, precision timestamping
4–7(same clocks)Soft IRQIdentical clocks, but callbacks run in softirq contextnanosleep(), timerfd, most user-facing timers

The hard/soft split was introduced to support PREEMPT_RT. On standard kernels, the distinction is mostly about callback execution context: hard-IRQ timers run with interrupts disabled in hrtimer_interrupt(), while soft-IRQ timers run in hrtimer_run_softirq() with interrupts enabled and preemption possible. On PREEMPT_RT kernels, all timers that are not explicitly marked HRTIMER_MODE_HARD are automatically moved to soft-IRQ bases — this is critical because softirq-context timers can take sleeping locks (regular spinlock_t, which becomes a sleeping mutex on RT).

Timer Modes

The mode argument passed to hrtimer_setup() and the start functions is a small bitmask, and it is worth reading as three independent yes/no choices rather than a list of named constants. Each choice answers a different question: is the expiry time you are giving me an absolute instant or a duration from now; may I move this timer to another CPU if yours goes idle; and does your callback need hardirq context or can it wait for a softirq? Combining them gives the constants below, which is why the list is longer than the number of decisions it encodes.

The third choice is the one most often got wrong, because its meaning changes with the kernel configuration. On a normal kernel, a timer that specifies neither HARD nor SOFT runs in hardirq context; on PREEMPT_RT the same timer is silently promoted into softirq context, because running arbitrary callbacks with interrupts disabled would destroy the latency guarantees the RT kernel exists to provide. Only an explicit HRTIMER_MODE_HARD keeps a timer in hardirq context there, and it is reserved for the handful of users — the scheduler tick and the watchdog among them — that genuinely cannot tolerate the deferral.

Table 6-158. hrtimer Mode Flags
FlagValueMeaning
HRTIMER_MODE_ABS0x00Expiry time is absolute (relative to the clock epoch)
HRTIMER_MODE_REL0x01Expiry time is relative to "now" at start time
HRTIMER_MODE_PINNED0x02Timer must not migrate to another CPU
HRTIMER_MODE_SOFT0x04Callback executes in softirq context
HRTIMER_MODE_HARD0x08Callback executes in hardirq context (even on PREEMPT_RT)

These flags can be combined. For example, the scheduler tick uses HRTIMER_MODE_ABS_PINNED_HARD — an absolute timer pinned to a specific CPU that must fire in hardirq context even on RT kernels. The nanosleep() system call uses HRTIMER_MODE_REL (relative time, soft context by default).

A subtle POSIX requirement is handled at initialization time: relative CLOCK_REALTIME timers are transparently converted to CLOCK_MONOTONIC. POSIX specifies that relative timers should not be affected by clock adjustments — only absolute REALTIME timers should jump when the wall clock changes.

The Timer Lifecycle

An hrtimer goes through a well-defined lifecycle: initialization → start → expiry (or cancellation) → optional restart. Each phase has specific API functions and internal mechanics.

Initialization: hrtimer_setup()

Before an hrtimer can be used it must be initialized with hrtimer_setup(), which combines initialization and callback assignment into a single call. The older two-step form — hrtimer_init() followed by a bare timer->function = cb; assignment — is gone. This was not a cosmetic rename but a multi-release migration: hrtimer_setup() was introduced in 6.13 alongside the whole tree being converted call site by call site, hrtimer_init() was deleted in 6.15, and the callback pointer was made private in the same release so the old idiom could not creep back in.

The motivation was a class of bug the two-step API made easy. A driver could initialize a timer and then, on some error path or in some configuration, start it before assigning the callback — at which point expiry would jump through a NULL pointer in hardirq context. Worse, code that reused a timer sometimes re-ran hrtimer_init() to change the clock base, silently clearing the callback that had been assigned earlier. Folding both steps into one call makes the omission impossible to express:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c */
void hrtimer_setup(struct hrtimer *timer,
                   enum hrtimer_restart (*function)(struct hrtimer *),
                   clockid_t clock_id, enum hrtimer_mode mode)
{
    debug_setup(timer, clock_id, mode);
    __hrtimer_setup(timer, function, clock_id, mode);
}

static void __hrtimer_setup(struct hrtimer *timer, ...)
{
    bool softtimer = !!(mode & HRTIMER_MODE_SOFT);

    /* On PREEMPT_RT: timers not marked HARD are moved to softirq */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT) && !(mode & HRTIMER_MODE_HARD))
        softtimer = true;

    memset(timer, 0, sizeof(struct hrtimer));

    /* POSIX: relative CLOCK_REALTIME → CLOCK_MONOTONIC */
    if (clock_id == CLOCK_REALTIME && mode & HRTIMER_MODE_REL)
        clock_id = CLOCK_MONOTONIC;

    /* Select the correct clock base (hard or soft half) */
    base = softtimer ? HRTIMER_MAX_CLOCK_BASES / 2 : 0;
    base += hrtimer_clockid_to_base(clock_id);

    timer->is_soft = softtimer;
    timer->is_hard = !!(mode & HRTIMER_MODE_HARD);
    timer->base = &cpu_base->clock_base[base];
    timerqueue_init(&timer->node);

    /* Last-resort guard: a NULL callback becomes a harmless no-op */
    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!function))
        ACCESS_PRIVATE(timer, function) = hrtimer_dummy_timeout;
    else
        ACCESS_PRIVATE(timer, function) = function;
}

Note the belt-and-braces guard at the end. Even though the callback is now a required argument, __hrtimer_setup() still checks it: a NULL callback triggers a warning and installs hrtimer_dummy_timeout(), which does nothing and returns HRTIMER_NORESTART. The result is a loud complaint in the log instead of a silent kernel panic in interrupt context. The timerqueue_init() call initializes the red-black tree node; the surrounding memset() has already zeroed state, is_rel, and the rest.

Two variants exist for timers that live on the stack, which is common for short-lived waits inside a system call:

/* include/linux/hrtimer.h */
void hrtimer_setup_on_stack(struct hrtimer *timer,
                            enum hrtimer_restart (*function)(struct hrtimer *),
                            clockid_t clock_id, enum hrtimer_mode mode);

void hrtimer_setup_sleeper_on_stack(struct hrtimer_sleeper *sl,
                                    clockid_t clock_id, enum hrtimer_mode mode);

These differ from hrtimer_setup() only in which debug-object hook they call: they register the timer with the DEBUG_OBJECTS_TIMERS infrastructure as stack-resident, so that if the function returns while the timer is still active — leaving a live timer pointing at a stack frame that is about to be reused — the debug machinery catches it. Callers of the stack variants must pair them with destroy_hrtimer_on_stack(), which is a no-op when the debug option is off. hrtimer_setup_sleeper_on_stack() is the one used by nanosleep() and futex timeouts; it initializes the embedded timer and installs the wakeup callback described later in this section.

Starting: hrtimer_start() and hrtimer_start_range_ns()

Starting an hrtimer involves several coordinated steps: removing the timer if already enqueued, converting relative times to absolute, applying slack, choosing the optimal CPU, inserting into the RB-tree, and potentially reprogramming the clockevent hardware:

/* The public API — just a wrapper with range_ns = 0 */
static inline void hrtimer_start(struct hrtimer *timer, ktime_t tim,
                                 const enum hrtimer_mode mode)
{
    hrtimer_start_range_ns(timer, tim, 0, mode);
}

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c — the real start path */
void hrtimer_start_range_ns(struct hrtimer *timer, ktime_t tim,
                            u64 delta_ns, const enum hrtimer_mode mode)
{
    base = lock_hrtimer_base(timer, &flags);

    if (__hrtimer_start_range_ns(timer, tim, delta_ns, mode, base))
        hrtimer_reprogram(timer, true);  /* New earliest → reprogram HW */

    unlock_hrtimer_base(timer, &flags);
}

The internal __hrtimer_start_range_ns() performs the heavy lifting:

static int __hrtimer_start_range_ns(struct hrtimer *timer, ktime_t tim,
                                    u64 delta_ns, const enum hrtimer_mode mode,
                                    struct hrtimer_clock_base *base)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *this_cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);
    struct hrtimer_clock_base *new_base;
    bool force_local, first, was_armed;

    /* Optimization: if restarting the current first-to-expire timer,
     * avoid double HW reprogramming (on removal + on enqueue) */
    force_local = base->cpu_base == this_cpu_base;
    force_local &= base->cpu_base->next_timer == timer;
    /* ...but never force-local onto a CPU that is already going away */
    force_local &= this_cpu_base->online;

    /* Step 1: Remove if queued (reprogram suppressed when force_local) */
    was_armed = remove_hrtimer(timer, base, true, force_local);

    /* Step 2: Convert relative → absolute, using THIS base's clock */
    if (mode & HRTIMER_MODE_REL)
        tim = ktime_add_safe(tim, __hrtimer_cb_get_time(base->clockid));

    /* Step 3: Apply low-res slack (CONFIG_TIME_LOW_RES) */
    tim = hrtimer_update_lowres(timer, tim, mode);

    /* Step 4: Set expiry range [tim, tim + delta_ns] */
    hrtimer_set_expires_range_ns(timer, tim, delta_ns);

    /* Step 5: Possibly migrate to another CPU */
    if (!force_local)
        new_base = switch_hrtimer_base(timer, base, mode & HRTIMER_MODE_PINNED);
    else
        new_base = base;

    /* Step 6: Insert into RB-tree — O(log n) */
    first = enqueue_hrtimer(timer, new_base, mode, was_armed);

    /* Step 7a: the hrtimer interrupt is running; it will reevaluate the
     * clock bases and reprogram anyway, so do nothing. (Linux 7.0.10) */
    if (new_base->cpu_base->in_hrtirq)
        return false;

    if (!force_local) {
        /* Step 7b: normal case. An online CPU never enqueues a timer
         * remotely if it would expire first there, so the caller can
         * simply reprogram when first == true. */
        if (hrtimer_base_is_online(this_cpu_base))
            return first;

        /* Step 7c: this CPU is offline, so the timer went to a remote
         * base. If it is first there, that CPU has to be told. */
        if (first)
            smp_call_function_single_async(new_base->cpu_base->cpu,
                                           &new_base->cpu_base->csd);
        return 0;
    }

    /* Step 7d: the timer was kept local and the reprogram in step 1 was
     * suppressed, so reprogram unconditionally now. */
    hrtimer_force_reprogram(new_base->cpu_base, 1);
    return 0;
}

The return value indicates whether the caller must reprogram the clockevent device, and it is worth being precise that this is not the same question as "did the timer become the earliest?". It is only in step 7b that the two coincide. Everywhere else the function returns zero because it has either established that reprogramming is unnecessary or done it itself. This matters for systems with thousands of active timers: most hrtimer_start() calls do not trigger hardware reprogramming.

The four exits repay a closer look, because each one exists to suppress a redundant write to the clock event device, and between them they cover every awkward case the subsystem has.

Step 7a is the newest, added in Linux 7.0.10 by commit ed2d49c781b4. If in_hrtirq is set, this CPU is inside hrtimer_interrupt(), which always ends by re-evaluating every active base and reprogramming the hardware from scratch. Any programming done here would be overwritten moments later. The case is not exotic: a timer callback that rearms itself, or arms another timer, runs with in_hrtirq set, so this is the common path for periodic hrtimer users. The same guard already existed in hrtimer_reprogram(); this commit brought the start path into line with it.

Step 7d is the counterpart of the force_local optimization at the top. When the timer being restarted is already the first to expire on this CPU, the naive sequence would reprogram the hardware twice: once when remove_hrtimer() takes the earliest timer away, and again when the new one is enqueued. Passing force_local into remove_hrtimer() suppresses the first write, which leaves an obligation to perform the second unconditionally — hence the direct call to hrtimer_force_reprogram() rather than a true return. The timer is also pinned to this CPU for the duration, since migrating it would defeat the whole arrangement.

Steps 7b and 7c divide on whether the local CPU is still online. An online CPU never enqueues a timer on a remote base that would become the earliest one there — switch_hrtimer_base() declines such a migration — so first can only be true for the local base, and returning it is safe. Once this CPU is on its way out, that guarantee is gone: the timer must go somewhere, and it may well be the earliest timer on its new home. The owning CPU cannot be reprogrammed from here, so it is sent an IPI through the per-CPU csd, which is precisely why struct hrtimer_cpu_base carries a call_single_data_t. This is also why the online flag is folded into force_local at the top: a CPU that has already run hrtimer_cpu_dying() must never keep a timer for itself.

One detail in step 2 is easy to read past. A relative expiry is converted to absolute by adding the current time of the timer's own base, via __hrtimer_cb_get_time(base->clockid) — not by adding ktime_get(). For a CLOCK_MONOTONIC timer the two are identical, which is why the distinction is easy to lose, but a relative CLOCK_REALTIME or CLOCK_TAI timer must be anchored to its own clock or it would land at the wrong moment by the offset between them. Until Linux 6.18 this was reached through a get_time function pointer stored in every hrtimer_clock_base; commit 009eb5da29a9 removed the field and replaced the indirect call with a switch on the clock id, saving a pointer per base and an indirect branch on a path that runs whenever a timer is armed.

Enqueue and Remove

Enqueue and remove are deliberately thin. Almost all the work of ordering timers is delegated to the generic timerqueue layer, which maintains the red-black tree and keeps a cached pointer to its leftmost node; what the hrtimer code adds on top is the bookkeeping that the rest of the subsystem depends on.

Two pieces of that bookkeeping matter. The first is the active_bases bitmask: enqueue sets the bit for this base, and remove clears it when the queue becomes empty. Maintaining it costs a single bit operation on a path that is already holding the base lock, and it saves the expiry loop from visiting seven empty queues to find timers in the eighth. The second is the return value of the enqueue helper, which reports whether the newly inserted timer became the leftmost node — that is, whether it now expires sooner than anything else on this base. That single boolean is what tells the caller whether the clockevent device needs reprogramming, and it is available for free because the tree insertion had to walk to the leftmost position anyway:

/* Insert into the sorted tree — O(log n) */
static bool enqueue_hrtimer(struct hrtimer *timer, struct hrtimer_clock_base *base,
                            enum hrtimer_mode mode, bool was_armed)
{
    debug_activate(timer, mode, was_armed);   /* debugobjects + tracepoint */
    WARN_ON_ONCE(!base->cpu_base->online);

    base->cpu_base->active_bases |= 1 << base->index;

    /* Pairs with the lockless read in hrtimer_is_queued() */
    WRITE_ONCE(timer->state, HRTIMER_STATE_ENQUEUED);

    return timerqueue_add(&base->active, &timer->node);
    /* Returns true if timer became the new leftmost (earliest) node */
}

/* Remove from tree */
static void __remove_hrtimer(struct hrtimer *timer,
                             struct hrtimer_clock_base *base,
                             u8 newstate, int reprogram)
{
    WRITE_ONCE(timer->state, newstate);
    if (!timerqueue_del(&base->active, &timer->node))
        cpu_base->active_bases &= ~(1 << base->index);  /* Base now empty */

    if (reprogram && timer == cpu_base->next_timer)
        hrtimer_force_reprogram(cpu_base, 1);  /* Need new earliest */
}

The was_armed argument threaded through the start path is worth following to its destination, because it does not affect behaviour at all. It is the return value of remove_hrtimer() — "was this timer already queued when we were asked to start it?" — and it travels through enqueue_hrtimer() into debug_activate(), whose only use of it is trace_hrtimer_start(timer, mode, was_armed). It exists purely so that a tracing user can tell two situations apart.

Until Linux 7.0.10, restarting an already-armed timer emitted a hrtimer_cancel event immediately followed by hrtimer_start, because the internal dequeue went through the same helper as a real cancellation. No cancellation had occurred — only the expiry time had changed — and the spurious events made genuine cancellations impossible to pick out of a trace. Commit 74fe3904e174 removed the misleading event and added this flag to the start tracepoint instead, so the two cases now read as was_armed=0 and was_armed=1 on a single line. This is the kind of change that never appears in a changelog a reader would look at, yet it silently invalidates every older worked example of hrtimer trace analysis.

Cancellation: hrtimer_cancel() and hrtimer_try_to_cancel()

Timer cancellation must handle the case where the timer's callback is currently executing on another CPU. The API provides two levels of safety:

/* Non-blocking attempt — returns -1 if callback is running */
int hrtimer_try_to_cancel(struct hrtimer *timer)
{
    /* Fast path: lockless check */
    if (!hrtimer_active(timer))
        return 0;  /* Already inactive */

    base = lock_hrtimer_base(timer, &flags);

    if (!hrtimer_callback_running(timer)) {
        ret = remove_hrtimer(timer, base, false, false);
    } else {
        ret = -1;  /* Callback running — cannot cancel now */
    }
    unlock_hrtimer_base(timer, &flags);
    return ret;
}

/* Blocking cancel — waits for running callback to finish */
int hrtimer_cancel(struct hrtimer *timer)
{
    int ret;
    do {
        ret = hrtimer_try_to_cancel(timer);
        if (ret < 0)
            hrtimer_cancel_wait_running(timer);  /* cpu_relax() or RT lock wait */
    } while (ret < 0);
    return ret;
}

The spin-wait in hrtimer_cancel() is safe because hrtimer callbacks are expected to be short. On PREEMPT_RT, hrtimer_cancel_wait_running() uses a proper sleeping lock (softirq_expiry_lock) instead of busy-waiting, so it's safe to call from process context even if the callback takes a long time.

Periodic Timers: hrtimer_forward()

For periodic timers (e.g., the scheduler tick, POSIX interval timers), the callback function returns HRTIMER_RESTART and calls hrtimer_forward_now() to advance the expiry time by one interval. The function handles overruns — if the system was so busy that multiple periods elapsed, it advances by the correct number:

u64 hrtimer_forward(struct hrtimer *timer, ktime_t now, ktime_t interval)
{
    u64 orun = 1;
    ktime_t delta = ktime_sub(now, hrtimer_get_expires(timer));

    if (delta < 0)
        return 0;  /* Timer hasn't expired yet */

    if (interval < hrtimer_resolution)
        interval = hrtimer_resolution;  /* Floor at 1ns (highres) or 1 tick */

    if (delta >= interval) {
        orun = ktime_divns(delta, ktime_to_ns(interval));  /* Missed periods */
        hrtimer_add_expires_ns(timer, ktime_to_ns(interval) * orun);
        if (hrtimer_get_expires(timer) > now)
            return orun;
        orun++;  /* Rounding correction */
    }
    hrtimer_add_expires(timer, interval);
    return orun;  /* Total overruns (0 = not yet expired, ≥1 = expired) */
}

The overrun count is important for POSIX timers: timer_getoverrun() returns this value so applications can detect and compensate for missed timer expirations.

The Interrupt Handler: hrtimer_interrupt()

When the clockevent device fires, hrtimer_interrupt() is called in hardirq context. This is the hot path of the entire hrtimer subsystem — it must be fast because it runs with interrupts disabled on the current CPU:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c — the main hrtimer interrupt handler */
void hrtimer_interrupt(struct clock_event_device *dev)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);
    ktime_t expires_next, now, entry_time, delta;
    int retries = 0;

    cpu_base->nr_events++;
    dev->next_event = KTIME_MAX;

    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
    entry_time = now = hrtimer_update_base(cpu_base);

retry:
    cpu_base->in_hrtirq = 1;
    cpu_base->expires_next = KTIME_MAX;  /* Block migration */

    /* Phase 1: Check if any soft timers have expired */
    if (!ktime_before(now, cpu_base->softirq_expires_next)) {
        cpu_base->softirq_expires_next = KTIME_MAX;
        cpu_base->softirq_activated = 1;
        raise_timer_softirq(HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ);
    }

    /* Phase 2: Run all expired hard-IRQ timers */
    __hrtimer_run_queues(cpu_base, now, flags, HRTIMER_ACTIVE_HARD);

    /* Phase 3: Recompute next event across all bases */
    expires_next = hrtimer_update_next_event(cpu_base);
    cpu_base->expires_next = expires_next;
    cpu_base->in_hrtirq = 0;
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&cpu_base->lock, flags);

    /* Phase 4: Reprogram the clockevent device */
    if (!tick_program_event(expires_next, 0)) {
        cpu_base->hang_detected = 0;
        return;  /* Success — hardware armed for next event */
    }

    /* --- Hang detection: next timer already expired! --- */
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
    now = hrtimer_update_base(cpu_base);
    cpu_base->nr_retries++;
    if (++retries < 3)
        goto retry;  /* Try up to 3 times */

    /* After 3 failures, force a minimum delay to prevent livelock */
    cpu_base->nr_hangs++;
    cpu_base->hang_detected = 1;
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&cpu_base->lock, flags);

    delta = ktime_sub(now, entry_time);
    if ((unsigned int)delta > cpu_base->max_hang_time)
        cpu_base->max_hang_time = (unsigned int) delta;
    /* Give the CPU at least 100ms to catch up */
    if (delta > 100 * NSEC_PER_MSEC)
        expires_next = ktime_add_ns(now, 100 * NSEC_PER_MSEC);
    else
        expires_next = ktime_add(now, delta);
    tick_program_event(expires_next, 1);
    pr_warn_once("hrtimer: interrupt took %llu ns\n", ktime_to_ns(delta));
}

Two details of the recovery path deserve a second look. The first is the unlock: cpu_base->lock is dropped before the delta is computed and the clockevent is reprogrammed. The lock was reacquired only to update the clock offsets and read a coherent now; holding a raw spinlock across tick_program_event() would extend a section that already runs with interrupts disabled on a CPU that has just demonstrated it is falling behind. The second is that this is the only place max_hang_time is written, which is why the field is an unsigned int rather than a ktime_t: a hang worth recording is measured in microseconds or milliseconds, and truncating to 32 bits caps the recorded value at roughly 4.3 seconds — long past the point where the number is diagnostic anyway.

The mechanism matters most for virtual machines. A guest may be descheduled by the hypervisor for an arbitrary stretch, and when it is resumed every timer that came due in the interval is already expired, so tick_program_event() keeps failing however far ahead the next event is placed. Without the three-attempt limit and the forced delay the CPU would loop in the hrtimer interrupt indefinitely, never returning to task context to run the work the timers exist to trigger. Note that the loop gives up after three attempts, not three retries: retries starts at zero, so the third failure falls through. The forced expires_next is deliberately not a fixed value — it is the measured overrun, clamped to 100 ms, so a CPU that fell a little behind is given a little slack and one that fell far behind is given the maximum. All three counters are exported through /proc/timer_list (kernel/time/timer_list.c), which is the practical way to tell a genuinely overloaded machine from one whose clocksource is misbehaving.

Running Expired Timers: __hrtimer_run_queues()

This is the loop that turns “an interrupt happened” into “these particular callbacks run.” It is shared by both dispatch paths: the hardirq handler calls it with HRTIMER_ACTIVE_HARD and the softirq handler with HRTIMER_ACTIVE_SOFT, and the mask is simply AND-ed with active_bases so each caller sees only its own half of the eight queues.

The inner loop stops at the first timer whose soft expiry lies in the future, not its hard expiry, and the distinction is the whole of the coalescing strategy. A timer is run as soon as its earliest acceptable time has passed, rather than being deferred to its latest — because deferring it would require a second wakeup later, which is exactly what the range mechanism is trying to avoid. Stopping at the first unexpired timer is safe despite the ranges overlapping: a later timer in the tree cannot have an earlier hard expiry that has already passed without also having an earlier soft expiry, so nothing expired is left behind. The kernel comment explains this as the reason a plain binary search tree suffices where an interval-stabbing query would otherwise be needed.

static void __hrtimer_run_queues(struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base,
                                 ktime_t now, unsigned long flags,
                                 unsigned int active_mask)
{
    unsigned int active = cpu_base->active_bases & active_mask;

    for_each_active_base(base, cpu_base, active) {
        ktime_t basenow = ktime_add(now, base->offset);

        while ((node = timerqueue_getnext(&base->active))) {
            timer = container_of(node, struct hrtimer, node);

            /* Only run timers whose soft-expiry has passed */
            if (basenow < hrtimer_get_softexpires(timer))
                break;  /* All remaining timers are in the future */

            __run_hrtimer(cpu_base, base, timer, &basenow, flags);
        }
    }
}

The comparison uses _softexpires (not the hard expiry), which means a timer with a range [100ms, 110ms] will fire as soon as now ≥ 100ms, even if the hard deadline of 110ms hasn't been reached. This is the key to the range/slack optimization: timers fire at the earliest acceptable time, but the hardware is only programmed for the latest hard expiry — allowing other timers whose windows overlap to share the same wakeup.

Executing a Single Timer: __run_hrtimer()

Running a timer callback is surprisingly complex because of concurrency requirements: the callback must be able to rearm the same timer, free the timer, or perform other operations that would normally require the base lock:

static void __run_hrtimer(struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base,
                          struct hrtimer_clock_base *base,
                          struct hrtimer *timer, ktime_t *now,
                          unsigned long flags)
{
    base->running = timer;  /* Mark as running (for hrtimer_active()) */
    raw_write_seqcount_barrier(&base->seq);

    __remove_hrtimer(timer, base, HRTIMER_STATE_INACTIVE, 0);
    fn = timer->function;

    /* DROP THE LOCK — callback runs without holding cpu_base->lock */
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
    trace_hrtimer_expire_entry(timer, now);

    restart = fn(timer);  /* Execute the callback */

    trace_hrtimer_expire_exit(timer);
    raw_spin_lock_irq(&cpu_base->lock);

    /* If callback returned RESTART, re-enqueue */
    if (restart != HRTIMER_NORESTART &&
        !(timer->state & HRTIMER_STATE_ENQUEUED))
        enqueue_hrtimer(timer, base, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS, false);

    raw_write_seqcount_barrier(&base->seq);
    base->running = NULL;
}

Key points: the lock is dropped before calling the callback (line with raw_spin_unlock), which means the callback executes without holding any timer locks. This allows the callback to call hrtimer_start(), hrtimer_forward_now(), or even free its own memory. The running pointer and seqcount barrier ensure that hrtimer_active() correctly reports the timer as active even though it's been removed from the tree.

The Soft-IRQ Path

Soft-context timers are not run directly in hrtimer_interrupt(). Instead, the hardirq handler checks whether any soft timers have expired and raises HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ. The actual execution happens later in hrtimer_run_softirq():

static void hrtimer_run_softirq(void)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);

    hrtimer_cpu_base_lock_expiry(cpu_base);    /* RT: sleeping lock */
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&cpu_base->lock, flags);

    now = hrtimer_update_base(cpu_base);
    __hrtimer_run_queues(cpu_base, now, flags, HRTIMER_ACTIVE_SOFT);

    cpu_base->softirq_activated = 0;
    hrtimer_update_softirq_timer(cpu_base, true);

    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
    hrtimer_cpu_base_unlock_expiry(cpu_base);
}

/* Registered at boot: */
void __init hrtimers_init(void)
{
    hrtimers_prepare_cpu(smp_processor_id());
    hrtimers_cpu_starting(smp_processor_id());
    open_softirq(HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ, hrtimer_run_softirq);
}

On PREEMPT_RT, the softirq_expiry_lock is a sleeping lock that allows hrtimer_cancel() to wait for soft-timer callbacks to complete without busy-spinning. This is essential for RT because soft-timer callbacks may take sleeping locks themselves.

Where the Soft-IRQ Actually Runs

One detail in the listings above is easy to read past. Both this path and the timer wheel raise their softirq through raise_timer_softirq(), not through the usual __raise_softirq_irqoff(), and the difference matters on any kernel with forced IRQ threading:

/* include/linux/interrupt.h */
static inline void raise_timer_softirq(unsigned int nr)
{
    lockdep_assert_in_irq();
    if (force_irqthreads())
        raise_ktimers_thread(nr);      /* per-CPU ktimers/N thread */
    else
        __raise_softirq_irqoff(nr);    /* ordinary softirq */
}

The problem this solves is a priority inversion peculiar to threaded interrupts. When softirqs are forced into thread context they are run by ksoftirqd, which is a plain SCHED_OTHER task, so expiring timers end up competing for the CPU with every ordinary process on the run queue. A timer meant to fire in a hundred microseconds can then be delayed by a scheduling latency measured in milliseconds, and nothing real-time is responsible for the delay.

Linux 6.13 split the timer softirqs out into their own per-CPU threads, named ktimers/<N> and tracked through the per-CPU ktimerd pointer, whose setup callback raises them to low-priority SCHED_FIFO with sched_set_fifo_low(). They sit deliberately just above SCHED_NORMAL: high enough that no ordinary task can delay a timer, low enough that they do not compete with genuine real-time work. Because these threads run outside the normal softirq mechanism they need their own pending mask, which is the per-CPU pending_timer_softirq word that raise_ktimers_thread() sets and local_timers_pending() reads.

That last function is why this matters even on a kernel that never enables the feature. It is what the tick layer consults before stopping the tick — kernel/time/tick-sched.c tests local_timers_pending() & BIT(TIMER_SOFTIRQ). Had the timer softirqs been moved to a separate pending word without teaching that test about it, a CPU could have gone idle with timer work still outstanding. When forced threading is not in use force_irqthreads() is constant false, both helpers collapse to their ordinary counterparts, and nothing changes.

The Low-Resolution Fallback

Not all systems have hardware capable of one-shot mode — some older or embedded clockevent devices only support periodic operation. On such systems, high-resolution mode (hres_active) never activates, and hrtimers fall back to a polling model driven by the periodic tick:

/* Called from run_local_timers() in each tick */
void hrtimer_run_queues(void)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);

    if (hrtimer_hres_active(cpu_base))
        return;  /* High-res mode handles everything */

    /* Check if we can switch to highres mode now */
    if (tick_check_oneshot_change(!hrtimer_is_hres_enabled())) {
        hrtimer_switch_to_hres();
        return;
    }

    /* Low-res: poll expired timers at each tick */
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
    now = hrtimer_update_base(cpu_base);

    if (!ktime_before(now, cpu_base->softirq_expires_next)) {
        cpu_base->softirq_expires_next = KTIME_MAX;
        cpu_base->softirq_activated = 1;
        raise_timer_softirq(HRTIMER_SOFTIRQ);
    }

    __hrtimer_run_queues(cpu_base, now, flags, HRTIMER_ACTIVE_HARD);
    raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&cpu_base->lock, flags);
}

In this mode, timer resolution is limited to 1/HZ (4ms at HZ=250). The transition to high-resolution mode happens automatically when a suitable clocksource (with CLOCK_SOURCE_IS_CONTINUOUS) and a one-shot-capable clockevent device become available. The switch calls hrtimer_switch_to_hres(), which sets hres_active = 1, changes hrtimer_resolution from LOW_RES_NSEC to 1ns, and installs the hrtimer-based tick emulation via tick_setup_sched_timer().

Timer Range and Slack

The hrtimer range mechanism allows the kernel to batch nearby timer expirations into a single interrupt, reducing wakeup frequency and saving power. When a timer is started with hrtimer_start_range_ns(timer, tim, delta_ns, mode), it creates an expiry window:

  • _softexpires = tim — the earliest acceptable firing time
  • node.expires = tim + delta_ns — the latest acceptable firing time (hard deadline)

The hardware is programmed for node.expires (the hard deadline), but the timer will fire as soon as any interrupt occurs after _softexpires. If another timer fires in the window, both timers execute in the same interrupt — one wakeup instead of two.

For nanosleep(), the slack comes from the calling process's timer_slack_ns field (set via prctl(PR_SET_TIMERSLACK)):

long hrtimer_nanosleep(ktime_t rqtp, const enum hrtimer_mode mode,
                       const clockid_t clockid)
{
    struct hrtimer_sleeper t;

    hrtimer_setup_sleeper_on_stack(&t, clockid, mode);
    /* Apply the process's timer slack as the range */
    hrtimer_set_expires_range_ns(&t.timer, rqtp, current->timer_slack_ns);
    ret = do_nanosleep(&t, mode);
    /* ... */
}

The default timer_slack_ns is 50µs for non-RT processes. Real-time processes (SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_DEADLINE) have a slack of 0, meaning their timers fire at exactly the requested time.

Clock Reprogramming and Migration

When a new timer is enqueued and becomes the earliest to expire, the clockevent device must be reprogrammed. The hrtimer_reprogram() function handles this with several optimizations to avoid unnecessary hardware writes:

static void hrtimer_reprogram(struct hrtimer *timer, bool reprogram)
{
    struct hrtimer_cpu_base *cpu_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);
    ktime_t expires = ktime_sub(hrtimer_get_expires(timer), base->offset);

    /* Soft timers: update tracking only, no HW reprogram unless earlier
     * than the current hard timer */
    if (timer->is_soft) {
        if (timer_cpu_base->softirq_activated)
            return;  /* Softirq will re-evaluate anyway */
        if (!ktime_before(expires, timer_cpu_base->softirq_expires_next))
            return;  /* Not the new earliest soft timer */
        timer_cpu_base->softirq_next_timer = timer;
        timer_cpu_base->softirq_expires_next = expires;
        if (!ktime_before(expires, timer_cpu_base->expires_next))
            return;  /* Hard timer fires first anyway */
    }

    /* Can only reprogram local CPU's clockevent */
    if (base->cpu_base != cpu_base)
        return;  /* Remote CPU — IPI will handle it */

    if (expires >= cpu_base->expires_next)
        return;  /* Not earlier than current next event */

    if (cpu_base->in_hrtirq)
        return;  /* Interrupt handler will reprogram on exit */

    cpu_base->next_timer = timer;
    __hrtimer_reprogram(cpu_base, timer, expires);  /* → tick_program_event() */
}

Timer Migration Between CPUs

Unpinned hrtimers can be migrated to different CPUs for better load distribution or power efficiency. During hrtimer_start(), switch_hrtimer_base() selects the target CPU. The migration uses a clever locking protocol with a special migration_base sentinel:

/* The migration sentinel — while timer->base points here,
 * the timer is "in transit" and lock_hrtimer_base() will spin */
static struct hrtimer_cpu_base migration_cpu_base = {
    .clock_base = { { .cpu_base = &migration_cpu_base, }, },
};

/* lock_hrtimer_base() spins while timer is migrating */
struct hrtimer_clock_base *lock_hrtimer_base(const struct hrtimer *timer, ...)
{
    for (;;) {
        base = READ_ONCE(timer->base);
        if (likely(base != &migration_base)) {
            raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&base->cpu_base->lock, *flags);
            if (likely(base == timer->base))
                return base;  /* Stable — we have the lock */
            raw_spin_unlock_irqrestore(&base->cpu_base->lock, *flags);
        }
        cpu_relax();  /* Timer is mid-migration, try again */
    }
}

CPU Hotplug: Timer Migration on CPU Death

CPU offlining is the hardest case for the timer subsystem, because unlike idle migration — where the source CPU is merely inconvenient — the source CPU is about to stop executing entirely. Any timer still queued on it when the last instruction retires will simply never fire, and whatever was waiting on that timeout will wait forever. The teardown therefore has to be exhaustive rather than opportunistic: every timer on all eight clock bases moves, regardless of pinning, and the target must be told to re-evaluate its programming afterwards. The hrtimers_cpu_dying() function, invoked from the CPUHP_AP_HRTIMERS_DYING hotplug state, handles this:

int hrtimers_cpu_dying(unsigned int dying_cpu)
{
    /* Select target: any online CPU in the housekeeping set */
    int ncpu = cpumask_any_and(cpu_active_mask,
                               housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_TIMER));

    old_base = this_cpu_ptr(&hrtimer_bases);
    new_base = &per_cpu(hrtimer_bases, ncpu);

    raw_spin_lock(&old_base->lock);
    raw_spin_lock_nested(&new_base->lock, SINGLE_DEPTH_NESTING);

    /* Migrate all 8 clock bases */
    for (i = 0; i < HRTIMER_MAX_CLOCK_BASES; i++)
        migrate_hrtimer_list(&old_base->clock_base[i],
                             &new_base->clock_base[i]);

    /* Tell target CPU to reprogram its clockevent */
    smp_call_function_single(ncpu, retrigger_next_event, NULL, 0);

    raw_spin_unlock(&new_base->lock);
    old_base->online = 0;
    raw_spin_unlock(&old_base->lock);
    return 0;
}

The migration takes both locks (nested) to prevent races during the transfer. Taking two per-CPU base locks at once would normally be a lock-ordering hazard, but the hotplug machinery serializes teardown globally, so only one CPU can ever be executing this function. After migration, an IPI (retrigger_next_event) notifies the target CPU to re-evaluate its next timer event and reprogram its clockevent device — necessary because the timers that just arrived may expire sooner than anything the target already had queued.

The final assignment, old_base->online = 0, closes a subtler hole and deserves attention because it is easy to miss. Draining the queues is not sufficient on its own: CPUHP_AP_HRTIMERS_DYING is not the last teardown state, so other subsystems' teardown callbacks still run on the dying CPU after the timers have been migrated away. If any of them arms an hrtimer — and some do, directly or through a helper that takes a timeout — the timer would be enqueued on a CPU that has already been drained and will never take another timer interrupt. It would be stranded.

The online flag is what prevents that. Every arming path chooses its destination through get_target_base(), which consults the flag before anything else:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c */
static inline struct hrtimer_cpu_base *get_target_base(struct hrtimer_cpu_base *base,
                                                       int pinned)
{
    if (!hrtimer_base_is_online(base)) {
        int cpu = cpumask_any_and(cpu_online_mask,
                                  housekeeping_cpumask(HK_TYPE_TIMER));

        return &per_cpu(hrtimer_bases, cpu);
    }

#if defined(CONFIG_SMP) && defined(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON)
    if (static_branch_likely(&timers_migration_enabled) && !pinned)
        return &per_cpu(hrtimer_bases, get_nohz_timer_target());
#endif
    return base;
}

Once the local base is marked offline, the check fires first and the timer is forced onto a remote online housekeeping CPU — overriding even HRTIMER_MODE_PINNED, since honouring a pin to a dead CPU is worse than ignoring it. hrtimer_base_is_online() compiles to a constant true when CONFIG_HOTPLUG_CPU is disabled, so kernels that cannot offline a CPU pay nothing for the check. Note the ordering that makes this work: the flag is cleared while old_base->lock is still held, in the same critical section that drained the queues, so there is no window in which the queues are empty but the base still looks online.

The nanosleep() Implementation

The nanosleep() system call demonstrates how user-space blocking sleeps are built on hrtimers. The implementation uses the hrtimer_sleeper wrapper, which pairs an hrtimer with a task pointer for wakeup:

/* The sleeper callback — wakes the sleeping task */
static enum hrtimer_restart hrtimer_wakeup(struct hrtimer *timer)
{
    struct hrtimer_sleeper *t =
        container_of(timer, struct hrtimer_sleeper, timer);
    struct task_struct *task = t->task;

    t->task = NULL;  /* Mark timer as expired */
    if (task)
        wake_up_process(task);

    return HRTIMER_NORESTART;
}

/* The sleep loop — handles signals and restarts */
static int do_nanosleep(struct hrtimer_sleeper *t, enum hrtimer_mode mode)
{
    do {
        set_current_state(TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE | TASK_FREEZABLE);
        hrtimer_sleeper_start_expires(t, mode);

        if (likely(t->task))
            schedule();  /* Sleep until woken by timer or signal */

        hrtimer_cancel(&t->timer);
        mode = HRTIMER_MODE_ABS;  /* Restart uses absolute time */
    } while (t->task && !signal_pending(current));

    __set_current_state(TASK_RUNNING);

    if (!t->task)
        return 0;  /* Timer expired normally */

    /* Signal interrupted the sleep — set up restart block */
    /* ... remaining time handling for ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK ... */
}

/* The syscall entry point */
SYSCALL_DEFINE2(nanosleep, struct __kernel_timespec __user *, rqtp,
                struct __kernel_timespec __user *, rmtp)
{
    struct timespec64 tu;
    if (get_timespec64(&tu, rqtp))
        return -EFAULT;
    if (!timespec64_valid(&tu))
        return -EINVAL;

    current->restart_block.nanosleep.type = rmtp ? TT_NATIVE : TT_NONE;
    current->restart_block.nanosleep.rmtp = rmtp;
    return hrtimer_nanosleep(timespec64_to_ktime(tu), HRTIMER_MODE_REL,
                             CLOCK_MONOTONIC);
}

On PREEMPT_RT, an additional optimization applies: if the calling task has a real-time scheduling policy (SCHED_FIFO/SCHED_DEADLINE), the sleeper timer is automatically upgraded to HRTIMER_MODE_HARD. This ensures that RT tasks receive low-latency wakeups from hardirq context rather than waiting for softirq processing.

Surviving a Signal: The Restart Block

The listing above ends at the interesting part. When a signal interrupts the sleep, do_nanosleep() returns -ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK, and what happens next is the mechanism that lets nanosleep() be interrupted an arbitrary number of times without drifting:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c — tail of hrtimer_nanosleep() */
    ret = do_nanosleep(&t, mode);
    if (ret != -ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK)
        goto out;

    /* Absolute timers do not update the rmtp value and restart: */
    if (mode == HRTIMER_MODE_ABS) {
        ret = -ERESTARTNOHAND;
        goto out;
    }

    restart = &current->restart_block;
    restart->nanosleep.clockid = t.timer.base->clockid;
    restart->nanosleep.expires = hrtimer_get_expires(&t.timer);
    set_restart_fn(restart, hrtimer_nanosleep_restart);
out:
    destroy_hrtimer_on_stack(&t.timer);
    return ret;

/* ...and the resumption, after the signal handler has run */
static long __sched hrtimer_nanosleep_restart(struct restart_block *restart)
{
    struct hrtimer_sleeper t;
    int ret;

    hrtimer_setup_sleeper_on_stack(&t, restart->nanosleep.clockid,
                                   HRTIMER_MODE_ABS);
    hrtimer_set_expires(&t.timer, restart->nanosleep.expires);
    ret = do_nanosleep(&t, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS);
    destroy_hrtimer_on_stack(&t.timer);
    return ret;
}

The essential point is that what gets saved is an absolute deadline, and the restart re-arms in HRTIMER_MODE_ABS regardless of how the sleep was originally requested. A relative request was already converted to absolute when the timer was armed, so the deadline is fixed from the first call onwards. The obvious alternative — storing the remaining time and re-arming relative to now — would restart the clock after each signal, and the error would accumulate: a task receiving a signal every millisecond during a one-second sleep could be delayed indefinitely. Storing the absolute expiry makes an interrupted sleep end at the same instant it would have ended undisturbed, no matter how many times it is interrupted.

The rmtp pointer that nanosleep() accepts is therefore a courtesy to userspace, not the kernel's own bookkeeping. It is filled in on the way out to a signal handler so that a program which chooses to restart the call by hand knows how long is left; the kernel's automatic restart path does not consult it. That is also why the absolute case bails out with -ERESTARTNOHAND instead: clock_nanosleep() with TIMER_ABSTIME has no remaining-time output to update, and its deadline is meaningful to the caller directly.

set_restart_fn() is worth noting as more than an assignment. It stores the resumption function, invokes the arch_set_restart_data() hook — which some architectures use to record state their signal-return path needs — and returns -ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK, so callers can write return set_restart_fn(...). Architectures that need nothing extra compile the hook away to nothing.

One field here changed in Linux 6.19. restart->nanosleep.expires was a bare u64 of nanoseconds and is now a ktime_t (commit 4702f4eceb63), matching the type the rest of the hrtimer core uses. The two are the same width and the change is invisible at runtime, but it removes a place where a reader had to know which of the kernel's two time representations was in play. POSIX CPU timers share this restart block and still work in plain nanoseconds, so they now go through explicit conversions rather than relying on the types happening to line up.

Key Users in the Kernel

It is worth closing with the breadth of the dependency, because it explains why this subsystem is held to unusually strict standards. Hrtimers began as a specialist facility for applications that needed sub-jiffy precision; in Linux 7.0.12 they are closer to infrastructure. The tick itself is an hrtimer in oneshot mode, which means the timer subsystem schedules the very interrupt that drives the timer subsystem. Every user-space sleep, every POSIX interval timer, every epoll() timeout backed by a timerfd, every futex wait with a deadline and every io_uring timeout ends up on one of these red-black trees.

That ubiquity is the reason for design choices that would otherwise look excessive: the hang detection that bounds a runaway callback, the migration-base sentinel that keeps cancellation correct while a timer is in flight between CPUs, and the compile-time enforcement of the callback pointer. A bug in a specialist facility inconveniences its users; a bug here hangs the machine. The following table lists the major subsystems that depend on hrtimers:

Table 6-159. Major hrtimer Users in Linux 7.0.12
SubsystemSource FileUsage
Scheduler tickkernel/time/tick-sched.csched_timer hrtimer drives the periodic tick in oneshot mode
nanosleepkernel/time/hrtimer.chrtimer_sleeper for precise process sleep
POSIX timerskernel/time/posix-timers.cPer-process interval timers with signal delivery
timerfdfs/timerfd.cFile-descriptor-based timers for epoll()/select()
Futexkernel/futex/core.cTimed futex waits (futex_wait() with timeout)
io_uringio_uring/timeout.cAsync I/O timeout operations
Schedulerkernel/sched/core.cDeadline bandwidth replenishment timers
Perf eventskernel/events/core.cEvent multiplexing rotation timer
Alarm timerskernel/time/alarmtimer.cAndroid-style alarms that wake from suspend
Networknet/core/dev.cNAPI busy-poll timeout, TCP pacing
DRMdrivers/gpu/drm/drm_vblank.cVblank simulation for displays
IIO triggersdrivers/iio/trigger/iio-trig-hrtimer.cHigh-frequency sensor sampling triggers
Watchdogdrivers/watchdog/watchdog_hrtimer_pretimeout.cPre-timeout notification before hardware reset
Soundsound/core/hrtimer.cALSA timer backend for low-latency audio
The hrtimer subsystem has evolved substantially. Linux 2.6.16 introduced hrtimers with hrtimer_init() + separate function assignment. Linux 7.0.12 changes: (1) hrtimer_init() replaced by hrtimer_setup() combining init + callback in one call, with the callback pointer made __private so it can only be changed through hrtimer_update_function(); (2) hard/soft IRQ split (4.16+) with 8 clock bases instead of 4; (3) PREEMPT_RT support with sleeping softirq_expiry_lock and automatic soft-mode promotion; (4) timerqueue abstraction replaces direct RB-tree usage; (5) migration_base sentinel for safe cross-CPU migration; (6) active_bases bitmask optimization to skip empty clock bases; (7) hrtimer_suitable_target() for smarter CPU selection on remote enqueue; (8) hang detection with 3-retry limit and adaptive delay for VM environments.

The Timer Wheel (Classic Timers)

The classic timer wheel (struct timer_list) is the kernel's workhorse for coarse-grained timeouts. While hrtimers provide nanosecond precision for a relatively small number of active timers, the timer wheel is optimized for a different scenario: millions of timers, most of which are cancelled before they expire. This describes the vast majority of timeout use cases in the kernel — TCP retransmission timeouts, connection tracking timeouts, disk I/O deadlines, workqueue delayed work, RCU grace period monitoring, and device polling intervals.

The key design insight is that timeout timers almost never fire. A TCP retransmission timer is set on every packet send but fires only when a packet is genuinely lost, which on a healthy link is rare. An NFS RPC timeout is set on every remote procedure call but almost always cancelled when the response arrives. For this workload pattern, fast cancellation matters more than precise expiry. The timer wheel achieves O(1) insertion and O(1) cancellation, while tolerating imprecise expiry with a granularity that increases with the timer's distance into the future.

That inversion of priorities — cancellation over precision — is the key to reading everything below. Five pressures follow from it, and between them they account for almost every structure in this section:

  • Cancellation must be O(1) and must touch nothing global. If the common operation is remove a timer that never fired, then removal cannot involve a search, a re-sort, or a lock that other CPUs contend for. This is the single reason the wheel is an array of hashed buckets rather than the sorted tree hrtimers use: a timer is unlinked from a doubly-linked list in constant time, without reference to any other timer.
  • Precision is the currency used to pay for that. A bucket covers a range of expiry times, so every timer in it fires at the same moment. Rather than accept one fixed granularity, the wheel is built in levels whose granularity coarsens by 8× each step — precise for the near future, deliberately vague for the distant future. A timeout 30 seconds away does not care about 4ms of error; a 10ms timeout does.
  • Nothing may ever be rescanned. The 2.6 wheel met the granularity problem by cascading: timers were placed in a coarse level and later physically moved down into finer levels as their expiry approached. That made a small number of ticks unpredictably expensive, walking and relinking whole buckets while holding the base lock. The modern wheel refuses to move timers at all — a timer is placed directly in its final bucket at enqueue time and stays there until it expires or is cancelled.
  • The tick must not scan the wheel. With 576 buckets per base and three bases per CPU, checking “has anything expired?” by inspection would cost more than the timers save. The base therefore caches the next expiry as a single value and maintains a bitmap of which buckets are occupied, so the overwhelmingly common answer — nothing — costs one comparison.
  • An idle CPU should not be woken for work another CPU could do. A timer pinned to a CPU must fire there; a timer that merely happens to have been armed there need not. Separating the two into different bases is what makes it possible to let an idle CPU sleep through its own non-pinned timeouts and have a CPU that is awake anyway expire them instead.

The rest of this section works through nine questions, in the order the subsections answer them:

  1. What shape is the wheel, and what does a bucket actually cover? The level geometry, the granularity ladder, and the maximum timeout the wheel can express.
  2. What is a timer, and what is a base? struct timer_list, the flags packed into it, and the three per-CPU bases.
  3. Given an expiry time, which bucket does the timer go in? calc_wheel_index(), and how the level is chosen from the distance to expiry.
  4. What does a timer's life look like from the caller's side? Setup, arming and re-arming, and the three flavours of deletion — including the one that makes a timer permanently dead.
  5. How does the tick turn into callbacks? The softirq, the multi-level collection scan, and the guarantees callbacks may and may not rely on.
  6. How does any of this survive a CPU that has stopped ticking? Idle base marking, and why the answer differs for pinned and global timers.
  7. Who runs an idle CPU's global timers? The timer-migration hierarchy, the migrator role, and which CPUs are deliberately kept out of it.
  8. What happens when a CPU disappears entirely? Hotplug teardown and bucket-by-bucket migration.
  9. Which of the two timer subsystems should new code use? The decision criteria, and why “more precision” is usually the wrong reason to reach for hrtimers.

Version history. The API survives; the implementation does not. Code written against the 2.6 interface would still look broadly familiar — a timer_list, an expiry in jiffies, a function to arm it — but every layer beneath that has been replaced. The cascading tvec_base with its tv1–tv5 arrays was removed in 4.8 in favour of the non-cascading hierarchical wheel described here; the per-CPU base was split in three to support tickless operation; and the timer-migration hierarchy was added in 6.9 so that idle CPUs need not wake for their own global timeouts. The names have moved too: a treewide rename retired del_timer() and del_timer_sync() in 6.15 and from_timer() in 6.16, in favour of timer_delete(), timer_delete_sync() and timer_container_of(), so the 2.6-era identifiers will not be found in a 7.0.12 tree at all.

The Hierarchical Wheel Architecture

Linux 7.0.12 uses a redesigned timer wheel that eliminates the cascading overhead of the Linux 2.6 implementation. Instead of the old tv1–tv5 arrays where timers were physically moved ("cascaded") from higher to lower levels as time advanced, the modern wheel places each timer directly into its final bucket at enqueue time. There is no cascading at all.

The wheel consists of multiple levels, each with 64 buckets (LVL_SIZE = 2^6 = 64). Each successive level has 8× coarser granularity (LVL_CLK_DIV = 2^3 = 8):

/* kernel/time/timer.c — wheel geometry constants */
#define LVL_CLK_SHIFT   3                       /* Each level: 8x coarser */
#define LVL_CLK_DIV     (1UL << LVL_CLK_SHIFT)  /* = 8 */
#define LVL_BITS        6                       /* 64 buckets per level */
#define LVL_SIZE        (1UL << LVL_BITS)       /* = 64 */

#if HZ > 100
# define LVL_DEPTH      9   /* 9 levels: HZ = 250, 300 or 1000 */
#else
# define LVL_DEPTH      8   /* 8 levels: HZ = 100 only */
#endif

#define WHEEL_SIZE      (LVL_SIZE * LVL_DEPTH)  /* 576 (or 512) buckets total */

/* Granularity at level n = LVL_CLK_DIV ^ n ticks
 * Level 0: 1 tick    (4ms at HZ=250)
 * Level 1: 8 ticks   (32ms)
 * Level 2: 64 ticks  (256ms)
 * Level 3: 512 ticks (2.048s)
 * ... and so on exponentially */

The practical effect at HZ=250 is shown in the following table:

Table 6-160. Timer Wheel Level Geometry (HZ=250)
LevelBucket OffsetGranularityRangeTypical Use
00–634ms (1 tick)0 – 256msTCP retransmit, ARP timeouts
164–12732ms (8 ticks)256ms – 2sNetwork socket timeouts
2128–191256ms (64 ticks)2s – 16sDevice polling intervals
3192–2552.048s (512 ticks)16s – 2minConnection tracking, NFS
4256–31916.4s (4096 ticks)2min – 17minTCP keepalive
5320–3832.2min17min – 2.3hrLong-lived session timeouts
6384–44717.5min2.3hr – 18.6hrConntrack established timeout
7448–5112.3hr18.6hr – 6.2dRarely used
