Core Data Structures

The wheel needs only two structures, and the contrast with hrtimers is instructive: there is no per-clock queue here, because a timer wheel timer has no clock to choose. Every expiry is expressed in jiffies on the monotonic tick count, so the two-level arrangement of timer and per-CPU base is all that is required. What the timer wheel spends its complexity on instead is density — packing state into as few bytes as possible, since the kernel may hold millions of these at once.

The timer_list Structure

Each timer wheel timer is a struct timer_list, deliberately kept small — 40 bytes on 64-bit, against 64 for a struct hrtimer — because the kernel may have millions of them active simultaneously:

/* include/linux/timer_types.h */
struct timer_list {
    struct hlist_node   entry;      /* Bucket list linkage (16 bytes) */
    unsigned long       expires;    /* Absolute expiry time in jiffies */
    void                (*function)(struct timer_list *);  /* Callback */
    u32                 flags;      /* CPU ID + TIMER_* flags + wheel index */
};

The flags field packs multiple pieces of information into a single 32-bit word:

Table 6-161. Timer Flags
Flag / FieldBitsMeaning
TIMER_CPUMASK[0:17]CPU number the timer is bound to (supports up to 262,144 CPUs)
TIMER_MIGRATING[18]Timer is being migrated between CPUs (transient sentinel)
TIMER_DEFERRABLE[19]Don't wake CPU from idle for this timer — service it when CPU wakes for another reason
TIMER_PINNED[20]Must expire on the CPU that started it — no migration to other CPUs
TIMER_IRQSAFE[21]Callback runs with IRQs disabled; safe to delete from IRQ context
TIMER_ARRAYMASK[22:31]Wheel bucket index (stored at enqueue for fast same-bucket detection)

The TIMER_DEFERRABLE flag is particularly important for power management. Deferrable timers are placed in a separate per-CPU timer base (BASE_DEF) and are never considered when the NOHZ subsystem calculates the next wakeup time. This means a CPU can remain in deep idle even when deferrable timers are pending — they'll be serviced the next time the CPU wakes for a non-deferrable reason. Typical deferrable timers include vmstat updates, memory compaction, and workqueue delayed work for non-urgent housekeeping.

The timer_base Structure

The base is the per-CPU container: it owns the wheel itself, the lock that protects it, and the cached state that lets the tick decide in a single comparison whether anything needs doing. Each CPU has not one base but three, and the reason is tickless operation rather than any property of the timers themselves. A timer pinned to this CPU must be expired here; a timer that merely happens to have been armed here may be expired anywhere. Keeping them in separate wheels is what allows an idle CPU to declare the second category someone else's problem while still honouring the first — a distinction that would be impossible to make cheaply if all the timers shared a wheel. A third base holds deferrable timers, which are permitted to be late indefinitely rather than wake a sleeping CPU at all:

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
struct timer_base {
    raw_spinlock_t      lock;               /* Protects this base */
    struct timer_list   *running_timer;     /* Currently executing callback */
#ifdef CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT
    spinlock_t          expiry_lock;        /* Held across callback execution */
    atomic_t            timer_waiters;      /* Deleters waiting on it */
#endif
    unsigned long       clk;               /* Wheel clock (jiffies-based) */
    unsigned long       next_expiry;        /* Earliest pending timer */
    unsigned int        cpu;                /* CPU this base belongs to */
    bool                next_expiry_recalc; /* Must recalculate next_expiry */
    bool                is_idle;            /* NOHZ: base marked idle */
    bool                timers_pending;     /* Any timers in the wheel? */
    DECLARE_BITMAP(pending_map, WHEEL_SIZE); /* 1 bit per bucket */
    struct hlist_head   vectors[WHEEL_SIZE]; /* The actual timer buckets */
} ____cacheline_aligned;

/* Per-CPU allocation: 3 bases when NOHZ, 1 otherwise */
static DEFINE_PER_CPU(struct timer_base, timer_bases[NR_BASES]);

#ifdef CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON
# define NR_BASES   3
# define BASE_LOCAL 0   /* Local (pinned) timers */
# define BASE_GLOBAL 1  /* Global (migratable) timers */
# define BASE_DEF   2   /* Deferrable timers */
#else
# define NR_BASES   1   /* Everything in one base */
#endif

The three-base split serves power management: when a CPU enters idle, only BASE_LOCAL timers require the CPU to wake up. BASE_GLOBAL timers can be expired by another CPU through the timer migration hierarchy (tmigr), and BASE_DEF timers can wait indefinitely until the CPU wakes for another reason.

The pending_map bitmap is a key optimization: one bit per bucket (576 bits = 72 bytes). The timer_recalc_next_expiry() function uses find_next_bit() on this bitmap to quickly locate the next bucket with pending timers, avoiding a linear scan of 576 list heads. On x86_64, find_next_bit() leverages the BSF/TZCNT hardware instruction, making the scan extremely fast.

Bucket Selection: calc_wheel_index()

When a timer is enqueued, its expiry distance from the current wheel clock determines which level and bucket it goes into. The algorithm is pure arithmetic — no loops, no cascading:

/* Compute the bucket for a single level */
static inline unsigned calc_index(unsigned long expires, unsigned lvl,
                                  unsigned long *bucket_expiry)
{
    /* Round UP to prevent early firing due to truncation */
    expires = (expires >> LVL_SHIFT(lvl)) + 1;
    *bucket_expiry = expires << LVL_SHIFT(lvl);
    return LVL_OFFS(lvl) + (expires & LVL_MASK);
}

/* Select the level based on expiry distance */
static int calc_wheel_index(unsigned long expires, unsigned long clk,
                            unsigned long *bucket_expiry)
{
    unsigned long delta = expires - clk;

    if (delta < LVL_START(1))       /* 0 – 63 ticks */
        return calc_index(expires, 0, bucket_expiry);
    else if (delta < LVL_START(2))  /* 64 – 511 ticks */
        return calc_index(expires, 1, bucket_expiry);
    else if (delta < LVL_START(3))  /* 512 – 4095 ticks */
        return calc_index(expires, 2, bucket_expiry);
    /* ... levels 3–7 ... */
    else if ((long)delta < 0) {     /* Already expired! */
        *bucket_expiry = clk;       /* Caller needs this set too */
        return clk & LVL_MASK;      /* Fire immediately */
    }
    else {
        /* Cap at maximum wheel capacity */
        if (delta >= WHEEL_TIMEOUT_CUTOFF)
            expires = clk + WHEEL_TIMEOUT_MAX;
        return calc_index(expires, LVL_DEPTH - 1, bucket_expiry);
    }
}

The round-up in calc_index() (+ 1 after the right shift) is essential: it guarantees that a timer never fires early, even when the expiry time falls at the boundary of a granularity step. This does mean that a timer at level 2 (256ms granularity at HZ=250) may fire up to 256ms late — but for timeout use cases, this is acceptable and far cheaper than maintaining per-timer precision.

Two further details of this function repay attention. The first is the constant that draws the level boundaries:

#define LVL_START(n)    ((LVL_SIZE - 1) << (((n) - 1) * LVL_CLK_SHIFT))

The - 1 is easy to read past and is not cosmetic. A level has 64 buckets of its own granularity, so the obvious cutoff would be LVL_SIZE granules; the kernel stops one granule short. The reason is the round-up that was just described. Suppose level 0 accepted a delta of exactly 64 ticks: calc_index() would compute expires + 1 and mask with LVL_MASK, landing the timer on the bucket the wheel clock is standing on right now. It would either fire immediately or, worse, sit unnoticed until the clock came round again a full 64 ticks later. Reserving the last granule guarantees the round-up always has somewhere to go, and the timer spills into the next level instead, where the coarser granularity absorbs it.

The second is the (long)delta < 0 branch. delta is an unsigned long, so a timer whose expiry has already passed does not produce a small number — it produces a value close to ULONG_MAX, which would sail past every LVL_START test and be treated as the longest possible timeout. Casting to long and testing the sign is how the kernel recovers the intended meaning, and the ordering matters: the test sits after all the level comparisons, because a genuine long timeout and an expired one are indistinguishable until the sign is examined. Such a timer is filed in the bucket the wheel clock currently occupies with *bucket_expiry set to clk, so it is collected on the very next pass of __run_timers(). This is not a rare corner: arming a timer with an expiry in the past is a perfectly legal thing for a caller to do, and mod_timer() with an already-elapsed jiffies value is a common way to say “run this soon”.

Finally, the fall-through case caps absurd timeouts. Anything at or beyond WHEEL_TIMEOUT_CUTOFF is rewritten to expire at clk + WHEEL_TIMEOUT_MAX — roughly 49 days at HZ=250 — rather than being rejected. The wheel simply has no representation for a longer delay, and the kernel would rather fire such a timer early than refuse the request or silently lose it. Callers that genuinely need multi-year timeouts are expected to re-arm.

The Timer Lifecycle

From a caller's point of view the timer wheel presents a much smaller interface than hrtimers: initialize, arm, delete. There are no modes to choose, because there is only one clock and one expiry context; the flags that do exist are set once at initialization and rarely thought about again. The subtleties are concentrated almost entirely at the end of the lifecycle, in the difference between the three ways a timer can be removed — and that is where the use-after-free bugs live.

A warning about names before the code. The timer-wheel API was renamed wholesale between Linux 6.15 and 6.16, and the identifiers used throughout this section are the current ones. Older kernels and older documentation use the previous names; the correspondence is worth keeping to hand when reading code written before 6.16.

Table 6-162. Timer API Renames Landing in Linux 6.15 and 6.16
Former nameName in Linux 7.0.12Old name removed in
del_timer()timer_delete()6.15
del_timer_sync()timer_delete_sync()6.15
try_to_del_timer_sync()timer_delete_sync_try()6.16
from_timer()timer_container_of()6.16
destroy_timer_on_stack()timer_destroy_on_stack()6.16
init_timer_key()timer_init_key()6.16
__init_timer()__timer_init()6.16

NEXT_TIMER_MAX_DELTATIMER_NEXT_MAX_DELTA6.16

The pattern is consistent — the subsystem prefix moved to the front, so that every timer-wheel identifier now sorts and greps together as timer_*. These were mechanical renames with no behavioural change.

The two dates in the last column are worth separating, because the first pair has a longer history than the rest. timer_delete_sync() was not invented in 6.15: it was added back in Linux 6.2 (commit 9b13df3fb64e), with del_timer_sync() left in place as a wrapper so that the thousands of call sites across the tree could be converted at leisure. What 6.15 did was finish that job and delete the wrapper (8fa7292fee5c), which is why a kernel between 6.2 and 6.14 accepts both spellings and anything from 6.15 accepts only the new one. The remaining seven renames were done in a single burst during the 6.16 merge window, this time without a transition period — the identifiers involved have far fewer users, and most are internal.

Two casualties of the same cleanup are worth knowing about because they are still referenced in older code and documentation. The CPU-explicit absolute helpers __round_jiffies() and __round_jiffies_up() were removed outright in 6.16 (49916e22d953). Neither had a caller in a very long time — the commit notes that __round_jiffies() had been unused since 2008 and __round_jiffies_up() since 2019 — and the rest of the family is untouched: round_jiffies(), round_jiffies_up(), their _relative forms and the CPU-explicit __round_jiffies_relative() and __round_jiffies_up_relative() all remain. Separately, 6.13 moved schedule_timeout() and its relatives out of kernel/time/timer.c into a new kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c (da7bd0a9e0fc), so a search for the sleep helpers in the file that implements the wheel now comes up empty.

Initialization: timer_setup()

Initialization binds the callback and sets the initial flags. Note that unlike an hrtimer, whose callback receives a pointer to the hrtimer it was armed on and must recover its container itself, a timer wheel callback receives a struct timer_list * and does the same — the timer_container_of() macro in the example below is simply container_of() under a name that documents what is being recovered:

/* include/linux/timer.h — macro wrapping the init function */
#define timer_setup(timer, callback, flags) \
    __timer_init((timer), (callback), (flags))

/* Static (compile-time) initialization: */
#define DEFINE_TIMER(_name, _function) \
    struct timer_list _name = __TIMER_INITIALIZER(_function, 0)

/* Usage: */
struct my_device {
    struct timer_list   watchdog_timer;
    /* ... */
};

static void watchdog_timeout(struct timer_list *t)
{
    struct my_device *dev = timer_container_of(dev, t, watchdog_timer);
    /* Handle timeout... */
}

/* In probe: */
timer_setup(&dev->watchdog_timer, watchdog_timeout, 0);

/* kernel/time/timer.c — what every path above converges on */
static void do_init_timer(struct timer_list *timer,
                          void (*func)(struct timer_list *),
                          unsigned int flags,
                          const char *name, struct lock_class_key *key)
{
    timer->entry.pprev = NULL;
    timer->function = func;
    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(flags & ~TIMER_INIT_FLAGS))
        flags &= TIMER_INIT_FLAGS;
    timer->flags = flags | raw_smp_processor_id();
    lockdep_init_map(&timer->lockdep_map, name, key, 0);
}

Only three flags are legal here. TIMER_INIT_FLAGS is TIMER_DEFERRABLE | TIMER_PINNED | TIMER_IRQSAFE, and anything else is caught by the WARN_ON_ONCE and masked away rather than being allowed to corrupt the low bits of the word — which is essential, because those low bits are not free space. do_init_timer() ORs in raw_smp_processor_id(), so from this moment the timer is associated with the CPU that initialized it, not the CPU that later arms it. For most drivers those are the same CPU, and for the rest __mod_timer() will move the timer when it is first armed; the initial value simply guarantees that lock_timer_base() always has a valid base to lock.

The reason timer_setup() is a macro rather than a function is visible in __timer_init(): under CONFIG_LOCKDEP it declares a static struct lock_class_key __key at the call site and passes it down with the stringified variable name. Every distinct timer_setup() call in the tree therefore gets its own lockdep class, which is what lets lockdep distinguish one driver's watchdog timer from another's when it reports a lock-order violation involving a timer callback. A function could not do this, because the key must be a separate static object per call site.

Timers on the stack need different treatment, and getting it wrong is a classic source of hard-to-debug corruption. Use timer_setup_on_stack(), and the kerneldoc is emphatic that it “must be balanced with a call to timer_destroy_on_stack()”. The reason is debugobjects: under CONFIG_DEBUG_OBJECTS_TIMERS, timer_init_key_on_stack() calls debug_object_init_on_stack(), which records the object's address and the stack frame it belongs to, so that debugobjects can scream if the function returns while the timer is still armed and the tracking entry outlives the memory it describes. Skipping the destroy call leaks that entry; skipping the _on_stack variant loses the check entirely. Without CONFIG_DEBUG_OBJECTS_TIMERS both reduce to the ordinary path and timer_destroy_on_stack() is an empty inline, which is exactly why the mistake survives testing on production configs.

The static form differs in one further respect. __TIMER_INITIALIZER() sets .entry.next to TIMER_ENTRY_STATIC rather than leaving it NULL — a poison value from include/linux/poison.h that the debugobjects callback timer_is_static_object() tests for, so that a statically defined timer is not reported as being used before initialization. DEFINE_TIMER() passes flags of 0, so a timer that needs TIMER_DEFERRABLE or TIMER_PINNED cannot use it and must call timer_setup() at runtime.

Starting: mod_timer()

mod_timer() is the primary API for arming or rearming a timer. It is specifically designed to be called frequently on the same timer — the most common pattern in networking, where every received packet resets a timeout:

/* kernel/time/timer.c — simplified __mod_timer() */
static inline int __mod_timer(struct timer_list *timer,
                              unsigned long expires, unsigned int options)
{
    unsigned long clk = 0, flags, bucket_expiry;
    struct timer_base *base, *new_base;
    unsigned int idx = UINT_MAX;
    int ret = 0;

    /* Fast path 1: Same expiry time — no work needed */
    if (!(options & MOD_TIMER_NOTPENDING) && timer_pending(timer)) {
        long diff = timer->expires - expires;

        if (!diff)
            return 1;
        if (options & MOD_TIMER_REDUCE && diff <= 0)
            return 1;

        /* Fast path 2: Compute bucket index under lock.
         * If the timer lands in the SAME bucket as before,
         * just update expires — no dequeue/enqueue needed. */
        base = lock_timer_base(timer, &flags);

        if (!timer->function)       /* Shut down under us? */
            goto out_unlock;

        forward_timer_base(base);

        clk = base->clk;
        idx = calc_wheel_index(expires, clk, &bucket_expiry);

        if (idx == timer_get_idx(timer)) {
            if (!(options & MOD_TIMER_REDUCE))
                timer->expires = expires;
            else if (time_after(timer->expires, expires))
                timer->expires = expires;
            ret = 1;
            goto out_unlock;
        }
    }

    /* Slow path: Dequeue from old bucket, enqueue in new one */
    ret = detach_if_pending(timer, base, false);
    /* ... possibly switch to a different CPU's base ... */
    internal_add_timer(base, timer);  /* → calc_wheel_index → enqueue_timer */
}

Both fast paths exist because of networking, and the kernel says so directly: “This is a common optimization triggered by the networking code - if the timer is re-modified to have the same timeout or ends up in the same array bucket then just return”. They are not the same optimization, though, and they fire under quite different conditions.

The first needs no lock at all: re-arming a timer to the identical jiffies value is extremely common when several packets for one socket arrive within a single tick, and it is settled by one subtraction. The second is the interesting one, and it is worth being precise about when it actually helps, because the answer is the opposite of what intuition suggests. Two expiry times share a bucket only when they differ by less than the granularity of the level they land in — so it is long timeouts that benefit, not short ones. A 30-second connection-tracking timer at HZ=250 sits in level 3, whose buckets are 2.048 s wide, so refreshing it every few hundred milliseconds keeps hitting the same bucket and never touches a list. A 200 ms retransmission timer, by contrast, sits in level 0 where a bucket is a single tick; extending it by another 200 ms moves it fifty buckets along and takes the slow path every time. Short timers get their speed from level 0 being exact, not from this optimization.

When it does fire, mod_timer() writes the new expires value and returns — no list manipulation, no bitmap update, no contention with the timer softirq. The kernel is candid about the price: “The downside of this optimization is that it can result in larger granularity than you would get from adding a new timer with this expiry.” The timer stays in the bucket chosen for its original expiry, so it fires when that bucket comes round rather than when a freshly armed timer would have.

The related API timer_reduce() only modifies the timer if the new expiry is earlier than the current one — useful for implementing "minimum timeout" patterns where multiple code paths may want to shorten a timer but never extend it.

Deletion: timer_delete() and timer_delete_sync()

Deletion is where the timer wheel API demands the most care, because the operation the caller usually wants is not the one with the simplest name. Three functions are available, and they differ in what they promise about a callback that is already running — the case that matters, since it is the one that produces use-after-free crashes when a driver frees the object its callback is about to touch:

/* Non-blocking delete — may return while callback is running */
int timer_delete(struct timer_list *timer);

/* Blocking delete — waits for any running callback to complete */
int timer_delete_sync(struct timer_list *timer);

/* Shutdown — permanently disables the timer (function = NULL) */
int timer_shutdown_sync(struct timer_list *timer);

The timer_delete_sync() function spins if the timer's callback is currently executing on another CPU, similar to hrtimer_cancel(). On PREEMPT_RT, it uses a sleeping lock (expiry_lock) to avoid priority inversion. The shutdown variants permanently disable the timer by setting function = NULL, causing any subsequent mod_timer() calls to be silently discarded — this is used during device teardown to prevent use-after-free races.

The PREEMPT_RT arrangement is worth a closer look, because spinning is not merely inefficient there — it can deadlock outright. Two fields exist for it. expiry_lock is taken by the softirq around every callback invocation, and by timer_delete_sync() when its first attempt finds the timer running; timer_waiters records that somebody is waiting, so the expiry side knows to drop and retake the lock between callbacks rather than holding it across the whole batch. The kernel's own comment names two distinct hazards. The first is ordinary priority inversion: on PREEMPT_RT a callback can be preempted mid-execution, so a high-priority deleter spinning on a remote CPU would burn its quantum waiting for a task that may not be scheduled for some time. The second is sharper — a livelock that arises when the deleter and the callback are on the same CPU. Timer callbacks run in a softirq thread on PREEMPT_RT, so a task that preempted that thread and then spun waiting for it would never yield, and the callback it is waiting for could never make progress. Blocking on a sleeping lock resolves both: the waiter is descheduled and the callback's thread inherits its priority.

The shutdown variant deserves the extra emphasis it gets here, because it solves a problem that timer_delete_sync() alone cannot. Waiting for the callback to finish is not enough if the callback — or anything else still running — can re-arm the timer afterwards. A driver that deletes a timer synchronously and then frees the enclosing object can still lose the race if some other thread calls mod_timer() in between. Setting function to NULL makes the timer permanently unarmable, so the teardown sequence has a definite end. A timer that has been shut down cannot be revived; it must be re-initialized from scratch.

Linux 6.18 fixed a narrow race in that mechanism which is worth noting as an illustration of how delicate this path is. The expiry loop reads timer->function into a local variable and warns loudly if it finds NULL, on the grounds that a timer in a bucket should always have a callback. But timer_shutdown_sync() was clearing function unconditionally, including in the case where the timer being shut down was the one currently being dispatched — producing exactly the NULL the expiry loop refuses to believe in, and a spurious warning with it. The fix moves the assignment inside the check that the timer is not the running one, so shutdown of a timer that is already executing waits rather than sabotaging the dispatch in progress.

Timer Expiry: __run_timers()

Timer expiry is driven by TIMER_SOFTIRQ, raised from run_local_timers() in the tick interrupt path when jiffies ≥ base->next_expiry. The softirq handler runs each base in order:

/* Softirq handler for timer wheel */
static void run_timer_softirq(void)
{
    run_timer_base(BASE_LOCAL);     /* Pinned timers first */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON)) {
        run_timer_base(BASE_GLOBAL);  /* Migratable timers */
        run_timer_base(BASE_DEF);     /* Deferrable timers */

        if (is_timers_nohz_active())
            tmigr_handle_remote();    /* Expire remote CPUs' global timers */
    }
}

/* Registered at boot: */
void __init timers_init(void)
{
    init_timer_cpus();
    open_softirq(TIMER_SOFTIRQ, run_timer_softirq);
}

Between the softirq handler and the expiry loop sits a small function that the listings above skip over, and it carries two things worth naming:

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
static void __run_timer_base(struct timer_base *base)
{
    /* Can race against a remote CPU updating next_expiry under the lock */
    if (time_before(jiffies, READ_ONCE(base->next_expiry)))
        return;

    timer_base_lock_expiry(base);       /* PREEMPT_RT: spin_lock(&expiry_lock) */
    raw_spin_lock_irq(&base->lock);
    __run_timers(base);
    raw_spin_unlock_irq(&base->lock);
    timer_base_unlock_expiry(base);
}

/* The remote-expiry entry point used by the migration hierarchy */
void timer_expire_remote(unsigned int cpu)
{
    struct timer_base *base = per_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[BASE_GLOBAL], cpu);

    __run_timer_base(base);
}

The first is the lockless early exit. Almost every invocation of the timer softirq finds nothing to do — the tick raises it whenever jiffies reaches next_expiry for any of the three bases, so two of the three calls typically bail out immediately. Testing next_expiry before taking either lock keeps that common case down to a single load. The READ_ONCE() is not decorative. A remote CPU may be updating next_expiry under the base lock while this test reads it without, which the kernel calls “an intentional and harmless data race” — but an unannotated one made KCSAN complain, so Linux 6.13 added the marking (commit 1d4199cbbe95). A stale value is harmless in both directions — reading too large a value simply defers the work to the next tick, and reading too small a one costs a wasted lock acquisition.

The second is timer_base_lock_expiry(), which is where the expiry_lock discussed earlier is actually taken. On a standard kernel it compiles to nothing at all; under CONFIG_PREEMPT_RT it wraps the entire expiry batch, so a task blocked in timer_delete_sync() is released only when the batch is done — or sooner, if timer_sync_wait_running() notices timer_waiters and hands the lock over between callbacks.

The same function is also the remote-expiry entry point. timer_expire_remote() is called by the migration hierarchy described later in this section when one CPU takes responsibility for another's global timers, and it reaches for BASE_GLOBAL explicitly — never BASE_LOCAL, which is precisely the guarantee that makes a timer pinned to a CPU stay there.

The core expiry loop in __run_timers() advances the wheel clock and collects expired timers:

static inline void __run_timers(struct timer_base *base)
{
    struct hlist_head heads[LVL_DEPTH];
    int levels;

    lockdep_assert_held(&base->lock);

    if (base->running_timer)
        return;                 /* Reentrancy guard */

    while (time_after_eq(jiffies, base->clk) &&
           time_after_eq(jiffies, base->next_expiry)) {

        /* Collect all expired timers across levels */
        levels = collect_expired_timers(base, heads);

        /* Finding nothing is legal only if every matching timer was
         * dequeued, or nothing has been queued since next_expiry was
         * parked at clk + TIMER_NEXT_MAX_DELTA */
        WARN_ON_ONCE(!levels && !base->next_expiry_recalc
                     && base->timers_pending);

        /* Advance the wheel clock (set 1 ahead to prevent
         * infinite requeuing to the current tick) */
        base->clk++;
        timer_recalc_next_expiry(base);

        /* Execute all collected timers */
        while (levels--)
            expire_timers(base, heads + levels);
    }
}

Collecting Expired Timers: The Multi-Level Scan

The collect_expired_timers() function is where the no-cascading design shines. It checks each level at the bucket corresponding to the current clock position, but only continues to the next level if the current level's clock bits are all zero (indicating a level boundary):

static int collect_expired_timers(struct timer_base *base,
                                  struct hlist_head *heads)
{
    unsigned long clk = base->clk = base->next_expiry;
    int i, levels = 0;

    for (i = 0; i < LVL_DEPTH; i++) {
        unsigned int idx = (clk & LVL_MASK) + i * LVL_SIZE;

        if (__test_and_clear_bit(idx, base->pending_map)) {
            hlist_move_list(base->vectors + idx, heads++);
            levels++;
        }
        /* Only check next level if current level clock bits are 0
         * (i.e., we've crossed a granularity boundary) */
        if (clk & LVL_CLK_MASK)
            break;
        clk >>= LVL_CLK_SHIFT;  /* Shift for next level's view */
    }
    return levels;
}

This means that on most ticks, only level 0 is checked. Level 1 is checked every 8th tick, level 2 every 64th tick, and so on. The amortized cost of running the timer wheel is therefore O(1) per tick, regardless of how many timers are enqueued.

Executing Timer Callbacks

The expire_timers() function runs each timer's callback with the base lock dropped (to allow reentrant timer operations). The lock handling differs based on the TIMER_IRQSAFE flag:

static void expire_timers(struct timer_base *base, struct hlist_head *head)
{
    /* Needed only for tracing: base->clk was incremented just before
     * expire_timers() was called, but expiry relates to the old value */
    unsigned long baseclk = base->clk - 1;

    while (!hlist_empty(head)) {
        struct timer_list *timer;
        void (*fn)(struct timer_list *);

        timer = hlist_entry(head->first, struct timer_list, entry);
        base->running_timer = timer;
        detach_timer(timer, true);
        fn = timer->function;

        if (WARN_ON_ONCE(!fn)) {
            /* Should never happen. Emphasis on should! */
            base->running_timer = NULL;
            continue;
        }

        if (timer->flags & TIMER_IRQSAFE) {
            raw_spin_unlock(&base->lock);
            call_timer_fn(timer, fn, baseclk);
            raw_spin_lock(&base->lock);
            base->running_timer = NULL;
        } else {
            raw_spin_unlock_irq(&base->lock);  /* Enable IRQs */
            call_timer_fn(timer, fn, baseclk);
            raw_spin_lock_irq(&base->lock);
            base->running_timer = NULL;
            timer_sync_wait_running(base);     /* PREEMPT_RT handshake */
        }
    }
}

Three details in this loop are easy to skip and all of them matter. The WARN_ON_ONCE(!fn) is the warning discussed earlier in this section: a timer sitting in a bucket is supposed to have a callback, and a NULL here means somebody cleared function out from under the dispatcher. Note the recovery — the timer has already been detached, so the loop clears running_timer and simply moves on rather than jumping to a NULL pointer.

The placement of base->running_timer = NULL is likewise deliberate. It is assigned inside each branch, after the lock has been retaken, rather than once at the bottom of the loop. That ordering is what timer_delete_sync() depends on: it decides whether a callback is still in flight by comparing base->running_timer against its own timer under the base lock, so the field must be cleared while the lock is held. In the non-IRQSAFE branch it must also be cleared before timer_sync_wait_running(), which drops the lock to let a waiter through — publishing “nothing is running” after opening that window would be too late.

Finally, the choice between raw_spin_unlock() and raw_spin_unlock_irq() is the whole meaning of the TIMER_IRQSAFE flag. An ordinary callback runs with interrupts enabled, which is what makes the timer softirq preemptible by hardware interrupts and keeps a long callback from adding to interrupt latency. A callback marked TIMER_IRQSAFE runs with interrupts still disabled, and the reason is not the callback’s own needs but the deleter’s: it is what makes it legal to call timer_delete_sync() on that timer from an interrupt handler and wait for the running instance to finish. The flag is passed through the flags argument of timer_setup() like TIMER_DEFERRABLE and TIMER_PINNED, but it is not a general-purpose option. Its real constituency is the workqueue and kthread-worker layers, where delayed_work and kthread_delayed_work set it unconditionally to resolve a locking problem of their own; outside those two, in-tree users number a handful of DRM fence timeouts. The kernel is unusually direct about this in the header: “The irq disabled callback execution is a special case for workqueue locking issues. It’s not meant for executing random crap with interrupts disabled. Abuse is monitored!”

NOHZ Integration: Idle Base Marking

The timer wheel cooperates with the NOHZ subsystem through the is_idle flag and the timer_base_try_to_set_idle() function. When a CPU prepares to stop its tick, the NOHZ code calls this function to determine the next timer wheel expiry and mark the bases as idle:

/* Called from tick_nohz_stop_tick() */
u64 timer_base_try_to_set_idle(unsigned long basej, u64 basem, bool *idle)
{
    if (*idle)
        return KTIME_MAX;  /* Already idle, nothing to do */

    return __get_next_timer_interrupt(basej, basem, idle);
    /* Sets base->is_idle = true for LOCAL (and GLOBAL on nohz_full)
     * Returns monotonic time of next pending timer */
}

/* On exit from idle: */
void timer_clear_idle(void)
{
    __this_cpu_write(timer_bases[BASE_LOCAL].is_idle, false);
    if (tick_nohz_full_cpu(smp_processor_id()))
        __this_cpu_write(timer_bases[BASE_GLOBAL].is_idle, false);
    tmigr_cpu_activate();  /* Re-join the migration hierarchy */
}

When is_idle is true and a new pinned timer is enqueued remotely on that CPU, trigger_dyntick_cpu() sends an IPI to wake the CPU — ensuring the timer isn't missed despite the tick being stopped. Deferrable timers (TIMER_DEFERRABLE) skip this IPI entirely, which is the key power-saving mechanism for housekeeping timers.

The IPI is rarer than that description suggests, and the guards around it are informative:

/* kernel/time/timer.c */
static void enqueue_timer(struct timer_base *base, struct timer_list *timer,
                          unsigned int idx, unsigned long bucket_expiry)
{
    hlist_add_head(&timer->entry, base->vectors + idx);
    __set_bit(idx, base->pending_map);
    timer_set_idx(timer, idx);

    trace_timer_start(timer, bucket_expiry);

    /* Is this the new first expiring timer?  The *effective* expiry
     * (bucket_expiry) is required here, not timer->expires */
    if (time_before(bucket_expiry, base->next_expiry)) {
        WRITE_ONCE(base->next_expiry, bucket_expiry);
        base->timers_pending = true;
        base->next_expiry_recalc = false;
        trigger_dyntick_cpu(base, timer);
    }
}

static void trigger_dyntick_cpu(struct timer_base *base,
                                struct timer_list *timer)
{
    /* A deferrable timer must never drag a CPU out of dynticks */
    if (!is_timers_nohz_active() || timer->flags & TIMER_DEFERRABLE)
        return;

    if (base->is_idle) {
        WARN_ON_ONCE(!(timer->flags & TIMER_PINNED ||
                       tick_nohz_full_cpu(base->cpu)));
        wake_up_nohz_cpu(base->cpu);
    }
}

The first thing to notice is that trigger_dyntick_cpu() is not reached on every remote enqueue — only when the timer just added becomes the base’s earliest. A CPU sleeping until a timer 5 seconds out does not need waking because a second timer was queued behind it; its programmed wakeup already covers that one. Only a timer that expires sooner than anything already pending invalidates the sleeping CPU’s plan.

The second is which value that comparison uses. The kernel is explicit in its comment that bucket_expiry is required rather than timer->expires, and the reason goes back to calc_wheel_index(): a timer filed into a coarse level does not expire when the caller asked, it expires when its bucket comes round. Comparing the requested time against next_expiry would make a timer look like the new earliest when its effective expiry is in fact later than one already queued, and the CPU would be woken for nothing.

The WARN_ON_ONCE encodes an invariant that is easy to miss. If the base is idle, the timer being enqueued must be either TIMER_PINNED or destined for a nohz_full CPU. A non-pinned timer only lands on a remote base at all if that base was running when the timer was queued, in which case the remote CPU handles everything itself; and a CPU on its way to idle cannot set is_idle behind this code’s back, because is_idle is set under the base lock that the enqueue path holds.

The deferrable exemption has a sharper rationale than “power saving”. Deferrable timers live in BASE_DEF, and the idle path does not consult that base at all — so waking the CPU would rouse it and then find nothing to do, since nothing in the idle exit path expires deferrable timers. The IPI would be pure loss.

The reverse transition is deliberately sloppy. timer_clear_idle() writes is_idle without taking the base lock, and the kernel explains why: the worst outcome of losing the race is that a remote enqueue sends a pointless IPI to a CPU that has already woken, whereas taking the lock would add cost to every single idle exit to shrink a window by a few instructions. The error is in the safe direction — a spurious wakeup, never a missed one.

Timer Migration: The tmigr Hierarchy

The previous subsection left a problem unsolved. Splitting the bases lets an idle CPU ignore its own global timers, but it does not say who runs them instead — and "whoever happens to be awake" is not an answer a kernel can act on, because no CPU knows what the others have queued. The timer migration (tmigr) subsystem, added in Linux 6.9, is the mechanism that turns that vague hope into a definite assignment.

Consider the concrete case: CPU 0 has a global timer expiring in 5 seconds and wants to enter a deep idle state. Without tmigr its only safe option is to program its clockevent device to wake it in 5 seconds, which defeats the purpose — deep C-states are only worth entering if you stay in them. With tmigr, responsibility for that timer is pushed up a hierarchy of groups and a designated migrator CPU — one that is awake anyway — takes it over. CPU 0 then sleeps with no timer of its own left to service.

The hierarchy is organized as a tree of tmigr_group nodes, with CPUs as leaves and progressively larger groups as internal nodes (similar to how the scheduler's load-balancing domains work, and likewise built to follow NUMA topology so that a migrator is usually taking over timers from CPUs on its own node). When the last CPU in a group goes idle, it becomes the migrator and inherits the group's timers. When a migrator itself goes idle, its timers propagate up to the next level. The invariant the tree maintains is the one that makes the whole scheme safe: so long as any CPU in the system is awake, exactly one CPU is responsible for the global timers of every idle CPU beneath it.

That the tree follows NUMA topology is an intent rather than an automatic consequence, and until recently the intent was not always achieved. The hierarchy is not built in one pass from a known topology; it grows incrementally as CPUs come up, each arriving CPU attaching itself and, when it exhausts the capacity of the current root, creating a new level above it. Because the shape therefore depends on boot order, a CPU from a second NUMA node that booted after the first node's group was complete would create a new root for its own node and connect the other node's group underneath it. The result was an imbalanced tree in which, as the fixing commit puts it, “some node 0 CPUs migrate node 1 timers (and vice versa) way before reaching the crossnode groups, resulting in more frequent remote memory accesses than expected”. Nothing was incorrect — timers still ran on time — but the locality the design was built for quietly did not materialize. Linux 6.19 fixed this (5eb579dfd46b) by refusing to connect groups whose nodes do not match, forcing the mismatched case up to a genuine cross-node level marked NUMA_NO_NODE. Tree construction has proved unusually difficult to get right in general: 6.14 corrected an off-by-one in the child count that could leave a system running with more than one top level (868c9037df62), defeating the single-migrator invariant outright.

/* From run_timer_softirq() — handle timers migrated from idle CPUs */
static void run_timer_softirq(void)
{
    run_timer_base(BASE_LOCAL);
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_NO_HZ_COMMON)) {
        run_timer_base(BASE_GLOBAL);
        run_timer_base(BASE_DEF);
        if (is_timers_nohz_active())
            tmigr_handle_remote();  /* Expire global timers from idle CPUs */
    }
}

Which CPUs Take Part

A CPU only participates in this scheme if it is available, a notion that Linux 6.19 broadened considerably. Availability began as a synonym for “online” — an offline CPU obviously cannot be a migrator — and the flag was called online accordingly. It was renamed to available because a second, quite different reason to exclude a CPU was added: isolation.

The motivation is a direct conflict between two features that had been developed independently. Timer migration improves idle residency by moving timer work towards CPUs that are awake. CPU isolation exists to keep work away from certain CPUs entirely. On a machine running a latency-critical workload on isolated cores, tmigr was doing exactly the wrong thing: an isolated core running a busy poll loop is, by definition, always awake, which made it an ideal migrator candidate and earned it a steady stream of other CPUs’ timer callbacks — precisely the interference isolation was configured to prevent.

Linux 6.19 resolves this by excluding domain-isolated CPUs from the hierarchy altogether (commits 8312cab5ff47 and 7dec062cfcf2):

/* kernel/time/timer_migration.c */
static cpumask_var_t tmigr_available_cpumask;

/* Enabled during late initcall */
static DEFINE_STATIC_KEY_FALSE(tmigr_exclude_isolated);

static inline bool tmigr_is_not_available(struct tmigr_cpu *tmc)
{
    return !(tmc->tmgroup && tmc->available);
}

static inline bool tmigr_is_isolated(int cpu)
{
    if (!static_branch_unlikely(&tmigr_exclude_isolated))
        return false;

    return (!housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_DOMAIN) &&
            housekeeping_cpu(cpu, HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE));
}

The condition in tmigr_is_isolated() repays a careful reading, because it deliberately treats the two kinds of isolation introduced in the previous section differently. A CPU is excluded when it is not a housekeeping CPU for HK_TYPE_DOMAIN — that is, it was isolated by isolcpus=domain or by an isolated cpuset partition — and it is a housekeeping CPU for HK_TYPE_KERNEL_NOISE, meaning it is not a nohz_full CPU.

So domain-isolated CPUs are removed from the tree entirely, while nohz_full CPUs stay in it. That asymmetry is deliberate. A nohz_full CPU already reports itself idle to tmigr whenever it stops its tick, so the timekeeping CPU picks up its global timers through the ordinary mechanism and no special case is needed. A domain-isolated CPU makes no such report — it may be running flat out with its tick enabled — so the only way to keep timer work off it is to remove it from the hierarchy. Marking it idle instead would mean maintaining idle state for a CPU that is manifestly busy, which the kernel comment describes as too costly.

One CPU is exempt from exclusion even if it is isolated: the timekeeping CPU. Removing it would leave the nohz_full CPUs with no global migrator at all, which is the one outcome worse than a little interference. The static key is likewise enabled only at late initcall, so the isolation logic is inert during early boot when the housekeeping masks are not yet final.

Because cpuset partitions can be reconfigured at runtime — the capability noted at the end of the NOHZ section — this is not purely a boot-time decision. Writing a new isolated partition causes tmigr_isolated_exclude_cpumask() to run, which un-isolates CPUs that have left the partition and marks newly isolated ones unavailable, rebuilding the affected parts of the hierarchy while the system runs.

CPU Hotplug: Timer Migration on CPU Death

When a CPU goes offline, all its pending timers must be migrated to a surviving CPU:

int timers_dead_cpu(unsigned int cpu)
{
    struct timer_base *old_base;
    struct timer_base *new_base;
    int b, i;

    for (b = 0; b < NR_BASES; b++) {
        old_base = per_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[b], cpu);
        new_base = get_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[b]);
        /*
         * The caller is globally serialized and nobody else
         * takes two locks at once, deadlock is not possible.
         */
        raw_spin_lock_irq(&new_base->lock);
        raw_spin_lock_nested(&old_base->lock, SINGLE_DEPTH_NESTING);

        /* The current CPU's base clock might be stale. Update
         * it before moving the timers over. */
        forward_timer_base(new_base);

        WARN_ON_ONCE(old_base->running_timer);
        old_base->running_timer = NULL;

        /* Migrate all WHEEL_SIZE (576) buckets */
        for (i = 0; i < WHEEL_SIZE; i++)
            migrate_timer_list(new_base, old_base->vectors + i);

        raw_spin_unlock(&old_base->lock);
        raw_spin_unlock_irq(&new_base->lock);
        put_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases);
    }
    return 0;
}

static void migrate_timer_list(struct timer_base *new_base,
                               struct hlist_head *head)
{
    struct timer_list *timer;
    int cpu = new_base->cpu;

    while (!hlist_empty(head)) {
        timer = hlist_entry(head->first, struct timer_list, entry);
        detach_timer(timer, false);
        timer->flags = (timer->flags & ~TIMER_BASEMASK) | cpu;
        internal_add_timer(new_base, timer);
    }
}

The destination is not a CPU chosen by any policy: get_cpu_ptr() simply returns the base of whichever CPU is running the hotplug callback, which by then is guaranteed not to be the dying one. Its matching put_cpu_ptr() re-enables preemption at the end of each iteration — easy to overlook, because unlike the two raw_spin_lock calls it does not look like a lock, but it is one.

Taking both bases' locks at once would normally be a lock-ordering hazard. The kernel argues it away rather than solving it: “The caller is globally serialized and nobody else takes two locks at once, deadlock is not possible.” Both halves matter. CPU hotplug is serialized by cpus_write_lock(), so two teardowns can never run concurrently, and no other code path in timer.c holds two timer_base locks simultaneously — lock_timer_base() takes exactly one. The SINGLE_DEPTH_NESTING subclass exists only to stop lockdep complaining about the same lock class being taken twice.

WARN_ON_ONCE(old_base->running_timer) asserts the invariant that makes all of this safe: a CPU that still has a callback in flight has not finished dying. This is the same field the expiry path publishes and timer_delete_sync() polls, so a non-NULL value here would mean a concurrent waiter is spinning on a base that is about to be emptied. Clearing it afterwards is defensive housekeeping for the offline base.

The re-insertion is more interesting than a straight list splice. migrate_timer_list() detaches each timer, rewrites the CPU index in the low bits of flags, and calls internal_add_timer(), which runs calc_wheel_index() again against the new base's freshly forwarded clk. Because expires is an absolute jiffies value, this recomputation is what keeps the deadline correct — and it can move a timer to a different level than it occupied before. A timer parked in level 4 on the dead CPU because it was armed far in advance may now be only milliseconds away and land in level 0, where it gains the tick-exact granularity it never had. The three bases are migrated independently, so a TIMER_DEFERRABLE timer stays deferrable; what it does not preserve is pinning. A TIMER_PINNED timer was pinned to a CPU that no longer exists, so the pin is silently transferred along with everything else.

The mirror image runs on the way up. timers_prepare_cpu() resets each of the incoming CPU's three bases — clk to the current jiffies, next_expiry to clk + TIMER_NEXT_MAX_DELTA, and the next_expiry_recalc, timers_pending and is_idle flags to false. Without this the base would resume with a clk frozen at the moment it went offline, and forward_timer_base() would have to walk it forward across the entire offline interval. Both functions are registered at the same hotplug state, CPUHP_TIMERS_PREPARE, one as the startup callback and one as the teardown callback.

Choosing Between hrtimers and the Timer Wheel

Having described both subsystems, it is worth stating plainly how to choose between them, because the intuitive rule — reach for hrtimers when you want accuracy — leads new code astray more often than not.

The right question is not how precise the timeout needs to be but whether it is expected to fire at all. A timeout that is normally cancelled belongs in the timer wheel however short it is, because the wheel is optimized for exactly that: arming and cancelling are both O(1) and touch nothing outside the timer itself. A timer that is expected to expire, and whose expiry time carries real meaning, belongs in an hrtimer — even a long one. Put a periodic sub-millisecond hrtimer where a wheel timer would do and the cost is a stream of hardware reprogramming operations and interrupts that the wheel would have absorbed into the tick for free. Put a TCP retransmission timeout in an hrtimer and you have paid for red-black tree insertion and removal on every packet to get precision that will be discarded when the acknowledgement arrives.

The following table summarizes the decision criteria:

Table 6-163. Choosing Between hrtimers and Timer Wheel
Criterionhrtimertimer_list (wheel)
ResolutionNanosecond (1ns in high-res mode)Tick (4ms at HZ=250)
PrecisionGuaranteed within hardware interrupt latency (~µs)Best-effort — up to 1 granularity step late (ms–seconds)
Insertion costO(log n) — RB-tree insertionO(1) — hash into bucket, linked list append
Cancellation costO(log n) — RB-tree removalO(1) — unlink from hash list
Memory per timer64 bytes (struct hrtimer)40 bytes (struct timer_list)
Scalability (millions)Moderate (tree depth limits throughput)Excellent (O(1) operations)
Cancellation-before-expiryUncommon (most sleep timers fire)The design assumption — the kernel calls it “the vast majority”
Clock baseMONOTONIC, REALTIME, BOOTTIME, TAIjiffies only (monotonic)
Typical use caseSleep, scheduling, futex, timerfd, precise intervalsNetwork timeouts, device polling, GC, deferred work

The rule of thumb: if the timer usually fires, use an hrtimer; if the timer usually gets cancelled, use the timer wheel. The hrtimer's RB-tree cost is justified by its precision for timers that actually fire. The timer wheel's O(1) operations are justified by the high cancellation rate of timeout timers — the insertion and removal costs dominate, not the execution cost.

This is not a rule of thumb invented for this book; it is the stated design premise of the wheel, recorded at the top of kernel/time/timer.c: “This is an optimization of the original timer wheel implementation for the majority of the timer wheel use cases: timeouts. The vast majority of timeout timers (networking, disk I/O ...) are canceled before expiry. If the timeout expires it indicates that normal operation is disturbed, so it does not matter much whether the timeout comes with a slight delay.” Read carefully, that is a stronger claim than it first appears. It says the imprecision is not a tolerated cost but a correct trade: on the rare occasion a timeout actually fires, something has already gone wrong, and a few extra milliseconds of delay are irrelevant next to the fault being reported.

The same comment records the one documented exception — “networking timers with a small expiry time. They rely on the granularity. Those fit into the first wheel level, which has HZ granularity” — which is why level 0 is exact to the tick and only the outer levels batch. It also explains why forcing over-long timeouts to the wheel’s capacity is safe rather than reckless: “From data sampling we know that the maximum value observed is 5 days (network connection tracking)”, comfortably inside the roughly 49-day ceiling at HZ=250.

The timer wheel has been redesigned from the ground up. Linux 2.6 used a cascading five-level wheel (tvec_base with tv1–tv5) where timers physically moved from higher to lower levels as time advanced — cascading added O(n) worst-case latency spikes. Linux 7.0.12 changes: (1) No-cascading hierarchical wheel with 9 levels × 64 buckets; (2) pending_map bitmap for O(1) next-timer lookup via find_next_bit(); (3) Three per-CPU bases (BASE_LOCAL, BASE_GLOBAL, BASE_DEF) for NOHZ power optimization; (4) Timer migration hierarchy (tmigr) allowing idle CPUs to delegate global timer expiry; (5) timer_setup() replaces init_timer() + setup_timer(); (6) timer_shutdown_sync() for safe permanent disabling; (7) Same-bucket mod_timer() optimization (no list manipulation when bucket unchanged); (8) round_jiffies() family for aligning timer expiry to second boundaries, reducing wakeups.

Updating System Time and Statistics

Every tick triggers a cascade of time-related updates that keep the system's clock accurate, charge CPU time to the correct process, and maintain statistics used by tools like top, uptime, and /proc/stat. In Linux 2.6, these duties were split between a global timer interrupt handler (updating xtime and jiffies) and a per-CPU local timer interrupt handler (accounting and scheduling). In Linux 7.0.12, the architecture has been completely restructured: a single per-CPU tick handler (tick_sched_handle()) drives everything through update_process_times(), while a designated "duty CPU" handles the global timekeeping updates.

Everything so far in this chapter has been about producing time: counting it, reading it, and arranging to be interrupted at the right moment. This section is about what the kernel actually does with the interrupt when it arrives — and it is worth pausing on how little of that work is timekeeping proper. Advancing jiffies and updating the wall clock is one line of the pipeline, performed by one CPU. The rest is bookkeeping on behalf of subsystems that have no other reason to run periodically and have simply adopted the tick as their heartbeat.

That opportunism is the organizing principle of this section, and it creates three tensions worth holding in mind:

  • The tick is a sample, not a measurement. Charging CPU time by observing what is running at the instant of each interrupt is statistical: a tick's worth of time — 4ms at HZ=250 — is charged in full to whichever task happened to be current, even if it started 10µs ago. Over a long run the errors cancel, which is why the cheap method survives; over a short run they emphatically do not, which is why two more precise accounting modes exist alongside it.
  • Some of this work must happen exactly once system-wide; the rest must happen on every CPU. Advancing jiffies globally from every CPU would be both wrong and a scalability disaster, so it is delegated to a single duty CPU. Charging CPU time, by contrast, is meaningless anywhere but on the CPU that ran the task. The split between do_timer() and update_process_times() is exactly this division.
  • The tick runs in hardirq context, and some of the work does not belong there. Delivering a signal requires locks that cannot be taken with interrupts disabled on a PREEMPT_RT kernel, and are expensive to take even on a normal one. Where a step cannot complete safely in the interrupt, the pattern is always the same: do a cheap check in the tick, and defer the real work to a context that can afford it.

The rest of this section walks the pipeline in execution order, then steps back:

  1. What, exactly, runs on every tick? The update_process_times() call chain, which is short enough to read in full and is the spine of everything that follows.
  2. How is CPU time charged to a process? Tick sampling, and the two higher-precision modes that replace it when sampling is not good enough.
  3. Who advances the clock? The duty CPU, do_timer(), and the handoff to the timekeeping machinery described earlier in the chapter.
  4. Where does the number in uptime come from? The load average, why it counts tasks that are not running at all, and how it survives CPUs that have stopped ticking.
  5. What about the timers themselves? The tick's hook into the timer wheel and the low-resolution hrtimer path.
  6. What do RCU and the scheduler get out of the tick? Quiescent-state reporting and time-slice enforcement — both covered in depth in later chapters, summarized here for the tick's sake.
  7. How are CPU-time limits enforced? POSIX CPU timers, and why on x86_64 and ARM64 the tick does not actually expire them.
  8. What does it all cost? A step-by-step summary of the whole cascade, and an honest look at where the price actually lies.

Version history. The work is recognizable; the structure around it is not. Linux 2.6 split these duties between a global timer interrupt handler that updated xtime under xtime_lock and a per-CPU local APIC handler that did accounting and scheduling. Linux 7.0.12 has a single per-CPU tick handler for everything, with the global portion guarded not by a lock but by a CPU identity check — only the CPU whose number matches tick_do_timer_cpu performs it. That change is what made tickless operation possible, because it turned “update the global clock” from something every CPU raced to do into a duty that can be handed from a CPU going idle to one that is staying awake.

The Tick Pipeline: update_process_times()

The central function called on every tick (or on every tick emulation in NOHZ mode) is update_process_times(). It is short — short enough to read in full — and reading it is the fastest way to understand what the tick is for, because the function is essentially a list of subsystems that asked to be called periodically. Nothing here dispatches based on state or priority; the tick calls each one unconditionally, in a fixed order, and each decides for itself whether it has work to do. That design is deliberate: it keeps the hot path branch-free and puts the burden of being cheap on the callee, which is why most of the functions below begin with a fast-path test that returns immediately.

The one argument, user_tick, is the only piece of information the pipeline needs from the interrupted context: whether the CPU was executing user-mode code at the instant the interrupt arrived. It is derived from the saved registers, and it is what makes tick-based CPU accounting possible.

/* kernel/time/timer.c — called from tick_sched_handle() */
void update_process_times(int user_tick)
{
    struct task_struct *p = current;

    /* 1. CPU time accounting — charge this tick to user/system/idle */
    account_process_tick(p, user_tick);

    /* 2. Run timer softirq if any timer wheel timers have expired */
    run_local_timers();

    /* 3. RCU: report quiescent state, advance callbacks */
    rcu_sched_clock_irq(user_tick);

    /* 4. IRQ work: deferred work that must run in hardirq context */
#ifdef CONFIG_IRQ_WORK
    if (in_hardirq())
        irq_work_tick();
#endif

    /* 5. Scheduler tick: update time slices, load balancing */
    sched_tick();

    /* 6. POSIX CPU timers: check process/thread CPU time limits */
    if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS))
        run_posix_cpu_timers();
}

Each of these steps performs a critical function. Let's examine them in detail.

CPU Time Accounting: account_process_tick()

The kernel must track how much CPU time each process consumes, broken down by execution context (user mode, system mode, idle, I/O wait, IRQ handling, steal time in VMs). This information is reported via /proc/[pid]/stat, /proc/stat, and the getrusage() system call.

On each tick, account_process_tick() charges one tick's worth of CPU time (typically 4ms at HZ=250) to the appropriate accounting bucket:

/* kernel/sched/cputime.c */
void account_process_tick(struct task_struct *p, int user_tick)
{
    u64 cputime, steal;

    /* vtime mode (NO_HZ_FULL): precise ns accounting, not tick-based */
    if (vtime_accounting_enabled_this_cpu())
        return;

    /* IRQ time accounting: if CONFIG_IRQ_TIME_ACCOUNTING, split
     * this tick into user/system/irq/softirq portions */
    if (irqtime_enabled()) {
        irqtime_account_process_tick(p, user_tick, 1);
        return;
    }

    /* Standard tick-based accounting */
    cputime = TICK_NSEC;  /* One tick = 4,000,000 ns at HZ=250 */

    /* Subtract any steal time (time stolen by hypervisor) */
    steal = steal_account_process_time(ULONG_MAX);
    if (steal >= cputime)
        return;  /* Entire tick was stolen */
    cputime -= steal;

    /* Classify: user, system, or idle */
    if (user_tick)
        account_user_time(p, cputime);
    else if ((p != this_rq()->idle) || (irq_count() != HARDIRQ_OFFSET))
        account_system_time(p, HARDIRQ_OFFSET, cputime);
    else
        account_idle_time(cputime);
}

The user_tick parameter is determined by examining whether the interrupted context was running in user mode (checking the saved CPU registers). Three accounting modes exist, each with different precision:

Table 6-164. CPU Time Accounting Modes
ModeConfigPrecisionMechanismUse Case
Tick-basedDefault1 tick (4ms at HZ=250)Sample at each tick, charge entire tick to interrupted contextStandard systems
IRQ timeCONFIG_IRQ_TIME_ACCOUNTING~ns for IRQ timeMeasures actual time in IRQ/softirq handlers using sched_clock()Systems where IRQ overhead matters
vtimeCONFIG_VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_GENNanosecondContext-tracking-based: timestamps every kernel/user boundary crossingNO_HZ_FULL CPUs (no tick to sample)

The tick-based mode is inherently imprecise — a process that runs for 3.9ms and sleeps for 0.1ms might get charged 0 or 1 tick depending on whether the tick interrupt catches it running. This imprecision is acceptable for general-purpose systems but inadequate for NO_HZ_FULL CPUs where there may be no ticks at all. On such CPUs, vtime (virtual time) accounting is used instead, recording exact timestamps at every kernel entry/exit transition.

The three modes are a Kconfig choice, so exactly one is active in any given build, and the dependencies between them are worth knowing because they rule out the combination the table might seem to suggest. VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_NATIVE — the hardware-assisted variant that reads a dedicated CPU counter on every entry, exit and in-kernel state transition — depends on HAVE_VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING && !NO_HZ_FULL. It is therefore mutually exclusive with full dynticks, and in any case only s390 and PowerPC provide the counter it needs. The mode that NO_HZ_FULL actually uses is VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_GEN, which needs no special hardware because it hooks the context-tracking subsystem the kernel already maintains for those CPUs, timestamping — in the Kconfig’s words — “every kernel-user boundaries”. On x86_64 and ARM64, HAVE_VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_GEN is default y if 64BIT, so this is the only precise mode either architecture can offer.

The Kconfig is also candid about the price, which is why this is not simply the best mode to select on any machine: the accounting “is thus performed at the expense of some significant overhead”, and the help text still advises saying N unless you are working on full dynticks. Every boundary crossing costs a timestamp read and an update, so a syscall-heavy workload pays on every syscall — a trade that only makes sense when the alternative is no sampling at all. IRQ_TIME_ACCOUNTING sits outside the choice as an independent option, but it too depends on !VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING_NATIVE, since the native mode already measures interrupt time directly.

What User Space Actually Sees

The values above are the raw ones the kernel maintains, and they are not the values reported by /proc/[pid]/stat or getrusage(). Between the two sits cputime_adjust(), and understanding why it exists explains a class of confusing observations.

Tick sampling produces a utime/stime split that is statistical, but the kernel separately maintains sum_exec_runtime — the task's total CPU time, measured precisely by the scheduler at every context switch. These two numbers disagree. The precise total is trustworthy; only the user/system ratio came from sampling. So cputime_adjust() keeps the ratio and rescales it to fit the precise total:

/* kernel/sched/cputime.c */
    raw_spin_lock_irqsave(&prev->lock, flags);
    rtime = curr->sum_exec_runtime;          /* precise */

    if (prev->stime + prev->utime >= rtime)  /* reordered, or a bug */
        goto out;

    stime = curr->stime;                     /* sampled */
    utime = curr->utime;                     /* sampled */

    /* If either stime or utime are 0, assume all runtime is userspace.
     * Once a task gets some ticks, the monotonicity code at 'update:'
     * will ensure things converge to the observed ratio. */
    if (stime == 0) { utime = rtime; goto update; }
    if (utime == 0) { stime = rtime; goto update; }

    stime = mul_u64_u64_div_u64(stime, rtime, stime + utime);

    /* mul_u64_u64_div_u64() can approximate; enforce a*b/(b+c) <= a */
    if (unlikely(stime > rtime))
        stime = rtime;
update:
    /* ... monotonicity clamp against prev, then: ... */
    utime = rtime - stime;

Two properties follow. First, the reported utime + stime always equals the precise runtime, so a task's total CPU time is accurate even though its user/system split is not. Second, the function enforces monotonicity through the cached prev_cputime under a lock — reported values may stall but can never go backwards, because a monitoring tool that saw CPU time decrease between two reads would compute a negative rate. This is why two consecutive reads of /proc/[pid]/stat on a lightly-loaded task can show identical values even though the task ran in between.

The two zero cases deserve a closer look, because the kernel’s own comment above them overstates what the code does. It reads “If either stime or utime are 0, assume all runtime is userspace”, but only the first branch does that. When stime is zero the whole runtime is charged to user; when utime is zero it is charged to system. Each branch is really saying that the sampler only ever caught this task in one mode, so everything should be attributed to that mode — a sensible guess, and a self-correcting one, since the first tick that lands in the other mode gives the ratio something to work with.

A short-lived task illustrates the limits of the whole scheme, and shows why the ordering of those two tests matters. A process that runs for 500µs and exits will have sum_exec_runtime recorded to the nanosecond, but it may never have been observed by a tick at all — so utime and stime are both zero. The stime == 0 test comes first, so the tie is broken in favour of user time and the entire 500µs is reported as user regardless of where it was actually spent. In /proc, a short-lived process that did nothing but call into the kernel is indistinguishable from one that spent its whole life in a tight userspace loop.

The same function serves whole thread groups through thread_group_cputime_adjusted(), which first sums the per-thread totals via thread_group_cputime() and then applies the identical scaling against the group's own prev_cputime. That is the path behind the aggregate figures in /proc/[pid]/stat and times().

One implementation note on the IRQ-time path shown in the listing above: irqtime_enabled() is a static key rather than a variable read, and it became one only in Linux 7.0. When CONFIG_IRQ_TIME_ACCOUNTING is compiled in but not enabled at boot, static_branch_likely(&sched_clock_irqtime) compiles to a jump the kernel patches at runtime, so the feature costs nothing on the tick path until someone turns it on.

The obvious motivation — avoiding a branch on a path that runs on every CPU on every tick — is not the one the kernel gives, and the real one is more interesting. The variable is read-mostly, and it happened to share a cacheline with the frequently updated NOHZ structure; the commit message’s complaint is that this “may share the same cacheline with frequently updated nohz struct”, so the cost was not the branch but a cacheline bounced between CPUs that had no interest in the flag at all. Converting it to a static key removes the load entirely, and with it the sharing.

Getting there took three attempts, which is a small illustration of why static keys are not a free substitute for a variable. Linux 6.14-rc1 made the conversion (8722903cbb8f) and 6.14-rc7 reverted it (f3fa0e40df17), because disabling a static key can sleep and the only caller of disable_sched_clock_irqtime() is mark_tsc_unstable(), which KVM reaches from vcpu_load() with preemption disabled. Linux 7.0 succeeded (505da6689305) by not disabling the key from that context at all: the disable is deferred to the existing sched_clock_work workqueue item, which the same code path already schedules when it calls clear_sched_clock_stable().

Updating Wall-Clock Time: do_timer() and update_wall_time()

The global system time (wall-clock time returned by clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)) must be updated periodically. In Linux 7.0.12, this responsibility belongs to the "duty CPU" — a designated CPU that advances jiffies and updates the timekeeping subsystem. The duty is managed by tick_do_timer_cpu (see the earlier section on the Timekeeping Duty CPU).

When the duty CPU's tick fires, it calls:

/* kernel/time/timekeeping.c */
void do_timer(unsigned long ticks)
{
    jiffies_64 += ticks;   /* Advance the global tick counter */
    calc_global_load();    /* Update the 1/5/15-minute load averages */
}

/* Called from tick_do_update_jiffies64() after advancing jiffies */
void update_wall_time(void)
{
    if (timekeeping_advance(TK_ADV_TICK))
        clock_was_set_delayed();  /* Notify if REALTIME offset changed */
    tk_aux_advance();  /* Update auxiliary timekeepers (coarse clocks) */
}

The timekeeping_advance() function reads the current clocksource value, computes how much real time has elapsed since the last update, and advances the internal timekeeping state. This is where NTP adjustments are applied — the kernel can slightly speed up or slow down the apparent passage of time to converge with the NTP reference clock. The details of this mechanism are covered in the Timekeeping section earlier in this chapter.

System Load Average: calc_global_load()

The load average — the numbers shown by uptime and top — represents the average number of runnable plus uninterruptible tasks over three time windows (1 minute, 5 minutes, 15 minutes). The phrase “plus uninterruptible” deserves emphasis, because it is where Linux parts company with every other Unix. Traditional systems count only tasks that are runnable, so the load average is a measure of demand for the CPU. Linux also counts tasks blocked in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE — overwhelmingly, tasks waiting on disk or network storage. The result is not a CPU utilization metric at all but a measure of overall system demand: a machine with a saturated disk and an idle CPU can show a load average of 20, and a machine with all cores pinned at 100% can show a load average of 4. Interpreting the number as “how busy is the CPU” is the single most common mistake made with it.

The calculation itself is an exponential moving average (EMA), sampled every five seconds rather than every tick:

/* kernel/sched/loadavg.c */
void calc_global_load(void)
{
    unsigned long sample_window;
    long active, delta;

    sample_window = READ_ONCE(calc_load_update);
    if (time_before(jiffies, sample_window + 10))
        return;  /* Not yet time for the next sample (every 5 seconds) */

    /* Fold in NOHZ CPUs that haven't reported recently */
    delta = calc_load_nohz_read();
    if (delta)
        atomic_long_add(delta, &calc_load_tasks);

    active = atomic_long_read(&calc_load_tasks);
    active = active > 0 ? active * FIXED_1 : 0;

    /* Exponential moving average with different decay constants */
    avenrun[0] = calc_load(avenrun[0], EXP_1, active);   /* 1 min */
    avenrun[1] = calc_load(avenrun[1], EXP_5, active);   /* 5 min */
    avenrun[2] = calc_load(avenrun[2], EXP_15, active);  /* 15 min */

    WRITE_ONCE(calc_load_update, sample_window + LOAD_FREQ);  /* Next: +5s */

    /* In case we went to NO_HZ for multiple LOAD_FREQ intervals
     * catch up in bulk. */
    calc_global_nohz();
}

The calc_load_tasks atomic counter is fed by each CPU every LOAD_FREQ from calc_global_load_tick(). LOAD_FREQ is defined as (5*HZ+1), and the stray +1 is not a rounding artefact but a fix for an observed bug. The kernel has several other five-second timers, and when one of them drifts into phase with the sampler it is seen by every single sample, inflating the load average with work that is barely there. It was reported on a machine where JBD’s five-second commit timer had synchronized with the load calculation; the fix, from Linus in 2007, was simply to offset the sampling period by one tick so that nothing running on a whole number of seconds can stay in phase with it. Note carefully what calc_global_load_tick() contributes: not a count, but a delta.

The + 10 in the window test is the other unexplained constant, and it is what makes the distributed scheme work without any synchronization at all. The per-CPU folds and the global average are not coordinated; each CPU folds its own delta when its own tick notices the window has opened, and calc_global_load() simply waits ten ticks before reading the total, on the assumption — stated in the file’s header comment — that “10 ticks is sufficient time for every CPU to have completed this task”. There is no check that they have. The comment is equally frank about what happens if a CPU is late: this “places an upper-bound on the IRQ-off latency of the machine. Then again, being late doesn’t loose the delta, just wrecks the sample.” A delta that misses its window is not dropped — it is still sitting in calc_load_tasks and will be included next time. Only that one five-second sample is slightly wrong, in a fifteen-minute exponential average. This is the whole design philosophy of the load average in one constant: never pay for accuracy that nobody can perceive.

/* kernel/sched/loadavg.c */
long calc_load_fold_active(struct rq *this_rq, long adjust)
{
    long nr_active, delta = 0;

    nr_active  = this_rq->nr_running - adjust;
    nr_active += (long)this_rq->nr_uninterruptible;

    if (nr_active != this_rq->calc_load_active) {
        delta = nr_active - this_rq->calc_load_active;
        this_rq->calc_load_active = nr_active;
    }

    return delta;
}

Each runqueue remembers the value it last reported in calc_load_active and adds only the difference to the global atomic. A CPU whose load has not changed since the previous sample performs no atomic operation at all — which on an idle or steady-state machine is the common case. This is the same delta-folding trick used throughout the kernel to keep a globally visible aggregate from becoming a per-CPU cache-line hotspot.

The (long) cast on nr_uninterruptible is not cosmetic, and the reason is one of the more surprising facts about this counter: a single CPU's nr_uninterruptible value is meaningless in isolation, and may legitimately be enormous or negative. Tracking it accurately per-CPU would require a cross-CPU cache-line miss and an atomic operation on the wakeup path — far too expensive for a statistic. So the kernel increments the counter on whichever CPU the task was running on when it went uninterruptible, and decrements on whichever CPU performed the wakeup. Those are frequently different CPUs. Only the sum across all CPUs is correct.

Linux 6.16 made this explicit by reverting nr_uninterruptible to unsigned long after an earlier change had narrowed it to unsigned int on the assumption that the value could never grow large. On a busy machine with heavy task migration it can, in fact, exceed INT_MAX on an individual CPU without anything being wrong — the matching decrements simply landed elsewhere. The wide unsigned type plus the signed cast at fold time is what makes the wrap-around arithmetic come out right when the deltas are summed.

Tickless CPUs need two separate accommodations, and the listing shows one at each end. A CPU that has stopped its tick is not running calc_global_load_tick(), so it cannot report its own delta. Instead it folds its contribution into a separate NOHZ accumulator on the way into idle, and calc_load_nohz_read() at the top of the function drains that accumulator into calc_load_tasks before the average is computed. Without this, load averages on a mostly-idle many-core machine would decay toward zero regardless of what the busy CPUs were doing.

The second problem is different and is handled by calc_global_nohz() at the bottom. Draining the accumulator fixes the value, but it does not fix the number of times the average should have decayed. If every CPU capable of running the sample went tickless for half a minute, calc_global_load() is not called at all during that period, and when it finally runs it would apply a single decay step for what should have been six. calc_global_nohz() detects this by checking how far jiffies has run past the window, computes n = 1 + (delta / LOAD_FREQ), and uses calc_load_n() to apply n decay steps in one go — raising the decay constant to the nth power rather than looping. Its own comment is terse about the purpose: “In case we went to NO_HZ for multiple LOAD_FREQ intervals catch up in bulk.”

It has a second job that is easy to miss because it is not conditional on anything. Outside that if, and after a smp_wmb(), it increments calc_load_idx. The NOHZ accumulator is a two-element array indexed by that counter, and flipping the index is what lets CPUs entering idle write to one slot while calc_load_nohz_read() drains the other, without a lock and without losing a delta that arrives during the drain. The barrier orders the new window time before the flip, so that a CPU reading the new index cannot pair it with the old time — the comment warns that otherwise “a double flip messing things up” becomes possible.

Two consequences of the five-second sampling period are worth noting, because they surprise people reading the numbers. A workload shorter than five seconds may not appear in the load average at all, and a load spike is visible for far longer than it lasted — the one-minute average needs roughly a minute of subsequent idleness to decay back down. The load average is a smoothed, coarse indicator, and it was never designed to be anything else.
