Table 6-165. Load Average Decay Constants
IntervalConstantTime constant τHalf-life (τ ln 2)EMA formula
1 minuteEXP_1 = 188460 s~42 sload = load × exp(-5s/60s) + active × (1 - exp(-5s/60s))
5 minutesEXP_5 = 2014300 s~3.5 minload = load × exp(-5s/300s) + active × (1 - exp(-5s/300s))
15 minutesEXP_15 = 2037900 s~10.4 minload = load × exp(-5s/900s) + active × (1 - exp(-5s/900s))

The distinction between the two middle columns matters when reading the numbers, and conflating them is a common error. The interval in the first column is the exponential time constant, not a half-life: the “one-minute” average is an exponential decay with τ = 60 s, which means that after a load spike ends the reported figure falls by half in about 42 seconds and is still showing roughly a third of the spike a minute later. Nothing about the one-minute average is confined to the last minute — it is a weighted average over all history, with the last minute contributing about 63% of the weight. The constants themselves are simply exp(-5/τ) in 11-bit fixed point: 1884/2048 = 0.9199 against exp(-5/60) = 0.9200.

Running Local Timers: run_local_timers()

This is the step that connects the tick to the timer wheel described earlier in the chapter. It is worth being precise about what it does and does not do: run_local_timers() never runs a timer callback. Running callbacks with interrupts disabled would let an arbitrary amount of driver code execute in hardirq context, so the tick only notices that timers are due and raises TIMER_SOFTIRQ; the actual expiry happens later in softirq context, where it can be preempted and where callbacks at least run with interrupts enabled. The check itself is a comparison against the next_expiry cache in the per-CPU timer_base, so on a tick with no due timers the cost is a single load and branch per base.

The same function also invokes hrtimer_run_queues(), which is the low-resolution fallback path for high-resolution timers — the route hrtimers take on a system that has no suitable one-shot clock event device, or before high-resolution mode has been enabled during boot. On a normal x86_64 or ARM64 system running in high-resolution mode this call returns almost immediately, because hrtimers are being driven by their own clock event interrupt rather than by the tick.

static void run_local_timers(void)
{
    struct timer_base *base = this_cpu_ptr(&timer_bases[BASE_LOCAL]);

    hrtimer_run_queues();  /* Low-res hrtimer check + mode switch probe */

    for (int i = 0; i < NR_BASES; i++, base++) {
        /* Only raise softirq if a timer has actually expired */
        if (time_after_eq(jiffies, READ_ONCE(base->next_expiry)) ||
            (i == BASE_DEF && tmigr_requires_handle_remote())) {
            raise_timer_softirq(TIMER_SOFTIRQ);
            return;
        }
    }
}

The check against base->next_expiry is more than an optimization; it is a deliberate, documented data race. next_expiry can be written by a remote CPU holding the base lock at the same instant this CPU reads it without one, and the kernel devotes a thirty-line comment to arguing that this is acceptable. It enumerates exactly two ways the remote write can happen and what each costs when the read misses it. If a remote CPU has just expired this CPU’s global timers and updated BASE_GLOBAL’s next_expiry, a stale read raises TIMER_SOFTIRQ once for nothing. If a remote CPU has enqueued a new first pinned timer and updated BASE_LOCAL, a stale read is covered by the IPI that the enqueue path sends anyway when this CPU was idle; if it was not idle, “then the timer would expire one jiffy late - bad luck”.

Both outcomes are bounded and neither is a correctness failure, which is what justifies the choice: the comment concludes that these cases are “not that expensive as doing the check always while holding the lock”. Taking a lock on every base on every tick, on every CPU, to eliminate a one-jiffy delay that can only occur when a remote CPU modifies a non-idle CPU’s timers in a specific window, would be a bad trade. The race is made explicit rather than merely tolerated: remote writers use WRITE_ONCE() and this reader uses READ_ONCE(), so the compiler cannot invent a second load and the sanity checkers know the access is intentional.

The TIMER_SOFTIRQ handler (run_timer_softirq()) performs the actual timer expiry work in softirq context, as described in the Timer Wheel section.

RCU Bookkeeping: rcu_sched_clock_irq()

The Read-Copy-Update (RCU) subsystem uses the tick interrupt to detect "quiescent states" — points where a CPU is guaranteed not to hold any RCU-protected references. Each tick that finds a CPU in user mode or idle constitutes a quiescent state. This information is used to determine when RCU grace periods have elapsed and when deferred memory can be safely freed.

Detecting quiescent states is only part of what the tick does for RCU, and the function is worth reading because each line is a different subsystem obligation:

/* kernel/rcu/tree.c */
void rcu_sched_clock_irq(int user)
{
    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();

    /* 1. Stall detection: prove this CPU is still taking ticks */
    raw_cpu_inc(rcu_data.ticks_this_gp);

    /* 2. Urgent request from a stalled grace period */
    if (smp_load_acquire(this_cpu_ptr(&rcu_data.rcu_urgent_qs))) {
        /* Idle and userspace execution already are quiescent states. */
        if (!rcu_is_cpu_rrupt_from_idle() && !user)
            set_need_resched_current();
        __this_cpu_write(rcu_data.rcu_urgent_qs, false);
    }

    /* 3. Flavour-specific quiescent state detection */
    rcu_flavor_sched_clock_irq(user);

    /* 4. Callbacks or grace-period work to do? Raise RCU_SOFTIRQ */
    if (rcu_pending(user))
        invoke_rcu_core();

    /* 5. RCU-tasks: a voluntary context switch equivalent */
    if (user || rcu_is_cpu_rrupt_from_idle())
        rcu_note_voluntary_context_switch(current);
}

The first line is not detection at all but evidence. ticks_this_gp is zeroed when a grace period starts and reported in the RCU CPU stall warning, so when RCU eventually complains that a CPU has not passed through a quiescent state it can also say whether that CPU was taking ticks at the time. A stalled CPU with a rising tick count is stuck in a long RCU read-side section or a preemption-disabled loop; one with a frozen count has stopped taking interrupts entirely. Those are different bugs, and the counter is what distinguishes them in the stall message.

Step 2 is the tick being used as a lever rather than a sensor. When a grace period has been waiting too long, RCU sets rcu_urgent_qs on the offending CPU; the next tick sees it and, if the CPU is not already quiescent, forces a reschedule — because for non-preemptible RCU a context switch is by definition a quiescent state. The nested test is the interesting part: if the tick arrived from idle or user mode the CPU is quiescent already, so the flag is simply cleared and no reschedule is forced.

Step 3 is where the two RCU flavours diverge, and which one a kernel gets is a build-time consequence of its preemption model rather than a choice anyone makes directly: PREEMPT_RCU is default y if (PREEMPT || PREEMPT_RT || PREEMPT_DYNAMIC). The two architectures this book follows land on opposite sides of that by default. x86_64 selects HAVE_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC_CALL, which makes PREEMPT_DYNAMIC — and therefore preemptible RCU — the default; ARM64 selects HAVE_PREEMPT_DYNAMIC_KEY instead, which offers the option without turning it on, so an ARM64 kernel built PREEMPT_NONE gets the non-preemptible flavour. For non-preemptible RCU the rule is the simple one stated above with one addition: a tick that interrupted kernel code holding no preempt count is also a quiescent state, since read-side sections in that flavour are delimited by preemption being disabled. For preemptible RCU the rule is weaker, because a task can be preempted in the middle of an rcu_read_lock() section and a tick in user mode proves nothing about it. rcu_flavor_sched_clock_irq() therefore checks rcu_preempt_depth() and the preempt and softirq counts, and where it cannot report a quiescent state it does the next best thing — it flags the deferred report so that the eventual rcu_read_unlock() reports it instead, and if the grace period is more than a second old it sets need_qs to ask rcu_read_unlock_special() for help.

Steps 4 and 5 are unrelated to quiescent states. rcu_pending() asks whether this CPU has callbacks ready to invoke or grace-period bookkeeping outstanding, and if so invoke_rcu_core() raises RCU_SOFTIRQ — the same deferral pattern the tick uses for the timer wheel, and for the same reason. rcu_note_voluntary_context_switch() serves RCU-tasks, a separate flavour whose grace periods end when every task has voluntarily blocked, and for which reaching user mode or idle counts as such an event.

On NO_HZ_IDLE CPUs, the act of entering idle itself is a quiescent state (reported by the NOHZ idle path). On NO_HZ_FULL CPUs, the context tracking mechanism (ct_kernel_exit()) reports quiescent states when returning to user space.

The Scheduler Tick: sched_tick()

Of everything the tick does, sched_tick() is the step with the most direct effect on what runs next. Preemption in Linux is not purely event-driven: a CPU-bound task that never blocks and never makes a system call would run forever if nothing interrupted it. The tick is that something. On every tick the scheduler is handed the current task and asked, in effect, “has this one had its turn?” — and if the answer is yes, it sets TIF_NEED_RESCHED so that the return path from the interrupt calls schedule() instead of resuming the interrupted task. This is why a CPU running a single busy task still cannot enter NOHZ mode and stop its tick: with more than one runnable task, the tick is the preemption mechanism.

The scheduler tick (detailed in Chapter 7) performs time-slice management, including:

  • Time-slice enforcement — update_deadline() checks whether the current entity's vruntime has reached its virtual deadline; if so it grants a fresh request by recomputing the deadline as vd_i = ve_i + r_i / w_i and calls resched_curr_lazy()
  • SCHED_RR time-slice counting — round-robin tasks decrement their time quantum; when it reaches zero, the task is moved to the end of its priority queue
  • SCHED_DEADLINE bandwidth — replenishment of deadline task budgets
  • Load balancing trigger — sched_balance_trigger() checks whether load balancing is needed across scheduling domains
  • Per-CPU load statistics — calc_global_load_tick() samples the runqueue task count for the load average calculation
  • NUMA balancing — periodic scanning for memory placement optimization

Two details in the first item date the description, and both are recent enough that older documentation describes something that no longer exists. There is no ideal_runtime any more: EEVDF replaced CFS’s proportional-share heuristic in Linux 6.6, and a task is now preempted when its virtual time reaches an explicit per-entity deadline rather than when it has run longer than a computed fair share. And the tick does not set TIF_NEED_RESCHED directly for a fair task; resched_curr_lazy() sets TIF_NEED_RESCHED_LAZY, which asks for a reschedule at the next convenient point rather than forcing one at the next preemption opportunity. That distinction is the subject of the lazy preemption work covered in Chapter 7; for the tick’s purposes what matters is that the mechanism is still the same — a flag set in interrupt context and acted on when the interrupt returns.

POSIX CPU Timers: run_posix_cpu_timers()

POSIX defines per-process and per-thread CPU time clocks (CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID, CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID). Unlike every other clock in this chapter, these do not advance with real time — they advance only while the task in question is on a CPU. That makes them impossible to arm a hardware timer against: there is no future instant at which the hardware could interrupt, because the clock's rate depends on scheduling decisions that have not been made yet. The only way to expire a CPU-time timer is to keep checking, and the tick is the natural place to check, because the tick is also where the CPU time was just charged.

The work falls into two halves that are worth separating carefully, because the tick performs only the first of them:

/* kernel/time/posix-cpu-timers.c */
void run_posix_cpu_timers(void)
{
    struct task_struct *tsk = current;

    lockdep_assert_irqs_disabled();

    /* Ensure that release_task(tsk) can't happen while
     * handle_posix_cpu_timers() is running. */
    if (tsk->exit_state)
        return;

    /* If expiry is deferred to task work and the work is already
     * scheduled, there is no point doing anything here. */
    if (posix_cpu_timers_work_scheduled(tsk))
        return;

    /* Fast path: are there any expired thread or thread-group timers? */
    if (!fastpath_timer_check(tsk))
        return;

    __run_posix_cpu_timers(tsk);
}

The first three checks are the entire cost on an overwhelming majority of ticks. Almost no process has a CPU-time timer armed, and the expensive path is not merely rare, it is designed to be rare, because it cannot be made cheap.

fastpath_timer_check() is doing more than the name suggests, and it is worth unpacking because it answers three separate questions without taking a lock for any of them. The first is per-thread: expiry_cache_is_inactive() tests whether this task has any CPU-time expiry armed at all, and on almost every tick the answer is no, so the sampling that would follow never happens. The second is per-thread-group, and it is guarded by a pair of READ_ONCE() reads of timers_active and expiry_active — the latter ensuring that only one thread in a group pursues expiry at a time. Those fields are deliberately read without sighand held, and the kernel spells out why that is acceptable: it is “meant to be a fastpath heuristic to determine whether we should try to acquire the sighand lock”, and if a thread misses a concurrent update, “the timer checks are delayed until the next thread in the group gets a scheduler interrupt”. A tick’s delay in delivering a CPU-time signal is not observable; a contended lock on every tick would be.

The third question has nothing to do with POSIX timers at all. fastpath_timer_check() also returns true for dl_task(tsk) && tsk->dl.dl_overrun, which is how a SCHED_DEADLINE task that has exceeded its declared runtime gets its SIGXCPU. Deadline bandwidth enforcement itself happens in the scheduler, but the signal rides out on this path, so the same task-work deferral described below applies to it.

Why the Tick Does Not Expire the Timer

Expiring a CPU-time timer means delivering a signal, and delivering a signal means taking sighand->siglock and walking the thread group. Both are problems in hardirq context. On a PREEMPT_RT kernel siglock is a sleeping lock and simply cannot be acquired with interrupts disabled; even on a normal kernel, holding it across a thread-group walk from inside the timer interrupt adds unbounded latency to a path every other subsystem depends on.

The kernel's answer is to split the operation across contexts. On architectures that select HAVE_POSIX_CPU_TIMERS_TASK_WORK — which includes both x86_64 and ARM64, so this is the normal path for the architectures this book follows — __run_posix_cpu_timers() does not expire anything:

/* kernel/time/posix-cpu-timers.c, CONFIG_POSIX_CPU_TIMERS_TASK_WORK */
static inline void __run_posix_cpu_timers(struct task_struct *tsk)
{
    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(tsk->posix_cputimers_work.scheduled))
        return;

    /* Schedule task work to actually expire the timers */
    tsk->posix_cputimers_work.scheduled = true;
    task_work_add(tsk, &tsk->posix_cputimers_work.work, TWA_RESUME);
}

task_work_add() queues a callback that the kernel runs on the way back out to user space, in task context, with interrupts enabled and preemption possible. The callback, posix_cpu_timers_work(), takes a per-task mutex and calls handle_posix_cpu_timers() — the function that actually collects expired timers and sends the signals. The delay this introduces is bounded and harmless: the task cannot reach user space to consume more CPU time without first running the work that decides whether it is allowed to.

What the deferral does create is a window, and Linux 6.13 was the release that finally decided what happens inside it. Between the tick queuing the work and the work running, the task can reach user space only via the exit path that runs the work — but another thread can call timer_settime() or timer_delete() on the same timer in the meantime. Should the signal that the tick set in motion still arrive? POSIX declines to answer, saying only that “the effect of disarming or resetting a timer with pending expiration notifications is unspecified” and that “the disposition of pending signals for the deleted timer is unspecified”. Linux now answers no. Every operation that invalidates a timer’s configuration increments it_signal_seq — do_timer_settime() does it with the comment “Prevent signal delivery and rearming”, and so does deletion — while the sequence value in force when the signal was queued is stashed in it_sigqueue_seq. Delivery then begins with a comparison:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c */
    /*
     * Check if the timer is still alive or whether it got modified
     * since the signal was queued. In either case, don't rearm and
     * drop the signal.
     */
    if (timr->it_signal_seq != timr->it_sigqueue_seq || WARN_ON_ONCE(!posixtimer_valid(timr)))
        return false;

Returning false discards the signal. The rule is worth stating plainly because it is the kind of thing that only becomes visible once expiry is deferred: a signal generated by a tick is not a promise, it is a proposal, and reprogramming or deleting the timer withdraws it. Interval timers get the same treatment for their overrun counts, which are reset rather than carried across a reprogramming.

The scheduled flag closes the obvious hole. Once work is queued, subsequent ticks see posix_cpu_timers_work_scheduled() return true and skip the fast-path check entirely, so a task that is slow to reach the exit path does not accumulate a queue of redundant callbacks. On PREEMPT_RT, where a tick can arrive while expired timers are being collected under siglock, re-enabling that fast path is done carefully by posix_cpu_timers_enable_work(), which re-runs the fast-path check if jiffies advanced during collection and forces another collection pass if new timers expired in the meantime.

Architectures without HAVE_POSIX_CPU_TIMERS_TASK_WORK fall back to calling handle_posix_cpu_timers() directly from the interrupt, bracketed by lockdep_posixtimer_enter()/_exit() so that lockdep knows to expect the unusual locking context. This was the behavior in Linux 2.6, and it remains the behavior on architectures that have not opted in — but it is no longer what happens on the machines most readers will be running.

The tsk->exit_state check at the top of the function is newer than the rest, added in Linux 6.16. Without it, a task could enter handle_posix_cpu_timers() and then be reaped by release_task() concurrently; a posix_cpu_timer_del() racing against that would fail to lock_task_sighand() and miss the fact that the timer was marked as firing, leaving the deletion to complete while expiry was still in progress.

Once expiry does run, the signals sent are the ones POSIX specifies: the user-chosen signal for a timer created with timer_create() on a CPU clock, SIGXCPU when the soft RLIMIT_CPU limit is crossed, and SIGKILL at the hard limit. Interval timers set with setitimer(ITIMER_VIRTUAL) and setitimer(ITIMER_PROF) ride the same machinery, which is why a process consuming CPU purely in kernel mode still receives SIGPROF but never SIGVTALRM.

Summary: The Tick Cascade

It is worth stepping back to see the whole cascade at once, because no single step below is expensive and the point is cumulative. Each item is a few tens to a few hundred nanoseconds; together they are the fixed price the system pays every 4ms, on every online CPU that is still ticking, whether or not anything needed doing. That total is the number that motivated the entire NOHZ effort described earlier in this chapter: not because a microsecond matters on one CPU, but because it is a microsecond multiplied by the core count, multiplied by 250 per second, forever.

The following table summarizes the complete sequence of work performed on each tick. Steps 1 through 6 are exactly the order in which update_process_times() issues them; step 0 happens earlier, in tick_sched_do_timer(), and step 7 after update_process_times() has returned. The figures in the last column are illustrative orders of magnitude for a modern x86_64 core rather than measurements — the real numbers depend on the microarchitecture, on cache state, on which of the optional accounting modes is compiled in, and above all on HZ. They are given only to show which steps dominate; anyone who needs the actual cost on a specific machine can obtain it from ftrace’s function profiler or from a perf record of the timer interrupt.

Table 6-166. Per-Tick Work Items
StepFunctionDutyOrder of magnitude
0tick_do_update_jiffies64()Advance jiffies, update_wall_time() (duty CPU only)~200ns (duty CPU); 0 (others)
1account_process_tick()Charge tick to user/system/idle/steal~50ns
2run_local_timers()Check timer wheel, possibly raise TIMER_SOFTIRQ~30ns (no expired); ~200ns (raise)
3rcu_sched_clock_irq()Report quiescent state, advance RCU callbacks~100ns
4irq_work_tick()Execute deferred IRQ work items (only when CONFIG_IRQ_WORK and in_hardirq())~20ns (none pending)
5sched_tick()Scheduler time-slice, load balance trigger~300ns
6run_posix_cpu_timers()Fast-path check of CPU-time limits and POSIX timers; queues task work on expiry (only when CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS)~50ns
7profile_tick()Statistical profiling sample (after update_process_times() returns)~10–30ns (NOP unless profiling enabled)
Total~750ns – 1µs per tick
The introduction to this section described the structural change from Linux 2.6 — the split between a global handler and a per-CPU one collapsing into a single per-CPU tick, and xtime under xtime_lock giving way to the timekeeper structure under a seqcount. Now that the pipeline has been walked end to end, four further differences can be stated more precisely than they could at the outset.

The two functions that survived by name did not survive by content. do_timer() in 2.6 was the whole of global tick processing; in 7.0.12 it is two statements, having handed the wall-clock work to update_wall_time() and thence to timekeeping_advance(), where NTP-aware sub-tick interpolation now lives. profile_tick() is still called, but it is the legacy sampler and it does nothing at all unless CONFIG_PROFILING is built in and profiling was armed on the kernel command line; perf events superseded it for every practical purpose.

Two of the section’s subjects did not exist in 2.6 in any form. Neither vtime accounting nor IRQ time accounting had an analogue, because both answer a question the 2.6 tick could not be asked: what happens when the tick is not running, and what happens when the sampled mode is a lie? They belong to the same lineage as NOHZ rather than to the lineage of the tick itself.

Finally, one piece of the pipeline exists purely to repair damage done by another. The NOHZ folding in calc_load_nohz_read() and the catch-up arithmetic in calc_global_nohz() have no counterpart in 2.6, because in 2.6 there was nothing to repair — every CPU ticked, so every CPU was sampled. The load average is the clearest case in this section of a mechanism whose complexity is entirely the price of a feature that lives somewhere else.

Software Timer Delay Functions

Kernel code frequently needs to wait for brief, precisely-bounded time intervals — typically while a hardware device completes an operation. For example, a device driver may need to wait 5 µs for a register write to take effect before reading back a status bit, or a USB controller may require a 10 ms reset settling time. These delays are too short or too timing-critical for the timer wheel (which has tick-granularity precision and scheduling overhead), so the kernel provides a family of specialized delay and sleep functions.

The fundamental distinction is between busy-wait delays (which spin the CPU, wasting cycles but guaranteeing the processor remains available) and sleeping delays (which yield the CPU to other tasks but require a schedulable context). The choice between them depends on whether the caller holds atomic context (spinlocks, interrupt handlers, preempt-disabled sections) and the required duration.

Two further points shape everything in this section. The first is that a delay function's contract is a lower bound, never an upper one: every function here guarantees only that at least the requested time has passed. How much more is the interesting question, and the answer differs by an order of magnitude between the mechanisms. The second is that the “correct” choice is not a matter of taste. Picking a busy-wait where a sleep would do burns a core; picking a sleep in atomic context is a bug that may not manifest until a rarely-taken path executes on a preemptible kernel.

Three forces have reshaped this small API since Linux 2.6, and they explain most of what follows:

  • Calibrated loops gave way to hardware counters. The classic delay loop measured the CPU by executing it, then counted iterations. Frequency scaling made that assumption false, and the answer on both architectures this book follows is to stop counting instructions and start reading a clock — the TSC on x86_64, the architected generic timer on ARM64. loops_per_jiffy survives as a name, but on both architectures it no longer counts loops.
  • Busy-waiting stopped meaning “burn the core”. A spin that keeps a pipeline full starves a hyperthread sibling and wastes power for no benefit. Every architecture now has instructions that let a core wait cheaply — PAUSE, TPAUSE and MWAITX on x86_64, WFE and the ARMv8.7 WFIT/WFET pair on ARM64 — and on the newest ARM64 hardware a udelay() does not spin at all.
  • Slack became something the caller declares rather than discovers. A driver that asks to sleep 100µs almost always means “at least 100µs, and I do not care much about the upper end”. Saying so explicitly lets the kernel coalesce the wakeup with an interrupt that was going to happen anyway. usleep_range() exists to make that statement, and fsleep() exists because most callers should not have to think about it at all.

The rest of this section answers six questions:

  1. How does a busy-wait delay actually measure time? udelay(), ndelay() and mdelay(), and the very different machinery underneath them on x86_64 and ARM64.
  2. What should process-context code use instead? usleep_range() on hrtimers, msleep() on the timer wheel, and why the split exists.
  3. Can the choice be automated? fsleep(), and the 25%-slack rule that sets its thresholds.
  4. Which one should I call? A comparison table covering duration, mechanism, context and precision.
  5. What underlies the sleeping variants? schedule_timeout(), still the foundation and still used directly.
  6. Where do the calibration constants come from? loops_per_jiffy, BogoMIPS, and why both are largely vestigial on modern hardware.

Version history. Linux 2.6 offered udelay(), ndelay(), mdelay() and schedule_timeout(), and that was the whole toolbox — a driver needing to wait 200µs in process context had no good option and typically busy-waited. The sleeping family (usleep_range(), msleep() and friends) filled that gap, and Linux 6.13 gathered all of it out of kernel/time/timer.c into a dedicated kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c. In the same cycle udelay() and ndelay() became real inline functions rather than macros, and fsleep()'s thresholds were reworked after it was noticed that the values inherited from the documentation could produce 100% slack rather than the 25% they promised.

Busy-Wait Delays: udelay(), ndelay(), mdelay()

The busy-wait delay functions spin the processor for a specified duration. They are the only valid delay mechanism in atomic context (interrupt handlers, spinlock-held code, preempt-disabled sections) because they never call the scheduler:

/* include/asm-generic/delay.h */
static __always_inline void udelay(unsigned long usec)
{
    if (__builtin_constant_p(usec)) {
        if (usec >= DELAY_CONST_MAX)  /* 20,000 µs safety limit */
            __bad_udelay();  /* Compile-time error if constant > 20ms */
        else
            __const_udelay(usec * UDELAY_CONST_MULT);
    } else {
        __udelay(usec);
    }
}

static __always_inline void ndelay(unsigned long nsec)
{
    if (__builtin_constant_p(nsec)) {
        if (nsec >= DELAY_CONST_MAX)
            __bad_ndelay();
        else
            __const_udelay(nsec * NDELAY_CONST_MULT);
    } else {
        __ndelay(nsec);
    }
}

/* mdelay: millisecond busy-wait (avoid — prefer msleep() in process context) */
#define mdelay(n) \
    ((__builtin_constant_p(n) && (n) <= MAX_UDELAY_MS) ? \
        udelay((n) * 1000) : \
        ({unsigned long __ms = (n); while (__ms--) udelay(1000);}))

The UDELAY_CONST_MULT and NDELAY_CONST_MULT constants convert microseconds/nanoseconds into "loop counts" using fixed-point arithmetic based on the CPU's loops_per_jiffy value, which is calibrated at boot time by calibrate_delay().

Two things about this pair of near-identical functions are worth more attention than their symmetry suggests, because both are places where the symmetry breaks.

The first is the constant limit. DELAY_CONST_MAX is 20,000 and it is compared against the raw argument in both functions, without regard to units — so the compile-time ceiling is 20,000µs for udelay() but 20,000ns, that is 20µs, for ndelay(). The header is candid about where the number came from: “The maximum constant udelay/ndelay value picked out of thin air to prevent too long constant udelays/ndelays.” Note also that __bad_udelay() and __bad_ndelay() are declared but never defined anywhere in the tree; that is the mechanism, not an oversight. Exceeding the limit with a constant argument produces a link error naming a function whose name is the diagnostic. A variable argument bypasses the check entirely, which is why the overflow warning about MAX_UDELAY_MS still matters.

The second is the odd-looking line that closes the header:

#define ndelay(x) ndelay(x)

A macro that expands to a call of the function it shadows looks like a no-op, and as a macro it very nearly is. Its purpose is to be visible to the preprocessor. include/linux/delay.h wraps its own fallback definition in #ifndef ndelay, and that fallback is worth knowing about:

/* include/linux/delay.h — used only if the architecture supplies no ndelay */
#ifndef ndelay
static inline void ndelay(unsigned long x)
{
    udelay(DIV_ROUND_UP(x, 1000));
}
#define ndelay(x) ndelay(x)
#endif

On an architecture with no nanosecond delay of its own, ndelay(100) rounds up to udelay(1) and waits ten times as long as asked. That is a defensible fallback — the contract is a lower bound, so waiting longer is legal — but a driver author reading ndelay() as a precise instrument would be badly misled. The self-referential #define is how an architecture (or the generic header) announces that it has provided a definition and the fallback must not be substituted, and every one of the dozen definitions in the tree ends with a #define of the bare name for that reason. The exact form varies — #define ndelay ndelay, #define ndelay(ns) __ndelay(ns), or the self-referential version above — because all the #ifndef needs is that the name be defined at all.

These two functions were only converted from macros to real inline functions in Linux 6.13, and the conversion is a cautionary tale about how alike they are. The rework (19e2d91d8cb1) transcribed udelay()’s body into ndelay() and left two calls unchanged, so every ndelay() on an architecture using the generic header dispatched to __udelay() and __bad_udelay() — multiplying every nanosecond delay by a thousand. The result was not a subtle timing regression but boot hangs, and it was fixed a few weeks later in the same release cycle by 4d17c25eaf5d, whose entire diff is those two identifiers.

Architecture-Specific Implementations

The actual spin mechanism is architecture-specific. On modern hardware, the kernel uses hardware timer counters rather than naive instruction loops for accurate delay measurement:

Table 6-167. Architecture-Specific Delay Mechanisms
ArchitectureMethodMechanismWhat Bounds the Overshoot
x86_64 (modern)delay_tsc()Spin reading TSC via rdtsc_ordered(); yields to RT tasks between readsThe deadline is only tested between native_pause() calls, so one PAUSE latency — tens of nanoseconds on recent parts
x86_64 (TPAUSE)delay_halt_tpause()Intel TPAUSE instruction enters C0.2 until TSC target; saves powerC0.2 exit latency, which the code judges “small compared to the ‘microseconds’ that usleep() will delay”
x86_64 (MWAITX)delay_halt_mwaitx()AMD MWAITX with timer; low-power spinWake latency, plus any early wake from a MONITORX store — hence the retry loop in delay_halt()
x86_64 (fallback)delay_loop()Tight dec/jnz assembly loop; aligned to avoid cache effectsOne loop iteration, whose duration is whatever loops_per_jiffy calibration decided it was
ARM64 (ARMv8.7+)__delay() / WFITWait-For-Interrupt-with-Timeout: the core stops executing until the CNTVCT_EL0 deadlineOne counter tick — 40 ns at the common 25 MHz architected timer
ARM64 (event stream)__delay() / WFESleeps until the architected timer event stream wakes the core; finishes on cpu_relax()The event stream fires only every 100 µs, which is why the loop exits a full period early and lets the cpu_relax() tail close the remaining gap to one counter tick
ARM64 (fallback)__delay()Reads CNTVCT_EL0 in a cpu_relax() loopOne counter tick — 40 ns at 25 MHz

The last column deserves a word, because it is easy to read a delay function’s resolution as its accuracy. Every mechanism in the table guarantees only a lower bound: the delay is at least as long as requested, never shorter. What the column names is therefore the granularity of the overshoot — how far past the deadline the call can return — and for the low-power variants that quantity is not the counter’s resolution at all but the latency of waking the core back up. This is why the kernel documentation reaches for “very, very short delays” rather than a number: the achievable accuracy depends on which of these seven rows the boot-time selection landed on, which the driver author cannot know.

On x86_64, the delay function is selected once at boot and stored in a function pointer (delay_fn). The TSC-based method is preferred because it provides nanosecond precision regardless of CPU frequency scaling. The implementation handles CPU migration by detecting changes in smp_processor_id() and rebalancing the cycle count:

/* arch/x86/lib/delay.c */
static void delay_tsc(u64 cycles)
{
    u64 bclock, now;
    int cpu;

    preempt_disable();
    cpu = smp_processor_id();
    bclock = rdtsc_ordered();
    for (;;) {
        now = rdtsc_ordered();
        if ((now - bclock) >= cycles)
            break;
        preempt_enable();
        native_pause();       /* Yield to hyperthreads, reduce power */
        preempt_disable();
        if (unlikely(cpu != smp_processor_id())) {
            /* Migrated — recalibrate from new CPU's TSC */
            cycles -= (now - bclock);
            cpu = smp_processor_id();
            bclock = rdtsc_ordered();
        }
    }
    preempt_enable();
}

The native_pause() instruction (x86 PAUSE) between TSC reads reduces power consumption and avoids starving hyper-thread siblings. On systems with Intel TPAUSE support, the kernel can enter a light C-state (C0.2) while waiting, further reducing power without sacrificing wakeup latency.

Note what delay_tsc() does about preemption, because it is the opposite of what one might expect from a function that must not be preempted. It does not hold preemption off for the duration of the delay; it drops it around every native_pause() and takes it again, precisely so that a higher-priority task can run during a long udelay(). The price is that the task may come back on a different CPU whose TSC is not the one it started measuring against, which is why the loop re-reads smp_processor_id() and, on a mismatch, subtracts the cycles already served and restarts from the new CPU’s counter. The delay is preserved in duration, not in the identity of the clock that measured it.

The two halting variants share a single driver function, and its structure is worth seeing because it is the same one ARM64 arrives at from a completely different direction:

/* arch/x86/lib/delay.c */
static void delay_halt(u64 __cycles)
{
    u64 start, end, cycles = __cycles;

    /*
     * Timer value of 0 causes MWAITX to wait indefinitely, unless there
     * is a store on the memory monitored by MONITORX.
     */
    if (!cycles)
        return;

    start = rdtsc_ordered();

    for (;;) {
        delay_halt_fn(start, cycles);   /* TPAUSE or MWAITX */
        end = rdtsc_ordered();

        if (cycles <= end - start)
            break;

        cycles -= end - start;          /* Woken early: wait out the rest */
        start = end;
    }
}

Both TPAUSE and MWAITX can return before their deadline — the Intel comment lists three exit conditions, of which “an external interrupt occurs” is the common one, and the global timeout in IA32_UMWAIT_CONTROL can cut the wait short as a matter of policy. So the halt is issued in a loop, with the remaining cycle count recomputed each time. The zero-cycle guard at the top is not an optimization: it is there because “timer value of 0 causes MWAITX to wait indefinitely”, so a delay of zero would become a delay of forever. The C0.2 state is chosen deliberately over the lighter C0.1, and the code says why — “exit latency is small compared to the ‘microseconds’ that usleep() will delay”.

Which of the four implementations a machine uses is decided once, at boot, and never revisited: delay_fn and delay_halt_fn are both __ro_after_init function pointers, so the dispatch costs an indirect call and the pointers themselves are write-protected once initialization finishes. The default is delay_loop, the naive instruction loop, which is replaced by delay_tsc once the TSC is known good and then by delay_halt if the CPU advertises TPAUSE or MWAITX.

ARM64: A Busy-Wait That Does Not Spin

ARM64 takes the same idea considerably further, and the result is worth reading closely because it undermines the term “busy-wait” entirely. __delay() has three tiers, chosen by what the hardware supports:

/* arch/arm64/lib/delay.c */
void __delay(unsigned long cycles)
{
    cycles_t start = __delay_cycles();

    if (alternative_has_cap_unlikely(ARM64_HAS_WFXT)) {
        u64 end = start + cycles;

        /* Start with WFIT. If an interrupt makes us resume
         * early, use a WFET loop to complete the delay. */
        wfit(end);
        while ((__delay_cycles() - start) < cycles)
            wfet(end);
    } else if (arch_timer_evtstrm_available()) {
        const cycles_t timer_evt_period =
            USECS_TO_CYCLES(ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US);

        while ((__delay_cycles() - start + timer_evt_period) < cycles)
            wfe();
    }

    while ((__delay_cycles() - start) < cycles)
        cpu_relax();
}

The first tier uses WFIT and WFET — Wait For Interrupt / Event with Timeout, added by the ARMv8.7 FEAT_WFxT extension and detected as the ARM64_HAS_WFXT capability. These instructions take an absolute counter deadline and stop the core until either the deadline passes or an interrupt arrives. On such hardware a udelay(500) issues one instruction and the core executes nothing at all for 500µs. This is a busy-wait in name and in contract — it is still not safe to call from a context where sleeping is required, because the CPU is not available to the scheduler — but it consumes almost no power and does not compete for shared pipeline resources. The WFET loop after the initial WFIT exists because an unrelated interrupt will wake the core early; the delay's guarantee is a lower bound, so the code simply waits again.

The second tier covers hardware without FEAT_WFxT but with the architected timer's event stream enabled. The event stream makes the generic timer emit an event at a fixed period (ARCH_TIMER_EVT_STREAM_PERIOD_US), which is enough to wake a core parked in WFE. The delay therefore sleeps in event-period-sized steps, stopping one period short of the deadline so that it never overshoots, and finishes with the third tier.

The third tier is the classic loop: read the counter, cpu_relax(), repeat. It runs unconditionally at the end of the function, which is what makes the first two tiers safe to be approximate — neither has to land exactly on the deadline, only to avoid passing it.

Two subtleties in the counter read are new in Linux 7.0. __delay_cycles() deliberately forces CNTVCT_EL0, the virtual counter, rather than accepting whichever counter the generic accessor would pick. WFIT and WFET interpret their deadline argument against the virtual counter, so the value used to compute the deadline must come from the same base; on a KVM host running at EL1, CNTVOFF_EL2 is not necessarily zero until the first vcpu_put(), and mixing the two counters would produce a deadline in the distant past or future. It also wraps the read in guard(preempt_notrace)(), because __arch_counter_get_cntvct_stable() consults a per-CPU variable to decide which erratum workaround applies and must not be preempted mid-read.

Sleeping Delays: usleep_range() and msleep()

When code runs in process context (not holding spinlocks, not in interrupt handlers), sleeping delays are strongly preferred over busy-waits because they free the CPU for other work. Two sleeping functions serve different precision/duration ranges:

usleep_range(min, max) — High-Resolution Sleep

This function uses an hrtimer to provide microsecond-precision sleeping. The caller specifies both a minimum and maximum sleep duration, giving the kernel freedom to coalesce the wakeup with other pending interrupts (reducing power consumption):

/* kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c */
void __sched usleep_range_state(unsigned long min, unsigned long max,
                                unsigned int state)
{
    ktime_t exp = ktime_add_us(ktime_get(), min);
    u64 delta = (u64)(max - min) * NSEC_PER_USEC;

    if (WARN_ON_ONCE(max < min))
        delta = 0;

    for (;;) {
        __set_current_state(state);
        /* Do not return before the requested sleep time has elapsed */
        if (!schedule_hrtimeout_range(&exp, delta, HRTIMER_MODE_ABS))
            break;
    }
}

The WARN_ON_ONCE(max < min) guard is newer than the rest of the function and catches a real class of caller bug: the two arguments are easy to transpose, and before the check was added a reversed pair produced a negative difference that was cast to u64, yielding a slack of several thousand years. The sleep still returned after min microseconds, so the mistake was invisible in testing and merely destroyed any chance of a well-timed wakeup. The guard forces the slack to zero and complains.

The delta parameter tells the hrtimer subsystem the acceptable "slack" — the timer may fire anywhere between min and max microseconds. This enables timer coalescing: if another interrupt is already scheduled within the range, the kernel piggybacks the wakeup on that interrupt rather than programming a new one. Typical usage:

/* Driver example: wait 100-150 µs for hardware reset */
usleep_range(100, 150);

/* Sleeps in TASK_IDLE, so it does not inflate the load average */
usleep_range_idle(500, 600);

The for (;;) loop deserves a word, because at first reading it looks like it could sleep for longer than requested. It cannot, and the reason is the line above it: exp is an absolute deadline computed once, before the loop, and passed with HRTIMER_MODE_ABS. schedule_hrtimeout_range() returns non-zero when the task was woken before that deadline — by an explicit wake_up_process(), or by a signal if the caller chose an interruptible state — and the loop simply waits again on the same deadline rather than recomputing one. Retrying is therefore idempotent, and the comment states the contract being upheld: “Do not return before the requested sleep time has elapsed”. This is the third appearance of the same shape in this section, and it is not a coincidence: ARM64’s __delay() re-issues wfet() against a fixed cycle count, and x86’s delay_halt() re-enters TPAUSE or MWAITX with the remaining cycles. Every mechanism in this section can be woken early, so every one of them is written as a loop around an absolute target.

The choice of state is the whole difference between the three wrappers, and it is not merely cosmetic. usleep_range() sleeps in TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE, which means — as the load average discussion later in this chapter explains — that the sleeping task is counted by calc_load_fold_active() and shows up in the number uptime prints. A driver that polls hardware with a usleep_range() loop therefore raises the system’s reported load for as long as it polls, even though it is consuming no CPU at all. usleep_range_idle() exists for exactly that case: the kerneldoc says it uses TASK_IDLE “to prevent contribution to the load average”. It is easy to mistake this for a question of how the sleeping task’s own time is accounted; it is not. The task consumes no time either way. What changes is the number the whole machine reports.

msleep() — Millisecond Sleep

For delays of 1ms or longer where precision is less critical, msleep() uses the timer wheel (jiffy-based timeout) rather than an hrtimer. This has lower overhead but coarser granularity (up to one extra tick of delay):

/* kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c */
void msleep(unsigned int msecs)
{
    unsigned long timeout = msecs_to_jiffies(msecs);

    while (timeout)
        timeout = schedule_timeout_uninterruptible(timeout);
}

/* Signal-aware variant — returns remaining time on signal delivery */
unsigned long msleep_interruptible(unsigned int msecs)
{
    unsigned long timeout = msecs_to_jiffies(msecs);

    while (timeout && !signal_pending(current))
        timeout = schedule_timeout_interruptible(timeout);
    return jiffies_to_msecs(timeout);
}

The schedule_timeout_uninterruptible() function creates a timer wheel timer that calls process_timeout() — which simply calls wake_up_process() on the sleeping task — and then invokes the scheduler. The while (timeout) loop handles spurious early returns, ensuring the full sleep duration is honored.

The slack of msleep() is worth stating precisely, because the commonly quoted figure is only half the story. The timer wheel's 12.5% bound applies to timers that land in level 1 or above. A short sleep lands in level 0, where the granularity is one tick and the slack is therefore a function of both the requested duration and HZ:

slack = MSECS_PER_TICK / msecs        (never less than 12.5%)

At HZ=250 one tick is 4ms, so msleep(10) has a potential slack of 4/10 = 40% — it may return anywhere up to roughly 14ms, not the 11.25ms that the 12.5% figure would suggest. Turning the formula around gives the useful rule: to keep msleep() within 25% slack you need MSECS_PER_TICK / 0.25 milliseconds, which is 16ms at HZ=250 and 4ms at HZ=1000. Below that threshold, usleep_range() is the function you actually want. This is the calculation that sets fsleep()'s thresholds, described next.

The Unified Interface: fsleep()

Choosing between udelay(), usleep_range(), and msleep() requires understanding the duration, context, and precision requirements. The fsleep() (flexible sleep) function automates this decision for non-atomic contexts:

/* include/linux/delay.h */
static inline void fsleep(unsigned long usecs)
{
    if (usecs <= 10)
        udelay(usecs);          /* Too short for scheduler overhead */
    else if (usecs < USLEEP_RANGE_UPPER_BOUND)  /* 4 ticks: 16ms at HZ=250 */
        usleep_range(usecs, usecs + (usecs >> max_slack_shift));
    else
        msleep(DIV_ROUND_UP(usecs, USEC_PER_MSEC));
}

Every threshold here exists to hold the total slack at or below 25%. For delays of 10µs or less, the cost of arming an hrtimer and entering the scheduler exceeds the delay itself, so a busy-wait is the honest choice. For intermediate delays, usleep_range() supplies precision, and the >> max_slack_shift shift (a right shift by 2) requests exactly a quarter of the duration as slack. Above the crossover, msleep() is preferred because the timer wheel costs less per timer than an hrtimer and the requested duration is by then long enough that a tick of granularity is within budget.

The crossover point is the interesting part, and it is not a constant:

/* include/linux/delay.h */
static const unsigned int max_slack_shift = 2;
#define USLEEP_RANGE_UPPER_BOUND  ((TICK_NSEC << max_slack_shift) / NSEC_PER_USEC)

The bound is four ticks — precisely the duration at which msleep()'s level-0 slack of one tick first falls to 25%. Because it is expressed in ticks it scales with the kernel's HZ: 16ms at HZ=250, 4ms at HZ=1000, 40ms at HZ=100. Quoting a fixed millisecond figure for fsleep()'s crossover is therefore wrong on three-quarters of configurations.

This HZ-awareness is the whole point of the Linux 6.13 rework. The original fsleep() simply encoded the thresholds recommended by Documentation/timers/timers-howto.rst — udelay() below 10µs, usleep_range() to 20ms, msleep() beyond — and those fixed numbers ignored two effects. A 20ms sleep on a HZ=100 system lands in a wheel level whose buckets are 10ms wide, giving 50% slack; and usleep_range() is entitled to sleep all the way to its max, so a range spanning the full requested duration permits 100% overshoot. A function whose entire purpose is to relieve the caller of thinking about slack was quietly delivering four times what it promised. Deriving the thresholds from TICK_NSEC and requesting a quarter-duration range fixed both.

One caveat survives the rework, and the kerneldoc states it rather than hiding it: the 25% figure is a property of the hrtimer path, so it evaporates when there is no hrtimer path. “When %CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS is not set, all sleeps are processed with the granularity of jiffies and the slack might exceed 25% especially for short sleep durations.” On such a kernel the middle branch still calls usleep_range(), but the hrtimer underneath it is being expired from the tick, so a request for 50µs cannot resolve any finer than one jiffy — 4ms at HZ=250, eighty times the requested duration. Neither architecture in this book would normally be built that way, but embedded configurations do turn HIGH_RES_TIMERS off, and code that treats fsleep()’s bound as a guarantee rather than a normal-case expectation will be surprised there.

Function Selection Guide

The table below collects the whole family. Two columns deserve more weight than the rest when choosing. Context is not a recommendation but a correctness requirement: anything marked “Process only” calls the scheduler, and calling it while holding a spinlock, inside an interrupt handler, or with preemption disabled is a bug that may sleep in atomic context. Precision is the resolution of the underlying mechanism, not a bound on how late the call can return — a ~1 tick entry means the wakeup is quantized to ticks, and the actual overshoot depends on the duration and HZ as described above. The final column matters more often than its width suggests: fsleep() has no interruptible form at all, so a driver that needs a long wait to remain killable cannot delegate the choice to it and must reach for msleep_interruptible() or usleep_range_state() directly.

A table invites the reader to pick the row that fits, which is not quite the advice the kernel gives. Documentation/timers/delay_sleep_functions.rst — the successor to the timers-howto.rst that the original fsleep() thresholds came from — states a preference order instead, and it is worth internalizing because it runs against the instinct that a more precise mechanism is a better one:

  1. Use fsleep() whenever unsure, “as it combines all the advantages of the others”.
  2. Use the *sleep() family “whenever possible”.
  3. Use usleep_range*() only “whenever accuracy of *sleep() is not sufficient”.
  4. Use *delay() “for very, very short delays”.

The reason msleep() outranks usleep_range() rather than the other way round is cost, and the document is specific about where the cost lies: hrtimers “are more expensive as they are using an rb-tree (instead of hashing)”, and more expensive again “when the requested sleeping duration is the first timer which means real hardware has to be programmed”. Both points connect directly to material earlier in this chapter. The first is the structural difference between the timer wheel’s array of buckets and the hrtimer red-black tree; the second is hrtimer_reprogram() writing a new deadline to the clock event device, which on some hardware is a slow bus access. A driver that sleeps a millisecond with usleep_range() because it looks more modern is paying a tree insertion and possibly a hardware write to obtain precision the caller does not need.

The document is equally direct about the busy-wait family on long intervals, where its entry is not a caveat but an instruction: Do not use! A udelay() long enough to matter is a core removed from the scheduler for the duration, and the section’s ARM64 discussion notwithstanding — where the core genuinely stops executing — it is still a core the scheduler cannot have.

Table 6-168. Delay and Sleep Function Comparison
