Waiting for Hardware Rather Than for Time

Every function in this section answers the question “how do I wait for N microseconds?” Drivers rarely want to know that. What a driver usually wants is “wait until this status bit clears, but give up after 50 ms,” and a driver author who reaches for the delay family to build that loop by hand will get the sleep interval, the timeout arithmetic, or both slightly wrong. The kernel provides the loop already written, in include/linux/iopoll.h, and it is worth knowing about here because it is built directly on usleep_range() and demonstrates the advice of the preceding sections applied properly.

/* include/linux/iopoll.h -- condensed */
#define poll_timeout_us(op, cond, sleep_us, timeout_us, sleep_before_op)  \
({                                                                        \
    u64 __timeout_us = (timeout_us);                                      \
    unsigned long __sleep_us = (sleep_us);                                \
    ktime_t __timeout = ktime_add_us(ktime_get(), __timeout_us);          \
    int ___ret;                                                           \
    might_sleep_if((__sleep_us) != 0);                                    \
    if ((sleep_before_op) && __sleep_us)                                  \
        usleep_range((__sleep_us >> 2) + 1, __sleep_us);                  \
    for (;;) {                                                            \
        bool __expired = __timeout_us &&                                  \
            ktime_compare(ktime_get(), __timeout) > 0;                    \
        /* guarantee 'op' and 'cond' are evaluated after timeout expired */ \
        barrier();                                                        \
        op;                                                               \
        if (cond) { ___ret = 0; break; }                                  \
        if (__expired) { ___ret = -ETIMEDOUT; break; }                    \
        if (__sleep_us)                                                   \
            usleep_range((__sleep_us >> 2) + 1, __sleep_us);              \
        cpu_relax();                                                      \
    }                                                                     \
    ___ret;                                                               \
})

Three details repay attention. First, the sleep interval is not the caller’s sleep_us but the range [(sleep_us >> 2) + 1, sleep_us] — a window three-quarters as wide as the maximum the caller has authorized. This is the “always provide a range” rule from the pitfalls list, applied automatically and far more generously than the 10–25% a hand-written call typically offers, because the macro knows that sleep_us is a polling interval and not a deadline.

Second, the ordering inside the loop is deliberate and was rearranged in Linux 6.18. The timeout is evaluated before the operation, but acted on after it, so a device that becomes ready in the same instant the timeout expires is reported as success rather than as -ETIMEDOUT. The barrier() exists to keep the compiler from reordering the clock read past the operation, which the commit that added it describes as preventing “false positive timeouts”.

Third, there are two families, and the split is exactly the one this section has been drawing all along. poll_timeout_us() and the read_poll_timeout()/readl_poll_timeout() wrappers above it sleep, and their kerneldoc says so with a qualifier worth reading: they “must not be called from atomic context if sleep_us or timeout_us are used”. Passing zero for both turns the macro into a pure tight loop with no timeout, which is legal anywhere — and is also a loop with no way out, so the qualifier is a narrower licence than it first appears. The _atomic variants busy-wait with udelay() instead, and because they cannot afford a ktime_get() on every iteration they track the remaining time by subtracting the delay they just performed. That substitution costs accuracy — the time spent in op itself goes uncounted — which is a reasonable trade in a context where the alternative is not sleeping at all.

The poll_timeout_us() spelling is new in Linux 6.18, which generalized the older read_poll_timeout() so that the polled operation need not produce a value. The older names remain and are still the ones most drivers use.

schedule_timeout(): The Foundation

Everything in the sleeping half of this section eventually reaches schedule_timeout(), and it is worth seeing once because the pattern it establishes — set the task state, arm a timer that will wake you, call schedule(), then clean up — recurs throughout the kernel wherever a wait needs a deadline.

msleep() is a thin loop around it, but schedule_timeout() remains widely used directly, because the wrappers all answer the same narrow question (“wait this long”) while the general form answers a more useful one: wait for either a condition or a deadline, whichever comes first. That is the shape of nearly every driver timeout, and it is why the return value matters — it is how the caller distinguishes “my event happened” from “I gave up”:

/* kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c */
struct process_timer {
    struct timer_list timer;
    struct task_struct *task;
};

static void process_timeout(struct timer_list *t)
{
    struct process_timer *timeout = timer_container_of(timeout, t, timer);
    wake_up_process(timeout->task);
}

signed long __sched schedule_timeout(signed long timeout)
{
    struct process_timer timer;
    unsigned long expire;

    switch (timeout) {
    case MAX_SCHEDULE_TIMEOUT:
        schedule();  /* Sleep forever (until explicit wake) */
        goto out;
    default:
        if (timeout < 0) {
            pr_err("%s: wrong timeout value %lx\n", __func__, timeout);
            dump_stack();
            __set_current_state(TASK_RUNNING);
            goto out;
        }
    }

    expire = timeout + jiffies;
    timer.task = current;
    timer_setup_on_stack(&timer.timer, process_timeout, 0);
    timer.timer.expires = expire;
    add_timer(&timer.timer);

    schedule();  /* Sleep — will be woken by timer or explicit wakeup */

    timer_delete_sync(&timer.timer);
    timer_destroy_on_stack(&timer.timer);  /* Remove from object tracker */

    timeout = expire - jiffies;

 out:
    return timeout < 0 ? 0 : timeout;  /* Remaining time, or 0 if expired */
}

The timer is allocated on the kernel stack (marked with timer_setup_on_stack() for debug checking). When the timer fires, process_timeout() wakes the sleeping task. The return value indicates how much time remained — zero means the full timeout elapsed, while a positive value indicates early wakeup (by signal or explicit wake_up_process()).

The single most important thing about this function is not in its body at all. schedule_timeout() never sets the task state; it inherits whatever the caller set, and its entire behaviour follows from that choice. The kerneldoc enumerates the three cases, and the first is the trap:

  • TASK_RUNNING — “the scheduler is called, but the task does not sleep at all”. The timer is still armed and torn down, schedule() is still entered, and the function still returns a plausible-looking remaining time. It simply does not wait. A caller that forgets to set a state before calling gets a busy loop with a timer allocation in it, and nothing in the return value distinguishes that from a legitimate early wakeup.
  • TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE — at least the requested jiffies pass unless someone calls wake_up_process() explicitly. This is what msleep() uses, and it is why a task sleeping in msleep() contributes to the load average.
  • TASK_INTERRUPTIBLE — the sleep may end early on signal delivery. This is the variant a driver wants when the wait is on behalf of a system call that should remain killable.

Two guarantees fall out of the code that are worth naming because callers rely on them. The first is stated by the kerneldoc: “The current task state is guaranteed to be %TASK_RUNNING when this routine returns.” That holds ordinarily because schedule() restores it, and on the error path because the function does it by hand. That __set_current_state(TASK_RUNNING) in the negative-timeout arm is easy to read as defensive noise, but without it a caller that passed a bad value would return with the task still marked TASK_UNINTERRUPTIBLE and then run on until something else happened to change the state. The second is that the return value is never negative, which is why the out: label is shared by all three exits rather than each returning its own value.

The negative case is a diagnostic rather than a defence. A negative timeout is nonsense, and the code says so in its own comment — the pr_err() and dump_stack() exist because “no piece of kernel is supposed to do a check for a negative retval”, so rather than propagating a value nobody tests, the function prints the stack of whoever computed it. This is a common shape in timeout code: the usual cause is arithmetic on a deadline that has already passed, and the backtrace names the subtraction.

The three named wrappers exist to make the state explicit and are what most call sites should use: schedule_timeout_interruptible(), schedule_timeout_uninterruptible(), and schedule_timeout_idle(), which sleeps in TASK_IDLE and therefore stays out of the load average. Each is a two-line function that sets the state and calls schedule_timeout().

Calibration: loops_per_jiffy and BogoMIPS

Every conversion in this section, on every architecture, funnels through a single global: loops_per_jiffy. Its name and its original meaning belong to an era that has largely passed, and understanding the gap between the two explains a number in the boot log that still confuses people.

The classic scheme is a measurement by execution. At boot, calibrate_delay() runs a tight loop, watches jiffies advance, and binary-searches for the iteration count that fills exactly one tick — that count is loops_per_jiffy, and __const_udelay() later scales it to convert a duration into iterations. The scheme has an obvious flaw on any CPU whose clock rate can change after boot, which is every CPU this book is concerned with.

So on both x86_64 and ARM64 the loop is not run at all. Each architecture sets the global lpj_fine from a known hardware frequency — the TSC frequency on x86_64, arch_timer_rate on ARM64, where lpj_fine = arch_timer_rate / HZ — and calibrate_delay() takes the shortcut, printing Calibrating delay loop (skipped), value calculated using timer frequency... The value it stores is counter ticks per jiffy, and the delay routines that consume it read the corresponding counter rather than counting anything. loops_per_jiffy has become a unit conversion factor that no longer refers to loops.

Running the loop is in fact only one of six possibilities. calibrate_delay() is a ladder of increasingly expensive answers, and it takes the first that applies: a value already calibrated for this CPU, held in the per-CPU cpu_loops_per_jiffy; a value forced on the command line; lpj_fine; an architecture hook, calibrate_delay_is_known(); a measurement against a registered delay timer, calibrate_delay_direct(); and only then calibrate_delay_converge(), the binary search described above. Each rung prints a different message, which is why the boot log tells you which one you got.

The second rung is the useful one to know about. Passing lpj=value on the kernel command line sets preset_lpj and skips calibration entirely — historically a boot-time optimization on machines where the converging search cost a noticeable fraction of a second, and still occasionally used to make boot timing reproducible. Because it sits above lpj_fine in the ladder, it overrides the hardware-derived value rather than merely substituting for a measurement, so a wrong value here silently mis-scales every busy-wait delay on the system.

One qualification on calling loops_per_jiffy a single global: it is the variable the generic code exports, but it is not always the one consulted. x86’s __const_udelay() reads this_cpu_read(cpu_info.loops_per_jiffy) and falls back to the global only when the per-CPU value is zero, because on a system whose cores calibrate to different values a single number would be wrong for all but one of them. The global is the default, not the authority.

The number still surfaces as BogoMIPS (“bogus MIPS”) in the boot log, which is where the confusion arises. It was never a performance benchmark — the name was chosen to say so — and today it is not even a measurement, merely the timer frequency divided by a constant. Two machines with identical BogoMIPS values may differ by a factor of several in real throughput.

The arithmetic is worth doing once, because it explains a number that surprises people who look at ARM64 boot logs. calibrate_delay() prints lpj / (500000 / HZ) as the integer part. On ARM64 lpj is arch_timer_rate / HZ, so the HZ terms cancel and the whole expression collapses to arch_timer_rate / 500000 — the generic timer frequency, and nothing else. The architected timer very commonly runs at 25 MHz, which is why an enormous range of ARM64 machines, from development boards to server-class parts, all report exactly 50.00 BogoMIPS. The value is not merely a poor benchmark; on that hardware it is not a property of the CPU at all.

Common Pitfalls and Best Practices

  • Never use mdelay() in process context — it wastes CPU for milliseconds. Use msleep() or fsleep() instead. The only valid use of mdelay() is in early boot (before the scheduler is running) or in interrupt context where you truly need a multi-millisecond hardware wait.
  • Always provide a range for usleep_range() — a zero-width range (usleep_range(100, 100)) defeats timer coalescing. Use at least 10-25% slack: usleep_range(100, 120).
  • Use fsleep() when in doubt — it encapsulates the selection logic and normally holds the slack to 25% or less — but only on a kernel built with CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS, as described above. It has no interruptible form, so a long wait that must stay killable has to be spelled out with msleep_interruptible() rather than delegated.
  • udelay() may return slightly early on some platforms due to: computed loops_per_jiffy being slightly too low (timer IRQ overhead during calibration), cache effects on loop timing, or CPU frequency changes between calibration and use.
  • Avoid large udelay() values — a constant argument at or above DELAY_CONST_MAX (20,000) fails to link, because the compiler resolves the __builtin_constant_p() branch and leaves a call to the deliberately undefined __bad_udelay(). Note that the constant is compared against the raw argument, so the effective ceiling is 20,000 µs for udelay() but 20,000 ns — 20 µs — for ndelay(). The check does not apply to variable arguments at all, and there values above MAX_UDELAY_MS (5 ms) risk arithmetic overflow in the loop-count conversion; use mdelay() instead.
  • Do not transpose the arguments to usleep_range() — passing max first produces an enormous slack rather than an error. Since Linux 6.13 this triggers a WARN_ON_ONCE(), but on older kernels it is silent.
The arrival of the sleeping family, and the 6.13 consolidation that gathered it into kernel/time/sleep_timeout.c, were described at the start of this section. Three deeper changes are easier to state now that the mechanisms have been read.

The busy-wait no longer busy-waits, and on ARM64 it may not execute at all. Linux 2.6 chose between the TSC and a tight instruction loop through a runtime vtable, cur_timer->delay(); 7.0.12 chooses once at boot into an __ro_after_init pointer, and the set of things it can choose has grown to include instructions whose purpose is to make the core stop doing work — TPAUSE, MWAITX, WFE and, since ARMv8.7, WFIT and WFET. The term “busy-wait” now names a contract — this call will not schedule, so it is safe in atomic context — rather than a description of what the hardware does.

The calibration that gives the section its constants has been hollowed out. loops_per_jiffy is still computed, still consumed by every conversion, and still printed as BogoMIPS, but on both of this book’s architectures it is derived from a counter frequency rather than measured, and the code that consumes it reads a counter rather than counting iterations. Every name in that pipeline now refers to something it no longer does.

Finally, the interface has acquired opinions. Linux 2.6 offered mechanisms; 7.0.12 offers a recommendation order, an auto-selecting front end in fsleep() whose thresholds are derived from TICK_NSEC rather than fixed, and a documentation file — Documentation/timers/delay_sleep_functions.rst, successor to timers-howto.rst — whose comparison table opens not with precision but with the row “Usage in atomic Context”. The 6.13 rework of fsleep()’s thresholds, and the WARN_ON_ONCE() added to usleep_range_state() in the same cycle, are both instances of the same shift: the API is being changed to make the common mistake impossible rather than documented.

The vDSO: Accelerating Time System Calls

The vDSO (virtual Dynamic Shared Object) is one of the most significant performance optimizations in the Linux timing subsystem. It is a small, kernel-provided shared library that the kernel maps into every process's virtual address space at load time, enabling time-related system calls to execute entirely in user space — without the overhead of a kernel trap, context switch, or privilege level transition.

On modern systems, clock_gettime() is one of the most frequently invoked system calls. High-frequency trading applications may call it millions of times per second; databases use it for transaction timestamps; and even simple programs call it indirectly through gettimeofday(), logging frameworks, and standard library time functions. The vDSO removes the kernel entry entirely, taking clock_gettime() from the hundreds of nanoseconds a system call costs to the tens of nanoseconds a counter read costs — an order of magnitude, which for latency-sensitive workloads is the difference between a measurement and an interference.

The vDSO is best understood as an answer to a question the rest of this chapter has been building toward. Everything so far has been about the kernel knowing the time. But almost nobody who wants the time is the kernel — the overwhelming majority of time queries come from user space, and for those, the expensive part is not reading the clock at all. It is the privilege transition needed to ask.

That observation shapes the entire design, and four constraints follow from it:

  • The data must be readable without a privilege change. Which means it lives on a page the kernel writes and user space maps read-only — a shared-memory protocol between rings, not an interface.
  • The reader cannot take a lock. A user-space thread holding a lock that the kernel's timekeeping update needs could be descheduled indefinitely, or killed while holding it. The only workable arrangement is one where the reader can be interrupted at any point and simply retry, which is why a seqlock sits at the center of the design.
  • The computation must be the same computation the kernel performs. If user space and kernel derive the time by different routes, they disagree, and a program that mixes clock_gettime() with a syscall that returns a timestamp sees time move backwards. So the vDSO does not approximate — it runs the identical mult/shift arithmetic against the identical snapshot.
  • Every path must have a way out. Some clocks cannot be computed in user space, some clocksources are not user-readable, and some conditions (a very stale snapshot, a time namespace) need kernel help. Each of these ends in a real system call, and getting those exits right is most of the subtlety in the code.

The rest of this section follows the data from the kernel to the caller and back:

  1. What is the vDSO, physically? A shared object the kernel maps into every process, and the pages behind it.
  2. What does the kernel publish? The vdso_time_data and vdso_clock structures on the data page.
  3. How does user space turn that into a timestamp? The seqlock retry loop and the counter arithmetic.
  4. Who writes the data, and when? update_vsyscall(), called from the timekeeping update.
  5. What happens when the fast path cannot work? The fallback to a real syscall.
  6. Which calls are accelerated, and which clocks? The exported symbols and the clock-ID routing.
  7. How do containers get their own view of time? Time namespace integration, which reuses the seqlock's odd state as a sentinel.
  8. How is all this mapped and protected? Page layout, the fault handler, and the sealing that stops user space tampering.
  9. What does the hardware access look like? RDTSC and CNTVCT_EL0, and when neither is usable.
  10. What goes wrong after a long idle? Overflow protection on the cycle delta.

Version history. Linux 2.6 had the vsyscall page, which shared the basic idea but little else: a single fixed address, x86_64 only, two accelerated functions, and — because the address was fixed — a reliable gadget source for exploits after ASLR became standard. The vDSO replaced it with a properly randomized, per-architecture ELF object, and Linux has since spent a decade consolidating the per-architecture copies into the generic implementation in lib/vdso/ that this section describes. That consolidation largely finished in Linux 6.15, which in a single cycle moved both x86 and ARM64 onto a common data-store implementation and replaced the flat per-architecture data structure with the vdso_time_data/vdso_clock split shown below. The split was made specifically to allow more than one independently-updated clock on the page, which is exactly what auxiliary clock support needed when it arrived in 6.17.

Architecture Overview

Although programs call it like a library, the vDSO is not one. Nothing links against it, no file on disk corresponds to it, and it appears in a process’s address space before the dynamic loader has done anything at all — the kernel maps it during execve(). What the loader finds is a complete, valid ELF shared object with a symbol table, which it treats like any other, and that is the whole trick: a normal-looking library whose code the kernel wrote and whose data the kernel keeps current.

The vDSO mechanism consists of three components that work together:

  1. The vDSO shared library — a small ELF shared object ([vdso]) containing user-space implementations of time functions, mapped read-only + execute into every process's address space
  2. The vvar pages — kernel-maintained data pages ([vvar]) mapped read-only into user space, containing timekeeping state that the vDSO code reads
  3. The kernel update path — code in update_vsyscall() that refreshes the vvar data on every tick or whenever the timekeeping state changes

When a user process calls clock_gettime(), the C library resolves the symbol to __vdso_clock_gettime() inside the vDSO. This function reads the pre-computed timekeeper snapshot from the vvar page, reads the hardware counter (TSC on x86_64, CNTVCT_EL0 on ARM64), and computes the current time — all without leaving user space.

The vvar Data Page

The vvar page is a kernel-owned page mapped read-only into user space. It contains a vdso_time_data structure with all the information needed to compute the current time from user space:

/* include/vdso/datapage.h */
struct vdso_timestamp {
    u64  sec;    /* Base seconds */
    u64  nsec;   /* Base nanoseconds (left-shifted by 'shift' for hires clocks) */
};

struct vdso_clock {
    u32  seq;           /* Sequence counter for lockless read consistency */
    s32  clock_mode;    /* VDSO_CLOCKMODE_* — which HW counter to read */
    u64  cycle_last;    /* Counter value at last update */
#ifdef CONFIG_GENERIC_VDSO_OVERFLOW_PROTECT
    u64  max_cycles;    /* Overflow protection limit */
#endif
    u64  mask;          /* Counter bitmask */
    u32  mult;          /* Cycles-to-nanoseconds multiplier */
    u32  shift;         /* Right-shift after multiplication */
    union {
        struct vdso_timestamp basetime[VDSO_BASES];  /* Per-clock base times */
        struct timens_offset  offset[VDSO_BASES];    /* Time namespace offsets */
    };
};

struct vdso_time_data {
    struct arch_vdso_time_data  arch_data;
    struct vdso_clock           clock_data[CS_BASES];      /* [CS_HRES_COARSE, CS_RAW] */
    struct vdso_clock           aux_clock_data[MAX_AUX_CLOCKS];
    s32                         tz_minuteswest;
    s32                         tz_dsttime;
    u32                         hrtimer_res;  /* clock_getres() answer */
} ____cacheline_aligned;

The clock_data array has two entries: CS_HRES_COARSE (index 0) serves CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_BOOTTIME, CLOCK_TAI, and the coarse variants; CS_RAW (index 1) serves CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW. Each entry contains a complete timekeeping snapshot that the user-space code can use independently.

The #ifdef around max_cycles is not the usual noise, and it is the one place in this structure where the two architectures this book covers genuinely differ. x86 selects CONFIG_GENERIC_VDSO_OVERFLOW_PROTECT and ARM64 does not, so struct vdso_clock is eight bytes shorter on ARM64 and every field after cycle_last sits at a different offset. That is tolerable only because the vvar page is not an ABI in the usual sense: the vDSO code that reads it is compiled from the same tree as the kernel that writes it and is shipped inside it, so the two can never disagree about the layout. A user-space program that tried to parse the page itself would be relying on something the kernel has never promised. Overflow Protection, at the end of this section, explains what the field is for and why only one of the two architectures needs it.

The Time Computation Algorithm

This is where the two halves meet. The kernel has published a base time and the counter value it corresponds to; the caller reads the counter now and must close the gap. The arithmetic itself is the same (delta * mult) >> shift conversion the clocksource layer uses, and deliberately so — the vDSO is not a cheaper approximation of the kernel’s answer, it is the kernel’s answer computed somewhere else.

What makes the code look unfamiliar is everything wrapped around that one multiply. The reader can be preempted between any two instructions, and the writer may run on another CPU at any moment, so the computation sits inside a retry loop and every value it uses must come from a single consistent snapshot.

Stripped of the defences, the conversion is two lines:

/* the arithmetic, without the guards discussed later */
u64 delta = (cycles - vc->cycle_last) & VDSO_DELTA_MASK(vc);
u64 ns    = ((delta * vc->mult) + base) >> vc->shift;

The real vdso_calc_ns() has a second branch for deltas large enough to overflow the 64-bit multiply, and x86 replaces the function outright to cope with a counter that can appear to move backwards. Both are deferred to Overflow Protection at the end of this section, where the full function is shown. Introducing them here would obscure the point, which is that the arithmetic is identical to the clocksource layer’s and everything difficult about the vDSO is what surrounds it.

In pseudo-code, the full algorithm is:

  1. Read the sequence counter seq from the vvar page (must be even — odd means kernel is updating)
  2. Read base time: base_sec, base_nsec from basetime[clock_id]
  3. Read the hardware counter: cycles = RDTSC (x86) or cycles = MRS CNTVCT_EL0 (ARM64)
  4. Compute delta: delta = (cycles - cycle_last) & mask
  5. Convert to nanoseconds: nsec = (delta × mult + base_nsec) >> shift
  6. Re-read the sequence counter — if it changed, retry from step 1
  7. Normalize: carry nanoseconds > 10⁹ into seconds

The sequence counter provides a lockless read-side protocol (similar to a seqlock). The kernel increments seq to an odd value before updating the data, then to an even value after. If the user-space code reads an odd seq or the seq changes between the start and end of its read, it retries. This ensures consistent data without any locks or atomic operations on the fast path.

One feature of that list is worth pausing on, because it looks like an accident of presentation and is in fact a requirement. Step 7, the normalization that carries surplus nanoseconds into seconds, comes after step 6’s retry check rather than inside the loop with the rest of the arithmetic. In the kernel this is vdso_set_timespec(), called below the do { } while (vdso_read_retry(...)), and its comment states the rule directly: it “must not be invoked within the sequence read section as a race inside that loop could result in __iter_div_u64_rem() being extremely slow.”

The reason is that __iter_div_u64_rem() does not divide. It subtracts in a loop, and it takes trouble to keep doing so:

/* include/vdso/math64.h */
static __always_inline u32
__iter_div_u64_rem(u64 dividend, u32 divisor, u64 *remainder)
{
    u32 ret = 0;

    while (dividend >= divisor) {
        /* The following asm() prevents the compiler from
           optimising this loop into a modulo operation.  */
        asm("" : "+rm"(dividend));

        dividend -= divisor;
        ret++;
    }

    *remainder = dividend;
    return ret;
}

For a legitimate nanosecond value the loop runs once or not at all, which is why this is faster than a 64-bit division on the machines that matter. For a torn read it is a disaster: a nanosecond count assembled from two different snapshots can be arbitrarily large, and the loop would then iterate hundreds of millions of times before producing a result the retry check was going to throw away anyway. Correctness is never at risk — the answer is discarded either way — but a thread could disappear into that loop for seconds. Placing the normalization outside the retry section means it only ever sees values that have already been confirmed consistent.

This is a recurring shape in the vDSO and one of the things that makes the code hard to read at first: several of its arrangements are defences not against wrong answers but against pathological cost, because a user-space fast path has no way to be preempted out of trouble by the kernel.

Kernel-Side Update: update_vsyscall()

Everything the vDSO does depends on the data page being correct, and this is the function that makes it so. It is the writer half of the seqlock whose reader half was shown above, and it is called from inside the timekeeping update described earlier in this chapter — which means it runs with the timekeeper lock held and interrupts disabled, on one CPU, while every other CPU in the system may be spinning in a vDSO read loop waiting for the sequence number to go even again.

That lock is worth a moment, because its history is the same history as the data page’s. Through Linux 6.12 it was a global named timekeeper_lock, and the vDSO update path reached for it by name. It is now tk_core.lock, a field of the timekeeper it protects, private to kernel/time/timekeeping.c and reachable only through timekeeper_lock_irqsave() and timekeeper_unlock_irqrestore(). The commit that did this says why: the lock “needs to be part of tk_core” because “the timekeeper infrastructure will be reused for per ptp clock timekeepers”. A single global lock and a single global sequence counter were the same assumption expressed twice, and both had to go before one machine could carry several independently-steered clocks. The restructuring of the data page described below is the other half of this change.

Architecture code that needs to modify its own portion of the page uses the exported pair vdso_update_begin() and vdso_update_end(), which wrap the lock acquisition and the sequence-counter bump together so that a caller cannot get one without the other.

That context explains the shape of the function. It does no computation of its own; it copies already-computed values. Anything expensive would extend the window during which every reader in the system is blocked.

Every time the kernel updates its internal timekeeping state (on each tick, or when settimeofday()/adjtimex() is called), it copies a snapshot to the vvar page:

/* kernel/time/vsyscall.c */
void update_vsyscall(struct timekeeper *tk)
{
    struct vdso_time_data *vdata = vdso_k_time_data;
    struct vdso_clock *vc = vdata->clock_data;

    vdso_write_begin(vdata);  /* seq++ (now odd — readers will spin) */

    /* Set clock mode: tells vDSO which HW counter to read */
    vc[CS_HRES_COARSE].clock_mode = tk->tkr_mono.clock->vdso_clock_mode;
    vc[CS_RAW].clock_mode         = tk->tkr_mono.clock->vdso_clock_mode;

    /* CLOCK_REALTIME */
    vc[CS_HRES_COARSE].basetime[CLOCK_REALTIME].sec  = tk->xtime_sec;
    vc[CS_HRES_COARSE].basetime[CLOCK_REALTIME].nsec = tk->tkr_mono.xtime_nsec;

    /* CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE — no counter read needed, tick-granularity */
    vc[CS_HRES_COARSE].basetime[CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE].sec  = tk->xtime_sec;
    vc[CS_HRES_COARSE].basetime[CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE].nsec = tk->coarse_nsec;

    /* CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_BOOTTIME, CLOCK_TAI, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW... */
    update_vdso_time_data(vdata, tk);

    /* Copy clocksource parameters: cycle_last, mult, shift, mask */
    fill_clock_configuration(&vc[CS_HRES_COARSE], &tk->tkr_mono);
    fill_clock_configuration(&vc[CS_RAW],         &tk->tkr_raw);

    vdso_write_end(vdata);  /* seq++ (now even — readers proceed) */
}

The clock_mode field tells the vDSO which hardware counter to read. If the current clocksource is not vDSO-capable (e.g., a platform with no user-accessible counter), clock_mode is set to VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE, causing the vDSO to fall through to the syscall fallback path. Note that when this is the case, update_vdso_time_data() is skipped entirely — there is no point publishing base times that no reader will use.

The Architecture Hooks

Two hooks let an architecture adjust the published data. Both default to nothing, and reading ARM64's use of the first is instructive:

/* arch/arm64/include/asm/vdso/vsyscall.h */
#define VDSO_PRECISION_MASK  ~(0xFF00ULL << 48)

static __always_inline
void __arch_update_vdso_clock(struct vdso_clock *vc)
{
    vc->mask = VDSO_PRECISION_MASK;
}

ARM64 overwrites the counter mask the clocksource supplied with a fixed 56-bit mask. The architecture guarantees the generic timer counter is at least 56 bits wide, and pinning the mask to that known value lets the vDSO's arithmetic be compiled against a constant rather than a value loaded from the page. It is a small thing, but it sits on the hottest path in the kernel's user-facing API.

The second hook, __arch_sync_vdso_time_data(), runs after vdso_write_end() and exists for architectures whose instruction or data caches do not automatically make the update visible to user space. On x86_64 and ARM64 it is empty; the ordering supplied by the seqlock's memory barriers is sufficient.

A Separate Path for Auxiliary Clocks

Auxiliary clocks (CLOCK_AUX through CLOCK_AUX_LAST, described earlier in this chapter) are not updated by update_vsyscall() at all. They have their own writer, vdso_time_update_aux(), and the difference is not cosmetic:

/* kernel/time/vsyscall.c */
void vdso_time_update_aux(struct timekeeper *tk)
{
    struct vdso_clock *vc;
    ...
    vc = &vdata->aux_clock_data[tk->id - TIMEKEEPER_AUX_FIRST];
    ...
    vdso_write_begin_clock(vc);      /* Bump *this clock's* seq only */
    vc->clock_mode = clock_mode;
    if (clock_mode != VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE) {
        fill_clock_configuration(vc, &tk->tkr_mono);
        /* ... derive the aux base time from monotonic_to_aux ... */
    }
    __arch_update_vdso_clock(vc);
    vdso_write_end_clock(vc);
}

The core update calls vdso_write_begin(), which bumps the sequence counters of all the core clocks together, because they are all derived from one timekeeper and must be published as one consistent snapshot. An auxiliary clock is independent: it has its own shadow timekeeper, can be enabled, disabled and steered on its own, and is updated at its own cadence. Bumping the shared sequence for it would stall every reader of CLOCK_MONOTONIC on the machine for no reason.

The vdso_write_begin_clock()/vdso_write_end_clock() pair, which operate on a single vdso_clock, exist precisely for this. Their arrival alongside auxiliary clock support is the clearest evidence of why the 6.15 restructuring happened: the flat data page had one sequence counter for one timekeeper, and the whole point of splitting vdso_clock out of vdso_time_data was to give each independently-updated clock its own.

The Fallback Path

Not all clock IDs can be served from user space. When the vDSO cannot compute a time (unsupported clock, no vDSO-capable clocksource, or dynamic clock ID), it falls back to a real system call:

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c */
static int __cvdso_clock_gettime_data(const struct vdso_time_data *vd,
                                      clockid_t clock, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    bool ok = __cvdso_clock_gettime_common(vd, clock, ts);

    if (unlikely(!ok))
        return clock_gettime_fallback(clock, ts);  /* Real syscall */
    return 0;
}

The fallback is a direct system call instruction — syscall on x86_64, svc #0 on ARM64 — issued from inline assembly inside the vDSO itself, not a call back into libc. Two consequences follow, and both matter to anyone who resolves these symbols by hand rather than letting libc do it.

The first is that the fallback is not only for clocks that can never work. CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID and CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID are permanently excluded, because they need per-task accounting the kernel cannot publish to a shared page. But do_hres() also returns false at run time when the clock mode is one it cannot read, and the clock mode changes when the kernel switches clocksources. The same clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) call can therefore take the fast path on one invocation and trap on the next, on the same machine, in the same process — if the TSC was declared unstable in between, or a paravirtualized counter stopped advertising itself as stable. Code that has measured the vDSO as fast has measured the machine in the state it was in.

The second is the error convention. __cvdso_clock_gettime_data() returns the value the syscall instruction produced, unchanged, and that value is a negative errno — the vDSO has no errno to set and no way to reach the caller’s. Calling __vdso_clock_gettime directly therefore means checking for a negative return, not for -1; the conversion into the familiar -1-plus-errno convention happens in libc’s wrapper, above the vDSO.

vDSO-Accelerated Functions

Not every system call is worth accelerating. The vDSO exports a deliberately small set, and the selection criterion is the same in each case: the call must be read-only, frequent enough that the syscall overhead dominates its cost, and computable from data the kernel can safely publish. Calls that change state, that need to consult per-task data, or that must serialize against other threads cannot qualify, which is why clock_settime() and adjtimex() are not here.

The vDSO provides user-space implementations for several time-related functions, not just clock_gettime():

Table 6-169. vDSO Exported Functions
Libc Wrapperx86_64 SymbolARM64 SymbolDescription
clock_gettime()__vdso_clock_gettime__kernel_clock_gettimeHigh-resolution time for all supported clocks
gettimeofday()__vdso_gettimeofday__kernel_gettimeofdayLegacy µs-resolution time (CLOCK_REALTIME only)
clock_getres()__vdso_clock_getres__kernel_clock_getresClock resolution query (reads hrtimer_res)
getrandom()__vdso_getrandom__kernel_getrandomUser-space CSPRNG (Linux 6.11+)
time()__vdso_time—Second-resolution wall time (reads coarse seconds)
getcpu()__vdso_getcpu—Current CPU and NUMA node (via RDTSCP or a segment register)
— (signal return)—__kernel_rt_sigreturnSignal trampoline; not a time function, but it is why every ARM64 process needs the vDSO mapped

Three things about this table are more interesting than the individual rows.

The naming differs by architecture and is not merely cosmetic: x86_64 uses an __vdso_ prefix and ARM64 a __kernel_ one, and libc has to know which to look for. x86_64 additionally exports every symbol twice, once prefixed and once bare — clock_gettime as well as __vdso_clock_gettime — while ARM64 exports only the prefixed names. Both architectures place their symbols in an ELF version node, LINUX_2.6 on x86_64 and LINUX_2.6.39 on ARM64, and those tags are frozen: they name the release in which the interface first appeared and will never be bumped, because doing so would break every binary that already looks them up.

ARM64 has no time() and no getcpu(). A program calling time() on ARM64 is served by libc calling the vDSO’s clock_gettime and discarding the nanoseconds, which is still far cheaper than a syscall; getcpu() has no such workaround and traps. The difference is a hardware one — x86’s RDTSCP returns a CPU identifier as a side effect of reading the counter, so getcpu() costs almost nothing to add, while ARM64 has no equivalent free source of the same information.

Finally, both architectures export things that have nothing to do with time. ARM64’s __kernel_rt_sigreturn is the signal trampoline, which is the reason an ARM64 process needs the vDSO even if it never asks what time it is, and x86_64 conditionally exports __vdso_sgx_enter_enclave under CONFIG_X86_SGX. The vDSO began as a timing optimization and has become the general mechanism for anything the kernel wants to hand user space as executable code.

Table 6-170. What a clock_gettime() Call Costs
PathOrder of MagnitudeWhat Dominates It
vDSO, coarse clocka few nanosecondsTwo loads from an already-hot cache line; no counter read at all
vDSO, high-resolutiontens of nanosecondsThe counter read and the barriers around it (see below)
Syscall fallbackhundreds of nanosecondsKernel entry and exit, whose cost depends on which CPU vulnerability mitigations the machine has enabled

The table gives orders of magnitude rather than figures because the ratio between the two paths is not a property of Linux. It is a property of the machine, and on current hardware the spread is wide enough that any single number would be misleading.

On the syscall side, the variable is mitigations. The x86_64 entry path in arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S contains IBRS_ENTER, IBRS_EXIT and CLEAR_CPU_BUFFERS, all of which are alternative-patched at boot according to what the CPU is vulnerable to. A kernel booted with mitigations=off on an unaffected part executes none of them; the same kernel on an affected part writes a speculation-control MSR twice and flushes internal buffers on every entry and exit. The syscall is the same syscall; what it costs is not.

On the vDSO side, the variable is how the architecture keeps a counter read from being reordered. rdtsc can be speculated ahead of prior loads — the comment in arch/x86/include/asm/tsc.h says the manuals are vague on the point but that it is observable — so rdtsc_ordered() is an ALTERNATIVE_2 that patches in rdtscp where available, lfence; rdtsc where it is not, and bare rdtsc only where the CPU needs no barrier at all. ARM64 has the same problem in a different shape: reading CNTVCT_EL0 normally requires a preceding isb, which drains the pipeline, but ARMv8.6’s Enhanced Counter Virtualization adds a self-synchronizing CNTVCTSS_EL0, and the kernel patches the barrier out to a nop when ARM64_HAS_ECV is present. Two machines running identical binaries can differ by tens of nanoseconds on this one instruction.

ARM64 then pays once more, and the reason is the seqlock this section has been describing. A system-register read is not a memory access, so a subsequent barrier does not order it, and a counter value could be sampled outside the sequence-protected region that was supposed to contain it. arch_counter_enforce_ordering() fixes this by manufacturing a data dependency: it exclusive-ORs the value with itself to get a guaranteed zero, adds that to the stack pointer, and loads from the result into xzr — a load that goes nowhere, from an address that is always the stack, which exists purely so that the counter read must complete before it. The comment above it in arch/arm64/include/asm/barrier.h is worth quoting in full: “This insanity brought to you by speculative system register reads, out-of-order memory accesses, sequence locks and Thomas Gleixner.”

The practical conclusion is unchanged — the vDSO is an order of magnitude faster and a program that reads the clock in a hot loop should use it — but a reader who benchmarks this and gets a ratio of four, or of thirty, has not made a mistake.

Clock ID Routing

A single entry point serves every clock ID, and its first job is to decide which of three things the caller is asking for: a high-resolution clock that needs the counter read, a coarse clock that can be answered from the published base time alone, or something the vDSO cannot compute at all. Doing that with a chain of comparisons would put a branch mispredict on the hot path, so the code uses a bitmask test instead — the clock ID becomes a bit position, and a constant mask says which category it falls in.

The vDSO classifies clock IDs into categories using bitmasks, routing each to the appropriate handler:

/* include/vdso/datapage.h */
#define VDSO_HRES   (BIT(CLOCK_REALTIME) | BIT(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) | \
                     BIT(CLOCK_BOOTTIME) | BIT(CLOCK_TAI))
#define VDSO_COARSE (BIT(CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE) | BIT(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE))
#define VDSO_RAW    (BIT(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW))
#define VDSO_AUX    __GENMASK(CLOCK_AUX_LAST, CLOCK_AUX)

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c — routing logic */
if (!vdso_clockid_valid(clock))     /* (u32)clock <= CLOCK_AUX_LAST */
    return false;

msk = 1U << clock;
if (likely(msk & VDSO_HRES))         → do_hres()   /* Read HW counter */
else if (msk & VDSO_COARSE)          → do_coarse() /* Just read basetime, no counter */
else if (msk & VDSO_RAW)             → do_hres()   /* HW counter via CS_RAW */
else if (msk & VDSO_AUX)             → do_aux()    /* Auxiliary clocks */
else                                  → fallback    /* Real syscall */

The guard on the first line is not decoration. 1U << clock is undefined behaviour if clock is negative, and negative clock IDs are not hypothetical — they are how POSIX encodes a dynamic clock backed by a file descriptor, so a program timing against a PTP device on /dev/ptp0 passes a negative number here. vdso_clockid_valid() disposes of the whole problem with one comparison by casting to u32 first, which turns every negative value into something far above CLOCK_AUX_LAST:

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c */
static __always_inline bool vdso_clockid_valid(clockid_t clock)
{
    /* Check for negative values or invalid clocks */
    return likely((u32) clock <= CLOCK_AUX_LAST);
}

The VDSO_AUX arm is the newest, and it behaves unlike the others in a way worth recording. An auxiliary clock that has never been enabled still occupies its slot on the data page, but carries VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE, so do_aux() returns failure and the caller lands in the syscall fallback. The same clock ID therefore takes the fast path or the slow path depending on run-time configuration rather than on anything intrinsic to the clock. do_aux() also fails outright when CONFIG_POSIX_AUX_CLOCKS is not built, which the compiler resolves by deleting the branch.

The coarse clocks (CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE, CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE) are particularly fast because they skip the hardware counter read entirely — they simply return the pre-computed value from the vvar page, which was written at the last tick. Their precision is limited to one tick (e.g., 4ms at HZ=250), but the latency is even lower (~10ns) because there is no RDTSC/CNTVCT_EL0 instruction.

Table 6-171. vDSO Clock Coverage
Clock IDvDSO?HandlerWhat clock_getres() ReportsNotes
CLOCK_REALTIME✓do_hres()hrtimer_resAffected by settimeofday()/NTP
CLOCK_MONOTONIC✓do_hres()hrtimer_resNever goes backward
CLOCK_BOOTTIME✓do_hres()hrtimer_resIncludes suspend time
CLOCK_TAI✓do_hres()hrtimer_resUTC + leap seconds
CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE✓do_coarse()LOW_RES_NSEC (one tick)No HW counter read, very fast
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE✓do_coarse()LOW_RES_NSEC (one tick)No HW counter read, very fast
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW✓do_hres()hrtimer_resNo NTP adjustment
CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID✗fallback—Requires kernel per-process accounting
CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID✗fallback—Requires kernel per-thread accounting
CLOCK_AUX … CLOCK_AUX_LASTConditionaldo_aux()aux_clock_resolution_ns()Eight IDs; each takes the fast path only while that clock is enabled, and only with CONFIG_POSIX_AUX_CLOCKS
CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM, CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM✗fallback—In no mask; these exist to arm wakeups, not to be read on a hot path
Negative IDs (dynamic POSIX clocks)✗fallback—Rejected by vdso_clockid_valid() before the mask is formed

The renamed column is a correction, not a rewording. The original said “precision” and gave ~1 ns for the high-resolution clocks, which conflates two unrelated quantities. What __cvdso_clock_getres_common() returns for those clocks is vd->hrtimer_res, a copy of the kernel’s hrtimer_resolution, which is 1 when CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS is enabled and a full tick otherwise. That is a statement about how finely the kernel can schedule a timer. It says nothing about how finely the counter you just read actually advances, and on ARM64 the two are three orders of magnitude apart: an architected timer running at 24 MHz advances once every 41 ns or so, while clock_getres() answers 1 ns.

The coarse clocks are the honest ones. They return LOW_RES_NSEC, which is TICK_NSEC, and the comment above its definition in include/vdso/ktime.h is candid about the purpose of the whole interface — the value exists “to give application programmers an idea of the (in)accuracy of timers.” An idea, not a bound. Code that needs to know the real granularity of the clock it is reading has to measure it; the kernel does not export it.

Time Namespace Integration

Linux time namespaces (CONFIG_TIME_NS) allow containers to have different views of CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME — essential for container live migration where the monotonic clock must appear continuous despite moving between hosts with different boot times.

The vDSO is fully namespace-aware. When a process belongs to a non-root time namespace, the kernel installs a special vvar page with seq set to 1 (odd) and clock_mode set to VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TIMENS. When the vDSO detects this sentinel, it follows an alternate path:

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c — time namespace handling */
static bool do_hres(const struct vdso_time_data *vd, const struct vdso_clock *vc,
                    clockid_t clk, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    do {
        while (unlikely((seq = READ_ONCE(vc->seq)) & 1)) {
            /* seq is odd: either a concurrent update or time namespace */
            if (IS_ENABLED(CONFIG_TIME_NS) &&
                vc->clock_mode == VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TIMENS)
                return do_hres_timens(vd, vc, clk, ts);  /* Namespace path */
            cpu_relax();  /* Normal concurrent update — spin */
        }
        smp_rmb();
        /* ... read data and compute time ... */
    } while (unlikely(vdso_read_retry(vc, seq)));
    return true;
}

The do_hres_timens() function reads the real time data from a second vvar page (at PAGE_SIZE offset), computes the actual time, then adds the per-clock namespace offset. This costs one extra page access but still avoids a syscall.

Memory Layout and Mapping

The layout is worth examining for two reasons. The first is practical: these mappings show up in every process’s address space, and knowing what they are makes the output of /proc/[pid]/maps and of tools like pmap intelligible. The second is that the permissions and flags on these pages are a security boundary. User space can read the data page and execute the code page, and must be unable to do anything else to either — if a process could write the data page it would control the time every library in it computes, and if it could unmap or replace the code page it would have a way to redirect calls that look like ordinary libc.

The vDSO and vvar pages are visible in /proc/[pid]/maps:

7fff8d5fe000-7fff8d600000 r--p  [vvar]    ← Read-only data pages (timekeeping state)
7fff8d600000-7fff8d602000 r-xp  [vdso]    ← Executable code (clock_gettime impl)

The vvar mapping uses a fault handler (vvar_fault()) that resolves pages on demand based on pgoff:

Table 6-172. vvar Page Layout
Page OffsetContentPurpose
VDSO_TIME_PAGE_OFFSETvdso_time_dataTimekeeping state (clocks, mult, shift, basetime)
VDSO_TIMENS_PAGE_OFFSETReal time data (or timens offsets)Time namespace support — swapped for non-root NS
VDSO_RNG_PAGE_OFFSETvdso_rng_datagetrandom() vDSO state (generation counter)
VDSO_ARCH_PAGES_STARTArch-specific dataPlatform-specific extensions

Two behaviours of this handler are easy to miss. A page offset whose feature is not configured returns VM_FAULT_SIGBUS rather than a zero page, so a program that reaches for the RNG page on a kernel without CONFIG_VDSO_GETRANDOM gets a fault instead of plausible-looking garbage. And for a task in a non-root time namespace the handler installs two pages on the first fault rather than one, with the reasoning stated in the code: the real data page “will be accessed to get clock data anyway”, so faulting it separately would only cost a second trap.

The mapping is installed during execve() by arch_setup_additional_pages() (x86_64) or the equivalent on ARM64, with the flags VM_READ | VM_MAYREAD | VM_IO | VM_DONTDUMP | VM_PFNMAP | VM_SEALED_SYSMAP. Two different protections are bundled there, and they are worth separating because only one of them is unconditional.

The data page can never be written. VM_WRITE is absent, and so is VM_MAYWRITE, which means user space cannot even acquire write permission afterwards through mprotect() — the absence of VM_MAYWRITE is what makes the read-only-ness permanent rather than merely current. That much holds on every configuration.

Whether the mapping can be moved or removed is a build-time decision. VM_SEALED_SYSMAP expands to VM_SEALED only when CONFIG_MSEAL_SYSTEM_MAPPINGS is enabled, and to VM_NONE — nothing at all — when it is not. Both x86_64 and ARM64 declare support for it, but the option cannot simply be turned on everywhere, and the Kconfig text is unusually candid about why: it “breaks programs which rely on relocating or unmapping system mappings”, naming UML, gVisor and rr among the casualties, and it carries a hard depends on !CHECKPOINT_RESTORE.

That dependency deserves notice here of all places. The time namespace support described in the previous subsection exists, as that subsection says, so that a container’s monotonic clock can survive live migration — and the tool that performs such migrations is precisely the checkpoint/restore machinery that sealing excludes. A kernel configured for the use case that motivates time namespaces is therefore a kernel in which these mappings are not sealed. The sealing genuinely does close an attack avenue, by stopping a process from unmapping the vDSO and putting its own code at the address libc will call; but describing it as a property of the vDSO rather than of a particular build overstates it.

Architecture-Specific Counter Access

Everything described so far is generic code shared by every architecture. This is the one place that cannot be: reading a hardware counter is a single instruction, and it is a different instruction on every machine. It is also the one operation with a hard prerequisite the kernel cannot supply — the counter has to be readable at the lowest privilege level, and whether it is depends on the hardware, on firmware configuration, and on whether the kernel has decided the counter is trustworthy.

The hardware counter read is the most architecture-dependent part of the vDSO. It must be accessible from user space without privilege, and the clock_mode field on the data page is what selects between the possibilities. The enumeration is deliberately open: include/vdso/clocksource.h defines only VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE and a sentinel, and each architecture appends its own names through a macro. Reading the full list is more informative than reading either architecture alone.

Table 6-173. User-Space Counter Access by Architecture
Architectureclock_modeUser-Space AccessSelected When
x86_64VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TSCRDTSC / RDTSCPThe TSC is constant, non-stop and judged reliable. RDTSCP additionally returns the CPU ID
x86_64VDSO_CLOCKMODE_PVCLOCKRDTSC scaled by a per-vCPU structure the hypervisor maintainsRunning under KVM with kvm-clock, and the guest TSC is stable
x86_64VDSO_CLOCKMODE_HVCLOCKRDTSC scaled by the Hyper-V TSC reference pageRunning under Hyper-V with the reference page available
ARM64VDSO_CLOCKMODE_ARCHTIMERMRS CNTVCT_EL0The architected timer is usable from EL0 with no erratum in the way
ARM64VDSO_CLOCKMODE_ARCHTIMER_NOCOMPATSame, but only from the 64-bit vDSOAn erratum makes the 32-bit compat counter access unsafe while the 64-bit one is fine
BothVDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE— (every call becomes a syscall)The current clocksource has no user-readable counter — HPET, the ACPI PM timer, or an architected timer behind an out-of-line erratum workaround

Two things this table makes visible are worth drawing out.

The first is that a virtual machine is not automatically condemned to the syscall path. It is often said that the vDSO stops working under virtualization, and the reasoning is sound as far as it goes — a guest TSC that the hypervisor may rescale, or that jumps on migration, cannot be trusted for timekeeping. But the paravirtualized clocks exist exactly to close that gap. Under KVM, kvm-clock publishes a per-vCPU structure containing a multiplier, a shift and an offset, versioned with its own seqlock; the guest reads the TSC and applies the hypervisor’s correction in user space. Hyper-V does the same through a TSC reference page. A cloud VM on either hypervisor gets the fast path, and falls back only when the hypervisor itself signals that the TSC has stopped being stable — which the guest discovers by finding PVCLOCK_TSC_STABLE_BIT clear on the very read it was attempting.

The second is that ARCHTIMER_NOCOMPAT exists to express a distinction no boolean could. ARM64 errata are not uniform in their effect: some make counter reads unsafe everywhere, and those set VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE; others affect only the 32-bit access path. A single extra enum value handles the second case, and the mechanism is elegantly minimal — the 64-bit __arch_get_hw_counter() rejects only VDSO_CLOCKMODE_NONE, while its compat counterpart in arch/arm64/include/asm/vdso/compat_gettimeofday.h insists on VDSO_CLOCKMODE_ARCHTIMER exactly. NOCOMPAT therefore passes the first test and fails the second, and a 32-bit process on such a machine takes the syscall path while its 64-bit neighbours do not. The kernel comment on the code that makes this choice notes that it “may change our mind pretty late in the game (with a per-CPU erratum, for example)” — which is why clock_mode is a field to be re-read rather than a boot-time constant.

Signalling a Failed Read

A subtlety hides in all of this. The generic code checks clock_mode before calling __arch_get_hw_counter(), but the check and the read are not atomic with respect to the kernel changing the mode, and a paravirtualized clock can fail on the read itself. So the counter accessor needs a way to say “no answer”, and the two architectures answer differently.

ARM64 returns zero, with a comment explaining the reasoning: the situation “raced against a concurrent update”, so “return something. Core will do another round and then see the mode change and fallback to the syscall.” A wrong answer is harmless because the seqlock retry is going to discard it anyway.

x86 cannot use that trick, because zero is a legitimate counter reading and its paravirtualized readers can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with a mode change. Instead they return U64_MAX, and arch_vdso_cycles_ok() rejects any value whose sign bit is set:

/* arch/x86/include/asm/vdso/gettimeofday.h */
static inline bool arch_vdso_cycles_ok(u64 cycles)
{
    return (s64)cycles >= 0;
}
#define vdso_cycles_ok arch_vdso_cycles_ok

Reserving the whole top half of the range as an error space is only affordable because the pv and hv readers mask their genuine results with S64_MAX before returning them, so a real reading can never be mistaken for the sentinel. That single decision is what forces x86 to supply its own vdso_calc_ns() rather than using the generic one, as the next subsection describes: the effective counter mask on x86 is not the clocksource’s mask field at all but S64_MAX, imposed by this convention.

Overflow Protection

There is one assumption in the computation above that has not yet been questioned. delta × mult is a 64-bit multiplication, and it is only safe while the delta stays small. The clocksource layer computes max_cycles — the largest delta that cannot overflow — and the kernel's own conversion path is careful never to exceed it, because the timekeeping update runs at least once per tick.

The vDSO has no such guarantee. A tickless CPU can leave the base time hours old, and a VM can be descheduled by its host between reading the counter and using it. So the fast path checks the delta first:

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c — generic version */
static __always_inline
u64 vdso_calc_ns(const struct vdso_clock *vc, u64 cycles, u64 base)
{
    u64 delta = (cycles - vc->cycle_last) & VDSO_DELTA_MASK(vc);

    if (likely(vdso_delta_ok(vc, delta)))          /* delta < vc->max_cycles */
        return vdso_shift_ns((delta * vc->mult) + base, vc->shift);

    return mul_u64_u32_add_u64_shr(delta, vc->mult, base, vc->shift);
}

Note what the slow branch does not do: it does not fall back to a system call. mul_u64_u32_add_u64_shr() performs the same conversion through a 128-bit intermediate, so the answer is still correct — just computed more slowly. The vDSO returns a real timestamp in both cases.

Two details are easy to miss. First, when CONFIG_GENERIC_VDSO_OVERFLOW_PROTECT is not selected, vdso_delta_ok() is compiled as an unconditional true, so the wide-multiply branch is dead code the compiler removes entirely. Of our two architectures, only x86 selects the option; ARM64 does not, because its 56-bit counter at typical generic-timer frequencies cannot produce a delta large enough to overflow. Second, x86 does not use the generic function at all — it defines its own vdso_calc_ns, because the TSC brings a second problem the generic code never has to consider:

/* arch/x86/include/asm/vdso/gettimeofday.h */
if (unlikely(delta > vc->max_cycles)) {
    /* Filter out negative motion: effective sign bit is bit 62 */
    if (delta & (1ULL << 62))
        return base >> vc->shift;

    return mul_u64_u32_add_u64_shr(delta & S64_MAX, vc->mult, base, vc->shift);
}

On x86 the TSC can appear to run backwards by a small amount across sockets, which in unsigned arithmetic produces an enormous delta. A single > comparison catches both cases at once, since a wrapped-negative value is always larger than max_cycles; the branch then distinguishes them by testing what is effectively the sign bit. Genuine negative motion returns the base time unchanged — the clock stands still rather than jumping forward by centuries. Overflow protection arrived in Linux 6.10 (0c68458b0a58).

What to take away. The vDSO began as a way to make one system call cheaper and has become something more general: the place the kernel puts code and data that user space may execute and read directly. Three things about it are worth carrying out of this section.

The first is that the vDSO does not approximate the kernel’s answer. It is the same mult/shift arithmetic against the same snapshot, which is why a program can mix clock_gettime() with a syscall that returns a timestamp and never see time move backwards. Every optimization in this section had to be compatible with that, and several — the wide-multiply fallback, the negative-motion check, the retry loop — exist precisely because the cheap version of the arithmetic would not have been.

The second is that the hard part of a lockless protocol is not correctness but cost. The seqlock guarantees that a torn read is discarded, and once that is settled the remaining design work is about making sure a discarded read is also a cheap one — hence normalization outside the retry loop, hence the sentinel values that let a failed counter read fall through the existing retry rather than needing a branch of its own. A kernel fast path can rely on being able to disable preemption; a user-space one cannot rely on anything.

The third is that the fallbacks are the interface. A vDSO that only worked would be easy; what makes the code intricate is that every path must degrade into a real system call — for an unreadable clocksource, an unsupported clock ID, a time namespace, a paravirtualized counter that has stopped being trustworthy — and must do so without the caller being able to tell. The subsections on clock routing, the fallback path and clock modes are all describing the same requirement from different sides.

Two historical footnotes. The vsyscall page at 0xFFFFFFFFFF600000 is still nominally present on x86_64 but is now emulated through page-fault traps, or disabled entirely, and nothing should be using it. And the generic implementation described here is recent: the consolidation of the per-architecture copies into lib/vdso/ only completed during the 6.13–6.17 cycles, so older kernels will not match this description in detail even where they match it in principle.

System Calls Related to Timing

Everything up to this point has been machinery the kernel runs for its own purposes. This section is the other side: the interfaces user space actually calls, and how each one lands on the subsystems already described. The list is longer than it needs to be, and understanding why is most of the story.

Three forces have shaped it:

  • Nothing is ever removed. alarm() dates from Version 7 Unix, setitimer() from 4.2BSD, gettimeofday() from the same era. Each was superseded, none was deleted, and all of them still work — so the kernel carries three generations of timer API simultaneously, with the older ones reimplemented on top of the newest machinery.
  • POSIX specified an interface, not an implementation. timer_create() promised timers on any clock, including per-process and per-thread CPU time, delivering any signal to any thread. Meeting that promise required the kernel to invent an indirection layer — struct k_clock — and to find room in the clockid_t number space for clocks that are not fixed constants at all.
  • Signals are a poor delivery mechanism. They cannot be waited on with epoll(), they are hard to attribute when several timers share one signal number, and they interact badly with threads. This is why timerfd exists, and why it is the interface most new code should use.

The section works through the interfaces roughly in the order a program would meet them:

  1. Reading and setting a clock — clock_gettime(), clock_settime(), clock_getres(), and the dispatch layer that makes an arbitrary clock ID mean something.
  2. Sleeping — nanosleep(), clock_nanosleep(), and what happens when a signal arrives mid-sleep.
  3. POSIX timers — timer_create() and friends, and how the kernel finds a timer given only an integer ID.
  4. timerfd — the same timers delivered as file descriptors.
  5. The legacy interval timers — setitimer() and alarm().
  6. Disciplining the clock — adjtimex() and clock_adjtime().
  7. The oldest interfaces — gettimeofday(), settimeofday(), and time().

Version history. The visible API is remarkably stable — almost every call described here would compile against a 2.6 kernel. What changed is underneath. Linux 2.6 had just acquired POSIX timers and had not yet acquired timerfd; every timer was ultimately a timer-wheel entry with jiffy granularity, and the whole subsystem was rebuilt on hrtimers over the following years. More recently, Linux 6.15 reworked how POSIX timers are looked up and freed — the per-process list that used to serve as the lookup path was replaced by a global RCU hash table, for reasons discussed below — and 6.17 brought the auxiliary clocks into the same dispatch table, so clock_gettime() and clock_adjtime() reach them through exactly the path described below (though not timer_create() — clock_aux deliberately provides no timer operations). A separate strand of change is the y2038 work: every interface here now has a __kernel_timespec form with a 64-bit tv_sec, and the 32-bit compatibility entry points are conversion wrappers around the same code.

The table below summarizes the complete set of timing-related system calls in Linux 7.0.12:

Table 6-174. Timing System Calls Overview

clock_settime()Set wall-clock time (CAP_SYS_TIME)posix-timers.c
clock_getres()Query clock resolutionvDSO or posix-timers.c
clock_nanosleep()Sleep with specified clock and flagsposix-timers.c → hrtimer
nanosleep()Relative sleep (CLOCK_MONOTONIC)hrtimer.c
timer_create()Create a POSIX per-process timerposix-timers.c
timer_settime()Arm/disarm a POSIX timerposix-timers.c
timer_gettime()Query remaining time on a POSIX timerposix-timers.c
timer_getoverrun()Get overrun count for a POSIX timerposix-timers.c

time()Get seconds since epoch (legacy)vDSO fast path, else time.c

Two qualifications on that last column. Every path named there is under kernel/time/ unless the table says otherwise, and the vDSO rows name a fast path rather than an alternative implementation — the system call still exists, is still the fallback, and is the only path taken when the active clocksource is not vDSO-capable. Second, the four clock_*() entry points are compiled from kernel/time/posix-timers.c only when CONFIG_POSIX_TIMERS is set. A kernel built without it — the configuration a deeply embedded system might choose — still provides clock_gettime(), clock_getres(), clock_settime() and clock_nanosleep() from kernel/time/posix-stubs.c, restricted to the basic clock IDs, while timer_create() and its relatives return -ENOSYS. The reduced build is why this chapter treats the clock-reading calls and the timer-creating calls as separate facilities even though they share a header.

clock_gettime() and clock_settime()

The clock_gettime() system call is the primary interface for reading the current time. It accepts a clock ID and returns the time as a timespec structure (seconds + nanoseconds). For most clock IDs, it is accelerated through the vDSO (see the preceding section) and never enters the kernel at all. When the vDSO path is unavailable, the kernel implementation dispatches through a k_clock operations table:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c */
SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_gettime, const clockid_t, which_clock,
                struct __kernel_timespec __user *, tp)
{
    const struct k_clock *kc = clockid_to_kclock(which_clock);
    struct timespec64 kernel_tp;
    int error;

    if (!kc)
        return -EINVAL;

    error = kc->clock_get_timespec(which_clock, &kernel_tp);

    if (!error && put_timespec64(&kernel_tp, tp))
        error = -EFAULT;

    return error;
}

The clockid_to_kclock() function maps a clock ID to a k_clock structure containing the operations for that clock type. Standard clocks (REALTIME, MONOTONIC, etc.) use a common implementation that reads the timekeeper. It is worth looking at how that mapping actually works, because the clockid_t number space is not the flat enumeration it appears to be.

The Shape of the clockid_t Namespace

POSIX defines clockid_t as an integer and hands out a handful of named constants. Linux needed more than constants: it had to name a clock that measures one particular process’s CPU time, and later, a clock that lives on one particular piece of hardware. Neither can be a compile-time constant, because both are chosen at runtime. The solution was to partition the integer:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c */
static const struct k_clock *clockid_to_kclock(const clockid_t id)
{
    clockid_t idx = id;

    if (id < 0) {
        return (id & CLOCKFD_MASK) == CLOCKFD ?
            &clock_posix_dynamic : &clock_posix_cpu;
    }

    if (id >= ARRAY_SIZE(posix_clocks))
        return NULL;

    return posix_clocks[array_index_nospec(idx, ARRAY_SIZE(posix_clocks))];
}

A non-negative ID is an index into the static posix_clocks[] table — the eleven named clocks plus, since Linux 6.17, the whole CLOCK_AUX ... CLOCK_AUX_LAST range mapped to a single clock_aux entry. The index is passed through array_index_nospec(), which clamps it to the array bound in a way the CPU’s speculative execution cannot bypass; without it, a bounds check that is correct architecturally still allows a Spectre v1 gadget to speculatively load past the end of the table.

A negative ID carries a payload. The low three bits say which kind of clock, bit 2 distinguishes per-thread from per-process, and the remaining bits hold a bitwise-complemented PID or file descriptor:

/* include/linux/posix-timers.h */
static inline clockid_t make_process_cpuclock(const unsigned int pid,
                                              const clockid_t clock)
{
    return ((~pid) << 3) | clock;
}

static inline clockid_t fd_to_clockid(const int fd)
{
    return make_process_cpuclock((unsigned int) fd, CLOCKFD);
}

Complementing the PID is what makes the result negative, which is how the encoded IDs stay clear of the static table. Two families share the space, told apart by CLOCKFD_MASK:

  • CPU-time clocks (clock_posix_cpu). CLOCK_PROCESS_CPUTIME_ID and CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID are just the encodings for the calling process and thread; the same encoding with someone else’s PID names their CPU clock, which is what clock_getcpuclockid() in libc returns.
  • Dynamic clocks (clock_posix_dynamic, kernel/time/posix-clock.c). Here the payload is an open file descriptor. This is the mechanism behind PTP: opening /dev/ptp0 and passing fd_to_clockid(fd) to clock_gettime() reads the network card’s hardware clock, and passing it to clock_adjtime() disciplines that clock rather than the system one. The k_clock operations forward to the driver’s posix_clock_operations.

This is why the k_clock indirection exists at all. From the system call’s point of view clock_gettime() is one function; underneath, the same call can read a global timekeeper, sum a thread group’s scheduler runtime, or issue a register read to a NIC over PCIe.

clock_settime() modifies the system’s wall-clock time. It requires CAP_SYS_TIME and only works on CLOCK_REALTIME: of all the entries in posix_clocks[], exactly one supplies a clock_set method, and the syscall returns -EINVAL for every clock that does not. That is not a permission check but a structural one — there is no code path that can move CLOCK_MONOTONIC, which is what makes the guarantee in its name worth anything. Note also where the permission check lives: the comment in SYSCALL_DEFINE2(clock_settime, …) says it is deliberately deferred to the setter callback, because different clocks require different capabilities.

Changing the wall clock is the most disruptive thing in this chapter, and the kernel does three things at once to contain the damage. It writes the new time into the timekeeper under tk_core.seq; it calls update_vsyscall() inside that same seqcount write section, so a concurrent vDSO reader either retries or sees the new value and can never observe a mixture; and it calls clock_was_set(), which walks the CPUs and re-evaluates every armed CLOCK_REALTIME hrtimer, since an absolute deadline that was ten minutes away may now be in the past. This is also what wakes TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET readers. User space sees the new time immediately, without waiting for a tick.

clock_getres() returns the resolution (granularity) of a clock. For high-resolution clocks it returns hrtimer_resolution (typically 1 ns with CONFIG_HIGH_RES_TIMERS); for coarse clocks it returns TICK_NSEC (4 ms at HZ=250). This call is also vDSO-accelerated — it simply reads the hrtimer_res field from the vvar page.

clock_nanosleep() and nanosleep()

Sleeping looks like the simplest thing in this section and is not. A sleep has to survive a signal arriving in the middle of it, and POSIX requires that the call report how much time was left so the caller can resume — which sounds reasonable until you notice that "resume the remaining time" is the wrong behaviour for anything periodic. A task that wants to run every 10 ms and is interrupted at 7 ms should not sleep 3 ms more and then 10 ms from there; that way its period drifts by the cost of every signal it ever receives. The distinction between the two system calls here is largely about giving callers a way to say which they want.

These system calls put the calling process to sleep for a specified duration using hrtimer-based high-resolution timers. nanosleep() is the simpler interface — it always sleeps relative to CLOCK_MONOTONIC:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c */
SYSCALL_DEFINE2(nanosleep, struct __kernel_timespec __user *, rqtp,
                struct __kernel_timespec __user *, rmtp)
{
    struct timespec64 tu;

    if (get_timespec64(&tu, rqtp))
        return -EFAULT;
    if (!timespec64_valid(&tu))
        return -EINVAL;

    current->restart_block.fn = do_no_restart_syscall;
    current->restart_block.nanosleep.type = rmtp ? TT_NATIVE : TT_NONE;
    current->restart_block.nanosleep.rmtp = rmtp;

    return hrtimer_nanosleep(timespec64_to_ktime(tu), HRTIMER_MODE_REL,
                             CLOCK_MONOTONIC);
}

clock_nanosleep() offers more control — the caller can choose any POSIX clock and specify either relative or absolute sleep using the TIMER_ABSTIME flag. Absolute sleep is important for periodic tasks: instead of sleeping for a relative interval (which accumulates drift), the task sleeps until an absolute wall-clock time, adjusting for any time already spent processing.

What happens when a signal arrives is the part most often described wrongly, including in manual pages, so it is worth following the code. do_nanosleep() returns -ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK, which is an internal value the system call never returns to user space. What it becomes depends entirely on whether a signal handler is about to run:

  • A handler runs. handle_signal() rewrites the return value to -EINTR and stops. It does this for ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK unconditionally — unlike ERESTARTSYS, it does not consult SA_RESTART. Installing a handler with SA_RESTART therefore does not make a sleep resume automatically, which surprises almost everyone. The kernel writes the remainder to rmtp and it is the application’s job to sleep again.
  • No handler runs — the signal was a stop or continue, or was consumed some other way. Only then does the kernel use the restart block, rewinding the instruction pointer to re-enter through restart_syscall(2), which lands in hrtimer_nanosleep_restart().

Two details of the restart are worth noticing, because both exist to stop the sleep drifting. The restart block stores hrtimer_get_expires() — an absolute deadline — not the remaining duration, and hrtimer_nanosleep_restart() re-arms in HRTIMER_MODE_ABS. A sleep interrupted and restarted a hundred times therefore still ends at the instant the original relative interval named. The rmtp value handed to user space is a genuine remaining duration and cannot offer the same guarantee, since an arbitrary amount of time passes while the handler runs.
