Absolute sleeps skip the mechanism entirely. hrtimer_nanosleep() tests the mode and substitutes -ERESTARTNOHAND, with the comment “Absolute timers do not update the rmtp value and restart”. There is nothing to remember: re-executing the original clock_nanosleep() with the same arguments targets the same instant, so the no-handler path simply rewinds and re-issues the call. The handler path still yields EINTR, and rmtp is not written — an absolute sleep has no meaningful remainder to report. This is the concrete reason to prefer TIMER_ABSTIME for anything periodic: it is not merely that the caller avoids arithmetic, it is that the deadline survives interruption without the caller having to reconstruct it.

Table 6-175. nanosleep() vs. clock_nanosleep()
Featurenanosleep()clock_nanosleep()
ClockCLOCK_MONOTONIC onlyAny POSIX clock
ModeRelative onlyRelative or absolute (TIMER_ABSTIME)
Backinghrtimer on the task’s stackhrtimer on the task’s stack
Timer slack appliedYes — current->timer_slack_nsYes, both modes
Signal, handler installedEINTR; remainder in rmtpRelative: as nanosleep(). Absolute: EINTR, no rmtp
Signal, no handlerRestarted to the original absolute deadlineRelative: same. Absolute: original call re-issued
RecommendationSimple delaysPeriodic tasks, absolute deadlines

The row that most often disappoints is the third. It is tempting to write “precision: 1 ns” here, because these calls are hrtimer-backed and clock_getres() answers 1 ns, but neither figure describes when the task actually runs again. hrtimer_nanosleep() arms the timer with a range, not a point:

/* kernel/time/hrtimer.c */
hrtimer_set_expires_range_ns(&t.timer, rqtp, current->timer_slack_ns);

The default value of timer_slack_ns, set in init/init_task.c and inherited by every process, is 50,000 — fifty microseconds. A nanosleep() of one millisecond may therefore legitimately return anywhere in a 50 µs window after the deadline, and it is not a bug or a scheduling artifact when it does: the kernel was told it may fire the timer early into a batch with other nearby expiries, which is the whole purpose of the deferrable-timer machinery described earlier in this chapter. Fifty thousand nanoseconds of designed-in imprecision sits underneath an interface named for nanoseconds.

Two ways out exist, and the important one is automatic. Any task with a real-time scheduling policy has its slack forced to zero — __setscheduler_params() does it on every policy change, with the comment “rt-policy tasks do not have a timerslack”, and restores the saved default when the task returns to a fair policy. A SCHED_FIFO thread therefore gets the precision the interface advertises without asking. Everything else must ask, through prctl(PR_SET_TIMERSLACK, 1); passing zero restores the inherited default rather than requesting zero slack.

POSIX Timers: timer_create() / timer_settime() / timer_delete()

The interfaces so far let a program ask what time it is, or stop until a time arrives. Neither lets it be told when a time arrives while it gets on with something else. That is what POSIX timers add: a timer becomes an object with a lifetime and an identity, created once and then armed, re-armed, queried and destroyed independently of whatever the program is doing.

The cost of that generality is visible in the implementation. A timer can be based on any clock, including CPU-time clocks that no hardware timer can be programmed against; it can target the process or one specific thread; and its expiry must be delivered asynchronously through the signal machinery, which introduces problems — signals of the same number coalesce, and delivery is not instantaneous — that the overrun counter exists to paper over.

POSIX timers (defined by POSIX.1b) are kernel-managed timer objects that deliver notifications — typically signals — when they expire. They are the successor to the older setitimer() mechanism and offer significantly more flexibility:

  • Any clock — timers can be based on CLOCK_REALTIME, CLOCK_MONOTONIC, CLOCK_BOOTTIME, or even per-process/per-thread CPU time clocks
  • Flexible notification — SIGEV_SIGNAL delivers to the process, SIGEV_NONE delivers nothing at all (the timer is never queued; it exists only to be polled with timer_gettime()), and SIGEV_THREAD_ID targets one specific thread of the group
  • Overrun counting — timer_getoverrun() reports how many expirations were missed while the signal was pending, preventing signal queue overflow

Two things about that list are usually got wrong, and good_sigevent() settles both in twenty lines.

SIGEV_THREAD_ID is not a fourth value alongside the others; it is the bit 4, and the kernel matches on SIGEV_SIGNAL | SIGEV_THREAD_ID. The distinction matters enough that kernel/time/posix-timers.c opens with a compile-time assertion — an #error that fires if SIGEV_THREAD_ID ever comes to share a bit with SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_NONE or SIGEV_THREAD. The thread it names must be in the caller’s own thread group, which same_thread_group() checks; a timer cannot be aimed at another process’s thread.

And SIGEV_THREAD, the POSIX-specified mode in which each expiry runs a function on a new thread, is not implemented by the kernel at all. It appears in good_sigevent() only as a case label falling through to the same handling as SIGEV_SIGNAL: the kernel validates the signal number and queues an ordinary signal. Everything that makes the mode useful happens in libc. The comment beside the constant in include/uapi/asm-generic/siginfo.h has said so, in the same words, for the better part of three decades — that SIGEV_THREAD “will have to be handled from userspace, libpthread transmuting it to SIGEV_SIGNAL, which the thread manager then catches and does the appropriate nonsense.” It is worth knowing which side of the boundary that thread comes from before trying to reason about its priority, its stack, or what happens when expiries arrive faster than it can service them.

/* Creating and using a POSIX timer (user-space example) */
timer_t timerid;
struct sigevent sev = {
    .sigev_notify = SIGEV_SIGNAL,
    .sigev_signo  = SIGRTMIN,
};
struct itimerspec its = {
    .it_value    = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 500000000 },  /* First: 500ms */
    .it_interval = { .tv_sec = 1, .tv_nsec = 0 },          /* Then: every 1s */
};

timer_create(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &sev, &timerid);
timer_settime(timerid, 0, &its, NULL);
/* ... SIGRTMIN delivered periodically ... */
timer_delete(timerid);

Internally, each POSIX timer is represented by a k_itimer structure containing an hrtimer. When timer_settime() is called, the kernel arms the hrtimer with the requested expiry time. When the hrtimer fires, the kernel increments the overrun counter and queues a signal to the target process or thread. The timer is identified by a per-process timer_t ID, and every timer the process owns is linked on signal->posix_timers.

How the Kernel Finds a Timer

Every one of these system calls takes a timer_t and must turn it into a struct k_itimer. That lookup is on the hot path of every timer_settime(), and it used to be a walk of signal->posix_timers under the process’s sighand->siglock — which meant that a process with a few thousand timers paid a linear scan, and that the scan serialized against signal delivery. Linux 6.15 replaced it with a global hash table:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c */
static struct timer_hash_bucket *hash_bucket(struct signal_struct *sig,
                                             unsigned int nr)
{
    return &timer_buckets[jhash2((u32 *)&sig, sizeof(sig) / sizeof(u32), nr)
                          & timer_hashmask];
}

static struct k_itimer *posix_timer_by_id(timer_t id)
{
    struct signal_struct *sig = current->signal;
    struct timer_hash_bucket *bucket = hash_bucket(sig, id);
    struct k_itimer *timer;

    hlist_for_each_entry_rcu(timer, &bucket->head, t_hash) {
        /* timer->it_signal can be set concurrently */
        if ((READ_ONCE(timer->it_signal) == sig) && (timer->it_id == id))
            return timer;
    }
    return NULL;
}

Three points are worth drawing out.

First, the key is the pair (signal, ID), not the ID alone. Timer IDs are per-process, so two processes routinely hold the same numeric ID; hashing the signal_struct pointer together with the ID both disambiguates them and spreads different processes’ timers across buckets. The table is sized by alloc_large_system_hash() at 512 * num_possible_cpus() entries, so on a large machine it is genuinely large.

Second, the lookup takes no lock. It walks an RCU-protected list, and the timer is kept alive across the lookup by an rcuref_t in k_itimer rather than by holding the bucket lock. Only the insertion path takes bucket->lock, and then only to confirm that the ID it wants is not already present.

Third, the field the lookup compares against does double duty. it_signal is a pointer, so bit 0 is always zero in a valid value — and the kernel sets that bit deliberately, twice in a timer’s life:

  • Between allocating an ID and finishing initialization, so the timer occupies its slot (nothing else can be handed that ID) while posix_timer_by_id() still fails to match it. A concurrent timer_settime() on a guessed ID cannot reach a half-built timer.
  • At the start of deletion, before the timer is unhashed, so the ID cannot be reused while the old timer is still being torn down.

posix_sig_owner() masks the bit out for the paths that need the real pointer; posixtimer_valid() tests it. The per-process list survives, but its job is now teardown — exit_itimers() walks it when the last thread of a thread group exits — rather than lookup.

Key implementation detail: when timer_settime() is called on an already-armed timer, the kernel must cancel the existing hrtimer first. If the hrtimer callback is currently running on another CPU, timer_try_to_cancel() returns -1 and the operation reports TIMER_RETRY to its caller, which loops:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c — posix_timer_delete() */
while (timer->kclock->timer_del(timer) == TIMER_RETRY) {
    guard(rcu)();
    spin_unlock_irq(&timer->it_lock);
    timer_wait_running(timer);
    spin_lock_irq(&timer->it_lock);
}

This is not a busy-wait. The loop drops it_lock — continuing to hold it is precisely what would stop the callback from making progress — and calls the clock’s timer_wait_running(), which on a PREEMPT_RT kernel blocks on the hrtimer’s expiry lock rather than spinning. RCU protection is taken first, because once it_lock is dropped the timer could otherwise be freed underneath the loop.

Each timer also carries a three-state field, it_status, that both the retry logic and the query path depend on:

  • POSIX_TIMER_DISARMED — not queued in any timer base. A one-shot timer that has fired ends here, and a SIGEV_NONE timer stays here permanently, since such timers are never actually queued.
  • POSIX_TIMER_ARMED — queued and waiting to expire.
  • POSIX_TIMER_REQUEUE_PENDING — an interval timer that has expired and whose signal is queued, but which has not yet been re-armed. Re-arming deliberately waits until the signal is dequeued, and that is what makes the overrun count meaningful: every expiry falling inside that window is counted rather than generating another signal.

Signal Delivery and Overrun Accounting

The three-state field above hints at a subtlety: for an interval timer the interesting work does not happen when the timer expires, but when the signal it queued is finally dequeued. Expiry merely queues a signal and marks the timer POSIX_TIMER_REQUEUE_PENDING; everything else waits. Linux 6.13 reworked this path substantially, and the changes are visible to applications.

The reason for deferring is a race that is impossible to close any other way. A signal can sit queued for an arbitrary time, during which the application is free to call timer_settime() to re-arm the timer with a new interval, or timer_delete() to destroy it outright. If the kernel had already committed to re-arming at expiry time, it would be re-arming a timer whose parameters the application has since replaced, and delivering a signal describing an expiry the application has explicitly cancelled. The kernel therefore tags each queued signal with a sequence number and checks it on the way out:

/* kernel/time/posix-timers.c, abridged */
static bool __posixtimer_deliver_signal(struct kernel_siginfo *info,
                                        struct k_itimer *timr)
{
    guard(spinlock)(&timr->it_lock);

    /* Modified or deleted since the signal was queued?  Drop it. */
    if (timr->it_signal_seq != timr->it_sigqueue_seq ||
        WARN_ON_ONCE(!posixtimer_valid(timr)))
        return false;

    if (!timr->it_interval ||
        WARN_ON_ONCE(timr->it_status != POSIX_TIMER_REQUEUE_PENDING))
        return true;                       /* one-shot: nothing to rearm */

    timr->kclock->timer_rearm(timr);
    timr->it_status        = POSIX_TIMER_ARMED;
    timr->it_overrun_last  = timr->it_overrun;
    timr->it_overrun       = -1LL;
    ++timr->it_signal_seq;
    info->si_overrun = timer_overrun_to_int(timr);
    return true;
}

it_signal_seq is incremented by every operation that changes the timer’s identity, while it_sigqueue_seq records its value at the moment the signal was queued. A mismatch means the timer moved on while the signal was in flight, and returning false causes the signal-delivery code in kernel/signal.c to discard it silently. Before 6.13 such a stale signal could still be delivered, carrying an overrun count belonging to a timer configuration that no longer existed.

The same function shows where the overrun count now comes from. it_overrun accumulates as the timer keeps expiring with its signal still pending; at delivery it is snapshotted into it_overrun_last, the live counter is reset to -1, and the snapshot is what both si_overrun in the siginfo and a subsequent timer_getoverrun() report. Computing it here rather than at expiry is what makes the two agree: previously the signal and the syscall could sample the counter at different moments and return different numbers for the same expiry. timer_overrun_to_int() saturates the 64-bit internal count at INT_MAX, since the POSIX interface is an int.

One case remains, and it is the awkward one. If the target signal is set to SIG_IGN, there is no dequeue and so no delivery to hang the re-arm on — yet a periodic timer that stops re-arming is simply broken, and one that re-arms itself from the ignore path spins generating signals nobody reads. Linux 6.13 resolves it with a holding area: posixtimer_sig_ignore() puts a periodic timer whose signal is being ignored onto the per-process ignored_posix_timers list instead of dropping its reference. If the application later installs a handler, posixtimer_sig_unignore() walks that list and re-queues the sigqueue so the ordinary delivery path can decide whether to re-arm — deliberately not deciding it there, since re-arming needs it_lock and the caller holds sighand->siglock, which is the wrong order. Timers that are non-periodic, or already deleted, take the old path and just drop their reference.

The distinction matters to timer_gettime(), which must report a sensible remaining time for a timer that is logically periodic but momentarily not queued. Seeing anything other than POSIX_TIMER_ARMED on an interval timer, it calls the clock’s timer_forward() to advance the expiry past the present — accumulating overruns as it goes — before computing what to return.

timerfd: File-Descriptor Timers

The timerfd interface (added in Linux 2.6.22) provides timers as file descriptors, making them integrable with epoll(), poll(), and select(). This is the preferred timer mechanism for event-driven applications (servers, GUI frameworks, state machines) because timers can be multiplexed alongside sockets, pipes, and other I/O sources in a single event loop:

/* User-space example: timerfd with epoll */
int tfd = timerfd_create(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, TFD_NONBLOCK | TFD_CLOEXEC);
struct itimerspec its = {
    .it_value    = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 100000000 },  /* 100ms */
    .it_interval = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 100000000 },  /* periodic */
};
timerfd_settime(tfd, 0, &its, NULL);

/* Add to epoll alongside sockets */
struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = tfd };
epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, tfd, &ev);

/* In event loop: */
uint64_t expirations;
read(tfd, &expirations, sizeof(expirations));  /* Returns # of expirations */

Internally, a timerfd_ctx structure wraps an hrtimer (or an alarm timer for alarm clocks). When it fires, it increments a ticks counter and wakes any task waiting on the timerfd’s wait queue. A read() returns the accumulated expiration count as a 64-bit integer and resets the counter to zero.

The interesting part is where a periodic timerfd gets re-armed, because it is not where one would expect. timerfd_tmrproc(), the expiry callback, returns HRTIMER_NORESTART even for a timer with a non-zero interval. The re-arming happens in read(), and the comment says why:

/* fs/timerfd.c, in timerfd_read() */
if (ctx->expired && ctx->tintv) {
    /*
     * If tintv != 0, this is a periodic timer that
     * needs to be re-armed. We avoid doing it in the timer
     * callback to avoid DoS attacks specifying a very
     * short timer period.
     */
    ticks += hrtimer_forward_now(&ctx->t.tmr, ctx->tintv) - 1;
    hrtimer_restart(&ctx->t.tmr);
}

An unprivileged process can ask for a one-nanosecond interval. Re-arming from the callback would put that timer back into the clock-event hardware from inside the timer interrupt, forever, and the machine would make no further progress — a denial of service costing two system calls to mount. Deferring the re-arm to read() makes the cost self-limiting: a process that does not read gets exactly one expiry, and a process that does read pays for the catch-up in its own context, where hrtimer_forward_now() advances the timer past the present in one step and reports how many periods it skipped.

This has a consequence worth stating plainly, because it distinguishes timerfd from every other timer in this chapter. A periodic timerfd nobody reads is not running. It fired once and stopped; the count a later read() returns is computed at that moment from the interval and the elapsed time, not accumulated as the periods went by. For an event loop this is exactly right — the count answers “how many periods did I miss?” regardless of how long the loop was blocked — but code that assumes a timerfd keeps ticking in the background while the process is busy elsewhere has the model backwards.

The two _ALARM clocks in the table are a different mechanism wearing the same interface. An ordinary hrtimer stops when the system suspends; an alarm timer additionally programs the platform's real-time clock so that the expiry wakes the machine up. That is why they require CAP_WAKE_ALARM — any process able to arm one can prevent a device from staying asleep. They are the kernel side of Android's AlarmManager, and are shared by timerfd and POSIX timers alike: alarm_clock appears in the same posix_clocks[] dispatch table as every other clock.

That shared machinery had a long-standing defect fixed only in Linux 7.0. alarm_timer_forward(), the operation used to advance a periodic alarm timer past the present and count the expiries skipped, passed the interval and the current time to alarm_forward() in the wrong order — so the delta it computed was meaningless and the overrun count wrong. The bug (5d16467ae563) had been present since the callback was introduced, which says something about how rarely overrun counts on wake-up alarms are checked.

Table 6-176. timerfd Supported Clocks and Flags
Clock IDSupportedNotes
CLOCK_REALTIME✓TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET detects settimeofday() — but only together with TFD_TIMER_ABSTIME
CLOCK_MONOTONIC✓Default choice — immune to wall-clock changes
CLOCK_BOOTTIME✓Survives suspend; useful for hardware watchdogs
CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM✓Wakes system from suspend (CAP_WAKE_ALARM required)
CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM✓Wakes system from suspend (CAP_WAKE_ALARM required)
Table 6-177. POSIX Timers vs. timerfd Comparison
FeaturePOSIX Timerstimerfd
NotificationSignals (SIGEV_SIGNAL, SIGEV_THREAD_ID)File descriptor (readable when expired)
MultiplexingSignals only (no epoll)epoll/poll/select compatible
CPU time clocksSupported (CLOCK_*_CPUTIME_ID)Not supported
Overrun handlingtimer_getoverrun()read() returns count
Across fork()Not inherited — the child has noneDescriptor duplicated; both processes share one timer
Across exec()Destroyed — exit_itimers() runs from begin_new_exec()Survives unless created with TFD_CLOEXEC
Typical useReal-time apps, profilingEvent-driven servers, GUI frameworks

The two lifetime rows used to be one, and collapsing them hid the trap. A timerfd inherited across fork() is not a copy of the timer — both descriptors refer to the same timerfd_ctx, so the two processes draw from a single expiration counter and whichever reads first takes the ticks the other was waiting for. POSIX timers have the opposite asymmetry: nothing survives fork(), but a timer would survive exec() if the kernel let it, which is why begin_new_exec() calls exit_itimers() explicitly. Neither mechanism is simply “inherited” or simply “not”; each is inherited along one axis and destroyed along the other, and they disagree about which.

One flag in the preceding table also deserves more than a cell. TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET asks the kernel to abort the timer if wall-clock time is stepped, so that a program sleeping until an absolute CLOCK_REALTIME instant learns its deadline has moved rather than waking at the wrong moment; a subsequent read() returns -ECANCELED instead of a count. But timerfd_setup_cancel() arms the mechanism only when the clock is CLOCK_REALTIME or CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM and TFD_TIMER_ABSTIME is also set; any other combination silently takes the else branch and removes the timer from the cancel list. Passing the flag on a relative timer is not an error and produces no diagnostic — it simply does nothing, which is the most expensive kind of nothing.

Legacy: setitimer() and alarm()

These two calls are older than almost everything else in this chapter — alarm() goes back to Version 7 Unix, setitimer() to 4.2BSD — and they are worth reading for two reasons. They remain extremely common in existing code, so a kernel engineer will meet them; and their limitations are exactly the ones POSIX timers were designed to remove. There are three of them per process and no more, each hardwired to one signal, with no way to ask how many expiries were missed.

The setitimer() system call creates interval timers that deliver periodic signals. It predates POSIX timers and offers three timer policies:

Table 6-178. setitimer() Timer Types
TimerClock BasisSignalDescription
ITIMER_REALElapsed time (CLOCK_MONOTONIC)SIGALRMFires after the requested interval of elapsed time; an hrtimer in signal->real_timer
ITIMER_VIRTUALUser-mode CPU timeSIGVTALRMFires after process accumulates user-mode CPU time
ITIMER_PROFUser + kernel CPU timeSIGPROFFires after total (user + system) CPU time; used for profiling

alarm(seconds) is a simplified wrapper that sets ITIMER_REAL for a one-shot SIGALRM delivery after the specified number of seconds. Internally it calls do_setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, ...) with a zero interval:

/* kernel/time/itimer.c */
static unsigned int alarm_setitimer(unsigned int seconds)
{
    struct itimerspec64 it_new, it_old;

    it_new.it_value.tv_sec = seconds;
    it_new.it_value.tv_nsec = 0;
    it_new.it_interval.tv_sec = it_new.it_interval.tv_nsec = 0;

    do_setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, &it_new, &it_old);

    /* Round up remaining time — never return 0 if alarm is pending */
    if ((!it_old.it_value.tv_sec && it_old.it_value.tv_nsec) ||
          it_old.it_value.tv_nsec >= (NSEC_PER_SEC / 2))
        it_old.it_value.tv_sec++;

    return it_old.it_value.tv_sec;
}

The word “wrapper” is meant literally, and it has a consequence that catches people. alarm() is not a separate facility: it arms the same ITIMER_REAL timer, so a library that calls alarm() silently cancels a caller’s setitimer(ITIMER_REAL, …) and vice versa, and the value alarm() returns is the remaining time on whatever was armed before — possibly by someone else. There is exactly one of these timers per process and no way to find out who owns it. This is the concrete form of the limitation the section opened with, and it is unfixable within the interface: the timer is named by a constant rather than by a handle.

Notice also which clock ITIMER_REAL uses. Despite the name, and despite decades of documentation calling it real time, copy_signal() arms signal->real_timer on CLOCK_MONOTONIC, so a settimeofday() jump does not move an alarm(). “Real” here means elapsed rather than wall-clock, and the behaviour is the one callers want.

Three further properties follow from where the state lives. All three timers are fields of signal_struct, so they are shared by every thread in the group — two threads calling setitimer(ITIMER_PROF, …) are configuring one timer, and ITIMER_VIRTUAL and ITIMER_PROF measure the CPU time of the whole thread group rather than of the caller. They are not inherited across fork(): copy_signal() allocates a zeroed signal_struct and arms a fresh real_timer, so the child starts with all three disarmed. And they do survive exec(), because signal_struct survives it — the exact opposite of POSIX timers, which exit_itimers() destroys on the exec path. A program that arms an alarm() and then execs a helper has handed that helper a SIGALRM it knows nothing about.

These interfaces are largely obsolete — new code should use POSIX timers or timerfd. However, they remain widely used in existing software, and ITIMER_PROF in particular is still the mechanism behind sampling profilers, so they are maintained indefinitely.

In Linux 2.6, ITIMER_REAL was implemented using a timer wheel dynamic timer (real_timer in the process descriptor), while ITIMER_VIRTUAL and ITIMER_PROF were decremented on each tick by account_it_virt() and account_it_prof(). In Linux 7.0.12, ITIMER_REAL uses an hrtimer for nanosecond-precision delivery, and the virtual/profile timers are managed through the POSIX CPU timer subsystem (run_posix_cpu_timers()). The old it_real_value, it_virt_value, it_prof_value fields are gone from the process descriptor.

adjtimex() and clock_adjtime() — NTP Discipline

Abruptly changing the system clock with clock_settime() is disruptive — it can break make builds that depend on file timestamps, confuse log correlation, and violate monotonic clock guarantees for applications. Instead, systems use NTP (Network Time Protocol) to gradually slew the clock toward the correct time. The kernel's NTP state machine is controlled through adjtimex() (and the newer clock_adjtime() which can adjust clocks other than CLOCK_REALTIME).

The system call receives a timex structure containing adjustment parameters, updates the kernel's NTP state, and returns the current state. The NTP state machine in kernel/time/ntp.c uses these parameters to adjust the mult field of the timekeeping clocksource — making the clock tick slightly faster or slower to converge toward the reference time:

Table 6-179. NTP Adjustment Parameters (struct timex)
FieldUnitEffect
modesbitmaskSelects which of the other fields are inputs (ADJ_OFFSET, ADJ_FREQUENCY, ADJ_TICK, ADJ_TAI, …); a zero modes makes the call a pure query
offsetns if STA_NANO, else µsPhase offset to correct — the kernel slews toward this target
freqPPM scaled by 216Long-term frequency correction; compensates for crystal oscillator drift. Clamped to ±500 PPM (MAXFREQ)
maxerrorµsMaximum estimated error bound; the kernel adds 500 µs per second on its own and clamps at NTP_PHASE_LIMIT
esterrorµsEstimated time error (NTP dispersion), supplied by the daemon
statusbitmaskPLL/FLL mode, nanosecond mode (STA_NANO), leap second pending/in-progress, unsynchronized flag
constantshift countPLL time constant, clamped to 0–10 (MAXTC); the phase correction applied per second is offset >> (SHIFT_PLL + constant), so a larger value converges more slowly and rejects more noise
tickµsNominal tick duration (for coarse adjustments)
taisecondsTAI−UTC offset; readable by anyone, settable only through ADJ_TAI

Two things about that table are easy to miss and both cause real bugs. The first is modes: struct timex is used for both directions, and every call returns the full structure, so a program that fills in offset without setting ADJ_OFFSET has written a value the kernel ignores, while a program that sets a mode bit it did not mean to has silently disciplined the system clock. The idiomatic read is modes = 0, and it is also the only unprivileged one: timekeeping_validate_timex() rejects any non-zero modes with -EPERM unless the caller holds CAP_SYS_TIME. The second is that offset changes unit under the caller’s feet. When STA_NANO is set in status it is nanoseconds; otherwise ntp_adjtime() multiplies the incoming value by NSEC_PER_USEC on the way in and divides on the way out. The constant field is adjusted by the same flag — microsecond-mode callers get four added to their time constant to keep the loop behaving as it did before nanosecond resolution existed.

Finally, ADJ_SETOFFSET is not part of the discipline at all. It adds its time argument to the current time as a step, not a slew, and is the interface a daemon reaches for when the offset is too large to correct gradually — a discontinuity in CLOCK_REALTIME, with all the consequences described earlier for TFD_TIMER_CANCEL_ON_SET and absolute timers. The one field in the table the kernel never acts on is esterror: it is range-checked, stored, and handed back unchanged.

The kernel maintains an NTP synchronization state with two modes of operation:

  • PLL (Phase-Locked Loop) — for small offsets (< 500ms), the kernel adjusts the clock frequency smoothly to eliminate the phase error over time. The constant parameter controls how aggressively the correction is applied.
  • FLL (Frequency-Locked Loop) — for larger offsets or when the PLL is slow to converge, the FLL estimates the frequency error directly from successive offset measurements.

The adjustment is applied in timekeeping_advance() on every tick: the NTP correction modifies the mult value used by the timekeeping subsystem, causing each tick to be counted as slightly more or fewer nanoseconds than nominal. A typical NTP slew rate is limited to ±500 PPM (0.05%), meaning the clock can gain or lose at most 500 µs per second. At this rate, correcting a 1-second offset takes about 33 minutes.

The two system calls differ in one respect: adjtimex() always operates on the system clock, while clock_adjtime() takes a clock ID first. In practice that extra argument exists for one purpose — disciplining a dynamic clock. Passing fd_to_clockid(fd) for an open /dev/ptpN routes the call through clock_posix_dynamic to the PTP driver's own adjfine/adjtime operations, so the same timex structure that steers the system clock's mult value steers a network card's oscillator instead. A PTP daemon typically uses both: clock_adjtime() on the NIC to lock it to the grandmaster, and adjtimex() on the system clock to follow the NIC. Since Linux 6.17 the auxiliary clocks are reachable the same way, through their own entry in the dispatch table.

The same interface carries the leap second mechanism. A daemon sets STA_INS or STA_DEL; second_overflow() notices at the next second boundary, computes the end of the current UTC day, and moves a small state machine through TIME_INS to TIME_OOP and finally TIME_WAIT. When the moment arrives the kernel logs “Clock: inserting leap second 23:59:60 UTC” and steps CLOCK_REALTIME back by one second — so wall-clock time repeats a second, and any code that assumes CLOCK_REALTIME increases monotonically is wrong twice over, once for leap seconds and once for settimeofday().

What the state machine deliberately does not touch is the other clocks. CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME are unaffected by construction, and CLOCK_TAI is unaffected by definition: TAI has no leap seconds, which is the entire reason it is offered. The tai field of struct timex holds the current TAI−UTC offset, and a program that needs a continuous, unambiguous time scale across a leap second should read CLOCK_TAI rather than trying to correct CLOCK_REALTIME after the fact.

The offset has stood at 37 seconds since 1 January 2017, and the mechanism may never be exercised again: the 27th General Conference on Weights and Measures resolved in November 2022 to stop inserting leap seconds by 2035 at the latest. The kernel code will stay — it costs nothing when idle, and nothing that already works is removed — but a reader encountering this for the first time should know they are looking at machinery with a scheduled end date rather than an ongoing operational concern.

gettimeofday(), settimeofday(), and time() — Legacy Interfaces

These were the primary time interfaces in Linux 2.6. They survive unchanged because the kernel does not break user space, but each has a successor that new code should prefer: they offer coarser resolution, they are tied to CLOCK_REALTIME and therefore to a clock that can jump, and two of the three carry a timezone argument the kernel has never meaningfully supported.

These older system calls are preserved for backward compatibility:

  • time() — returns seconds since the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970 UTC). Accelerated through the vDSO; essentially reads basetime[CLOCK_REALTIME].sec from the vvar page.
  • gettimeofday() — returns wall-clock time as a timeval (seconds + microseconds), plus an optional timezone structure. Also vDSO-accelerated. Superseded by clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) which provides nanosecond precision.
  • settimeofday() — sets the wall-clock time and optionally the timezone. Requires CAP_SYS_TIME. Like clock_settime(), it only modifies the kernel's time — the hardware RTC is not updated unless the user explicitly runs hwclock.

What to take away. Three generations of interface are described above and all three still work, which is the single most important fact about this part of the kernel. Nothing here was ever removed; what happened instead is that each generation was reimplemented on top of the next one’s machinery, so alarm() is a setitimer() call, setitimer()’s ITIMER_REAL is an hrtimer, and gettimeofday() is clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) with the nanoseconds thrown away. A reader who finds an old interface in a code base is not looking at an old code path.

This is where Linux 2.6 and 7.0.12 diverge most, and it is worth being specific about how. Linux 2.6 answered gettimeofday() by reading xtime under the xtime_lock seqlock and then adding a sub-tick correction from cur_timer->get_offset(), with fixups for lost ticks — six steps, several counter reads, entirely inside the kernel. None of those names survive. xtime, wall_jiffies and the cur_timer vtable were replaced by the single timekeeper structure, and the call itself usually does not enter the kernel at all.

Two design lessons are worth carrying forward from the section as a whole. The first is that generality has a price paid in the implementation rather than the interface: timer_create() looks barely more complex than setitimer(), but supporting arbitrary clocks and arbitrary delivery targets is what forces the k_clock dispatch table, the encoded negative clock IDs, the global hash table and the sequence-numbered signals. The second is that the delivery mechanism, not the timer, is what dates an interface. Every generation here uses good timers; what separates them is whether expiry arrives as a signal, which cannot be waited on or attributed, or as a readable file descriptor, which can. That is why timerfd is the recommendation for new code even though it is the least capable of the three — it has no CPU-time clocks and no per-thread targeting — and why the one thing it does better matters more than everything it does not do.

Time Namespaces

Linux 7.0.12 supports time namespaces (CONFIG_TIME_NS), allowing containers to have their own independent views of CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME. This is the newest of the Linux namespace types (added in Linux 5.6) and was designed specifically to enable container live migration — moving a running container from one host to another without breaking applications that depend on monotonic clocks being continuously increasing.

Chapter 3 introduces the time namespace alongside the other namespace types, and Chapter 25 places it among the namespaces a container runtime combines; this section concentrates on the clock and vDSO machinery that makes it work.

Time namespaces are the odd one out among Linux namespaces, and it is worth saying why before looking at the code. Every other namespace virtualizes a set of names — process IDs, mount points, network interfaces — and the kernel can simply hand a task a different table to look things up in. A clock has no names. It is a monotonically increasing number that the hardware produces and that user space may already be holding copies of. Virtualizing it means changing the value of something a process has already observed, which is exactly what the clock is contractually forbidden to do.

Three constraints follow, and they explain almost every design decision in this section:

  • A running process’s clock must never jump. A namespace can only be adopted at a moment when the process has no accumulated timestamps to be inconsistent with — which turns out to mean at fork() or at execve(), and produces the two-pointer arrangement described below that has no counterpart in any other namespace except PID.
  • Not every clock may be virtualized. Offsetting CLOCK_REALTIME would let a container disagree with the outside world about what time it is, breaking TLS certificate validation, Kerberos tickets and log correlation. The kernel deliberately virtualizes only the clocks whose absolute value is meaningless.
  • The vDSO must not get slower. The whole point of the previous section is that reading a clock costs no system call. A feature that almost nobody uses must not add a branch to that path — so time namespaces are implemented by swapping the page a task reads, not by testing a flag.

The section works through these in order:

  1. Why the problem exists at all — what breaks when a container is migrated.
  2. What the kernel stores — the offsets and the per-namespace page.
  3. Which clocks are affected, and the reasoning behind each inclusion and exclusion.
  4. How a namespace is created and configured, and why the offsets can be set only before anybody is using them.
  5. How the vDSO handles it at zero cost to everyone else.
  6. What the kernel does at the system call boundary, where the vDSO trick does not apply.
  7. Lifecycle and restrictions.
  8. How container runtimes actually use it.

Version history. Time namespaces did not exist — they arrived in Linux 5.6 (2020) and are the newest namespace type in the kernel. They are also the one namespace whose implementation is mostly not in the namespace code: the interesting half lives in the vDSO data-page machinery described in the previous section. Linux 6.15 restructured that machinery, so the function this section shows was renamed from timens_setup_vdso_data() to timens_setup_vdso_clock_data() and now operates on a vdso_clock; Linux 6.18 then moved time namespaces onto the generic namespace infrastructure, giving them stable IDs, file-handle lookup, and the reference-counting helpers shown below.

The Problem: Container Migration and Monotonic Clocks

Consider a container that has been running on Host A for 10 hours. Applications inside the container see CLOCK_MONOTONIC at approximately 36000 seconds. If the container is migrated to Host B, which was booted only 1 hour ago, CLOCK_MONOTONIC on Host B is at approximately 3600 seconds — a jump backward in time that violates the monotonic guarantee. Applications using monotonic clocks for timeout management, elapsed-time measurement, or sequencing would malfunction.

Time namespaces solve this by adding a per-namespace offset to the host's monotonic and boottime clocks. The container on Host B gets a monotonic offset of +32400 seconds, making its view of CLOCK_MONOTONIC appear continuous across the migration. Similarly, CLOCK_BOOTTIME (which includes suspend time) gets its own independent offset.

Core Data Structures

The namespace object itself is small, because almost everything a time namespace does is done by other subsystems on its behalf. It holds two offsets, one page, and a flag:

/* include/linux/time_namespace.h */
struct timens_offsets {
    struct timespec64 monotonic;  /* Offset for CLOCK_MONOTONIC */
    struct timespec64 boottime;   /* Offset for CLOCK_BOOTTIME */
};

struct time_namespace {
    struct user_namespace  *user_ns;        /* Owning user namespace */
    struct ucounts         *ucounts;        /* Resource counter */
    struct ns_common       ns;             /* Common namespace ops (refcount, etc.) */
    struct timens_offsets  offsets;         /* Per-namespace time offsets */
    struct page            *vvar_page;     /* Namespace-specific vvar page */
    bool                   frozen_offsets; /* True after first task joins */
};

The key design element is the offsets structure: it contains a seconds + nanoseconds offset for each adjustable clock. When a process in the namespace calls clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), the returned time is host_monotonic + offsets.monotonic. The frozen_offsets flag prevents modifying the offsets after any task has entered the namespace — this avoids a class of race conditions where applications could observe time going backward within a namespace.

The vvar_page is the namespace’s private copy of the vDSO data page, discussed below. It is allocated when the namespace is created but left zeroed; it is filled in only when the first task actually joins. The frozen_offsets flag is what marks that transition, and it does double duty — it means both “the offsets may no longer be changed” and “the page has been initialized.” The two facts are the same fact, which is why one flag suffices: the moment the page is written is the moment the offsets become observable, and therefore the last moment at which changing them would be safe.

The embedded ns_common is shared with every other namespace type, and its contents changed noticeably in Linux 6.18, when time namespaces were moved onto the generic namespace infrastructure. The reference count that used to live directly in ns_common is now __ns_ref, reached through ns_ref_inc()/ns_ref_put() wrappers rather than touched directly, and Linux 6.19 added a second, active reference count (__ns_ref_active) that distinguishes namespaces currently in use by a running task from those merely kept alive by an open file descriptor. The same series gave every namespace a stable ns_id and list linkage, which is what allows a time namespace to be looked up by ID or referred to by a file handle rather than only through an open /proc/[pid]/ns/time descriptor.

Affected and Unaffected Clocks

Which clocks a time namespace may shift is a policy decision, and the dividing line is sharper than it first looks: a clock is virtualized precisely when its absolute value carries no meaning outside the machine. CLOCK_MONOTONIC qualifies — its zero point is an arbitrary boot-time instant, so no two hosts agree on it anyway, and shifting it breaks no contract. CLOCK_REALTIME does not: it names an instant in a globally agreed timeline, and a container that disagreed with the outside world about it would fail TLS certificate validation, reject Kerberos tickets, and produce logs that cannot be correlated with the host’s.

Note the practical consequence: a container’s wall clock is not isolated. Anything inside the container able to call settimeofday() changes the time for the entire machine, which is why container runtimes drop CAP_SYS_TIME rather than relying on the namespace for that. The CPU-time clocks need no treatment at all — they measure a process’s own consumption and are already relative to it.

Table 6-180. Clock Behavior in Time Namespaces
Clock IDNamespace Aware?Offset AppliedRationale
CLOCK_MONOTONIC✓offsets.monotonicMust appear continuous across migration
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW✓offsets.monotonicSame base as MONOTONIC, without NTP adjustment
CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE✓offsets.monotonicCoarse variant of MONOTONIC
CLOCK_BOOTTIME✓offsets.boottimeMust include virtualized suspend time
CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM✓offsets.boottimeAlarm variant of BOOTTIME
CLOCK_REALTIME✗—Names an instant on a globally agreed timeline; a container must agree with the outside world
CLOCK_REALTIME_COARSE✗—Coarse variant of REALTIME
CLOCK_REALTIME_ALARM✗—Alarm variant of REALTIME — unlike its boottime counterpart, no entry is written for it
CLOCK_TAI✗—International atomic time — absolute reference
CLOCK_*_CPUTIME_ID✗—Per-process CPU time — already process-relative

Creating and Configuring a Time Namespace

Creating a time namespace and putting a process into it are two separate acts, separated in time, and the interface reflects that in a way that surprises most people the first time they meet it. The sequence below is the one every container runtime performs, and the ordering is not a matter of taste — the offsets can only be written while nobody is in the namespace, and the process doing the writing is deliberately not in it either.

Time namespaces are created using unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) or clone3() with the CLONE_NEWTIME flag. The offsets are configured through /proc/[pid]/timens_offsets before any task enters the namespace:

/* The sequence a runtime performs, in order */
unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME);          /* creates the namespace; caller stays outside */

fd = open("/proc/self/timens_offsets", O_WRONLY);
write(fd, "monotonic 32400 0\n", 18);   /* +9 hours  */
write(fd, "boottime   7200 0\n", 18);   /* +2 hours  */
close(fd);                               /* offsets still unfrozen */

execv("/container/init", argv);  /* THIS is what enters the namespace */

/* Inside the namespace: */
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) → host_monotonic + 32400s
clock_gettime(CLOCK_BOOTTIME)  → host_boottime  + 7200s
clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)  → host_realtime  (unchanged)

/* From a shell, util-linux does all of the above in one command: */
$ unshare --time --monotonic 32400 --boottime 7200 --fork /container/init

The single-command form is not a convenience. There is no way to write the offsets from a shell that is already inside the namespace, and every obvious attempt to do so fails: unshare --time --fork bash puts the forked bash in the namespace through timens_on_fork(), and even without --fork the execve() of bash commits it through exec_task_namespaces(). Either way the offsets are frozen before the first prompt, and echo > /proc/self/timens_offsets returns EACCES. unshare(1) grew --monotonic and --boottime for exactly this reason: the write has to happen in the process that called unshare(), in the window before it forks or execs.

The write itself is handled by proc_timens_set_offset(), and its ordering is deliberate. Each requested offset is validated first — only CLOCK_MONOTONIC and CLOCK_BOOTTIME are accepted, anything else giving -EINVAL, and the offset must not take the clock negative or past KTIME_SEC_MAX / 2, which yields -ERANGE. Note what that bound is measured against: the function reads the current value of the clock and adds the proposed offset, so validity depends on when the write happens, and the halving is there, in the words of the comment, “to be sure that KTIME_MAX is still unreachable” for absolute deadlines computed later. Only once every offset in the request has passed does the function take offset_lock, re-check frozen_offsets — returning -EACCES if a task has entered in the meantime — and apply them all under a comment reading “Don’t report errors after this line.” A multi-line write is therefore atomic: either both clocks move or neither does.

The Namespace You Are Not In Yet

The sequence above contains something that looks like a formality and is not. After unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) the offsets are written and only then is execv() used to start the real program. That execv() is load-bearing: until it happens, the calling process is not in the new time namespace at all.

This is the defining peculiarity of time namespaces. unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) creates a namespace and does not move the caller into it. It cannot — the caller is a running process that has already read the monotonic clock, possibly cached deadlines derived from it, and may have timers armed against it. Moving it would make its clock jump, which is the one thing the whole feature exists to prevent. So nsproxy carries two pointers instead of one:

/* include/linux/nsproxy.h */
struct nsproxy {
    refcount_t                count;
    struct uts_namespace     *uts_ns;
    struct ipc_namespace     *ipc_ns;
    struct mnt_namespace     *mnt_ns;
    struct pid_namespace     *pid_ns_for_children;
    struct net               *net_ns;
    struct time_namespace    *time_ns;                /* what I see now */
    struct time_namespace    *time_ns_for_children;   /* what my children will see */
    struct cgroup_namespace  *cgroup_ns;
};

Only the PID namespace shares this shape, and for the same underlying reason: a process cannot change its own PID any more than it can change its own uptime. unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) sets time_ns_for_children and leaves time_ns alone, which is also why /proc/[pid]/timens_offsets is writable at that moment — the namespace exists but nobody is using it, so the offsets are not yet frozen.

A task then actually adopts the namespace by one of three routes:

  • fork() — timens_on_fork() notices that the two pointers differ, points the child’s time_ns at the pending namespace, and calls timens_commit(). The child has no clock history, so nothing can be inconsistent. Note the guard in copy_namespaces(): this is skipped when CLONE_VM is set, because a thread sharing its parent’s address space cannot have a different vvar page mapped into it.
  • execve() — exec_task_namespaces() performs the same fix-up for the calling task. This is the step the sequence above relies on, and it is safe for the same reason: execve() discards the entire address space, so no timestamp survives the transition.
  • setns() — timens_install() is the one path that moves a task directly, setting both pointers. It is allowed only because of the conditions it enforces first: the task must be single-threaded (otherwise -EUSERS), and it must hold CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the target namespace’s user namespace and its own. The caller is assumed to know its clock is about to change.

The practical upshot for anyone reading container-runtime code: the runtime unshares the time namespace in the parent, writes the offsets, and lets the subsequent fork()/exec() of the container init do the actual entering. There is no system call that means “put me in this time namespace now” short of setns().

vDSO Integration

The most interesting aspect of time namespaces is how they integrate with the vDSO fast path without adding overhead to the common case (processes in the root time namespace).

When the first task enters a non-root time namespace (via timens_commit()), two things happen:

  1. The namespace's vvar_page is initialized by timens_setup_vdso_clock_data(): the seq field is set to 1 (permanently odd) and clock_mode is set to VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TIMENS
  2. The process's vvar page table entries are zapped by vdso_join_timens(), so the next access triggers a page fault that installs the namespace's vvar page instead of the system-wide one
/* kernel/time/namespace.c */
static void timens_setup_vdso_clock_data(struct vdso_clock *vc,
                                         struct time_namespace *ns)
{
    struct timens_offset *offset = vc->offset;

    vc->seq        = 1;                       /* Permanently odd → forces slow path */
    vc->clock_mode = VDSO_CLOCKMODE_TIMENS;   /* Sentinel: "this is a timens page" */

    /* Store offsets in the vvar page itself */
    offset[CLOCK_MONOTONIC]        = offset_from_ts(ns->offsets.monotonic);
    offset[CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW]    = offset_from_ts(ns->offsets.monotonic);
    offset[CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE] = offset_from_ts(ns->offsets.monotonic);
    offset[CLOCK_BOOTTIME]         = offset_from_ts(ns->offsets.boottime);
    offset[CLOCK_BOOTTIME_ALARM]   = offset_from_ts(ns->offsets.boottime);
}

Two details of that first step are easy to overlook. timens_setup_vdso_clock_data() is called once per clock base — the loop runs over all CS_BASES entries, and since Linux 6.17 over the auxiliary clock array as well — because each vdso_clock carries its own sequence counter and each must be given the sentinel independently. And the whole of it runs under offset_lock with a double-checked frozen_offsets test, so that the second and subsequent tasks joining the namespace take an early return and never touch the lock at all.

The vvar mapping is then swapped for namespace tasks, and the mechanism is easiest to see from the page ordering itself:

/* include/vdso/datapage.h */
enum vdso_pages {
    VDSO_TIME_PAGE_OFFSET,
    VDSO_TIMENS_PAGE_OFFSET,
    VDSO_RNG_PAGE_OFFSET,
    VDSO_ARCH_PAGES_START,
    VDSO_ARCH_PAGES_END = VDSO_ARCH_PAGES_START + VDSO_ARCH_DATA_PAGES - 1,
    VDSO_NR_PAGES
};

The timens page is deliberately adjacent to the time page, and that adjacency is the whole trick. For a task in the root namespace, slot 0 holds the real timekeeping data and slot 1 is unused. For a namespaced task the fault handler installs the sentinel page in slot 0 and the real data in slot 1, so whichever page a task finds at the primary address, the other one is exactly one page further on. Nothing needs to be told which case it is in; the mapping already encodes it, and the vDSO reaches the real data by adding PAGE_SIZE.

The long comment above timens_setup_vdso_clock_data() still draws this as a four-page layout with PVCLOCK and HVCLOCK pages between the two, which was the x86-specific arrangement before the generic vDSO data storage arrived in Linux 6.15. The comment’s explanation of the sentinel is still correct and still worth reading; its diagram no longer matches enum vdso_pages, and could not, since the fixed + PAGE_SIZE in the fast path requires the two pages to be neighbours.

That swap is performed by the same fault handler introduced in the previous section. Zapping the page tables does not decide anything; it just guarantees the next access faults, and the decision is made then:

/* lib/vdso/datastore.c — vvar_fault(), abridged */
struct page *timens_page = find_timens_vvar_page(vma);

switch (vmf->pgoff) {
case VDSO_TIME_PAGE_OFFSET:
    pfn = __phys_to_pfn(__pa_symbol(vdso_k_time_data));
    if (timens_page) {
        /* Fault in the real VVAR page too, since it will be
         * accessed to get clock data anyway. */
        addr = vmf->address + VDSO_TIMENS_PAGE_OFFSET * PAGE_SIZE;
        err = vmf_insert_pfn(vma, addr, pfn);
        if (unlikely(err & VM_FAULT_ERROR))
            return err;
        pfn = page_to_pfn(timens_page);   /* swap */
    }
    break;

find_timens_vvar_page() returns NULL for a task in the root namespace, in which case the branch is skipped entirely and the real page is installed as normal — the root-namespace cost is one already-NULL pointer test in a page fault that would happen anyway. For a namespaced task, both pages are installed in one fault rather than two, since a timens read is certain to need the real page immediately afterwards.

That function also carries a small security check worth noticing. It returns the current task’s namespace page, which is only correct if the faulting mm belongs to the current task; anything else means the fault was triggered from outside, through an interface like /proc/[pid]/mem or process_vm_readv(). Such an access would otherwise install one process’s namespace page into another process’s address space. The VM_PFNMAP | VM_IO flags on the mapping are supposed to make this unreachable, so the handler treats it as a kernel bug and fires a WARN() rather than silently coping.

When the vDSO code then detects the sentinel, it reads the real time from the swapped page and adds the namespace offset:

/* lib/vdso/gettimeofday.c — timens fast path */
static bool do_hres_timens(const struct vdso_time_data *vdns,
                           const struct vdso_clock *vcns,
                           clockid_t clk, struct __kernel_timespec *ts)
{
    /* The real vvar page sits exactly one page further on */
    const struct vdso_time_data *vd = __arch_get_vdso_u_timens_data(vdns);
    const struct timens_offset *offs = &vcns->offset[clk];
    const struct vdso_clock *vc = vd->clock_data;
    u64 ns;
    s64 sec;

    if (clk != CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW)
        vc = &vc[CS_HRES_COARSE];
    else
        vc = &vc[CS_RAW];

    do {
        seq = vdso_read_begin(vc);
        if (!vdso_get_timestamp(vd, vc, clk, &sec, &ns))
            return false;  /* Fallback to syscall */
    } while (vdso_read_retry(vc, seq));

    /* Add the namespace offset */
    sec += offs->sec;
    ns  += offs->nsec;

    vdso_set_timespec(ts, sec, ns);
    return true;  /* Success — no syscall needed */
}

Three things in that function repay a second look. The two arguments named vdns and vcns are the namespace page and its clock, carrying nothing but offsets and the sentinel; the real data is reached by __arch_get_vdso_u_timens_data(), whose entire body is (void *)vd + PAGE_SIZE. That is the swap the previous subsection described, expressed as pointer arithmetic: the fault handler arranged for the real page to be adjacent, so finding it costs an add. The function then re-selects the clock base — CS_RAW for CLOCK_MONOTONIC_RAW, CS_HRES_COARSE otherwise — because the base it was handed belongs to the namespace page, not to the page it is about to read. And the retry loop it runs is an ordinary one: the sentinel lives only on the namespace page, so there is no risk of recursing into the timens path a second time.

The offset lookup is vcns->offset[clk], indexed by clock ID with no filtering, which explains something the table above leaves implicit. A namespaced task reading CLOCK_REALTIME also comes through here, finds the zero that alloc_page(__GFP_ZERO) left in the array, and adds it. Non-virtualized clocks are not special-cased anywhere; they are simply the entries timens_setup_vdso_clock_data() never wrote to. do_coarse_timens() is the same function again for the coarse clocks, which is why CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE appears in the table with an offset of its own.

This design has zero overhead for the common case. The kernel comment above do_hres() makes the argument precisely: tasks in the root time namespace see an even seq and never take the branch, and “if vc->seq is odd, i.e. a concurrent update is in progress the extra check for vc->clock_mode is just a few extra instructions while spin waiting for vc->seq to become even again.” The cost is paid where it is already being wasted. Tasks in a non-root namespace pay one extra page read and an addition — still entirely in user space, no syscall needed.

Kernel-Side Time Translation

The vDSO handles the common case, but it only handles times flowing outward — the kernel computing a timestamp for a process to read. Times also flow inward: a namespaced process that calls clock_nanosleep(TIMER_ABSTIME) or arms a timer with an absolute expiry is quoting a moment in its own timeline, and the kernel must convert it before handing it to machinery that thinks in host time. Get this wrong in either direction and a container’s timers fire at the wrong moment by exactly the namespace offset — potentially hours.

The inward conversion is a single inline function, written so that the root-namespace case is a pointer comparison and a return:

/* include/linux/time_namespace.h */
static inline ktime_t timens_ktime_to_host(clockid_t clockid, ktime_t tim)
{
    struct time_namespace *ns = current->nsproxy->time_ns;

    if (likely(ns == &init_time_ns))
        return tim;  /* Root namespace — no translation needed */

    return do_timens_ktime_to_host(clockid, tim, &ns->offsets);
}

Two properties of that conversion matter. It is a saturating subtraction, not an arithmetic one: do_timens_ktime_to_host() treats an absolute time earlier than the namespace offset as already expired and returns 0 rather than a negative ktime_t, and clamps the result at KTIME_MAX at the other end. And it is a switch on the clock ID with a default that returns the value unchanged, so a caller may hand it any clock and only the virtualized ones are touched — which is why the call sites do not have to know which clocks are namespaced. With CONFIG_TIME_NS=n the whole family collapses further still: every helper becomes an empty inline or an identity function, and copy_time_ns() returns -EINVAL for CLONE_NEWTIME, which is what a process sees when it tries to unshare a time namespace on a kernel built without the feature.

Those call sites are more numerous than the timer interfaces suggest. timerfd_settime(), timer_settime(), clock_nanosleep(TIMER_ABSTIME) and the alarm timers all convert inward, and so does futex() — kernel/futex/syscalls.c translates the absolute timeout of FUTEX_WAIT_BITSET, which is the deadline underneath most user-space condition-variable and mutex timeouts. A container whose pthread_cond_timedwait() deadlines were off by the namespace offset would be far more visibly broken than one whose timers were.

The reverse translation (host → namespace) is performed by timens_add_monotonic() and timens_add_boottime(), which the syscall path uses for CPU-time clocks and whenever the vDSO is unavailable. It also reaches well outside the time subsystem, and this is the part most descriptions of the feature omit:

  • /proc/uptime adds the boottime offset, so uptime inside a container reports the container’s age rather than the host’s.
  • /proc/stat’s btime field — the wall-clock instant of boot — is moved the other way with timens_sub_boottime(), so that it stays consistent with the virtualized uptime.
  • /proc/[pid]/stat reports each process’s starttime through timens_add_boottime_ns(), which is what lets ps compute a sane elapsed time inside the namespace.
  • sysinfo() adjusts its uptime field the same way.

The pattern is worth naming: the namespace does not merely offset a clock, it offsets every derived quantity the kernel exports that would otherwise let a process work out the host’s real uptime by subtraction. A leak in any one of them would defeat the whole feature, since a migrated container could then detect that it had moved.

Lifecycle and Restrictions

Most of the rules below exist to enforce the invariant stated at the start of this section: a task must never observe its own monotonic clock moving. The restrictions are what make that possible, and each one closes a way the invariant could otherwise be violated.

  • Creating one is privileged — unshare_nsproxy_namespaces() requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in the caller’s user namespace, and copy_namespaces() enforces the same for clone3(). The usual unprivileged route is to unshare a user namespace first and acquire the capability inside it. A per-user-namespace limit also applies: UCOUNT_TIME_NAMESPACES, exposed as /proc/sys/user/max_time_namespaces, makes clone_time_ns() return -ENOSPC once it is exhausted.
  • Single-threaded requirement — this applies to setns(), not to unshare(). timens_install() calls current_is_single_threaded() and returns -EUSERS if the caller has siblings, because it is the only path that changes the calling task’s own time_ns and all threads share one mm and therefore one vvar mapping. unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) has no such restriction precisely because it does not move the caller; a multi-threaded process may create a time namespace perfectly well, it just cannot enter it without forking or execing.
  • Offsets are inherited, then frozen — clone_time_ns() copies old_ns->offsets rather than starting from zero, so a time namespace created inside another one begins where its parent left off and the offsets compose. Once any task enters (timens_commit()), frozen_offsets is set and further writes return -EACCES. init_time_ns is statically declared with frozen_offsets = true, so the root namespace can never be offset at all.
  • Capability requirements — writing offsets requires CAP_SYS_TIME in the target namespace’s user namespace, checked with file_ns_capable() against the credentials of whoever opened timens_offsets rather than whoever writes to it. Entering an existing namespace with setns() requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the target’s user namespace and the caller’s.
  • Inheritance — children created with fork() inherit the parent’s time_ns, or adopt time_ns_for_children if the parent has unshared one. clone() with CLONE_VM does not: copy_namespaces() skips timens_on_fork() in that case, so a thread always stays in its creator’s time namespace.
  • procfs interface — there are two namespace files, matching the two nsproxy pointers. /proc/[pid]/ns/time names the namespace the task is in; /proc/[pid]/ns/time_for_children names the one its children will get, and differs from the first exactly in the window between unshare() and the next fork() or execve(). Both are backed by the same timens_install(), so setns() on either has the same effect. /proc/[pid]/timens_offsets reads and writes the offsets of time_ns_for_children — which is what makes the configure-then-enter sequence possible.

Container Runtime Integration

Time namespaces exist because of one workload, and it is worth closing with how that workload actually drives them — not least because the feature is easy to misread as general-purpose clock virtualization, which it is not. Nothing here isolates a container’s wall clock or lets it run at a different rate; the only thing on offer is a constant offset on two clocks, applied once, before anything starts.

Container runtimes (Docker, Podman, CRI-O, LXC) use time namespaces to provide each container with an independent monotonic clock. The typical workflow is:

  1. Container runtime calls unshare(CLONE_NEWTIME) (often combined with other namespace flags)
  2. Writes the desired offsets to /proc/self/timens_offsets (calculated from the container's saved monotonic time minus the host's current monotonic time)
  3. Calls exec() to enter the namespace with the configured offsets
  4. Container processes see a continuous monotonic clock, even after live migration

For CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace), which performs the actual container migration: when restoring a container on a new host, CRIU calculates the necessary offsets from the checkpointed clock values and the host's current clocks, writes them to the time namespace, and then restores the container's process tree within that namespace.

Before the namespace existed. It is worth recording what migration tools did before Linux 5.6. There were three options and all of them were bad: intercept clock_gettime() with LD_PRELOAD or a seccomp filter, which is slow, misses static binaries and misses the vDSO entirely unless it is also disabled; ship a patched vDSO, which is fragile and architecture-specific; or accept that monotonic clocks jump on migration and hope nothing important notices. The last was the common choice, and the bugs it produced — timeouts that never fire, rate limiters that stall for hours — are the reason the feature was eventually built into the kernel.

What it is not. A time namespace is a consistency mechanism, not a security boundary, and reading the code makes that unusually clear. /proc/[pid]/timens_offsets is mode 0444 for reading, so a process can simply ask what its own offsets are; and since CLOCK_REALTIME is untouched, anything inside a container can recover the host’s true monotonic clock by subtraction whenever it likes. Nothing here is hidden. The guarantee on offer is narrower and more useful than concealment: an application that measures elapsed time will get an answer that stays consistent across a migration it was never told about.

The design lesson. The hard part of this feature was never the arithmetic — it is one addition — but finding a moment at which the addition could be introduced without anybody noticing. The kernel’s answer was to identify the two points at which a task provably holds no derived state, fork() and execve(), and to make the namespace change happen only there, carrying the pending namespace in a second pointer until one of them arrives. That is a pattern worth recognising: when a value cannot be changed under a running observer, change it for a new observer instead.

Summary

This chapter opened with a claim that sounds almost too simple to need a chapter: the kernel does two timing jobs, keeping the time and running timers, and they want different hardware. Everything since has been the consequence. Because the two duties are separate they get two frameworks — clocksource and clock event device — and because those frameworks are generic, every layer above them could be written once instead of once per architecture. That single decision, taken during the Linux 2.6 series, is why a chapter that in Linux 2.6 was largely a tour of the PIT and the local APIC is now a tour of abstractions.

The price of the abstraction is that no single mechanism is responsible for anything a user would recognise. A clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) that returns in twenty nanoseconds is the joint work of a hardware counter, a mult/shift pair computed once at registration, a seqcount-protected structure updated on every tick, a page mapped into the calling process, and possibly a namespace offset added on the way out. A msleep(1) is the joint work of the timer wheel, the tick layer’s decision about whether the tick may stop, the timer migration hierarchy’s decision about which CPU should be watching while it is stopped, and the scheduler. Neither can be understood in isolation, which is why this chapter is long.

The diagram below is the assembled picture: every mechanism the chapter has described, in the layer it belongs to, with the paths that connect them.

The Six Layers

The architecture is organized into six layers, each building on the one below. The rule that governs the boundaries is worth stating explicitly, because it is what makes the diagram readable: each layer knows only the interface of the layer beneath it, never the hardware two levels down. The timekeeping core has never heard of the TSC; it reads whatever struct clocksource it was given. The hrtimer subsystem has never heard of the local APIC; it asks the tick layer for an event at a time. Every piece of architecture-specific code this chapter has shown — __arch_get_hw_counter(), CNTVOFF_EL2, the x86 override of vdso_calc_ns() — sits at exactly one of these boundaries and nowhere else.

  1. Hardware — physical oscillators and counter circuits (TSC, HPET, ARM Arch Timer, ACPI PM Timer, RTC) that provide raw timing signals. The RTC provides the initial wall-clock seed at boot; the others provide continuous counters and programmable interrupts.
  2. Abstraction Frameworks — the clocksource framework wraps free-running counters into a uniform read() interface with mult/shift conversion parameters; the clock event device framework wraps interrupt-capable timers into a uniform set_next_event() interface. These allow all higher layers to be hardware-independent.
  3. Core Subsystems — timekeeping maintains the current time-of-day using the best clocksource, and since Linux 6.17 maintains a set of independent auxiliary timekeepers alongside it so that PTP hardware clocks can be read through the same machinery; the tick layer programs clock event devices to generate periodic or one-shot interrupts (with NOHZ idle/full suppression); NTP discipline adjusts the timekeeping rate to converge with network time; CPU accounting charges CPU time to processes on each tick.
  4. Timer Subsystems — hrtimers provide nanosecond-resolution timers sorted in an RB-tree; the timer wheel provides efficient coarse-grained timers in a hierarchical wheel that never cascades, and delegates the question of who watches a sleeping CPU’s timers to the timer migration hierarchy; POSIX timers are kernel objects that deliver signals on expiry; delay functions provide busy-wait and sleeping delays; the scheduler tick manages time-slices and load balancing.
  5. User-Space Bridge — the vDSO maps timekeeping data into user space so that clock_gettime() costs a counter read rather than a syscall; timerfd provides file-descriptor timers for event loops; time namespaces give containers independent monotonic/boottime offsets; the syscall interface covers everything else (clock_nanosleep, setitimer, alarm, adjtimex).
  6. Applications — databases and trading systems that need sub-microsecond timestamps; servers and GUIs using epoll+timerfd event loops; containers requiring namespace-virtualized clocks; device drivers using delay functions for hardware timing.

Key Architectural Principles

Several principles run through the whole subsystem, and they are worth remembering in preference to any individual function, because they predict how the code will behave in the places this chapter did not reach:

  • Hardware independence — the clocksource and clock event device frameworks ensure that higher layers never interact directly with hardware registers. Adding a new timer chip requires only registering a new clocksource or clock event device; all existing functionality works automatically.
  • Layered precision — applications choose the precision they need: coarse clocks (~4ms, cheapest), timer wheel (~4ms, low overhead per timer), hrtimers (~1ns, higher overhead), or busy-wait delays (~1ns, CPU-burning). Each layer has a different cost/precision tradeoff.
  • Zero-cost when idle — the NOHZ mechanism suppresses tick interrupts on idle CPUs, and the vDSO eliminates syscall overhead for time reads. A fully idle system consumes essentially no timing overhead.
  • Namespace isolation — time namespaces provide per-container clock virtualization with zero overhead for the common (non-namespace) case, using the clever vDSO sequence-counter sentinel.
  • Readers are never blocked; they are made to retry. Nothing on the path that reads the time takes a lock. The seqcount pattern appears at every level — in timekeeping_get_ns(), in the vDSO’s vdso_read_begin(), in the per-clock counters of the auxiliary timekeepers — because a reader that occasionally spins through a rare update is cheaper than one that serialises against every other reader. It is also what makes the vDSO possible at all: a lock cannot be shared with user space, but a counter can.
  • Cost is moved, not removed. It is tempting to read NOHZ and the vDSO as free wins. They are not. Stopping the tick means something must decide when to restart it, and that is the whole timer migration hierarchy. Skipping the system call means the kernel must publish a consistent snapshot of its state into a page that user space can read, and that is the whole vDSO data-page machinery, down to the parts that exist only to stop the multiplication overflowing. Every optimisation in this chapter has a structure somewhere else that pays for it.
  • The special case is made to look like the general one. A time namespace is not a branch in the vDSO; it is a different page. A one-shot tick is not a mode of the periodic tick; it is the same set_next_event() call with a different argument. A PTP clock is not a side door into the timekeeper; it is another timekeeper. Where the kernel could have added a test to a hot path it has repeatedly chosen instead to arrange for the hot path to be unable to tell the difference.
  • Correctness is increasingly enforced by types and by tooling. init_timer() with an opaque unsigned long argument became timer_setup() and then timer_delete_sync(); hrtimer_init() plus a separate function assignment became a single hrtimer_setup(). In each case a rule that used to live in a comment — initialise before arming, do not free a timer that may still be running — was moved somewhere the compiler or a debug option can check it. The same instinct produced the clocksource watchdog, which assumes the hardware is lying and checks.

What Changed Since Linux 2.6

Twenty years of changes are easier to remember as three movements than as a list.

The first was separation. Linux 2.6.11 had one per-architecture timer_opts object that both read the time and generated the tick, and one global xtime that the tick advanced. Splitting that into a clocksource, a clock event device, and a timekeeper is the single change from which most of this chapter follows. It is what allowed the tick to become optional, because once nothing reads the time from the tick, the tick is only an interrupt and interrupts can be skipped.

The second was the removal of fixed granularity. In 2.6 the resolution of essentially everything was one jiffy: timers expired on tick boundaries, sleeps rounded up to them, and process accounting sampled at them. hrtimers gave the kernel a second timer subsystem with no relationship to HZ at all, the timer wheel was rebuilt around the admission that its users do not actually want precision, and the two now coexist as a deliberate choice rather than an accident — which is why this chapter spends as long on when to use which as on how either works.

The third, and the most recent, was moving work off the critical CPU. NO_HZ_FULL, the timer migration hierarchy, deferrable and pinned timers, per-CPU accounting and the vDSO all serve the same end: whatever a CPU is doing, nothing else should be allowed to interrupt it merely because it exists. This is the movement still in progress; the auxiliary PTP clocks added in 6.17 and the ongoing PREEMPT_RT work are both continuations of it.

The table below summarises the concrete differences between the timing subsystem in Linux 2.6.11 and the current implementation (Linux 7.0.12):

Time storagextime (struct timespec)struct timekeeper (multiple bases)
Timer interruptFixed periodic (PIT/APIC)Clock event devices (periodic/oneshot)
High-res timersNot availablehrtimer subsystem (ns resolution)
Timer wheel5-level cascade (tv1–tv5)Flat hierarchical wheel (9 levels, no cascading)
TicklessNot availableNO_HZ_IDLE (default) + NO_HZ_FULL
Default HZ1000 (x86)Kconfig default 250; x86_64_defconfig still selects 1000
vDSO timeMinimal (vsyscall, fixed address)Full coverage (ASLR'd, x86_64 + ARM64)

Time namespacesNot availableFull support (container migration)
NTP integrationupdate_wall_time_one_tick()Dedicated ntp.c with PLL/FLL
CPU accountingTick sampling onlyFine-grained VIRT_CPU_ACCOUNTING + irqtime
ARM64 supportNot applicableFirst-class (arch timer, vDSO, CNTVCT_EL0)
Delay functionsudelay/ndelay only+ usleep_range, msleep, fsleep
Timer APIinit_timer() + func/datatimer_setup() / hrtimer_setup() (type-safe)
Timer teardowndel_timer_sync()timer_delete_sync() / timer_delete_sync_try()

Hardware clock disciplineNo kernel supportPTP hardware clocks via /dev/ptpN and clock_adjtime()

Real-time preemptionOut-of-tree patch setPREEMPT_RT merged; hrtimers split hard/soft

What has not changed is the difficulty the chapter started from. A counter still has to be trusted, and hardware still lies — which is why the watchdog exists, why the TSC has a stability history rather than a specification, and why ARM64 has to be told at boot which of its architected-timer errata apply. Time still cannot be allowed to move backwards, and every mechanism added since 2.6 has had to be fitted around that constraint rather than the other way round: it is why namespace offsets are frozen before use, why NTP corrects the rate instead of the value, and why a leap second is still, after all this time, awkward. The frameworks have replaced the per-architecture code, but they have not replaced the physics.
